  40. 40.40Security as a practice

Security is the one area of backend engineering where a single missing if statement is a headline. A slow query costs you latency. A missing index costs you money. A missing ownership check on GET /orders/:id costs you every customer's address, and possibly the company.

This part is written for the engineer who ships NestJS services against PostgreSQL and Redis and wants to stop treating security as "the thing the pentest company finds once a year". We go through identity and access (who are you, what may you do), the small amount of cryptography you actually need to understand, the OWASP Top 10 as it appears in a real NestJS + PostgreSQL codebase, and finally a complete, production-shaped auth module you can lift into a project.

Three rules run through everything that follows:

  1. Never trust input. Not the body, not the headers, not the URL, not the JWT until it is verified, not the row you just read from the database if a user wrote it.
  2. Deny by default. Every route is private unless explicitly marked public. Every query is filtered by owner or tenant unless there is a written reason not to be.
  3. Defense in depth. Assume each layer will fail at some point. The guard will be forgotten on one route; the row-level security policy catches it. The API key will leak into a log; the key is hashed and scoped so the damage is bounded.

Keep the senior mantra in mind, with a security twist: Can it be forged? Can it be replayed? Can it be guessed? Can it be bypassed? Can it leak? Can it be abused at scale?

40.1 Authentication vs Authorization

Concept

Authentication (AuthN) answers who are you? Authorization (AuthZ) answers what are you allowed to do?

In one sentence: authentication turns an anonymous request into a request from a known principal; authorization decides whether that principal may perform this action on this resource.

In code, they are two different checks that run at two different times:

TypeScript
// Authentication: turn credentials into an identity, or reject.
const user = await authService.validateAccessToken(token); // who are you?
if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException();              // HTTP 401

// Authorization: decide if THIS identity may do THIS thing to THIS resource.
const order = await ordersRepo.findOneBy({ id: orderId });
if (order.customerId !== user.id && !user.roles.includes('support')) {
  throw new ForbiddenException();                          // HTTP 403
}

The two HTTP status codes encode the difference. 401 Unauthorized (badly named; it means unauthenticated) says "I do not know who you are; present credentials". 403 Forbidden says "I know exactly who you are, and the answer is no".

Why does it exist?

Without authentication every request is anonymous and the system cannot tell a customer from an attacker. Without authorization every authenticated user is an administrator. Real systems break in both directions, but the second failure is far more common. Most production data leaks are not "someone broke the login". They are "someone logged in as themselves and then asked for someone else's data, and the server said yes".

Separating the two concepts matters because they are implemented in different places and fail in different ways. Authentication is centralised: one login flow, one token format, one guard. Authorization is spread across the whole codebase: every controller, every service method, every query. That is why authorization bugs outnumber authentication bugs ten to one.

Mental model

Imagine an office building. At the front desk you show your ID and the receptionist hands you a badge. That is authentication: one check, at one door, producing a badge that proves who you are. Now you walk around the building. The badge opens the floors you work on and refuses the server room and the CEO's office. Every door does its own check of your badge against its own list. That is authorization: many checks, at many doors, each about a specific resource.

A building with a strict front desk and no locks on internal doors is exactly a backend with a strong login and no ownership checks.

How it works

  1. A request arrives with a credential: a session cookie, a Authorization: Bearer <token> header, an API key, or a client certificate.
  2. The authentication layer validates the credential. For a session it looks up the session store. For a JWT it verifies the signature and expiry. For an API key it hashes the key and looks it up. The result is a principal: { id, roles, tenantId, scopes }. In NestJS this is a Passport strategy plus an AuthGuard, and the principal lands on request.user.
  3. If no valid credential is present and the route is not public, the request stops here with 401.
  4. The coarse authorization layer checks route-level rules: does this route require the admin role? Does the token carry the orders:write scope? In NestJS this is a RolesGuard or ScopesGuard running after the auth guard.
  5. The fine-grained authorization layer runs inside the service, where the resource is loaded: is this user the owner of this order? Is this support agent in the same region as this customer? This check needs data and therefore belongs next to the data access.
  6. Optionally the database enforces a last line of defense with PostgreSQL row-level security, so that even a query that forgot the WHERE tenant_id = ... returns nothing it should not.
Text
 request --> [AuthGuard: who?] --> [RolesGuard: role ok?] --> [Controller]
                  |                       |                       |
                401                     403                 [Service: owner?]
                                                                  |
                                                                403 / data
                                                                  |
                                                     [PostgreSQL RLS: tenant?]

Practical example

A food-delivery platform has three kinds of principals: customers, restaurant staff and internal support agents. All of them log in with the same POST /auth/login endpoint and receive the same token format. That is authentication, and it is identical for everyone.

Then they diverge. A customer may read their own orders. Restaurant staff may read orders for their restaurant and change the status from accepted to preparing. Support agents may read any order in their region and issue refunds up to a limit. None of those rules live in the login code. They live in guards and services, and each of them is a separate decision.

NestJS example

The cleanest way to keep the two concerns separate is to give each its own guard and keep resource ownership in the service.

TypeScript
// orders.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { AuthenticatedUser } from '../auth/authenticated-user';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Controller('orders')
@UseGuards(AuthGuard('jwt')) // AuthN: reject anonymous requests with 401
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  getOne(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
    @CurrentUser() user: AuthenticatedUser,
  ) {
    // AuthZ happens in the service, where the order is loaded.
    return this.orders.getForPrincipal(id, user);
  }
}
TypeScript
// orders.service.ts
import { ForbiddenException, Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { AuthenticatedUser } from '../auth/authenticated-user';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly repo: Repository<Order>) {}

  async getForPrincipal(id: string, user: AuthenticatedUser): Promise<Order> {
    const order = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id } });
    // Return 404 for both "missing" and "not yours" to avoid leaking existence.
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundException();
    const isOwner = order.customerId === user.id;
    const isSupport = user.roles.includes('support') && order.region === user.region;
    if (!isOwner && !isSupport) throw new NotFoundException();
    return order;
  }
}

Note the deliberate choice to return 404 rather than 403 for a foreign order. A 403 tells an attacker that the order id exists. With UUIDs this matters little; with sequential integer ids it turns your API into an oracle for counting orders.

PostgreSQL example

Authentication data and authorization data are different tables with different access patterns.

SQL
-- Authentication: credentials and identity.
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email         citext NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- citext: case-insensitive unique email
  password_hash text   NOT NULL,             -- argon2id hash, never the password
  status        text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                CHECK (status IN ('active','locked','disabled')),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Authorization: what each user may do.
CREATE TABLE roles (
  id   smallint PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL UNIQUE                   -- 'customer', 'support', 'admin'
);

CREATE TABLE user_roles (
  user_id uuid     NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role_id smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id)
);

-- Lookups during login hit users(email); lookups during authz hit user_roles(user_id).
-- The PK on user_roles already covers user_id as the leading column.

The citext extension (CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS citext;) avoids the classic bug where Alice@Example.com and alice@example.com become two accounts, which later enables account takeover through password reset.

Production scenario

A B2B invoicing product with 40,000 companies and 300,000 users. Login traffic is tiny (about 5 requests per second) and is dominated by the cost of argon2 (roughly 50 to 100 ms per attempt by design). Authorization, on the other hand, runs on every one of the 3,000 requests per second the API serves. That asymmetry decides the architecture: the roles and tenant id are placed in the access token so that the coarse check costs nothing, while fine-grained ownership is checked against the row already being loaded, so it adds no extra query.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 on a Tuesday, a customer emailed support: "Why can I see invoices from a company I have never heard of?" A new GET /invoices/export endpoint had been added the week before. It was protected by AuthGuard('jwt'), so the developer's manual test with their own token worked, and code review focused on the CSV formatting. The service method built its query from the companyId in the query string, not from the token. Anyone could export any company's invoices by changing a number. The system authenticated perfectly and authorized nothing.

The fix was three lines. The incident response, customer notification and regulator report took three weeks.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A route with no guard at all: NestJS routes are public by default. The fix is a global guard with an explicit @Public() opt-out (see 40.37).
  • Guard applied to the controller but a new method added with a different guard that accidentally overrides it.
  • Authorization data in the token drifts from the database: a user demoted from admin keeps the role until the token expires.
  • 401 vs 403 confusion in clients: a 401 should trigger token refresh; a 403 should not, or you get a refresh loop.
  • Identity present but account disabled: authentication succeeds cryptographically, but the principal must still be rejected. Check status on every request or on every refresh.
  • Service-to-service calls with no principal: internal endpoints often skip authorization "because only our services call it", until an SSRF bug (40.23) lets an attacker call it too.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior engineer treats authentication as a solved, centralised problem and authorization as the real work. Their questions on every new endpoint: Who can call this? What resource does it touch? Where is the ownership check, and does it use the principal from the token or a value from the request? They refuse to accept "it is behind the auth guard" as an answer to "is it secure". To a product manager they explain: "Login proves who you are. It does not decide what you can see; that is a separate rule for every screen, and every rule needs to be written down."

Common mistakes

  • Using userId from the request body or query string instead of from the verified token. The attacker controls the request; they do not control the token.
  • Returning 403 on missing resources, leaking existence.
  • Treating "is logged in" as the only authorization rule.
  • Putting authorization only in the controller and not in the service, so the same service called from a job or another controller has no check at all.
  • Skipping authorization on internal or admin endpoints because "they are not linked from the UI".

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between 401 and 403, and why does it matter for clients?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 401 means unauthenticated, retry with credentials or refresh; 403 means authenticated but not permitted, do not retry. Follow-up: when would you return 404 instead of 403?
  2. Where should an ownership check live: controller, guard or service?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: in the service next to the data load, because it needs the resource; guards are for route-level rules. Follow-up: how would you make it impossible to forget?
  3. Roles in the token or roles from the database on each request?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: token for speed, with short expiry and a revocation path; database when changes must be immediate. Follow-up: how would you handle "demote an admin now"?
  4. A developer says an endpoint is secure because it is behind the JWT guard. What do you ask next?
  5. How would you design authorization for a multi-tenant SaaS so that a missing filter cannot leak data?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: tenant id from token, repository-level filtering, PostgreSQL row-level security as defense in depth.

Practical exercise

Take an existing NestJS service with an orders module. Write an integration test that logs in as user A, creates an order, then logs in as user B and requests GET /orders/:id with A's order id. Acceptance criteria: the response is 404 (or 403 by documented policy), no order fields are present in the body, and the test fails if the ownership check is removed from the service.

40.2 Sessions

Concept

A session is server-side state that remembers who a client is between requests. After login the server creates a record (in Redis, PostgreSQL, or memory), gives the client an opaque random identifier, usually in a cookie, and on each request looks the identifier up to recover the user.

The important word is opaque. A session id carries no information. It is a random 128-bit or larger string whose only job is to be unguessable and to serve as a lookup key. Everything about the user lives on the server.

Why does it exist?

HTTP is stateless. Each request arrives with no memory of the previous one. Something has to bridge "the user typed a correct password ten minutes ago" and "this request should be treated as that user". Sessions are the oldest and simplest bridge, and they solve a problem tokens struggle with: instant revocation. Delete the session record and the user is logged out on the next request, everywhere. There is no waiting for expiry.

Mental model

Imagine a coat check at a theatre. You hand over your coat and get a numbered ticket. The ticket says nothing about your coat. It is just a number. When you come back, the attendant looks up the number and returns your coat. If the theatre wants to end your visit, they simply throw away the coat check record; your ticket becomes a meaningless piece of paper. If someone steals your ticket, they can claim your coat, which is why the ticket must be hard to forge and kept in your pocket, not pinned to your back.

The ticket is the session id. The coat check book is Redis. The pocket is an HttpOnly cookie.

How it works

  1. POST /auth/login with email and password. The server verifies the password hash (40.14).
  2. The server regenerates the session: any session id that existed before login is discarded and a fresh random id is generated. This defeats session fixation, an attack where the attacker plants a known session id in the victim's browser before login and then uses that same id after the victim logs in.
  3. The server writes { userId, roles, createdAt, ip, userAgent } to Redis under key sess:<id> with a TTL, and adds <id> to a set user:<userId>:sessions so it can find all sessions of a user later.
  4. The server sends Set-Cookie: sid=<id>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=1209600.
  5. On every subsequent request the browser attaches the cookie automatically. Middleware reads the cookie, loads sess:<id> from Redis (about 0.3 ms on the same network) and sets request.session.userId.
  6. A guard converts request.session.userId into the principal, or rejects with 401.
  7. POST /auth/logout deletes sess:<id> and clears the cookie. "Logout everywhere" reads the set user:<userId>:sessions and deletes every member.
  8. Sliding expiry: on each request the TTL is refreshed, so an active user stays logged in while an idle one is logged out after the TTL. An absolute maximum (say 30 days) is enforced separately using createdAt.

Cookie flags, and what each one defends against:

Flag Meaning Attack it blocks
HttpOnly JavaScript cannot read the cookie XSS stealing the session id
Secure Sent only over HTTPS Network sniffing on plain HTTP
SameSite=Lax Not sent on cross-site POSTs; sent on top-level GET navigations Most CSRF
SameSite=Strict Never sent cross-site, even on links All CSRF, but breaks "click link in email, land logged in"
Path=/ Scope within the site Minor; keeps cookies off unrelated paths
Domain (omitted) Only the exact host Subdomain takeover reading cookies
__Host- prefix Browser enforces Secure, no Domain, Path=/ Cookie injection from sibling subdomains
Max-Age Lifetime in seconds Sessions that live forever in a stolen laptop

Practical example

An e-commerce storefront rendered by a Next.js frontend on shop.example.com with the NestJS API on api.example.com. The team chooses cookie sessions because they want instant logout, they want the "sign out of all devices" button on the account page, and the frontend is a browser they control. Mobile apps for the same platform use JWTs (40.3) instead, because cookies are awkward in native HTTP clients.

NestJS example

NestJS runs on Express by default, so the well-trodden express-session plus connect-redis combination is the standard approach. It is configured in main.ts, not in a module, because it is HTTP-layer middleware.

TypeScript
// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import session from 'express-session';
import { RedisStore } from 'connect-redis';
import { createClient } from 'redis';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
  await redis.connect();

  app.set('trust proxy', 1); // behind a load balancer: needed for Secure cookies
  app.use(
    session({
      name: '__Host-sid',                 // prefix forces Secure, Path=/, no Domain
      secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET!, // signs the cookie; rotate via array of secrets
      store: new RedisStore({ client: redis, prefix: 'sess:', ttl: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14 }),
      resave: false,
      saveUninitialized: false,           // no session row for anonymous visitors
      rolling: true,                      // sliding expiry
      cookie: {
        httpOnly: true,
        secure: true,
        sameSite: 'lax',
        maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days
      },
    }),
  );
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

The login service regenerates the session and records it in the per-user index so "logout everywhere" is possible.

TypeScript
// session-auth.service.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request } from 'express';
import { UsersService } from '../users/users.service';
import { RedisService } from '../redis/redis.service'; // thin wrapper over the redis client

@Injectable()
export class SessionAuthService {
  constructor(private users: UsersService, private redis: RedisService) {}

  async login(req: Request, email: string, password: string): Promise<void> {
    const user = await this.users.verifyCredentials(email, password); // argon2 verify inside
    if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid credentials');

    // Session fixation defense: discard whatever id the browser had before login.
    await new Promise<void>((res, rej) => req.session.regenerate((e) => (e ? rej(e) : res())));

    req.session.userId = user.id;
    req.session.roles = user.roles;
    req.session.createdAt = Date.now();
    await this.redis.client.sAdd(`user:${user.id}:sessions`, req.sessionID);
  }

  async logoutEverywhere(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    const key = `user:${userId}:sessions`;
    const ids = await this.redis.client.sMembers(key);
    if (ids.length) await this.redis.client.del(ids.map((id) => `sess:${id}`));
    await this.redis.client.del(key);
  }
}

A guard turns the session into a principal. It also fails closed: if Redis is unreachable, express-session leaves req.session empty, and the guard rejects. Users get a 401 during the outage, which is the correct behaviour; the wrong behaviour would be to let requests through as anonymous-but-trusted.

TypeScript
// session-auth.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request } from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class SessionAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly absoluteMaxMs = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 30; // 30-day hard cap

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const s = req.session;
    if (!s?.userId) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (Date.now() - (s.createdAt ?? 0) > this.absoluteMaxMs) {
      s.destroy(() => undefined);
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Session expired');
    }
    req.user = { id: s.userId, roles: s.roles ?? [] };
    return true;
  }
}

You will need a small type augmentation so TypeScript knows about userId on the session:

TypeScript
// express-session.d.ts
import 'express-session';
declare module 'express-session' {
  interface SessionData {
    userId?: string;
    roles?: string[];
    createdAt?: number;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Sometimes you want sessions in PostgreSQL instead of Redis: an audit requirement to keep login history, or a small system with no Redis. The table below doubles as the "active devices" list in an account page.

SQL
CREATE TABLE sessions (
  id           text PRIMARY KEY,            -- 32+ random bytes, base64url; never sequential
  user_id      uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ip           inet,
  user_agent   text,
  revoked_at   timestamptz
);

-- "Logout everywhere" and "list my devices" both need this.
CREATE INDEX sessions_user_active_idx ON sessions (user_id) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;
-- Cleanup job: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now() - interval '7 days';
CREATE INDEX sessions_expires_idx ON sessions (expires_at);

-- Lookup on every request (about 1 ms on a warm cache):
-- SELECT user_id FROM sessions WHERE id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now();

The cost is one PostgreSQL round trip per request rather than one Redis round trip. At 3,000 requests per second that is 3,000 small indexed reads per second on top of your real workload; PostgreSQL handles that easily, but it is one more reason the read replica and connection pool sizing in Part 27 matter.

TypeORM example

TypeScript
@Entity('sessions')
export class Session {
  @PrimaryColumn('text') id: string;
  @Column('uuid') userId: string;
  @CreateDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz' }) createdAt: Date;
  @Column({ type: 'timestamptz' }) expiresAt: Date;
  @Column({ type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true }) revokedAt: Date | null;
  @Column({ type: 'inet', nullable: true }) ip: string | null;
}

// Revoke all sessions of a user, e.g. after a password change:
await dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .update(Session)
  .set({ revokedAt: () => 'now()' })
  .where('user_id = :userId AND revoked_at IS NULL', { userId })
  .execute();

Production scenario

A marketplace with 1.2 million monthly active users keeps sessions in a Redis cluster with three primaries and three replicas. Session records are about 300 bytes; 2 million live sessions occupy roughly 600 MB. Every API request costs one GET (0.2 to 0.5 ms). Login rate at peak is 40 per second; each login costs an argon2 verify (about 60 ms of CPU) and two Redis writes. The rolling: true sliding expiry means every request also issues an EXPIRE, which doubles Redis command volume; the team accepted that cost for the UX. A nightly job scans user:*:sessions sets and removes ids whose sess: key has expired, so the per-user index does not grow forever.

Monitoring: Redis memory, GET p99 latency, 401 rate (a sudden jump means Redis trouble or a cookie change), and login failure rate (a spike means credential stuffing, 40.25).

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: 401 rate went from 0.3 percent to 92 percent in one minute. Every logged-in user was thrown out. Cause: a config change had rotated SESSION_SECRET to a single new value. express-session signs the cookie with the secret; every existing cookie now failed the signature check and was treated as absent. The fix was to set secret to an array [newSecret, oldSecret]: the first is used to sign new cookies, all are accepted for verification. After 14 days (the session TTL) the old secret is removed. Rotation without an overlap window is a self-inflicted outage.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Session fixation: forgetting regenerate() on login. Any pre-login session id survives into the authenticated session.
  • Redis down: fail closed (401), never fail open. Add a circuit breaker so the app does not hang on Redis timeouts; a 2-second connect timeout is better than a 30-second one.
  • Session store restart with no persistence: everyone is logged out. Acceptable if documented; enable AOF or accept the blast radius.
  • Cookie too large: browsers cap cookies at about 4 KB. Sessions store data server-side, so this only bites you if someone stores state in the cookie itself.
  • Cross-subdomain leaks: setting Domain=example.com sends the cookie to blog.example.com too; if that host is compromised, so is the session.
  • Privilege change while logged in: roles cached in the session are stale until re-login. Either reload roles from the DB every request, or bump a rolesVersion in Redis and reject sessions with an older version.
  • Concurrent logins: allow many sessions per user, but cap them (for example 20) and evict the oldest, or one leaked credential creates thousands of sessions.
  • Clock skew: sliding expiry uses server time. If two app nodes disagree by minutes, sessions expire unpredictably. Run NTP.
  • Sticky sessions are not needed with a shared store; if someone proposes them, the store is probably in memory, which is wrong for more than one replica.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior engineer's first question is: do I need instant revocation? If yes (banking, admin panels, anything where "log them out now" is a real requirement), sessions are the honest answer, and they accept the Redis dependency. If the clients are mobile apps or third-party services, or the system spans many services that must all validate identity without a shared store, they lean towards tokens (40.3) and accept the revocation compromise.

They also insist on the __Host- prefix, SameSite=Lax, secret rotation with overlap, and an index of sessions per user from day one, because retrofitting "logout everywhere" after an account-takeover incident is painful.

Common mistakes

  • Storing sessions in process memory (MemoryStore) and then scaling to two replicas.
  • Skipping regenerate() on login and on privilege change.
  • Setting saveUninitialized: true, which creates a Redis key for every anonymous crawler hit and turns a bot scan into a memory problem.
  • Rotating the cookie secret without the overlap array.
  • Setting a Domain attribute "so it works on all subdomains" and thereby sharing the session with the marketing site.
  • Not indexing sessions by user, making "logout everywhere" impossible.

Interview questions

  1. What is session fixation and how do you prevent it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: attacker plants a session id before login; regenerate the id at login so the planted one is worthless. Follow-up: does the same risk exist with JWTs?
  2. Explain each cookie flag and the attack it prevents.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: table above. Follow-up: when would you choose SameSite=Strict over Lax?
  3. How do you implement "log out of all devices"?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: per-user index of session ids (Redis set or DB index) and delete them all. Follow-up: how do you keep that index from growing unbounded?
  4. Redis is down. What should the auth layer do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: fail closed with 401 and a short timeout; never treat the user as anonymous-but-allowed.
  5. How do you rotate the session signing secret with zero logouts?
  6. Compare a session table in PostgreSQL with Redis sessions on cost, latency and features.

Practical exercise

Implement session login in a NestJS app with express-session and connect-redis. Add POST /auth/logout-all and GET /auth/sessions (listing active devices with IP, user agent and last-seen time). Acceptance criteria: logging in from two browsers and calling logout-all from one invalidates both within one request; the cookie carries HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax and the __Host- prefix; stopping Redis causes 401 responses within 2 seconds rather than hanging requests.

40.2.1 Session vs token: the decision table

Dimension Server-side session Stateless token (JWT)
Revocation Instant: delete the record Wait for expiry, or add a denylist (state again)
Per-request cost One store lookup (Redis 0.2 to 1 ms) Signature verify (HS256 microseconds, RS256 about 0.1 to 0.3 ms)
Horizontal scaling Needs shared store Any node can verify with the key
Cross-service auth Each service needs the store Each service needs only the public key
Client type Browsers (cookies) Mobile, SPAs, service-to-service
CSRF exposure Yes when cookie-based; mitigate with SameSite and tokens No if sent in a header; yes if placed in a cookie
XSS exposure Cookie unreadable with HttpOnly localStorage readable by any script
Data in credential None (opaque) Claims visible to anyone who holds it (base64, not encrypted)
Best fit Web apps, admin panels, anything needing "log out now" APIs consumed by many clients and services

Many mature systems use both: a short-lived JWT as the access credential and a server-side record for the refresh token, which gives you cheap stateless verification for 99 percent of requests and a revocation point for the remaining 1 percent. That design is the subject of the next section.

40.3 JSON Web Tokens (JWT)

Concept

A JWT is a small, self-contained credential: a JSON payload of claims ("this is user 42, with role customer, valid until 14:05") that is signed so that anyone with the right key can verify it was issued by your server and has not been changed. Because the token carries its own proof, the server that receives it does not need to look anything up. It reads the claims, checks the signature and the expiry, and trusts the content.

That last sentence is both the appeal and the danger. No lookup means fast, stateless, easy to scale. No lookup also means no way to change your mind about a token once it is out in the world, until it expires.

Why does it exist?

Sessions require every service that authenticates a request to reach the same store. When the system is one NestJS app and one Redis, that is fine. When there are eight services, an API gateway, a mobile app and three partner integrations, a shared session store becomes a bottleneck and a coupling point. JWTs let each service validate identity locally with a public key and nothing else.

They also fit machine-to-machine and third-party access (OAuth 2.0, 22.4) where there is no browser and no cookie jar.

Mental model

Imagine a concert wristband. The venue puts it on you at the gate after checking your ticket. Every bar and every door inside checks the wristband, not your ticket, and they do not phone the gate to ask. The wristband is hard to forge (special print, tamper-evident), it shows what you are entitled to (VIP area, free drinks), and it stops working when the festival ends. But if security decides to throw you out, they cannot remotely deactivate the wristband. They have to find you and cut it off. And if someone steals it from you, they are you until it expires.

That is the JWT tradeoff in one picture. Everything in this section is about making the wristband short-lived and making the "find you and cut it off" path possible.

How it works

A JWT is three base64url-encoded parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature.

JSON
// header
{ "alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT", "kid": "2026-08-key-1" }
// payload (claims)
{
  "sub": "8b1e2c1a-0f7f-4a5e-9f31-6c2f2a0e0d11",
  "iss": "https://api.example.com",
  "aud": "example-api",
  "iat": 1788900000,
  "exp": 1788900900,
  "jti": "c0a9c3d2-2f0a-4c22-8e02-5c7a8c0f1f2a",
  "roles": ["customer"],
  "tenant_id": "t_9f2"
}

The signature is computed over base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload) using the algorithm named in the header. Note that the payload is encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who holds the token can read every claim. Never put secrets, passwords, card numbers or personal data you would not show the user into a JWT.

Standard claims you should always set and always verify:

Claim Meaning Why it matters
iss Issuer Reject tokens minted by a different auth server that happens to share a key format
sub Subject (user id) The principal; use a stable id, not an email
aud Audience A token for the payments API must not be accepted by the admin API
exp Expiry (seconds since epoch) Bounds the damage of a stolen token
iat Issued at Lets you reject tokens issued before a "revoke all" timestamp
nbf Not before Rarely needed; verify it if present
jti Token id Needed for denylists and reuse detection

Signing algorithms:

Algorithm Type Key Verify cost Use when
HS256 HMAC with SHA-256 One shared secret About 5 microseconds One service issues and verifies; nobody else needs to verify
RS256 RSA signature Private key signs, public key verifies About 100 to 300 microseconds (2048-bit) Many services or third parties verify; publish the public key via JWKS
ES256 ECDSA on P-256 Private/public pair About 50 to 100 microseconds; much smaller signatures Same as RS256, with smaller tokens and keys

The rule: with HS256, every service that can verify can also forge, because it is the same secret. The moment a second service needs to verify tokens, move to RS256 or ES256 and hand out only the public key.

The alg=none attack. Early JWT libraries trusted the alg field in the header. An attacker took a valid token, changed the header to {"alg":"none"}, removed the signature, edited the payload to "roles":["admin"], and the library said "no signature required, looks fine". A related trick: change RS256 to HS256 and sign the forged token with the server's public key as the HMAC secret; a library that picks the verification routine from the header would then verify it with the public key and accept it. The defense in every modern library, including jsonwebtoken used by @nestjs/jwt and passport-jwt, is to pin the allowed algorithms on the verifying side: algorithms: ['RS256']. Never let the token tell you how to verify it.

Expiry and clock skew. Access tokens should live minutes, not days: 5 to 15 minutes is typical. Verification compares exp to the server clock. If the issuing server's clock runs 30 seconds ahead of a verifying server, brand-new tokens fail with "token not yet valid" (nbf/iat checks) or expire 30 seconds early. Libraries expose a clockTolerance (typically 30 to 60 seconds); set it, and run NTP on every node.

Why you cannot revoke a JWT, and the three answers. The verifier does not call home, so nothing you do on the server changes the outcome until exp. The answers, from cheapest to most complete:

  1. Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens. Access token: 10 minutes, stateless. Refresh token: days or weeks, stored server-side (hashed), exchanged for a new access token at POST /auth/refresh. Revocation happens at the refresh step; the maximum window of a stolen access token is 10 minutes.
  2. Refresh token rotation with reuse detection. Every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old (already used) refresh token is presented again, someone has a copy: either the legitimate client replayed a request, or an attacker stole the token. Either way, revoke the whole token family and force re-login.
  3. A denylist in Redis keyed by jti with TTL equal to the token's remaining life, checked on every request. This reintroduces a lookup per request, but only a GET that returns nothing 99.99 percent of the time. Use it for the rare "log this user out now" case (password change, account compromise) rather than for normal logout.

Where to store the token on the client.

Storage XSS risk CSRF risk Notes
localStorage / sessionStorage Any injected script can read and exfiltrate the token None (not sent automatically) Easiest; unacceptable for high-value apps
In memory (JS variable) Script can read it while the page is open; lost on reload None Combine with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie
HttpOnly cookie Script cannot read it Sent automatically, so CSRF defenses are required (SameSite, CSRF token, 40.22) Best for browser clients
Native secure storage (Keychain, Keystore) Not applicable Not applicable Mobile apps

The pattern most teams settle on for browsers: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to Path=/auth/refresh. XSS cannot read the refresh token; CSRF cannot use it because SameSite=Strict stops cross-site sending, and even if it could, the refresh endpoint returns the access token in the response body, which the attacker's page cannot read.

Practical example

A ride-booking platform: a rider app, a driver app, and internal services (pricing, dispatch, payments). The auth service issues ES256 access tokens (10 minutes) with aud: "rider-api" or aud: "driver-api" and a roles claim. Every service verifies with the public key fetched from https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json and cached for an hour. The refresh token lives in the app's secure storage and is rotated on each use. When a driver is deactivated, the auth service revokes the driver's refresh family; the driver's access token dies within 10 minutes. For the "deactivate a driver during a live safety incident" case, the driver's jti is added to a Redis denylist and the driver API checks it, so the cut-off is immediate.

NestJS example

The building blocks: @nestjs/jwt to sign, @nestjs/passport plus passport-jwt to verify, and a strategy that turns a verified payload into the request principal.

TypeScript
// auth.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtModule } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { PassportModule } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { JwtStrategy } from './jwt.strategy';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { AuthController } from './auth.controller';

@Module({
  imports: [
    PassportModule.register({ defaultStrategy: 'jwt' }),
    JwtModule.registerAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
        privateKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PRIVATE_KEY'), // PEM, from a secrets manager
        publicKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'),
        signOptions: {
          algorithm: 'ES256',
          expiresIn: '10m',
          issuer: 'https://api.example.com',
          audience: 'example-api',
          keyid: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_KEY_ID'), // "kid" header for rotation
        },
      }),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [AuthService, JwtStrategy],
  controllers: [AuthController],
  exports: [AuthService],
})
export class AuthModule {}
TypeScript
// jwt.strategy.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { UsersService } from '../users/users.service';
import { TokenDenylist } from './token-denylist';

export interface AccessTokenPayload {
  sub: string; roles: string[]; tenant_id: string; jti: string; iat: number; exp: number;
}

@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor(cfg: ConfigService, private users: UsersService, private denylist: TokenDenylist) {
    super({
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
      secretOrKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'),
      algorithms: ['ES256'],          // pin the algorithm: defeats alg=none and key confusion
      issuer: 'https://api.example.com',
      audience: 'example-api',
      ignoreExpiration: false,
      jsonWebTokenOptions: { clockTolerance: 30 }, // seconds of skew we forgive
    });
  }

  // Runs only after signature, exp, iss and aud have been verified.
  async validate(payload: AccessTokenPayload) {
    if (await this.denylist.has(payload.jti)) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    // Optional, costs one cached lookup: reject tokens issued before "revoke all" or for disabled users.
    const status = await this.users.getAuthStatus(payload.sub); // cached in Redis for 60 s
    if (!status || status.disabled || payload.iat * 1000 < status.tokensInvalidBefore.getTime()) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException();
    }
    return { id: payload.sub, roles: payload.roles, tenantId: payload.tenant_id, jti: payload.jti };
  }
}

Whatever validate returns becomes request.user. The strategy is used by AuthGuard('jwt') from @nestjs/passport; a thin subclass lets you add a @Public() bypass (shown in full in 40.37).

The refresh flow stores only a hash of the refresh token. If the refresh_tokens table leaks (backup, SQL injection, a curious DBA), the attacker gets hashes they cannot use.

TypeScript
// auth.service.ts (refresh part)
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { createHash, randomBytes, randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { RefreshToken } from './refresh-token.entity';

@Injectable()
export class AuthService {
  constructor(private jwt: JwtService, @InjectRepository(RefreshToken) private tokens: Repository<RefreshToken>) {}

  private hash(raw: string) { return createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest('hex'); } // fast hash is fine: token is high-entropy

  async issuePair(user: { id: string; roles: string[]; tenantId: string }, familyId = randomUUID()) {
    const raw = randomBytes(48).toString('base64url');            // 384 bits of entropy
    await this.tokens.save(this.tokens.create({
      tokenHash: this.hash(raw), userId: user.id, familyId,
      expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 3600 * 1000),   // 30 days
    }));
    const accessToken = await this.jwt.signAsync(
      { roles: user.roles, tenant_id: user.tenantId },
      { subject: user.id, jwtid: randomUUID() },
    );
    return { accessToken, refreshToken: raw };
  }

  async refresh(raw: string) {
    const row = await this.tokens.findOne({ where: { tokenHash: this.hash(raw) }, relations: { user: true } });
    if (!row || row.expiresAt < new Date()) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (row.usedAt || row.revokedAt) {
      // Reuse detected: revoke the whole family, force re-login on every device sharing it.
      await this.tokens.update({ familyId: row.familyId }, { revokedAt: new Date() });
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Refresh token reuse detected');
    }
    await this.tokens.update({ id: row.id }, { usedAt: new Date() });
    return this.issuePair({ id: row.user.id, roles: row.user.roleNames(), tenantId: row.user.tenantId }, row.familyId);
  }
}

One subtle race remains: two legitimate refresh requests in flight at the same time (a mobile app with two tabs) will trigger reuse detection for the second one. Mitigate by making the UPDATE ... SET used_at conditional (WHERE used_at IS NULL) and checking the affected row count, and by allowing a short grace window (for example 10 seconds after used_at) during which the same replacement token is returned again. The complete module in 40.37 includes this.

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE refresh_tokens (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  token_hash  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- sha256 hex of the raw token
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  family_id   uuid NOT NULL,                 -- all rotations of one login share a family
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  used_at     timestamptz,                   -- set on rotation
  revoked_at  timestamptz,                   -- set on logout or reuse detection
  replaced_by uuid REFERENCES refresh_tokens(id),
  user_agent  text,
  ip          inet
);

-- Revoke a family on reuse; list a user's live tokens; purge expired.
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_family_idx ON refresh_tokens (family_id);
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_user_live_idx ON refresh_tokens (user_id)
  WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND used_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_expires_idx ON refresh_tokens (expires_at);

-- The refresh lookup is a single unique-index probe:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, user_id, family_id, used_at, revoked_at, expires_at
FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = 'e3b0c442...';
Text
Index Scan using refresh_tokens_token_hash_key on refresh_tokens
  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=88) (actual time=0.031..0.032 rows=1 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (token_hash = 'e3b0c442...'::text)
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Planning Time: 0.090 ms
Execution Time: 0.052 ms

The users table should carry a tokens_invalid_before timestamptz column. Setting it to now() on password change or "log out everywhere" invalidates every access token issued earlier, provided the strategy compares iat against it (as in the validate method above). It is a cheap, coarse revocation that costs one cached read.

Sequelize example

The same reuse detection with Sequelize, using a transaction and a row lock so that two concurrent refreshes with the same token cannot both succeed.

TypeScript
async refresh(raw: string) {
  const tokenHash = sha256(raw);
  return this.sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
    const row = await RefreshToken.findOne({
      where: { tokenHash },
      lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE,        // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE: serialises concurrent refreshes
      transaction: t,
    });
    if (!row || row.expiresAt < new Date()) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (row.usedAt || row.revokedAt) {
      await RefreshToken.update({ revokedAt: new Date() }, { where: { familyId: row.familyId }, transaction: t });
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Refresh token reuse detected');
    }
    await row.update({ usedAt: new Date() }, { transaction: t });
    return this.issuePair(row.userId, row.familyId, t);
  });
}

Production scenario

A SaaS API at 4,000 requests per second. Each request verifies an ES256 token: about 80 microseconds of CPU, so 0.3 CPU-seconds per second across the fleet, negligible. Refreshes arrive at roughly 4,000 / (10 minutes of token life / average session) which works out to about 7 per second, each costing two small PostgreSQL writes. The refresh_tokens table grows by about 600,000 rows a day; a nightly job deletes rows where expires_at < now() - interval '7 days', keeping it under 25 million rows. The Redis denylist holds a few hundred entries at any time.

Key rotation: the auth service generates a new key pair monthly. The JWKS endpoint serves both the new and previous public keys, each with its kid. Tokens are signed with the new key; verifiers pick the key by kid. After the longest access-token lifetime plus a safety margin (one hour), the old key is removed from the JWKS. Verifiers cache JWKS for an hour but refresh immediately on an unknown kid, with a rate limit so an attacker cannot force JWKS fetches by sending random kid values.

Failure scenario

At 09:03 the payments service started rejecting 100 percent of requests with 401. The auth team had rotated the signing key at 09:00 and, to be tidy, removed the old key from JWKS at the same moment. Every access token in circulation (issued up to 10 minutes earlier) now referenced a kid that no longer existed. The payments service's JWKS cache refreshed, found no matching key, and rejected everything. Users saw "session expired" and their clients hit /auth/refresh all at once: a retry storm of 40,000 refreshes in one minute against a table designed for 7 per second. PostgreSQL held, but p99 latency on refresh went to 4 seconds and several mobile clients gave up and forced re-login.

Two lessons. Old keys stay in JWKS for at least one full token lifetime. And refresh endpoints need their own rate limiting and connection pool budget, because they are the thing everything falls back to.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Token replay within its lifetime: a captured access token works until exp. Keep lifetimes short and bind tokens to TLS where possible (mTLS or DPoP for high-value APIs).
  • Refresh token theft: rotation with reuse detection bounds the damage to one refresh; whoever refreshes second triggers family revocation.
  • Legitimate double refresh: two tabs, one token. Use a conditional update plus a short grace window.
  • Clock skew: tokens rejected as "not yet valid" or expiring early. Set clockTolerance, run NTP, alert on skew.
  • JWKS rotation removing keys too early: keep old keys for at least the token lifetime.
  • JWKS endpoint down: verifiers must cache keys with a long stale-while-revalidate window; never fail open.
  • Huge tokens: a roles claim with 400 permissions pushes the token past 8 KB and past header-size limits on some proxies. Put permission versions or a role id in the token, not the full list.
  • Deleted or disabled user with a valid token: verify status on each request from a short-lived cache, or accept a 10-minute window and document it.
  • aud not checked: a token for the public API accepted by the admin API.
  • iss not checked: tokens from staging accepted in production because both share a key format (or, worse, a key).
  • Secrets in the payload: claims are readable by anyone with the token.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior engineer asks: what is the blast radius of a stolen token, and how long does it last? Every design decision follows from that: short exp, rotation, denylist for emergencies, hashed storage of refresh tokens, aud per API. They pick ES256 over HS256 as soon as a second verifier exists, and they build key rotation before they need it, because rotating for the first time during an incident is how outages happen. They refuse to put anything in a token they would not print on a receipt.

To a product manager: "When you press 'deactivate this account', the app is locked out within ten minutes in the normal case and immediately in the emergency case. Making every case immediate would cost a database lookup on every request; here is what that costs and why we chose the hybrid."

Common mistakes

  • Verifying with the algorithm named in the token header instead of pinning it.
  • One long-lived access token (30 days) and no refresh flow.
  • Storing raw refresh tokens in the database.
  • Storing the access token in localStorage on a site that renders any user-generated content.
  • Putting the whole user object, including email and address, into the token.
  • Not setting or not verifying aud and iss.
  • Rotating keys by replacing rather than by overlapping.
  • Using the same key pair in staging and production.
  • Treating logout as "delete the token on the client" only, with no server-side revocation of the refresh token.

Interview questions

  1. Why can't you revoke a JWT, and what are the practical answers?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no lookup during verification; short expiry plus refresh rotation, reuse detection, denylist for emergencies. Follow-up: what does the denylist cost per request?
  2. Explain the alg=none and key-confusion attacks and the single configuration that prevents both.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pin algorithms on the verifier.
  3. HS256 or RS256/ES256 for a system with three services?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: asymmetric, because a shared HMAC secret lets any verifier forge. Follow-up: how do you rotate the key without downtime?
  4. Where do you store the token in a browser SPA and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: access token in memory, refresh token in HttpOnly SameSite cookie; discuss XSS vs CSRF.
  5. Describe refresh token rotation with reuse detection. What is the race condition and how do you handle it?
  6. A user's role changes. When does the API notice?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: at next token issue; sooner with a status cache or version claim.
  7. What is clockTolerance and why would a 30-second skew take down authentication?

Practical exercise

Build the refresh flow: POST /auth/login returns an access token (10 minutes, ES256) and a refresh token (raw, 48 random bytes); POST /auth/refresh rotates; the database stores only hashes. Write tests for: normal rotation; replay of a used refresh token revokes the whole family; a token with alg changed to none is rejected; a token signed with the wrong key is rejected; a token with aud: "other-api" is rejected; a token 20 seconds past expiry is accepted with clockTolerance: 30 and rejected at 40 seconds. Acceptance criteria: all tests pass, and no raw refresh token ever appears in a log line or a database column.

40.4 OAuth 2.0

Concept

OAuth 2.0 is a protocol for delegated authorization: letting one application access a user's data in another application, with the user's consent, without ever giving the first application the user's password. When a scheduling app asks "may I read your Google Calendar?" and you click Allow, that is OAuth. The scheduling app ends up with an access token that works only for the calendar, only for you, only until it expires.

OAuth is not a login protocol, even though everyone uses it for login. "Login with Google" is OpenID Connect (40.5), a thin identity layer on top of OAuth. Keep the two separate in your head: OAuth answers "what may this app do on this user's behalf"; OIDC answers "who is this user".

Why does it exist?

Before OAuth, integrating with another service meant asking the user for their password to that service and storing it. Every integration was a full-access credential, unrevocable except by changing the password, and stored in dozens of third-party databases. OAuth replaces that with scoped, revocable, expiring tokens issued by the service that owns the data.

Inside a company it solves the same problem: a mobile app, a partner API, and internal services all need bounded, revocable access to the same resources without sharing passwords or a master key.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel. You are the guest (resource owner). The room is the resource. The front desk is the authorization server. A valet is a client: he needs to move your car but does not need your room key or your wallet. The front desk gives the valet a key card that opens only the garage, only today. That card is an access token with a scope of garage:drive and an expiry of tonight. If the valet loses the card, the front desk deactivates it; your room is never at risk.

How it works

The four roles:

Role Meaning In a NestJS system
Resource owner The user who owns the data The customer
Client The app that wants access Your SPA, mobile app, or a partner's server
Authorization server Issues tokens after authenticating the user and getting consent Your auth service, Auth0, Keycloak, Cognito, Google
Resource server Holds the data and accepts tokens Your NestJS API

The grant types that matter today:

  1. Authorization code with PKCE: for anything with a user in a browser or on a device. The client redirects the user to the authorization server, the user logs in and consents, the authorization server redirects back with a short-lived code, and the client exchanges the code for tokens at the token endpoint. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, pronounced "pixie") binds the code to the client instance that started the flow so that a stolen code is useless.
  2. Client credentials: for service-to-service calls with no user. The client authenticates with its own id and secret (or a private key) and receives a token representing itself.
  3. Refresh token: exchanges a refresh token for a new access token; not a separate login, a continuation of one of the above.

Grants that are dead: the implicit grant (tokens in the URL fragment, no PKCE, leaks through browser history and referrers) and the resource owner password grant (the client collects the password, which is exactly what OAuth exists to avoid). OAuth 2.1 removes both. If a library or a vendor still proposes them, say no.

Authorization code + PKCE, step by step:

  1. The client generates a random code_verifier (43 to 128 characters) and computes code_challenge = base64url(sha256(code_verifier)).
  2. It redirects the browser to GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=...&redirect_uri=...&scope=orders:read&state=<random>&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256.
  3. The authorization server authenticates the user (password, MFA, existing session) and shows a consent screen listing the scopes.
  4. It redirects to redirect_uri?code=<code>&state=<same random>. The code lives about 60 seconds and can be used once.
  5. The client verifies state matches what it sent (CSRF defense for the callback), then calls POST /token with grant_type=authorization_code&code=...&redirect_uri=...&client_id=...&code_verifier=<original>.
  6. The server hashes the verifier, compares to the stored challenge, and only then issues { access_token, token_type: "Bearer", expires_in: 600, refresh_token, scope }.
  7. The client calls the resource server with Authorization: Bearer <access_token>.
  8. The resource server validates the token (signature via JWKS, exp, iss, aud, required scope) and serves the request.

Scopes are strings that name a permission bundle: orders:read, orders:write, profile. The authorization server records which scopes the user consented to; the token carries them; the resource server checks them per endpoint. Scopes are about what the client app may do, not what the user may do. A user with admin rights using a client that only has orders:read still cannot write orders through that client. Both checks apply.

Practical example

An e-commerce platform opens its API to third-party inventory tools. A vendor's tool wants to read a merchant's orders and update stock levels. The merchant clicks "Connect" in the vendor's tool, is redirected to auth.example.com, logs in, sees "This app wants to: read your orders, update your inventory", and approves. The vendor's server receives tokens scoped to orders:read inventory:write for that merchant. The platform's NestJS API checks the scope on every endpoint and the merchant id inside the token on every query. If the merchant disconnects the app, the platform revokes the refresh token; the vendor loses access within the access token's 10-minute life.

For internal traffic, the pricing service calls the catalog service with a client-credentials token (scope: catalog:read, sub: "svc-pricing"), so the catalog service can enforce which services may call which endpoints and can attribute traffic in its logs.

NestJS example

A NestJS API acting as a resource server for tokens issued by an external authorization server. The trick is jwks-rsa, which fetches and caches the public keys and selects the right one by kid.

TypeScript
// oauth-resource.strategy.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';
import { passportJwtSecret } from 'jwks-rsa';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Injectable()
export class OAuthResourceStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'oauth') {
  constructor(cfg: ConfigService) {
    super({
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
      secretOrKeyProvider: passportJwtSecret({
        jwksUri: `${cfg.getOrThrow('OAUTH_ISSUER')}/.well-known/jwks.json`,
        cache: true,
        cacheMaxAge: 60 * 60 * 1000,   // 1 hour; refreshed early on unknown kid
        rateLimit: true,
        jwksRequestsPerMinute: 5,      // attacker cannot force JWKS fetches with random kids
        timeout: 3000,
      }),
      algorithms: ['RS256'],
      issuer: cfg.getOrThrow('OAUTH_ISSUER'),
      audience: 'https://api.example.com',
      jsonWebTokenOptions: { clockTolerance: 30 },
    });
  }

  validate(payload: { sub: string; scope: string; client_id?: string; merchant_id?: string }) {
    return {
      id: payload.sub,
      scopes: payload.scope?.split(' ') ?? [],
      clientId: payload.client_id,
      merchantId: payload.merchant_id,
    };
  }
}

Scopes are enforced by a small decorator and guard pair using Reflector, exactly the same mechanism as roles (40.8).

TypeScript
// scopes.decorator.ts + scopes.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable, SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';

export const SCOPES_KEY = 'required_scopes';
export const RequireScopes = (...scopes: string[]) => SetMetadata(SCOPES_KEY, scopes);

@Injectable()
export class ScopesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector) {}
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(SCOPES_KEY, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]) ?? [];
    if (required.length === 0) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { scopes: string[] } | undefined;
    const ok = required.every((s) => user?.scopes.includes(s));
    if (!ok) throw new ForbiddenException(`Missing scope: ${required.join(' ')}`);
    return true;
  }
}

// usage
// @UseGuards(AuthGuard('oauth'), ScopesGuard)
// @RequireScopes('inventory:write')
// @Patch('inventory/:sku') updateStock(...) {}

A client-credentials call from one NestJS service to another, with the token cached until shortly before expiry so that you do not hit the token endpoint on every request:

TypeScript
// service-token.provider.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Injectable()
export class ServiceTokenProvider {
  private token?: { value: string; expiresAt: number };
  constructor(private cfg: ConfigService) {}

  async get(): Promise<string> {
    if (this.token && this.token.expiresAt - Date.now() > 30_000) return this.token.value; // 30 s safety margin
    const body = new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: 'client_credentials',
      scope: 'catalog:read',
    });
    const basic = Buffer.from(`${this.cfg.getOrThrow('SVC_CLIENT_ID')}:${this.cfg.getOrThrow('SVC_CLIENT_SECRET')}`).toString('base64');
    const res = await fetch(`${this.cfg.getOrThrow('OAUTH_ISSUER')}/token`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { Authorization: `Basic ${basic}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
      body,
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`token endpoint ${res.status}`);
    const json = (await res.json()) as { access_token: string; expires_in: number };
    this.token = { value: json.access_token, expiresAt: Date.now() + json.expires_in * 1000 };
    return this.token.value;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

If you run your own authorization server, three tables carry the state: registered clients, consents, and authorization codes (which you may also keep in Redis with a 60-second TTL).

SQL
CREATE TABLE oauth_clients (
  id                 text PRIMARY KEY,                 -- public client_id
  secret_hash        text,                             -- NULL for public clients (SPA, mobile)
  name               text NOT NULL,
  redirect_uris      text[] NOT NULL,                  -- exact-match only, never prefix-match
  allowed_scopes     text[] NOT NULL,
  allowed_grants     text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{authorization_code,refresh_token}',
  require_pkce       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  created_at         timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE oauth_consents (
  user_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  client_id  text NOT NULL REFERENCES oauth_clients(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  scopes     text[] NOT NULL,
  granted_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  revoked_at timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, client_id)
);

CREATE TABLE oauth_codes (
  code_hash      text PRIMARY KEY,                     -- hash of the code, never the raw code
  client_id      text NOT NULL,
  user_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  redirect_uri   text NOT NULL,
  scopes         text[] NOT NULL,
  code_challenge text NOT NULL,
  expires_at     timestamptz NOT NULL,                 -- now() + 60 s
  used_at        timestamptz                           -- single use; reuse revokes issued tokens
);

redirect_uris must be matched exactly. Prefix or wildcard matching is the root of a whole family of token-theft bugs: an attacker registers https://app.example.com.evil.com or finds an open redirect on your domain and the code is delivered to them.

Production scenario

A platform with 3,000 registered third-party apps and 120,000 merchants. The authorization server (Keycloak, tuned) handles about 150 token requests per second at peak, most of them refreshes. The NestJS resource servers verify roughly 6,000 bearer tokens per second using cached JWKS; JWKS is fetched once per hour per pod. Scope checks are metadata lookups and cost nothing measurable. Consent revocation by a merchant marks oauth_consents.revoked_at and revokes the client's refresh tokens; existing access tokens die within 10 minutes. The dashboard tracks token requests per client, refresh failure rate per client (a spike means a partner's integration broke), and JWKS fetch errors per pod.

Failure scenario

A partner reported that their integration "randomly logs merchants out". Investigation showed their server ran two instances behind a load balancer, each holding its own copy of the refresh token in memory. Instance A refreshed; the token rotated; instance B later used the old token; the authorization server's reuse detection revoked the family. Correct behaviour on our side, but it took the partner three weeks to find. The fix on their side was a shared token store with a lock around refresh. The lesson for us: document rotation and reuse detection loudly in the partner API docs, and expose a clear error code (invalid_grant with error_description: "refresh token reused") instead of a generic 401.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Open redirect on your own domain turns exact-match redirect URIs into token leaks. Audit every redirect in the app.
  • Authorization code reuse: a code presented twice must fail and revoke tokens already issued from it (the spec's recommendation), because it means the code was stolen.
  • Missing state check: the callback becomes a CSRF target: an attacker can log the victim into the attacker's account (login CSRF) and later read what the victim saved there.
  • Scope escalation: the token request asks for more scopes than the user consented to; the server must issue the intersection, never the request.
  • Token endpoint without rate limits: brute force on client_secret or code.
  • Long-lived access tokens for third parties: revocation becomes impossible in practice; keep them short and use refresh.
  • JWKS unreachable: cache with stale-while-revalidate; fail closed for unknown kid, but do not evict a still-valid cached key just because the refresh failed.
  • Confused deputy: a resource server accepts a token whose aud names a different API; always check aud.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They do not build an authorization server unless the business is identity. They pick Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito or Ory and spend their effort on scopes, audiences, and the resource-server side, which is where their product's data is. They insist on PKCE for every public client, exact redirect URIs, aud per API, and client-credentials tokens (not shared API keys) for service-to-service traffic, because the audit trail of "which service called what" is worth the setup cost. When a vendor proposes the implicit or password grant, that is the end of the evaluation.

Common mistakes

  • Using OAuth access tokens as proof of identity ("the token is valid so the user is logged in"). Access tokens are for the resource server; identity is OIDC's id token.
  • Prefix-matching redirect URIs.
  • Skipping state or PKCE "because it is a confidential client".
  • Treating scopes as user permissions instead of client permissions and skipping the user-level check.
  • Calling the token endpoint on every outgoing request instead of caching the token.
  • Sharing one client id and secret across all internal services, which makes attribution and revocation impossible.

Interview questions

  1. Explain authorization code + PKCE and what PKCE protects against.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: binds the code to the client instance; a stolen code cannot be exchanged without the verifier. Follow-up: why is implicit grant dead?
  2. What is the difference between scopes and roles?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scopes bound the client app; roles bound the user; both apply.
  3. How does a resource server validate a token from an external authorization server?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: JWKS by kid, pinned algorithm, iss, aud, exp, scope; caching and rate-limiting of JWKS fetches.
  4. Client credentials vs a shared API key for service-to-service calls?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: expiring, scoped, attributable tokens vs a static secret.
  5. Why must redirect URIs be matched exactly?
  6. What should happen when an authorization code is used twice?

Practical exercise

Configure a NestJS API as a resource server for a local Keycloak (or Ory Hydra) instance. Register a public client with PKCE, a confidential client for client credentials, and two scopes. Acceptance criteria: an endpoint annotated with @RequireScopes('inventory:write') returns 403 for a token with only orders:read; a token with the wrong aud returns 401; stopping Keycloak after the first successful request does not break verification for the next hour (cached JWKS); a token with an unknown kid triggers at most 5 JWKS fetches per minute.

40.5 OpenID Connect (OIDC)

Concept

OpenID Connect adds identity to OAuth 2.0. It defines one new token, the id token (a JWT that says who the user is and how and when they authenticated), a standard userinfo endpoint, a discovery document so clients can configure themselves from a single URL, and a nonce parameter that binds the id token to the login request. "Login with Google", "Login with Microsoft", and your company's single sign-on all speak OIDC.

Why does it exist?

Teams were using OAuth access tokens as proof of login, which is wrong: an access token proves that some client was granted some access, not that this user just authenticated to this client. A malicious app could take a token a user granted to it and present that token to your app's "login with X" endpoint; your app would look up the user and log the attacker in as them. OIDC fixes this by issuing an id token with aud set to your client id and a nonce you chose, so an id token obtained by another app is useless against yours.

Mental model

Imagine the hotel again. OAuth gave the valet a garage key card. OIDC is the front desk also handing you a printed slip: "This is guest Priya Sharma, checked in at 14:02 with passport verification, for hotel booking reference 8812." The slip is signed by the hotel, addressed to a specific booking, and useless for any other booking. The valet's key card says nothing about who you are; the slip says nothing about what you can open.

How it works

  1. Discovery. The client fetches https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration and learns authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, userinfo_endpoint, jwks_uri, supported scopes and algorithms. No hand-typed URLs.
  2. The client starts an authorization code + PKCE flow with scope=openid email profile, a random state, and a random nonce, both stored in the user's pre-login session.
  3. On callback, the client checks state, exchanges the code, and receives { access_token, id_token, refresh_token? }.
  4. The client verifies the id token: signature against jwks_uri, iss equals the discovered issuer, aud equals the client id, exp valid, and nonce equals the stored nonce. Only then is the user considered authenticated.
  5. Claims in the id token (sub, email, email_verified, name, picture) identify the user. sub is the stable identifier; email can change. Link accounts on (issuer, sub), never on email alone, and require email_verified: true before trusting the email at all.
  6. Optionally the client calls userinfo with the access token for extra claims.
  7. The client then creates its own session or its own JWT (40.2, 40.3). The Google tokens are not used to authenticate requests to your API; they only established who the user is.

Id token vs access token:

Id token Access token
Audience Your client (the app that started login) The resource server (Google's APIs, or your API if you are the issuer)
Purpose Prove who authenticated and how Authorize API calls
Format Always a JWT Opaque or JWT; you should not parse Google's
Should your API accept it as a bearer credential? No Only if your API is its intended audience

Practical example

A food-delivery app offers "Continue with Google". The NestJS backend implements the flow, verifies the id token, upserts a users row keyed on (provider='google', provider_sub), and issues its own access and refresh tokens. If the same email later registers with a password, the two are linked only after the password account proves ownership (login) and explicitly links, never automatically, because automatic linking by email is a classic account takeover: an attacker creates a Google account with the victim's unverified email at some identity provider and gets merged into the victim's account.

NestJS example

A self-contained implementation using jose for id-token verification. Libraries such as openid-client do this for you; seeing the steps once makes their configuration options meaningful.

TypeScript
// google-oidc.service.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify, type JWTPayload } from 'jose';
import { createHash, randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';
import { RedisService } from '../redis/redis.service';

interface Discovery { issuer: string; authorization_endpoint: string; token_endpoint: string; jwks_uri: string; }

@Injectable()
export class GoogleOidcService {
  private discovery?: Discovery;
  private jwks?: ReturnType<typeof createRemoteJWKSet>;
  constructor(private cfg: ConfigService, private redis: RedisService) {}

  private async discover(): Promise<Discovery> {
    if (this.discovery) return this.discovery;
    const res = await fetch('https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration', { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) });
    this.discovery = (await res.json()) as Discovery;
    this.jwks = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(this.discovery.jwks_uri)); // caches keys, refetches on unknown kid
    return this.discovery;
  }

  async beginLogin(): Promise<{ url: string; flowId: string }> {
    const d = await this.discover();
    const flowId = randomBytes(16).toString('hex');
    const state = randomBytes(16).toString('base64url');
    const nonce = randomBytes(16).toString('base64url');
    const verifier = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
    const challenge = createHash('sha256').update(verifier).digest('base64url');
    await this.redis.client.set(`oidc:${flowId}`, JSON.stringify({ state, nonce, verifier }), { EX: 600 });
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
      client_id: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID'),
      redirect_uri: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI'),
      response_type: 'code', scope: 'openid email profile',
      state, nonce, code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
    });
    return { url: `${d.authorization_endpoint}?${params}`, flowId };
  }

  async completeLogin(flowId: string, code: string, state: string): Promise<JWTPayload> {
    const d = await this.discover();
    const raw = await this.redis.client.getDel(`oidc:${flowId}`);  // single use
    if (!raw) throw new UnauthorizedException('Login flow expired');
    const flow = JSON.parse(raw) as { state: string; nonce: string; verifier: string };
    if (flow.state !== state) throw new UnauthorizedException('State mismatch');

    const res = await fetch(d.token_endpoint, {
      method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
      body: new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'authorization_code', code, code_verifier: flow.verifier,
        client_id: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID'),
        client_secret: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET'),
        redirect_uri: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI'),
      }),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new UnauthorizedException('Token exchange failed');
    const { id_token } = (await res.json()) as { id_token: string };

    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(id_token, this.jwks!, {
      issuer: d.issuer, audience: this.cfg.getOrThrow('GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID'), clockTolerance: 30,
    });
    if (payload.nonce !== flow.nonce) throw new UnauthorizedException('Nonce mismatch');
    if (payload.email_verified !== true) throw new UnauthorizedException('Email not verified');
