    return payload; // sub, email, name, picture
  }
}

The controller stores flowId in a short-lived cookie before redirecting and reads it back on the callback, then hands the verified payload to the users service to upsert and to the auth service to issue the app's own tokens.

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE user_identities (
  user_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  provider      text NOT NULL,                  -- 'google', 'microsoft', 'okta:acme'
  provider_sub  text NOT NULL,                  -- stable subject from the id token
  email         citext,                         -- informational; may change
  linked_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (provider, provider_sub)          -- one identity maps to exactly one user
);
CREATE INDEX user_identities_user_idx ON user_identities (user_id);

-- Upsert on login:
INSERT INTO user_identities (user_id, provider, provider_sub, email)
VALUES ($1, 'google', $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (provider, provider_sub) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email
RETURNING user_id;

Production scenario

A B2C app where 70 percent of sign-ins come through Google and Apple. The OIDC callback handler runs at about 25 requests per second at peak; each does one token-exchange call to the provider (100 to 250 ms) and one upsert. Provider outages happen a few times a year; the app shows "Google sign-in is temporarily unavailable, use email" based on a circuit breaker around the token endpoint rather than letting users stare at a spinner. JWKS from Google rotates roughly daily; createRemoteJWKSet handles the refetch on unknown kid.

Failure scenario

An attacker created an account on a small identity provider using the victim's email address, which that provider did not verify. The app supported "Login with any OIDC provider" for enterprise customers and linked identities by email. The attacker logged in and landed in the victim's account. Root cause: linking by email plus trusting a provider's email claim without email_verified. Fix: link on (provider, sub); treat email from a new provider as unverified; require an explicit, authenticated linking step.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing or unchecked nonce: id token replay from another flow.
  • aud unchecked: an id token issued to another client accepted by yours.
  • Account linking by email: takeover through unverified emails.
  • Provider changes a user's sub (rare, but happens on tenant migration): keep a manual re-link path for support.
  • Discovery document fetched on every login: cache it (with a TTL of hours) and refresh in the background.
  • Login flow state stored in a cookie without integrity: attacker sets state themselves. Store it server-side (Redis) or sign the cookie.
  • Provider tokens used as your API's bearer tokens: coupling to the provider's rotation and outages, and no audience separation.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior engineer treats external identity providers as sources of identity, not as session mechanisms. After the id token is verified, the provider is out of the picture; the app runs its own sessions or tokens. They insist on (provider, sub) as the linking key, email_verified, and an explicit link flow. They also plan for the provider being down and for a customer's IT department moving from Google Workspace to Microsoft, which changes every sub.

Common mistakes

  • Accepting the access token instead of the id token as proof of login.
  • Skipping nonce because "we already have state".
  • Linking by email.
  • Hard-coding endpoints instead of using discovery.
  • Never rotating the client secret.

Interview questions

  1. Id token vs access token: what is each for, and which one proves login?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: id token, audience is the client, verified locally. Follow-up: why must your API not accept a Google access token?
  2. What does nonce prevent that state does not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: state protects the callback against CSRF; nonce binds the id token to the login request and prevents replay of an id token obtained elsewhere.
  3. How do you link an external identity to a local user safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: (issuer, sub), verified email, explicit link step.
  4. What is the discovery document and why does it matter operationally?

Practical exercise

Implement "Continue with Google" in a NestJS app without a Passport strategy, using discovery, PKCE, state, nonce, and jose. Acceptance criteria: an id token with the wrong aud or a mismatched nonce is rejected; a login flow older than 10 minutes fails; a second login by the same Google account maps to the same users row; a different Google account with the same email does not merge into the existing user.

40.6 Single Sign-On (SSO)

Concept

Single sign-on lets a user authenticate once at a central identity provider (IdP) and be recognised by many applications (service providers, SPs) without logging in again. In enterprise settings this is how an employee opens their email, the HR system, and your SaaS product with one corporate login. Two protocols dominate: SAML 2.0 (XML, older, deeply embedded in enterprise IT) and OIDC (JSON and JWT, newer, simpler, what everything new should use).

Why does it exist?

Companies do not want employees to have 40 passwords, and they need to disable a leaving employee's access everywhere with one click. From your side as a SaaS vendor, "supports SSO with our Okta / Azure AD" is a requirement on every enterprise procurement checklist. SSO also moves password policy, MFA and device checks to the IdP, where the customer's security team controls them.

Mental model

Imagine an airport with many airlines. You pass security once (the IdP), and each airline gate (an SP) accepts the boarding pass stamped by security instead of running its own screening. If security revokes your pass, every gate refuses you. Each gate still checks that the pass is for its flight (audience) and has not expired.

How it works

OIDC-based SSO is the flow from 40.5, with the corporate IdP (Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace, Keycloak) in the role of Google. The customer's admin registers your app as a client, gives you a client id and secret and the issuer URL; you store those per tenant and run discovery per issuer.

SAML-based SSO:

  1. The user hits your app; you look up their tenant (by email domain or a subdomain like acme.yourapp.com) and find the tenant's IdP metadata (entity id, SSO URL, signing certificate).
  2. You redirect the browser to the IdP with a signed AuthnRequest (SP-initiated) or the user starts from the IdP's app launcher (IdP-initiated).
  3. The IdP authenticates the user and posts a signed XML Response containing an Assertion (subject, attributes such as email and groups, conditions with audience and validity window) to your Assertion Consumer Service URL.
  4. You verify the signature against the tenant's certificate, check Audience, NotBefore / NotOnOrAfter, InResponseTo (SP-initiated only), and the Destination. You also reject an assertion id you have seen before (replay).
  5. You map attributes to a local user (by NameID, ideally a persistent id, and never by email alone across tenants), then create your own session or token pair. Session propagation ends here: your session is independent of the IdP's session.

Logout is the messy part. Single Logout (SLO) tries to end every SP session when the IdP session ends; in practice it is unreliable, and many vendors implement "logout ends our session; the IdP session is the customer's concern" and enforce short session lifetimes plus periodic re-authentication instead. When an employee is offboarded, the customer expects immediate loss of access; a short session lifetime (8 hours) or SCIM-based deprovisioning (the IdP calls your API to disable the user) is the honest way to deliver that.

SAML vs OIDC in enterprise:

Aspect SAML 2.0 OIDC
Format XML, signed with XML-DSig JSON, JWT
Complexity and known bugs XML signature wrapping, comment injection in NameID, canonicalisation issues Far smaller attack surface
Mobile and SPA support Poor Native
Enterprise IdP support Universal, including 15-year-old systems Universal in modern IdPs
Library in Node @node-saml/passport-saml openid-client, jose, passport-jwt
Choose when The customer only offers SAML Everything else

NestJS example

Per-tenant IdP configuration stored in PostgreSQL, selected at login time. The SAML strategy is created per request via @node-saml/passport-saml's MultiSamlStrategy, which calls getSamlOptions with the request so the tenant's settings can be loaded.

TypeScript
// saml.strategy.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { MultiSamlStrategy, type Profile, type SamlConfig } from '@node-saml/passport-saml';
import type { Request } from 'express';
import { TenantsService } from '../tenants/tenants.service';
import { SamlReplayCache } from './saml-replay.cache';

@Injectable()
export class SamlStrategy extends PassportStrategy(MultiSamlStrategy, 'saml') {
  constructor(private tenants: TenantsService, private replay: SamlReplayCache) {
    super(
      {
        passReqToCallback: true,
        getSamlOptions: async (req: Request, done: (err: Error | null, opts?: SamlConfig) => void) => {
          const tenant = await this.tenants.findBySlug(req.params.tenant);
          if (!tenant?.saml) return done(new UnauthorizedException('SSO not configured'));
          done(null, {
            entryPoint: tenant.saml.ssoUrl,                       // IdP SSO URL
            issuer: `https://app.example.com/saml/${tenant.slug}`, // our SP entity id
            callbackUrl: `https://app.example.com/saml/${tenant.slug}/acs`,
            idpCert: tenant.saml.certificatePem,                  // verify assertion signature
            audience: `https://app.example.com/saml/${tenant.slug}`,
            wantAssertionsSigned: true,
            acceptedClockSkewMs: 30_000,
            identifierFormat: 'urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent',
          });
        },
      },
      async (req: Request, profile: Profile | null, done: (err: Error | null, user?: unknown) => void) => {
        if (!profile?.nameID) return done(new UnauthorizedException());
        if (await this.replay.seen(profile.ID)) return done(new UnauthorizedException('Assertion replay'));
        const user = await this.tenants.resolveSsoUser(req.params.tenant, profile.nameID, profile);
        done(null, user);
      },
    );
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE tenant_sso (
  tenant_id        uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  protocol         text NOT NULL CHECK (protocol IN ('saml', 'oidc')),
  issuer           text,             -- OIDC issuer URL or SAML IdP entity id
  sso_url          text,             -- SAML only
  certificate_pem  text,             -- SAML signing cert
  client_id        text,             -- OIDC
  client_secret_enc bytea,           -- OIDC secret, encrypted with the app data key (22.16)
  email_domains    citext[] NOT NULL,-- 'acme.com' -> route login to this tenant
  enforce_sso      boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false, -- block password login for these domains
  updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX tenant_sso_domains_idx ON tenant_sso USING gin (email_domains);

Production scenario

A SaaS with 900 enterprise tenants: 600 on OIDC, 300 on SAML. Login volume is low (a few per second), but every failure is a support ticket from an IT admin. The team runs a self-service SSO setup page that validates metadata, tests a login, and shows the exact failed check ("audience mismatch: expected X, got Y"). They log every assertion's id, issuer and validity window (never the attributes) for 30 days, which resolves most "SSO stopped working" tickets in minutes (usually an expired IdP certificate).

Failure scenario

On a Monday morning 40 tenants could not log in. All used the same IdP vendor, which had rotated its signing certificate over the weekend and published the new one via metadata. The SaaS stored a static certificate per tenant. Fix: support IdP metadata URLs with periodic refresh, and accept both current and previous certificates for a grace period.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Expired or rotated IdP certificates.
  • Clock skew between IdP and SP causing NotBefore failures; allow 30 to 60 seconds.
  • Assertion replay: cache assertion ids until their NotOnOrAfter.
  • IdP-initiated SAML has no InResponseTo, which makes it easier to spoof; many teams disable it.
  • Email-domain routing with a personal email domain (gmail.com) listed by a careless admin, which would route every Gmail user to that tenant.
  • enforce_sso not applied to API keys and existing sessions, leaving a bypass.
  • Offboarding expectations: without SCIM or short sessions, a fired employee keeps access until session expiry.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never write SAML parsing themselves. They isolate SSO behind an interface ("resolve an external identity for tenant T into a local user") so the rest of the system does not know whether SAML or OIDC happened. They build the self-service setup page early because SSO support tickets otherwise consume an engineer permanently. They set session lifetimes with offboarding in mind and offer SCIM to customers who need instant deprovisioning.

Common mistakes

  • Mapping SSO users by email across tenants.
  • Trusting unsigned assertions or only the response signature but not the assertion signature.
  • No replay cache.
  • Static certificates with no rotation path.
  • Leaving password login enabled for domains that require SSO.

Interview questions

  1. SAML or OIDC for a new enterprise integration, and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: OIDC unless the customer cannot; smaller attack surface, better tooling.
  2. What checks must you perform on a SAML assertion?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: signature, audience, validity window, InResponseTo, destination, replay.
  3. How does session propagation work between the IdP and your app, and what happens on logout?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: your session is independent after login; SLO is unreliable; use short sessions and SCIM.
  4. A customer rotates their IdP certificate. What breaks and how do you prevent it?

Practical exercise

Add per-tenant OIDC SSO to a NestJS app. Store issuer, client id and encrypted secret per tenant; route POST /auth/sso/start by email domain; run discovery per issuer with a cached document; enforce enforce_sso by rejecting password login for those domains. Acceptance criteria: two tenants with different IdPs can log in concurrently; a user from tenant A cannot be resolved into tenant B even with the same email; discovery is fetched at most once per hour per issuer.

40.7 Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

Concept

Multi-factor authentication requires two or more independent proofs of identity from different categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, hardware key), something you are (fingerprint). A password plus a six-digit code from an authenticator app is the common form. A password plus a security question is not MFA; both are things you know.

The mainstream mechanisms, in rising order of strength: SMS codes (phishable, SIM-swappable, better than nothing), TOTP apps (phishable in real time but not SIM-swappable), and WebAuthn / passkeys (bound to the site's origin, so phishing does not work).

Why does it exist?

Passwords leak. Billions of email-and-password pairs from past breaches are traded and replayed against every login form on the internet (credential stuffing, 40.25). People reuse passwords. MFA makes a leaked password insufficient. For a backend engineer the question is not whether to offer MFA but how to make it mandatory for admins, available to everyone, and impossible to bypass through a side door (password reset, API keys, "remember this device").

Mental model

Imagine a bank vault that needs two keys turned at the same time, held by two different people. Stealing one key from one person's pocket is not enough. TOTP is a key that changes every 30 seconds; a passkey is a key that only fits the door of the real bank and will not turn in a fake door that looks the same.

How it works

TOTP (RFC 6238):

  1. During enrolment the server generates a random secret (20 bytes, base32-encoded) and shows it as a QR code (otpauth://totp/Example:alice@example.com?secret=...&issuer=Example). The authenticator app stores the secret.
  2. Both sides compute HMAC-SHA1(secret, floor(now / 30s)), truncate to 6 digits. The app shows the digits; the user types them.
  3. The server accepts the code for the current 30-second step and typically one step on each side (window of 1) to absorb clock drift, and records the last used step so the same code cannot be replayed within its window.
  4. The secret must be stored encrypted (40.16); a database leak that exposes TOTP secrets removes the second factor for everyone.

Backup codes: 8 to 10 single-use codes generated at enrolment, shown once, stored hashed like passwords (argon2 or at least a keyed hash; they are low-entropy compared to tokens). Each successful use deletes the code.

WebAuthn / passkeys: the browser creates a key pair per site. The public key is stored on your server; the private key stays in the device's secure hardware or the platform's password manager. Login is a challenge-response signature over a server-issued random challenge and the origin. A phishing site on a different origin cannot produce a valid signature. Use @simplewebauthn/server on the NestJS side; do not implement the CBOR and attestation parsing yourself.

Step-up authentication: the session or token records when and how the user authenticated (auth_time, amr: ["pwd","otp"]). Sensitive actions (change email, add a payout account, pay above a threshold) require a recent strong authentication, for example MFA within the last 5 minutes; otherwise the API returns 403 with a reason code and the client prompts for the second factor again.

Rate limiting OTP attempts: a 6-digit code has one million possibilities; with a window of 3 steps, an attacker who can make 300,000 guesses has a 90 percent chance. Limit to about 5 attempts per user per 15 minutes, lock the MFA step after that, and alert.

Practical example

A ride-booking company's driver-payout portal. Every finance user must enrol TOTP or a passkey; admins cannot disable MFA for themselves. Changing a driver's bank account requires MFA within the last 5 minutes (step-up). Backup codes exist for lost phones, and using one triggers an email and an audit entry. OTP verification is limited to 5 attempts per 15 minutes per user; the sixth attempt locks the MFA step for an hour and pages nobody but shows on the security dashboard.

NestJS example

Enrolment, verification with replay protection and rate limiting, using otplib.

TypeScript
// mfa.service.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException, HttpException, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { authenticator } from 'otplib';
import * as argon2 from 'argon2';
import { randomInt } from 'node:crypto';
import { UserMfa } from './user-mfa.entity';
import { FieldCipher } from '../crypto/field-cipher';   // AES-256-GCM wrapper from 22.16
import { RedisService } from '../redis/redis.service';

@Injectable()
export class MfaService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(UserMfa) private mfa: Repository<UserMfa>,
    private cipher: FieldCipher,
    private redis: RedisService,
  ) {
    authenticator.options = { window: 1, step: 30 }; // accept previous/next 30 s step
  }

  async beginEnrolment(userId: string, email: string) {
    const secret = authenticator.generateSecret(20);              // base32, 160 bits
    await this.mfa.upsert({ userId, totpSecretEnc: this.cipher.encrypt(secret), confirmed: false }, ['userId']);
    return { otpauthUrl: authenticator.keyuri(email, 'Example', secret) }; // render as QR on the client
  }

  async confirmEnrolment(userId: string, code: string) {
    const row = await this.mfa.findOneByOrFail({ userId });
    if (!this.verifyTotp(this.cipher.decrypt(row.totpSecretEnc), code, row)) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid code');
    const backupCodes = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => String(randomInt(0, 1e8)).padStart(8, '0'));
    row.backupCodeHashes = await Promise.all(backupCodes.map((c) => argon2.hash(c)));
    row.confirmed = true;
    await this.mfa.save(row);
    return { backupCodes }; // shown exactly once
  }

  async verify(userId: string, code: string): Promise<void> {
    const key = `mfa:attempts:${userId}`;
    const attempts = await this.redis.client.incr(key);
    if (attempts === 1) await this.redis.client.expire(key, 900);
    if (attempts > 5) throw new HttpException('Too many attempts', HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS);

    const row = await this.mfa.findOneByOrFail({ userId });
    const secret = this.cipher.decrypt(row.totpSecretEnc);
    if (/^\d{6}$/.test(code) && this.verifyTotp(secret, code, row)) {
      row.lastTotpStep = Math.floor(Date.now() / 30_000);          // replay protection
      await this.mfa.save(row);
      await this.redis.client.del(key);
      return;
    }
    if (await this.consumeBackupCode(row, code)) { await this.redis.client.del(key); return; }
    throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid code');
  }

  private verifyTotp(secret: string, code: string, row: UserMfa): boolean {
    const step = Math.floor(Date.now() / 30_000);
    if (row.lastTotpStep !== null && step <= row.lastTotpStep) return false; // code for this step already used
    return authenticator.verify({ token: code, secret });
  }

  private async consumeBackupCode(row: UserMfa, code: string): Promise<boolean> {
    for (const [i, hash] of row.backupCodeHashes.entries()) {
      if (await argon2.verify(hash, code)) {
        row.backupCodeHashes.splice(i, 1);          // single use
        await this.mfa.save(row);
        return true;
      }
    }
    return false;
  }
}

A step-up guard that requires a recent strong authentication, read from claims placed in the access token at MFA time:

TypeScript
// recent-mfa.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable, SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';

export const RequireRecentMfa = (maxAgeSeconds = 300) => SetMetadata('recent_mfa', maxAgeSeconds);

@Injectable()
export class RecentMfaGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector) {}
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const maxAge = this.reflector.get<number>('recent_mfa', ctx.getHandler());
    if (maxAge === undefined) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { amr: string[]; authTime: number };
    const strong = user.amr.includes('otp') || user.amr.includes('hwk');
    const fresh = Date.now() / 1000 - user.authTime <= maxAge;
    if (!strong || !fresh) throw new ForbiddenException({ code: 'STEP_UP_REQUIRED', maxAge });
    return true;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE user_mfa (
  user_id            uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  totp_secret_enc    bytea NOT NULL,          -- AES-256-GCM: iv || ciphertext || tag, key id prefixed
  confirmed          boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  last_totp_step     bigint,                  -- replay protection
  backup_code_hashes text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  enrolled_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE webauthn_credentials (
  id               bytea PRIMARY KEY,         -- credential id from the authenticator
  user_id          uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  public_key       bytea NOT NULL,
  sign_count       bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, -- clone detection: must increase
  transports       text[],
  name             text,                      -- "MacBook Touch ID"
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_used_at     timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX webauthn_user_idx ON webauthn_credentials (user_id);

Production scenario

A fintech app with 2 million users, 35 percent enrolled in TOTP and 10 percent in passkeys. MFA verifications run at about 60 per second at peak. TOTP verification is microseconds; the cost is the decrypt of the secret and the row update. Backup-code verification with argon2 costs 50 ms per code hash checked, so up to 10 hashes per attempt; it is rare enough not to matter. The security dashboard tracks MFA failure rate per user (attack indicator), backup-code usage (lost phones), and step-up prompts per sensitive action.

Failure scenario

Support received a wave of "my code is always wrong" tickets after a deploy. The new pods had a clock 90 seconds behind; with a TOTP window of one step (30 seconds each side) every code failed. NTP on the node image had been disabled by a hardening script. Clock skew alerting (compare each pod's clock to an NTP source and alert over 5 seconds) was added the same day.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Clock drift on server or phone; window of 1 step plus NTP.
  • TOTP code replay within the window; store last_totp_step.
  • Brute force on the code; rate limit per user and per IP; lock the MFA step.
  • Backup codes stored in plaintext or shown more than once.
  • MFA bypass through password reset: reset must not disable MFA; recovery needs a separate, slower path with identity verification.
  • MFA bypass through API keys or long-lived sessions created before enrolment.
  • "Remember this device" cookies that never expire or are not bound to the user.
  • Secret leak via a database dump if secrets are not encrypted.
  • WebAuthn sign_count going backwards indicates a cloned authenticator; treat as compromise.
  • Users losing both phone and backup codes: a recovery process with human verification and a waiting period, or you have built a lockout machine.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make MFA mandatory for staff and admins first, because those accounts have the widest blast radius. They prefer passkeys because phishing resistance removes an entire class of incident, and they keep TOTP for users without passkey support. They design step-up from the start by putting amr and auth_time in the token, because retrofitting "prove it again for this action" is expensive. And they audit every alternative path into an account (reset, recovery, API keys, SSO) with the question: does this path skip the second factor?

Common mistakes

  • SMS as the only second factor for high-value accounts.
  • No rate limit on the OTP endpoint.
  • Not recording the last used TOTP step.
  • Allowing enrolment without confirming the first code (locks the user out).
  • Storing the TOTP secret in plaintext next to the password hash.
  • Letting a password reset remove MFA.

Interview questions

  1. How does TOTP work and why does a window of 1 exist?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: HMAC of a time counter; window absorbs clock drift. Follow-up: how do you stop replay inside the window?
  2. Why are passkeys phishing-resistant when TOTP is not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the signature covers the origin.
  3. Design step-up authentication for payouts.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: amr and auth_time in the token; a guard enforcing freshness; a client flow to re-prompt.
  4. What is the attack if the OTP endpoint has no rate limit? Do the arithmetic.
  5. How would you store backup codes and why?
  6. Enumerate the ways MFA can be bypassed in a typical app.

Practical exercise

Add TOTP MFA to a NestJS auth module: enrolment with QR, confirmation, verification with replay protection and a 5-per-15-minutes limit, backup codes stored with argon2, and a @RequireRecentMfa(300) guard on PATCH /me/payout-account. Acceptance criteria: the same code is rejected on second use; the sixth wrong attempt returns 429; the payout endpoint returns 403 with STEP_UP_REQUIRED for a token whose auth_time is 10 minutes old; a database dump contains no readable TOTP secret.

40.8 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Concept

RBAC assigns users to roles (customer, support, warehouse, admin) and grants permissions to roles rather than to users. A request is allowed when the caller holds a role that is permitted for that action. It is the simplest authorization model that scales past a handful of users and it covers the majority of business applications.

Why does it exist?

Granting permissions per user does not scale and is impossible to audit: "who can refund orders?" becomes a query over thousands of rows that nobody trusts. Roles turn that into "the support and admin roles can refund", which a product manager can read and a compliance auditor can sign off on. Roles also make onboarding and offboarding a single change.

Mental model

Imagine the badges from 40.1 again, but now the badge says "Warehouse Staff" rather than listing 40 doors. Each door has a sign: "Warehouse Staff, Managers". The door does not know your name; it knows your role. Adding a new warehouse worker means printing one badge, not reprogramming 40 doors.

How it works

  1. A roles table defines the roles. A user_roles table maps users to roles (many-to-many; a user can be both support and warehouse).
  2. At login, the user's roles are loaded and either placed in the token as a claim or cached.
  3. Each route declares the roles it requires with a decorator, @Roles('admin', 'support').
  4. A RolesGuard runs after the authentication guard, reads the required roles through Reflector, compares with the principal's roles, and returns true or throws 403.
  5. Optional role hierarchy: admin implies support implies customer. Implement it by expanding roles at token-issue time (admin becomes ["admin","support","customer"]) or by a lookup table in the guard. Expansion at issue time keeps the guard trivial.
  6. Roles in the JWT vs from the database on each request: the token is fast and stateless but stale until refresh; the database is always current and costs a query (or a Redis read) per request. A common compromise is roles in the token plus a roles_version claim; the guard compares it to a cached per-user version in Redis and rejects the token when a role change has bumped the version.

Practical example

An e-commerce back office. customer can read their own orders. support can read any order and issue refunds up to 100 units of currency. support_lead can issue any refund. warehouse can change fulfilment status. admin can manage users and roles. The refund limit is not RBAC (it is an attribute check, 40.9), but which roles may refund at all is pure RBAC and lives in the guard.

NestJS example

The decorator and guard pair, with hierarchy expansion done once at token issue time.

TypeScript
// roles.decorator.ts
import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
export const ROLES_KEY = 'roles';
export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata(ROLES_KEY, roles);

// roles.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ROLES_KEY } from './roles.decorator';

@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    // Method-level @Roles overrides class-level; no metadata means "any authenticated user".
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(ROLES_KEY, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]);
    if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { roles?: string[] } | undefined;
    if (!user) throw new ForbiddenException(); // JwtAuthGuard should have run first
    const ok = required.some((r) => user.roles?.includes(r));
    if (!ok) throw new ForbiddenException('Insufficient role');
    return true;
  }
}
TypeScript
// role-hierarchy.ts: expand roles when issuing the token
const IMPLIES: Record<string, string[]> = {
  admin: ['support_lead', 'warehouse'],
  support_lead: ['support'],
  support: ['customer'],
};
export function expandRoles(direct: string[]): string[] {
  const out = new Set<string>();
  const stack = [...direct];
  while (stack.length) {
    const r = stack.pop()!;
    if (out.has(r)) continue;
    out.add(r);
    stack.push(...(IMPLIES[r] ?? []));
  }
  return [...out];
}
TypeScript
// refunds.controller.ts
@Controller('refunds')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard)
export class RefundsController {
  @Post()
  @Roles('support')             // support_lead and admin inherit this via expansion
  create(@Body() dto: CreateRefundDto, @CurrentUser() user: AuthenticatedUser) {
    return this.refunds.create(dto, user); // service enforces the amount limit per role
  }
}

Register the guards globally so a forgotten @UseGuards cannot open a route (with a @Public() decorator for the few open endpoints; full code in 40.37):

TypeScript
// app.module.ts
providers: [
  { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: JwtAuthGuard },
  { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: RolesGuard },   // order of registration is execution order
]

Role freshness without a database hit per request: bump a per-user version on role change and compare in the strategy.

TypeScript
// in JwtStrategy.validate
const currentVersion = await this.redis.client.get(`user:${payload.sub}:roles_v`); // ~0.3 ms
if (currentVersion && Number(currentVersion) !== payload.roles_v) {
  throw new UnauthorizedException('Roles changed, please refresh'); // client refreshes, gets new roles
}

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE roles (
  id          smallint PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  description text
);

CREATE TABLE role_hierarchy (
  parent_role_id smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id),
  child_role_id  smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (parent_role_id, child_role_id)
);

CREATE TABLE user_roles (
  user_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role_id    smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id),
  granted_by uuid REFERENCES users(id),
  granted_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id)
);
CREATE INDEX user_roles_role_idx ON user_roles (role_id);  -- "who has admin?"

-- Effective roles for a user, expanding the hierarchy:
WITH RECURSIVE eff AS (
  SELECT r.id, r.name FROM user_roles ur JOIN roles r ON r.id = ur.role_id WHERE ur.user_id = $1
  UNION
  SELECT c.id, c.name FROM eff JOIN role_hierarchy h ON h.parent_role_id = eff.id JOIN roles c ON c.id = h.child_role_id
)
SELECT array_agg(DISTINCT name) FROM eff;

Role changes should be audited (40.35): who granted admin to whom and when is one of the first questions after an incident.

TypeORM example

TypeScript
@Entity('users')
export class User {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column({ type: 'citext', unique: true }) email: string;
  @Column() passwordHash: string;
  @ManyToMany(() => Role, { eager: false })
  @JoinTable({ name: 'user_roles', joinColumn: { name: 'user_id' }, inverseJoinColumn: { name: 'role_id' } })
  roles: Role[];
  roleNames(): string[] { return this.roles.map((r) => r.name); }
}

// Load roles only at login/refresh, not on every request:
const user = await usersRepo.findOne({ where: { email }, relations: { roles: true } });

Sequelize example

TypeScript
User.belongsToMany(Role, { through: 'user_roles', foreignKey: 'user_id', otherKey: 'role_id' });
Role.belongsToMany(User, { through: 'user_roles', foreignKey: 'role_id', otherKey: 'user_id' });

const user = await User.findOne({ where: { email }, include: [{ model: Role, attributes: ['name'] }] });
const roles = expandRoles(user.Roles.map((r) => r.name));

Production scenario

A SaaS with 300,000 users and 9 roles. Roles ride in the access token; a Redis roles_v check adds 0.3 ms per request and lets an admin demotion take effect within one request. Role grants are about 200 per day, all audited. The user_roles table is small (400,000 rows) and fully cached. The team reviews the "who has admin" list monthly; it is a single indexed query.

Failure scenario

A developer added @UseGuards(RolesGuard) to a new admin controller but forgot JwtAuthGuard. RolesGuard saw request.user undefined and, in an early version of the code, returned true when no user was present ("nothing to check"). Anonymous requests reached admin endpoints for six days. The fix: RolesGuard throws when request.user is missing and required roles exist, and both guards are registered globally so per-controller omission is impossible.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Role removed but token still carries it until refresh; use the version check.
  • Guard order: RolesGuard before JwtAuthGuard sees no user. Register globally in the correct order.
  • Role names as free strings with typos (suport); use an enum or constants and a test that every @Roles value exists in the roles table.
  • Hierarchy cycles (a implies b implies a); guard against them in the expansion code and with a check on insert.
  • Role explosion: 60 roles each slightly different means you need permissions (40.10), not more roles.
  • Roles used for ownership decisions ("support can read all orders") without regional or tenant limits; that is ABAC territory.
  • Cross-tenant admin: an admin role must be scoped to a tenant unless it is explicitly a platform role.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start with RBAC because it is understandable, and they move to permissions or ABAC only when roles stop describing the rules. They keep the guard tiny and put anything that needs data in the service. They register guards globally, deny by default, and write a test that walks every route and asserts it is either @Public() or guarded. They put role changes in the audit log and give security a one-click "who has this role" report.

Common mistakes

  • Roles checked only in the controller, so a job or another service path bypasses them.
  • Role in the request body ({ role: 'admin' } on signup) accepted by a DTO without a whitelist (40.24).
  • Hard-coded if (user.email === 'ceo@example.com') instead of a role.
  • Treating admin as global in a multi-tenant system.
  • No audit of role grants.

Interview questions

  1. Roles in the JWT or from the database on each request?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: token plus version check, or DB with cache; tradeoff freshness vs cost.
  2. How does Reflector work in a NestJS guard and what does getAllAndOverride do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: reads metadata set by SetMetadata; method-level wins over class-level.
  3. Implement role hierarchy; where would you expand it and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: at token issue time or via recursive CTE; keep guard trivial.
  4. When does RBAC stop being enough?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when decisions depend on attributes of the resource or context.
  5. How do you make sure no route is accidentally unprotected?

Practical exercise

Implement @Roles(), RolesGuard, hierarchy expansion, and a Redis roles_v freshness check. Write a test that enumerates all routes via the NestJS DiscoveryService (from @nestjs/core) and asserts each is either marked @Public() or reachable only through the global guards. Acceptance criteria: demoting a user from admin causes their existing token to fail on the very next request; a route without @Roles still requires authentication; a RolesGuard running with no request.user throws rather than allowing.

40.9 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

Concept

ABAC decides access by evaluating policies over attributes of the subject (the user: id, roles, region, department), the resource (the order: owner, region, status, amount), the action (read, refund), and the environment (time, IP, MFA freshness). A policy reads like a sentence: "a user can view an order if they own it, or if they are support in the same region as the order." RBAC is a special case of ABAC where the only attribute is the role.

Why does it exist?

Real rules have conditions. "Support can refund" is a role. "Support can refund up to 100, support leads up to 1,000, and nobody can refund an order older than 90 days" is not something roles express without an explosion of support_under_100_recent pseudo-roles. ABAC lets you write the condition once, in one place, and evaluate it wherever the decision is needed: in a guard, in a service, and in the query that lists what the user may see.

Mental model

Imagine a bouncer with a rule card instead of a guest list. The card says: "Admit if on the list, or if over 21 and with a member, or if staff and it is after closing time." The bouncer looks at the person (subject attributes), the door (resource), what they want (enter, or enter the VIP room), and the clock (environment), and applies the rules. Adding a rule is editing the card, not printing new badges.

How it works

  1. Define abilities per subject: a function that takes the user and returns the set of (action, subject type, conditions) triples they are allowed. CASL (@casl/ability) is the standard TypeScript library for this and is what the NestJS documentation uses.
  2. Check an ability against a specific resource instance: ability.can('read', order) evaluates the conditions (owner id, region) against the order's fields.
  3. Convert the same conditions into a database filter for list endpoints so that users only see what they may see, without loading everything and filtering in memory. CASL provides @casl/ability/extra helpers for this; for SQL you typically translate conditions into a where object.
  4. Use a policy guard for route-level checks that need only the user and the subject type ("may this user create refunds at all?") and keep instance-level checks in the service where the row is loaded.

Practical example

Food delivery. Rules:

  • A customer can read an order if order.customerId === user.id.
  • A restaurant staff member can read and update an order if order.restaurantId is in user.restaurantIds and order.status is not delivered.
  • A support agent can read any order in order.region === user.region, and can refund if order.total <= 100 or the agent has the support_lead role.
  • Nobody can refund an order with createdAt older than 90 days.

Every one of these is a condition over attributes. All of them can be evaluated against a loaded order, and all except the date rule can be pushed down into a WHERE clause for listings.

NestJS example

Ability definition with CASL, then a service check and a list query derived from the same rules.

TypeScript
// ability.factory.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AbilityBuilder, createMongoAbility, MongoAbility, InferSubjects } from '@casl/ability';
import { Order } from '../orders/order.entity';
import { AuthenticatedUser } from '../auth/authenticated-user';

export type Action = 'read' | 'update' | 'refund' | 'manage';
export type Subjects = InferSubjects<typeof Order> | 'all';
export type AppAbility = MongoAbility<[Action, Subjects]>;

@Injectable()
export class AbilityFactory {
  define(user: AuthenticatedUser): AppAbility {
    const { can, cannot, build } = new AbilityBuilder<AppAbility>(createMongoAbility);

    can('read', Order, { customerId: user.id });                                   // owner
    if (user.restaurantIds?.length) {
      can(['read', 'update'], Order, { restaurantId: { $in: user.restaurantIds }, status: { $ne: 'delivered' } });
    }
    if (user.roles.includes('support')) {
      can('read', Order, { region: user.region });
      can('refund', Order, { region: user.region, total: { $lte: 100 } });
    }
    if (user.roles.includes('support_lead')) can('refund', Order, { region: user.region });
    if (user.roles.includes('admin')) can('manage', 'all');

    // Absolute rule: cannot() after can() wins.
    const ninetyDaysAgo = new Date(Date.now() - 90 * 86_400_000);
    cannot('refund', Order, { createdAt: { $lt: ninetyDaysAgo } }).because('Order older than 90 days');

    return build({ detectSubjectType: (obj) => obj.constructor as typeof Order });
  }
}
TypeScript
// orders.service.ts (instance check + list filter from the same rules)
import { ForbiddenError, subject } from '@casl/ability';
import { rulesToQuery } from '@casl/ability/extra';

async refund(orderId: string, amount: number, user: AuthenticatedUser) {
  const order = await this.repo.findOneByOrFail({ id: orderId });
  const ability = this.abilities.define(user);
  ForbiddenError.from(ability).throwUnlessCan('refund', subject('Order', order)); // throws with the reason
  return this.refunds.execute(order, amount, user);
}

async listVisible(user: AuthenticatedUser) {
  const ability = this.abilities.define(user);
  const q = rulesToQuery(ability, 'read', 'Order', (rule) => rule.conditions ?? {}); // { $or: [...] } or null
  if (q === null) return [];                                   // no rule allows read at all
  const where = toTypeOrmWhere(q);                             // small translator: $in -> In(), $ne -> Not(), $or -> array
  return this.repo.find({ where, take: 50, order: { createdAt: 'DESC' } });
}

A route-level policy guard for checks that only need the subject type:

TypeScript
// policies.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, Injectable, SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AbilityFactory, AppAbility } from './ability.factory';

type PolicyHandler = (ability: AppAbility) => boolean;
export const CheckPolicies = (...handlers: PolicyHandler[]) => SetMetadata('policies', handlers);

@Injectable()
export class PoliciesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector, private abilities: AbilityFactory) {}
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const handlers = this.reflector.get<PolicyHandler[]>('policies', ctx.getHandler()) ?? [];
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user;
    const ability = this.abilities.define(user);
    return handlers.every((h) => h(ability));
  }
}
// @CheckPolicies((a) => a.can('refund', 'Order'))  -> "may refund some orders"; instance check still in service

PostgreSQL example

The same policy as a database view for reporting, and as an index that keeps the support listing fast:

SQL
-- Support agents list orders by region, newest first: index matches the filter and sort.
CREATE INDEX orders_region_created_idx ON orders (region, created_at DESC);

-- Owner listing:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total, status FROM orders
WHERE region = 'eu-west' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
Text
Limit  (cost=0.56..12.31 rows=50 width=44) (actual time=0.041..0.112 rows=50 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_region_created_idx on orders
        (cost=0.56..48210.11 rows=205000 width=44) (actual time=0.039..0.101 rows=50 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (region = 'eu-west'::text)
        Buffers: shared hit=7
Execution Time: 0.140 ms

Production scenario

A marketplace support tool serving 1,200 agents across 6 regions, 40 million orders. Every order view runs ability.can on the loaded row (microseconds). Listings translate CASL conditions into indexed WHERE clauses; the p95 for a region listing is 8 ms. Policy changes (raise the refund limit to 150) are one line in the ability factory, reviewed by security and deployed like code. The team logs every ForbiddenError with the rule reason so product can see which policies are being hit.

Failure scenario

An agent in the EU region could refund orders in the US region. The listing was correctly filtered by region, but the refund endpoint took an order id and only checked user.roles.includes('support'). The ABAC rule existed in the ability factory; the refund service simply did not call it. The fix was to route every mutation through throwUnlessCan and to add a test that constructs a user from region A and an order from region B for each action.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rules defined but not applied in a code path (the failure above). Centralise enforcement.
  • Conditions that cannot be translated to SQL (computed fields), forcing in-memory filtering; keep policy attributes as stored columns.
  • Time-based rules evaluated with the server clock; clock skew and time zones.
  • Attribute staleness: user.region from the token is stale after a transfer; version the claims (40.8).
  • Performance: an ability with hundreds of rules per request; cache the built ability per request, not per user across requests.
  • cannot rules and rule ordering surprises; test the precedence explicitly.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They adopt ABAC when a rule cannot be said with roles alone, and they keep the policy in one file per domain so it can be reviewed like a contract. They insist that the same rules drive both the instance check and the list query, because two implementations of the same rule drift. They resist externalising policy to a general-purpose engine (OPA, Cedar) until multiple services need to share it, because a network call per authorization decision is a real cost and a new failure mode.

Common mistakes

  • Evaluating policy only in listings and not in mutations.
  • Encoding policy in scattered if statements across services.
  • Loading all rows and filtering in memory.
  • Putting mutable attributes in the token without versioning.

Interview questions

  1. When is ABAC needed over RBAC? Give a rule that RBAC cannot express.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: any condition over resource attributes, like region or amount.
  2. How do you keep list filtering and instance checks consistent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: derive both from one rule set (CASL rulesToQuery).
  3. Where do policy decisions belong: gateway, guard, service, database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: type-level in guard, instance-level in service, tenant-level in DB as a backstop.
  4. What is the cost of an external policy engine per request?

Practical exercise

Implement the food-delivery rules above with CASL. Acceptance criteria: unit tests cover each rule with positive and negative cases, including the 90-day cannot; the listing endpoint for a support agent returns only their region and uses an index (verify with EXPLAIN); the refund endpoint rejects a cross-region refund with the CASL reason in the 403 body.

40.10 Permissions, Scopes and Tenant Isolation

Concept

Permissions are fine-grained named capabilities (orders.read, orders.refund, users.invite) that roles bundle. Scopes are the same idea applied to third-party clients through OAuth (40.4): which capabilities this app was granted for this user. Least privilege is the principle behind both: grant only what is needed for the task, for as short a time as possible. Tenant isolation is the specific and unforgiving case of least privilege in multi-tenant SaaS: a query that forgets the tenant filter leaks another company's data.

Why does it exist?

Roles get coarse. Product wants a "billing-only" role, then a "billing read-only" role, then "billing read-only except invoices". A permissions table lets roles be composed from small capabilities without changing code. Scopes exist because third-party apps must be bounded independently of the user's own rights. Tenant isolation exists because the single most damaging class of SaaS bug is cross-tenant data exposure, and it is caused by an ordinary missing WHERE.

Mental model

Imagine an apartment building (the SaaS) with many tenants (customers). Each apartment has its own lock (tenant filter). A cleaner (support role) has a master key for their floor only (permission scoped by tenant). A delivery app (third-party client) is given a code that opens only the parcel locker (scope). And the building has a second safeguard: even with the wrong key, the doors on floor 7 will not open for a keycard registered to floor 3 (row-level security).

How it works

Permissions:

  1. permissions table with stable string keys. role_permissions maps roles to permissions. Effective permissions of a user are the union over their roles.
  2. Guards check permissions rather than roles: @RequirePermission('orders.refund'). Roles become configuration; code references permissions.
  3. Effective permissions are computed at login and cached (Redis, 60 seconds) or placed in the token as a compact form (a perm_v version plus a role list; never 200 strings).

Scopes: enforced by the ScopesGuard from 40.4. The effective right is the intersection of the client's scopes and the user's permissions.

Tenant isolation:

  1. The tenant id comes from the verified token (or from the API key's record), never from the URL or body.
  2. Every repository method receives the tenant id and includes it in the WHERE clause. Composite indexes lead with tenant_id.
  3. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) is enabled on tenant tables. Before running queries, the app sets SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '<uuid>' inside the transaction, and the policy compares each row's tenant_id with that setting. A query that forgets the filter returns only the current tenant's rows. A query with no tenant set returns nothing.
  4. The application's database user is not the table owner and has no BYPASSRLS, otherwise RLS is silently skipped.

Practical example

A B2B invoicing SaaS with 40,000 tenants in one PostgreSQL database. Every table with customer data has a tenant_id uuid NOT NULL column. The JwtStrategy puts tenantId on request.user. A request-scoped TenantContext carries it into repositories. A TypeORM subscriber or a wrapping withTenant() helper opens a transaction, runs SET LOCAL app.tenant_id, and executes the unit of work. RLS policies exist on every tenant table, and a CI test runs each repository method with RLS enabled for tenant A and asserts that tenant B's rows never appear.

NestJS example

A helper that binds the tenant to the transaction, so RLS applies to everything inside it, and a repository that also filters explicitly (belt and braces).

TypeScript
// tenant-db.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class TenantDb {
  constructor(private ds: DataSource) {}

  // Everything inside `work` runs with RLS bound to the tenant.
  async withTenant<T>(tenantId: string, work: (em: EntityManager) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      // SET LOCAL is transaction-scoped: safe with PgBouncer transaction pooling, resets on commit.
      // set_config with parameters avoids string interpolation of the tenant id.
      await em.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)`, [tenantId]);
      return work(em);
    });
  }
}
TypeScript
// invoices.repository.ts
@Injectable()
export class InvoicesRepository {
  constructor(private db: TenantDb) {}

  findForCustomer(tenantId: string, customerId: string) {
    return this.db.withTenant(tenantId, (em) =>
      em.getRepository(Invoice).find({
        where: { tenantId, customerId },          // explicit filter uses the composite index
        order: { issuedAt: 'DESC' }, take: 100,
      }),
    );
  }
}
TypeScript
// permission.guard.ts
export const RequirePermission = (...perms: string[]) => SetMetadata('permissions', perms);

@Injectable()
export class PermissionGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector, private perms: PermissionsService) {}
  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>('permissions', [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]) ?? [];
    if (!required.length) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as AuthenticatedUser;
    const effective = await this.perms.effectiveFor(user.id, user.tenantId); // Redis-cached 60 s, invalidated on role change
    if (!required.every((p) => effective.has(p))) throw new ForbiddenException(`Missing permission ${required.join(', ')}`);
    return true;
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Permissions tables, RLS policy, and the least-privilege database user.

SQL
CREATE TABLE permissions (
  key         text PRIMARY KEY,           -- 'orders.refund'
  description text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE role_permissions (
  role_id        smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  permission_key text NOT NULL REFERENCES permissions(key) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (role_id, permission_key)
);

-- Effective permissions of a user (cached by the app):
SELECT DISTINCT rp.permission_key
FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_permissions rp ON rp.role_id = ur.role_id
WHERE ur.user_id = $1;
SQL
-- Tenant isolation with RLS.
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL,
  total_cents bigint NOT NULL,
  issued_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX invoices_tenant_customer_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, customer_id, issued_at DESC);

ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;    -- apply even to the table owner

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)         -- reads, updates, deletes
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);   -- inserts and updated rows

-- Least-privilege application role: no ownership, no BYPASSRLS, only needed grants.
CREATE ROLE app_api LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOBYPASSRLS;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON invoices TO app_api;
REVOKE DELETE ON invoices FROM app_api;                                    -- soft delete only
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_api;

current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) returns NULL (rather than erroring) when the setting is missing; NULL = anything is not true, so a query with no tenant bound returns zero rows. That is the fail-closed behaviour you want.

Check that the plan still uses the index with RLS on: the policy predicate becomes an extra filter, and because the query also filters on tenant_id explicitly, the index scan is unchanged.

Text
Index Scan using invoices_tenant_customer_idx on invoices
  Index Cond: ((tenant_id = '9a1f...'::uuid) AND (customer_id = '4c2e...'::uuid))
  Filter: (tenant_id = (current_setting('app.tenant_id'::text, true))::uuid)

Sequelize example

TypeScript
await sequelize.transaction(async (t) => {
  await sequelize.query(`SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', :tenantId, true)`, {
    replacements: { tenantId }, transaction: t,
  });
  return Invoice.findAll({ where: { tenantId, customerId }, order: [['issuedAt', 'DESC']], limit: 100, transaction: t });
});

Production scenario

The invoicing SaaS runs 2,500 requests per second against a 1.8 TB database; RLS adds under 2 percent CPU because every query already filters on tenant_id. The team measured a synthetic "forgotten filter" query with RLS on: it returned the correct tenant's rows only, at a cost of a sequential scan; RLS saved the data, and the slow-query alert caught the bug. Permission caches are invalidated by publishing a Redis message on role change; propagation takes under a second.

Failure scenario

A reporting endpoint used a raw query written by a data engineer: SELECT ... FROM invoices WHERE issued_at > $1. No tenant filter. It ran through a separate "analytics" database user that had been created as the table owner for convenience, so RLS did not apply. The endpoint leaked revenue figures across tenants for 3 hours before a customer noticed unfamiliar customer names in an export. Two fixes: the analytics user was recreated without ownership and with NOBYPASSRLS, and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY was set on every tenant table.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RLS bypassed by the table owner or a superuser connection; enforce FORCE and least-privilege roles.
  • SET instead of SET LOCAL with a connection pool: the tenant setting leaks to the next request on the same connection. Always SET LOCAL inside a transaction, or set_config(..., true).
  • Background jobs with no tenant context querying tenant tables: bind the tenant explicitly per job.
  • Cross-tenant admin tools that need to see everything: a separate role with a BYPASSRLS policy exception, heavily audited, never used by the API.
  • Permission cache stale after a role change; invalidate on write.
  • Scope and permission both required: checking only one of them is a bug.
  • Tenant id taken from the URL for "convenience" and not compared to the token's tenant.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat tenant isolation as a property to be proven, not hoped for: token-derived tenant id, repository-level filtering, RLS, a least-privilege DB user, and a test suite that tries to cross tenants for every repository method. They accept the small RLS overhead as the cheapest insurance the company will ever buy. They grant permissions, not roles, in code, so that reorganising roles is a data change. And they ask, for every new database user or IAM role: what is the minimum this needs?

Common mistakes

  • Trusting tenantId from the request.
  • Creating the app's DB user as the table owner.
  • Using SET without LOCAL on pooled connections.
  • Not indexing with tenant_id first.
  • Putting hundreds of permission strings in the token.

Interview questions

  1. How do you guarantee tenant isolation in a shared-database SaaS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: token-derived tenant, repository filter, RLS with SET LOCAL, least-privilege user, tests.
  2. Why does RLS silently not apply for some connections?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: table owner, superuser, or BYPASSRLS; fix with FORCE and roles.
  3. What is the difference between a permission and a scope?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: user capability vs client-app grant; both apply.
  4. What breaks if you use SET instead of SET LOCAL behind PgBouncer?
  5. How do you keep a permission cache fresh?

Practical exercise

Enable RLS on orders and invoices, create an app_api role without ownership, and implement withTenant. Write a test that inserts rows for two tenants and runs every repository method as tenant A. Acceptance criteria: no method returns tenant B rows; a deliberately unfiltered raw query inside withTenant still returns only tenant A rows; a query outside withTenant returns zero rows; EXPLAIN shows the composite index is used.

40.11 API Keys for Machine Clients

Concept

An API key is a long random secret that identifies and authenticates a machine client: a partner's server, a CI pipeline, an internal cron job. Unlike OAuth tokens, keys are long-lived and manually managed, which makes them convenient and dangerous in equal measure. The engineering job is to make a leaked key as harmless as possible: hashed at rest, scoped, expiring, revocable, and easy to rotate.

Why does it exist?

Not every client can run an OAuth flow. A partner's nightly batch job has no user to log in and often no ability to store and refresh tokens. A key in a config file is what they can do. API keys are the pragmatic answer, provided they are treated like passwords, not like identifiers.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel key card issued to a cleaning contractor. It has the contractor's name on it (prefix, so you know whose it is), it opens only the floors they clean (scopes), it stops working at the end of the contract (expiry), the front desk keeps only a fingerprint of the card, not a copy (hash at rest), and when the contractor loses it, a new one is issued and the old one dies after a short overlap (rotation).

How it works

  1. Generate: 32 random bytes, base64url encoded, with a recognisable prefix: sk_live_7Qm3.... The prefix lets secret scanners (GitHub, gitleaks) recognise leaked keys, and lets you tell live from test keys at a glance.
  2. Store: only sha256(key) in the database, plus a short key_id (the first 8 characters after the prefix) for lookup and display, and last4 for the dashboard. SHA-256 is fine here, not bcrypt, because the key has 256 bits of entropy and cannot be brute-forced; bcrypt would just make every request cost 50 ms.
  3. Show once: the full key is returned exactly once at creation. Afterwards only sk_live_7Qm3...ab9f is displayed.
  4. Authenticate: read Authorization: Bearer sk_live_... or X-API-Key, hash it, look up by hash, check revoked_at and expires_at, load the owner, scopes and tenant, and set request.user.
  5. Scope and bound: each key has scopes (orders:read), optional IP allow-list, optional rate-limit tier, and belongs to exactly one tenant.
  6. Rotate: create a new key, keep both valid for an overlap window (say 7 days), then revoke the old one. Store last_used_at so you can see whether the old key is still in use before revoking.
  7. Detect leaks: run secret scanning on your own repos and logs; subscribe to GitHub secret scanning partner program if you are big enough; revoke and notify automatically on a hit.

NestJS example

TypeScript
// api-key.strategy.ts
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { Strategy } from 'passport-custom';
import type { Request } from 'express';
import { createHash, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import { ApiKeysService } from './api-keys.service';

@Injectable()
export class ApiKeyStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'api-key') {
  constructor(private keys: ApiKeysService) { super(); }

  async validate(req: Request) {
    const raw = (req.headers['x-api-key'] as string | undefined)
      ?? (req.headers.authorization?.startsWith('Bearer sk_') ? req.headers.authorization.slice(7) : undefined);
    if (!raw || !/^sk_(live|test)_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{43}$/.test(raw)) throw new UnauthorizedException();

    const hash = createHash('sha256').update(raw).digest();
    const key = await this.keys.findActiveByHash(hash);           // indexed unique lookup
    if (!key) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    // Defensive constant-time compare even though the DB lookup already matched the hash.
    if (!timingSafeEqual(hash, key.keyHash)) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (key.ipAllowList?.length && !key.ipAllowList.includes(req.ip!)) throw new UnauthorizedException();

    await this.keys.touch(key.id, req.ip!);                       // last_used_at, throttled to once per minute
    return { id: `key:${key.id}`, tenantId: key.tenantId, scopes: key.scopes, roles: ['machine'], apiKeyId: key.id };
  }
}

The AuthGuard(['jwt', 'api-key']) form from @nestjs/passport tries strategies in order, so a route can accept either a user token or a machine key without duplication.

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE api_keys (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  name          text NOT NULL,                     -- "Warehouse sync (prod)"
  key_id        text NOT NULL,                     -- first 8 chars after prefix, for display and support
  key_hash      bytea NOT NULL UNIQUE,             -- sha256(raw key)
  last4         text NOT NULL,
  scopes        text[] NOT NULL,
  ip_allow_list inet[],
  rate_tier     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'standard',
  created_by    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at    timestamptz,                       -- NULL = no expiry (discouraged)
  last_used_at  timestamptz,
  last_used_ip  inet,
  revoked_at    timestamptz,
  replaced_by   uuid REFERENCES api_keys(id)       -- rotation chain
);
CREATE INDEX api_keys_tenant_idx ON api_keys (tenant_id) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;

-- Lookup on every machine request: unique index probe on key_hash, ~0.05 ms.

Production scenario

A logistics API with 4,000 partner keys handling 900 requests per second. The key lookup is a unique index probe, cached in Redis for 60 seconds keyed by hash (with revocation publishing an invalidation), so PostgreSQL sees about 15 key lookups per second. last_used_at writes are throttled per key to once per minute. Keys expire after 12 months by policy; the dashboard warns 30 days before. Secret scanning on the company's GitHub organisation has caught three leaked test keys and one live key in two years; the live key was revoked automatically within 4 minutes of the commit.

Failure scenario

A partner pasted their live key into a support ticket. The support tool indexed tickets into a search system readable by every employee. The key was found by an internal red-team exercise five months later. Because it was scoped to orders:read for one tenant, the damage was limited, but the lesson was to add key-pattern redaction to the support ingestion pipeline and to the application logs (40.30).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Keys logged in request logs (Authorization header) or in URLs (query-string keys end up in access logs and browser history); never accept keys in the query string.
  • Key lookup without an index: a sequential scan per request.
  • Keys without expiry living for years across employee and partner turnover.
  • Revocation not propagating through the cache.
  • Rate tier per key not enforced, so one partner's bug becomes everyone's outage.
  • Key belonging to a user rather than a tenant, so the key dies when the employee leaves.
  • Timing leak in string comparison if you compare raw strings rather than looking up by hash.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They prefer OAuth client credentials for anything that can run it and offer API keys for everything else, built once, centrally, with hashing, prefixes, scopes, expiry, rotation and last-used tracking. They put keys through the same guard chain as users so that scopes and tenant isolation apply identically. They also assume every key will leak eventually and design the blast radius accordingly.

Common mistakes

  • Storing raw keys.
  • Comparing keys with === on the raw string against a stored raw key.
  • Accepting keys in query strings.
  • No prefix, so scanners cannot recognise them.
  • No overlap window on rotation, which breaks partners at 03:00.

Interview questions

  1. Why SHA-256 for API keys but argon2 for passwords?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: entropy; passwords are guessable, 256-bit keys are not.
  2. Design key rotation for a partner with zero downtime.
  3. What does a key prefix buy you?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: secret scanning, environment identification.
  4. How do you bound the damage of a leaked key?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scopes, tenant binding, expiry, IP allow-list, rate tier, revocation.

Practical exercise

Implement API keys with the schema above, a Passport custom strategy, AuthGuard(['jwt','api-key']) on a read endpoint, rotation with a 7-day overlap, and last_used_at. Acceptance criteria: the raw key appears only in the creation response; a revoked key fails within one second; a key with orders:read cannot call a write endpoint; request logs never contain the key.

40.12 Object-Level Authorization and IDOR

Concept

An Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) is what happens when an endpoint takes an object id from the client and returns or modifies that object without checking that the caller may access it. GET /orders/1042 returns order 1042 to anyone logged in. Change the number, get someone else's order. It is the most common serious vulnerability in real APIs, year after year, because it is not a framework bug or a crypto bug; it is a missing line of code in ordinary business logic.

Why does it exist?

Authentication is centralised and hard to forget. Object-level authorization must be written per endpoint, per object type, per action, and is easy to forget. Sequential integer ids make the attack trivial; UUIDs make guessing hard but do nothing about ids that appear in emails, shared links, or other users' responses.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel locker where you type a locker number and it opens. There is a login at the door (authentication), but once inside, every locker opens for every visitor. The fix is not a stronger door; it is a check at each locker that the code belongs to the person standing in front of it.

How it works

  1. Every load or mutation of an object that has an owner or a tenant takes the principal from the verified token and the object id from the request.
  2. The query includes the ownership predicate: WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2. If no row comes back, respond 404. This is better than load-then-check because it cannot be forgotten in a later branch and it does one round trip.
  3. For objects with more complex rules (support in the same region), load the object and evaluate the ABAC rule (40.9).
  4. Protect related objects too: PATCH /orders/:id/items/:itemId must check that the item belongs to the order and the order to the user. Attackers move an item id from their order into a request for another order.
  5. Make it hard to forget: an ownership-scoped repository whose methods all require a principal, and a lint rule or test that flags direct repository.findOne({ where: { id } }) calls in controllers and services for owned entities.

Practical example

A ride-booking app exposes GET /rides/:id/receipt. Rides belong to a rider and a driver. The rule: the rider, the driver, or support in the region may view the receipt. The repository method is findRideForPrincipal(rideId, principal) and encodes exactly that predicate. There is no findRideById for use in request handlers.

NestJS example

Guard for the simple ownership case, plus a repository that makes the safe path the easy path.

TypeScript
// owned-orders.repository.ts
@Injectable()
export class OwnedOrdersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private repo: Repository<Order>) {}

  // The ONLY way to fetch a single order in request handling. The predicate cannot be forgotten.
  async findForPrincipal(id: string, p: AuthenticatedUser): Promise<Order> {
    const qb = this.repo.createQueryBuilder('o').where('o.id = :id', { id });
    if (p.roles.includes('support')) {
      qb.andWhere('o.region = :region', { region: p.region });
    } else {
      qb.andWhere('o.customer_id = :uid', { uid: p.id });
    }
    const order = await qb.getOne();
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundException();   // 404 for both missing and foreign
    return order;
  }

  // Nested object: the item must belong to the order AND the order to the principal.
  async findItemForPrincipal(orderId: string, itemId: string, p: AuthenticatedUser): Promise<OrderItem> {
    const order = await this.findForPrincipal(orderId, p);
    const item = await this.repo.manager.findOne(OrderItem, { where: { id: itemId, orderId: order.id } });
    if (!item) throw new NotFoundException();
    return item;
  }
}
TypeScript
// ownership.guard.ts: a route-level guard for the plain "owner only" case
@Injectable()
export class OrderOwnerGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private repo: Repository<Order>) {}
  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const exists = await this.repo.exist({ where: { id: req.params.id, customerId: req.user.id } });
    if (!exists) throw new NotFoundException();
    return true;
  }
}
// The guard is convenient for simple cases but the service must ALSO scope its queries:
// a guard checks the route parameter, not every id inside the body.

Mass assignment is IDOR's sibling: PATCH /orders/:id with { "customerId": "<other user>" } reassigns the order if the DTO is not whitelisted. Enable ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }) globally and never spread the raw body into an entity (40.24).

PostgreSQL example

Ownership predicates need indexes that include the owner column, and RLS can enforce ownership for customer-facing tables, not only tenants.

SQL
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_idx ON orders (customer_id, id);

-- Optional RLS for owner scoping in a B2C app; app sets app.user_id per transaction.
CREATE POLICY order_owner ON orders
  USING (customer_id = current_setting('app.user_id', true)::uuid
         OR current_setting('app.role', true) = 'support');

Production scenario

A bug-bounty programme for a 5-million-user marketplace paid out on 23 valid reports in a year; 14 were IDORs, all in endpoints added after the original auth design: exports, webhooks management, invoice PDFs, address book entries. The team added a repository convention, a lint rule flagging findOneBy({ id }) on owned entities, and an integration test template ("user B cannot access user A's X") that every new owned resource must include.

Failure scenario

A "download invoice" endpoint accepted ?invoiceId= and streamed the PDF from S3. The developer had checked ownership on the invoice list endpoint and assumed the ids were therefore safe. A researcher enumerated integer invoice ids and downloaded 1,200 invoices in ten minutes. The fix was the ownership predicate on the download query and a switch to signed, short-lived S3 URLs generated only after the check (40.32).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Nested ids: item ids, address ids, attachment ids inside an owned parent.
  • Ids in bodies, not just in URLs: { "paymentMethodId": ... } on checkout must belong to the caller.
  • Bulk endpoints: POST /orders/cancel with { ids: [...] } must filter the whole set by owner, and report which were skipped.
  • Sequential ids leak counts and enable enumeration; prefer UUIDv4 or v7 for exposed ids, but do not rely on unguessability as the control.
  • 403 vs 404 leaking existence.
  • Support tooling that legitimately crosses ownership needing its own scoped rules and audit.
  • Background jobs reusing request-handler repositories without a principal; give jobs an explicit system principal and log it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every id in a request is hostile. They make ownership part of the query, not a check after it. They design repositories so the unsafe method does not exist for request handling, and they require a negative test per owned resource. They know IDOR is the vulnerability most likely to appear in their next pentest report and they budget for it.

Common mistakes

  • Checking ownership on the list and not on the item.
  • Loading by id and forgetting the check in one of several branches.
  • Trusting UUIDs as a security control.
  • Returning 403 for foreign objects.
  • Accepting userId or customerId in bodies.

Interview questions

  1. What is IDOR and why is it so common?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: per-endpoint authorization forgotten; not a framework bug.
  2. Load-then-check or check-in-query?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: in-query where possible; one round trip, cannot be forgotten in branches.
  3. How would you make IDOR structurally hard in a NestJS codebase?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scoped repositories, global whitelist validation, negative tests, lint rules.
  4. Do UUIDs solve IDOR?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; they reduce enumeration, not authorization.

Practical exercise

Audit an existing orders module. For every endpoint that takes an id (path, query or body), write a test where user B uses user A's id.
