The module:

TypeScript
@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([User, Credential, Session, RefreshToken, MfaSecret, EmailToken, Role]),
    PassportModule.register({ defaultStrategy: 'jwt', session: false }),
    JwtModule.registerAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
        privateKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PRIVATE_KEY'),   // Ed25519 PKCS8 PEM
        publicKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'),
        signOptions: {
          algorithm: 'EdDSA', expiresIn: '15m',
          issuer: 'https://api.example.com', audience: 'example-api',
          keyid: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_KID'),              // enables key rotation
        },
        verifyOptions: { algorithms: ['EdDSA'], issuer: 'https://api.example.com',
                         audience: 'example-api', clockTolerance: 30 },
      }),
    }),
    ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => ({
        throttlers: [{ name: 'default', ttl: 60_000, limit: 100 }],
        storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(cfg.getOrThrow('REDIS_URL')),
      }),
    }),
  ],
  controllers: [AuthController],
  providers: [
    AuthService, TokenService, MfaService, PasswordService, JwtStrategy,
    { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard },   // order matters: throttle first,
    { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: JwtAuthGuard },     // then authenticate,
    { provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: RolesGuard },       // then authorize.
  ],
  exports: [AuthService, TokenService],
})
export class AuthModule {}

Decorators:

TypeScript
// public.decorator.ts
export const IS_PUBLIC_KEY = 'isPublic';
export const Public = () => SetMetadata(IS_PUBLIC_KEY, true);

// roles.decorator.ts
export const ROLES_KEY = 'roles';
export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata(ROLES_KEY, roles);

// current-user.decorator.ts
export interface JwtUser { sub: string; sid: string; roles: string[]; tenantId?: string; jti: string }
export const CurrentUser = createParamDecorator((data: keyof JwtUser | undefined, ctx: ExecutionContext) => {
  const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ user: JwtUser }>().user;
  return data ? user?.[data] : user;
});

Strategy and guards:

TypeScript
// jwt.strategy.ts
@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor(cfg: ConfigService, private readonly users: UserLookupService) {
    super({
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
      ignoreExpiration: false,
      algorithms: ['EdDSA'],
      secretOrKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'),
      issuer: 'https://api.example.com',
      audience: 'example-api',
      jsonWebTokenOptions: { clockTolerance: 30 },   // seconds; see 22.39 on clock skew
    });
  }

  // Runs only after the signature, exp, iss and aud have been verified.
  async validate(payload: JwtPayload): Promise<JwtUser> {
    // One cached lookup (Redis, 30 s TTL) enforces the things a stateless token cannot know.
    const state = await this.users.getAuthState(payload.sub);      // status, tokensInvalidBefore, session state
    if (!state || state.status !== 'active') throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (payload.iat * 1000 < state.tokensInvalidBefore.getTime()) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    if (state.revokedSessionIds.has(payload.sid)) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    return { sub: payload.sub, sid: payload.sid, roles: payload.roles, tenantId: payload.tenant, jti: payload.jti };
  }
}
TypeScript
// jwt-auth.guard.ts: global, opt out with @Public()
@Injectable()
export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) { super(); }

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext) {
    const isPublic = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<boolean>(IS_PUBLIC_KEY, [
      ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass(),     // handler beats controller
    ]);
    return isPublic ? true : super.canActivate(ctx);
  }
}

// roles.guard.ts
@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(ROLES_KEY, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]);
    if (!required?.length) return true;                       // no @Roles() means authentication is enough
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ user?: JwtUser }>().user;
    if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException();             // 401, not 403: we do not know who you are
    const ok = required.some((r) => user.roles.includes(r));
    if (!ok) throw new ForbiddenException('Insufficient role');
    return ok;
  }
}

DTOs:

TypeScript
export class RegisterDto {
  @IsEmail() @MaxLength(254) @Transform(({ value }) => String(value).trim().toLowerCase()) email: string;
  @IsString() @MinLength(12) @MaxLength(128) password: string;   // length beats character classes
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @Length(1, 80) displayName?: string;
}
export class LoginDto {
  @IsEmail() @MaxLength(254) @Transform(({ value }) => String(value).trim().toLowerCase()) email: string;
  @IsString() @MaxLength(128) password: string;
  @IsOptional() @Matches(/^\d{6}$/) totp?: string;               // present on the second leg of MFA login
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @Length(1, 64) deviceLabel?: string;
}
export class RefreshDto { @IsString() @Length(43, 64) refreshToken: string; }
export class ResetConfirmDto {
  @IsString() @Length(43, 64) token: string;
  @IsString() @MinLength(12) @MaxLength(128) password: string;
}

With the global pipe new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true }), a body containing roles or emailVerified is a 400, not a privilege escalation.

PasswordService:

TypeScript
@Injectable()
export class PasswordService {
  // Tuned so hashing takes 100-150 ms on the API instance. Measure on YOUR hardware.
  private readonly opts = { type: argon2.argon2id, memoryCost: 65536, timeCost: 3, parallelism: 1 } as const;
  // A real hash of a random value, computed once, used to burn the same CPU for unknown emails.
  private readonly dummyHash = argon2.hashSync?.(randomBytes(32).toString('hex'), this.opts);

  hash(plain: string) { return argon2.hash(plain, this.opts); }

  async verify(hash: string | null, plain: string): Promise<boolean> {
    if (!hash) { await argon2.verify(this.dummyHash, plain).catch(() => false); return false; }
    try { return await argon2.verify(hash, plain); } catch { return false; }
  }

  // Upgrade parameters silently when a user logs in with an older hash.
  needsRehash(hash: string) { return argon2.needsRehash(hash, this.opts); }
}

Login, end to end:

TypeScript
// auth.service.ts
async login(dto: LoginDto, meta: RequestMeta): Promise<LoginResult> {
  const failKey = `login:fail:${dto.email}`;
  if (Number((await this.redis.get(failKey)) ?? 0) >= 5) {
    throw new HttpException({ code: 'TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS', retryAfter: 300 }, 429);
  }

  const row = await this.users.findWithCredentials(dto.email);          // LEFT JOIN credentials
  const ok = await this.passwords.verify(row?.passwordHash ?? null, dto.password); // constant work either way

  if (!row || !ok || row.status !== 'active') {
    await this.redis.multi().incr(failKey).expire(failKey, 900).exec();
    await this.audit.record({ action: 'login.failed', actorType: 'system', targetType: 'user',
                              targetId: dto.email, details: { reason: 'invalid_credentials' }, ...meta });
    throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid email or password');       // one message for every failure
  }
  if (this.passwords.needsRehash(row.passwordHash)) {
    await this.credentials.update(row.id, { passwordHash: await this.passwords.hash(dto.password) });
  }

  const mfa = await this.mfa.getConfirmed(row.id);
  if (mfa && !dto.totp) {
    const challengeId = await this.mfa.startChallenge(row.id, meta);    // 5-minute Redis entry
    return { mfaRequired: true, challengeId };
  }
  if (mfa) await this.mfa.verifyOrThrow(row.id, dto.totp!);             // consumes the step, blocks replay

  await this.redis.del(failKey);
  const session = await this.sessions.create(row.id, dto.deviceLabel ?? deriveLabel(meta.userAgent), meta);
  const pair = await this.tokens.issuePair(row, session.id);            // new family
  await this.audit.record({ action: 'login.success', actorType: 'user', actorId: row.id,
                            targetType: 'session', targetId: session.id, ...meta });
  if (await this.sessions.isNewDevice(row.id, meta)) await this.mailer.newDeviceLogin(row.email, meta);
  return { ...pair, mfaRequired: false };
}

Register:

TypeScript
async register(dto: RegisterDto, meta: RequestMeta): Promise<{ status: string }> {
  if (await this.breached.isCompromised(dto.password)) {   // HIBP range API, k-anonymity
    throw new BadRequestException({ code: 'PASSWORD_BREACHED' });
  }
  const hash = await this.passwords.hash(dto.password);
  try {
    await this.ds.transaction(async (tx) => {
      const user = await tx.getRepository(User).save({ email: dto.email, displayName: dto.displayName ?? '' });
      await tx.getRepository(Credential).save({ userId: user.id, passwordHash: hash });
      await tx.query(`INSERT INTO user_roles (user_id, role_id) SELECT $1, id FROM roles WHERE name = 'customer'`,
                     [user.id]);
      await this.emailTokens.issue(tx, user.id, 'verify_email', 60);   // 60 minutes
    });
  } catch (err) {
    if (isUniqueViolation(err, 'users_email_key')) {
      // The email exists. Tell the OWNER, not the requester, and return the same response either way.
      await this.mailer.registrationAttemptOnExistingAccount(dto.email);
    } else { throw err; }
  }
  return { status: 'verification_email_sent' };            // identical response in both branches
}

Refresh with rotation and reuse detection. This is the core algorithm of the module.

TypeScript
// token.service.ts
async rotate(presented: string, meta: RequestMeta): Promise<TokenPair> {
  const hash = createHash('sha256').update(presented).digest();          // fast hash: 256 bits of entropy
  const row = await this.refresh.findOne({ where: { tokenHash: hash } });
  if (!row) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid refresh token');

  // REUSE: this token was already exchanged or already revoked. Two copies exist. Kill the family.
  if (row.usedAt || row.revokedAt) {
    await this.revokeFamily(row.familyId, 'reuse_detected');
    await this.sessions.revoke(row.sessionId, 'reuse_detected');
    await this.audit.record({ action: 'refresh.reuse_detected', actorType: 'system',
                              targetType: 'user', targetId: row.userId,
                              details: { familyId: row.familyId, tokenId: row.id }, ...meta });
    await this.alerts.securityEvent('refresh_reuse', { userId: row.userId, ip: meta.ip });
    throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'SESSION_REVOKED' });
  }
  if (row.expiresAt <= new Date()) throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid refresh token');

  return this.ds.transaction(async (tx) => {
    // Atomic single-use consume: a concurrent request loses this race and gets 0 rows.
    const res = await tx.query(
      `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET used_at = now(), revoked_at = now(), revoked_reason = 'rotated'
       WHERE id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL RETURNING id`, [row.id]);
    if (res.length === 0) throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'SESSION_REVOKED' });

    const user = await tx.getRepository(User).findOneByOrFail({ id: row.userId });
    if (user.status !== 'active') throw new UnauthorizedException();
    await tx.query(`UPDATE sessions SET last_seen_at = now(), ip = $2 WHERE id = $1`, [row.sessionId, meta.ip]);
    return this.issueInto(tx, user, row.sessionId, row.familyId, row.id);   // same family, parent = old id
  });
}

private async revokeFamily(familyId: string, reason: string) {
  await this.refresh.query(
    `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now(), revoked_reason = $2
     WHERE family_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL`, [familyId, reason]);
}

Why this works: after rotation, the old token is used. If an attacker stole it before you used it, they get the new one and you present the old one on your next refresh — reuse detected, family killed, both of you logged out, and the user gets an alert. If they use it after you, same result. Either way the theft becomes a detected event instead of a silent second session. The cost is a real logout for a legitimate user in a race (see the grace window in edge cases).

Logout and logout-everywhere:

TypeScript
async logout(user: JwtUser) {
  await this.refresh.query(
    `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now(), revoked_reason = 'logout'
     WHERE session_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL`, [user.sid]);
  await this.sessions.revoke(user.sid, 'logout');
  await this.redis.del(`authstate:${user.sub}`);        // drop the cached state so the JWT stops working
  await this.audit.record({ action: 'logout', actorType: 'user', actorId: user.sub,
                            targetType: 'session', targetId: user.sid });
}

async logoutEverywhere(userId: string, reason: 'user_request' | 'password_changed') {
  await this.ds.transaction(async (tx) => {
    await tx.query(`UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now(), revoked_reason = 'logout_all'
                    WHERE user_id = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL`, [userId]);
    await tx.query(`UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at = now(), revoked_reason = $2 WHERE user_id = $1
                    AND revoked_at IS NULL`, [userId, reason]);
    // Access tokens are stateless: this timestamp is what invalidates the ones already issued.
    await tx.query(`UPDATE users SET tokens_invalid_before = now() WHERE id = $1`, [userId]);
  });
  await this.redis.del(`authstate:${userId}`);
}

tokens_invalid_before is the switch that makes stateless tokens revocable. JwtStrategy.validate compares it against iat. The Redis cache of auth state has a 30-second TTL, so the worst case for a revocation to take effect is 30 seconds, and deleting the key makes it immediate.

Password reset:

TypeScript
async requestPasswordReset(email: string, meta: RequestMeta) {
  const user = await this.users.findByEmail(email);
  if (user) {
    const token = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
    await this.ds.transaction(async (tx) => {
      // The partial unique index means the previous live token must go first.
      await tx.query(`UPDATE email_tokens SET used_at = now()
                      WHERE user_id = $1 AND purpose = 'password_reset' AND used_at IS NULL`, [user.id]);
      await tx.query(`INSERT INTO email_tokens (user_id, purpose, token_hash, expires_at, request_ip)
                      VALUES ($1,'password_reset',$2, now() + interval '15 minutes', $3)`,
                     [user.id, sha256(token), meta.ip]);
    });
    await this.mailer.passwordReset(user.email, token);
  } else {
    await this.timing.burn(120);          // match the work done in the found branch
  }
  return { status: 'accepted' };          // identical response and timing either way
}

async confirmPasswordReset(dto: ResetConfirmDto, meta: RequestMeta) {
  const rows = await this.ds.query(
    `UPDATE email_tokens SET used_at = now()
     WHERE token_hash = $1 AND purpose = 'password_reset' AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
     RETURNING user_id`, [sha256(dto.token)]);        // atomic consume: two concurrent uses, one winner
  if (rows.length === 0) throw new BadRequestException({ code: 'INVALID_OR_EXPIRED_TOKEN' });

  const userId = rows[0].user_id;
  await this.credentials.update(userId, {
    passwordHash: await this.passwords.hash(dto.password), passwordChangedAt: new Date(), failedAttempts: 0,
  });
  await this.logoutEverywhere(userId, 'password_changed');   // every device, everywhere
  await this.audit.record({ action: 'password.changed', actorType: 'user', actorId: userId,
                            targetType: 'user', targetId: userId, details: { via: 'reset' }, ...meta });
  await this.mailer.passwordChanged(userId);
}

Email verification uses the same email_tokens machinery with purpose = 'verify_email' and a 60-minute expiry; consuming it sets users.email_verified = true in the same transaction. Unverified accounts can log in but are blocked from checkout and from receiving marketing mail — decide that policy explicitly rather than leaving it to whichever guard someone remembers.

TOTP enrolment and verification with a replay window:

TypeScript
@Injectable()
export class MfaService {
  private readonly totp = new TOTP({ digits: 6, period: 30, window: [1, 1] });   // otplib; +/- 1 step

  async startEnrolment(userId: string, email: string) {
    const secret = authenticator.generateSecret(20);                 // 160 bits, base32
    const enc = await this.crypto.encryptForUser(userId, Buffer.from(secret, 'utf8'));  // envelope, 22.16
    await this.repo.upsertPending(userId, enc);                      // confirmed_at stays NULL
    const uri = authenticator.keyuri(email, 'Example Shop', secret); // otpauth:// for the QR code
    return { otpauthUri: uri, secret };                              // shown once, never logged
  }

  async confirmEnrolment(userId: string, code: string) {
    const pending = await this.repo.findPending(userId);
    if (!pending) throw new BadRequestException({ code: 'NO_PENDING_ENROLMENT' });
    const secret = (await this.crypto.decryptForUser(userId, pending.secretEnc)).toString('utf8');
    const step = this.currentStep();
    if (!authenticator.check(code, secret)) throw new BadRequestException({ code: 'INVALID_CODE' });

    const recovery = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => randomBytes(10).toString('base64url'));
    await this.repo.confirm(userId, step, await Promise.all(recovery.map((c) => this.passwords.hash(c))));
    await this.audit.record({ action: 'mfa.enrolled', actorType: 'user', actorId: userId,
                              targetType: 'user', targetId: userId, details: { type: 'totp' } });
    return { recoveryCodes: recovery };                              // displayed once
  }

  async verifyOrThrow(userId: string, code: string) {
    const row = await this.repo.findConfirmed(userId);
    if (!row) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    const secret = (await this.crypto.decryptForUser(userId, row.secretEnc)).toString('utf8');
    if (!authenticator.check(code, secret)) {
      await this.redis.incr(`mfa:fail:${userId}`);                   // 5 failures -> temporary block
      throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'INVALID_CODE' });
    }
    const step = this.currentStep();
    // Replay defence: the same 30-second step can be used exactly once, even inside the +/- 1 window.
    const updated = await this.repo.bumpStep(userId, step);          // UPDATE ... WHERE last_step IS DISTINCT FROM $step AND (last_step IS NULL OR last_step < $step)
    if (!updated) throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'CODE_ALREADY_USED' });
  }

  private currentStep() { return Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000 / 30); }
}

The exception filter that never leaks account existence:

TypeScript
@Catch()
export class AuthExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(AuthExceptionFilter.name);
  // Anything thrown from an auth route collapses into one of these.
  private static readonly SAFE: Record<number, { code: string; message: string }> = {
    400: { code: 'BAD_REQUEST', message: 'Invalid request' },
    401: { code: 'INVALID_CREDENTIALS', message: 'Invalid email or password' },
    403: { code: 'FORBIDDEN', message: 'Not allowed' },
    429: { code: 'TOO_MANY_REQUESTS', message: 'Too many requests' },
  };

  catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const req = host.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const correlationId = (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID();
    const status = exception instanceof HttpException ? exception.getStatus() : 500;

    // Full detail to the log, including WHY, so on-call can debug without the client learning anything.
    this.logger.warn({ correlationId, path: req.path, status,
                       reason: exception instanceof HttpException ? exception.getResponse() : String(exception) },
                     'auth request failed');

    const safe = AuthExceptionFilter.SAFE[status] ?? { code: 'INTERNAL', message: 'Internal server error' };
    // Preserve machine-readable codes the client legitimately needs (MFA required, token expired).
    const passthrough = exception instanceof HttpException &&
      ['MFA_REQUIRED', 'SESSION_REVOKED', 'PASSWORD_BREACHED', 'INVALID_OR_EXPIRED_TOKEN', 'OTP_LOCKED']
        .includes((exception.getResponse() as any)?.code);
    const body = passthrough ? (exception as HttpException).getResponse() : safe;
    res.status(status === 500 ? 500 : status).json({ ...(body as object), correlationId });
  }
}

The rule the filter enforces: the client learns the category, the log learns the reason. UserNotFoundException and WrongPasswordException may exist internally and be useful in logs; neither may ever reach the wire.

Production scenario

A retail API with 900,000 monthly active users: 1.4 million logins a month, 26 million refreshes (a 15-minute access token means roughly one refresh per active user per 15 minutes), and about 40,000 password resets. refresh_tokens holds around 4 million rows; a nightly job deletes rows where expires_at < now() - interval '7 days' in batches of 10,000 to keep vacuum happy. Rotation adds one UPDATE and one INSERT per refresh, p99 under 6 ms. Reuse detection fires 30 to 60 times a day, and roughly 90 percent of those are the double-refresh race from mobile clients on flaky networks rather than theft, which is why the grace window below matters.

Failure scenario

A mobile release shipped without a mutex around token refresh. When the app resumed from background, four queued requests all got 401, all called /auth/refresh with the same token, and one won. The other three hit the reuse branch: family revoked, session killed, user logged out. Support tickets went from 12 to 900 a day.

The fix was two-part. Client: a single-flight refresh with the other callers awaiting the same promise. Server: a 10-second grace window — if a token was used within the last 10 seconds, from the same session, and the replacement token has not itself been used, return the same replacement pair instead of treating it as reuse. Genuine theft almost never lands inside a 10-second window from the same session id, and the false-positive rate went to nearly zero.

SQL
-- The grace-window query: return the child of a just-rotated token instead of killing the family.
SELECT c.* FROM refresh_tokens p
JOIN refresh_tokens c ON c.parent_id = p.id
WHERE p.token_hash = $1 AND p.used_at > now() - interval '10 seconds'
  AND c.used_at IS NULL AND c.revoked_at IS NULL AND c.session_id = p.session_id;

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Concurrent refresh from multiple tabs or a resumed mobile app: use the grace window plus a single-flight client.
  • Deleted or suspended user with a valid access token: the cached auth state has a 30-second TTL, so there is a window; delete the cache key on status change to close it.
  • Password change during an active session: logoutEverywhere sets tokens_invalid_before, so the current device is logged out too. Decide whether to re-issue a pair for the initiating session (most products do).
  • Clock skew between the signer and a verifier rejecting fresh tokens: clockTolerance: 30 and NTP on every node.
  • Refresh token in localStorage where XSS can read it: prefer an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to /auth/refresh for browsers, and the response body only for native apps.
  • Session table growth: revoke and prune, or the device list becomes a hundred rows of "Chrome on Windows".
  • MFA lockout when a user loses their phone: recovery codes, and a documented, identity-verified support path that writes an audit event.
  • Enumeration through the MFA step: challengeId must be returned for a valid password on an MFA account only, and the timing of the invalid-password path must match.
  • Argon2 parameters too high for the instance size: 64 MB per hash times 50 concurrent logins is 3.2 GB. Cap concurrency, or the login endpoint OOMs the pod under a stuffing attack.
  • Unique violation on refresh_one_live_per_family_idx under a race: map it to the same 401 as reuse, or retry once after re-reading.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick one design and write it down, because the failure mode of auth is not usually a broken algorithm, it is five half-implemented ideas in one codebase. They make revocation possible from day one, since "we chose stateless tokens so we cannot log anyone out" is a sentence that ends careers during an incident. They keep the number of things a client can send small and the number of ways the server can answer smaller. And they treat the reuse-detection alert as a real signal with a real runbook: notify the user, list active sessions, and offer a password change.

They also know what this module does not solve: a compromised device, a phished TOTP code (only phishing-resistant WebAuthn stops that), or a malicious insider with database access. Those need different controls.

Common mistakes

  • Storing refresh tokens in plaintext, or as JWTs that cannot be revoked.
  • Rotation without reuse detection, which is just a shorter-lived token.
  • Reuse detection without a grace window, which logs out real users daily.
  • No tokens_invalid_before, so a password change leaves old access tokens working.
  • Putting roles in the JWT and never bounding the staleness window.
  • Returning different errors for unknown email, wrong password, and locked account.
  • One AuthService method that does registration, login and MFA with six boolean flags.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through refresh token rotation with reuse detection.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: opaque token, hashed at rest, family id, atomic consume, reuse revokes the family, alert and audit.
  2. Why store refresh tokens hashed, and why is SHA-256 enough there when passwords need argon2?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 256 bits of entropy means no brute force; slow hashing protects low-entropy secrets only.
  3. How do you revoke a stateless access token?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: short lifetime, tokens_invalid_before, session revocation list, cached with a bounded TTL.
  4. Two tabs refresh at the same moment. What happens, and how do you avoid logging the user out?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the race, the grace window, client single-flight.
  5. Where does the MFA replay window come from and how do you close it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: TOTP accepts +/- 1 step; store last_step and reject a repeat.
  6. Design the password reset flow so it is safe against enumeration and races.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: uniform response and timing, hashed single-use token, atomic consume, session invalidation, notification.
  7. What is in your access token, and what is deliberately not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sub, sid, roles, tenant, jti; no email, no PII, no permissions list that changes often.

Practical exercise

Implement this module against the schema above, then prove it with integration tests.

Acceptance criteria: registering an existing email returns the same body and status as a new one, and the existing owner receives an email; login with an unknown email and login with a wrong password have identical bodies and timings within 10 percent over 50 samples; refresh rotates the token and the old one fails; using an old token after rotation revokes the whole family, kills the session, and writes an audit event; two concurrent refreshes within 10 seconds both succeed and return the same pair; a password reset logs out all sessions and the previously issued access token stops working within 30 seconds; TOTP code reuse inside the same 30-second step is rejected; every route is protected by default and adding a controller without @Public() or a valid token returns 401 in the route-walker test.

40.37 Threat modeling in one page

Concept

Threat modeling is a structured conversation that answers four questions about a feature: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we doing about it, and did we do a good job? It is not a document produced by a consultant. It is a 45-minute whiteboard session with the people who are about to write the code, and its output is a short table of threats and controls that turns into tickets.

STRIDE is the checklist that stops the conversation from drifting into whatever the loudest person is worried about. Six categories, one per letter:

Letter Threat The property it breaks
S Spoofing Authentication
T Tampering Integrity
R Repudiation Non-repudiation
I Information disclosure Confidentiality
D Denial of service Availability
E Elevation of privilege Authorization

Why does it exist?

Because security bugs are cheapest to fix before the code exists. A missing tenant filter found on a whiteboard costs ten minutes; found in production it costs a breach notification. And because engineers are good at imagining failures (timeouts, retries, partial writes) and bad at imagining adversaries, unless something prompts them. STRIDE is the prompt.

Mental model

Imagine walking through a new shop with a security consultant before it opens. They do not read a policy document; they walk the customer's path, stopping at each point where something changes hands: the door, the shelves, the fitting room, the till, the stockroom door, the safe. At each point they ask one question: what would a dishonest person try here? Threat modeling is that walk, and STRIDE is the six questions they ask at each stop.

How it works

Step 1: draw the flow with trust boundaries. A trust boundary is any place where data crosses from a less-trusted zone to a more-trusted one. Every boundary is where validation and authorization must happen.

The boundaries here: browser to API, admin console to API, and payment provider to webhook handler. Note that the payment provider sits in the untrusted zone even though you trust the company: the network path is untrusted, so the webhook must be authenticated by signature (40.18), not by source IP or by hope.

Step 2: run STRIDE at each boundary. The output is one table. This is the deliverable; there is no document behind it.

# STRIDE Threat against checkout Likelihood Impact Control
1 S Attacker replays a stolen JWT to check out as another customer Medium High 15-minute access tokens, refresh rotation with reuse detection, device/session binding, new-device email
2 S Forged payment webhook marks an unpaid order as paid Medium High HMAC signature verification with timestamp and replay cache; reconcile against the provider API before fulfilment
3 T Client posts { "priceCents": 1 } with the cart High High Server recomputes every price from products; the client sends only ids and quantities
4 T Coupon applied twice by concurrent requests Medium Medium UPDATE coupons SET used = used + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND used < max_uses RETURNING, unique (coupon_id, order_id)
5 T Quantity -5 produces a negative line total and a refund Medium High @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(100) on the DTO; CHECK (quantity > 0) in Postgres
6 R Customer denies placing a 1,200 euro order Low Medium audit_events with actor, ip, user agent, request id, hash chain; payment provider record
7 R Support agent refunds to their own card and denies it Low High Refund audit event with on_behalf_of, destination change alert, four-eyes approval above a threshold
8 I GET /orders/:id returns another customer's address High High Owner-scoped query WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2; row-level security; 404 not 403
9 I Order confirmation email leaks the full PAN Low High Only last4 ever leaves the payment service; never-log list; redaction
10 I Error response leaks SQL and table names Medium Low Global exception filter with a correlation id
11 D Payment endpoint flooded, blocking real checkouts Medium High Cost-weighted rate limit per user, per IP; circuit breaker on the PSP call; separate connection pool for checkout
12 D One customer creates 50,000 carts, filling the table Medium Medium Per-user cart limit; TTL cleanup job; quota
13 E POST /admin/orders/:id/refund without a role guard Medium High Global RolesGuard, route-walker test that fails CI on an unguarded admin route
14 E role: "admin" in the registration body Medium High ValidationPipe whitelist plus forbidNonWhitelisted; per-audience DTOs

Step 3: decide. Every row gets one of four outcomes: mitigate (build the control, make a ticket now), accept (write down why, with an owner and a review date), transfer (the PSP takes card data so PCI scope moves to them), or eliminate (drop the feature). Rows 3, 8, 13 and 14 are always "mitigate before merge". Row 12 might be "accept for now, revisit at 10,000 users".

Step 4: verify. Each mitigate row needs a test. "The server recomputes prices" is a claim until there is a test that posts a tampered price and asserts the order total is unchanged.

How to run it in 45 minutes. The agenda that works:

Text
0-5    One person draws the flow on the board. Data stores, services, boundaries. No detail.
5-10   Everyone silently lists threats on sticky notes, one per note. Silence matters:
       it stops the first idea from anchoring the room.
10-30  Walk STRIDE letter by letter at each boundary. Notes go on the board under a letter.
       Timebox each letter to 3-4 minutes. Duplicates are a signal, not a problem.
30-40  Score likelihood and impact as High/Medium/Low by show of hands. Do not compute a
       risk number to two decimal places; you are sorting, not measuring.
40-45  Assign an outcome to every row. Mitigations become tickets before people leave.

Rules that keep it to 45 minutes: the room is the engineers building the feature plus one person who has seen an incident, no slides, no template document, and no arguing about likelihood for more than 30 seconds (when in doubt, call it Medium and move on). Repeat only when the design changes materially, not on a calendar.

Production scenario

A payments team threat-models every design doc before implementation. The session is 45 minutes and produces 8 to 15 rows, of which typically 3 become tickets and the rest are already covered by platform controls. Over two years the sessions caught: a webhook handler that trusted a source IP, a "resend invoice" endpoint that took an email address from the request, and an admin export that had no tenant filter. Each of those was a 20-minute fix at design time.

Failure scenario

A team skipped threat modeling for a "simple" gift card feature because it was two endpoints. Nobody asked the D question. The balance check endpoint accepted a card code with no rate limit, and codes were 8 alphanumeric characters. An attacker enumerated 40 million combinations over a weekend from 200 IPs and drained 60,000 euros of balances. The threat is row 12's cousin, and it takes one letter of STRIDE and 30 seconds to find on a whiteboard.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Modeling the happy path only and missing the admin, support and internal-service paths.
  • Forgetting that the mobile app is untrusted code running on a device the user controls.
  • Treating "internal network" as a trust boundary; it is not, in a Kubernetes cluster with 200 pods.
  • Producing a document nobody reads instead of tickets somebody builds.
  • Threat modeling once at project start and never again after the design changed twice.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They run the session early, keep it short, and insist the output is tickets with tests. They know the highest-value letters for a typical CRUD backend are I and E (information disclosure and elevation of privilege), so they spend the most time there. They treat "accepted risk" as a real answer that must be written down with an owner, because an undocumented accepted risk is indistinguishable from an oversight during the postmortem.

Common mistakes

  • Inviting only the security team, so the people who write the code never build the intuition.
  • Scoring risk with a formula instead of sorting by gut and moving on.
  • Skipping repudiation because it feels legalistic, then having no audit trail during a dispute.

Interview questions

  1. Apply STRIDE to a checkout flow. Give one concrete threat per letter.
  2. What is a trust boundary and where are they in a typical NestJS deployment?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: client to API, webhook sender to handler, service to service, human to admin console; not "inside the VPC".
  3. A threat model row says "accepted". What must be written next to it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: reason, owner, review date, and the signal that would change the decision.
  4. How do you keep threat modeling from becoming a document nobody reads?

Practical exercise

Run a 45-minute STRIDE session on the checkout flow of a project you know. Produce the table above with your own rows.

Acceptance criteria: at least one threat per STRIDE letter; every High/High row has a ticket; every mitigate row names a test; every accepted row names an owner and a review date; the session ended on time.

40.38 The security review checklist for pull requests

Concept

Most security bugs enter the codebase through a normal pull request reviewed by a normal engineer on a normal Tuesday. A checklist turns "does this look fine" into "did we check these specific things", and it works because human reviewers are excellent at pattern matching once told which patterns to match.

Use it as a filter, not a ritual: most PRs touch none of these areas and get a normal review. The moment a PR touches a route, a query, a template, a dependency, a config file or a log line, the relevant group applies.

How it works

Group Check What to look for
Authentication Is every new route authenticated? A new controller without @Public() should still be covered by the global guard; a new @Public() needs a reason in the PR description
Token handling No token logged, no token in a URL, no token in localStorage for a browser client, expiry set
Credential changes Password change or reset invalidates sessions; a notification email is sent
MFA paths The MFA step cannot be skipped by calling the second endpoint directly
Authorization Ownership check on every read and write by id WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2, not findOne(id) then compare after loading
Role or permission check for privileged actions @Roles() present; admin routes not reachable with a customer token
Tenant filter present in every query Especially in raw SQL, query builders, bulk operations and reports
404 not 403 for resources the caller may not see Otherwise the status code is an existence oracle
Input DTO with class-validator on every body, query and param No any, no Record<string, unknown> reaching a service
Whitelist active Global ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true }); nested objects use @Type() and @ValidateNested()
Numeric and length bounds @Min, @Max, @MaxLength; pagination has a hard cap
No user input in an interpreter No string-built SQL, no exec, no path from a parameter, no template compiled from data, no ORDER BY from a string
Output No sensitive field in the response @Exclude() on hashes and secrets, or an explicit response DTO; check the serializer is applied
Error responses generic No stack trace, SQL, file path, or "user not found"
Correct content type and disposition for files nosniff, attachment, forced type from sniffed bytes
Data Migration is reversible and non-destructive No column drops in the same deploy as the code that stops using them
Indexes for new query patterns And a WHERE clause the index can actually serve
PII columns encrypted or justified New personal data has a retention answer and an erasure answer
Audit event for privileged or money-moving actions Actor, target, before/after, ip
Dependencies New package justified Downloads, last publish, maintainer count, install scripts, transitive size
Lockfile updated and npm ci still reproducible No floating range added
npm audit clean at the policy level No new high or critical
Configuration No secret in the diff gitleaks passes; new config comes from the secrets manager
Production-safe defaults synchronize: false, debug off, Swagger off, CORS explicit
New environment variable added to the config schema and to every environment A missing variable must fail at boot, not at 3 am on the first request that needs it
Observability No sensitive value logged Structured fields, not interpolated strings; check err.config.headers
New failure paths emit a metric or a log with enough context Correlation id present
Rate limit on any new expensive or public endpoint With a cost weight if the bucket is shared

Automate the mechanical half of this list so reviewers spend attention on the parts that need judgement: gitleaks for secrets, Semgrep rules for exec/path.join(req/raw SQL concatenation, an ESLint rule banning any in DTOs, a route-walker test asserting every route has a guard, and npm audit plus Trivy in CI. A checklist item that a machine can check should never be a human's job twice.

Practical exercise

Add the automatable half of the checklist to CI and the judgement half to your pull request template.

Acceptance criteria: a PR adding an unguarded route fails CI; a PR adding a hard-coded secret fails CI; a PR adding child_process.exec fails CI; the template's manual items fit on one screen so people actually read them.

40.39 Edge cases and failure modes

Concept

These are the ones that get through design reviews and appear at 03:00. Each is a real pattern with a symptom you can recognise and a fix you can implement.

1. Token replay after logout. Symptom: a user clicks "log out", the client deletes the token, and a request replayed from a proxy log or a browser extension still succeeds for the next 14 minutes. Cause: logout deleted the refresh token but access tokens are stateless. Fix: revoke the session and set users.tokens_invalid_before = now() (or maintain a revoked-sid set in Redis with a TTL equal to the access token lifetime); check it in JwtStrategy.validate; delete the cached auth state key so the check is immediate rather than eventually consistent. Accept that with a 30-second state cache your worst case is 30 seconds, and write that number down.

2. A stolen refresh token used from another country. Symptom: a refresh succeeds from an IP 4,000 km from the last one, 90 seconds later. Cause: the token leaked through a compromised device, a shared computer, or an XSS. Fix: bind the refresh token to a session and record the ip and user agent; compute an "impossible travel" signal on refresh (distance divided by elapsed time exceeding, say, 900 km/h) and on a hit require re-authentication, revoke the family, email the user with the device list, and write an audit event. Do not silently block: a VPN produces the same signal, so the response must be "prove it is you", not "you are locked out".

3. Clock skew rejecting valid tokens. Symptom: a small percentage of requests fail with jwt not active or jwt expired right after issuing, always on the same pod. Cause: the signer's clock is ahead of the verifier's by a few seconds, so nbf/iat is in the verifier's future. Fix: clockTolerance: 30 (seconds) in verifyOptions and in passport-jwt's jsonWebTokenOptions; run NTP (chrony) on every node and alert when offset exceeds 1 second; never set nbf unless you need it. Tolerance is a band-aid over a clock problem, so monitor the clock too.

4. JWKS rotation breaking verification mid-deploy. Symptom: during a rollout, some requests fail with invalid signature and it clears when the rollout finishes. Cause: new pods signed with key B while old pods and downstream verifiers still had only key A, or the JWKS cache TTL was longer than the rollout. Fix: the two-phase rotation: publish first, sign later. Deploy the new key into the JWKS with a distinct kid and let every verifier pick it up (cache TTL 5 minutes, plus a forced refetch on an unknown kid, rate limited to avoid a stampede). Only in a later deploy switch signing to the new kid. Keep the old key published for at least the maximum token lifetime plus skew before removing it.

5. The session store being unavailable. Symptom: Redis is down and every request either 500s or, worse, succeeds without a session check. Cause: an error handler that treats a lookup failure as "no revocation found". Fix: auth fails closed. A store error is a 503, not an implicit allow. Write the check so the safe branch is the default: const state = await lookup(); if (!state) throw new UnauthorizedException(); never if (state?.revoked) throw. Separately, reduce the blast radius: cache auth state locally in-process for a few seconds so a brief Redis blip does not become a full outage, and make the non-security uses of Redis (rate limiting on read endpoints) fail open, which is the opposite decision for a reason you can articulate.

6. An API key leaked into logs or a git commit. Symptom: GitHub's secret scanner emails you, or the key turns up in a log search. Cause: the key was logged in an error, printed in a debug branch, or committed in a .env. Fix: run the runbook from 40.32 (rotate, revoke, audit, contain, rewrite, close the path). Structurally: give keys a visible prefix (ak_live_) so scanners can find them, store only the hash, keep last_used_at and last_used_ip so you can prove the old key is dead, scope each key to the minimum permissions and to an IP range where the client allows, and add the prefix to your own log-scanning rules so you find your leaks before a scanner does.

7. A permission cache still allowing access after a role was revoked. Symptom: an offboarded employee's admin access works for another ten minutes. Cause: roles are cached in Redis with a 15-minute TTL, or baked into a JWT with a 15-minute life, and revocation only wrote the database. Fix: make revocation an event, not just a write: the same transaction that deletes the user_roles row publishes an invalidation that deletes authstate:{userId} and bumps tokens_invalid_before. Keep the TTL short enough that a missed invalidation self-heals (30 to 60 seconds), and write a test that revokes a role and asserts a 403 within the documented window. Decide and document the window; "immediately" is not an implementable requirement for a distributed cache.

8. A deleted user holding a valid JWT for 15 more minutes. Symptom: a deactivated account keeps placing orders. Cause: the token is stateless and nothing checks user status. Fix: the same mechanism as 7 — status is part of the cached auth state that validate() checks, and deletion invalidates the cache key. If your access tokens are longer-lived than a minute or two, you need this check; if you insist on no per-request lookup, then your token lifetime is your revocation window, so make it 5 minutes and say so out loud.

9. Tenant data leaking through one query that forgot the filter. Symptom: a customer of tenant A sees a row from tenant B in a report or an export. Cause: one query out of 400 was written by hand without tenant_id. Fix: stop relying on discipline. Enable PostgreSQL row-level security on every tenant-scoped table, with a policy on a session variable set per request:

SQL
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY orders_tenant ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
-- Per request, on the connection checked out of the pool:
SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = '2f1c...';

SET LOCAL scopes it to the transaction, so a pooled connection cannot leak the setting to the next request. Also add a CI test that runs every repository method as tenant A and asserts zero rows from tenant B, and make sure the app role is not BYPASSRLS.

10. Timing attacks on token comparison. Symptom: none, until a researcher demonstrates it. Cause: a === b on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, and over enough samples the difference is measurable, especially on a local network. Fix: crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers, and hash both sides first so the lengths always match and the comparison never reveals the length:

TypeScript
export function safeEqual(a: string, b: string): boolean {
  const ha = createHash('sha256').update(a).digest();
  const hb = createHash('sha256').update(b).digest();
  return timingSafeEqual(ha, hb);           // both are 32 bytes, always
}

Use it for API keys, webhook signatures, OTP codes and reset tokens. timingSafeEqual throws if the buffer lengths differ, which is why the hash step matters. Note that a database lookup by hash is already constant-ish time and is the better pattern where it applies.

11. A race in password reset where two tokens are valid at once. Symptom: a user requests two reset emails, uses the first, and the second still works an hour later; or two concurrent submissions of the same token both succeed and the second sets a password the attacker chose. Cause: issue-then-check logic instead of atomic consumption, and no invalidation of the previous token. Fix: the partial unique index (WHERE used_at IS NULL) so only one live token per user per purpose can exist, invalidation of the previous token inside the same transaction that issues the new one, and atomic consumption with UPDATE ... WHERE used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now() RETURNING user_id. Zero rows returned means someone else won; return the same generic error either way.

12. Mass assignment through a nested DTO. Symptom: a user updates their profile and their address.id now points at someone else's address row, or their subscription.plan becomes enterprise. Cause: whitelist: true without forbidNonWhitelisted, or a nested object without @Type() so class-transformer never converts it and validation silently skips it. Fix: forbidNonWhitelisted: true and forbidUnknownValues: true globally; @ValidateNested() with @Type(() => AddressDto) on every nested object and array; no id field on nested input DTOs (the server resolves ownership); and never Object.assign(entity, dto). Add a test that posts an unexpected property to every write route and asserts a 400 naming the property.

13. CORS misconfiguration exposing authenticated responses. Symptom: a bug bounty report shows an attacker page reading GET /api/me for any logged-in visitor. Cause: origin: true (reflection) with credentials: true, or a suffix match like endsWith('example.com') that also matches evil-example.com, or allowing Origin: null. Fix: an exact allow-list from configuration, credentials: true only with a specific origin, never null, and a boot-time assertion plus a unit test that a forged origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. Remember that CORS protects browsers only; it is not an authorization control for server-to-server callers.

14. SSRF through an HTTP redirect after the allow-list check. Symptom: a "fetch product data from your URL" feature is used to read http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Cause: the code validated the initial URL against an allow-list, then let the HTTP client follow a 302 to an internal address. The DNS variant is worse: the hostname resolves to a public IP during validation and to 127.0.0.1 on the actual request (DNS rebinding). Fix:

TypeScript
const res = await axios.get(url, {
  maxRedirects: 0,                                   // follow redirects yourself, revalidating each hop
  timeout: 5_000,
  validateStatus: (s) => s < 400,
  // Resolve and pin the IP: validate the address you will actually connect to.
  httpAgent: new http.Agent({ lookup: allowListedLookup }),
});

allowListedLookup resolves the hostname, rejects any address in a private, loopback, link-local or unique-local range (including IPv6 and IPv4-mapped forms like ::ffff:127.0.0.1), and hands the resolved IP to the connection so the name cannot be re-resolved to something else. Follow redirects manually, applying the same check to each Location, with a hop limit of 3. Then add the control that survives a code bug: an egress network policy or proxy that only permits the destinations this service legitimately needs.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Every item above is a place where a correct-looking implementation is wrong because of timing, caching, concurrency or a second request. So they ask the same six questions about every security control that they ask about every other piece of the system: Can it time out? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? — plus the security additions: Can it be forged? Can it be replayed? Can it be guessed? Can it be bypassed? Can it leak? Can it be abused at scale?

They also write down the windows. "Revocation takes effect within 30 seconds." "Access tokens live 15 minutes." "The reuse grace window is 10 seconds." A number you have chosen is a design; a number you have not chosen is a surprise during an incident.

40.40 Security as a practice

Concept

Everything so far is a control. This section is about the routine that keeps controls working after the people who built them have moved on: scanning, testing, external reporting, and the ability to respond when it goes wrong anyway.

How it works

Dependency scanning in CI. The baseline, running on every pull request and nightly on the default branch:

YAML
# .github/workflows/security.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, security-events: write, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2          # secrets in the diff and in history
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high
      - run: npx semgrep --config .semgrep.yml --error   # exec, path.join(req, raw SQL, eval
      - run: npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0     # OS and image layers
        with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/example/api:${{ github.sha }}", severity: "HIGH,CRITICAL", exit-code: "1" }

Nightly matters as much as per-PR: a dependency that was clean on Monday has a CVE on Thursday, and nobody opened a PR in between. Route the results into one place with an owner and an SLA (critical in 24 hours, high in 7 days, medium in 30), or the scanner becomes noise everyone mutes.

Penetration testing cadence. A useful rhythm for a mid-sized product: an external pentest annually, plus one after any major architectural change (new auth system, new tenant model, first mobile app). Two weeks of a good tester's time on a scoped target beats a month of automated scanning. Give them credentials for two accounts in two tenants and one admin account — an unauthenticated test on a product that is 95 percent behind login tests 5 percent of your attack surface. Insist that findings come with reproduction steps, and treat the retest as part of the engagement.

Bug bounty. Start with a vulnerability disclosure policy before a paid bounty: a security.txt file, a monitored security@ address, a public promise not to pursue researchers acting in good faith, and a stated response time. That alone converts a percentage of "found a bug, posted it on Twitter" into "found a bug, emailed you". Move to a paid programme only when you can triage within a day and fix within a week; a bounty with a slow queue produces angry researchers and public disclosure. Start private and scoped, with a clear out-of-scope list (denial of service testing, social engineering, physical, third-party services).

Incident response for a breach. The shape of the first four hours, written down before you need it:

Text
1. Declare.       One incident commander. One channel. One document. Say the word "incident".
2. Contain.       Revoke credentials, disable the endpoint, block the IP, scale down the
                  compromised workload. Containment beats investigation in the first hour.
3. Preserve.      Snapshot pods and volumes before restarting anything. Export logs to a
                  place with a longer retention than the source. Note the times in UTC.
4. Assess.        What data, whose data, how much, over what period? Query the audit log.
                  "We do not know" is an answer that must be written down and worked on.
5. Eradicate.     Rotate every secret in the blast radius, not only the one you think leaked.
                  Patch the entry point. Rebuild rather than clean.
6. Recover.       Restore service, monitor closely, keep the incident open.
7. Notify.        Legal and privacy counsel decide the obligations. GDPR is 72 hours to the
                  supervisory authority from becoming aware. Start that clock in the document.
8. Learn.         Blameless postmortem within a week: timeline, contributing factors, actions
                  with owners and dates. Publish internally.

The two things teams get wrong under pressure: restarting the compromised pod (destroying the evidence) and rotating only the one credential they can prove was used. Snapshot first; rotate wide.

The disclosure conversation. When you have to tell customers, three principles beat any amount of wordsmithing. Say what happened in plain language and be specific about scope, including what was not affected. Say what you are doing and what they should do, with the useful actions first (change your password, check your sessions, watch for phishing that references this incident). And do not promise what you cannot verify — "no data was accessed" is only sayable if you have logs proving it, and "we take security seriously" costs you credibility because it is what everyone says.

Practise it: a tabletop exercise where the team is handed a scenario ("a researcher emails you a screenshot of another tenant's orders") and runs the playbook for an hour is the cheapest preparation available, and it always finds that nobody knows who can revoke production credentials at 2 am.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know security is a rate, not a state: you will introduce vulnerabilities continuously, so what matters is how fast you find and remove them. They spend their budget on the controls that keep working when someone forgets — global guards, row-level security, database grants, egress rules, scanners in CI, short-lived credentials — rather than on documents that describe what everyone should remember. They keep the incident runbook short enough to be followed at 3 am. And they are honest with the business: perfect security is not on the menu; bounded, understood, monitored risk is.

Senior Checklist — Part 40

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain the difference between authentication and authorization, and when each returns 401 versus 403
  • I can implement refresh token rotation with reuse detection, including the concurrency race and the grace window
  • I can choose and tune a password hash, and explain why argon2id beats bcrypt and why both beat SHA-256
  • I can name the parameterised form for every interpreter my service talks to
  • I can write an ownership-scoped query and back it up with row-level security
  • I can design a file upload pipeline with quarantine, magic-byte checks, re-encoding and a separate serving domain
  • I can configure pino redaction and explain why it is a backstop rather than the control
  • I can answer a right-to-erasure request without breaking an append-only audit log
  • I can rotate a database credential and a JWT signing key with zero downtime
  • I can write a CSP for an API and for a server-rendered page, and explain why origin: true with credentials is a data leak
  • I can build a tamper-evident audit log and verify the chain
  • I can run a 45-minute STRIDE session and turn the output into tickets with tests
  • I can run the first hour of a breach response without improvising

Part 40 — Key Takeaways

  • Authentication asks who you are; authorization asks what you may do. Deny by default, and make the deny the framework's job, not the developer's memory.
  • Short-lived access tokens plus rotating, revocable refresh tokens with reuse detection is the design that survives a stolen token; rotation without detection is only a shorter fuse.
  • Every injection is the same bug: data became syntax. Learn the parameterised form for SQL, shells, paths, Redis, Lua, logs, templates and dynamic SQL, and allow-list where no parameterised form exists.
  • Hash passwords with argon2id tuned to about 100 ms on your hardware; hash high-entropy tokens with SHA-256 and compare with timingSafeEqual.
  • Uploaded bytes are hostile until your own pipeline has re-encoded them; only a clean state is servable, and user content belongs on its own domain.
  • The never-log list is short and absolute; structured logging plus redaction is a backstop, and crypto-shredding is how erasure coexists with append-only history.
  • Secrets should be short-lived and narrowly scoped, because then a leak is survivable; every rotation needs an overlap window before the old value dies.
  • PostgreSQL has an authorization system: per-service roles, column grants, statement timeouts and row-level security back up application code that will eventually be wrong.
  • Security headers are the cheapest control you own, and CORS reflection with credentials is the most expensive mistake in that file.
  • An audit log is a business record, not a debug log: append-only, hash-chained, retained for years, and queryable by the people who need it.
  • Rate limit on the unit that matters — account for auth, key for partners, user for cost — in shared storage, before the expensive work, with Retry-After on the way out.
  • Threat model for 45 minutes with the people writing the code; the output is tickets with tests, not a document.
  • Security is a rate, not a state. Invest in controls that keep working when someone forgets, write down your windows, and rehearse the incident before you have one.

A test suite is the only part of your codebase that gets to say "no" to a deploy. Everything else is opinion. That is why senior engineers care so much about what the suite is actually proving. A green pipeline that mocks the database, mocks the ORM, mocks time and mocks the payment gateway proves that your mocks agree with each other. It proves nothing about the unique constraint that will reject a duplicate order at 02:14 on a Saturday.

This part is about tests that prove something. We use Jest, @nestjs/testing, supertest, Testcontainers, nock and a real PostgreSQL. We cover the three levels (unit, integration, end-to-end), the doubles you are allowed to use at each level, the things you must never mock, how to test transactions, concurrency, time and async flows, and how to organise all of it in CI so that it stays fast and stays trusted. The running example is the same one used through the book: PlaceOrder in an e-commerce backend, with inventory, payment and an outbox event.

Keep the senior mantra next to you: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? A good test suite has at least one test per question for every critical path.

41.1 The testing pyramid and the testing trophy

Concept

The testing pyramid is the classic shape: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, very few slow end-to-end (e2e) tests at the top. The testing trophy is a newer shape that argues the middle layer (integration) should be the widest, because integration tests give the most confidence per minute of maintenance. Both agree on one thing: the higher a test sits, the slower and more expensive it is, and the more real failures it can catch.

For a backend service that sits in front of PostgreSQL, the most expensive bugs live at the boundary between your code and the database (constraints, transactions, locks, migrations) and at the boundary between your service and other services (contracts, timeouts, retries). Unit tests cannot see either boundary. That is the whole argument for the trophy shape.

Why does it exist?

Without a shape, teams drift into one of two failure modes. The first is "unit tests only": thousands of tests that mock the repository, run in eight seconds, and never notice that the production schema differs from the entity definition. The second is "e2e only": a hundred tests that each boot the whole app and take twenty minutes, so developers stop running them locally and start ignoring them when they fail. The shape is a budget. It tells you where to spend test time to get the most confidence.

Mental model

Imagine inspecting a car. A unit test is checking one spark plug on the bench: fast, precise, and it tells you nothing about whether the car starts. An integration test is starting the engine in the garage: slower, but now you know the fuel line, the battery and the plugs work together. An e2e test is driving it around the block: slowest, most realistic, and when it fails you only know "something is wrong somewhere". You want a lot of bench checks, a solid number of engine starts, and a few drives.

How it works

The cost, speed and confidence of each layer for a NestJS + PostgreSQL service:

Layer Typical runtime per test What it exercises What it cannot see Confidence per test Maintenance cost
Static (tsc, ESLint) 0 ms (once per build) Types, obvious mistakes Any runtime behaviour Low but free Very low
Unit 1–20 ms Pure functions, aggregates, one class with fakes SQL, constraints, wiring, HTTP Medium for logic, none for I/O Low if you test behaviour, high if you test implementation
Integration 20–300 ms Service + real PostgreSQL / Redis / Kafka in a container Full HTTP stack, auth, other services High Medium (needs containers and data builders)
E2E 200 ms – 3 s Full NestJS app over HTTP with real DB, external HTTP mocked The real third party Highest for "does the feature work" High (slow, brittle if data is shared)
Contract 10–100 ms Shape of requests/responses/events between services Business logic High for integration between teams Medium

The recommended ratio for a typical NestJS + PostgreSQL service is discussed in section 41.17. The short version: roughly 40% unit (concentrated on domain logic), 45% integration (services against a real database), 15% e2e and contract. If your domain layer is thin (a CRUD service), shift further toward integration.

Practical example

An orders service has these behaviours worth testing:

  • Pricing: subtotal, discounts, tax rounding. Pure logic. Unit.
  • Order state machine: PENDING -> PAID -> SHIPPED, with illegal transitions rejected. Pure logic. Unit.
  • "Two customers cannot buy the last unit." Depends on SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and a CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint. Integration against real PostgreSQL.
  • "Payment failure rolls back the order and inventory." Depends on transaction boundaries. Integration.
  • "POST /orders returns 201 with the right body, requires a JWT, and writes an outbox event." E2E.
  • "Our order.placed event still matches what the shipping team consumes." Contract.

Notice how quickly the important behaviours leave the unit layer. That is normal for backend systems and it is the reason the trophy exists.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer asks, for every test: what production bug would this test have caught? If the answer is "none, it only checks that I called the mock", the test is deleted. They also ask what production bug would this test miss? and add the missing layer. They treat test runtime as a budget: the unit suite must run in under a minute on a laptop, integration under five minutes in CI, e2e in under fifteen. When a suite exceeds the budget, they fix the suite (sharding, container reuse, fewer redundant tests) instead of letting people stop running it.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the pyramid as a rule about counts instead of cost. The goal is confidence per minute, not a ratio.
  • Writing integration tests that could be unit tests (booting a container to test a rounding rule).
  • Writing unit tests that should be integration tests (mocking repository.findOne to "test" a query).
  • Having no e2e tests at all, so the first time the real HTTP pipeline (guards, pipes, filters, serialization) runs together is in staging.

Interview questions

  1. Why does the testing trophy put integration tests in the widest band for backend services?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the most expensive backend bugs live at the code/database and service/service boundaries, and unit tests cannot observe those boundaries. Follow-up: what does that imply for a thin CRUD service?
  2. How do you decide which layer a test belongs in?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: by what it needs to observe. If the behaviour depends on SQL semantics, it is an integration test. If it depends on HTTP pipeline behaviour, it is e2e.
  3. What is the cost of an e2e test beyond runtime?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: data setup, flakiness from shared state, harder debugging, and slower feedback that pushes developers to skip them.

41.2 Where tests sit in the architecture

Before writing a single test it helps to draw where each kind of test cuts the system. Each cut defines what is real and what is a double on either side.

  • Unit tests touch AGG and SVC with in-memory fakes for REPO, PAY, OUT.
  • Integration tests touch SVC with a real PG in a container, a fake or stubbed PAY, and the real OUT (it writes to PG).
  • E2E tests go through C -> GW -> CTRL -> SVC -> PG, with STRIPE replaced by nock at the network boundary.

The rule of thumb: the further right on that diagram a component sits, the more it should be real in your tests, until you reach a system you do not own. Systems you do not own are mocked at the network boundary, never inside your code.

41.3 Unit testing domain logic and services

Concept

A unit test exercises a small piece of code in isolation and asserts on its observable behaviour: return values, thrown errors, state changes on the object under test, and calls to collaborators when the call itself is the behaviour (for example "the payment gateway was charged exactly once"). "In isolation" means no network, no database, no filesystem, no real clock.

Why does it exist?

Domain rules are where money is made and lost: pricing, discounts, tax, stock reservation rules, order state transitions. These rules have many branches. Exercising every branch through HTTP and PostgreSQL would take minutes; through a pure function it takes milliseconds. Unit tests also act as executable documentation of rules that product managers argue about ("is the discount applied before or after tax?").

Mental model

Imagine a pharmacist checking a prescription. She does not need the patient present, the pharmacy open, or the insurance company on the phone. She needs the rules (dosage, interactions) and the inputs (patient weight, other medications). A unit test is the same: rules plus inputs, nothing else in the room.

How it works

A good unit test has a structure called AAA: Arrange (build inputs), Act (call the thing), Assert (check one behaviour). One behaviour per test, named as a sentence that describes the behaviour, not the method name.

  1. Arrange: build a valid object using a builder with sensible defaults (section 41.6), then change only the field the test cares about.
  2. Act: call exactly one public method.
  3. Assert: check the outcome. Prefer asserting on state or return value over asserting on which private method was called.

The most reliable unit tests target code that has no dependencies at all. Push logic into the aggregate and value objects (see Part 14 — Domain-Driven Design) and the tests become trivial.

Practical example — the Order aggregate

The aggregate holds the invariants: an order cannot be empty, quantities must be positive, and only certain state transitions are legal.

TypeScript
// src/orders/domain/order.ts
export type OrderStatus = 'PENDING' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED' | 'CANCELLED';

export class DomainError extends Error {}

export interface OrderLine { sku: string; unitPriceCents: number; qty: number }

export class Order {
  private constructor(
    public readonly id: string,
    public readonly customerId: string,
    private lines: OrderLine[],
    private status: OrderStatus,
  ) {}

  static place(id: string, customerId: string, lines: OrderLine[]): Order {
    if (lines.length === 0) throw new DomainError('order must have at least one line');
    for (const l of lines) {
      if (!Number.isInteger(l.qty) || l.qty <= 0) throw new DomainError(`invalid qty for ${l.sku}`);
      if (l.unitPriceCents < 0) throw new DomainError(`negative price for ${l.sku}`);
    }
    return new Order(id, customerId, [...lines], 'PENDING');
  }

  get totalCents(): number {
    // integer cents only; never floats for money
    return this.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.unitPriceCents * l.qty, 0);
  }

  getStatus(): OrderStatus { return this.status; }

  markPaid(): void { this.transition('PENDING', 'PAID'); }
  ship(): void { this.transition('PAID', 'SHIPPED'); }
  cancel(): void {
    if (this.status === 'SHIPPED') throw new DomainError('cannot cancel a shipped order');
    this.status = 'CANCELLED';
  }

  private transition(from: OrderStatus, to: OrderStatus) {
    if (this.status !== from) throw new DomainError(`cannot go from ${this.status} to ${to}`);
    this.status = to;
  }
}

The tests read like a specification:

TypeScript
// src/orders/domain/order.spec.ts
import { Order, DomainError } from './order';
import { anOrderLine } from '../../../test/builders/order-line.builder';

describe('Order aggregate', () => {
  it('rejects an order with no lines', () => {
    expect(() => Order.place('o1', 'c1', [])).toThrow(DomainError);
  });

  it('rejects a non-positive quantity', () => {
    const line = anOrderLine({ qty: 0 });
    expect(() => Order.place('o1', 'c1', [line])).toThrow(/invalid qty/);
  });

  it('computes the total in integer cents', () => {
    const order = Order.place('o1', 'c1', [
      anOrderLine({ unitPriceCents: 1999, qty: 3 }),
      anOrderLine({ unitPriceCents: 501, qty: 1 }),
    ]);
    expect(order.totalCents).toBe(1999 * 3 + 501);
  });

  it('moves PENDING to PAID to SHIPPED', () => {
    const order = Order.place('o1', 'c1', [anOrderLine()]);
    order.markPaid();
    order.ship();
    expect(order.getStatus()).toBe('SHIPPED');
  });

  it('refuses to ship an unpaid order', () => {
    const order = Order.place('o1', 'c1', [anOrderLine()]);
    expect(() => order.ship()).toThrow(/cannot go from PENDING to SHIPPED/);
  });

  it('refuses to cancel a shipped order', () => {
    const order = Order.place('o1', 'c1', [anOrderLine()]);
    order.markPaid();
    order.ship();
    expect(() => order.cancel()).toThrow(DomainError);
  });
});

Every test name is a sentence. Every test asserts one behaviour. No mocks anywhere, because the aggregate has no dependencies. When a product manager asks "what happens if I cancel after shipping?", the answer is a test name.

NestJS example — a service with fakes

Services orchestrate: load data, call the aggregate, persist, publish. Their unit tests replace the collaborators with fakes and assert on orchestration behaviour.

TypeScript
// src/orders/place-order.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Order, OrderLine } from './domain/order';

export interface OrderRepository {
  findByIdempotencyKey(key: string): Promise<Order | null>;
  save(order: Order, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void>;
}
export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(input: { orderId: string; amountCents: number }): Promise<{ paymentId: string }>;
}
export interface Clock { now(): Date }
export interface IdGenerator { next(): string }

export const ORDER_REPOSITORY = Symbol('ORDER_REPOSITORY');
export const PAYMENT_GATEWAY = Symbol('PAYMENT_GATEWAY');
export const CLOCK = Symbol('CLOCK');
export const ID_GENERATOR = Symbol('ID_GENERATOR');

@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderService {
  constructor(
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    @Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAY) private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
    @Inject(CLOCK) private readonly clock: Clock,
    @Inject(ID_GENERATOR) private readonly ids: IdGenerator,
  ) {}

  async execute(customerId: string, lines: OrderLine[], idempotencyKey: string): Promise<Order> {
    const existing = await this.orders.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey);
    if (existing) return existing; // idempotent replay

    const order = Order.place(this.ids.next(), customerId, lines);
    await this.payments.charge({ orderId: order.id, amountCents: order.totalCents });
    order.markPaid();
    await this.orders.save(order, idempotencyKey);
    return order;
  }
}

(Inject comes from @nestjs/common; the import is omitted above to keep the sample focused.) The unit test uses an in-memory fake repository and a Jest mock for the gateway:

TypeScript
// src/orders/place-order.service.spec.ts
import { PlaceOrderService, PaymentGateway } from './place-order.service';
import { InMemoryOrderRepository } from '../../test/fakes/in-memory-order.repository';
import { anOrderLine } from '../../test/builders/order-line.builder';

describe('PlaceOrderService', () => {
  let repo: InMemoryOrderRepository;
  let gateway: jest.Mocked<PaymentGateway>;
  let service: PlaceOrderService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    gateway = { charge: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ paymentId: 'pay_1' }) };
    const clock = { now: () => new Date('2026-09-06T10:00:00Z') };
    const ids = { next: jest.fn().mockReturnValue('order-1') };
    service = new PlaceOrderService(repo, gateway, clock, ids);
  });

  it('charges the exact order total and persists a PAID order', async () => {
    const order = await service.execute('cust-1', [anOrderLine({ unitPriceCents: 2500, qty: 2 })], 'idem-1');

    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ orderId: 'order-1', amountCents: 5000 });
    expect(order.getStatus()).toBe('PAID');
    expect(await repo.findByIdempotencyKey('idem-1')).toBe(order);
  });

  it('returns the existing order and does not charge again on idempotent replay', async () => {
    await service.execute('cust-1', [anOrderLine()], 'idem-1');
    const second = await service.execute('cust-1', [anOrderLine()], 'idem-1');

    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(second.id).toBe('order-1');
  });

  it('does not persist the order when the charge fails', async () => {
    gateway.charge.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('card declined'));

    await expect(service.execute('cust-1', [anOrderLine()], 'idem-2')).rejects.toThrow('card declined');
    expect(await repo.findByIdempotencyKey('idem-2')).toBeNull();
  });
});
