Note what is asserted: the gateway was charged with the right amount (that is the behaviour), the order is persisted, replays are safe. Note what is not asserted: the order in which private methods ran, or that repo.save was called with a specific internal shape. That is implementation detail and testing it makes refactoring painful.

Failure scenario

A team had a PricingService.spec.ts with 140 tests, all green, and a production incident where every order in one region was charged 0.00. The root cause: tax rates were loaded from the tax_rates table, and the region's row had rate = NULL. NULL * price in TypeScript became NaN, then Math.round(NaN) became NaN, then the ORM wrote it as NULL, then the payment gateway received amount: null and defaulted to zero. Not one of the 140 tests loaded a rate from a database; they all passed rates in as numbers. A single integration test that seeded a real row with NULL would have failed. The lesson is not "unit tests are bad"; it is "unit tests are blind to the boundary, so the boundary needs its own tests".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Tests that assert on toHaveBeenCalledWith for every collaborator become a mirror of the implementation; any refactor breaks them without any behaviour change.
  • Number money arithmetic (19.99 * 3) produces 59.97000000000001; test with integer cents and the tests will force you into the right design.
  • Tests that construct entities with 20 fields inline drift from the real shape; use builders.
  • Tests that depend on Date.now() pass on the day they are written and fail on the first day of the next month.
  • async tests without await on the assertion pass trivially; always await expect(...).rejects.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They push logic down into classes with no dependencies so that most rules can be unit tested with zero doubles. They inject time, randomness and ids as small interfaces (Clock, IdGenerator) so the service is deterministic. They resist mocking anything they own: if a service is hard to unit test because it needs six mocks, they treat that as a design smell (the service is doing too much) rather than a testing problem.

Common mistakes

  • Naming tests after methods (test execute()) instead of behaviours (does not charge twice on replay).
  • Asserting multiple unrelated things in one test, so the first failure hides the rest.
  • Sharing mutable fixtures across tests via module-level let without beforeEach reset.
  • Mocking the class under test's own private methods with jest.spyOn(service as any, 'validate').
  • Using toEqual on huge objects instead of asserting the field that matters.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a unit test brittle?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: coupling to implementation details (call order, private methods, internal data shapes). Follow-up: how do you refactor a brittle test?
  2. How do you unit test code that depends on the current time?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inject a Clock; in tests supply a fixed one. Fake timers are a second option with pitfalls (section 41.11).
  3. Should a service unit test verify that repository.save was called?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: only if persistence is the behaviour under test and there is no better observable outcome; prefer an in-memory fake and assert on what can be read back.

Practical exercise

Extract a Money value object (integer cents, currency code) from the Order aggregate. Write unit tests for: adding two amounts, multiplying by a quantity, rejecting mixed currencies, and rounding a percentage discount half-up. Acceptance: all tests are pure (no doubles), each test name is a full sentence, and 19.99 * 3 style float arithmetic cannot appear anywhere because the type does not allow it.

41.4 Test doubles: dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake

Concept

A test double is any object that stands in for a real dependency in a test. The five kinds have precise meanings, and using the right word makes design conversations clearer:

Double What it does Jest API Example
Dummy Passed to satisfy a signature, never used a plain object or {} as X A Logger passed to a constructor when the test never logs
Stub Returns canned answers, no assertions on it jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(...) rates.getFor('IN') returns 0.18
Spy Wraps the real thing and records calls jest.spyOn(obj, 'method') Verify metrics.increment('orders.placed') was called while the real metrics client runs
Mock Pre-programmed with expectations; test fails if they are not met jest.fn() plus expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...) gateway.charge must be called once with the right amount
Fake A working, simplified implementation Hand-written class InMemoryOrderRepository backed by a Map

Why does it exist?

A dependency is replaced for three reasons: it is slow (network, disk), it is non-deterministic (time, random, third-party outages), or it is expensive or dangerous to call for real (charging a card, sending an SMS). Each reason maps to a different double. Slow-but-deterministic (a database) is best handled by a real instance in a container, not by a double, which is why section 41.5 exists.

Mental model

Imagine a fire drill. The alarm is real (spy: we record that it rang). The fire is a stub (a sign saying "fire here"). The fire brigade is a mock (we expect them to be called exactly once). The evacuation route is a fake (a real route through the building, just shorter). The receptionist's phone is a dummy (it is on the desk, nobody uses it).

How it works — the Jest APIs

TypeScript
// stub: canned answer, no expectations
const rates = { getFor: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(0.18) };

// mock: expectation on the interaction
const sms = { send: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) };
await service.notify(order);
expect(sms.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ to: '+91...' }));

// spy: keep real behaviour, observe calls
const spy = jest.spyOn(metrics, 'increment');
await service.execute(...);
expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('orders.placed');
spy.mockRestore(); // always restore in afterEach

// spy with replaced behaviour (be careful: this is now a stub on a real object)
jest.spyOn(Date, 'now').mockReturnValue(1_757_152_800_000);

A fake is a real class. It is the most valuable double because it can be reused across dozens of tests and it behaves consistently:

TypeScript
// test/fakes/in-memory-order.repository.ts
import { Order } from '../../src/orders/domain/order';
import { OrderRepository } from '../../src/orders/place-order.service';

export class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  private byKey = new Map<string, Order>();
  private byId = new Map<string, Order>();

  async findByIdempotencyKey(key: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    return this.byKey.get(key) ?? null;
  }

  async save(order: Order, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void> {
    if (this.byKey.has(idempotencyKey) && this.byKey.get(idempotencyKey)!.id !== order.id) {
      // mimic the UNIQUE constraint so unit tests see the same failure shape
      throw new Error('duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_idempotency_key_key"');
    }
    this.byKey.set(idempotencyKey, order);
    this.byId.set(order.id, order);
  }

  // helper for assertions only, not part of the interface
  all(): Order[] { return [...this.byId.values()]; }
}

The fake mimics the one database rule the service depends on (uniqueness). This is the honest boundary of a fake: it can model rules you know about. It cannot model rules you forgot, which is why the integration test still exists.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • jest.spyOn without mockRestore leaks into other tests in the same file; use afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks()).
  • jest.fn() with no implementation returns undefined; an await on it resolves to undefined and code that does result.id throws a confusing TypeError far from the cause.
  • Fakes drift from the real implementation. Run the same behavioural test suite against the fake and the real repository ("contract tests for fakes") to keep them honest.
  • jest.mock('../module') auto-mocks every export; an accidental auto-mock of a utility module turns real logic into undefined-returning stubs and tests still pass.

Common mistakes

  • Calling everything a "mock". A stub and a mock have different failure modes: an unmet mock expectation fails the test; an unused stub silently does nothing.
  • Using a mock where a fake would make ten tests simpler.
  • Spying on the object under test itself.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a stub supplies answers; a mock verifies interactions. Follow-up: when is verifying an interaction the right assertion?
  2. When would you write a fake instead of using jest.fn()?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when the dependency has state that multiple tests rely on (a repository, a cache, a queue) and you want consistent behaviour across tests.
  3. How do you keep a fake from drifting away from the real implementation?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: run the same contract test suite against both.

41.5 What SHOULD and SHOULD NOT be mocked

This section is the one to bookmark. Most bad test suites are bad because of a wrong answer to this question.

Concept

The rule: mock what you do not own and cannot control; run for real what you do own and can control. Third-party HTTP, time, randomness and the network are not yours. Your database schema, your ORM configuration, your transactions, your modules and your own services are yours, and running them for real is cheap once you have containers.

The definitive table

Dependency Unit test Integration test E2E test Why
Third-party HTTP (payment gateway, email/SMS provider, shipping API) Mock or stub the client interface Stub the client interface, or nock nock/msw at the network boundary You cannot control it, it costs money, it is slow and non-deterministic
Time (Date.now, cron schedules, TTL expiry) Inject a Clock or use fake timers Inject a Clock; avoid fake timers with real DB calls Inject a Clock via config Real time makes tests non-deterministic and slow
Randomness / ids (crypto.randomUUID, Math.random) Inject an IdGenerator or seed Inject Usually real (assert on shape, not value) Deterministic assertions
Message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ producer) Mock the producer interface Real container, or outbox table assertion Real container or outbox assertion The publish call is a behaviour, but the broker semantics matter for consumers
Message broker consumer logic Unit test the handler with a fake message Real container with real messages Rarely Ordering, retries, rebalancing only show up for real
PostgreSQL Not present (pure logic only) Never mock. Real container. Real container Constraints, transactions, locks, types, NULL handling, plans
Redis Fake (in-memory Map) acceptable Real container Real container TTL and atomic ops (SET NX, Lua) behave differently in fakes
ORM (repository.find, queryBuilder) Not present Never mock. Never mock Mocking repository.find tests that you called find, nothing more
Your own modules and services Fake at interface boundaries only when needed Real Real Mocking your own internals hides wiring bugs
NestJS guards/pipes/interceptors Unit test them in isolation Real, or overrideGuard for auth convenience Real (with a test JWT) They are yours
Filesystem / S3 Fake or in-memory LocalStack or MinIO container, or a fake Container or fake External and slow
Logger, metrics Dummy or spy Real (silent) Real (silent) Rarely the behaviour under test
Environment config Plain object Plain object or .env.test .env.test Never read real secrets in tests

Why mocking the ORM tests nothing real

Consider this common "repository test":

TypeScript
// anti-pattern: this test can never fail for a real reason
it('finds orders by customer', async () => {
  const repo = { find: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue([{ id: 'o1' }]) };
  const service = new OrdersQueryService(repo as any);
  expect(await service.forCustomer('c1')).toEqual([{ id: 'o1' }]);
  expect(repo.find).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ where: { customerId: 'c1' } });
});

What can break in production here? The column might be named customer_id and the entity mapping wrong. The where might need deletedAt: IsNull(). The query might need an index and time out on 40 million rows. The result might need ordering. None of that is visible to this test; it only checks that a JavaScript object was passed to a function. The test is green, the query is broken, and the team thinks the repository is "covered".

The same test against a real database in a container is about 20 lines and catches all of the above:

TypeScript
it('finds only the customer\'s non-deleted orders, newest first', async () => {
  await seedOrders(dataSource, [
    anOrder({ customerId: 'c1', createdAt: '2026-09-01' }),
    anOrder({ customerId: 'c1', createdAt: '2026-09-03' }),
    anOrder({ customerId: 'c1', deletedAt: '2026-09-02' }),
    anOrder({ customerId: 'c2' }),
  ]);
  const result = await service.forCustomer('c1');
  expect(result.map((o) => o.createdAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10))).toEqual(['2026-09-03', '2026-09-01']);
});

When an in-memory fake is acceptable

  • At the unit level, for a repository or cache interface you defined and the test is about orchestration, not persistence.
  • When the fake is verified by the same contract tests as the real implementation.
  • When the rule the fake models is simple and stable (uniqueness by key, TTL expiry as "now > expiresAt").

An in-memory fake is not acceptable as a substitute for integration tests of queries, transactions, locks, migrations or constraints.

A special warning about pg-mem. It is an in-memory PostgreSQL emulator for Node with a TypeORM adapter (newDb().adapters.createTypeormDataSource(...)). It is fast and fun, and it is not PostgreSQL. It does not implement large parts of the language: many functions, partial and expression indexes, FOR UPDATE semantics, most of ON CONFLICT, advisory locks, extensions and real transaction isolation. A test that passes on pg-mem and fails on PostgreSQL is a common story. Use it only for throwaway experiments, never for the tests that gate a deploy. Testcontainers starts a real PostgreSQL in about two seconds; that cost is worth paying.

The "mock everything" anti-pattern

The story repeats in every company. A team is told to reach 80% coverage. The fastest way is to mock every dependency of every class and assert that the mocks were called. Coverage hits 85%. The suite runs in 9 seconds. Six months later:

  • A migration renames orders.total to orders.total_cents; the entity is updated; a raw SQL report query is not. Tests: green. Production: 500s on the finance dashboard.
  • A developer wraps two writes in a transaction but passes the wrong EntityManager to the second one; it runs outside the transaction. Tests: green (the mock manager.save was "called"). Production: orders with missing items after a partial failure.
  • nock is never used; the payment client is mocked at the class level. The provider changes a response field from id to payment_id. Tests: green. Production: undefined stored as payment_id, every refund fails.

The suite was green for every one of these because it never ran anything real. The fix is not more mocks. The fix is the table above.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They draw the boundary at "things I do not own". Inside the boundary, everything runs for real in tests, because the cost of a container is small and the cost of a hidden wiring bug is an incident. They accept that this makes the integration suite slower than a mocked suite, and they invest in container reuse, parallel schemas and test sharding to keep it under budget rather than retreating to mocks. When a colleague proposes mocking DataSource "just for speed", they ask which production bug the resulting test would catch.

Interview questions

  1. Should you mock the database in a repository test?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; a repository test that mocks the database tests nothing. Use a real database in a container. Follow-up: how do you keep it fast?
  2. What do you mock in an e2e test?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: only systems you do not own, at the network boundary (nock/msw), plus time and possibly ids.
  3. What is wrong with pg-mem for gating tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it is not PostgreSQL; it lacks many features and semantics (locks, isolation, partial indexes, functions), so green on pg-mem does not imply green on PostgreSQL.
  4. Give an example of a bug that a fully mocked suite cannot catch.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a unique constraint violation, a query outside the transaction, a column rename, a third-party response shape change.

Practical exercise

Take one existing test in your codebase that mocks Repository or DataSource. Rewrite it against a Testcontainers PostgreSQL. Then introduce a deliberate bug the old test could not see (rename a column in the entity but not in a raw query, or drop the where clause) and confirm the new test fails. Acceptance: the old test is deleted, the new test runs in under 300 ms after container startup, and the deliberate bug is caught.

41.6 Fixtures, factories and builders

Concept

A fixture is data that exists before a test runs. A factory (or builder) is a function that creates a valid object or row with sensible defaults, letting the test override only what matters. The difference decides whether your suite is readable at 500 tests or a swamp of copy-pasted 30-field object literals.

Why does it exist?

Every test needs a valid Order, a valid Customer, a valid Product. If each test builds them inline, the first schema change (adding a required currency column) touches 300 files. If tests share one giant fixtures.json, every test depends on every row in it, nobody dares delete a row, and the file becomes a second, undocumented schema. This is fixture drift: the test data slowly stops looking like production data, and tests keep passing on shapes production never sees.

Mental model

Imagine a film set. The props department has a standard "office desk" kit: a lamp, a phone, three folders. A scene that needs a red folder asks for the standard kit with one red folder. Nobody rebuilds the desk from raw wood per scene, and nobody drags a single shared desk between every set (someone would eventually knock the lamp over in scene 12 and break scene 40).

How it works

  1. One builder per aggregate or table, living under test/builders/.
  2. Defaults are valid and boring: a normal customer, an in-stock product, a small order.
  3. Randomised fields use @faker-js/faker with a fixed seed so failures reproduce.
  4. Overrides are a partial object merged on top.
  5. A separate seed* helper writes the built objects to the real database in integration tests, returning the persisted rows (with generated ids).
TypeScript
// test/builders/order-line.builder.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { OrderLine } from '../../src/orders/domain/order';

faker.seed(20260906); // deterministic across runs; change on purpose only

export function anOrderLine(overrides: Partial<OrderLine> = {}): OrderLine {
  return {
    sku: `SKU-${faker.string.alphanumeric({ length: 8, casing: 'upper' })}`,
    unitPriceCents: faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 }),
    qty: faker.number.int({ min: 1, max: 5 }),
    ...overrides,
  };
}
TypeScript
// test/builders/product.builder.ts
import { faker } from '@faker-js/faker';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Product } from '../../src/products/product.entity';

export function aProduct(overrides: Partial<Product> = {}): Product {
  const p = new Product();
  p.sku = `SKU-${faker.string.alphanumeric({ length: 8, casing: 'upper' })}`;
  p.name = faker.commerce.productName();
  p.priceCents = faker.number.int({ min: 100, max: 50_000 });
  p.stock = 10;
  Object.assign(p, overrides);
  return p;
}

export async function seedProducts(ds: DataSource, products: Product[]): Promise<Product[]> {
  // save() returns entities with generated columns filled in
  return ds.getRepository(Product).save(products);
}

A test then reads as intent:

TypeScript
const [last] = await seedProducts(ds, [aProduct({ stock: 1, priceCents: 9_999 })]);

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unseeded faker produces a different email each run; a unique-constraint failure appears once a month and nobody can reproduce it.
  • Builders that default stock: 0 make half the tests fail for the wrong reason. Defaults must be the happy path.
  • A builder that generates a random createdAt "in the past" occasionally lands on a daylight-saving boundary and breaks a date-diff assertion. Pin dates unless the test is about dates.
  • Seeding via the ORM runs entity hooks and default values; seeding via raw SQL bypasses them. Choose deliberately; if your production writes go through the ORM, seed through the ORM.

Common mistakes

  • One fixtures.sql with 4,000 rows loaded in beforeAll. Every test depends on all of it.
  • Builders that hit the database implicitly on construction, making unit tests secretly integration tests.
  • Overriding ids by hand (id: 1) and colliding with sequences later in the same test file.

Interview questions

  1. What is fixture drift and how do you prevent it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: test data diverging from production shapes over time; prevent with builders that default from the real entity and with integration tests that go through real migrations.
  2. Why seed faker?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: reproducibility; a failing test must fail the same way tomorrow.

41.7 Integration testing with a real PostgreSQL (Testcontainers)

Concept

An integration test runs your real code (service, repository, ORM configuration, migrations) against a real dependency (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) that is started just for the test run. Testcontainers is a library that starts Docker containers from test code, waits for them to be ready, hands you the connection details, and stops them afterwards.

Why does it exist?

The bugs unit tests cannot see are exactly the ones a real database exposes: a NOT NULL you forgot, a UNIQUE that fires on retry, a foreign key that blocks a delete, a FOR UPDATE that does not lock what you think, a migration that does not match the entity, a timestamp vs timestamptz mismatch, a query plan that seq-scans 30 million rows. Every one of those has caused a production incident that a mocked repository could not have prevented. Integration tests are the cheapest place to find them.

Mental model

Imagine a flight simulator. It is not a real flight, but the instruments, the physics and the failure modes are real. Pilots train on it because a checklist on paper (unit tests) does not prepare you for what the aircraft actually does when an engine fails.

How it works

  1. Global setup starts one PostgreSQL container for the whole run (startup about 1.5–3 s for postgres:16-alpine on a warm Docker cache). Starting one per test file would multiply that by the number of files.
  2. The connection URI is shared with workers through environment variables (set in global setup) or a temp file.
  3. Migrations run once against the container. Never use synchronize: true in tests; it creates a schema from entities that can differ from what migrations create in production (section 41.20 lists the incident).
  4. Each Jest worker gets an isolated slice of the database (a schema or a database per worker) so parallel files do not interfere.
  5. Each test gets a clean state using one of the isolation strategies below.
  6. Global teardown stops the container.

The per-test isolation strategies, with tradeoffs:

Strategy Speed Isolation Works with Catches Fails on
Transaction rollback (open BEGIN before test, ROLLBACK after) Fastest (no I/O for cleanup) Per test Code that accepts an injected EntityManager/QueryRunner Most SQL bugs Code that opens its own transactions (nested BEGIN is a savepoint, COMMIT inside commits the savepoint, not the outer), concurrency tests, anything that needs another connection to see the data
Truncate all tables after each test (TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE) Fast (about 5–20 ms for 30 tables) Per test Any code Everything including real transactions and concurrency Tests running in parallel in the same schema
Schema per worker + truncate Fast Per worker and per test Any code, parallel files Everything Slight setup cost (migrations per schema)
Database per worker (CREATE DATABASE w1 TEMPLATE app_test) Medium (template copy about 100–300 ms) Strongest Any code Everything Slower start; connection limits with many workers
Fresh container per file Slowest (2–3 s per file) Strongest Any code Everything CI budget; Docker resource limits

The recommended default for a NestJS + TypeORM/Sequelize service is schema per worker plus truncate after each test. It works with real transactions and with concurrency tests, and it lets Jest run files in parallel.

Practical example — global setup with Testcontainers

TypeScript
// test/global-setup.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:os';

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const container: StartedPostgreSqlContainer = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withDatabase('app_test')
    .withUsername('app')
    .withPassword('app')
    // fsync off makes the test DB much faster; never do this in production
    .withCommand(['postgres', '-c', 'fsync=off', '-c', 'synchronous_commit=off', '-c', 'full_page_writes=off'])
    .start();

  const uri = container.getConnectionUri();
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL = uri;

  // Workers are separate processes: persist what they need on disk
  writeFileSync(join(process.cwd(), '.test-db.json'), JSON.stringify({ uri }));

  // Keep a handle for teardown
  (globalThis as any).__PG_CONTAINER__ = container;

  // Create one schema per potential worker and migrate each once
  const admin = new DataSource({ type: 'postgres', url: uri });
  await admin.initialize();
  const workers = Number(process.env.JEST_MAX_WORKERS ?? 4);
  for (let w = 1; w <= workers; w++) {
    await admin.query(`CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS w${w}`);
    const ds = new DataSource({
      type: 'postgres', url: uri, schema: `w${w}`,
      migrations: ['src/migrations/*.ts'], migrationsTableName: 'migrations',
    });
    await ds.initialize();
    await ds.runMigrations();
    await ds.destroy();
  }
  await admin.destroy();
}
TypeScript
// test/global-teardown.ts
export default async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  await (globalThis as any).__PG_CONTAINER__?.stop();
}
TypeScript
// test/db.ts  (used by every integration test file)
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

export function workerSchema(): string {
  // JEST_WORKER_ID is "1", "2", ... per worker process
  return `w${process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID ?? '1'}`;
}

export async function createTestDataSource(entities: Function[]): Promise<DataSource> {
  const { uri } = JSON.parse(readFileSync('.test-db.json', 'utf8'));
  const ds = new DataSource({
    type: 'postgres', url: uri, schema: workerSchema(), entities,
    synchronize: false, logging: process.env.SQL_LOG === '1' ? 'all' : false,
    extra: { max: 5 },
  });
  return ds.initialize();
}

export async function truncateAll(ds: DataSource): Promise<void> {
  const schema = workerSchema();
  const tables = await ds.query(
    `SELECT tablename FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = $1 AND tablename <> 'migrations'`, [schema],
  );
  if (tables.length === 0) return;
  const list = tables.map((t: { tablename: string }) => `"${schema}"."${t.tablename}"`).join(', ');
  await ds.query(`TRUNCATE ${list} RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE`);
}
TypeScript
// jest.integration.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';
const config: Config = {
  rootDir: '.',
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.int-spec.ts'],
  globalSetup: '<rootDir>/test/global-setup.ts',
  globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/test/global-teardown.ts',
  testTimeout: 30_000,
  maxWorkers: 4,
  transform: { '^.+\\.ts$': 'ts-jest' },
};
export default config;

NestJS example — a repository test with real constraints

TypeScript
// src/orders/typeorm-order.repository.int-spec.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { createTestDataSource, truncateAll } from '../../test/db';
import { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';
import { OrderItemEntity } from './order-item.entity';
import { TypeormOrderRepository } from './typeorm-order.repository';
import { Order } from './domain/order';
import { anOrderLine } from '../../test/builders/order-line.builder';

describe('TypeormOrderRepository (integration)', () => {
  let ds: DataSource;
  let repo: TypeormOrderRepository;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    ds = await createTestDataSource([OrderEntity, OrderItemEntity]);
    repo = new TypeormOrderRepository(ds);
  });
  afterEach(() => truncateAll(ds));
  afterAll(() => ds.destroy());

  it('persists an order with its items and reads it back by idempotency key', async () => {
    const order = Order.place('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'cust-1', [anOrderLine({ qty: 2 })]);
    await repo.save(order, 'idem-1');

    const found = await repo.findByIdempotencyKey('idem-1');
    expect(found?.id).toBe(order.id);
    expect(found?.totalCents).toBe(order.totalCents);
  });

  it('rejects a second order with the same idempotency key at the database', async () => {
    const a = Order.place('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'cust-1', [anOrderLine()]);
    const b = Order.place('22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222', 'cust-1', [anOrderLine()]);
    await repo.save(a, 'idem-1');

    await expect(repo.save(b, 'idem-1')).rejects.toMatchObject({ code: '23505' }); // unique_violation
    const rows = await ds.query(`SELECT count(*)::int AS n FROM orders`);
    expect(rows[0].n).toBe(1);
  });
});

The second test is impossible with a mocked repository and it is the one that protects you from double-charging on client retries. 23505 is the PostgreSQL SQLSTATE for unique_violation; asserting on it, not on the message text, is stable across PostgreSQL versions.

PostgreSQL example — proving a plan inside a test

Integration tests can assert on EXPLAIN output. This is the only automated way to catch "someone dropped the index in a migration" or "the query stopped using the index after a refactor":

TypeScript
it('uses the customer index for the order list query', async () => {
  const sql = `SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`;
  const plan = await ds.query(`EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) ${sql}`, ['cust-1']);
  const root = plan[0]['QUERY PLAN'][0]['Plan'];
  // Walk to the scan node; with LIMIT it is usually Limit -> Index Scan
  const scan = root['Plans']?.[0] ?? root;
  expect(scan['Node Type']).toMatch(/Index Scan|Index Only Scan/);
  expect(scan['Index Name']).toBe('idx_orders_customer_created');
});

Be careful: on an empty table the planner may prefer a sequential scan because it is cheap, and the test will fail for the wrong reason. Seed a few thousand rows first, run ANALYZE, and then assert. Alternatively set enable_seqscan = off for the session and assert only that the index exists and is usable, which is a weaker but stabler claim.

Sequelize example — the same setup

TypeScript
// test/sequelize-db.ts
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize-typescript';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { OrderModel } from '../src/orders/order.model';

export async function createTestSequelize(): Promise<Sequelize> {
  const { uri } = JSON.parse(readFileSync('.test-db.json', 'utf8'));
  const schema = `w${process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID ?? '1'}`;
  const sequelize = new Sequelize(uri, {
    dialect: 'postgres', logging: false, schema,
    models: [OrderModel],
    define: { schema },
    pool: { max: 5 },
  });
  await sequelize.authenticate();
  // Do NOT call sequelize.sync(); the schema was created by migrations in global setup
  return sequelize;
}

With Sequelize the temptation is sequelize.sync({ force: true }). It is the same trap as TypeORM's synchronize: a schema generated from models, not from migrations. Run migrations (with umzug or sequelize-cli db:migrate) in global setup instead.

Testing Redis and Kafka with containers

Redis starts in under a second and is worth running for real whenever TTLs, SET NX, Lua scripts or pub/sub are involved:

TypeScript
// test/redis-setup.ts
import { RedisContainer } from '@testcontainers/redis';

export async function startRedis() {
  const container = await new RedisContainer('redis:7-alpine').start();
  return { container, url: container.getConnectionUrl() }; // redis://host:port
}

A rate-limiter test with real Redis:

TypeScript
it('allows 10 requests per minute per key then rejects', async () => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) expect(await limiter.tryAcquire('cust-1')).toBe(true);
  expect(await limiter.tryAcquire('cust-1')).toBe(false);
  const ttl = await redis.ttl('rl:cust-1');
  expect(ttl).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  expect(ttl).toBeLessThanOrEqual(60);
});

Kafka takes longer to start (about 8–20 s for a single-broker confluentinc/cp-kafka image, faster with the KRaft-mode images) and is worth it for consumer tests: at-least-once handling, idempotent processing, and the consumer surviving a poison message.

TypeScript
// test/kafka-setup.ts
import { KafkaContainer } from '@testcontainers/kafka';

export async function startKafka() {
  const container = await new KafkaContainer('confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0').withExposedPorts(9093).start();
  const brokers = [`${container.getHost()}:${container.getMappedPort(9093)}`];
  return { container, brokers };
}
TypeScript
// src/inventory/stock-consumer.int-spec.ts (excerpt)
import { Kafka } from 'kafkajs';

it('processes a duplicate order.placed message exactly once', async () => {
  const producer = kafka.producer();
  await producer.connect();
  const message = { key: 'order-1', value: JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'order-1', sku: 'SKU-1', qty: 2 }) };
  await producer.send({ topic: 'order.placed', messages: [message, message] }); // duplicate on purpose
  await producer.disconnect();

  await waitFor(async () => (await stockOf(ds, 'SKU-1')) === 8, { timeoutMs: 10_000 });
  // still 8 after the duplicate: the consumer's processed_messages table did its job
  await expect(waitFor(async () => (await stockOf(ds, 'SKU-1')) < 8, { timeoutMs: 1_500 })).rejects.toThrow();
});

(waitFor is the polling helper from section 41.10.)

Production scenario — container lifecycle and CI

A typical orders service suite: 380 unit tests (6 s), 140 integration tests (55 s including 3 s container start), 35 e2e tests (70 s). In CI on GitHub Actions the runner already has Docker, so Testcontainers works with no extra configuration. Two ways to provide containers in CI:

  • Docker on the runner (GitHub-hosted runners, GitLab with Docker-in-Docker or the Docker socket mounted): Testcontainers starts containers itself, the same as on a laptop. Simplest; startup cost paid per job.
  • Service containers (services: in GitHub Actions, services: in GitLab CI): the CI starts PostgreSQL alongside the job; your global setup detects TEST_DATABASE_URL and skips Testcontainers. Faster start, but the test environment now differs between laptop and CI, which is a small but real source of "works on my machine".
YAML
  # .github/workflows/test.yml (integration job, Testcontainers on the runner)
jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED: 'false'   # Ryuk reaps containers if the job is killed
          JEST_MAX_WORKERS: '4'

Reuse across suites: set TESTCONTAINERS_REUSE_ENABLE=true and call .withReuse() on the container to keep it running between local runs; the second run then skips the 2–3 s startup. Do not enable reuse in CI, where each job should start clean.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on a Monday the integration job started failing with Error: Could not find a working container runtime strategy on 30% of runs. The CI provider had moved to a new runner image where the Docker socket path changed. Locally everything passed. The team lost half a day before finding the DOCKER_HOST environment variable. The lesson: container-based tests add a dependency on the CI environment; pin runner images, set DOCKER_HOST explicitly, and keep a fallback path where TEST_DATABASE_URL from a service container is honoured so a broken Docker socket does not block every merge.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Container startup timeout in CI (default 60 s) when the image is not cached and the registry is slow; pre-pull images in a cached layer or use a smaller image (-alpine).
  • Exhausting the PostgreSQL max_connections (default 100) with many workers each holding a pool of 10: set extra.max to a small number in tests.
  • TRUNCATE waiting on a lock held by a leaked open transaction from a previous test; add SET lock_timeout = '5s' in the test connection so the leak surfaces as an error with a stack trace instead of a hang.
  • Migrations that depend on extensions (uuid-ossp, pgcrypto, pg_trgm) fail on a plain image; run CREATE EXTENSION in global setup or use an image that includes them.
  • Time zone: the container runs in UTC; a developer laptop may be in IST. A test that compares DATE(created_at) with a JS Date passes on one and fails on the other. Set TZ=UTC for the Node process in tests and in production.
  • Windows and macOS Docker Desktop are slower at file I/O; a suite that takes 50 s on Linux CI may take 3 minutes locally. Use tmpfs for the data directory (.withTmpFs({ '/var/lib/postgresql/data': 'rw' })) to speed it up.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They budget the container cost once (global setup) and never per test. They choose the isolation strategy based on what the tests need to prove: transaction rollback is elegant but it cannot prove concurrency or real transaction behaviour, so they default to truncate and accept the few milliseconds. They treat the integration suite as the primary safety net for anything touching SQL and refuse to merge a repository or migration change without one.

Common mistakes

  • synchronize: true in the test DataSource. The schema under test is not the schema in production.
  • One shared database for parallel Jest workers, then "fixing" flakiness with --runInBand, then the suite takes 12 minutes.
  • Asserting on ORM-returned objects with toEqual including createdAt, so every test is time-sensitive.
  • Leaving the pool open (ds.destroy() missing in afterAll), so Jest prints "did not exit one second after the test run" and CI hangs.
  • Starting Kafka per test file. Start it once in global setup.

Interview questions

  1. Compare transaction-rollback isolation with truncation.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rollback is fastest and gives per-test isolation but cannot test code that manages its own transactions or concurrency across connections; truncate is universal at a small cost.
  2. How do you run integration tests in parallel against one PostgreSQL container?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: schema or database per Jest worker, keyed by JEST_WORKER_ID.
  3. Why not synchronize: true in tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it creates a schema from entities that can differ from what migrations create; tests then pass on a schema production does not have.
  4. How do you test that a query uses an index?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) in the test, after seeding enough rows and running ANALYZE.

Practical exercise

Set up Testcontainers global setup with schema-per-worker for a service with three tables. Write integration tests for: a unique constraint violation on retry (assert SQLSTATE 23505), a foreign key preventing deletion of a product with orders (assert 23503), and a CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint rejecting an oversell (assert 23514). Acceptance: the suite runs with maxWorkers: 4 without interference, total runtime under 30 s on a laptop, and each test fails if the corresponding constraint is removed from the migration.

41.8 Testing NestJS specifics: guards, pipes, interceptors, filters, modules

Concept

NestJS has a request pipeline: middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, handler, interceptors (after), exception filters. Each piece is a class you own, so each is testable in isolation (unit) and together (e2e). @nestjs/testing provides Test.createTestingModule, which builds a real dependency-injection container for a test and lets you swap providers with overrideProvider, overrideGuard, overrideInterceptor, overridePipe and overrideFilter.

Why does it exist?

The pipeline is where authorization, validation, serialization and error mapping live. A bug in a guard is a security incident; a bug in a pipe is a 500 instead of a 400; a bug in a filter leaks a stack trace to a client. These classes are small and pure enough for unit tests, but their ordering and wiring only shows up when the app boots, which is why the same behaviours get an e2e test too.

How it works

  • Guards implement canActivate(context: ExecutionContext). Unit test by building a fake ExecutionContext with createMock-style objects or a tiny hand-written one.
  • Pipes implement transform(value, metadata). Unit test by calling transform directly. ValidationPipe with a DTO is tested by passing a plain object and asserting BadRequestException.
  • Interceptors implement intercept(context, next), returning an Observable. Unit test with of(value) as next.handle() and lastValueFrom.
  • Exception filters implement catch(exception, host). Unit test with a fake ArgumentsHost exposing a fake response object.
  • Request-scoped providers (@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })) are not created by module.get; use module.resolve(Provider) which returns a promise, and optionally module.registerRequestByContextId to supply a request.

NestJS example — unit tests for each pipeline piece

A guard that requires a role:

TypeScript
// src/auth/roles.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ROLES_KEY } from './roles.decorator';

@Injectable()
export class RolesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const required = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>(ROLES_KEY, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]);
    if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user;
    if (!user) throw new ForbiddenException('no user on request');
    const ok = required.some((r) => user.roles?.includes(r));
    if (!ok) throw new ForbiddenException(`requires one of ${required.join(', ')}`);
    return true;
  }
}
TypeScript
// src/auth/roles.guard.spec.ts
import { ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { RolesGuard } from './roles.guard';

function contextWith(user: unknown): ExecutionContext {
  return {
    getHandler: () => function handler() {},
    getClass: () => class Ctrl {},
    switchToHttp: () => ({ getRequest: () => ({ user }) }),
  } as unknown as ExecutionContext;
}

describe('RolesGuard', () => {
  const reflector = new Reflector();
  const guard = new RolesGuard(reflector);

  it('allows when the handler declares no roles', () => {
    jest.spyOn(reflector, 'getAllAndOverride').mockReturnValue(undefined);
    expect(guard.canActivate(contextWith({ roles: [] }))).toBe(true);
  });

  it('forbids a user without the required role', () => {
    jest.spyOn(reflector, 'getAllAndOverride').mockReturnValue(['admin']);
    expect(() => guard.canActivate(contextWith({ roles: ['customer'] }))).toThrow(ForbiddenException);
  });

  it('forbids when there is no authenticated user', () => {
    jest.spyOn(reflector, 'getAllAndOverride').mockReturnValue(['admin']);
    expect(() => guard.canActivate(contextWith(undefined))).toThrow(/no user/);
  });

  afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks());
});

A DTO with ValidationPipe:

TypeScript
// src/orders/dto/create-order.dto.spec.ts
import { ValidationPipe, BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CreateOrderDto } from './create-order.dto';

describe('CreateOrderDto validation', () => {
  const pipe = new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true });
  const metadata = { type: 'body' as const, metatype: CreateOrderDto };

  it('rejects an empty lines array', async () => {
    await expect(pipe.transform({ lines: [] }, metadata)).rejects.toThrow(BadRequestException);
  });

  it('rejects unknown properties so clients cannot smuggle fields', async () => {
    await expect(pipe.transform({ lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1 }], isAdmin: true }, metadata))
      .rejects.toThrow(/property isAdmin should not exist/);
  });

  it('transforms a valid payload into a class instance', async () => {
    const dto = await pipe.transform({ lines: [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1 }] }, metadata);
    expect(dto).toBeInstanceOf(CreateOrderDto);
  });
});

An interceptor that adds timing, and an exception filter that maps domain errors:

TypeScript
// src/common/domain-error.filter.spec.ts
import { ArgumentsHost } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DomainErrorFilter } from './domain-error.filter';
import { DomainError } from '../orders/domain/order';

it('maps a DomainError to 422 with a stable error code and no stack', () => {
  const json = jest.fn();
  const status = jest.fn().mockReturnValue({ json });
  const host = {
    switchToHttp: () => ({ getResponse: () => ({ status }), getRequest: () => ({ url: '/orders', id: 'req-1' }) }),
  } as unknown as ArgumentsHost;

  new DomainErrorFilter().catch(new DomainError('cannot cancel a shipped order'), host);

  expect(status).toHaveBeenCalledWith(422);
  expect(json).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ code: 'DOMAIN_RULE_VIOLATION', requestId: 'req-1' }));
  expect(json.mock.calls[0][0]).not.toHaveProperty('stack');
});

NestJS example — Test.createTestingModule with overrides

Building a module for a service test with a real DataSource from Testcontainers and an overridden payment gateway:

TypeScript
// src/orders/orders.module.int-spec.ts
import { Test, TestingModule } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { OrdersModule } from './orders.module';
import { PAYMENT_GATEWAY, PlaceOrderService } from './place-order.service';
import { createTestDataSource, truncateAll } from '../../test/db';
import { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';
import { OrderItemEntity } from './order-item.entity';

describe('OrdersModule wiring (integration)', () => {
  let ds: DataSource;
  let module: TestingModule;
  const gateway = { charge: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ paymentId: 'pay_test' }) };

  beforeAll(async () => {
    ds = await createTestDataSource([OrderEntity, OrderItemEntity]);
    module = await Test.createTestingModule({
      imports: [
        // Reuse the already-initialised DataSource instead of letting Nest create one
        TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({ useFactory: () => ds.options, dataSourceFactory: async () => ds }),
        OrdersModule,
      ],
    })
      .overrideProvider(PAYMENT_GATEWAY).useValue(gateway)
      .compile();
  });

  afterEach(async () => { gateway.charge.mockClear(); await truncateAll(ds); });
  afterAll(async () => { await module.close(); await ds.destroy(); });

  it('resolves PlaceOrderService with the real repository and the stubbed gateway', async () => {
    const service = module.get(PlaceOrderService);
    const order = await service.execute('cust-1', [{ sku: 'SKU-1', unitPriceCents: 500, qty: 2 }], 'idem-1');
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ orderId: order.id, amountCents: 1000 });
    const [row] = await ds.query(`SELECT status, total_cents FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, [order.id]);
    expect(row).toEqual({ status: 'PAID', total_cents: 1000 });
  });
});

dataSourceFactory is a real option of TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync; it lets the test hand Nest an existing DataSource rather than having Nest open a second one against the container. Note module.close() in afterAll: it runs onModuleDestroy hooks and prevents the "open handles" warning.

overrideGuard is the typical convenience in e2e tests when the behaviour under test is not auth:

TypeScript
const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] })
  .overrideGuard(JwtAuthGuard).useValue({ canActivate: (ctx) => { ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user = testUser; return true; } })
  .compile();

Use this sparingly. At least one e2e test per protected route must run the real guard with a real test JWT; otherwise the day someone forgets @UseGuards on a new controller, nothing notices.

Request-scoped providers:

TypeScript
import { ContextIdFactory } from '@nestjs/core';

const contextId = ContextIdFactory.create();
moduleRef.registerRequestByContextId({ headers: { 'x-tenant-id': 't-42' } }, contextId);
const tenantCtx = await moduleRef.resolve(TenantContext, contextId);
expect(tenantCtx.tenantId).toBe('t-42');

Sequelize example — module with SequelizeModule

TypeScript
const module = await Test.createTestingModule({
  imports: [
    SequelizeModule.forRoot({
      dialect: 'postgres', uri: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL, schema: workerSchema(),
      models: [OrderModel, OrderItemModel], autoLoadModels: false, synchronize: false, logging: false,
    }),
    OrdersModule,
  ],
}).compile();

synchronize: false again. Sequelize's SequelizeModule.forRoot accepts the same options as the Sequelize constructor plus synchronize, autoLoadModels and retryAttempts.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • module.get(RequestScopedProvider) throws; use module.resolve.
  • overrideProvider(X).useValue(...) silently does nothing if X is not part of the compiled module graph (for example, provided by a dynamic module with a different token). Assert the override took effect in a test.
  • A test that overrides ValidationPipe globally hides validation bugs. Keep the real global pipe in e2e tests.
  • Reflector metadata comes from decorators; a guard test with a hand-built context must stub getAllAndOverride or apply the real decorator to a real class.
  • Interceptors returning an Observable that never completes (a forgotten finalize) cause tests to hang; wrap in lastValueFrom with a timeout.

Common mistakes

  • Testing the guard through HTTP only, so a failure reads as "expected 200, got 403" with no clue why.
  • Using app.useGlobalGuards in production but forgetting to set them up in the e2e test app, so the test passes without auth.
  • Creating a TestingModule per test with a real database connection, then running out of connections.

Interview questions

  1. How do you test a request-scoped provider with @nestjs/testing?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: module.resolve with a ContextId registered via registerRequestByContextId.
  2. When is overrideGuard acceptable in e2e tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: as a convenience when the test is not about auth, provided the real guard is exercised elsewhere by at least one test per protected route.
  3. How do you give Nest an existing DataSource in tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync with dataSourceFactory.

41.9 Testing transactions and concurrency against a real database

Concept

A concurrency test runs several operations at the same time against the real database and asserts that invariants hold afterwards. The most valuable one in any commerce system is "N customers try to buy the last M units; exactly M succeed and stock never goes negative". You cannot write this test with mocks, and you cannot write it with transaction-rollback isolation, because it needs multiple real connections.

Why does it exist?

Oversell, double refund, double job execution and lost updates are all concurrency bugs (see Part 21 — Database Transactions). They pass every single-threaded test and appear only under load. A concurrency test makes them reproducible on a laptop in 200 ms.

How it works

  1. Seed the contended row (stock = 3).
  2. Launch N concurrent calls with Promise.allSettled (not Promise.all, which stops at the first rejection and hides the count).
  3. Count fulfilled vs rejected.
  4. Assert on the database state, not on which call won.

Practical example — proving oversell protection

TypeScript
// src/inventory/reserve-stock.int-spec.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { createTestDataSource, truncateAll } from '../../test/db';
import { Product } from '../products/product.entity';
import { ReserveStockService, OutOfStockError } from './reserve-stock.service';
import { aProduct, seedProducts } from '../../test/builders/product.builder';

describe('ReserveStockService under concurrency', () => {
  let ds: DataSource;
  let service: ReserveStockService;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    // A pool of 20 so the 20 concurrent transactions really run in parallel
    ds = await createTestDataSource([Product]);
    service = new ReserveStockService(ds);
  });
  afterEach(() => truncateAll(ds));
  afterAll(() => ds.destroy());

  it('sells exactly 3 units when 20 customers race for stock=3', async () => {
    const [p] = await seedProducts(ds, [aProduct({ stock: 3 })]);

    const results = await Promise.allSettled(
      Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => service.reserve(p.id, 1, `order-${i}`)),
    );

    const ok = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'fulfilled').length;
    const outOfStock = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'rejected' && r.reason instanceof OutOfStockError).length;
    expect(ok).toBe(3);
    expect(outOfStock).toBe(17);

    const [row] = await ds.query(`SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1`, [p.id]);
    expect(row.stock).toBe(0);
    const [{ n }] = await ds.query(`SELECT count(*)::int AS n FROM reservations WHERE product_id = $1`, [p.id]);
    expect(n).toBe(3);
  });
});

For this test to be meaningful, the pool must be at least as large as the concurrency; with extra: { max: 5 } the 20 calls would queue and the test would pass even without locking. In the test file, create the DataSource with extra: { max: 20 } and note why in a comment.

The service under test uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) or an atomic conditional UPDATE:

TypeScript
// src/inventory/reserve-stock.service.ts (core)
async reserve(productId: string, qty: number, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  await this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
    const res = await m.query(
      `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock >= $1 RETURNING stock`,
      [qty, productId],
    );
    if (res[1] === 0) throw new OutOfStockError(productId); // rowCount 0: condition failed
    await m.query(`INSERT INTO reservations (product_id, order_id, qty) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)`, [productId, orderId, qty]);
  });
}

Remove the AND stock >= $1 and the test fails with stock = -17. Add a CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint and the test still passes, but now the failure is a 23514 error instead of OutOfStockError, which is a different contract; the test documents which one you chose.

PostgreSQL example — a deadlock retry test

Two transactions that lock the same two rows in opposite orders deadlock. PostgreSQL detects it after deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) and aborts one with SQLSTATE 40P01. Code that retries on 40P01 (and on 40001 serialization failure) must be tested for real:

TypeScript
it('retries and completes both transfers when they deadlock', async () => {
  const [a, b] = await seedProducts(ds, [aProduct({ stock: 10 }), aProduct({ stock: 10 })]);

  // Move stock a->b and b->a concurrently; without retry, one of them dies with 40P01
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    service.transferStock(a.id, b.id, 2), // locks a then b
    service.transferStock(b.id, a.id, 3), // locks b then a
  ]);

  expect(results.every((r) => r.status === 'fulfilled')).toBe(true);
  const rows = await ds.query(`SELECT id, stock FROM products ORDER BY id`);
  expect(rows.map((r: any) => r.stock).reduce((x: number, y: number) => x + y, 0)).toBe(20); // conserved
});

To make the deadlock reproducible rather than occasional, the service can accept an optional delayBetweenLocksMs in tests, or the test sets deadlock_timeout = '50ms' on the test connection so detection is fast. A deterministic alternative is to lock rows in a fixed order (ORDER BY id) in the service, which makes the deadlock impossible; the test then verifies that both complete without any retry and pg_stat_database.deadlocks did not increase.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The test passes because the pool serialised the requests, not because the locking works. Pool size must exceed concurrency.
  • Promise.all hides the count of failures. Use allSettled.
  • Fake timers and concurrency tests do not mix; the database does not care about Jest's clock.
  • On a slow CI runner, 20 concurrent transactions plus a 1 s deadlock_timeout can exceed the default 5 s Jest timeout; set testTimeout explicitly.
  • Transaction-rollback isolation cannot host this test (single connection). Use truncate.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prove oversell protection in an automated test?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: real database, N concurrent calls with Promise.allSettled, pool larger than N, assert exact success count and final stock.
  2. Why might a concurrency test pass while production oversells?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the pool serialised the calls, or the test hit a different code path (for example a cached stock value).

41.10 Testing async flows: jobs, sagas, outbox relay, consumers

Concept

Many backend behaviours complete after the request returns: an outbox relay publishes an event, a worker processes a job, a saga advances after a reply. Tests for these must wait for eventual state instead of asserting immediately.

Why does it exist?

await service.execute() returning does not mean the email was sent or the event was published. Asserting immediately gives a flaky test that passes on a fast laptop and fails in CI. A polling helper with a timeout turns "eventually" into a deterministic assertion.

How it works — the polling helper

TypeScript
// test/wait-for.ts
export async function waitFor<T>(
  probe: () => Promise<T>,
  opts: { timeoutMs?: number; intervalMs?: number; until?: (v: T) => boolean } = {},
): Promise<T> {
  const { timeoutMs = 5_000, intervalMs = 50, until = (v) => Boolean(v) } = opts;
  const deadline = Date.now() + timeoutMs;
  let last: T | undefined;
  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    last = await probe();
    if (until(last)) return last;
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, intervalMs));
  }
  throw new Error(`waitFor timed out after ${timeoutMs}ms; last value: ${JSON.stringify(last)}`);
}

Use it to test the outbox relay end to end with real PostgreSQL and a captured publisher:

TypeScript
it('relays an unpublished outbox row and marks it published', async () => {
  await ds.query(
    `INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)`,
    ['e1', 'order-1', 'order.placed', JSON.stringify({ orderId: 'order-1' })],
  );
  const published: unknown[] = [];
  const relay = new OutboxRelay(ds, { publish: async (e) => { published.push(e); } }, { batchSize: 50 });

  await relay.runOnce(); // one tick, no timers involved

  const row = await waitFor(() => ds.query(`SELECT published_at FROM outbox WHERE id = 'e1'`).then((r) => r[0]),
    { until: (r) => r?.published_at != null });
  expect(row.published_at).toBeTruthy();
  expect(published).toHaveLength(1);
});

Design tip visible in that test: the relay exposes runOnce() separately from its setInterval loop. Tests call runOnce() directly and never need fake timers.

The fake timers pitfall with async database calls

jest.useFakeTimers() replaces setTimeout, setInterval, Date and friends. It does not speed up I/O. This code hangs forever:

TypeScript
jest.useFakeTimers();
const p = relay.start();          // internally: setInterval(() => this.runOnce(), 1000)
jest.advanceTimersByTime(1000);   // fires the callback, which awaits a real DB query
await p;                          // the DB response arrives on a real timer that is now frozen

The pg driver's own timeouts, the pool's idle checks and the container's readiness checks all use timers. Freezing them freezes the database client. Rules:

  • Never enable fake timers in a test that touches a real database, Redis, Kafka or HTTP.
  • If you must advance a timer and await I/O, use jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync (Jest 29.5+) and enable fake timers with doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate']; even then, prefer redesigning the code so the tick can be triggered directly.
  • Inject the clock and the scheduler into anything that loops, so tests call the tick function.

Testing a BullMQ job processor

TypeScript
it('generates the invoice PDF and stores its key on the order', async () => {
  const processor = module.get(InvoiceProcessor);
  const job = { id: '1', data: { orderId: order.id }, attemptsMade: 0 } as Job<InvoiceJobData>;

  await processor.process(job); // call the processor method directly; no real queue needed

  const [row] = await ds.query(`SELECT invoice_key FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, [order.id]);
  expect(row.invoice_key).toMatch(/^invoices\/.+\.pdf$/);
  expect(storage.objects.has(row.invoice_key)).toBe(true); // in-memory storage fake
});

The queue itself (retries, backoff, dead-letter) is BullMQ's responsibility and is tested by BullMQ. Your test covers your processor. An integration test with a real Redis container that enqueues and waits for completion is still worth having for the wiring (queue name, processor registration), but one per queue is enough.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A polling helper with no timeout hangs CI silently; always include one, and include the last observed value in the error.
  • Polling every 1 ms hammers the database; 25–100 ms is enough.
  • Waiting for "count increased" is flaky if a previous test left rows; truncate first.
  • Consumer tests must wait for the consumer to join the group before producing (kafkajs consumer.run resolves before assignment); wait for a first heartbeat or use fromBeginning: true.

Interview questions

  1. How do you test an outbox relay?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: real DB, insert a row, call the relay's single-tick method, assert the row is marked published and the publisher received the event; no timers.
  2. Why do fake timers hang tests that use a real database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the driver relies on timers for I/O; freezing them freezes the client.

41.11 Testing time: frozen clocks, cron logic and TTL expiry

Concept

Anything that depends on "now" (expiry, scheduling, grace periods, createdAt ordering, daily reports) must be tested at fixed, chosen instants: just before the boundary, exactly at it, just after it.

How it works — three techniques

1. Inject a Clock (best). The service never calls Date.now(); it calls this.clock.now(). Tests supply { now: () => new Date('2026-09-06T23:59:59.999Z') }.

2. jest.useFakeTimers + jest.setSystemTime for code you do not control that reads Date:

TypeScript
beforeEach(() => { jest.useFakeTimers({ doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate'] }); jest.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-09-06T10:00:00Z')); });
afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers());

it('expires a reservation after 15 minutes', () => {
  const r = Reservation.create('order-1', new Date());
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(15 * 60 * 1000 - 1);
  expect(r.isExpired(new Date())).toBe(false);
  jest.advanceTimersByTime(1);
  expect(r.isExpired(new Date())).toBe(true);
});

3. Let the database decide, and test in the database. For TTLs enforced by SQL (WHERE expires_at < now()), do not fight now(); insert rows with explicit expires_at in the past and future and assert which are selected:

TypeScript
it('cleanup deletes only expired reservations', async () => {
  await ds.query(`INSERT INTO reservations (id, expires_at) VALUES
    ('past', now() - interval '1 minute'), ('future', now() + interval '1 minute')`);
  await cleanup.runOnce();
  const rows = await ds.query(`SELECT id FROM reservations ORDER BY id`);
  expect(rows.map((r: any) => r.id)).toEqual(['future']);
});

Cron logic. Do not test that @Cron('0 2 * * *') fires at 02:00; that is the library's job. Test your function with an injected "as of" date: dailyReport.run(new Date('2026-09-06T02:00:00Z')) and assert it covers 2026-09-05 in the configured time zone. Test the time zone explicitly: the same instant is 2026-09-06 07:30 in IST.

Redis TTL. With a real Redis container, set a key with EX 1, assert ttl > 0, then await sleep(1100) and assert null. One such test per TTL-dependent feature is enough; longer TTLs are tested by asserting the TTL value, not by waiting.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • jest.setSystemTime does not affect PostgreSQL's now(); a test mixing both compares two different clocks.
  • Time zone of the CI runner (TZ unset means UTC on Linux) differs from a developer laptop; set TZ=UTC in jest.config via process.env.TZ = 'UTC' at the top of the config file.
  • Month-end and leap-day arithmetic: 2026-01-31 + 1 month is ambiguous; pin tests at those dates.
  • Tests that sleep to wait for expiry are slow and flaky; prefer injecting time and using the database for the rest.

41.12 Testing migrations

Concept

A migration is production code that runs once, under load, and often cannot be undone. It deserves a test: does up apply cleanly on the current schema? Does down reverse it? Does it take locks that block traffic?

How it works

  1. In an integration test, start from the schema at the previous migration (run all migrations except the last, or restore a snapshot).
  2. Run up; assert the resulting schema (information_schema.columns, pg_indexes).
  3. Run down; assert the previous schema is restored.
  4. Measure the wall-clock time of up on a table seeded with a realistic number of rows and assert it stays within a budget; long durations usually mean a full-table rewrite or a lock held while backfilling.
TypeScript
// src/migrations/1757152800000-add-orders-currency.int-spec.ts
it('adds currency with a default without rewriting the table, and reverses', async () => {
  await ds.query(`INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total_cents, status) SELECT gen_random_uuid(), 'c', 100, 'PAID' FROM generate_series(1, 200000)`);

  const start = Date.now();
  await ds.runMigrations(); // applies only the pending one
  const ms = Date.now() - start;
  expect(ms).toBeLessThan(2_000); // ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT is metadata-only on PG 11+

  const [col] = await ds.query(`SELECT column_default, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'orders' AND column_name = 'currency'`);
  expect(col).toEqual({ column_default: "'INR'::text", is_nullable: 'NO' });

  await ds.undoLastMigration();
  const gone = await ds.query(`SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'orders' AND column_name = 'currency'`);
  expect(gone).toHaveLength(0);
});

To assert on lock behaviour, run the migration in one connection while a second connection holds a short transaction on the table and assert the migration either waits less than lock_timeout or fails fast (SET lock_timeout = '2s' inside the migration is a production best practice; see Part 24 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction blocks writes for the whole build; a migration test on 200k rows will show hundreds of milliseconds where you expected metadata-only.
  • down migrations that drop data cannot be reversed; the test should at least assert they run.
  • Migrations tested only on an empty table hide rewrites; seed rows.
  • TypeORM's migrationsRun: true at app boot in tests races with parallel workers; run migrations in global setup only.

Practical exercise

Write an integration test for your next migration that (1) seeds 100k rows, (2) asserts up completes under a budget, (3) asserts the exact schema change via information_schema, and (4) asserts down restores the previous state. Acceptance: the test fails if CONCURRENTLY is removed from an index creation, because the duration budget is exceeded.

41.13 End-to-end testing the NestJS app with supertest and nock

Concept

An e2e test boots the whole NestJS application (all modules, global pipes, guards, interceptors, filters), talks to it over real HTTP with supertest, uses a real PostgreSQL and Redis from containers, and replaces only the systems you do not own by intercepting their HTTP calls at the network boundary with nock (or msw). It asserts on the HTTP response and on the resulting database state, because a 201 with nothing persisted is a bug.

Why does it exist?

Unit and integration tests prove the pieces. E2E proves the wiring: that @UseGuards is on the route, that ValidationPipe is global, that the exception filter maps errors, that the serializer hides passwordHash, that the DTO shape in the OpenAPI spec is what the handler actually accepts. Every one of those has been broken in production by a change that passed all lower-level tests.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant's soft opening. Real kitchen, real waiters, real tables, invited guests. The only thing that is not real is the credit card terminal, which is in demo mode. You are not testing whether the chef can cook (unit) or whether the oven works (integration); you are testing whether a guest can walk in, order, eat and pay.

How it works

  1. beforeAll: create the app with Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }), apply the same global setup as main.ts (a shared configureApp(app) function is the trick), await app.init().
  2. nock.disableNetConnect() and nock.enableNetConnect('127.0.0.1') so any un-mocked external call fails loudly instead of hitting the internet.
  3. Per test: seed data, set up nock interceptors, send the request, assert status, body, headers, database rows, outbox rows, and that every nock scope was consumed (scope.isDone()).
  4. afterEach: nock.cleanAll(), truncate tables.
  5. afterAll: await app.close().

NestJS example — the e2e harness

TypeScript
// src/app.setup.ts  (shared by main.ts and tests, so tests boot the real pipeline)
import { INestApplication, ValidationPipe, ClassSerializerInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { DomainErrorFilter } from './common/domain-error.filter';

export function configureApp(app: INestApplication): void {
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true }));
  app.useGlobalInterceptors(new ClassSerializerInterceptor(app.get(Reflector)));
  app.useGlobalFilters(new DomainErrorFilter());
  app.enableShutdownHooks();
}
TypeScript
// test/e2e/app.harness.ts
import { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import nock from 'nock';
import { JwtService } from '@nestjs/jwt';
import { AppModule } from '../../src/app.module';
import { configureApp } from '../../src/app.setup';
import { truncateAll } from '../db';

export async function createE2EApp() {
  process.env.DATABASE_URL = JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync('.test-db.json', 'utf8')).uri;
  process.env.DATABASE_SCHEMA = `w${process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID ?? '1'}`;
  process.env.PAYMENT_BASE_URL = 'https://api.payments.test';

  const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }).compile();
  const app: INestApplication = moduleRef.createNestApplication();
  configureApp(app);
  await app.init();

  nock.disableNetConnect();
  nock.enableNetConnect('127.0.0.1');

  const jwt = app.get(JwtService);
  const ds = app.get(DataSource);
  return {
    app,
    ds,
    tokenFor: (sub: string, roles: string[] = ['customer']) => jwt.sign({ sub, roles }),
    reset: async () => { nock.cleanAll(); await truncateAll(ds); },
    close: async () => { nock.enableNetConnect(); await app.close(); },
  };
}

Two important details. The app reads config from process.env, so the harness sets env before compiling the module; @nestjs/config reads it at that moment. The test signs a JWT with the app's own JwtService, so the real JwtAuthGuard runs with a real signature; there is no overrideGuard here.

TypeScript
// test/e2e/orders.e2e-spec.ts
import request from 'supertest';
import nock from 'nock';
import { createE2EApp } from './app.harness';
import { aProduct, seedProducts } from '../builders/product.builder';

describe('POST /orders (e2e)', () => {
  let h: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createE2EApp>>;
  beforeAll(async () => { h = await createE2EApp(); });
  afterEach(() => h.reset());
  afterAll(() => h.close());

  it('creates a PAID order, decrements stock and writes an outbox event', async () => {
    const [p] = await seedProducts(h.ds, [aProduct({ stock: 5, priceCents: 1200 })]);
    const payment = nock('https://api.payments.test')
      .post('/v1/charges', (body) => body.amount === 2400 && body.currency === 'INR')
      .reply(200, { id: 'ch_123', status: 'succeeded' });

    const res = await request(h.app.getHttpServer())
      .post('/orders')
      .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${h.tokenFor('cust-1')}`)
      .set('Idempotency-Key', 'idem-e2e-1')
      .send({ lines: [{ sku: p.sku, qty: 2 }] })
      .expect(201);

    expect(res.body).toMatchObject({ id: expect.any(String), status: 'PAID', totalCents: 2400 });
    expect(res.body).not.toHaveProperty('customerInternalNotes'); // serializer hides @Exclude fields
    expect(payment.isDone()).toBe(true);

    const [stock] = await h.ds.query(`SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1`, [p.id]);
    expect(stock.stock).toBe(3);
    const outbox = await h.ds.query(`SELECT event_type, payload FROM outbox WHERE aggregate_id = $1`, [res.body.id]);
    expect(outbox).toEqual([{ event_type: 'order.placed', payload: expect.objectContaining({ orderId: res.body.id }) }]);
  });

  it('returns 402 and rolls back stock when the gateway declines', async () => {
    const [p] = await seedProducts(h.ds, [aProduct({ stock: 5 })]);
    nock('https://api.payments.test').post('/v1/charges').reply(402, { error: { code: 'card_declined' } });

    await request(h.app.getHttpServer())
      .post('/orders')
      .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${h.tokenFor('cust-1')}`)
      .set('Idempotency-Key', 'idem-e2e-2')
      .send({ lines: [{ sku: p.sku, qty: 1 }] })
      .expect(402);

    const [stock] = await h.ds.query(`SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1`, [p.id]);
    expect(stock.stock).toBe(5);
    expect(await h.ds.query(`SELECT 1 FROM orders`)).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  it('returns 401 without a token and 400 with an invalid body', async () => {
    await request(h.app.getHttpServer()).post('/orders').send({ lines: [] }).expect(401);
    await request(h.app.getHttpServer())
      .post('/orders').set('Authorization', `Bearer ${h.tokenFor('cust-1')}`)
      .send({ lines: [{ sku: 'X', qty: -1 }] })
      .expect(400)
      .expect((r) => expect(r.body.message).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([expect.stringMatching(/qty/)])));
  });

  it('treats a replay with the same Idempotency-Key as the same order and charges once', async () => {
    const [p] = await seedProducts(h.ds, [aProduct({ stock: 5 })]);
    const payment = nock('https://api.payments.test').post('/v1/charges').once().reply(200, { id: 'ch_1', status: 'succeeded' });
    const send = () => request(h.app.getHttpServer()).post('/orders')
      .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${h.tokenFor('cust-1')}`).set('Idempotency-Key', 'idem-e2e-3')
      .send({ lines: [{ sku: p.sku, qty: 1 }] });

    const first = await send().expect(201);
    const second = await send().expect(201);
    expect(second.body.id).toBe(first.body.id);
    expect(payment.isDone()).toBe(true); // .once() means a second call would have failed with "no match"
  });

  it('times out the gateway and returns 503 without charging or persisting', async () => {
    const [p] = await seedProducts(h.ds, [aProduct({ stock: 5 })]);
    nock('https://api.payments.test').post('/v1/charges').delayConnection(3_000).reply(200, {});

    await request(h.app.getHttpServer()).post('/orders')
      .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${h.tokenFor('cust-1')}`).set('Idempotency-Key', 'idem-e2e-4')
      .send({ lines: [{ sku: p.sku, qty: 1 }] })
      .expect(503);
    expect(await h.ds.query(`SELECT 1 FROM orders`)).toHaveLength(0);
  }, 10_000);
});

The last test is the senior mantra in code: can it timeout? The payment client has a 2 s timeout; the test proves that a hung gateway does not become a hung order.

msw is an alternative to nock with the same idea and a request-handler style:

TypeScript
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
const server = setupServer(
  http.post('https://api.payments.test/v1/charges', () => HttpResponse.json({ id: 'ch_1', status: 'succeeded' })),
);
beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

msw intercepts fetch and undici as well as http; nock (v13+) intercepts http/https and, from v14, fetch via undici interception. Pick one per repository.

Smoke tests against staging

E2E tests in CI run against containers. A smoke test runs a tiny subset (health, login, one read, one write with a test account) against the deployed staging environment after each deploy and against production after a release, with real third parties in sandbox mode. It is the only automated check that catches a wrong environment variable, a broken secret, or a firewall rule. Keep it under ten requests and under a minute, and make it the gate between "deployed" and "traffic shifted".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • nock set up after the request, or with a path or body matcher that does not match, produces Nock: No match for request and a 500 from your app; assert scope.isDone() so unused interceptors also fail the test.
  • Persisted interceptors (.persist()) leak between tests; nock.cleanAll() in afterEach.
  • app.getHttpServer() with the Fastify adapter needs await app.getHttpAdapter().getInstance().ready() before the first request.
  • Forgetting configureApp(app) means the e2e app has no global pipe; validation tests then fail or, worse, pass because the test expected the unvalidated behaviour.
  • Running e2e files in parallel against one schema; use the same per-worker schema strategy.

Interview questions

  1. What do you assert in an e2e test beyond the status code?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: body shape, hidden fields, headers, database state, outbox/side-effects, and that every external interceptor was consumed.
  2. Why mock at the network boundary rather than the client class?
    Show answerHide answer
