        `SELECT id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
         WHERE created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $2 ORDER BY created_at, id`,
        [from, to], { batchSize: 1_000 }, // rows fetched from the server cursor per round trip
      ));
      const toCsv = new Transform({
        objectMode: true,
        transform(row, _enc, cb) {
          cb(null, `${row.id},${row.customer_id},${row.status},${row.total_cents},${row.created_at.toISOString()}\n`);
        },
      });
      await pipeline(stream, toCsv, res); // backpressure: slow clients slow the cursor, not memory
    } finally {
      await queryRunner.release();
    }
  }
}

pg-query-stream opens a server-side cursor, so PostgreSQL does not materialise the result either. pipeline propagates backpressure: if the client reads slowly, the cursor stops fetching. Memory stays under a few MB for a 10-million-row export. Note @Res() disables Nest's response handling for this route, which is intended; alternatively return a StreamableFile wrapping the transformed stream.

For JSON, stream JSON Lines (application/x-ndjson, one object per line) rather than a JSON array; the client can parse as it goes and you never need the closing bracket in memory. If the client insists on an array, write [, then rows joined by ,, then ], still streaming.

Streaming also applies to file uploads (pipe the request to S3 with multipart upload instead of buffering into memory) and to large HTTP responses from third parties (response.body as a stream in undici/fetch).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A streaming response cannot change its status code after the first byte; validate everything before res.write.
  • Client disconnect must abort the cursor (req.on('close')) or the connection stays busy until the query finishes.
  • Streaming inside a transaction holds the connection for the whole export; use a dedicated read-replica pool for exports.
  • Compression middleware buffering the whole stream defeats the purpose; ensure it flushes per chunk or compress at the LB.

Interview questions

  1. Why is OFFSET 500000 slow and what replaces it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the scan reads and discards 500k rows; keyset pagination enters the index at the cursor.
  2. How do you export 20 million rows without OOM?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: server-side cursor (pg-query-stream), transform stream, pipeline for backpressure, streaming response.

42.9 Compression, serialization and HTTP client tuning

42.9.1 Compression

Concept

Compression trades CPU for bytes. gzip at level 6 turns a 200 KB JSON response into about 25 KB (JSON compresses 6–10×). Brotli at quality 4–5 gets 10–15% smaller than gzip for similar CPU; at quality 11 it is smaller still but 10–50× slower to compress, which is only sensible for static assets compressed once at build time.

Why does it exist?

For a mobile client on a 5 Mbit/s connection, 200 KB is 320 ms of transfer; 25 KB is 40 ms. For API-to-API traffic inside one data centre, bandwidth is plentiful and the CPU spent compressing is often the larger cost.

How it works — where to compress

Location Pros Cons Use when
In the Node process (compression middleware, @fastify/compress) Simple; works everywhere Uses event loop CPU: about 1–3 ms per 100 KB at gzip level 6, which is a significant fraction of a 20 ms request Small deployments without a smart edge
At the load balancer / ingress (NGINX, Envoy, ALB does not compress; CloudFront and most CDNs do) Offloads CPU from the app; centralised config Needs the edge to see plaintext (TLS terminates there) Default for production
At the CDN for cacheable responses Compress once, serve millions Only for cacheable responses Static assets, public catalog endpoints

Measure the CPU: node --cpu-prof on a load test with and without compression; zlib frames in the flame graph tell you the share. A common finding is that gzip costs 8–15% of the event loop at level 6 on an API returning 50–100 KB responses. Move it to the edge and the pod handles 10% more traffic for free.

TypeScript
// main.ts: compress only when the edge cannot; skip small bodies and already-compressed types
import compression from 'compression';
app.use(compression({
  threshold: 1024,       // bodies under 1 KB are not worth it
  level: 4,              // level 6 is default; 4 is ~30% cheaper with ~5% larger output
  filter: (req, res) => !req.headers['x-no-compression'] && compression.filter(req, res),
}));

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Compressing a streaming response buffers it unless the middleware flushes per chunk; res.flush() after each write with compression.
  • Double compression (app and edge) wastes CPU and can corrupt responses when Content-Encoding is set twice; pick one layer.
  • Content-Length is unknown for compressed streams, so responses become chunked; some old clients misbehave.
  • BREACH-style attacks: compressing responses that mix secrets and attacker-controlled input leaks the secret through size; do not compress responses containing CSRF tokens next to reflected input.

42.9.2 Serialization cost

Concept

Turning objects into bytes (JSON.stringify) and applying transformation layers (class-transformer, DTO mapping) runs on the event loop. For small responses it is negligible; for large ones it is the single biggest CPU cost in the request.

How it works — numbers

  • JSON.stringify runs at roughly 100–300 MB/s depending on the shape. A 50 KB response: about 0.3 ms. A 5 MB response: 20–50 ms, during which the event loop is blocked for every other request.
  • ClassSerializerInterceptor calls class-transformer's instanceToPlain on the result. It walks every object and property, checks @Expose/@Exclude/@Transform metadata, and builds a new object graph. Cost scales with object count: 1,000 nested entities with 20 fields each is typically 15–40 ms. On a list endpoint that is the whole latency budget.
  • fast-json-stringify compiles a JSON Schema into a specialised serializer that is 2–5× faster than JSON.stringify for known shapes, and it drops unknown properties by construction, which doubles as an allow-list.

NestJS example — measure, then decide per route

TypeScript
// Measure: how much of the request is serialization?
// Wrap the interceptor call with a timer for one hot route
@Injectable()
export class SerializationTimingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    return next.handle().pipe(map((body) => {
      const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
      const plain = instanceToPlain(body);            // what ClassSerializerInterceptor does
      const json = JSON.stringify(plain);
      const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - t0) / 1e6;
      serializationHistogram.labels(ctx.getHandler().name).observe(ms / 1000);
      return json.length > 0 ? plain : plain;
    }));
  }
}

If the histogram shows serialization above 10–15% of route latency, act:

  1. Return DTOs built explicitly (a mapper function that picks fields) rather than entities passed through class-transformer. A hand-written mapper for an Order list is 10–30× cheaper than instanceToPlain and easier to read.
  2. Apply ClassSerializerInterceptor per controller where it is needed rather than globally with APP_INTERCEPTOR.
  3. For the few very hot, fixed-shape endpoints, fast-json-stringify with a schema.
  4. Shrink the payload: fewer fields, no nested graphs on list endpoints, pagination caps.
TypeScript
// A plain mapper: no reflection, no metadata, explicit allow-list
export function toOrderSummary(o: OrderEntity): OrderSummaryDto {
  return { id: o.id, status: o.status, totalCents: o.totalCents, createdAt: o.createdAt.toISOString() };
}

Fastify adapter vs Express

Nest supports both through @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify. On a hello-world benchmark Fastify serves roughly 2× the requests per second of Express (tens of thousands versus around 15–20k RPS on one core, numbers vary by machine). On a realistic endpoint that does two database queries and returns 20 KB of JSON, the difference shrinks to 5–15%, because the request is dominated by the database and serialization, not routing. Fastify also brings schema-based serialization (fast-json-stringify built in) and faster body parsing. Choose Fastify for new services if your middleware ecosystem allows it; do not migrate an existing Express-based service for performance until a profile shows the framework is where time goes, which it rarely is.

42.9.3 HTTP client tuning

Concept

Every outbound call (payment gateway, search service, another team's API) pays DNS, TCP and TLS setup unless connections are reused. A keep-alive pool with sensible limits and timeouts turns a 60 ms cold call into a 20 ms warm one and prevents a slow dependency from consuming all your sockets.

How it works

  1. Keep-alive. Node's default http.globalAgent has keepAlive: true since Node 19; before that, each request opened a new socket. Explicit agents let you set maxSockets (per host concurrency), maxFreeSockets and timeout.
  2. undici (the engine behind Node's fetch) has its own Agent/Pool with connections, keepAliveTimeout, headersTimeout, bodyTimeout and pipelining; setGlobalDispatcher applies it to every fetch.
  3. DNS caching. Node resolves DNS on every new connection through the OS resolver (getaddrinfo, in the libuv thread pool). With keep-alive, resolution is rare; without it, a slow resolver adds 5–50 ms per call and DNS timeouts appear as random 5 s hangs. cacheable-lookup caches results with TTL and can be attached to agents.
  4. Timeouts at three levels: connect (fail fast when the host is unreachable), headers (time to first byte), body (total). A request with no timeout is a leak waiting for an incident.
TypeScript
// src/payments/http-client.provider.ts
import { Agent, setGlobalDispatcher, request } from 'undici';

export const paymentsDispatcher = new Agent({
  connections: 32,            // max sockets to this origin per pod; ties to Little's law: 600 RPS x 30 ms = 18 busy
  keepAliveTimeout: 30_000,   // shorter than the server's idle timeout to avoid reusing a socket the server just closed
  keepAliveMaxTimeout: 60_000,
  connect: { timeout: 1_000 },
  headersTimeout: 2_000,
  bodyTimeout: 3_000,
});
setGlobalDispatcher(paymentsDispatcher); // applies to global fetch too

export async function charge(body: ChargeRequest, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const res = await request(`${process.env.PAYMENT_BASE_URL}/v1/charges`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'idempotency-key': idempotencyKey },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    dispatcher: paymentsDispatcher,
  });
  if (res.statusCode >= 500) throw new UpstreamError(res.statusCode);
  return res.body.json();
}

With axios or Nest's HttpModule (which wraps axios), pass explicit agents:

TypeScript
import { Agent as HttpsAgent } from 'node:https';
HttpModule.register({
  timeout: 3_000,
  maxRedirects: 0,
  httpsAgent: new HttpsAgent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 32, maxFreeSockets: 8, timeout: 30_000 }),
});

The keep-alive mismatch 502

A classic incident: the app's agent keepAliveTimeout is 5 s, the upstream load balancer's idle timeout is 4 s. The LB closes an idle connection at 4.0 s; the client reuses it at 4.5 s; the request fails with ECONNRESET or, when your service is the upstream behind an ALB, the ALB returns intermittent 502s. Rule: the server's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the client's (or the LB in front of it). For a Node server behind an AWS ALB (60 s idle default), set server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000 and server.headersTimeout = 66_000.

TypeScript
// main.ts
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
await app.listen(3000);
const server = app.getHttpServer();
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;
server.headersTimeout = 66_000;

Edge cases & failure modes

  • maxSockets too low queues requests inside the agent with no visible error; expose the queue length or set connections from Little's law with headroom.
  • maxSockets unlimited plus a slow upstream opens thousands of sockets, exhausting file descriptors (EMFILE).
  • Retries without a budget turn one slow upstream into a retry storm (section 42.14).
  • DNS TTL of 60 s with a resolver that takes 2 s under load: cache, and set dns.setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first') if IPv6 resolution fails slowly in your network.

Interview questions

  1. Why must the server's keep-alive timeout exceed the client's?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: otherwise the server closes an idle socket the client is about to reuse, producing resets and 502s at the LB.
  2. What three timeouts does an HTTP client need?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: connect, headers (first byte), body (total); each catches a different failure.
  3. How does Little's law size maxSockets?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: outbound RPS × average call duration = busy sockets; add headroom.

42.10 Async offloading, Node/NestJS tuning and the client-facing edge

42.10.1 Move work off the request path

Concept

Anything the client does not need in the response goes to a queue: sending the confirmation email, rendering the invoice PDF, generating thumbnails, syncing to the CRM, updating search indexes. The request writes the order and an outbox row; a worker does the rest. Part 36 — Background Jobs and Schedulers covers the machinery (BullMQ, retries, idempotent workers). The performance effect is direct: a POST /orders that awaited a 400 ms email API now returns in 90 ms, and the email provider's outage no longer becomes your outage.

TypeScript
// Request path: enqueue, do not await the side effect
await this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
  await m.save(order);
  await m.insert(OutboxEvent, { type: 'order.placed', payload: { orderId: order.id } });
});
return order; // the relay publishes; a consumer sends the email

// Worker path (BullMQ processor)
@Processor('emails')
export class EmailProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  async process(job: Job<{ orderId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    await this.email.sendOrderConfirmation(job.data.orderId); // idempotent by orderId
  }
}

Decision rule: if the client cannot act on the result within this request, it does not belong in this request.

42.10.2 Node and NestJS specifics

Request-scoped providers on hot paths

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST }) makes Nest create a new instance of the provider for every request and of every provider that depends on it (scope bubbles up through the injection graph, including controllers). On a hot route that means dozens of allocations and constructor calls per request plus the loss of singleton caches. Measured on a mid-size module graph, request scope adds 0.3–2 ms per request and a noticeable GC increase. Use it only where per-request state is unavoidable (a DataLoader, a tenant context) and consider durable: true providers, which are created once per tenant key rather than per request, or pass request data as method arguments instead.

Synchronous crypto and CPU-bound work

bcrypt.hashSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync, scryptSync, zlib.gzipSync, JSON.parse of multi-megabyte bodies, image resizing in pure JS: all block the event loop. Use the async variants (bcrypt.hash, crypto.pbkdf2, which run in the libuv thread pool), and for real CPU work use worker_threads through a pool such as piscina:

TypeScript
// src/pdf/pdf.service.ts
import Piscina from 'piscina';
import { resolve } from 'node:path';

@Injectable()
export class PdfService {
  private readonly pool = new Piscina({ filename: resolve(__dirname, 'render-invoice.worker.js'), maxThreads: 2 });
  render(invoice: InvoiceData): Promise<Buffer> {
    return this.pool.run(invoice); // runs on a worker thread; the event loop keeps serving requests
  }
}

Set the thread pool size for async crypto/DNS/fs with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (default 4) if profiles show queueing there.

Parallelism: cluster vs pods

One Node process uses one core. To use a 4-core machine you run 4 processes: either Node's cluster module (one master forking workers on the same port) or, in Kubernetes, 4 single-process pods with 1 CPU each. Pods are preferred: the scheduler spreads them across nodes, a crash affects one pod, memory limits apply per process, and horizontal autoscaling works on the same unit. cluster is fine on a VM without an orchestrator.

Heap size

node --max-old-space-size=768 dist/main.js for a pod with a 1 GiB limit (about 75%). Without it, V8 may grow past the cgroup limit and the kernel kills the pod with exit code 137 and no stack trace, which shows up as OOMKilled with a healthy-looking heap graph right up to the kill.

Heavy interceptors and loggers per route

A global logging interceptor that serialises the request and response body at info level costs JSON.stringify twice per request and floods the log pipeline. Rules: log bodies only at debug and only when a flag is on; exclude health and metrics routes from logging and metrics interceptors; bind expensive interceptors per controller with @UseInterceptors rather than globally; use a fast structured logger (pino) with async transport rather than a synchronous console.log into a slow stdout pipe (section 42.14 tells the incident).

42.10.3 The client-facing edge: CDN, cache headers, ETags, HTTP/2

The fastest request is the one that never reaches your pod.

  • Cache-Control. Public, rarely changing responses (product details, category trees, static config) get public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 so the CDN serves them and refreshes in the background. Per-user responses get private, no-store or private, max-age=0, must-revalidate.
  • ETags. Express (and therefore Nest's Express adapter) generates weak ETags for buffered responses by default; a client sending If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified with no body. The pod still computes the response to hash it, so ETags save bandwidth, not CPU, unless you compute the ETag from a version column and short-circuit before the query.
  • CDN. Put static assets and cacheable API responses behind CloudFront/Cloudflare/Fastly. A catalog endpoint at 2,000 RPS with a 60 s TTL becomes about 1 origin request per minute per edge location.
  • HTTP/2 at the load balancer multiplexes many requests on one connection and compresses headers; the pod can keep speaking HTTP/1.1 to the LB. HTTP/3 (QUIC) helps lossy mobile networks. Neither changes what your handler does; both cut the client's connection overhead.
TypeScript
@Get('products/:id')
@Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300')
async getProduct(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Promise<ProductDto> {
  return this.products.getPublic(id);
}

Interview questions

  1. Why is a request-scoped provider expensive?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it and everything depending on it are re-instantiated per request; caches are lost; GC pressure rises.
  2. What is the difference between bcrypt.hashSync and bcrypt.hash for a server?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sync blocks the event loop for the whole hash (100+ ms at cost 12); async runs in the thread pool.
  3. Do ETags reduce server CPU?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: not by default; the response is computed then hashed; they save bandwidth. To save CPU, derive the ETag from a version and short-circuit.

42.11 Capacity and load testing, performance budgets and regression tests

Concept

A load test sends controlled traffic at a system and records latency, throughput and errors as the traffic changes. Its purpose is to find the knee: the throughput at which latency starts climbing the hockey-stick curve from section 42.1. A soak test holds moderate load for hours to expose leaks and slow degradation. A performance budget is a number a change must not exceed (p95 under 300 ms at 500 RPS, response under 50 KB) and a regression test is a load test in CI that fails when the budget is broken.

Why does it exist?

Nobody knows the capacity of a system by reading its code. Capacity depends on the slowest resource under contention, and contention only appears under load. Teams that do not load test discover the knee on the day of the marketing campaign.

Mental model

Imagine testing a bridge by driving progressively heavier trucks across and measuring how much it bends. You stop well before it breaks; the point is to know the safe limit and to notice if this year's repairs made it weaker.

How it works — profiles

Profile Shape Answers
Smoke 1–5 virtual users for 1 minute Does the script and environment work at all?
Ramp / stress Increase load in steps (100, 200, 400, 800 RPS), each held 3–5 minutes Where is the knee? Which resource saturates first?
Steady state Target load held 10–30 minutes Does p99 stay within budget at expected peak?
Spike Jump from 100 to 1,000 RPS instantly, hold 2 minutes, drop Does autoscaling and queueing absorb a burst? Do retries storm?
Soak 60–70% of peak for 4–12 hours Memory leaks, pool leaks, log volume, disk growth, GC drift
Breakpoint Increase until errors exceed a threshold Absolute ceiling and failure mode (graceful 503 vs crash)

Practical example — k6 script for POST /orders

TypeScript
// perf/place-order.k6.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import { uuidv4 } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',   // controls RPS directly, not virtual users
      startRate: 50, timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 200, maxVUs: 1000,
      stages: [
        { target: 100, duration: '3m' },
        { target: 200, duration: '3m' },
        { target: 400, duration: '3m' },
        { target: 800, duration: '3m' },
        { target: 0, duration: '1m' },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:place_order}': ['p(95)<300', 'p(99)<800'],
    checks: ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

const skus = JSON.parse(open('./fixtures/skus.json')); // 5,000 real SKUs seeded in staging with high stock

export default function () {
  const sku = skus[Math.floor(Math.random() * skus.length)];
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/orders`, JSON.stringify({ lines: [{ sku, qty: 1 }] }), {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.TOKEN}`,
      'Idempotency-Key': uuidv4(),      // unique per request, or the idempotency path hides the real cost
    },
    tags: { endpoint: 'place_order' },
    timeout: '5s',
  });
  check(res, { 'created': (r) => r.status === 201 });
  sleep(0.1);
}

Run: k6 run --out json=perf/results.json -e BASE_URL=https://staging.example.com -e TOKEN=$TOKEN perf/place-order.k6.js. The ramping-arrival-rate executor is the right one for finding the knee: it holds the request rate constant per stage even as latency rises, which is how real traffic behaves. A virtual-user executor slows down automatically when latency rises and hides the knee.

Reading the results

Plot p50, p95, p99 and error rate against the stage's target RPS, next to the server-side saturation metrics: event loop lag, pod CPU, pg_pool_waiting, DB CPU, DB connections, Redis latency. The knee is where p99 turns upward. The resource whose graph turns at the same moment is the bottleneck. Typical findings for a NestJS + PostgreSQL service:

  • p99 climbs at 350 RPS, pg_pool_waiting starts rising at 340 RPS: pool-bound; check hold time (a query got slow, or a connection is held across an await).
  • p99 climbs at 500 RPS, event loop lag rises: CPU-bound in Node; profile (section 42.12); usually serialization, validation or logging.
  • p99 climbs at 200 RPS, DB CPU at 90%: query-bound; pg_stat_statements (section 42.6).
  • Errors appear at 800 RPS as 503s with p99 stable: the rate limiter or load shedder is doing its job, which is the desired failure mode.

Record the knee in the runbook: "orders-api: 6 pods, knee at about 650 RPS, bottleneck pool; safe peak 400 RPS". Re-measure after every significant change and monthly.

Soak tests for leaks

Run at 60% of peak for eight hours with nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes, pg_pool_total, open file descriptors and pod memory on a dashboard. A healthy service shows a sawtooth heap (grows, GC drops it) with a flat baseline. A rising baseline is a leak: unbounded in-memory cache, event listeners added per request, Map keyed by request id never cleared, setInterval created per request. A pool total that climbs to max and stays there while traffic is flat means connections are not released on an error path. Part 10 — Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime covers heap snapshot diffing to find the retained objects.

Never load test production without a plan

Production load tests are legitimate (they are the only way to test real infrastructure, real data sizes and real third-party sandboxes) and dangerous. The plan: a named owner and an abort switch; a time window announced to on-call and dependent teams; a tenant or synthetic account whose data is excluded from analytics and billing; third parties in sandbox or mocked at the edge; rate limits and autoscaling max verified; a rollback for any config changed for the test; and the test tagged in traces (x-load-test: 1) so its traffic is separable in every dashboard. Without those, a load test is an outage with a scheduled start.

Performance budgets and regression tests in CI

Budgets are written where they are checked. Three levels that work:

  1. Micro-benchmarks for pure code (pricing engine, serializer): tinybench or benchmark.js run in CI, failing when a function gets 30% slower than the committed baseline. Cheap, deterministic, catches algorithmic regressions.
  2. Integration-level query budgets: the integration tests from Part 41 — Testing assert EXPLAIN uses the expected index and that a hot endpoint issues at most N queries (count via a query logger). This catches N+1 and dropped indexes at PR time.
  3. Nightly k6 against staging with thresholds; the pipeline fails and posts the comparison with last night's run. Staging must be sized as a known fraction of production (for example 1/4 pods, same instance class for the database) so numbers translate.
YAML
  # .github/workflows/perf-nightly.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  k6:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
      - run: k6 run --out json=results.json -e BASE_URL=${{ vars.STAGING_URL }} -e TOKEN=${{ secrets.PERF_TOKEN }} perf/place-order.k6.js
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: k6-results, path: results.json }

SLOs give budgets their meaning: if the SLO is "p99 < 300 ms over 30 days" then the CI threshold is stricter (p99 < 250 ms on staging at target load) so production has margin. "Measure, don't guess" is the rule for every change made in the name of performance: a PR that claims to be faster carries a before/after number from a repeatable measurement, or it is not a performance PR. Premature optimisation is optimising something no measurement identified; necessary optimisation is fixing the thing the profile points at before it becomes an incident. The difference is not the technique; it is whether a number came first.

Interview questions

  1. How do you find the capacity of a service?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ramping arrival-rate load test, plot p99 and saturation metrics against RPS, identify the knee and the resource that turns with it.
  2. Why use an arrival-rate executor rather than virtual users?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: VUs slow down as latency rises and hide the knee; arrival rate models real traffic that does not wait.
  3. What does a soak test catch that a stress test does not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: leaks and slow degradation (heap, pool, descriptors, disk, log volume).
  4. What must be in place before a production load test?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: owner, abort switch, window, synthetic tenant, sandboxed third parties, tagged traffic, rollback.

42.12 The profiling toolkit

Concept

Profiling answers "where does the time go?" for one process or one query. Tracing answers it across services. Together with metrics they form the loop that every performance investigation follows.

The tools and when to reach for each

Tool Layer What it shows When
node --cpu-prof Node CPU .cpuprofile sampled stack traces; open in Chrome DevTools Performance tab or speedscope Event loop lag is high; find the hot function
node --heap-prof / v8.writeHeapSnapshot() Node memory Allocation sites; retained object graph Heap grows; find the leak
Chrome DevTools (node --inspect) Node Live CPU profile, heap snapshot diff, async stack traces Local reproduction of a slow path
clinic doctor Node Diagnoses event loop delay, CPU, memory, active handles and recommends the next tool First look at "something is slow and I do not know what"
clinic flame / 0x Node CPU Flame graph: width is time; look for wide frames in your code, JSON.stringify, zlib, class-transformer Confirmed CPU-bound
clinic bubbleprof Node async Where time is spent waiting between async operations Latency high but CPU low
OpenTelemetry traces (Jaeger/Tempo/Datadog) Cross-service Span waterfall per request: DB spans, HTTP spans, queue spans; which one is slow and whether they are serial Any p99 investigation starts here
pg_stat_statements PostgreSQL Top queries by total/mean time, calls, buffer hits DB CPU or I/O high; find the query
auto_explain PostgreSQL Actual plans of slow statements with real parameters A query is slow in prod but fast in psql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) PostgreSQL One query's plan, actual rows, buffers read vs hit Fixing a specific query
pg_stat_activity PostgreSQL Live sessions, wait_event_type, state, query age Locks, idle in transaction, long-running statements
Redis SLOWLOG GET 25 and redis-cli --latency Redis Commands over slowlog-log-slower-than (default 10 ms); round-trip latency Redis latency spikes; big keys, KEYS, Lua
kubectl top pod / kubectl top node Infra CPU and memory per pod and node Saturation and noisy neighbours
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay Node Event loop lag histogram exported as a metric Always-on saturation signal

Practical example — a CPU profile in production

You cannot attach DevTools to a production pod, but you can take a short profile on demand:

TypeScript
// src/ops/profile.controller.ts  (internal port, admin-only, rate limited)
import { Controller, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Session } from 'node:inspector/promises';
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

@Controller('internal/profile')
@UseGuards(InternalAdminGuard)
export class ProfileController {
  @Post('cpu')
  async cpu(): Promise<{ file: string }> {
    const session = new Session();
    session.connect();
    await session.post('Profiler.enable');
    await session.post('Profiler.start');
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 15_000)); // 15 s of samples under real traffic
    const { profile } = await session.post('Profiler.stop');
    session.disconnect();
    const file = `/tmp/cpu-${process.pid}-${Date.now()}.cpuprofile`;
    await writeFile(file, JSON.stringify(profile));
    return { file }; // copy out with kubectl cp, open in DevTools or speedscope
  }
}

The profiler adds a few percent of overhead for 15 seconds; taken from one pod out of six, it is safe. For memory, v8.writeHeapSnapshot() pauses the process for seconds on a large heap and doubles memory briefly; take it from a pod removed from the load balancer.

Interview questions

  1. Latency is high, CPU is low. What do you reach for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: traces to find the waiting span; clinic bubbleprof for async waits; pg_stat_activity for locks; pool wait metrics.
  2. How do you get a CPU profile from a production pod safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: on-demand short profile through the inspector API on one pod, admin-only, copied out; or continuous profiling agents.

42.13 Runbook: "The API suddenly became slow"

This is the page you open at 02:14 when the pager says p99 tripled. Work top to bottom; do not skip to the step you suspect, because the first three steps are what stop you from spending an hour on the wrong theory.

Step 1: Confirm and scope with metrics (5 minutes)

  • Which endpoints? All routes (infrastructure, database, GC) or one route (a query, a dependency)?
  • Since when? Exact minute from the latency graph. Write it down.
  • p50 vs p99? p50 up too means everything is slower (saturation, DB, network). p99 only means a subset is slow (locks, GC, one dependency, one tenant).
  • Error rate? Latency up with errors flat is queueing (pool, event loop, upstream). Latency up with 5xx rising is failing dependencies or timeouts.
  • Traffic? RPS up (organic, campaign, bot, retry storm) or flat?

Step 2: Correlate with change (5 minutes)

Deploys (app and every dependency), config changes, feature flags, migrations, cron jobs that started at that minute, autoscaling events, certificate rotations, a partner's release, a new tenant onboarded, time of day (end-of-month batch). Most sudden slowdowns are caused by something that changed. If a deploy matches the minute: roll back first, investigate second.

Step 3: Check saturation, in this order

Signal Where Healthy Suspect
Pod CPU kubectl top pod, container metrics under 65% above 80% sustained
Event loop lag p99 app metric under 20 ms above 100 ms
Heap used, GC pause app metrics sawtooth, flat baseline rising baseline, GC pauses over 100 ms
Pool waiting, pool wait time app metric 0 sustained above 0
DB CPU RDS/Cloud SQL metrics under 60% above 80%
DB connections pg_stat_activity well under max_connections near the limit, many idle in transaction
Replica lag pg_stat_replication, cloud metric under 1 s seconds to minutes (reads stale, or reads fail over to primary)
Redis latency, memory, evictions redis-cli --latency, INFO under 1 ms, no evictions spikes, evicted_keys rising (hit ratio collapse)
Queue depth, consumer lag broker metrics stable growing (consumers slow or dead; producers blocking)
Disk I/O, IOPS credits cloud volume metrics headroom burst credits exhausted

The first row that is red is where you look next.

Step 4: Traces for the slow span

Open the tracing UI, filter the slow route since the minute in step 1, sort by duration, open five. Which span grew? A DB span (go to step 5), an HTTP span to a dependency (step 7), a gap between spans with no child (event loop blocked or pool wait; step 3), or the whole thing uniformly slower (infrastructure; step 6).

Step 5: Database

SQL
-- What is waiting right now?
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS age, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' AND backend_type = 'client backend'
ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Who blocks whom?
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, left(blocking.query, 60) AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid));

-- New top query since the incident? (reset stats after a known-good baseline so deltas are visible)
SELECT round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms, calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms, left(query, 90)
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Autovacuum and bloat
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;

Things to look for: a lock chain (one long transaction, often a migration or a batch job, blocking hot rows); a query whose plan flipped after the table crossed a size threshold or stats went stale (EXPLAIN it now, compare to yesterday's auto_explain log); a missing index revealed by data growth (a query that was fine at 2 million rows seq-scans at 20 million); autovacuum falling behind after a mass delete or update (dead tuples in the millions, index bloat); a replica that fell behind so reads went to the primary; max_connections reached.

Step 6: Infrastructure

Noisy neighbour on the node (kubectl top node, other pods' CPU on the same node), memory pressure and throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total climbing means CPU limits are throttling the pod even though "usage" looks fine), DNS resolution slow or failing (dig from inside a pod, CoreDNS metrics), network partition or packet loss between zones, load balancer health checks failing some pods and concentrating traffic on the rest, disk credits exhausted on the database volume.

Step 7: External dependencies

Latency of each outbound HTTP span, the dependency's status page, your own timeout and retry configuration (are you retrying a slow dependency and tripling the load on it?), circuit breaker state, the third party's rate limits (429s in your logs).

Step 8: Mitigate first, then root cause

Mitigation options in rough order of speed and safety: roll back the correlated change; scale out pods (if CPU or event loop bound) or the pool (if pool bound and the database has room); shed load (rate limit the noisy tenant or bot, disable a non-critical feature flag, return cached or degraded responses); kill the blocker (pg_terminate_backend on the long transaction or the batch job); fail over reads away from a lagging replica; add the index CONCURRENTLY if the missing index is certain. Every mitigation is announced in the incident channel with the time.

Then root cause: reproduce with the load test or the query, write the fix, add the missing alert (the one that would have paged you at the right layer) and the missing test, and put the timeline in the post-mortem. Prevention items that come up repeatedly: alerts on saturation (pool waiting, event loop lag, replica lag, cl_waiting) rather than only on errors; statement_timeout and lock_timeout on every connection; short connectionTimeoutMillis; retry budgets; a per-tenant rate limit; nightly load tests; auto_explain on.

Incident story

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: POST /orders p99 1.9 s, p50 unchanged, error rate flat, RPS flat. Step 1 said "a subset of requests is slow, nothing is failing". Step 2 found no deploy; a nightly refund_reconciliation job had started at 02:00. Step 3 showed pool waiting at 0, DB CPU normal, but pg_stat_activity had 14 sessions in wait_event_type = Lock. Step 5's blocking query showed the reconciliation job holding row locks on orders inside a transaction that had been open for 14 minutes because it looped over 200k orders with one UPDATE each in a single BEGIN. Mitigation at 02:31: pg_terminate_backend on the job; p99 fell to 140 ms within a minute. Root cause: a refactor had moved the loop inside one transaction "for consistency". Fix: commit per 1,000 rows, lock_timeout = '2s' in the job, an alert on "any transaction older than 60 s on the primary", and a job schedule that avoids the order peak in the Americas region.

42.14 Edge cases & failure modes

  • p99 dominated by GC. A 1.8 GB heap with major GCs every 20 s pausing 150 ms; every route's p99 shows the pause, no query is slow, traces show a gap with no child span. Fix: reduce retained memory (bounded caches, no per-request closures on long-lived objects), smaller pods with more replicas, tune --max-semi-space-size for allocation-heavy workloads.
  • Pool exhaustion showing as latency, not errors. connectionTimeoutMillis at 30 s means every request waits up to 30 s and succeeds; dashboards on error rate stay green. Fix: short acquire timeout, alert on waiting, load shed with a 503.
  • Cache hit ratio drop after a deploy. A key format change (product:v2:{id}) or a serializer change invalidates every entry at once; the database takes the full read load; latency doubles for the TTL duration. Fix: warm the new keys before switching reads, or deploy the key change behind a flag with dual reads; alert on hit ratio.
  • Index bloat after a mass delete. Deleting 40 million archived rows leaves the index the same size; scans read empty pages; vacuum takes hours. Fix: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, partition so old data is dropped by partition instead of deleted by row.
  • Plan flip at a data threshold. At 9.8 million rows the planner used an index; at 10.1 million, after autoanalyze, it chose a hash join with a seq scan, and the query went from 8 ms to 2.4 s. Fix: better statistics (ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 1000), a covering or partial index that makes the index path clearly cheaper, auto_explain to catch the flip, and in extreme cases pg_hint_plan.
  • One tenant hogging. A B2B customer's integration polls GET /orders?limit=100 every second from 40 servers; their 4,000 RPS starve everyone; per-route metrics look uniform. Fix: per-tenant rate limits and quotas, per-tenant latency labels, a dedicated pool or priority for interactive traffic.
  • Retry storms. A dependency slows to 2 s; your client times out at 1 s and retries 3 times; the dependency now receives 4× the load and gets slower; your pools fill with waiting requests. Fix: retry budgets (at most 10% extra load), exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, retry only idempotent calls.
  • Compression CPU spike. A new endpoint returns 3 MB catalog dumps; gzip level 6 costs 40 ms of event loop per response; at 50 RPS the loop is fully busy compressing. Fix: compress at the edge, cache the compressed body, reduce the payload, lower the level.
  • Log volume slowing the app (sync stdout). Debug logging enabled in production writes 20 MB/s to stdout; the container runtime's pipe backs up; process.stdout.write becomes blocking; event loop lag hits 500 ms. Fix: async logger transport (pino with pino.transport or a separate worker), log sampling, never log bodies at info, alert on log rate.
  • DNS resolution timeouts. A resolver that drops 1% of queries turns into 5 s hangs (the default retry timeout) on 1% of new connections; without keep-alive that is 1% of requests. Fix: keep-alive so connections are reused, cacheable-lookup, resolver health monitoring, shorter dns timeouts via resolver.setServers plus a custom lookup.
  • Keep-alive mismatch 502s. The LB's idle timeout is longer than the Node server's keepAliveTimeout (5 s default); the LB reuses a connection Node just closed; clients get intermittent 502s that no application log explains. Fix: server.keepAliveTimeout a few seconds above the LB idle timeout, headersTimeout above that.
  • Load balancer health check load. Health checks every 2 s from 3 LB nodes to 40 pods, each running two database queries: 60 QPS of pointless load and a /health p50 dragging every dashboard. Fix: cheap liveness (200 OK with no I/O), readiness that checks dependencies with a cached result refreshed every 10 s, exclude health routes from metrics.
  • Event loop lag from a giant JSON payload. A client sends a 25 MB JSON body; JSON.parse blocks for 200 ms; class-validator walks 300k nested objects for another 800 ms; every other request on the pod waits. Fix: body size limits (bodyParser limit: '1mb'), @MaxLength/@ArrayMaxSize on DTOs, streaming parsers for legitimately large uploads.
  • Hot row contention. Every order updates one daily_stats row; at 500 orders/s the row lock serialises all of them and p99 climbs with throughput. Fix: shard the counter (N rows, random pick, sum on read), append events and aggregate asynchronously, or use Redis INCR with periodic flush.
  • SELECT FOR UPDATE on a popular product. A flash sale on one SKU means every checkout waits for the same row lock; throughput on that SKU is bounded by lock hold time. Fix: shorten the hold (no external calls inside the lock), reservation tokens issued from Redis, or a queue that admits buyers at the rate stock allows.

Senior Checklist — Part 42

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can apply Little's law to size a connection pool, an HTTP agent and a pod count from measured rate and latency
  • I can explain why 80% utilization is dangerous using the queueing curve
  • I report p99 from aggregated histogram buckets and can explain tail latency amplification across fan-out calls
  • I can detect N+1 from pg_stat_statements and traces, and fix it with joins, IN batching or a request-scoped DataLoader
  • I export pool.waitingCount and event loop lag as metrics and alert on saturation, not only on errors
  • I can run the EXPLAIN workflow and recognise SELECT *, COUNT(*), OFFSET, functions on indexed columns and plan flips
  • I can stream a large export with a server-side cursor and backpressure instead of building an array
  • I know where to compress, what serialization costs and when a hand-written mapper beats class-transformer
  • I configure keep-alive, connection limits and the three timeouts on every HTTP client, and I know the keep-alive mismatch rule
  • I move non-essential work to queues and keep request-scoped providers and sync crypto off hot paths
  • I can write a k6 arrival-rate test, find the knee, read the results against saturation metrics and run a soak test for leaks
  • I can execute the "API suddenly became slow" runbook top to bottom: confirm, correlate, saturation, traces, database, infra, dependencies, mitigate, root cause

Part 42 — Key Takeaways

  • Measure, then reason, then fix, then measure again; a performance change without a before-and-after number is a guess.
  • Little's law (concurrency = throughput × latency) sizes pools, agents and pods; queueing theory says the knee is around 80% utilization, so run at 50–65%.
  • Averages hide the tail; SLOs live on p99 computed from aggregated histograms; with 20 fan-out calls, a backend p99 becomes the page's p82.
  • Find which resource is saturated (event loop, heap and GC, pool, DB CPU, replica lag, Redis, queue) before touching code.
  • N+1 is the most common ORM performance bug; it is invisible with small N and shows in pg_stat_statements as a cheap query with an enormous call count.
  • Pool exhaustion fails as latency, not errors; alert on waiting count and use short acquire timeouts so it becomes visible.
  • Sort pg_stat_statements by total time; avoid SELECT *, exact COUNT(*) on big tables, OFFSET, and functions on indexed columns.
  • Batch writes with multi-row inserts, COPY and UNNEST; batch external calls with bounded concurrency; batch Kafka publishes per send.
  • Stream large exports with a server-side cursor and pipeline; never build a giant array in memory.
  • Compress at the edge, serialize with explicit mappers on hot paths, and keep request-scoped providers, sync crypto and body logging off the request path.
  • Every HTTP client needs keep-alive, a connection limit from Little's law and connect, headers and body timeouts; the server's keep-alive timeout must exceed the load balancer's.
  • Find the knee with an arrival-rate load test on a sized staging environment; soak for leaks; never load test production without an owner, a window, tagged traffic and an abort switch.
  • When the API suddenly gets slow: confirm scope, correlate with change, roll back if it matches, then check saturation, traces, database locks and plans, infra and dependencies; mitigate first, root cause second, add the missing alert third.

43.1 Monitoring versus observability

Every backend engineer has lived this moment: a customer says "checkout is broken", you open the dashboard, CPU is fine, memory is fine, the health check is green, and you still have no idea what happened to that one customer. The system is monitored. It is not observable.

This part teaches the difference and then builds, step by step, the three tools that close the gap: structured logs, metrics and distributed traces. All of it is shown in a NestJS service talking to PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka, because that is where you will meet it.

43.1.1 Known unknowns and unknown unknowns

Concept

Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance. You decide "alert me if error rate is above 1 percent" or "graph the database CPU". These are known unknowns: you know the question, you just do not know today's answer.

Observability is the property of a system that lets you answer questions you did not think of in advance, using only the data the system emits. "Why did order 8812 take 9 seconds at 14:02 when everything else was fast?" is an unknown unknown. Nobody wrote a dashboard for it. An observable system lets you find the trace for that order, see that 8.7 of the 9 seconds were spent waiting on a Redis GET, and see from the logs that the Redis pod was being evicted at that moment.

Observability is not a product you buy. It is a habit of emitting rich, correlated, structured data from every layer, and having tools that can slice it any way you want.

Why does it exist?

Modern backends are distributed. One request touches a load balancer, an API pod, a Redis cluster, a PostgreSQL primary, a Kafka topic and a worker. Each of those has its own logs and its own metrics. Without correlation, an incident is a treasure hunt across six consoles. Observability exists because "look at the logs" stopped being a sentence with a single meaning the day you had more than one process.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital. Monitoring is the row of monitors at the nurses' station: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen. They beep when a threshold is crossed. That tells you that something is wrong. Observability is the patient's full chart, the lab results and the ability to order any test you need: it tells you why. You need both. A hospital with only the beeping monitors cannot diagnose anything; a hospital with only lab tests will not notice a patient collapsing.

How it works

The classic model has three pillars. Two more are worth naming because you will meet them in production.

  1. Logs are discrete events with a timestamp and fields. They are the most detailed and the most expensive signal. One request can produce 5 to 50 lines.
  2. Metrics are aggregated numbers sampled over time: a counter of requests, a histogram of latencies. They are cheap to store because a million requests collapse into a handful of numbers per scrape interval.
  3. Traces record the path of a single request as a tree of timed spans. They are the only signal that natively answers "where did the time go across services".
  4. Events are business-level facts emitted deliberately (order_placed, payment_failed). Often they are just logs with a strict schema, or Kafka messages that analytics consumes.
  5. Profiles show which functions burn CPU or allocate memory. Continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Parca) samples a running process at low overhead. You reach for it after metrics tell you CPU is high and traces tell you which endpoint, and you still need to know which function.

The three pillars are not three separate products. Their value comes from correlation: a traceId in every log line, a trace exemplar attached to a latency bucket, a request id carried through Kafka. When they are linked, you move from a red dashboard to the exact line of code in under two minutes.

The cost of observability

Observability is not free, and a senior engineer budgets it like any other resource.

Signal Typical volume for a 500 RPS NestJS service Rough monthly cost driver
Logs at INFO with request logging 500 lines/s at 400 bytes = 17 GB/day Ingestion and retention; the most expensive signal by far
Metrics with 300 series per pod, 10 pods, 15 s scrape 3,000 series, 200 samples/s Series count (cardinality), not request volume
Traces at 10 percent sampling, 8 spans per request 400 spans/s Span count and retention; tail sampling reduces it further

Rule of thumb: logs cost 5 to 20 times more than metrics for the same service. Every time you add a log line to a hot path you are signing a monthly bill. We return to cost control in 43.9.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask two questions before adding any signal: "What question does this let me answer at 3 a.m.?" and "What does it cost per month?" If the answer to the first is "none", the signal goes. They refuse dashboards nobody looks at and alerts nobody acts on. They explain it to a product manager as: "Monitoring tells us we are losing money; observability tells us which line of code is losing it."

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: monitoring answers predefined questions with thresholds; observability lets you answer new questions from emitted data. Follow-up: give an example of a question only observability can answer.
  2. Why are logs more expensive than metrics?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: logs are per-event and unbounded; metrics aggregate into a fixed number of series per scrape. Follow-up: what makes metrics expensive? (Cardinality.)
  3. What links the three pillars together?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: trace id in logs, exemplars in metrics, consistent resource attributes (service, env, version).

43.2 Logs

43.2.1 Structured logging

Concept

A structured log is a log line that is a machine-readable record, almost always one JSON object per line, with named fields. {"level":"info","msg":"order created","orderId":"8812","durationMs":42} is structured. Order 8812 created in 42ms is not; a human can read it, but a query engine cannot filter on durationMs > 1000 without a fragile regular expression.

Why does it exist?

Unstructured logs work for one process on one machine that you tail -f. They fail the moment you have twenty pods, because the only way to find anything is text search, and text search cannot answer "show me all requests over 2 seconds for user 41 in the last hour". Structured logs turn a log store into a database you can query.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse receiving deliveries. Unstructured logging is a delivery driver shouting "big brown box from Mumbai, fragile!" as they drop it. Structured logging is a barcode label with origin, weight, fragile, orderId. The second one lets you find every fragile box from Mumbai in a second, and the first one lets you find nothing once the driver has left.

How it works

Every line carries a fixed core of fields. Agree on them across every service in the company, because cross-service queries only work when the field names match.

Field Example Why
time 2026-09-06T14:02:11.483Z ISO 8601 in UTC, millisecond precision. Never local time.
level info Filter and alert by severity.
msg order created Short, constant, lower-case. Variable data goes in fields, not in the message.
service orders-api Which deployable.
env prod Never mix environments in one query by accident.
version 2.14.3+a1b2c3d Which build. Essential when a deploy causes the incident.
requestId req_7f3c... Correlation id for one inbound request.
traceId 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 Links to the distributed trace.
userId u_41 Who. Internal id only, never email.
orderId 8812 The business key you will search by at 3 a.m.
durationMs 42 Numeric so you can filter and aggregate.
err { type, message, stack } Structured error, including stack.

What must never appear: passwords, tokens, session cookies, full card numbers, bank details, government ids, emails and phone numbers (these are personal data under GDPR and similar laws), full request bodies by default, and Authorization headers. Logs are copied to more places than your database ever will be, and they are read by more people. Treat them as public within the company.

Keep msg constant and put variables in fields. msg: "order created" with orderId: 8812 groups into one pattern in your log tool; msg: "order 8812 created" produces a million distinct messages and defeats pattern-based analysis.

NestJS example

pino is the fastest mainstream Node.js logger because it serializes to JSON with minimal work and writes to a stream without formatting. nestjs-pino wires it into the Nest Logger abstraction and adds request logging.

TypeScript
// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { LoggerModule } from 'nestjs-pino';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

@Module({
  imports: [
    LoggerModule.forRoot({
      pinoHttp: {
        level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info',
        // Fixed fields on every line from this process.
        base: {
          service: 'orders-api',
          env: process.env.NODE_ENV,
          version: process.env.APP_VERSION,
        },
        timestamp: () => `,"time":"${new Date().toISOString()}"`,
        // Reuse the incoming id so the gateway, this service and the worker agree.
        genReqId: (req) => (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID(),
        // Redact secrets before they are serialized. Paths use pino's redact syntax.
        redact: {
          paths: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie', '*.password', '*.cardNumber'],
          censor: '[REDACTED]',
        },
        // Keep request logs small: no bodies, no full header dumps.
        serializers: {
          req: (req) => ({ id: req.id, method: req.method, url: req.url }),
          res: (res) => ({ statusCode: res.statusCode }),
        },
        customProps: (req) => ({ requestId: req.id }),
        // Health checks are noise; do not log them.
        autoLogging: { ignore: (req) => req.url === '/health' || req.url === '/metrics' },
      },
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}
TypeScript
// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Logger } from 'nestjs-pino';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  // bufferLogs holds early lines until the pino logger is attached.
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true });
  app.useLogger(app.get(Logger));
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

In services, inject PinoLogger and log objects, not sentences.

TypeScript
// orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PinoLogger, InjectPinoLogger } from 'nestjs-pino';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectPinoLogger(OrdersService.name) private readonly log: PinoLogger) {}

  async create(userId: string, dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    try {
      const order = await this.repo.createOrder(userId, dto);
      this.log.info(
        { orderId: order.id, userId, itemCount: dto.items.length, durationMs: elapsedMs(started) },
        'order created',
      );
      return order;
    } catch (err) {
      // Pass the Error under the `err` key: pino serializes type, message and stack.
      this.log.error({ err, userId, itemCount: dto.items.length }, 'order creation failed');
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

function elapsedMs(start: bigint): number {
  return Number((process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1_000_000n);
}

The err key matters. this.log.error('failed: ' + err.message) throws away the stack, the error class and any cause. Logging the Error object under err keeps all of it, and pino's default serializer formats it as { type, message, stack }.

TypeORM example

Route the ORM's own logging through the same pino instance so slow queries land in the same stream with the same requestId. TypeORM accepts a custom Logger implementation and a maxQueryExecutionTime threshold.

TypeScript
// database/typeorm-pino.logger.ts
import { Logger as TypeOrmLogger, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';
import { PinoLogger } from 'nestjs-pino';

export class TypeOrmPinoLogger implements TypeOrmLogger {
  constructor(private readonly log: PinoLogger) {}

  logQuery() {} // Do not log every query in prod; that is a 3x log volume increase.

  logQueryError(error: string | Error, query: string, parameters?: unknown[]) {
    this.log.error({ err: error, query, paramCount: parameters?.length ?? 0 }, 'query failed');
  }

  logQuerySlow(time: number, query: string) {
    // Fires when a query exceeds maxQueryExecutionTime.
    this.log.warn({ durationMs: time, query: query.slice(0, 500) }, 'slow query');
  }

  logSchemaBuild(message: string) { this.log.info({ message }, 'schema build'); }
  logMigration(message: string) { this.log.info({ message }, 'migration'); }
  log(level: 'log' | 'info' | 'warn', message: unknown) { this.log.info({ message }, 'typeorm'); }
}

// In TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync(...) useFactory:
//   logger: new TypeOrmPinoLogger(pinoLogger),
//   maxQueryExecutionTime: 500,   // ms; anything slower triggers logQuerySlow

Never log query parameters in production. They contain the customer's data.

Sequelize example

Sequelize takes a logging function and, with benchmark: true, passes the elapsed time as the second argument.

TypeScript
// database/sequelize.config.ts
new Sequelize(process.env.DATABASE_URL!, {
  benchmark: true,
  logging: (sql: string, timingMs?: number) => {
    if (timingMs !== undefined && timingMs > 500) {
      pinoLogger.warn({ durationMs: timingMs, query: sql.slice(0, 500) }, 'slow query');
    }
  },
});

Production scenario

An orders API at 500 RPS logging one request line plus one business line per request emits about 1,000 lines per second, roughly 400 bytes each: 34 GB per day. At typical hosted log pricing ($0.50 to $2.50 per GB ingested plus retention) that is $500 to $2,500 a month for one service. The same service with DEBUG accidentally enabled in production emits 8 lines per request and the bill quadruples overnight. This is why LOG_LEVEL comes from the environment, and why someone reviews log volume per service every month.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged: checkout error rate is 4 percent. The error log says "msg":"payment failed" and nothing else, 600 times. Which provider? Which users? Which error code? The engineer has to enable DEBUG, redeploy, wait for the next failure, and read a stack trace, adding 40 minutes to the incident. The fix the next day was one line: this.log.error({ err, orderId, provider, providerCode: err.code, amount }, 'payment failed'). The following incident took four minutes because the log said providerCode: "insufficient_funds" on every line and the alert was rewritten to exclude customer-side declines.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Logging the whole request body "for debugging" captures passwords on /login and card numbers on /payments. Redact by path or log nothing by default.
  • A msg built with string interpolation creates unbounded unique messages and breaks pattern grouping.
  • Circular objects passed to the logger throw or produce [Circular]; log ids, not ORM entities.
  • Very large log lines (over 16 KB) are truncated or dropped by many shippers; do not log a 2 MB response.
  • Logging err.message instead of err loses the stack and the cause chain.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat log fields as a public API of the service and version them like one. They keep a short company-wide field dictionary and reject PRs that invent order_id when the standard is orderId. They ask of every line: "Would I search by this at 3 a.m.? If not, why is it here?"

Common mistakes

  • Using console.log in services: no levels, no fields, synchronous write to stdout, and no way to turn it off.
  • Different services using different field names for the same thing.
  • Logging at INFO inside loops that run per item; 10,000 items becomes 10,000 lines.
  • Emitting secrets through error objects (some HTTP client errors include the request headers).

43.2.2 Log levels and what belongs at each

Concept

A level is a severity tag that decides whether a line is written and how it is triaged. The mistake most teams make is not having a shared meaning for each level, so error becomes noise and nobody reads it.

How it works

Level Meaning Production default Examples
fatal Process cannot continue and will exit On Cannot bind port, cannot decrypt config, database unreachable at startup
error An operation failed and a human may need to act On Unhandled exception in a handler, payment provider 500, Kafka producer failure after retries
warn Something unexpected but handled; watch the trend On Retry succeeded on attempt 3, slow query over 500 ms, cache miss storm, deprecated endpoint used
info Business and lifecycle events you would want in an audit On Request completed, order created, worker started, config loaded
debug Developer detail for diagnosing a specific flow Off Cache key computed, branch taken, payload sizes
trace Everything, including per-item loops Off Raw SQL, per-message consumer processing

Two rules keep levels meaningful. First, an error must be actionable. A customer typing a wrong password is not an error; it is info with reason: "bad_credentials". A 4xx returned to a client is info or warn, never error, because the client caused it. Second, warn is for trends. One warn is fine; a thousand per minute is an alert, and you build that alert on the count rather than on any individual line.

Common mistakes

  • Logging expected validation failures as error, which drowns real errors and trains the team to ignore the level.
  • Leaving debug on in production because "it might be useful". It is useful in exactly the way a flooded basement is wet.

43.2.3 Request logging and correlation ids in NestJS

Concept

A correlation id (also called a request id) is a unique string attached to an inbound request and carried through everything that request causes: every log line, every downstream HTTP call, every Kafka message, every job. It is how you find "everything about this one request" across ten services.

Why does it exist?

Without it, an incident investigation is "find the log line at 14:02:11 in the API, then look in the worker's logs around 14:02:12 and hope only one order was being processed". With it, you type one id and see the whole story in order.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel's tracking number. Every depot, truck and courier scans the same number. You never ask "where is the brown box"; you ask "where is 1Z999AA1". A correlation id is the tracking number for one request.

How it works

  1. The API gateway or load balancer generates a request id if the client did not send one and sets X-Request-Id.
  2. The NestJS middleware reads X-Request-Id, or generates a UUID if it is missing, and stores it in AsyncLocalStorage (ALS), a Node.js mechanism that keeps a value attached to the current chain of async calls without passing it as a parameter.
  3. The logger reads the id from ALS on every call and adds it as a field.
  4. Outbound HTTP clients read it from ALS and set the header on every downstream call.
  5. Kafka producers add it as a message header. Consumers read the header, enter a new ALS context with that id, and every log line in the consumer carries it too.
  6. The response echoes X-Request-Id so a customer or support agent can quote it.

NestJS example

nestjs-cls wraps ALS as a NestJS module with middleware that opens a context per request.

TypeScript
// app.module.ts (correlation setup)
import { ClsModule } from 'nestjs-cls';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import type { Request } from 'express';

ClsModule.forRoot({
  global: true,
  middleware: {
    mount: true,        // registers the middleware for all routes
    generateId: true,
    idGenerator: (req: Request) => (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID(),
    setup: (cls, req: Request) => {
      cls.set('userId', (req as any).user?.id);   // filled later by the auth guard if present
    },
  },
}),

Feed the id into every pino line with a mixin, which pino calls on each log to merge extra fields.

TypeScript
// logging/logging.module.ts
import { ClsService } from 'nestjs-cls';
import { LoggerModule } from 'nestjs-pino';
import { trace } from '@opentelemetry/api';

LoggerModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ClsService],
  useFactory: (cls: ClsService) => ({
    pinoHttp: {
      mixin() {
        // Runs for every log call: attach correlation and trace ids from the current context.
        const span = trace.getActiveSpan()?.spanContext();
        return {
          requestId: cls.getId(),
          userId: cls.get('userId'),
          traceId: span?.traceId,
          spanId: span?.spanId,
        };
      },
    },
  }),
}),

Forward it on outbound HTTP calls with an Axios interceptor, and echo it on the response.

TypeScript
// http/outbound-http.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HttpService } from '@nestjs/axios';
import { ClsService } from 'nestjs-cls';

@Injectable()
export class OutboundHttpService {
  constructor(private readonly http: HttpService, private readonly cls: ClsService) {
    this.http.axiosRef.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
      config.headers['X-Request-Id'] = this.cls.getId();   // propagate downstream
      config.timeout = config.timeout ?? 3_000;             // never call without a timeout
      return config;
    });
  }
}

// request-id.interceptor.ts
@Injectable()
export class RequestIdInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly cls: ClsService) {}
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {
    ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().setHeader('X-Request-Id', this.cls.getId());
    return next.handle();
  }
}

Now Kafka. The producer adds the header; the consumer enters a new context per message.

TypeScript
// events/orders.producer.ts
await this.producer.send({
  topic: 'orders.created',
  messages: [{
    key: order.id,
    value: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.id, userId: order.userId }),
    headers: { 'x-request-id': this.cls.getId() },   // carry the correlation id across the broker
  }],
});

// workers/notifications.consumer.ts
await consumer.run({
  eachMessage: async ({ message }) => {
    const requestId = message.headers?.['x-request-id']?.toString() ?? randomUUID();
    // cls.run opens a fresh ALS context for this message; everything inside inherits it.
    await this.cls.run(async () => {
      this.cls.set(CLS_ID, requestId);
      await this.handler.handle(JSON.parse(message.value!.toString()));
    });
  },
});

CLS_ID is the constant exported by nestjs-cls for the id key. Inside handle, every log.info automatically carries requestId: req_7f3c, the same id the API used 200 ms earlier, even though this is a different process on a different node.

Production scenario

A support agent gets a complaint: "I was charged but my order shows cancelled". The agent asks for the request id from the app's error screen (req_7f3c...). One query in Loki, {env="prod"} | json | requestId="req_7f3c", returns 14 lines across orders-api, payments-api and orders-worker, in time order. Line 11 says the worker's warn: inventory reservation failed, cancelling order fired 300 ms after line 9's payment captured. Root cause found in three minutes, and the refund is issued before the agent hangs up.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • ALS loss. Context is lost across boundaries that break the async chain: callbacks from some native libraries, EventEmitter listeners registered outside the request, setTimeout scheduled during bootstrap, and message consumers, which have no inbound HTTP request at all. Use cls.run explicitly at those boundaries. Test it: log inside the consumer and assert requestId is present.
  • Trusting the client's id blindly. A client can send X-Request-Id: <script> or a 10 KB string. Validate the format (for example a UUID or a bounded alphanumeric string); otherwise generate your own and log the client's as clientRequestId.
  • Reusing one id for a batch. A worker that processes 500 messages under one id makes the id useless. One context per message.
  • Id collisions when two gateways generate short ids. Use UUIDs or 128-bit random values.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They consider correlation ids non-negotiable in any system with more than one process, and they test propagation in CI: an integration test sends X-Request-Id: test-123, consumes the resulting Kafka message, and asserts the worker's log line contains test-123. They know the difference between the correlation id (a business-friendly id for one inbound request) and the trace id (the tracing system's id, which may have a different lifetime); both live in every log line.

43.2.4 Sampling, rate limiting and the cost of volume

Concept

Log sampling means deliberately writing only a fraction of lines that match a rule. Rate limiting logs means capping how many identical lines can be written per second. Both exist because log volume is the single largest observability cost and because a flood of identical lines hides the one line you need.

How it works

  • Sample successes, keep failures. Log 100 percent of requests with status 5xx or duration over 1 second, and 1 to 10 percent of fast 2xx requests. Failures are rare and valuable; successes are common and mostly identical.
  • Rate limit repeated errors. When Redis is down, every request fails at the same line. Ten thousand identical ECONNREFUSED lines per minute are worse than one line per second plus a counter. Implement a small token bucket keyed by message, or rely on the log shipper's dedup feature.
  • Keep the audit trail off the sampled path. Business events that must exist (order placed, refund issued) are not logs to be sampled; they are records, and belong in a table or a Kafka topic.
TypeScript
// logging/sampled-request.interceptor.ts
@Injectable()
export class SampledRequestLoggerInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly log: PinoLogger) {}
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap({
        next: () => this.maybeLog(req, ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().statusCode, started),
        error: (err) => this.maybeLog(req, err.status ?? 500, started, err),
      }),
    );
  }
  private maybeLog(req: any, status: number, started: bigint, err?: Error) {
    const durationMs = Number((process.hrtime.bigint() - started) / 1_000_000n);
    const interesting = status >= 500 || durationMs > 1000 || !!err;
    if (!interesting && Math.random() > 0.05) return;   // keep 5 percent of boring requests
    this.log.info({ method: req.method, route: req.route?.path, status, durationMs, err, sampled: !interesting }, 'request');
  }
}

Metrics still count every request; sampling only affects the detailed record. That division of labour, metrics for counting and logs for detail, is the whole reason both exist.

43.2.5 Sync versus async logging and the event loop

Concept

Writing a log line means writing bytes to a file descriptor. If that write is synchronous, the event loop stops until the kernel accepts the bytes. If the destination is slow (a network socket, a full pipe, a disk under pressure), every request waits.

How it works

pino writes to stdout, and in a container stdout is a pipe read by the container runtime. Pipes have a buffer (64 KB on Linux by default). When the reader is slow, a synchronous write blocks the whole process. pino offers pino.destination({ sync: false }), which uses sonic-boom to buffer in memory and flush asynchronously, so a slow reader costs memory rather than latency. The tradeoff: on a hard crash, the last few kilobytes of buffered lines are lost. Flush on shutdown to keep them.

TypeScript
// logging/destination.ts
import pino from 'pino';

export const logDestination = pino.destination({
  sync: false,          // do not block the event loop on stdout backpressure
  minLength: 4096,      // buffer before writing; flushes automatically every so often
});

process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  logDestination.flushSync();   // push buffered lines before the container stops
});

Never ship logs directly from the application to a remote log service over the network in the request path. Write to stdout, let a node-level agent (Fluent Bit, Promtail, the CloudWatch agent) ship them. The agent has its own buffer and retry, and the application stays fast when the log backend is slow.

Production scenario

A team enabled a network transport inside the app to send logs straight to a hosted provider. During a provider outage the transport's queue grew, then the write blocked, and p99 latency went from 80 ms to 6 seconds while every dashboard showed the database perfectly healthy. The fix was to go back to stdout plus a node agent. The lesson: your logging library should never be able to make your API slow.

43.2.6 Aggregation, querying and log-based alerts

Concept

Log aggregation collects lines from every pod into one searchable store. The main choices are Loki (labels plus grep-like search, cheap), the Elastic stack (full-text indexes, expensive, powerful) and cloud-native stores (CloudWatch Logs, Google Cloud Logging).

How it works

Loki indexes only labels (service, env, pod, level) and stores the line as a compressed blob; it greps within the selected streams at query time. That makes ingestion 10 times cheaper than Elasticsearch, and queries on labels fast, but a query like "all lines containing orderId 8812 across all services for a week" scans a lot of data. Elasticsearch indexes every field so any query is fast, at the cost of 3 to 5 times more storage and CPU. CloudWatch Logs Insights sits between the two.

Typical LogQL queries you will actually run:

Text
{service="orders-api", env="prod"} | json | level="error" | line_format "{{.msg}} {{.orderId}}"
{env="prod"} | json | requestId="req_7f3c"
sum by (msg) (count_over_time({service="orders-api"} | json | level="error" [5m]))
{service="orders-api"} | json | durationMs > 2000

Log-based alerts fire on counts, never on single lines: count_over_time({service="payments-api"} | json | msg="provider timeout" [5m]) > 50. A single line is a story; fifty in five minutes is a symptom.

The "grep at 3 a.m." story

At 03:10 an SRE at a food-delivery company is paged: order placement latency p99 is 12 seconds. The metrics dashboard shows the API is slow, the database is idle and Redis is idle. Nothing is obviously broken. In the pre-observability days this meant SSH-ing into three API nodes, running grep "slow" /var/log/app.log | tail, and finding text lines like slow: 11842ms with nothing else. Which endpoint? Which dependency? Unknown. The engineer restarted the pods, latency recovered, and the post-mortem said "cause unknown".

With structured logs and a correlation id, the same engineer runs {service="orders-api"} | json | durationMs > 5000 | line_format "{{.route}} {{.dependency}} {{.dependencyMs}}" and sees every slow line says dependency="restaurant-service" dependencyMs=11500. The restaurant service's own logs, filtered by the same request ids, show warn: circuit open, falling back to slow path. Root cause in eight minutes, no restart, a real fix the next morning. The difference was not smarter people; it was fields.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The agent cannot keep up under load and drops lines silently. Watch the agent's own dropped_records metric.
  • Disk fills because a pod logs 200 MB a minute and log rotation is not configured. Kubernetes rotates container logs at 10 MB by default (five files), so the most verbose pod loses history first.
  • A log line contains invalid JSON (a stray console.log) and the whole line is stored unparsed; queries on fields miss it.
