  • Time zones: an app that logs local time and a store that assumes UTC puts your lines five and a half hours off from the metrics.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They choose Loki for most teams because the cost difference funds the retention difference, and structured logs plus labels cover 95 percent of queries. They move to Elasticsearch only when full-text search across unstructured bodies is a product requirement. They put the log-store's own health (ingest lag, dropped records) on the same dashboard as the service, because a dead log pipeline during an incident is a second incident.

Interview questions

  1. How do you propagate a request id across a Kafka boundary in Node.js?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: message header on produce; on consume, read the header and open a new AsyncLocalStorage context per message. Follow-up: what breaks if you forget the new context? (Logs in the consumer carry the previous message's id or none.)
  2. Why should the application write logs to stdout and not to a remote service directly?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: backpressure from a slow remote blocks the event loop or grows memory; a node agent buffers and retries outside the request path.
  3. What is wrong with logging a 4xx as error?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: not actionable, drowns real errors, breaks alerting on error counts.
  4. How would you find every log line for one customer's order across five services?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: shared correlation id and a shared field name, plus a query on that field in the aggregator.
  5. How do you keep log costs under control at 5,000 RPS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sample successful requests, keep all failures, rate limit repeated errors, cap retention, move audit facts out of logs.

Practical exercise

Build request logging and correlation for a NestJS orders service:

  1. Add nestjs-pino and nestjs-cls. Every log line must carry service, env, version, requestId, traceId (may be empty), userId when authenticated.
  2. Incoming X-Request-Id is reused if it matches ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,64}$, otherwise generated.
  3. Outbound Axios calls and Kafka messages carry the id; a consumer opens a new context per message.
  4. Log only 5 percent of successful requests under 1 second; log 100 percent of failures and slow requests.
  5. Acceptance: an integration test sends X-Request-Id: test-abc, triggers a Kafka message, and asserts the consumer's captured log output contains "requestId":"test-abc". A test also asserts that Authorization and password never appear in any log output.

43.3 Metrics

43.3.1 Metric types: counter, gauge, histogram, summary

Concept

A metric is a named number, with a small set of labels, sampled over time. http_requests_total{route="/orders",status="201"} is a metric. The value is stored every 15 seconds or so, and you can graph it, compare it with last week, and alert when it crosses a line. Metrics are the cheapest signal to store and the fastest to query, which is why almost every alert is built on them.

Why does it exist?

You cannot alert on logs at scale without paying to index every line, and you cannot alert on traces because they are sampled. Metrics exist to answer "how is the system doing right now, and is that different from normal" in one cheap query, regardless of how many requests happened.

Mental model

Imagine a car dashboard. The odometer only ever goes up (a counter). The fuel gauge goes up and down (a gauge). The trip computer that says "your average speed was 62 km/h, and you spent 15 percent of the trip above 100" is a histogram. Nobody wants the car to log every rotation of the wheel; the dashboard summarizes.

How it works

Type Behaviour Use for Query pattern
Counter Only increases; resets to 0 on restart Requests, errors, bytes, jobs processed, messages consumed rate(x[5m]) turns it into per-second
Gauge Goes up and down In-flight requests, pool connections in use, queue depth, memory, temperature Use the raw value; max_over_time for peaks
Histogram Counts observations into fixed buckets, plus sum and count Latency, payload size, job duration histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(x_bucket[5m]))
Summary Client-side quantiles over a sliding window Rarely; when you cannot aggregate across instances Cannot be aggregated across pods correctly

Histograms beat summaries almost always. A histogram is a set of counters (le="0.05", le="0.1", ...) that Prometheus can add across pods and then compute a quantile from. A summary computes p99 inside each pod; the average of ten pods' p99 is not the fleet's p99. Choose bucket boundaries deliberately: for HTTP latency, [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10] seconds covers a typical API; for a batch job, use seconds to minutes.

Common mistakes

  • Using a gauge for something that only goes up, and then being unable to compute a rate after restarts.
  • Recording latency in milliseconds under a metric named _seconds, or the reverse. Prometheus convention is base units: seconds, bytes.
  • Default buckets that stop at 10 seconds when your slow path is 30 seconds; everything above the last bucket lands in +Inf and the quantile lies.

43.3.2 RED, USE and the Golden Signals

Concept

Three small frameworks tell you which metrics to collect. They exist so that you do not have to invent a dashboard from scratch for every service.

  • RED for request-driven services: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second), Duration (latency distribution). Every API, every consumer, every worker gets these three.
  • USE for resources: Utilization (how busy: CPU percent, pool in-use over pool size), Saturation (how much work is queued: run queue, waiting connections, event loop lag), Errors (hardware or driver errors). Every CPU, disk, connection pool and queue gets these three.
  • Google's four Golden Signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. RED plus saturation, in practice.

Mental model

Imagine a bank branch. RED is about customers: how many arrive per minute, how many leave unhappy, how long each waits. USE is about tellers: how busy they are, how long the queue is, how many computers crashed. You need both to know whether to hire more tellers or fix the software.

How it works

For a NestJS service the RED metrics come from one interceptor. The USE metrics come from prom-client's default collectors (CPU, memory, event loop lag, GC) and from your own gauges on pools and queues.

The key backend metrics

This is the list a senior engineer expects to find for every service. If one is missing, the first outage will show why.

Area Metric Type Why it matters
Process process_cpu_seconds_total counter CPU usage as rate(); over 0.8 of a core means the loop is saturated
Process process_resident_memory_bytes, nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes gauge Leak detection; OOMKilled prediction
Process nodejs_eventloop_lag_seconds (p50, p99) gauge The most important Node.js metric: how long a callback waits to run. Over 100 ms means every request is slow regardless of dependencies
Process nodejs_gc_duration_seconds histogram Long GC pauses explain latency spikes with no dependency cause
HTTP http_requests_total{method,route,status} counter Rate and error rate
HTTP http_request_duration_seconds{method,route} histogram Latency per route
HTTP http_requests_in_flight gauge Saturation; rises before latency does
PostgreSQL `db_pool_connections{state="in_use idle waiting"}`
PostgreSQL db_query_duration_seconds{operation} histogram Slow queries by operation, not by full SQL text
Redis redis_command_duration_seconds{command} histogram Redis should be under 1 ms; a spike is network or a blocked Redis
Redis `cache_requests_total{result="hit miss"}` counter
Kafka kafka_consumer_lag{topic,group,partition} gauge The consumer is falling behind
Kafka kafka_messages_consumed_total{topic,result} counter Consumer RED
Jobs jobs_processed_total{queue,result}, job_duration_seconds{queue} counter, histogram Worker RED
Jobs queue_depth{queue,state} gauge Saturation
Dependencies outbound_request_duration_seconds{target} histogram Which third party is slow
Dependencies circuit_breaker_state{target} gauge 0 closed, 1 half-open, 2 open
Build app_build_info{version,commit} gauge, always 1 Join with any other metric to see which version is misbehaving

43.3.3 Cardinality

Concept

Cardinality is the number of distinct time series a metric produces, which is the product of the number of distinct values of each label. http_requests_total with 30 routes, 5 methods and 10 status codes is at most 1,500 series per pod. The same metric with a userId label and one million users is a million series, and it will take your Prometheus down.

Why it matters

Prometheus keeps an index and a recent-data chunk in memory for every active series. Roughly, 1 million active series costs 4 to 8 GB of RAM and slows every query. A single bad label added in a single service has taken down company-wide monitoring more than once.

Rules

  • Never label by user id, order id, session id, email, IP, request id, or any free-form value.
  • Use the route template (/orders/:id), never the raw path (/orders/8812).
  • Bound status codes to the ones you emit, or group them (2xx, 4xx, 5xx) if you must.
  • Keep a mental multiplication: routes × methods × statuses × pods. If the number is above 10,000 for one metric, redesign.
  • High-cardinality questions ("which user is slow?") belong to traces and logs, which is exactly why exemplars link the two.

43.3.4 Exposing /metrics in NestJS

NestJS example

prom-client is the standard Node.js Prometheus library. @willsoto/nestjs-prometheus wraps it with providers and a controller. Both are shown; the manual approach is ten more lines and has no dependency.

TypeScript
// metrics/metrics.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PrometheusModule, makeCounterProvider, makeHistogramProvider, makeGaugeProvider } from '@willsoto/nestjs-prometheus';

@Module({
  imports: [
    PrometheusModule.register({
      path: '/metrics',
      defaultMetrics: { enabled: true },   // process CPU, memory, event loop lag, GC, handles
      defaultLabels: { service: 'orders-api' },
    }),
  ],
  providers: [
    makeCounterProvider({
      name: 'http_requests_total',
      help: 'HTTP requests by method, route template and status',
      labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
    }),
    makeHistogramProvider({
      name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
      help: 'HTTP request latency',
      labelNames: ['method', 'route'],
      buckets: [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10],
    }),
    makeGaugeProvider({ name: 'http_requests_in_flight', help: 'Requests currently being handled' }),
  ],
  exports: [PrometheusModule],
})
export class MetricsModule {}
TypeScript
// metrics/http-metrics.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectMetric } from '@willsoto/nestjs-prometheus';
import { Counter, Gauge, Histogram } from 'prom-client';
import { finalize, Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class HttpMetricsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(
    @InjectMetric('http_requests_total') private readonly requests: Counter<string>,
    @InjectMetric('http_request_duration_seconds') private readonly duration: Histogram<string>,
    @InjectMetric('http_requests_in_flight') private readonly inFlight: Gauge<string>,
  ) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const http = ctx.switchToHttp();
    const req = http.getRequest();
    const method = req.method;
    // Route template, never the raw URL: "/orders/:id" not "/orders/8812".
    const route = req.route?.path ?? 'unmatched';
    this.inFlight.inc();
    const stop = this.duration.startTimer({ method, route });
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap({
        next: () => this.requests.inc({ method, route, status: String(http.getResponse().statusCode) }),
        error: (err) => this.requests.inc({ method, route, status: String(err.status ?? 500) }),
      }),
      finalize(() => { stop(); this.inFlight.dec(); }),
    );
  }
}

The manual alternative, if you prefer no wrapper:

TypeScript
// metrics/metrics.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header } from '@nestjs/common';
import { collectDefaultMetrics, Registry } from 'prom-client';

export const registry = new Registry();
registry.setDefaultLabels({ service: 'orders-api' });
collectDefaultMetrics({ register: registry, eventLoopMonitoringPrecision: 10 });

@Controller('metrics')
export class MetricsController {
  @Get()
  @Header('Content-Type', registry.contentType)
  async scrape(): Promise<string> {
    return registry.metrics();   // text exposition format, one line per series
  }
}

Two things to add on day one: the build info gauge and the database pool gauges.

TypeScript
// metrics/build-info.provider.ts
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';
new Gauge({
  name: 'app_build_info',
  help: 'Always 1; labels carry version and commit',
  labelNames: ['version', 'commit'],
  registers: [registry],
}).set({ version: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? 'dev', commit: process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'unknown' }, 1);

TypeORM example

TypeORM's PostgreSQL driver wraps a pg.Pool, which exposes totalCount, idleCount and waitingCount. Read them in a collect callback so the gauge is fresh at scrape time.

TypeScript
// metrics/db-pool.metrics.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';
import type { Pool } from 'pg';

@Injectable()
export class DbPoolMetrics implements OnModuleInit {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  onModuleInit() {
    const pool = (this.dataSource.driver as any).master as Pool;   // pg.Pool behind TypeORM
    new Gauge({
      name: 'db_pool_connections',
      help: 'PostgreSQL pool connections by state',
      labelNames: ['state'],
      registers: [registry],
      collect() {
        this.set({ state: 'total' }, pool.totalCount);
        this.set({ state: 'idle' }, pool.idleCount);
        this.set({ state: 'in_use' }, pool.totalCount - pool.idleCount);
        this.set({ state: 'waiting' }, pool.waitingCount);   // callers blocked waiting for a connection
      },
    });
  }
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize's connection manager holds a generic-pool instance with size, available, borrowed and pending.

TypeScript
// metrics/sequelize-pool.metrics.ts
const pool = (sequelize.connectionManager as any).pool;
new Gauge({
  name: 'db_pool_connections',
  help: 'PostgreSQL pool connections by state',
  labelNames: ['state'],
  registers: [registry],
  collect() {
    this.set({ state: 'total' }, pool.size);
    this.set({ state: 'idle' }, pool.available);
    this.set({ state: 'in_use' }, pool.borrowed);
    this.set({ state: 'waiting' }, pool.pending);
  },
});

PostgreSQL example

The database has its own metrics, exposed by postgres_exporter, which runs SQL against the catalog views. The three queries you would put on a dashboard:

SQL
-- Connections by state: watch "idle in transaction" and "active" trending up
SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database() GROUP BY state;

-- Cache hit ratio: below 0.99 on a hot OLTP database means shared_buffers or the working set is wrong
SELECT sum(blks_hit)::float / nullif(sum(blks_hit) + sum(blks_read), 0) AS cache_hit_ratio
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

-- Top statements by total time (requires pg_stat_statements)
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

43.3.5 Prometheus scraping, PromQL and recording rules

How it works

Prometheus is a pull system. Every 15 seconds (the scrape interval) it makes an HTTP GET to each target's /metrics, parses the text, and appends samples to its time-series database. In Kubernetes it discovers targets from the API server (pod annotations or a ServiceMonitor), so a new pod is scraped within one interval of becoming ready.

Pull has consequences. A pod that is overloaded may fail its scrape, which shows up as up == 0 and is itself an alert. A pod that lives for 10 seconds (a short job) is never scraped; for those you use the Pushgateway, or better, emit job metrics from the long-lived worker.

PromQL, the query language, is small. Five expressions cover most dashboards:

Text
# Request rate per second, per route, over the last 5 minutes
sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{service="orders-api"}[5m]))

# Error ratio: 5xx over all requests
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders-api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders-api"}[5m]))

# p99 latency per route from the histogram buckets
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="orders-api"}[5m])))

# Event loop lag p99 per pod
nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds{service="orders-api"}

# Pool exhaustion: callers waiting for a connection
max by (pod) (db_pool_connections{service="orders-api", state="waiting"})

rate() needs a range at least four times the scrape interval to be stable; [5m] with 15 second scrapes is conventional. histogram_quantile over sum by (le) is how you aggregate latency across pods correctly.

Recording rules precompute expensive expressions on a schedule and store the result as a new series. The p99 query above scans every bucket of every pod; on a dashboard refreshing every 10 seconds with 20 panels, that is real load. A rule turns it into a single series lookup.

YAML
# prometheus/rules/orders-api.yml
groups:
  - name: orders-api.rules
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - record: service:http_request_duration_seconds:p99_5m
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, service, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
      - record: service:http_requests:error_ratio_5m
        expr: |
          sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            / sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

The naming convention level:metric:operations is a Prometheus community standard and makes rules discoverable.

43.3.6 Grafana dashboards: the service overview

Concept

A dashboard is a question-answering layout, not a wall of graphs. The first screen for any service should answer, in 30 seconds, "is it healthy, and if not, where do I look next". A senior engineer builds one dashboard template and stamps it on every service using a service variable.

The recommended layout

Design rules that come from painful experience:

  • Put the error ratio next to its SLO line so anyone can see "we are burning budget" without reading a number.
  • Show latency as p50, p95 and p99 together, never as an average. An average of 40 ms can hide a p99 of 4 seconds.
  • Use per-pod lines for saturation panels; a single hot pod is a common failure mode and a fleet average hides it.
  • Add deploy annotations. Half of all incidents begin at a vertical line.
  • Link every panel to the query that would come next: from the error panel to the log query with level="error", from the latency panel to the trace search with duration > 2s.

43.3.7 Alerting rules

Concept

An alert is a promise: "when this fires, a human must act now". Every alert that does not meet that bar trains the on-call to ignore the pager. The goal is few alerts, each pointing at a symptom customers feel, each with a runbook.

How it works

Alert on symptoms, not causes. "Error ratio above 1 percent for 5 minutes" is a symptom. "CPU above 80 percent" is a cause, and a cause that may not matter; a batch job at 95 percent CPU with fine latency is not an incident. Causes go on dashboards for diagnosis; symptoms go to the pager.

Alert on SLOs with burn rates. If your SLO is 99.9 percent availability over 30 days, your error budget is 0.1 percent of requests, about 43 minutes of full outage a month. A burn rate of 1 means you are consuming the budget exactly on schedule; a burn rate of 14.4 means you will exhaust the month's budget in 50 hours. Multi-window burn rate alerting pages when the error ratio over both a long window (1 hour) and a short window (5 minutes) exceed a burn-rate threshold. The long window proves it is real; the short window proves it is still happening, so the alert resolves as soon as the fix lands.

YAML
# prometheus/rules/orders-api-alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: orders-api.slo
    rules:
      - alert: OrdersApiHighErrorBurn
        # 14.4x burn over 1h and 5m: exhausts a 30-day 99.9 percent budget in about 2 days
        expr: |
          (service:http_requests:error_ratio_1h{service="orders-api"} > (14.4 * 0.001))
          and
          (service:http_requests:error_ratio_5m{service="orders-api"} > (14.4 * 0.001))
        for: 2m
        labels: { severity: page, team: orders }
        annotations:
          summary: "orders-api is burning error budget fast"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.internal/orders-api/high-error-rate"
      - alert: OrdersApiLatencyP99
        expr: service:http_request_duration_seconds:p99_5m{service="orders-api", route="/orders"} > 1.5
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: page, team: orders }
        annotations:
          summary: "POST /orders p99 above 1.5 s for 10 minutes"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.internal/orders-api/latency"
      - alert: OrdersApiDbPoolExhausted
        expr: max by (pod) (db_pool_connections{service="orders-api", state="waiting"}) > 5
        for: 3m
        labels: { severity: ticket, team: orders }
        annotations:
          summary: "callers waiting for a DB connection on {{ $labels.pod }}"

Notice the two severities. page wakes someone. ticket creates a work item for business hours. Most cause-based conditions (pool nearly full, disk 70 percent) belong at ticket.

Avoiding alert fatigue.

  • Every alert has an owner team, a runbook link and a for: duration. No for: means one bad scrape pages someone.
  • Group in Alertmanager by service so a database outage produces one page, not forty.
  • Inhibit child alerts when a parent fires: if PostgresDown is firing, mute DbPoolExhausted.
  • Review the pager weekly: any alert that fired and needed no action gets fixed or deleted that week.
  • Never alert on averages; alert on ratios and quantiles.

Production scenario

A payments service with 200 RPS and an SLO of 99.95 percent. The monthly budget is 0.05 percent of about 518 million requests, roughly 259,000 failed requests. A provider outage causes a 3 percent error rate. The 5 minute window crosses the 14.4x threshold (0.72 percent) within 2 minutes; the 1 hour window crosses after 15 minutes; the alert pages at minute 17. That is deliberately slower than a naive "error rate above 1 percent for 1 minute" alert, but it never pages for a 90 second blip, and the on-call has learned to trust it.

Failure scenario

At 09:03 a deploy to the catalog service ships a query with a missing index. p99 goes from 40 ms to 900 ms. No alert fires because the only latency alert is on the average, which moves from 25 ms to 60 ms. Customers complain on social media at 09:40. The retrospective adds p99 alerts per route, deploy annotations to the dashboard and a canary step to the pipeline; the alert would have fired at 09:14.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A counter reset after a restart looks like a dip; rate() handles it, raw subtraction does not.
  • Scrapes failing under load produce gaps that look like zero traffic. Alert on up == 0 separately.
  • A metric registered twice (two modules creating the same Counter) throws at startup; keep one registry module.
  • Many pods restarting at once (a rollout) reset all counters; rate() over [5m] smooths it, [1m] does not.
  • Histogram buckets changed in a deploy make old and new series unmergeable for the overlap.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the alert set with the on-call rota in mind: what will I be woken for, and will I know what to do. They insist every page has a runbook and every runbook has been used at least once in a game day. They treat "alert fired, nothing to do" as a bug with the same priority as a real incident. When a product manager asks for "an alert if anything goes wrong", they translate it into two or three SLO burn-rate alerts and explain that anything more will be ignored within a month.

Interview questions

  1. Why histograms rather than summaries for latency?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: histograms aggregate across instances; summaries do not. Follow-up: how do you pick bucket boundaries?
  2. What is cardinality and why does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: number of distinct series; memory and query cost grow with it; never label by user id. Follow-up: where do per-user questions go? (Traces and logs.)
  3. Explain multi-window burn-rate alerting.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: long window proves severity, short window proves it is ongoing; thresholds derived from the SLO. Follow-up: why not alert on "error rate above 1 percent"?
  4. What is the single most important Node.js process metric?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: event loop lag; it explains latency that no dependency explains.
  5. What is the difference between a symptom-based and a cause-based alert, and which should page?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: symptoms page; causes inform.
  6. A dashboard shows average latency 50 ms but users complain. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: p95 and p99, per-route, per-pod; averages hide tails.

Practical exercise

Instrument a NestJS orders service and build its overview dashboard:

  1. Expose /metrics with default process metrics, http_requests_total, http_request_duration_seconds with explicit buckets, http_requests_in_flight, db_pool_connections{state}, app_build_info.
  2. Run Prometheus and Grafana locally in Docker Compose scraping the service every 15 seconds.
  3. Build the five-row overview dashboard with a service variable.
  4. Write two recording rules (p99 and error ratio) and one multi-window burn-rate alert for a 99.9 percent SLO.
  5. Acceptance: a load test with autocannon at 200 RPS shows rate, p99 and pool in-use panels moving; killing PostgreSQL makes the error-ratio panel cross the SLO line and the alert reach firing in Prometheus within 5 minutes; sum(count by (__name__) ({service="orders-api"})) stays under 500 series per pod.

43.4 Traces

43.4.1 Distributed tracing explained simply

Concept

A trace is the record of one request's journey through your system, as a tree of timed operations called spans. The API handler is a span. The PostgreSQL query it runs is a child span. The Kafka publish is another child. The worker that consumes the message starts a span whose parent is the publish span, even though it runs in a different process on a different node minutes later. Put the tree on a timeline and you see exactly where the time went.

Each span carries:

  • a trace id (128-bit, shared by every span in the request),
  • a span id (64-bit, unique to this operation),
  • a parent span id (empty for the root),
  • a name (POST /orders, SELECT orders, kafka.send orders.created),
  • start and end timestamps,
  • attributes: key-value pairs such as http.status_code, db.statement, order.id,
  • events: timestamped notes inside the span, such as an exception,
  • a status: unset, ok, or error.

Why does it exist?

Logs tell you what happened in one process. Metrics tell you how much and how often. Neither tells you that a 3 second request spent 2.8 seconds waiting for a lock in PostgreSQL after a 100 ms Redis timeout. Tracing exists because in a system of six processes, "where did the time go" is the first question of every latency incident, and it cannot be answered from any single process.

Mental model

Imagine a relay race where every runner wears a GPS watch and the baton has a barcode. After the race you can lay every runner's segment on one timeline, see that runner three stood still for 40 seconds waiting for a gate to open, and know exactly which baton it was. The barcode is the trace id. Each runner's segment is a span. The gate is your database lock.

How it works

Step by step, for the request above:

  1. The gateway sees no incoming trace context, so it starts a new trace: it generates a trace id and a root span.
  2. It forwards the request with a traceparent header, the W3C Trace Context standard: 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-<flags>. 00 is the version, the flags byte carries the sampled bit (01 means sampled).
  3. The NestJS HTTP instrumentation reads traceparent, creates a server span whose parent is the gateway's span, and stores the active span in an AsyncLocalStorage context, the same mechanism the correlation id uses.
  4. Every instrumented client call (pg, ioredis, kafkajs, http) creates a child span under whatever span is active, and ends it when the call completes.
  5. The Kafka instrumentation injects traceparent as a message header. When the worker consumes the message, the instrumentation extracts it and starts a span with that parent. The trace now crosses an asynchronous boundary and shows the 180 ms of queueing as a gap between the send span and the process span.
  6. Spans are batched in memory and exported to a collector every few seconds. The collector forwards them to a trace store: Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, AWS X-Ray or a vendor.

Sampling: head versus tail

Tracing every request in a 5,000 RPS system produces 40,000 spans per second. Nobody stores that. Sampling decides which traces to keep.

  • Head sampling decides at the root, when the trace starts, usually "keep 10 percent at random". The decision travels in the traceparent flags so every service agrees. It is simple and cheap, and it is blind: it cannot know that this request will fail in 3 seconds, so 90 percent of failures are discarded.
  • Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete. The OpenTelemetry Collector buffers all spans of a trace for a few seconds, then applies policies: keep every trace with an error, keep every trace slower than 1 second, keep 5 percent of the rest. This keeps the interesting traces at a fraction of the cost. The price is memory in the collector and the requirement that every span of a trace reach the same collector instance (load balance by trace id).

The usual production shape is head sampling at 100 percent inside the application (mark everything sampled, so the collector sees everything) and tail sampling in the collector, or head sampling at 10 to 20 percent when there is no collector budget. A ParentBasedSampler respects the upstream decision so a trace is never half-kept.

43.4.2 OpenTelemetry setup in NestJS

Concept

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs: an API your code calls, an SDK that implements it, auto-instrumentation libraries that patch popular packages, and a wire protocol (OTLP) to ship data. You instrument once and can switch from Jaeger to Tempo to a vendor by changing the exporter.

How it works

The SDK must start before any instrumented module is imported, because auto-instrumentation works by patching require. In NestJS that means a separate tracing.ts file loaded first, either via import './tracing' as the first line of main.ts or with node -r ./dist/tracing.js dist/main.js.

TypeScript
// tracing.ts (loaded before anything else)
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http';
import { resourceFromAttributes } from '@opentelemetry/resources';
import { ATTR_SERVICE_NAME, ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION } from '@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions';
import { ParentBasedSampler, TraceIdRatioBasedSampler, BatchSpanProcessor } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';

const exporter = new OTLPTraceExporter({
  url: process.env.OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT ?? 'http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces',
  timeoutMillis: 5_000,
});

export const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({
    [ATTR_SERVICE_NAME]: 'orders-api',
    [ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION]: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? 'dev',
    'deployment.environment': process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'dev',
  }),
  // Respect the upstream sampled flag; sample 20 percent of new roots.
  sampler: new ParentBasedSampler({ root: new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(0.2) }),
  spanProcessors: [
    new BatchSpanProcessor(exporter, {
      maxQueueSize: 4096,        // spans buffered before dropping; bounded so memory cannot explode
      scheduledDelayMs: 2_000,   // export at least every 2 s
      exportTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
    }),
  ],
  instrumentations: [
    getNodeAutoInstrumentations({
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http': {
        ignoreIncomingRequestHook: (req) => req.url === '/health' || req.url === '/metrics',
      },
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-express': {},
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-nestjs-core': {},
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-pg': { enhancedDatabaseReporting: false }, // no bound parameters in spans
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-ioredis': {},
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-kafkajs': {},
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-fs': { enabled: false },   // file system spans are noise
    }),
  ],
});

sdk.start();

// Flush spans on shutdown; bounded so a dead collector cannot block the pod from stopping.
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  Promise.race([sdk.shutdown(), new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3_000))])
    .finally(() => process.exit(0));
});
TypeScript
// main.ts
import './tracing';           // must be the first import
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true });
  app.enableShutdownHooks();
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

With only this file, every inbound HTTP request, every pg query, every ioredis command and every kafkajs send and consume produces spans with the right parents. The pg instrumentation names spans by operation and includes db.statement (the SQL text without parameters when enhancedDatabaseReporting is off); the Kafka instrumentation injects and extracts traceparent in message headers.

NestJS example: manual spans in services

Auto-instrumentation shows you dependencies. It does not show you your logic: "validate cart", "reserve inventory", "calculate pricing". Wrap meaningful business steps in manual spans and attach the business ids as attributes.

TypeScript
// orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { trace, SpanStatusCode, Span } from '@opentelemetry/api';

const tracer = trace.getTracer('orders-api');

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly inventory: InventoryService, private readonly repo: OrdersRepository) {}

  async place(userId: string, dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
    // startActiveSpan makes this span the parent of everything awaited inside the callback.
    return tracer.startActiveSpan('orders.place', async (span: Span) => {
      span.setAttributes({ 'user.id': userId, 'order.item_count': dto.items.length });
      try {
        const reservation = await this.reserve(dto);              // child span
        const order = await this.repo.create(userId, dto, reservation);
        span.setAttribute('order.id', order.id);                  // searchable in Tempo or Jaeger
        span.addEvent('order.persisted', { 'order.total_cents': order.totalCents });
        span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.OK });
        return order;
      } catch (err) {
        span.recordException(err as Error);                      // stack and message as a span event
        span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message: (err as Error).message });
        throw err;
      } finally {
        span.end();                                               // always end, or the span never exports
      }
    });
  }

  private reserve(dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    return tracer.startActiveSpan('inventory.reserve', async (span) => {
      try {
        return await this.inventory.reserve(dto.items);
      } finally {
        span.end();
      }
    });
  }
}

Attribute naming: use dotted namespaces (order.id, payment.provider), never PII (user.email), and keep values bounded. Attributes are indexed by most backends, so order.id makes the trace findable from a support ticket.

For a reusable pattern, a NestJS interceptor can open a span per handler with the controller and method name, so every route has a span even before you add manual ones:

TypeScript
// tracing/handler-span.interceptor.ts
@Injectable()
export class HandlerSpanInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const name = `${ctx.getClass().name}.${ctx.getHandler().name}`;
    return new Observable((subscriber) => {
      tracer.startActiveSpan(name, (span) => {
        next.handle().pipe(finalize(() => span.end())).subscribe({
          next: (v) => subscriber.next(v),
          error: (e) => { span.recordException(e); span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR }); subscriber.error(e); },
          complete: () => subscriber.complete(),
        });
      });
    });
  }
}

Exporters and where traces go

The application exports OTLP (over HTTP on port 4318 or gRPC on 4317) to a collector, never directly to the storage backend. The collector then exports to one or more of:

Backend Character Typical choice when
Jaeger Open source, mature UI, own storage (Cassandra, Elasticsearch, or Badger) Self-hosted, moderate volume
Grafana Tempo Object-storage backed, very cheap per span, searches by trace id and attributes, integrates with Loki and Prometheus Already on Grafana, high volume
AWS X-Ray Managed, integrates with AWS services Fully on AWS, low ops budget
Vendor (Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic) Managed, powerful, priced per span or per GB Budget exists, ops team is small

Switching backends is a collector config change. That is the entire point of exporting OTLP from the application.

Reading a trace to find the slow span

Open the trace for a slow request and read it like this:

  1. Look at the root span's duration. That is what the customer felt.
  2. Find the longest child. If children are sequential, the sum explains the root; if they overlap, the request did work in parallel.
  3. Look for gaps: time in the parent that no child accounts for. A gap is CPU work in your own process (JSON serialization, a synchronous loop) or event loop lag, and neither shows as a span.
  4. Look for fan-out: a hundred tiny sequential SELECT spans is an N+1 query; you will see them as a staircase.
  5. Look for waiting: a pg span of 2 seconds for an UPDATE that normally takes 2 ms is lock contention; the SQL is fine, the row was locked.
  6. Check the async gap between a Kafka send span and its consumer span: that is queueing delay and consumer lag, visible without any Kafka dashboard.

A trace that shows POST /orders at 3,100 ms with children redis GET 0.4 ms, pg INSERT 3,050 ms and everything else under 10 ms is a lock or a slow disk, not application code. A trace that shows the same root with children summing to 200 ms and a 2,900 ms gap is event loop blocking, and the next step is a CPU profile.

Linking logs to traces and metrics exemplars

Two links make the three pillars one tool.

Logs to traces. The mixin in 43.2.3 adds traceId and spanId from trace.getActiveSpan() to every log line. In Grafana, a Loki line with a traceId field gets a button that opens the trace in Tempo, and a Tempo trace gets a button that queries Loki for that id. You move between "what did the code say" and "where did the time go" in one click.

Metrics to traces via exemplars. An exemplar is a trace id attached to a histogram bucket observation. When the p99 panel shows a spike, you click a dot on the spike and open a real trace from that bucket. prom-client supports this with enableExemplars.

TypeScript
// metrics/http-metrics.interceptor.ts (exemplar variant)
const duration = new Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'HTTP request latency',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route'],
  buckets: [0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10],
  enableExemplars: true,
  registers: [registry],
});

// at the end of the request
const span = trace.getActiveSpan()?.spanContext();
duration.observe({
  labels: { method, route },
  value: elapsedSeconds,
  exemplarLabels: span ? { traceId: span.traceId } : {},   // exposed as # {traceId="..."} in the scrape
});

Prometheus must run with --enable-feature=exemplar-storage, and Grafana's Prometheus data source is configured to link the traceId exemplar label to Tempo.

Production scenario

An orders API at 800 RPS, 8 spans per request, head sampling 20 percent: 1,280 spans per second exported, batched in 2 second flushes of about 2,500 spans (roughly 1 MB). The collector tail-samples down to 100 percent of errors and slow traces plus 5 percent of the rest, storing about 300 spans per second in Tempo. At typical object-storage pricing this costs tens of dollars a month; the same traffic traced at 100 percent with no tail sampling into a per-span vendor plan costs thousands.

Failure scenario

At 16:20 the on-call sees POST /checkout p99 at 4 seconds. The dashboard shows PostgreSQL and Redis healthy. They click an exemplar on the p99 spike and land on a trace. The root is 3.9 seconds; the children are redis GET 0.5 ms, pg SELECT 2 ms and http POST https://pricing.internal/quote 3,850 ms. The pricing service's trace, linked by the same trace id, shows its own root at 3,840 ms with an http POST tax-provider child at 3,800 ms. The tax provider is slow; the checkout service has no timeout on the pricing call; the pricing service has no timeout on the tax provider. Fix: 800 ms timeouts at both hops and a cached fallback for tax rates. Without tracing this was "checkout is slow, nothing is wrong"; with it, the diagnosis took the time it takes to click twice.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Context loss. setTimeout, setImmediate, EventEmitter listeners and Promise chains created outside the request lose the active span. Use context.with(context.active(), fn) or bind the callback; test it.
  • Spans never ended (missing span.end() in an error path) never export, and the trace shows a hole exactly where the bug is.
  • Instrumentation not loaded because the SDK started after pg was required. The symptom is HTTP spans with no children.
  • Exporter blocking shutdown. sdk.shutdown() waits for the collector; if it is down, the pod hangs until Kubernetes kills it. Bound the wait.
  • Clock skew between hosts makes a child span appear to start before its parent, or a consumer span appear before the producer's. Trace stores tolerate it, but negative gaps confuse humans. Run NTP or chrony on every node.
  • Sampling hiding the rare failure. At 1 percent head sampling, a failure that happens once an hour is captured once every four days. Use tail sampling or force-sample on errors.
  • Attribute cardinality is fine (traces are meant for it) but attribute size is not: a 200 KB db.statement per span multiplies export cost and can exceed collector limits.

43.4.3 Correlation ID versus Trace ID versus Span ID

Correlation id (request id) Trace id Span id
Who generates it Gateway or first service, or the client Tracing SDK at the root of a trace Tracing SDK for every operation
Format Anything; usually UUID 32 hex characters (128-bit) 16 hex characters (64-bit)
Header X-Request-Id (convention) traceparent (W3C standard) Part of traceparent as the parent span id
Scope One inbound request and everything it causes, including async work One trace, which is usually the same thing but can be cut by sampling or by a new root One operation within a trace
Lives in logs Yes, on every line Yes, on every line Usually, to jump to the exact span
Survives sampling Always; it is just a string you carry The id exists always, but the trace data exists only if sampled Same
Shown to customers Yes, on error screens and in support tickets No No
Purpose Human-friendly "find everything about this request" Machine-friendly "reconstruct the timing tree" Locate one node in that tree

Many teams simplify by making the correlation id equal to the trace id. That works when every entry point is traced and the gateway generates the trace, but it breaks when a client wants to send its own id, or when sampling means the trace was never stored. The safest design keeps both: a request id that always exists and is always logged, and a trace id that links to the trace when there is one.

43.5 OpenTelemetry Collector and how the tools fit together

43.5.1 The collector

Concept

The OpenTelemetry Collector is a standalone process that receives telemetry (OTLP, Prometheus, Jaeger and other formats), processes it (batching, filtering, attribute manipulation, tail sampling, memory limiting) and exports it to one or more backends. It sits between your services and your storage so that the services do not need to know or care where the data goes.

Why does it exist?

Without a collector, every service holds credentials for every backend, retries against every backend, and changes when the backend changes. With a collector, the service speaks OTLP to otel-collector:4317 and everything else is a config file operated by the platform team. The collector also makes tail sampling possible, because tail sampling needs all spans of a trace in one place.

How it works

A pipeline is receivers, then processors in order, then exporters. Traces, metrics and logs each get their own pipeline. The processors that matter:

  • memory_limiter first, always. It refuses data when the collector approaches its memory limit instead of being OOMKilled and losing everything in its buffers.
  • tail_sampling holds spans per trace for a decision window (10 to 30 seconds) then applies policies.
  • attributes or transform to remove anything sensitive that slipped in, and to add cluster or region labels.
  • batch last, to compress export traffic.
YAML
# otel-collector.yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: { endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317 }
      http: { endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318 }

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 1500
    spike_limit_mib: 300
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 15s
    num_traces: 200000
    policies:
      - { name: errors, type: status_code, status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] } }
      - { name: slow, type: latency, latency: { threshold_ms: 1000 } }
      - { name: baseline, type: probabilistic, probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 5 } }
  attributes/scrub:
    actions:
      - { key: user.email, action: delete }
      - { key: http.request.header.authorization, action: delete }
  batch:
    timeout: 2s
    send_batch_size: 2048

exporters:
  otlp/tempo:
    endpoint: tempo:4317
    tls: { insecure: true }
  prometheusremotewrite:
    endpoint: http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, tail_sampling, attributes/scrub, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [prometheusremotewrite]

Deploy the collector two ways at once: an agent as a DaemonSet on every node (or a sidecar) that receives from local pods and forwards, and a gateway deployment behind a Service that does tail sampling. The agent must route by trace id to the gateway (the loadbalancing exporter does this) so all spans of a trace land on one gateway instance.

43.5.2 How Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo and the collector fit together

Each tool has one job. Prometheus stores metrics and evaluates alerts. Loki stores logs. Tempo stores traces. The collector receives and shapes traces (and can generate RED metrics from spans, so services without a /metrics endpoint still get rate, error and duration). Grafana is the single pane where a traceId in a log line, an exemplar on a histogram and a span in a trace are the same clickable thing. The senior engineer's rule: the on-call should never need to open more than one UI during an incident.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start tracing on day one of a multi-service system, because retrofitting context propagation across twelve services and three queues is a quarter of work, while adding it to the first two services is an afternoon. They keep auto-instrumentation on for dependencies and add manual spans only at business boundaries. They treat the collector as production infrastructure: it has its own dashboard (queue size, dropped spans, memory), it has a memory limit, and it is on the same deploy pipeline as everything else. They never let the application talk to a trace vendor directly, because the day the vendor has an outage must not be the day the API slows down.

Common mistakes

  • Starting the SDK after Nest bootstraps, so nothing is patched.
  • Sampling at 1 percent to save money, then having no trace for the one failing request that matters.
  • Putting db.statement with bound parameters, or a request body, in span attributes.
  • Forgetting to end spans in error paths.
  • Exporting straight from the app to a vendor over the public internet without a timeout.
  • Tail sampling without routing by trace id, so half of a trace is kept and the other half dropped.

Interview questions

  1. Explain how a trace crosses a Kafka boundary.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: producer instrumentation injects traceparent as a message header; consumer instrumentation extracts it and starts a span with that parent; the gap between them is queueing time. Follow-up: what if the consumer batches 100 messages? (One span per message with links, or a batch span with links to each producer span.)
  2. Head versus tail sampling: tradeoffs?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: head is cheap and blind; tail keeps interesting traces but needs a collector with memory and trace-id routing.
  3. What is traceparent and what is in it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: W3C header, version, trace id, parent span id, flags with the sampled bit.
  4. How do you connect a latency spike on a dashboard to a specific trace?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: exemplars on the histogram, linked in Grafana to the trace store.
  5. A trace shows a 2 second gap in the parent span with no child. What is it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CPU work or event loop lag in the process; next step is a profile.
  6. Why put a collector between the app and the backend?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: decoupling, retries, tail sampling, credential isolation, scrubbing, one place to change backends.

Practical exercise

Trace an order across services:

  1. Add tracing.ts to a NestJS orders-api and a notifications-worker with auto-instrumentation for http, express, nestjs-core, pg, ioredis and kafkajs. Export OTLP to a local collector; run Tempo (or Jaeger) and Grafana in Docker Compose.
  2. Add a manual orders.place span with order.id and user.id attributes; record exceptions.
  3. Configure the collector with memory_limiter, tail sampling (all errors, all traces over 500 ms, 10 percent baseline) and batch.
  4. Add traceId to every pino line and configure the Grafana Loki-to-Tempo link.
  5. Acceptance: placing an order produces one trace with spans in both processes and a visible queueing gap; forcing an inventory error produces a trace with an error status that is kept by tail sampling even at 10 percent baseline; searching Tempo by order.id finds the trace; clicking the trace id in the Loki log line opens it.

43.6 Health, readiness and build info as observability

43.6.1 Health endpoints tell the platform; metrics tell the humans

Concept

A liveness endpoint answers "is this process alive enough to keep, or should it be restarted". A readiness endpoint answers "can this pod take traffic right now". A build info metric answers "which exact version is this". All three are observability: the platform reads the first two, humans and dashboards read the third.

Why does it exist?

Kubernetes has no idea what your process is doing. It can only see whether the container is running. Liveness lets you tell it "I am deadlocked, restart me"; readiness lets you tell it "I am starting, or my database connection is gone, do not route to me yet". Without readiness, a rolling deploy sends requests to pods that have not finished connecting to PostgreSQL and the deploy itself causes an error spike.

How it works

  • Liveness must be cheap and must not depend on external systems. If liveness checks the database and the database is down, Kubernetes restarts every pod in a loop and the outage gets worse. Liveness answers 200 as long as the event loop is responsive.
  • Readiness may check dependencies you cannot serve without: the database pool can acquire a connection, Redis answers PING, the Kafka consumer has joined its group. It flips to 503 during shutdown so the load balancer drains before the process exits.
  • Startup probes exist for slow-starting processes so liveness does not kill them during boot.
TypeScript
// health/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator, MemoryHealthIndicator } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { RedisHealthIndicator } from './redis.health';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly memory: MemoryHealthIndicator,
    private readonly redis: RedisHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    // Only in-process checks. Never touch the network here.
    return this.health.check([() => this.memory.checkHeap('heap', 1_500 * 1024 * 1024)]);
  }

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1_000 }),
      () => this.redis.isHealthy('redis'),
    ]);
  }
}

Expose the build in three places so nobody has to guess what is running: the app_build_info gauge from 43.3.4, the version field on every log line, and service.version on every span's resource. During an incident the first question is "what changed", and the second is "which version is this pod". Both should be answerable from the dashboard.

A useful PromQL trick joins any metric with the build info to split it by version during a rollout:

Text
sum by (version) (
  rate(http_requests_total{service="orders-api", status=~"5.."}[5m])
  * on (pod) group_left(version) app_build_info
)

If the new version's error rate is higher than the old version's during a canary, that one panel tells you to roll back.

43.7 Observability for the database, Redis, Kafka and Kubernetes

43.7.1 PostgreSQL

Concept

The database is where most latency incidents end up, and it has excellent built-in instrumentation that most teams never turn on. postgres_exporter turns catalog views into Prometheus metrics; pg_stat_statements records per-query statistics; a handful of views cover replication, locks and vacuum.

The dashboard

Panel Source What it tells you
Connections by state pg_stat_activity idle in transaction climbing means an app is holding transactions open; active at max_connections means the pool math is wrong
Transactions per second, commits vs rollbacks pg_stat_database Rollback spike is an app error or deadlocks
Cache hit ratio pg_stat_database Below 99 percent on OLTP means the working set does not fit
Top queries by total time and by mean time pg_stat_statements The queries to fix, ranked
Replica lag in bytes and seconds pg_stat_replication on the primary, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on replicas Reads from a replica 30 seconds behind explain "I just saved it and it is gone"
Locks: waiting sessions pg_locks joined to pg_stat_activity where wait_event_type = 'Lock' Lock contention before it becomes a timeout storm
Dead tuples and last vacuum per table pg_stat_user_tables Bloat and the reason a table got slow with no code change
Long-running transactions pg_stat_activity with xact_start Anything over 5 minutes blocks vacuum and holds locks
Disk and WAL growth node exporter and pg_wal size A replication slot that fell behind fills the disk

The two queries a senior engineer runs by hand during an incident:

SQL
-- Who is blocking whom
SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocked.query AS blocked_query,
       blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocking.query AS blocking_query,
       now() - blocking.xact_start AS blocking_for
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE blocked.wait_event_type = 'Lock';

-- Replica lag as seen from the replica
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_lag;

43.7.2 Redis

redis_exporter exposes the fields of INFO. The panels that matter: used_memory against maxmemory (eviction begins at the line), evicted_keys rate (your cache is too small or a key leak), keyspace_hits versus keyspace_misses (hit ratio), connected_clients (a leak looks like a slow climb), blocked_clients, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, and rdb_last_bgsave_status plus aof_last_write_status (persistence failing silently). From the application side, the redis_command_duration_seconds histogram from 43.3.2 is the one that pages: Redis p99 above 5 ms from the app while the server reports sub-millisecond latency means the network or the client pool is the problem. SLOWLOG GET 10 shows commands over the configured threshold, typically KEYS * written by someone who should have used SCAN.

43.7.3 Kafka

The single metric is consumer lag per group per partition: the difference between the partition's latest offset and the group's committed offset. kafka_exporter or the broker's own metrics provide it, and kafkajs can report it from the client side. Alert on lag that grows for 10 minutes, not on a fixed number, because a burst can legitimately create lag that drains in a minute. Also watch rebalances per minute (a consumer that crashes in a loop rebalances the whole group and stops everyone), under-replicated partitions (a broker is sick), and request latency at the producer. Put the lag panel on the service dashboard of the consumer, not on a "Kafka" dashboard nobody opens.

43.7.4 Kubernetes

kube-state-metrics plus cAdvisor give the pod-level truth. The panels: restarts per pod (kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total rate), last termination reason (OOMKilled is the one that matters), CPU throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total, which explains latency on a pod whose CPU "looks" at 60 percent because it is being throttled against its limit), memory working set against the limit, HPA current versus desired replicas, and pending pods. A pod at 95 percent of its memory limit is a future OOMKilled; a pod being CPU-throttled is a present latency problem with no error anywhere.

43.8 Dashboards and on-call

43.8.1 What the first screen must answer in 30 seconds

Concept

On-call is a reading test under stress. The first screen is not for exploring; it is for deciding what to do next. It should let a tired engineer answer four questions without scrolling:

  1. Are customers affected right now? (error ratio versus SLO, p99 versus target)
  2. Since when? (the time the lines changed, with deploy annotations)
  3. Is it us or a dependency? (process saturation row versus dependency row)
  4. Is it getting worse? (the slope of the last 15 minutes)

Everything else, per-route breakdowns, per-pod detail, database internals, lives one click down.

Runbook links from alerts

Every alert carries runbook_url. The runbook is short: what the alert means, the dashboard to open, the three most likely causes with the query that confirms each, the mitigation for each, and who to escalate to. It is a checklist, not an essay. It is stored next to the code, reviewed in PRs, and updated in the incident retrospective. Part 49 — Site Reliability Engineering covers the runbook format and the incident process; here the rule is simply that no alert ships without one.

Incident-style example

At 02:14 the pager fires: OrdersApiHighErrorBurn. The runbook link opens the orders overview dashboard with the time range preset to the last hour. Row 1 shows error ratio at 6 percent since 02:09, a deploy annotation at 02:08. Row 2 shows nothing unusual. Row 3 shows db_pool_connections{state="waiting"} at 20 on every pod and DB query p99 at 4 seconds for operation="select_orders". The runbook's "pool exhausted after a deploy" branch says: check pg_stat_statements for a new slow query, roll back if found. The query is a new SELECT ... WHERE lower(email) = $1 with no index. Roll back at 02:19, error ratio recovers at 02:21. Total time: seven minutes, no exploring, no guessing. The retrospective adds the missing index and a lint rule for functions on indexed columns.

43.9 Cost control

43.9.1 Where the money goes and how to keep it

Lever Effect Typical setting
Log level in production Largest single lever; DEBUG is 5 to 10 times INFO info; debug per request via a header, never globally
Request log sampling Cuts the dominant line type 100 percent of errors and slow requests, 5 percent of the rest
Log retention Storage cost scales linearly 7 to 14 days hot, 30 to 90 days cold or archived to object storage
Metric cardinality Prometheus memory and query time Under 500 series per pod; no unbounded labels; drop unused default metrics with relabeling
Scrape interval Samples per second 15 s default; 60 s for slow-moving infrastructure
Trace head sampling Spans exported from the app 10 to 20 percent for high-traffic services; 100 percent for low-traffic
Trace tail sampling Spans stored All errors and slow traces, 5 percent baseline
Trace retention Object storage 7 to 30 days
Span attribute size Export bandwidth No bodies, no full SQL with parameters, truncate at 1 KB

A useful discipline is a monthly "observability bill review" with one table per service: log GB per day, series count, spans per second, and dollars. The service that produces 40 percent of the log volume with 3 percent of the traffic is always a surprise to its team and always has a debug loop that nobody remembers adding.

43.10 Edge cases & failure modes

This section collects the ways observability itself fails. Each one has taken down a real system or hidden a real incident.

  • Logging PII or secrets. A console.log(req.body) on /login writes passwords to a log store with 90 day retention and 200 readers. Redact by path in the logger config, scrub in the collector as a second line, and run a regular scan of the log store for patterns like card numbers and JWTs. Under GDPR a leak into logs is a reportable breach.
  • Logs dropping under load. The agent's buffer fills, and the lines you most need during the incident are the ones that vanish. Monitor the agent's dropped-records metric, size its buffer for a burst of 10 times normal, and alert when it drops anything.
  • Disk full from logs. A pod logging 500 lines per second of stack traces fills a node's disk in hours; Kubernetes then evicts unrelated pods from that node. Rotation limits (10 MB times 5 files per container by default) cap the damage, but a node with 40 chatty pods still suffers. Rate limit repeated errors at the source.
  • Metric cardinality explosion killing Prometheus. One service adds userId as a label. Within an hour Prometheus has 2 million series, uses 16 GB, and its queries time out; every team's dashboards go blank at once. Enforce a series limit per scrape target (sample_limit), review label additions in code review, and alert on prometheus_tsdb_head_series growth.
  • Missing trace context across queues, timers and Promise boundaries. A setTimeout scheduled at bootstrap, an EventEmitter created in a module constructor, a p-queue worker or a Promise created in a different request all lose the ALS context, and the logs from that code carry no requestId or the wrong one. Use cls.run or context.with at every boundary, and write a test that asserts the id survives.
  • Sampling hiding the rare failure. At 1 percent head sampling, an error that occurs 50 times a day is traced once every two days. The incident where "we have no trace of any failing request" is the tail sampling argument in one sentence.
  • Clock skew making spans negative. A node whose clock is 300 ms ahead produces child spans that end before they start relative to their parent. Traces render strangely and duration math goes wrong. Run chrony on every node and alert on node clock offset from node_timex_offset_seconds.
  • Alert storms during incidents. The database goes down, and 45 alerts fire across 12 services. The on-call cannot find the one that says "database down". Group by cluster, inhibit downstream alerts when an upstream fires, and page once per incident with a summary.
  • Dashboards lying because of averaging. Average latency 60 ms with p99 at 5 seconds. A fleet-average CPU of 40 percent while one pod is at 100 percent. A 1 hour graph resolution that smooths a 3 minute outage into a small bump. Always show quantiles, per-pod lines and enough resolution to see a deploy.
  • Logging inside hot loops. A log.debug inside a loop that runs 10,000 times per request costs nothing when debug is off, if and only if the arguments are cheap. log.debug({ item: JSON.stringify(item) }) serializes 10,000 objects per request even at info level, because the argument is evaluated before the level check. Guard with if (log.isLevelEnabled('debug')) or pass the raw object and let pino skip it.
  • The observability agent consuming more CPU than the app. A Fluent Bit with a regex parser on multi-line stack traces, or a collector doing tail sampling on a node-sized budget, or auto-instrumentation of fs producing a span per file read. Measure the agent's CPU next to the app's; budget observability overhead at 5 to 10 percent of the service's CPU and treat more as a bug.
  • Exporters blocking shutdown. sdk.shutdown() flushes to the collector; if the collector is down, the flush waits for its timeout, the pod exceeds its termination grace period, and Kubernetes kills it, losing the buffered spans anyway and delaying the rollout. Bound the flush with Promise.race and a 3 second timer.
  • The observability stack in the blast radius. Prometheus, Loki and Tempo running in the same cluster that is having the outage. When the cluster's network fails, the dashboards fail with it. Run the monitoring stack in a separate cluster or a managed service, and keep a minimal external uptime check that does not depend on anything internal.
  • Health checks that lie. A readiness endpoint that returns 200 while the Kafka consumer is dead, or a liveness endpoint that checks the database and restarts healthy pods during a database blip. Liveness checks only the process; readiness checks what the pod needs to serve.

43.10.1 How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat observability as a product with users (the on-call) and a budget, not as a checkbox. They design it before the first deploy: field names, correlation, metrics naming, alert ownership. They measure the cost of every signal and the overhead of every agent. They run game days where they break something and time how long the dashboards take to point at it; if the answer is more than five minutes, the dashboards change. They know that the most dangerous state is not "no monitoring" but "monitoring that looks fine while customers suffer", so they alert on symptoms, show quantiles, and keep an external check that does not trust anything inside the cluster.

43.10.2 Common mistakes

  • Building dashboards from whatever metrics exist rather than from the questions the on-call asks.
  • Twelve services with twelve different requestId field names.
  • One giant dashboard with 80 panels that takes 20 seconds to load during an incident.
  • Alerts with no owner, no runbook and no for: duration.
  • Treating the collector, Prometheus and Loki as "not real production" and giving them no memory limits, no dashboards and no on-call.
  • Sampling logs of business events that are actually audit records.

43.10.3 Interview questions

  1. Design the observability for a new NestJS service that talks to PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka. Expected: structured JSON logs to stdout with a shared field set and correlation id via ALS; /metrics with RED per route, process metrics, pool and consumer lag gauges, build info; OTel auto-instrumentation exporting to a collector with tail sampling; overview dashboard in five rows; two or three SLO burn-rate alerts with runbooks. Why it matters: shows the candidate can go from zero to observable without gold-plating.
  2. What should a liveness probe check and what must it never check? Expected: only in-process health; never external dependencies, or a dependency outage becomes a restart storm.
  3. How do you keep a debug log line from costing CPU in production? Expected: cheap arguments, level checks before expensive serialization, no string interpolation.
  4. A dashboard shows everything green but customers report failures. List three reasons. Expected: averages hiding tails; alerts on causes not symptoms; monitoring inside the blast radius; readiness lying; sampling dropping the failing traces.
  5. How would you find which deploy caused an error spike? Expected: app_build_info joined to error rate by version, deploy annotations, per-version canary panel.
  6. Where does tracing lose context in Node.js and how do you fix it? Expected: timers, emitters, external Promise chains, queue consumers; context.with or cls.run at the boundary.

43.10.4 Practical exercise

Run a game day against your instrumented service:

  1. With the stack from the earlier exercises running, inject four faults one at a time: kill Redis, add a 2 second sleep to one repository method, add a userId label to a counter, and set LOG_LEVEL=debug.
  2. For each fault, time how long it takes to identify the cause using only Grafana, starting from the overview dashboard.
  3. Acceptance: Redis down is visible on Row 3 and the correct alert fires within 5 minutes; the 2 second sleep is found through an exemplar to a trace showing the gap in under 3 minutes; the userId label is caught by a series-count alert before it reaches 10,000 series; the debug level is visible as a 5x jump on a log-volume panel and a ticket severity alert fires within 15 minutes.

Senior Checklist — Part 43

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • Every log line in my services is JSON with time, level, msg, service, env, version, requestId, traceId, and business ids, and never contains PII or secrets
  • I can propagate a correlation id from an inbound request through HTTP calls and Kafka messages into a worker and prove it with a test
  • I can expose RED metrics per route, process metrics, pool and lag gauges and app_build_info from NestJS and keep cardinality bounded
  • I can write the PromQL for request rate, error ratio and p99 from a histogram, and a recording rule for each
  • I can write a multi-window burn-rate alert from an SLO and explain why it beats a fixed threshold
  • I can set up OpenTelemetry in NestJS before bootstrap, add manual spans with attributes and exceptions, and read a trace to find the slow span or the gap
  • I can configure an OTel Collector pipeline with memory limiting, tail sampling and attribute scrubbing
  • I can explain the difference between correlation id, trace id and span id and where each lives
  • I can build the five-row service overview dashboard and say what the first screen answers in 30 seconds
  • I can list the PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka and Kubernetes panels that belong on a service dashboard
  • I can estimate the monthly cost of a service's logs, metrics and traces and name the levers that reduce it
  • I know where AsyncLocalStorage context is lost in Node.js and how to restore it

Part 43 — Key Takeaways

  • Monitoring answers questions you planned; observability answers questions you did not. You need both, and the second needs structured, correlated data.
  • Logs are for detail, metrics are for counting and alerting, traces are for "where did the time go". Their value comes from being linked by trace id and exemplars.
  • Structured JSON logs with a shared field set are a company-wide contract; msg is constant, variables are fields, PII and secrets never appear.
  • A correlation id lives in AsyncLocalStorage, on every log line, in every outbound header and every Kafka message header, and in a fresh context per consumed message.
  • Write logs to stdout asynchronously; let a node agent ship them. Your logger must never be able to slow your API.
  • Histograms over summaries, route templates over raw paths, and never a user id as a label. Cardinality is what kills Prometheus.
  • The event loop lag metric explains the latency that no dependency explains.
  • Alert on symptoms and SLO burn rates with runbooks and owners; put causes on dashboards. An alert with nothing to do is a bug.
  • Start the OpenTelemetry SDK before Nest bootstraps, auto-instrument dependencies, add manual spans at business boundaries, and export through a collector with tail sampling that keeps every error.
  • Dashboards show quantiles, per-pod lines and deploy annotations; averages lie.
  • The observability stack is production: give it limits, dashboards, an on-call, and a home outside the blast radius.
  • Budget observability like any resource: sample successes, keep failures, bound cardinality, tail-sample traces, and review the bill monthly.

Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers

  • 2 h 16 min read
  • 16 sections

What you will learn

  1. 44.1What a container really is
  2. 44.2Images: layers, digests, registries and base images
  3. 44.3Layers and the build cache
  4. 44.4The container as a process: PID 1, signals, exit codes and restart policies
  5. 44.5Dockerfile best practices
  6. 44.6Multi-stage builds
  7. 44.7Container networking
  8. 44.8Volumes and state
  9. 44.9Environment variables and configuration
  10. 44.10Container lifecycle, logs and resource limits
  11. 44.11Container security

  13. 44.13Containerizing a NestJS + PostgreSQL application
  14. 44.14Debugging containers

Docker is the tool most backend engineers use every day and understand the least. You copy a Dockerfile from the last project, it builds, it runs, and you move on. Then one night your NestJS pods take 30 seconds to shut down and drop in-flight orders, or a container is killed at 512 MB even though "Node only uses 200 MB", or a deploy that worked yesterday fails because a native module will not compile on Alpine. Every one of those incidents comes from not knowing what a container actually is.

This part teaches containers from the kernel up: what isolation really means, how images are built from layers, why the order of lines in a Dockerfile changes your build time from 8 minutes to 40 seconds, how signals reach your Node process, how to wire a NestJS API, PostgreSQL, Redis and a message broker together with Docker Compose, and how to ship a small, secure, non-root production image. The final sections are a full worked example, a debugging guide, CI build patterns and a catalogue of the failure modes that senior engineers have all met at least once.

44.1 What a container really is

Concept

A container is a normal Linux process (or a small tree of processes) that the kernel has been told to lie to. The process believes it has its own filesystem, its own process list starting at PID 1, its own network interface and hostname, and its own share of CPU and memory. None of that is a separate machine. It is the same kernel as the host, running your node dist/main.js, with a few kernel features wrapped around it.

Three kernel features do almost all of the work:

  • Namespaces change what the process can see: files, other processes, network interfaces, hostname, users.
  • Control groups (cgroups) limit what the process can use: CPU time, memory, disk I/O, number of PIDs.
  • A union filesystem (OverlayFS) stacks read-only image layers plus one writable layer so that many containers can share the same image files on disk while each thinks it owns a private copy.

Docker is the tooling that packages a filesystem into an image, ships it to a registry, and asks the kernel to start a process with those namespaces, cgroups and mounts configured. The container runtime underneath Docker (containerd and runc) is what actually makes the system calls.

Why does it exist?

Before containers, deploying a Node.js service meant a runbook: install this Node version, install these system libraries, set these environment variables, copy these files to these paths, hope nothing else on the machine conflicts. Two services on the same VM fought over global packages, OpenSSL versions and port numbers. Staging drifted from production because someone patched a library by hand. "It works on my machine" was a real, recurring cause of outages.

Virtual machines solved isolation but at a heavy price: each VM boots its own kernel, takes gigabytes of disk, minutes to start and hundreds of megabytes of memory before your application even runs. You could not afford a VM per microservice, and you certainly could not spin one up in two seconds when traffic spiked.

Containers give most of the isolation of a VM at the cost of a process. The image carries the exact filesystem your code was tested with, down to the byte, so the "my machine" problem disappears: the same image runs on your laptop, in CI, in staging and in production. Start time is milliseconds, memory overhead is close to zero, and a single 8 GB node can run dozens of them.

Mental model

Imagine an office building. A virtual machine is renting a whole separate building next door: its own foundation, plumbing, electricity, security desk. Total isolation, very expensive, takes months to set up.

A container is renting one office floor in a shared building. The building (the kernel) provides plumbing and electricity to everyone. Your floor has its own door with a lock (namespaces: you cannot see into other floors), your own electricity meter and a breaker that trips at an agreed limit (cgroups: you cannot consume more than your share), and your furniture is a standard kit that was photographed once and copied to every floor (image layers, shared on disk, with your own scratch desk on top as the writable layer). If you knock down a wall you only damage your floor. If the building's foundation cracks (a kernel bug), every floor feels it.

How it works

When you run docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1 -p 3000:3000 orders-api:1.4.2, this happens, step by step:
