  1. Image lookup. Docker checks whether the image layers are present locally. If not, it pulls each missing layer (a compressed tar archive) from the registry, verifying each one against its SHA-256 digest.
  2. Filesystem assembly. OverlayFS mounts the read-only layers as the "lower" directories and creates an empty "upper" directory as the container's writable layer. The merged view is the container's root filesystem (/).
  3. Namespaces. runc calls clone() with flags that create new namespaces:
    • CLONE_NEWPID: the first process becomes PID 1 inside; it cannot see host processes.
    • CLONE_NEWNS: a private mount table; the merged OverlayFS becomes / via pivot_root.
    • CLONE_NEWNET: a fresh network stack with its own lo and a virtual ethernet pair (veth) plugged into the Docker bridge.
    • CLONE_NEWUTS: its own hostname (the container ID by default).
    • CLONE_NEWIPC: private shared-memory segments and semaphores.
    • Optionally CLONE_NEWUSER: uid 0 inside maps to an unprivileged uid outside (user namespace remapping; not the default in Docker, which is one reason "root in the container" is dangerous).
  4. cgroups. runc writes the limits into the cgroup v2 hierarchy: memory.max = 536870912 and cpu.max = 100000 100000 (1 CPU: 100 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period). The kernel enforces them: exceed the memory limit and the OOM killer terminates a process in the cgroup; exceed the CPU quota and the process is paused (throttled) until the next period.
  5. Capabilities and seccomp. Docker drops most Linux capabilities (the container cannot load kernel modules, change the clock, or use raw sockets unless you allow it) and applies a default seccomp profile that blocks around 40 dangerous system calls.
  6. Port publishing. For -p 3000:3000 Docker adds iptables (or nftables) NAT rules so that traffic to the host's port 3000 is forwarded to the container's IP on port 3000.
  7. Exec. runc calls execve("/usr/local/bin/node", ["node", "dist/main.js"]). Your NestJS application is now running. It is visible in the host's ps output as an ordinary process with a strange root directory and a cgroup.

Here is the container-versus-VM comparison senior engineers keep in their heads:

Property Virtual machine Container
Kernel Own kernel per VM Shares the host kernel
Isolation boundary Hypervisor (hardware-assisted) Kernel namespaces and cgroups
Start time 30 s to minutes 50 ms to 2 s
Memory overhead 200 MB to 1 GB per VM before your app A few MB
Disk footprint Gigabytes per VM Shared layers; tens to hundreds of MB
Density on one 16 GB host 4 to 10 50 to 200
Security isolation Strong; kernel exploit in a VM does not reach the host Weaker; a kernel exploit escapes all containers on the node
Runs a different OS kernel Yes (Windows on Linux host) No; Linux containers need a Linux kernel (Docker Desktop hides a small Linux VM)
Typical use Untrusted multi-tenant workloads, legacy OS, kernel-level customisation Your own services, CI jobs, local dev dependencies

Why "it works on my machine" disappears: the image is a content-addressed snapshot of the filesystem. The Node binary, the OpenSSL your pg driver links against, the tzdata package, the exact node_modules tree from npm ci: all of it is inside the image with a digest. If the digest matches, the bytes match. What remains variable is only what you deliberately inject at run time (environment variables, mounted secrets) and the kernel itself.

Practical example

Your team runs an orders API in NestJS on three EC2 instances. One instance was set up in 2022 with Node 18.12, one was rebuilt last year with Node 18.19, and one was patched by hand to Node 20 during an incident. A dependency (undici) behaves differently across them: one instance returns ECONNRESET on keep-alive sockets under load and the other two do not. Nobody can reproduce it locally because every laptop has yet another Node version.

After containerising: one image, orders-api@sha256:9f3c..., built once in CI from node:20.18.1-alpine3.20, deployed to all three instances. The difference in behaviour is gone because there is no difference in environment. When the bug reappears, an engineer runs the same image locally with the same environment variables and reproduces it in ten minutes.

NestJS example

Nothing in your NestJS code changes to run in a container, and that is the point. What changes is what the code must not assume. The following main.ts is container-aware: it binds to all interfaces (not localhost), reads its port from the environment, logs to stdout, and shuts down on signals.

TypeScript
// src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Logger, ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap(): Promise<void> {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, {
    // JSON logs to stdout; the container runtime collects them
    logger: ['log', 'warn', 'error'],
  });

  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

  // Registers listeners for SIGTERM/SIGINT so OnModuleDestroy and
  // OnApplicationShutdown hooks run when the container is stopped.
  app.enableShutdownHooks();

  const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
  // 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1: inside the container, localhost is the
  // container's own loopback and is unreachable from outside.
  await app.listen(port, '0.0.0.0');
  Logger.log(`orders-api listening on ${port}`, 'Bootstrap');
}

bootstrap();

Production scenario

A food-delivery platform runs 40 NestJS services. On Kubernetes nodes with 16 vCPU and 64 GB, each node hosts 20 to 30 containers with memory limits between 256 MB and 1 GB. Container start-to-ready time is 2 to 4 seconds for an API (dominated by Node loading the module graph and opening the PostgreSQL pool), which is what makes autoscaling from 10 to 40 replicas in under a minute possible. The same 40 images run on developer laptops via Compose, in CI for integration tests, and in production; the only per-environment differences are environment variables and secrets.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 an on-call engineer is paged: payments-api is returning 502 from the load balancer. docker ps on the node shows the container restarting every 40 seconds. docker inspect shows "OOMKilled": true. The cgroup memory limit was 256 MB; a new report endpoint loaded 90,000 rows into memory and the process crossed the line. The kernel does not warn and does not negotiate: it kills the process. Nothing in the Node logs explains it, because Node never got a chance to log. The engineer learns the two lessons this part will keep repeating: the container's memory limit is a hard wall, and you must look at the container runtime, not just the application logs, to see why a process died.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shared kernel means shared kernel bugs. A kernel panic or a conntrack table overflow on the node affects every container on it.
  • Time and time zones come from the host kernel. A container cannot set the system clock (the CAP_SYS_TIME capability is dropped). Clock skew is a host problem; see 44.16.
  • PID 1 is special. The first process in the PID namespace does not get default signal handling from the kernel and must reap zombie children; see 44.4.
  • Docker Desktop is a VM. On macOS and Windows, containers run inside a Linux VM, so file bind mounts cross a VM boundary (slow) and the clock can drift after the laptop sleeps.
  • Namespaces are not a security boundary on their own. Running as root inside a container without user namespaces is root on the host if any escape exists. Treat non-root as mandatory; see 44.11.
  • Resource limits are not visible to the application by default. os.totalmem() in Node reports the host's memory, not the cgroup limit, unless you read /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max yourself.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer treats a container as "a process with a contract": the contract says what files it needs (the image), what it must not assume (writable disk, localhost, root, unlimited memory), how it receives configuration (environment), how it reports health (an HTTP endpoint) and how it is told to stop (SIGTERM). They design the application to honour that contract, because everything above it, from Compose to Kubernetes to ECS, relies on it.

They also know when a container is the wrong tool: for a workload that needs a custom kernel module, for a multi-tenant platform running untrusted customer code (use Firecracker micro-VMs or gVisor instead), or for a database where the operational maturity of a managed service is worth more than portability.

Explained to a product manager: "A container is a sealed box with our app and everything it needs inside. The box we test is the exact box we ship, so the surprises between 'works in test' and 'works in production' mostly go away."

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a container is a lightweight VM and expecting it to have its own kernel, its own clock, or a persistent disk.
  • Binding the HTTP server to 127.0.0.1 inside the container and then wondering why the published port returns "connection refused".
  • Running as root because "it's only a container".
  • Writing files to the container's filesystem (uploads, logs, SQLite) and losing them at the next restart.
  • Not knowing that docker inspect and the exit code (137, 143) tell you why a process died when the logs do not.

Interview questions

  1. What kernel features make a container possible, and what does each one do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: namespaces (visibility: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user), cgroups (resource limits: cpu, memory, pids, io), union filesystem (layered image plus writable layer), plus capabilities and seccomp for hardening. Follow-up: which of these does a VM not need, and why?
  2. Why does "it works on my machine" mostly disappear with containers, and what can still differ?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the image is a content-addressed filesystem snapshot; what can differ is the kernel, environment variables, mounted secrets, resources, and network. Follow-up: give an example of a kernel-level difference that broke an app.
  3. Is a container a security boundary?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: weaker than a VM; shared kernel; non-root plus dropped capabilities plus seccomp plus read-only fs makes it reasonable for your own code; for untrusted code use micro-VMs or gVisor.
  4. A container has exit code 137. What happened?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 128 + 9, killed by SIGKILL; either OOM (check OOMKilled in inspect) or the runtime gave up waiting after the stop grace period.
  5. How does the host reach a service listening on port 3000 inside a container?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: -p creates NAT rules forwarding host port to container IP; the process must bind to 0.0.0.0.

Practical exercise

Run docker run -d --name probe --memory=64m --cpus=0.5 node:20-alpine node -e "setInterval(()=>{},1000)". From the host, find the process in ps aux and confirm it is a normal host process. Inside the container (docker exec -it probe sh), run cat /proc/1/cgroup, cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max, hostname and ip addr, and explain each output in terms of a namespace or cgroup. Then run docker exec probe node -e "console.log(require('os').totalmem())" and explain why it does not print 64 MB. Acceptance criteria: a short written note mapping each observation to pid, mnt, net, uts namespaces or the memory cgroup, and a one-line statement of what Node would need to do to learn its real memory limit.

44.2 Images: layers, digests, registries and base images

Concept

An image is a read-only, layered snapshot of a filesystem plus a small JSON manifest that says how to run it (default command, environment, working directory, exposed ports, user). Each layer is a tar archive of filesystem changes, identified by the SHA-256 hash of its content. The image manifest lists the layer digests in order. Because everything is hashed, an image is immutable: change one byte and you get a different digest.

A registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry) is an HTTP server that stores manifests and layers and serves them by digest. A tag (orders-api:1.4.2) is a mutable pointer to a digest, like a Git branch pointing to a commit.

Why does it exist?

Shipping software as a full disk image (like a VM image) is slow: gigabytes for every change. Layers solve this. Ten services built on node:20-alpine share the same 130 MB base layers; the registry stores them once, the node pulls them once, and deploying a new version of one service transfers only the layers that changed, often just the 5 MB dist layer.

Content addressing solves trust and caching. If the digest matches, the bytes are identical; a cache anywhere in the chain (BuildKit, registry, node) can serve it without asking. That is why a pull of a 300 MB image can finish in two seconds when the base layers are already present.

Mental model

Imagine a stack of transparent sheets on an overhead projector. The bottom sheet has the operating system files drawn on it. The next sheet adds Node. The next adds your node_modules. The next adds your compiled code. Looking down through the stack you see one complete picture, but each sheet is stored separately. If you change only the top sheet, you only reprint that sheet. A tag is a sticky note on the pile saying "v1.4.2"; anyone can move the note to a different pile, but the sheets themselves never change.

How it works

  1. Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (FROM, COPY, ADD, RUN) produces a layer. Instructions that only change metadata (ENV, WORKDIR, USER, CMD, EXPOSE, LABEL) produce an empty layer with a config change.
  2. Layer content is hashed. The image config (JSON) references the layers by these digests. The manifest hashes the config plus layer list; that manifest digest is what sha256:... refers to when you pin an image.
  3. On docker push, the client asks the registry which layer digests it already has and uploads only the missing ones.
  4. On docker pull, the same happens in reverse. A multi-architecture image has a manifest list (an index) that maps linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 to separate manifests; the client picks the one for its CPU.
  5. Deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier layer. OverlayFS records a "whiteout" marker. The bytes are still in the image, still downloadable, still visible with docker history and extraction tools. This is why a secret copied in one layer and deleted in the next is still leaked.

Tags versus digests:

Reference Example Mutable? Use it for
Tag node:20-alpine Yes; can move to a new build tomorrow Human-readable intent
Pinned tag node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 Mostly stable but can be republished Dockerfiles, with regular bumps
Digest node@sha256:3b4c... Never Reproducible CI builds, production deploys
Tag plus digest node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:3b4c... Never (digest wins) Best of both: readable and exact

Base image choice for Node.js:

Base Size (approx.) libc Shell and package manager Tradeoffs
node:20 (Debian full) 1.1 GB glibc bash, apt, build tools Everything works; huge; large attack surface
node:20-slim (Debian minimal) 200 MB glibc bash, apt, no compilers Native modules with prebuilt glibc binaries work out of the box; good default
node:20-alpine 130 MB musl sh, apk Smallest with a shell; native modules may need to compile from source or lack musl builds; DNS resolver differences; no tzdata by default
gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 130 MB glibc none (no shell, no package manager) Smallest attack surface; cannot docker exec sh; HEALTHCHECK and preStop scripts must be Node code
Chainguard node 120 MB glibc none in the runtime variant Similar to distroless with daily rebuilds and SBOMs; commercial support

The musl versus glibc issue in practice: bcrypt, sharp, sqlite3, argon2, grpc and other native modules ship prebuilt binaries per platform and libc. When a prebuilt for linux-musl-x64 is missing for the version you use, npm ci falls back to compiling with node-gyp, which needs python3 make g++ inside the image. On Alpine that adds 200 MB of build tools to your build stage and several minutes of compile time, and it fails outright if you forgot the packages. The senior choices are: use -slim (glibc, prebuilts always available), or use pure-JavaScript alternatives (bcryptjs) where the performance difference is irrelevant, or accept Alpine and install build tools only in the build stage of a multi-stage build (see 44.6).

Practical example

Your orders-api image is built from node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:... (pinned by digest in the Dockerfile) and tagged three ways in CI: orders-api:1.4.2 (semver from the release), orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2 (git commit), and orders-api:1.4 (floating minor). Kubernetes manifests reference orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2 so that a rollout is tied to an exact commit and a rollback is a change of one string. Nothing in production references latest, because latest means "whatever was pushed most recently", which is not a version.

Production scenario

An e-commerce company with 60 services and 200 deploys a day keeps images in ECR. Because all services share the same base image digest, a node pulling a new version transfers 5 to 20 MB. When the platform team bumps the base image (monthly, for OS security patches), every service rebuilds and the first pull per node transfers the new 130 MB base once; subsequent services reuse it. ECR lifecycle rules keep the last 30 sha-* tags per repository and delete untagged manifests after 7 days, which keeps storage at a few hundred GB rather than tens of TB.

Failure scenario

A team pinned FROM node:20-alpine. On a Tuesday the official image was rebuilt: same tag, new Alpine minor, new musl. npm ci in CI started compiling bcrypt from source because the prebuilt binary for the new musl was not published yet, and failed with gyp ERR! find Python. No code had changed. The fix was to pin the digest and, separately, to move password hashing to argon2 with a prebuilt musl binary. The lesson: a tag is a promise from someone else; a digest is a fact.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deleted files are still in the image. RUN cp secret.pem /tmp && ... && rm /tmp/secret.pem leaks the secret in the earlier layer.
  • Tag drift. node:20 today and node:20 next month are different images; builds are not reproducible without a digest.
  • Multi-arch pulls. Building on an M-series Mac produces arm64 images by default; deploying them to amd64 nodes fails with exec format error. Always build with explicit --platform.
  • Registry rate limits. Docker Hub anonymous pulls are limited (around 100 per 6 hours per IP); a cluster of 50 nodes pulling node:20-alpine at once during a scale-out can hit the limit and fail. Mirror base images into your own registry.
  • Layer count and size. Hundreds of layers (from many RUN lines) slow pulls; a single 900 MB layer cannot be cached partially. Aim for a handful of well-ordered layers.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They decide base images once, per organisation, and publish an internal "golden" image (registry.internal/base/node:20) that pins the upstream digest, adds tini and tzdata, sets USER node, and is rebuilt weekly with a scan. Services inherit from it. That gives one place to patch OpenSSL and one place to change the Node version.

They treat digests as the unit of deployment and tags as documentation. They mirror third-party images to avoid depending on Docker Hub availability at 3 a.m. And they resist Alpine by default: 70 MB saved is not worth a week debugging DNS or a native module unless the team already knows the tradeoffs.

Common mistakes

  • Using FROM node:latest or node:20 in a production Dockerfile.
  • Choosing Alpine for size and then installing python3 make g++ into the final image to make bcrypt build, ending up larger than -slim.
  • Copying a .npmrc with a private registry token into a layer and deleting it later.
  • Pushing latest from a laptop and letting production pull it.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between an image tag and a digest, and which should a production manifest use?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: tag is a mutable pointer; digest is content hash; deploy by digest or immutable sha- tag.
  2. Why is a deleted file still a risk in an image?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: layers are additive; deletion is a whiteout; earlier layer still contains bytes; mitigate with multi-stage builds and never copying secrets.
  3. Compare node:20-alpine, node:20-slim and distroless for a NestJS API.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: musl versus glibc, native modules, shell availability, attack surface, size; give a recommendation with reasons.
  4. How does a multi-arch image work and why does it matter on Graviton or Apple Silicon?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: manifest list per platform; build with buildx --platform; wrong arch gives exec format error.

Practical exercise

Build the same NestJS application on node:20, node:20-slim, node:20-alpine and gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 (multi-stage for the last three). Record image size with docker images, pull time from a registry on a clean machine, and whether bcrypt and sharp install without compilers. Acceptance criteria: a table of size, pull time and native-module result for each base, and a one-paragraph recommendation for your team with the tradeoff you are accepting.

44.3 Layers and the build cache

Concept

Every RUN, COPY and ADD line creates a layer, and BuildKit caches each layer keyed by the instruction plus the content it depends on. If nothing that feeds an instruction has changed, the cached layer is reused and the instruction is skipped. The first time an instruction's input changes, that layer and every layer after it are rebuilt. This single rule determines whether your build takes 40 seconds or 8 minutes.

Why does it exist?

Installing dependencies is the slow part of building a Node service: npm ci for a NestJS project with 900 packages takes 60 to 180 seconds and downloads 200 MB. Your source code changes on every commit; your package-lock.json changes once a week. If the dependency install layer depends only on the lockfile, it is rebuilt once a week instead of on every commit. The cache turns the average build from minutes into seconds and makes CI pipelines and hotfixes fast.

Mental model

Imagine cooking a lasagne where each layer is prepared and photographed. Tomorrow, if the tomato sauce recipe has not changed, you reuse yesterday's sauce; but if you change the sauce, everything above it (cheese, pasta, top) has to be redone because it sits on the sauce. Put the things that rarely change (base, system packages, dependencies) at the bottom and the things that change constantly (your code) at the top.

How it works

The cache-invalidation rules BuildKit applies:

  1. FROM is cached by the image digest.
  2. RUN is cached by the exact command string plus the state of all previous layers. Changing a single character in the command invalidates it.
  3. COPY/ADD are cached by a checksum of the contents and permissions of the copied files (not their modification time). Copying package*.json first means that layer changes only when the lockfile changes.
  4. Once one layer misses, all following layers miss, even if their own inputs did not change.
  5. BuildKit builds stages in parallel where possible and skips stages that are not needed by the final target.

The classic wrong order:

Dockerfile
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .            # any source change invalidates everything below
RUN npm ci          # runs on every commit: 2 minutes wasted
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

The right order:

Dockerfile
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20
WORKDIR /app
# 1. Only the manifests. This layer changes when dependencies change.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
# 2. Deterministic install from the lockfile. Cached until the lockfile changes.
RUN npm ci
# 3. Source last. Changes every commit, but only this and later layers rebuild.
COPY tsconfig.json tsconfig.build.json nest-cli.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

.dockerignore is part of the cache story. Without it, COPY . . sends your local node_modules (often 500 MB), .git, dist, coverage reports and .env to the build context, slowing the build and, worse, invalidating the cache whenever any of those files change. A production-quality .dockerignore for a NestJS project:

Text
node_modules
dist
coverage
.git
.github
.vscode
.env
.env.*
*.md
test
**/*.spec.ts
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*.yml
npm-debug.log

Inspecting layers:

Shell
# Which instruction produced which size
docker history --no-trunc --format "table {{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}" orders-api:1.4.2

# Interactive layer browser: shows wasted space (files added then deleted)
dive orders-api:1.4.2

A typical docker history for a poorly built image shows a 480 MB layer for npm install (dev dependencies included) and a 210 MB layer for apk add python3 make g++. dive reports an "efficiency" score and lists files that exist in multiple layers, which is how you find the .npmrc token you forgot about.

Practical example

Your CI builds orders-api on every push. Before reordering, the average build is 6 min 40 s and the runner downloads 210 MB from the npm registry each time. After moving COPY package*.json and npm ci above COPY src and adding .dockerignore, builds where only source changed take 55 s, of which 35 s is the TypeScript compile. Dependency-changing builds still take 6 minutes, but they happen 5 times a week instead of 200.

NestJS example

NestJS projects have a small set of files that must be copied before the build step. Make the build layer depend on exactly those and nothing else:

Dockerfile
# Build stage of a NestJS project (see 26.6 for the full multi-stage file)
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY tsconfig.json tsconfig.build.json nest-cli.json ./
COPY src ./src
# nest build reads nest-cli.json and tsconfig.build.json; output goes to dist/
RUN npm run build

If your project uses TypeORM migrations in src/migrations and a data-source.ts, they live under src and are compiled into dist by the same step; there is nothing extra to copy.

Production scenario

A platform team measures build minutes across 60 services: 14,000 CI minutes per month, 70% spent in npm ci layers that should have been cached. Three changes cut it to 4,000 minutes: correct layer order, .dockerignore, and a registry-backed BuildKit cache (--cache-from, see 44.15) so that fresh CI runners start with yesterday's layers instead of an empty cache.

Failure scenario

A developer adds COPY . . before npm ci to "simplify" the Dockerfile. Nobody notices in review. Every build now runs npm ci from scratch: builds go from 1 minute to 7 minutes. A week later, a hotfix for a payment bug waits 7 minutes for a build, then 7 minutes again because a reviewer asked for a comment change. The regression cost 12 minutes on the one deploy that mattered. The reviewer's checklist now includes "does the dependency install layer depend only on the lockfile?"

Edge cases & failure modes

  • npm install versus npm ci. npm install may update the lockfile and pull newer minor versions; the layer is cached but the content can drift between machines. npm ci fails if lockfile and manifest disagree and installs exactly what the lockfile says.
  • File permissions change the checksum. Checking out the repo on a different OS can flip executable bits and invalidate COPY layers.
  • ARG before FROM versus after. An ARG used in a RUN line is part of the cache key; changing a build arg such as GIT_SHA early in the file invalidates everything after it. Put volatile args (version labels) at the end.
  • Timestamps do not matter, content does. Touching a file without changing its bytes does not invalidate the cache.
  • Cache poisoning in shared runners. A layer cache keyed on RUN apk add curl reuses a months-old layer with unpatched packages. Rebuild base layers on a schedule with --no-cache or bump the base digest.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read a Dockerfile top to bottom asking one question per line: "how often does the input to this line change?" The answer must be non-decreasing as they read down. They insist on npm ci, a committed lockfile, and a .dockerignore reviewed alongside the Dockerfile. They measure build time and cache hit rate in CI the way they measure p99 latency, because slow builds slow every incident response.

Common mistakes

  • COPY . . before dependency install.
  • No .dockerignore, so node_modules from macOS (with native binaries for Darwin) is copied into a Linux image and then overwritten, wasting hundreds of MB in a hidden layer.
  • Using npm install in the Dockerfile.
  • Installing dev dependencies in the final image because "the build needs them" (multi-stage fixes this; see 44.6).
  • Putting ARG BUILD_DATE at the top and passing a new value every build, guaranteeing a full rebuild.

Interview questions

  1. Explain how Docker's layer cache decides to rebuild a layer, and how you would order a Dockerfile for a Node service.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: instruction plus input checksum; first miss invalidates the rest; manifests then npm ci then source.
  2. What does .dockerignore protect you from?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: large build contexts, cache invalidation from irrelevant files, leaking .env and .git, copying the wrong platform's node_modules.
  3. Why npm ci and not npm install in a build?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: deterministic install from lockfile, fails on mismatch, no lockfile mutation, faster.
  4. How would you find why an image is 1.2 GB?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: docker history, dive, look for dev dependencies, build tools, copied node_modules, .git.

Practical exercise

Take an existing NestJS Dockerfile with COPY . . before npm ci. Measure a cold build, then a build after changing one line in a controller. Reorder the Dockerfile, add .dockerignore, and measure again. Run dive on both images. Acceptance criteria: the warm build after a source-only change must finish in under 90 seconds, the build context must be under 5 MB, and dive must report no node_modules or .git directory in any layer of the final image.

44.4 The container as a process: PID 1, signals, exit codes and restart policies

Concept

A running container is one process tree with a special first process. That first process is PID 1 inside the PID namespace, and Linux treats PID 1 differently from every other process: the kernel does not install default signal handlers for it, and it is responsible for adopting and reaping orphaned child processes. If your Node process is PID 1 and does not explicitly handle SIGTERM, the signal is silently ignored. The orchestrator waits its grace period, gives up, and sends SIGKILL. Your in-flight requests die with it.

Exit codes are the other half of the contract. When the process ends, the runtime records the code: 0 for success, 1 for an uncaught exception in Node, 137 for killed by SIGKILL (128 + 9), 143 for terminated by SIGTERM (128 + 15). Restart policies decide what the runtime does next.

Why does it exist?

Orchestrators need a reliable, universal way to tell a container "stop soon, cleanly" and to learn whether it stopped cleanly. Signals are that mechanism; they predate containers by decades and every runtime uses the same two: SIGTERM to request shutdown, SIGKILL to force it. A service that honours SIGTERM can finish the current requests, close database connections and let the load balancer drain it. A service that ignores it loses work on every deploy, every scale-down, every node drain.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. The head chef (PID 1) is told "we close in 10 minutes". A good head chef stops taking new orders, finishes the dishes in progress, and tells the staff to clean up. A chef who does not hear the announcement keeps cooking until the manager cuts the power (SIGKILL): half-cooked dishes, dirty pans, angry customers. And someone must sign off the staff as they leave (reaping child processes); otherwise the staff list fills with people who have already gone home (zombies).

How it works

  1. docker stop orders-api (or a Kubernetes pod deletion) sends SIGTERM to PID 1 of the container. Only PID 1. Child processes get nothing unless PID 1 forwards it.
  2. The runtime waits a grace period: Docker's default is 10 seconds (docker stop -t 30 to change); Kubernetes uses terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30.
  3. If PID 1 has exited, the container is stopped with PID 1's exit code. If not, the runtime sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, and records exit code 137.
  4. Zombie reaping: when a child of PID 1 exits, it stays as a zombie entry until PID 1 calls wait(). Node does not reap children it did not spawn. In a long-running container that spawns processes (for example child_process.exec for image conversion, or Puppeteer), zombies accumulate until the PID cgroup limit or the kernel's PID table is exhausted.

The three ways your Node process ends up not receiving SIGTERM:

  • Shell form CMD. CMD node dist/main.js is executed as /bin/sh -c "node dist/main.js". The shell is PID 1; node is its child. Most shells (dash on Debian, ash/busybox on Alpine) do not forward signals to children, so SIGTERM reaches the shell and stops there.
  • npm start. CMD ["npm", "start"] makes npm PID 1. npm spawns a shell, which spawns node. Signal forwarding through this chain is unreliable across npm versions, and npm adds 30 to 80 MB of memory and a slower start. Never use a package manager as your entrypoint in production.
  • Node as PID 1 without handlers. Even with the exec form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"], node is PID 1 and gets no default handler. Without process.on('SIGTERM', ...) (which NestJS installs when you call app.enableShutdownHooks()), the signal is ignored.

The fix that senior teams standardise on is a tiny init process plus the exec form:

Dockerfile
# Alpine: tini is a 25 KB init that becomes PID 1, forwards signals to its
# child, and reaps zombies.
RUN apk add --no-cache tini
ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

Or at run time with docker run --init, which injects Docker's bundled tini. In Kubernetes there is no --init flag; bake tini into the image or make sure your process is a correct PID 1. With tini, node is PID 2, gets normal kernel signal defaults, and SIGTERM terminates it even if you forgot a handler; with a handler, NestJS runs its shutdown hooks.

Restart policies decide what happens after exit:

Policy Restarts on exit 0? Restarts on non-zero? Survives daemon restart? Use for
no (default) No No No One-shot jobs, migrations
on-failure[:N] No Yes, up to N times No Batch workers that should retry crashes
always Yes Yes Yes Long-running services on a single host
unless-stopped Yes Yes Yes, unless you stopped it manually Local dev dependencies (PostgreSQL, Redis)

Docker applies exponential backoff between restarts (100 ms doubling to a cap). In Kubernetes the equivalent is restartPolicy at pod level plus the CrashLoopBackOff state (see Part 45).

Practical example

The orders API handles POST /orders in about 120 ms: insert the order, publish an order.created event, return 201. During a rolling deploy, each old container receives SIGTERM. With correct handling, NestJS stops accepting new connections, waits up to a few seconds for the 15 to 30 requests in flight, closes the PostgreSQL pool and the Kafka producer, and exits 0. The load balancer had already stopped sending new traffic. Zero failed requests. Without handling, the container is killed after 10 seconds with 20 requests mid-transaction: PostgreSQL rolls those transactions back, the clients receive connection resets, and some retry, creating duplicate orders if the API is not idempotent.

NestJS example

NestJS gives you lifecycle hooks that run on SIGTERM when shutdown hooks are enabled. The important detail is order: stop taking new work, finish current work, then close resources.

TypeScript
// src/shutdown/graceful-shutdown.service.ts
import {
  Injectable,
  Logger,
  OnApplicationShutdown,
  BeforeApplicationShutdown,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class GracefulShutdownService
  implements BeforeApplicationShutdown, OnApplicationShutdown
{
  private readonly logger = new Logger(GracefulShutdownService.name);

  constructor(
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly notificationsQueue: Queue,
  ) {}

  // Runs after the HTTP server stops accepting connections but before
  // providers are destroyed. In-flight handlers are still completing.
  async beforeApplicationShutdown(signal?: string): Promise<void> {
    this.logger.log(`Received ${signal}; draining in-flight work`);
    // Give the load balancer time to notice we are unready (see Part 45
    // for the preStop and readiness interplay).
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2_000));
  }

  // Runs last. Close outbound resources so no query or job is left hanging.
  async onApplicationShutdown(signal?: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.notificationsQueue.close();
    if (this.dataSource.isInitialized) {
      await this.dataSource.destroy(); // returns pooled connections cleanly
    }
    this.logger.log(`Shutdown complete after ${signal}`);
  }
}

The app.enableShutdownHooks() call in main.ts (shown in 44.1) is what registers the signal listeners. Without it, none of these hooks run on SIGTERM.

PostgreSQL example

What PostgreSQL sees when your container is killed matters. A SIGKILLed Node process leaves TCP connections that PostgreSQL only notices when the kernel closes the sockets (immediate for a killed process on the same host; up to tcp_keepalives_idle seconds across a network if the container's network namespace vanished first). Each open transaction is rolled back, but until the backend notices, it holds locks and a connection slot:

SQL
-- Sessions that belong to a dead client but have not been cleaned up yet
SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now() - state_change AS idle_for, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
  AND now() - state_change > interval '30 seconds';

-- Safety net: kill transactions idle longer than 60 s, per application role
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';

A graceful shutdown that calls dataSource.destroy() sends a clean Terminate message on each pooled connection, so PostgreSQL frees the slots immediately instead of waiting for TCP keepalives.

TypeORM example

TypeORM's DataSource.destroy() waits for the pool to release connections. If a query is still running, the pool waits for it; combine with a statement_timeout on the role so that a runaway query cannot block shutdown past the grace period:

TypeScript
// src/database/data-source.ts
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  entities: [__dirname + '/../**/*.entity.js'],
  migrations: [__dirname + '/../migrations/*.js'],
  extra: {
    max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 10),
    // Fail fast instead of hanging shutdown on a dead database
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
    statement_timeout: 10_000,
  },
});

Sequelize example

Sequelize exposes sequelize.close(), which drains the pool. Register it in the same OnApplicationShutdown hook:

TypeScript
// In a provider with access to the Sequelize instance
import { InjectConnection } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize-typescript';

constructor(@InjectConnection() private readonly sequelize: Sequelize) {}

async onApplicationShutdown(): Promise<void> {
  await this.sequelize.close(); // waits for checked-out connections to return
}

Production scenario

A ride-booking API deploys 30 times a day across 12 replicas. Each deploy stops 12 containers. At 800 RPS, roughly 100 requests are in flight at any instant per replica set. With correct SIGTERM handling and a 2-second drain, the deploy's error contribution is zero. Before the fix, each deploy produced 400 to 900 502/ECONNRESET errors, which showed up as a daily saw-tooth in the error-rate dashboard that everyone had learned to ignore.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 a scale-down event removes 6 of 18 payments-worker containers. The Dockerfile used CMD npm run start:prod. npm was PID 1, ignored SIGTERM, and after 10 seconds all 6 were SIGKILLed. Each worker was mid-way through a batch of 50 payment captures against a PSP. The captures had been sent but the acknowledgements were never processed; the jobs were retried by BullMQ and 214 customers were charged twice. The post-mortem fix was three lines: tini, exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/worker.js"], and idempotency keys on the capture call (see Part 31 — Reliability Engineering).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SIGTERM arrives before the app is ready. A rollback during startup can send SIGTERM while NestJS is still initialising modules; make sure hooks tolerate uninitialised resources (if (dataSource.isInitialized)).
  • Grace period shorter than drain. If shutdown takes 15 s and the grace period is 10 s, you are killed anyway. Align terminationGracePeriodSeconds with your real drain time plus margin.
  • Child processes. child_process.spawn for ImageMagick or headless Chrome creates children that need signal forwarding and reaping; tini -g forwards to the whole process group.
  • SIGINT in local dev, SIGTERM in production. Handle both; enableShutdownHooks() covers both by default.
  • Uncaught exceptions during shutdown. A throw inside a shutdown hook aborts the rest; wrap each resource close in its own try/catch and log.
  • Restart loops on config errors. With restart: always, a container that exits immediately because DATABASE_URL is missing restarts forever; alert on restart count, not just on "is it running".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They insist that every service passes a "kill test" before it is allowed in production: send SIGTERM under load, count failed requests, verify the exit code is 0 and that pg_stat_activity shows no leftover sessions. They standardise tini plus exec-form CMD in the base image so that no team can get it wrong. And they know the mantra: can it timeout? can it fail? can it partially succeed? A shutdown is a partial failure by design; the code must make it clean.

Common mistakes

  • CMD npm start or CMD npm run start:prod.
  • Shell-form CMD node dist/main.js.
  • Forgetting app.enableShutdownHooks().
  • Closing the database pool before the HTTP server has stopped accepting requests, so the last requests fail with "pool is closed".
  • Treating exit code 137 as "the app crashed" and looking for a bug in the code instead of an OOM or a missed SIGTERM.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a Node process running as PID 1 ignore SIGTERM, and what are two fixes?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: kernel installs no default handlers for PID 1; fix with tini/--init or explicit handlers; use exec-form CMD.
  2. What is the difference between CMD node main.js and CMD ["node","main.js"]?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: shell form wraps in sh -c, shell becomes PID 1 and does not forward signals; exec form runs node directly.
  3. Describe a correct shutdown sequence for a NestJS API with PostgreSQL and a Kafka producer.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: stop accepting, drain in-flight with a bound, flush producer, close pool, exit 0, all within the grace period.
  4. What do exit codes 0, 1, 137 and 143 tell you?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: clean, uncaught error, SIGKILL (OOM or forced), SIGTERM without handler.
  5. When would you use restart: on-failure versus always?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: batch/worker retries versus long-running service; note the infinite loop risk on config errors.

Practical exercise

Build the orders API with CMD ["npm", "start"] and run it with docker run. Fire 200 requests per second with autocannon for 30 seconds, and at second 10 run docker stop. Count non-2xx responses and note the exit code and the time until the container stopped. Repeat with tini, exec-form CMD, and enableShutdownHooks(). Acceptance criteria: the fixed version stops in under 5 seconds with exit code 0, zero failed requests during the drain, and pg_stat_activity shows no sessions from the stopped container within 2 seconds.

44.5 Dockerfile best practices

Concept

A Dockerfile is a build script that produces an image. Best practices are the set of rules that keep the resulting image small, cacheable, reproducible, secure and operable. Most of them are one line each; all of them exist because someone lost a night to their absence.

Why does it exist?

A Dockerfile that "works" is easy. A Dockerfile that builds in 40 seconds, produces a 200 MB image, runs as a non-root user, restarts cleanly, does not leak secrets and does not break when Docker Hub republishes a tag takes deliberate choices. The practices below encode those choices so that every service in the organisation starts from the same safe baseline.

Mental model

Imagine a packing list for a shipping container going to a remote site: bring only what is needed, label everything, do not pack the keys to the warehouse inside, put fragile things where they will not be crushed, and write on the outside how to open it. A Dockerfile is that packing list; the practices are the rules experienced shippers follow.

How it works

Each practice, what it does and why:

Practice Instruction Why
Pin the base image FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:... Reproducible builds; no surprise musl or OpenSSL changes
Set the working directory WORKDIR /app Absolute paths in later instructions; created if missing
Production mode ENV NODE_ENV=production Express/NestJS disable dev behaviours; npm ci skips dev deps when set
Non-root user USER node The node images ship uid 1000 node; a compromise does not get root
Copy with ownership COPY --chown=node:node dist ./dist Files owned by the runtime user; no RUN chown -R layer doubling size
Exec-form entrypoint ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini","--"] and CMD ["node","dist/main.js"] Signals reach node; see 44.4
Labels LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision=$GIT_SHA Traceability from a running container back to a commit
Health check HEALTHCHECK CMD node healthcheck.js Compose can wait for readiness; note the Kubernetes caveat below
Expose (documentation) EXPOSE 3000 Documents the port; does not publish it
One process per container Single CMD Restart, scale and monitor one thing

The HEALTHCHECK caveat: Kubernetes ignores Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK entirely. The kubelet uses its own liveness, readiness and startup probes defined in the pod spec. A HEALTHCHECK in the image is useful for Docker Compose (depends_on: condition: service_healthy) and for standalone Docker, but it also runs every 30 seconds by default even where nobody reads it, so keep it cheap. On Kubernetes, some teams remove it from the image to avoid the wasted work.

Labels follow the OCI annotation spec so that tooling recognises them:

Dockerfile
ARG GIT_SHA=unknown
ARG VERSION=0.0.0
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="orders-api" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="${VERSION}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/acme/orders-api"

Put the ARG and LABEL lines at the end of the Dockerfile. A GIT_SHA that changes on every commit would otherwise invalidate every layer after it.

Practical example

A production-quality single-stage Dockerfile (the multi-stage version in 44.6 is what you should actually ship; this one shows the practices in isolation):

Dockerfile
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:2d07db07a2df6830718ae2a47db6fedce6745f5bcd174c398f2acdda90a11c03

# tini for PID 1, tzdata so TZ works, no cache to keep the layer small
RUN apk add --no-cache tini tzdata

ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    TZ=UTC \
    PORT=3000

WORKDIR /app

COPY --chown=node:node package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force

COPY --chown=node:node dist ./dist

USER node
EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/live').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"

ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

NestJS example

The health endpoint that the HEALTHCHECK (and later the Kubernetes probes) call should be cheap and must not depend on the database for liveness. @nestjs/terminus gives you the pieces:

TypeScript
// src/health/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  HealthCheck,
  HealthCheckService,
  TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  MemoryHealthIndicator,
} from '@nestjs/terminus';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly memory: MemoryHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  // Liveness: is the process alive and not wedged? No external calls.
  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.memory.checkHeap('heap', 400 * 1024 * 1024), // 400 MB
    ]);
  }

  // Readiness: can we serve traffic? Check the database with a short timeout.
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 300 }),
    ]);
  }
}

Production scenario

A platform team publishes a Dockerfile template and a linter (hadolint) in CI that fails on FROM without a tag, USER missing, apt-get install without --no-install-recommends, or shell-form CMD. Across 60 services this removed an entire class of incidents: no more root containers, no more missed SIGTERM, no more 1 GB images. The template is versioned; when tini had a CVE fix, one PR to the template and 60 rebuilds later, done.

Failure scenario

An engineer adds RUN chown -R node:node /app after copying 300 MB of node_modules as root. OverlayFS cannot change ownership in place; it copies every file into a new layer. The image doubles to 700 MB, pulls slow down, and node disk fills faster. The fix is COPY --chown, which sets ownership at copy time with no extra layer.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • USER node before npm ci. The node user cannot write to /app unless WORKDIR was created with the right owner; run installs as root, then switch, or chown the directory first.
  • ENV NODE_ENV=production before npm ci in a build stage. Dev dependencies (TypeScript, Nest CLI) are skipped and the build fails. Set it only in the runtime stage.
  • Alpine tzdata. Without it, TZ=Asia/Kolkata is silently ignored and dates render in UTC. Install tzdata or use UTC everywhere and convert at the edge (the better choice).
  • HEALTHCHECK on distroless. No shell, no curl; only a node -e or a compiled binary works.
  • EXPOSE does not publish. Teams sometimes think EXPOSE 3000 makes the port reachable; it is documentation.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write Dockerfiles for the reader on call at 3 a.m.: obvious, linted, boring. They keep the runtime image free of anything not needed to run node dist/main.js. They put USER node as late as possible and ARGs as late as possible. And they refuse a Dockerfile in review that lacks a pinned base, a non-root user or an exec-form command, regardless of how urgent the feature is.

Common mistakes

  • Unpinned FROM.
  • Running as root because a file permission error appeared once.
  • RUN apt-get update in one layer and apt-get install in another (stale package lists cached).
  • Putting ARG GIT_SHA at the top.
  • Believing the Kubernetes probes come from HEALTHCHECK.

Interview questions

  1. List five Dockerfile practices that matter in production and the incident each prevents.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pinned base (drift), non-root (privilege escalation), exec-form CMD (lost SIGTERM), .dockerignore and layer order (slow builds, leaked .env), --chown (image bloat).
  2. Does Kubernetes use the image's HEALTHCHECK?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; kubelet probes only.
  3. What does ENV NODE_ENV=production change?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: framework behaviours, npm ci omitting dev deps, some libraries caching; must not be set before a build that needs dev deps.
  4. Why are ARG values part of the cache key?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a RUN that references an ARG changes when the value changes; volatile args go last.

Practical exercise

Run hadolint on three Dockerfiles from your company and fix every warning. For each fix, write one sentence naming the production failure it prevents. Acceptance criteria: zero hadolint errors, a non-root USER, exec-form ENTRYPOINT/CMD, pinned base digest, and a passing docker run --rm image node -e "console.log(process.getuid())" printing 1000.

44.6 Multi-stage builds

Concept

A multi-stage build uses several FROM sections in one Dockerfile. Early stages install dependencies and compile TypeScript; the final stage starts from a clean base image and copies in only the artefacts needed at run time: dist and production node_modules. Compilers, dev dependencies, source files and build caches never reach the shipped image.

Why does it exist?

A NestJS project needs TypeScript, the Nest CLI, Jest, ESLint and type definitions to build, and none of them to run. Installing everything in one stage produces images of 800 MB to 1.3 GB, most of which is dev tooling that also expands the attack surface (a vulnerable webpack transitive dependency is a CVE in your production image even though it never runs). Multi-stage builds separate the build environment from the runtime environment, cutting image size by 70 to 85% and CVE counts by a similar proportion.

Mental model

Imagine a furniture workshop and a showroom. In the workshop you have saws, glue, sandpaper, sawdust everywhere. The showroom receives only the finished chair. Nobody ships the workshop to the customer. Each FROM starts a new clean room; COPY --from= carries the chair across.

How it works

  1. deps stage. Copy package.json and package-lock.json, run npm ci. Full install including dev dependencies. Cached until the lockfile changes.
  2. build stage. Start from deps, copy source and config, run nest build (or tsc -p tsconfig.build.json). Output is dist/.
  3. prod-deps stage. Copy the manifests again and run npm ci --omit=dev to get only runtime packages. Optionally prune further (npm prune --omit=dev, remove *.md, *.ts, *.map inside node_modules with tools like node-prune or clean-modules).
  4. runtime stage. Fresh base image, tini, USER node, COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist, COPY --from=prod-deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules, CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"].

BuildKit builds the deps, build and prod-deps stages in parallel where the graph allows (deps and prod-deps both depend only on the manifests) and skips any stage not referenced by the final one. docker build --target build lets CI build only up to the build stage for running tests.

Practical example

Dockerfile
# ---------- 1. deps: full install for building and testing ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

# ---------- 2. build: compile TypeScript to dist ----------
FROM deps AS build
COPY tsconfig.json tsconfig.build.json nest-cli.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# ---------- 3. prod-deps: runtime dependencies only ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS prod-deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
# --omit=dev skips devDependencies; cache clean drops the 50-100 MB npm cache
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force

# ---------- 4. runtime: minimal, non-root, signal-safe ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS runtime
RUN apk add --no-cache tini tzdata
ENV NODE_ENV=production TZ=UTC PORT=3000
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=node:node --from=prod-deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --chown=node:node --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

Typical size numbers for a mid-sized NestJS API (TypeORM, pg, ioredis, bullmq, class-validator, @nestjs/swagger):

Build approach Image size Layers High/critical CVEs (Trivy, typical)
Single stage, node:20, npm install 1.35 GB 12 40 to 90
Single stage, node:20-alpine, all deps 610 MB 10 5 to 15
Multi-stage, node:20-slim, prod deps 290 MB 8 3 to 10
Multi-stage, node:20-alpine, prod deps 215 MB 8 0 to 5
Multi-stage, distroless nodejs20-debian12 205 MB 6 0 to 3

The dist folder for such an API is 2 to 8 MB; production node_modules is 60 to 120 MB; the rest is the base image. Once you are at 200 MB, the remaining cost is the Node runtime itself, and further shaving is rarely worth the operational loss of a shell.

NestJS example

Native modules that must compile on Alpine belong in the deps and prod-deps stages only. The runtime stage never sees the compilers:

Dockerfile
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS prod-deps
WORKDIR /app
# Build tools exist only in this stage; the runtime stage copies the
# compiled node_modules and never installs python3/make/g++.
RUN apk add --no-cache python3 make g++
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force

If the compiled binary links against a library not present in the runtime image (for example libstdc++ for some modules), add that runtime library to the runtime stage with apk add --no-cache libstdc++; do not add the compilers.

Production scenario

A company migrates 40 services from single-stage node:16 images (average 1.1 GB) to multi-stage node:20-alpine (average 210 MB). Effects measured over a month: node image pulls during autoscaling drop from 45 s to 6 s, which lets the HPA react a full minute faster during traffic spikes; registry storage falls from 9 TB to 1.4 TB; Trivy findings drop from 2,300 to 90; and the average build stays at 70 s because the cache order was preserved.

Failure scenario

During an incident a team needs to add a temporary debug endpoint. The build fails: Cannot find module '@nestjs/cli'. Someone had set ENV NODE_ENV=production at the top of the Dockerfile, above the deps stage, so npm ci skipped dev dependencies including the Nest CLI. The build had been "passing" only because a stale CI cache still had the layer from before the change. --no-cache in CI reproduced the break in 2 minutes. Moving ENV NODE_ENV to the runtime stage fixed it; adding a weekly --no-cache build to CI made sure the cache could not hide it again.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two npm ci runs double the dependency download (deps and prod-deps). A BuildKit cache mount (RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci) keeps the npm cache across builds so the second install is mostly local.
  • COPY --from with an absolute path must match the stage's WORKDIR; a mismatch copies an empty directory silently.
  • Lockfile mismatch between stages cannot happen (same file) but package.json scripts.postinstall may behave differently with --omit=dev (for example Husky's prepare script failing); guard with npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts when appropriate, and be aware that --ignore-scripts also skips native module builds.
  • Source maps. dist/**/*.map help stack traces but add 30 to 50% to dist; keep them, they are small compared to node_modules, and set NODE_OPTIONS=--enable-source-maps.
  • Copying package.json into runtime is needed if code reads its own version; do not copy the lockfile.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see the final stage as the only artefact that matters and audit it like a production server: what user, what files, what binaries, what listening ports. They keep the build and test stages rich (compilers, test runners) and the runtime stage austere. They use --target so that CI runs tests in the exact dependency set that produced the shipped dist.

Common mistakes

  • Copying the whole /app from the build stage (including dev node_modules and src) into runtime.
  • Setting NODE_ENV=production before the build stage's npm ci.
  • Installing build tools in the runtime stage to make a native module work.
  • Forgetting npm cache clean --force, leaving 80 MB of tarballs in a layer.

Interview questions

  1. Explain a multi-stage Dockerfile for a NestJS API and what each stage produces.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: deps (all packages), build (dist), prod-deps (runtime packages), runtime (base plus copies, non-root, tini).
  2. Why is the final image still around 200 MB after removing dev dependencies?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the Node runtime and base OS dominate; dist is a few MB.
  3. How do you handle a native module on Alpine without shipping compilers?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: compile in an intermediate stage, copy node_modules, add only runtime shared libraries.
  4. How would you run unit tests against exactly the image you ship?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: --target build for tests, same lockfile, same base digest.

Practical exercise

Convert a single-stage NestJS Dockerfile into the four-stage version above. Add a BuildKit cache mount for npm. Measure image size, number of layers, and trivy image high/critical counts before and after. Acceptance criteria: the runtime image is under 260 MB on Alpine (under 330 MB on slim), contains no typescript, jest or @nestjs/cli directory under node_modules, runs as uid 1000, and stops within 3 seconds on docker stop.

44.7 Container networking

Concept

Each container gets its own network namespace: a private loopback interface (lo), a private eth0, its own IP address, its own routing table and its own port space. Docker connects that eth0 to a virtual switch (a bridge) on the host. Containers on the same user-defined bridge can reach each other by IP and, more usefully, by name through Docker's embedded DNS server. The host reaches a container only through ports you explicitly publish.

Why does it exist?

Without network isolation, two containers could not both listen on port 3000, and a container could sniff or spoof traffic of another. With it, every service listens on whatever port it likes inside its own namespace, and the platform decides what is reachable from where. Name-based discovery means your NestJS config says DB_HOST=postgres, not an IP that changes on every restart.

Mental model

Imagine an apartment building with an internal phone system. Every apartment (container) has its own phone with extension numbers (ports); you can call another apartment by its name through the building's directory (Docker DNS). The outside world cannot ring an apartment directly; the building's reception (the host) forwards only the numbers listed at the front desk (published ports). Inside your apartment, dialling "myself" (localhost) rings your own phone, never the neighbour's. That last point is the single most common confusion in Docker networking.

How it works

Network drivers you will meet:

Driver What it does Name resolution Use it for
Default bridge (docker0) Legacy shared bridge; containers get IPs from 172.17.0.0/16 None (no DNS by name) Nothing; avoid
User-defined bridge Private bridge per network; embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 Yes, by container or service name Compose, local dev, single-host deployments
host Container shares the host's network namespace; no isolation, no NAT Host's resolver Performance-sensitive or port-heavy tools on Linux; not available on Docker Desktop in the same way
none Only loopback None Sandboxed batch jobs
overlay Multi-host network (Swarm) Yes Rarely; Kubernetes replaces this

Step by step for a Compose project with api and postgres services:

  1. Compose creates a user-defined bridge network named <project>_default, for example orders_default, with a subnet such as 172.20.0.0/16.
  2. Each service's container gets a veth pair: one end inside the container as eth0 with an IP like 172.20.0.3, the other end attached to the bridge.
  3. Docker's embedded DNS server listens on 127.0.0.11 inside each container's namespace and answers queries for service names (postgres), container names and network aliases with the container's IP. /etc/resolv.conf in the container points to it; unknown names are forwarded to the host's resolver.
  4. api connects to postgres:5432. The name resolves to 172.20.0.2, the packet goes over the bridge, no NAT involved. Latency is 30 to 80 microseconds, the same as loopback for practical purposes.
  5. ports: - "3000:3000" on api installs a NAT rule on the host: host 0.0.0.0:3000 forwards to 172.20.0.3:3000. Your browser talks to localhost:3000 on the host; the host forwards it in. PostgreSQL does not need a published port for api to reach it; publish 5432 only so that a GUI on your laptop can connect.

The localhost confusion, spelled out:

  • Inside the api container, localhost:5432 is the api container's own loopback. Nothing listens there. ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 is the symptom.
  • The database is at postgres:5432 (service name) on the shared network.
  • To reach something running on your laptop from inside a container (a local mock server, a debugger), use host.docker.internal on Docker Desktop. On Linux, add extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"] to the service.
  • Inside the container, your NestJS server must bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, or the published port will connect to the container and be refused.

Practical example

The orders API connects to PostgreSQL through a URL built from environment variables. Locally, Compose sets DB_HOST=postgres; in Kubernetes, the same variable becomes the Service name (orders-postgres.shop.svc.cluster.local) or an RDS hostname. The code never changes.

YAML
# docker-compose.yml (excerpt)
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"          # host:container; only the API is exposed to the laptop
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres        # service name, resolved by Docker DNS
      DB_PORT: "5432"
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
    # No "ports" needed for api -> postgres; add "5432:5432" only for a local GUI
  redis:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine

NestJS example

Config that produces the same connection whether the host is a Compose service name, a Kubernetes Service or RDS:

TypeScript
// src/config/database.config.ts
import { registerAs } from '@nestjs/config';

export default registerAs('database', () => ({
  host: process.env.DB_HOST ?? 'localhost',   // 'postgres' in Compose
  port: Number(process.env.DB_PORT ?? 5432),
  username: process.env.DB_USER ?? 'orders',
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD ?? '',
  database: process.env.DB_NAME ?? 'orders',
  // Only RDS/production have TLS; Compose PostgreSQL does not
  ssl: process.env.DB_SSL === 'true' ? { rejectUnauthorized: true } : false,
  poolMax: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 10),
}));

PostgreSQL example

PostgreSQL inside a container listens on 0.0.0.0 by default in the official image (listen_addresses = '*') and pg_hba.conf allows password auth from any address. From another container:

Shell
docker compose exec api sh -c 'nc -zv postgres 5432'      # TCP reachability
docker compose exec postgres psql -U orders -c "SELECT inet_server_addr(), inet_client_addr();"

The second command shows the server's address on the bridge (172.20.0.2) and the client's (172.20.0.2 for a local psql, or 172.20.0.3 if run from api), which is a quick way to confirm which network path is in use.

Production scenario

On a single-host staging server, 8 containers on one user-defined bridge talk to each other by name at bridge speed. In production on Kubernetes the same names become Services; the pattern of "connect by name, bind to 0.0.0.0, publish nothing you do not need" carries over unchanged. A team that learned networking through Compose finds Kubernetes Services familiar: a stable name in front of a changing IP.

Failure scenario

At 09:05 a new developer reports "the API cannot reach the database". Their .env has DB_HOST=localhost, copied from a colleague who runs PostgreSQL natively. Inside the container, localhost is the container. The error log says connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432. Fifteen minutes lost; the fix is DB_HOST=postgres. The team adds a comment in .env.example and a startup log line printing the resolved DB host, which turns the next occurrence into a 30-second fix.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Default bridge has no DNS. docker run without --network puts the container on docker0, where names do not resolve. Always create or use a user-defined network.
  • Port already allocated. Two Compose projects publishing 5432:5432 collide on the host; use different host ports or none.
  • IPv6 and localhost. Node 17+ resolves localhost to ::1 first; a server bound to 0.0.0.0 (IPv4 only) refuses it. Bind to :: to accept both, or use 127.0.0.1 explicitly in clients.
  • Alpine DNS behaviour. musl's resolver historically lacked TCP fallback for large responses and handles search domains differently; long service names or many search domains in Kubernetes can produce intermittent ENOTFOUND. glibc images are more forgiving.
  • Connection limits from many containers. Every container's pool counts toward max_connections in PostgreSQL; 20 containers with max: 20 is 400 connections. See Part 19 — PostgreSQL Internals.
  • Bridge MTU. VPNs on the host can shrink MTU; large responses stall inside containers. Rare but memorable.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never hardcode hosts; everything is a name from configuration. They publish the minimum set of ports and treat a published database port as a security finding outside local dev. They know that "connect by service name" is the same idea on Compose, ECS and Kubernetes, and they explain to juniors, once, that localhost inside a container is the container.

Common mistakes

  • DB_HOST=localhost inside a container.
  • Binding NestJS to 127.0.0.1.
  • Publishing every port "just in case".
  • Using the default bridge and then linking containers with deprecated --link.
  • Assuming the container can reach the host's services by localhost.

Interview questions

  1. A container logs ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432. What is wrong?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: localhost is the container's own loopback; use the service name.
  2. How does Docker resolve service names between containers?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 on user-defined networks; not on the default bridge.
  3. What does -p 3000:3000 actually do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: host NAT rule to container IP; container must bind to all interfaces.
  4. When would you use --network host and what do you lose?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: raw performance or many ports on Linux; lose isolation and port namespacing.

Practical exercise

Create a Compose project with api, postgres and redis. From inside api, run getent hosts postgres, cat /etc/resolv.conf, nc -zv postgres 5432 and nc -zv localhost 5432, and explain each result. Then bind the API to 127.0.0.1 and show the published port failing, then fix it. Acceptance criteria: a short write-up explaining the resolver address, why localhost:5432 fails, and a passing curl localhost:3000/health/live from the host.

44.8 Volumes and state

Concept

A container's writable layer is disposable: it is deleted when the container is removed, it is slow (copy-on-write through OverlayFS), and it is invisible to other containers. Anything that must outlive the container, be shared, or be fast for heavy writes goes in a volume. Docker has two main kinds: bind mounts, which map a host directory into the container, and named volumes, which Docker manages in its own storage area.

Why does it exist?

A PostgreSQL container that stores its data in the writable layer loses the whole database on docker compose down. A developer who wants hot reload needs the container to see the source files being edited on the host. A worker that writes uploaded files to /tmp and expects another container to read them needs a shared location. Volumes solve all three and, more importantly, they make the boundary explicit: this container is stateless; the only state is here.

Mental model

Imagine hotel rooms. The room (container) is cleaned and reset between guests; anything left inside is thrown away. The hotel safe deposit box (named volume) keeps your valuables between stays. A window into your own house (bind mount) lets you work on files at home while sitting in the hotel, but the hotel staff (container user) may not have the keys to your drawers (permissions).

How it works

Kind Syntax (Compose) Where the data lives Performance Use for
Writable layer (default) OverlayFS upper dir; deleted with container Slow for heavy writes Nothing important
Named volume pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data on the Docker host (inside the VM on Desktop) Native filesystem speed Databases, Redis persistence, broker logs
Bind mount ./src:/app/src Your host directory Native on Linux; slow across the Desktop VM boundary on macOS/Windows Source code for hot reload, config files
tmpfs tmpfs: - /tmp RAM Fastest; lost on stop Scratch space, especially with a read-only root filesystem

Step by step for a PostgreSQL named volume:

  1. docker compose up sees volumes: pgdata: and creates it if missing.
  2. The volume is mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data in the postgres container, over whatever the image had there. Because the volume is empty on first run, Docker copies the image's existing directory contents into it (this copy only happens for named volumes, not bind mounts).
  3. PostgreSQL's entrypoint sees an empty PGDATA, runs initdb, creates the user and database from POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB, and runs any *.sql in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/.
  4. On subsequent starts, PGDATA is populated, so init scripts are skipped. This surprises everyone once: changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in Compose does nothing to an existing volume.
  5. docker compose down removes containers but keeps volumes; docker compose down -v deletes them.

Permissions: the official PostgreSQL image runs as uid 999 (postgres). initdb requires PGDATA to be owned by that user with mode 0700 or 0750. With a named volume Docker handles it. With a bind mount on Linux, the directory takes your host uid and PostgreSQL fails with data directory has wrong ownership or permission denied. Your NestJS container runs as uid 1000 (node); a bind-mounted ./uploads directory owned by a host user with uid 501 (macOS default) works on Docker Desktop (it remaps) but fails on a Linux CI runner. The rule: named volumes for data the container owns; bind mounts for files the developer owns.

Practical example

YAML
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: orders
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: orders
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data                 # durable data
      - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro         # first-run SQL, read-only bind mount
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U orders -d orders"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: deps                 # dev image with the full toolchain
    command: ["npx", "nest", "start", "--watch"]
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src             # hot reload: edits on the host are seen in the container
      - /app/node_modules          # anonymous volume: keep the container's Linux node_modules
    environment:
      CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING: "true"  # file watching across the Desktop VM boundary

volumes:
  pgdata:

The /app/node_modules anonymous volume is the trick that prevents your host node_modules (built for macOS or Windows) from shadowing the container's Linux one when you bind-mount the project directory.

NestJS example

Stateless means the API writes nothing local that matters. File uploads are the usual violation. Stream them to object storage and keep only metadata in PostgreSQL:

TypeScript
// src/uploads/uploads.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Upload } from './upload.entity';

@Injectable()
export class UploadsService {
  private readonly s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });

  constructor(@InjectRepository(Upload) private readonly uploads: Repository<Upload>) {}

  async store(userId: string, file: Express.Multer.File): Promise<Upload> {
    const key = `users/${userId}/${crypto.randomUUID()}-${file.originalname}`;
    // Bytes go to S3 (or MinIO locally); nothing is written to the container disk
    await this.s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
      Bucket: process.env.UPLOADS_BUCKET,
      Key: key,
      Body: file.buffer,
      ContentType: file.mimetype,
    }));
    return this.uploads.save(this.uploads.create({ userId, key, size: file.size }));
  }
}

Locally, MinIO runs as another Compose service with its own named volume, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL points at it. The API code is identical in both places.

PostgreSQL example

Verifying where data lives and that it survives a restart:

Shell
docker compose exec postgres psql -U orders -c "SHOW data_directory;"   # /var/lib/postgresql/data
docker volume inspect orders_pgdata --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'
docker compose down && docker compose up -d
docker compose exec postgres psql -U orders -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"  # still there

And the one-time initialisation script pattern for local dev, mounted read-only:

SQL
-- db/init/01-extensions.sql : runs only when PGDATA is empty
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto";
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pg_stat_statements";

Production scenario

In production you rarely use Docker volumes directly: Kubernetes PersistentVolumes back StatefulSets, and most teams use RDS or Aurora for PostgreSQL anyway (see Part 45 for the honest discussion). The habit that carries over is stateless application containers: no local writes, logs to stdout, uploads to object storage, sessions in Redis. A stateless API can be scaled to 40 replicas or killed at any time with no data loss.

Failure scenario

A team runs PostgreSQL in Docker on a staging server with the data in the writable layer (no volume). A routine docker compose up --force-recreate after an image bump recreates the container; the database is empty. Three weeks of QA test data is gone. Staging is rebuilt from a production snapshot, which takes a day. The lesson is written into the Compose file as a named volume and into the team's checklist: any container with data has a volume, and the volume is backed up or reproducible.

Edge cases & failure modes
