  • Init scripts run once. Changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD or adding a script does nothing to an existing volume; docker compose down -v (destroying data) is the reset.
  • Bind-mount performance on Desktop. A node_modules bind mount on macOS can make nest start 5 to 10 times slower; keep node_modules in a volume or in the container.
  • Ownership on Linux hosts. Files created by the container as uid 1000 appear owned by uid 1000 on the host; if your user is 1001, you cannot delete them without sudo. Match uids or use named volumes.
  • Volume mounted over image content. A bind mount to /app hides the image's /app entirely, including dist; mount only src.
  • Read-only root filesystem plus volumes. With read_only: true, every writable path (/tmp, /app/.cache) needs an explicit tmpfs or volume.
  • Disk full. Named volumes live on the Docker host's disk; a PostgreSQL volume growing unbounded on a small root partition fills the disk and stops every container on the host.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "where does state live?" for every container, and the only acceptable answers are "nowhere" (stateless) or "in a named, backed-up volume or an external store". They keep bind mounts strictly for development. They know the initdb runs-once rule and the uid rules well enough to fix a permission error in one minute rather than by running everything as root.

Common mistakes

  • No volume for PostgreSQL or Redis in Compose.
  • Bind-mounting the whole project directory including node_modules.
  • Storing uploads on the container disk.
  • Fixing a bind-mount permission error with USER root.
  • Expecting environment changes to reconfigure an already-initialised database volume.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a bind mount and a named volume, and when do you use each?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: host path versus Docker-managed; dev source versus database data; performance and permissions differences.
  2. Why does changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD in Compose not change the password?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: init runs only on empty PGDATA.
  3. Why must application containers be stateless?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: restart, scale, replace freely; state goes to PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage.
  4. Your container runs as uid 1000 and cannot write to a bind-mounted directory. What are your options?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: match ownership on host, --chown/entrypoint chown for named volumes, use a named volume, avoid root.

Practical exercise

Set up Compose with PostgreSQL on a named volume and the API with a bind-mounted src. Insert 1,000 orders, run docker compose down, then up, and verify the rows exist. Then run down -v and show they are gone. Add a read_only: true API container with a tmpfs /tmp and make the app work. Acceptance criteria: data persists across down/up, hot reload works when editing a controller, and the read-only API passes its health check.

44.9 Environment variables and configuration

Concept

Configuration is everything that varies between deployments of the same image: database host, credentials, feature flags, log level, external API endpoints. The twelve-factor rule is that configuration lives in the environment, not in the image, so that one image serves every environment. Build-time settings (ARG) are baked into the image and cannot change later; run-time settings (ENV, -e, Compose environment, Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets) are read when the process starts.

Why does it exist?

If configuration is inside the image, you need a different image per environment, which means the image you tested is not the image you ship. If secrets are inside the image, anyone who can pull the image (every developer, every CI runner, every node) has production credentials, forever, in a layer. If configuration is unvalidated, a typo in a variable name is discovered by a customer at 2 a.m. Externalised, validated configuration solves all three.

Mental model

Imagine a delivery van (the image). The van is identical for every city. The route sheet (configuration) is handed to the driver at the depot each morning. You would never paint the route on the van, and you would never leave the depot's master key taped under the dashboard.

How it works

  1. Build time. ARG values exist only during docker build; they are visible in docker history (so never pass secrets as ARG) and are gone from the running container unless copied into an ENV.
  2. Image defaults. ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 sets defaults recorded in the image config. They are visible to anyone with the image. Safe for non-secrets that rarely change.
  3. Run time. docker run -e DB_PASSWORD=..., Compose environment: and env_file:, or Kubernetes env/envFrom. Overrides image defaults. This is where per-environment values and secrets go.
  4. Secrets as files. Docker Compose secrets: and Kubernetes Secret volumes mount secrets as files (/run/secrets/db_password) rather than environment variables, which keeps them out of docker inspect, crash dumps and child processes. Many libraries support DB_PASSWORD_FILE-style variables for this reason.
  5. Validation at startup. The application reads the environment once, validates the shape and types, and refuses to start on invalid config. Failing fast at boot with a clear message is far cheaper than failing at first use.

.env files: convenient for local development, never for production. Compose reads .env from the project directory for variable substitution and env_file: for container environment. Keep .env in .gitignore and .dockerignore, commit a .env.example with placeholder values.

ARG versus ENV:

ARG ENV
Available during build Yes Yes (after the line)
Available at run time No Yes
Visible in docker history Yes (value in the layer metadata) Yes
Overridable at run No Yes (-e)
Safe for secrets No No
Typical use Base image version, build target, Git SHA for a label NODE_ENV, PORT, TZ, non-secret defaults

Practical example

The orders API has around 25 configuration values. Locally they come from .env via Compose; in Kubernetes from a ConfigMap and a Secret; in CI from the workflow. In every case the app validates them the same way, and a missing DATABASE_URL produces Config validation error: "DATABASE_URL" is required and exit code 1 before any request is served.

NestJS example

@nestjs/config with a Joi schema. Validation runs when ConfigModule initialises, so the app never starts with bad config:

TypeScript
// src/app.module.ts (excerpt)
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule } from '@nestjs/config';
import * as Joi from 'joi';
import databaseConfig from './config/database.config';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({
      isGlobal: true,
      load: [databaseConfig],
      // Do not read .env in production: the environment is the source of truth
      ignoreEnvFile: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production',
      validationSchema: Joi.object({
        NODE_ENV: Joi.string().valid('development', 'test', 'production').required(),
        PORT: Joi.number().port().default(3000),
        DB_HOST: Joi.string().hostname().required(),
        DB_PORT: Joi.number().port().default(5432),
        DB_USER: Joi.string().required(),
        DB_PASSWORD: Joi.string().min(8).required(),
        DB_NAME: Joi.string().required(),
        DB_POOL_MAX: Joi.number().integer().min(1).max(50).default(10),
        REDIS_URL: Joi.string().uri({ scheme: ['redis', 'rediss'] }).required(),
        KAFKA_BROKERS: Joi.string().required(),           // comma-separated host:port
        JWT_SECRET: Joi.string().min(32).required(),
        LOG_LEVEL: Joi.string().valid('debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error').default('info'),
      }),
      validationOptions: { abortEarly: false }, // report every problem at once
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

The same with zod, using the validate option, which gives you a typed config object:

TypeScript
// src/config/env.schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const envSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url().startsWith('postgres'),
  REDIS_URL: z.string().url(),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
  DB_POOL_MAX: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(50).default(10),
});
export type Env = z.infer<typeof envSchema>;

// Used as ConfigModule.forRoot({ validate })
export function validate(raw: Record<string, unknown>): Env {
  const result = envSchema.safeParse(raw);
  if (!result.success) {
    // One line per problem; the container exits 1 and the orchestrator shows the log
    const issues = result.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join('.')}: ${i.message}`);
    throw new Error(`Config validation error:\n${issues.join('\n')}`);
  }
  return result.data;
}

TypeORM example

The DataSource reads the same validated config, and the migration CLI uses the same file, so migrations and the app can never disagree about which database they target:

TypeScript
// src/database/data-source.ts  (used by both TypeOrmModule and the CLI)
import 'reflect-metadata';
import { DataSource, DataSourceOptions } from 'typeorm';

export const dataSourceOptions: DataSourceOptions = {
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.DB_HOST,
  port: Number(process.env.DB_PORT ?? 5432),
  username: process.env.DB_USER,
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.DB_NAME,
  entities: [__dirname + '/../**/*.entity.js'],
  migrations: [__dirname + '/../migrations/*.js'],
  migrationsTableName: 'typeorm_migrations',
  synchronize: false,                     // never in a containerised deploy
  logging: process.env.LOG_LEVEL === 'debug',
  extra: { max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 10) },
};

export const AppDataSource = new DataSource(dataSourceOptions);

The migration runner in Compose (44.12) executes node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:run -d dist/database/data-source.js with the same environment as the API.

Sequelize example

TypeScript
// src/app.module.ts (excerpt)
import { SequelizeModule } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

SequelizeModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    dialect: 'postgres',
    host: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_HOST'),
    port: config.get<number>('DB_PORT', 5432),
    username: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_USER'),
    password: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_PASSWORD'),
    database: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_NAME'),
    autoLoadModels: true,
    synchronize: false,
    pool: { max: config.get<number>('DB_POOL_MAX', 10), acquire: 5_000 },
    logging: false,
  }),
});

getOrThrow turns a missing variable into a startup failure with the variable's name in the message.

Production scenario

A company with 60 services standardises on: image defaults for NODE_ENV, PORT, TZ; a ConfigMap per service for non-secret settings; secrets from AWS Secrets Manager synced into Kubernetes Secrets and mounted as files; Joi validation in every service. A dashboard counts "config validation failures at startup" per deploy. In a year, 31 bad deploys were caught by validation before serving a single request, each within 5 seconds of the pod starting.

Failure scenario

At 16:20 a deploy of notifications-api goes out with SMTP_HOST misspelled as SMPT_HOST in the ConfigMap. There was no validation. The pods started, passed liveness, and served traffic. Every email for 40 minutes failed with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND undefined until a customer asked support why they had not received an order confirmation. With required-field validation the pods would have crashed at boot, the rollout would have stalled at 1 of 6 replicas, and the old pods would have kept serving. The team added the schema that afternoon and, after that, kubectl rollout status did the catching.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Secrets in environment variables leak into docker inspect, /proc/<pid>/environ, crash reports, child processes and often logs. Prefer file-mounted secrets for the most sensitive values.
  • .env copied into the image because .dockerignore was missing. Now every developer has production credentials.
  • Booleans as strings. FEATURE_X=false is a non-empty string and truthy in JavaScript; coerce with a schema.
  • Numbers as strings. PORT="3000" works because listen coerces; DB_POOL_MAX="10" handed to a library expecting a number may silently become NaN. Coerce with a schema.
  • Build-time ARG used for a secret (an npm token) remains in docker history. Use BuildKit secret mounts: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci.
  • Config that changes after start. Environment variables are read once at process start; rotating a secret means restarting the pod (see Part 45 on checksum annotations).
  • Defaults that hide problems. A default DB_HOST=localhost masks a missing variable in Compose; use required for anything that differs per environment.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate identity (the image, immutable) from behaviour (the config, injected). They validate config at boot and treat validation failures as the cheapest possible incident. They keep secrets out of images, out of Git and, where feasible, out of environment variables. They give every variable a name that says its unit (HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS, not TIMEOUT) and a documented example in .env.example.

Common mistakes

  • Copying .env into the image or baking secrets with ENV.
  • No validation, so typos become runtime errors hours later.
  • Different config loading code for the app and the migration CLI, so they connect to different databases.
  • Reading process.env all over the codebase instead of through ConfigService, making the set of variables impossible to audit.
  • Setting synchronize: true in a containerised deploy.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between ARG and ENV and why neither is safe for secrets.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: build versus run scope; both visible in image metadata or history; use BuildKit secret mounts and run-time secret injection.
  2. How do you make a NestJS service refuse to start with bad configuration?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ConfigModule.forRoot with validationSchema (Joi) or validate (zod); exit non-zero; orchestrator halts rollout.
  3. Why are file-mounted secrets sometimes better than environment variables?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: environment leaks through inspect, /proc, children, crash dumps; files can be permissioned and rotated.
  4. One image for all environments: what has to be true?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no environment-specific code paths at build, all config injected, validated, and secrets external.

Practical exercise

Add Joi or zod validation to an existing NestJS service. Remove a required variable and confirm the container exits with code 1 and a readable message within 3 seconds. Move the database password to a Compose secrets: file mount and read it from DB_PASSWORD_FILE. Acceptance criteria: docker inspect of the running container shows no password in Config.Env, the app starts and connects, and a misspelled variable name fails startup with the exact variable name in the log.

44.10 Container lifecycle, logs and resource limits

Concept

A container moves through a small set of states: created, running, paused, stopped (exited), removed. Docker commands map directly onto them. While running, the container writes logs to stdout and stderr, which the runtime captures, and it lives inside cgroup limits for memory and CPU. Node.js does not automatically size itself to those limits, so a senior engineer sets the V8 heap explicitly and understands what the kernel does when the limit is crossed.

Why does it exist?

Orchestrators need a predictable state machine to reason about: "is it running, did it exit cleanly, should I restart it". Operators need logs without SSH-ing into containers. And the whole point of packing 30 containers on a node is that one runaway process cannot take the node down; that requires hard limits, and hard limits require the application to know about them.

Mental model

Imagine a conference room booking. Created is the booking; running is the meeting; stopped is the meeting ended; removed is the booking deleted. The room has a maximum occupancy (memory limit): one more person and the fire marshal ends the meeting immediately, no discussion. The room also has a time-sharing agreement with other rooms for the projector (CPU quota): you get 50% of the projector time per minute, and when you have used your 30 seconds you wait, even if the projector is idle.

How it works

The commands and what they send:

Command What happens Signal Exit code seen
docker create Allocates the container (filesystem, config) without starting none n/a
docker start Starts PID 1 none n/a
docker stop SIGTERM, wait grace period (default 10 s, -t N), then SIGKILL SIGTERM then SIGKILL 143 if handled, 137 if killed, or the app's own code
docker kill Immediate SIGKILL (or --signal) SIGKILL 137
docker restart stop then start as stop as stop
docker rm Removes a stopped container and its writable layer (-f kills first) n/a n/a
docker pause Freezes all processes via the freezer cgroup none n/a

Logs: the container runtime captures stdout and stderr. Docker's default json-file driver writes them to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log (unbounded unless you set max-size and max-file). docker logs -f --since 10m orders-api reads them. Your application should write structured JSON lines to stdout and nothing to files. In Kubernetes the same stream is read by a log agent (Fluent Bit) and shipped to Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch.

One subtle point: on Linux, Node writes to a pipe stdout synchronously. If the process reading the other end (the Docker logging driver) is blocked, console.log blocks the event loop. Docker's --log-opt mode=non-blocking --log-opt max-buffer-size=4m buffers in the driver and drops on overflow instead of stalling your service.

Resource limits and what Node sees:

  1. --memory=512m sets memory.max in the cgroup. The kernel counts everything the process touches: V8 heap, native buffers, code, stack, page cache for files it reads. When usage exceeds the limit, the OOM killer sends SIGKILL. Exit code 137, OOMKilled: true. No warning, no log line from Node.
  2. --cpus=1.5 sets cpu.max to 150,000 microseconds per 100,000 microsecond period. Node's main thread can use at most 1 CPU anyway, but libuv's thread pool (4 threads by default: DNS, fs, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib) and V8's garbage collector helper threads can use the rest. When the quota is exhausted the whole container is throttled until the next period, which appears as latency spikes of up to 100 ms with no CPU-bound work visible in the profile.
  3. --pids-limit=256 prevents fork bombs and zombie accumulation.

Node's default heap limit is derived from the memory it believes is available. Newer Node versions consult the cgroup limit when computing that default, but the result is still a heuristic (roughly a quarter to a half of "available" memory, with caps) and not tuned to your container. Set it explicitly:

Dockerfile
# Container limit is 512 MB; leave ~25% for native memory, buffers and the code cache
ENV NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=384"

The rule of thumb: --max-old-space-size at 70 to 80% of the container memory limit for a typical API; lower (60%) if the service handles large Buffers (file uploads, image processing) because those live outside the V8 heap. If the heap limit is higher than the container limit, V8 happily grows past the cgroup line and the kernel kills the process before V8 ever runs a full GC to reclaim space. If the heap limit is much lower than needed, V8 throws FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed and exits with code 134, which at least leaves a log line.

To read the real limit at run time:

TypeScript
// src/runtime/cgroup.ts
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

export function containerMemoryLimitBytes(): number | undefined {
  try {
    const raw = readFileSync('/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max', 'utf8').trim(); // cgroup v2
    return raw === 'max' ? undefined : Number(raw);
  } catch {
    return undefined; // not in a container, or cgroup v1
  }
}

Practical example

The orders API runs with --memory=512m --cpus=1. Steady-state heap is 120 MB; RSS is 210 MB. A Prometheus gauge from process.memoryUsage() exports heapUsed, rss and external so the team can see headroom. When a report endpoint pushes RSS to 480 MB the dashboard shows it before the kernel does, and the alert "rss above 85% of limit for 5 minutes" fires first.

NestJS example

A small interceptor-free health signal for memory pressure, wired into Terminus so readiness can go false before the OOM killer acts:

TypeScript
// src/health/memory-pressure.indicator.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicatorResult } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { containerMemoryLimitBytes } from '../runtime/cgroup';

@Injectable()
export class MemoryPressureIndicator {
  private readonly limit = containerMemoryLimitBytes();

  // Returns a Terminus-compatible result; used as () => indicator.check('memory')
  async check(key: string): Promise<HealthIndicatorResult> {
    const rss = process.memoryUsage().rss;
    const ratio = this.limit ? rss / this.limit : 0;
    const healthy = ratio < 0.9;
    return {
      [key]: {
        status: healthy ? 'up' : 'down',
        rssMb: Math.round(rss / 1_048_576),
        limitMb: this.limit ? Math.round(this.limit / 1_048_576) : null,
      },
    };
  }
}

Marking the pod unready at 90% lets the load balancer shift traffic away and gives the process a chance to recover, instead of dying mid-request.

Production scenario

A payments service on Kubernetes has limits.memory: 768Mi and NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=576. Over a quarter, its OOMKilled count is zero; before the flag was set, the same service was killed 3 to 5 times a week during end-of-month batch traffic, each time dropping 20 to 40 in-flight requests. CPU is requested at 500m with no limit, so the garbage collector can burst during peaks without throttling; p99 latency fell from 340 ms to 190 ms when the CPU limit was removed (see Part 45 for the requests-versus-limits discussion).

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged for inventory-sync restarting. docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' prints true 137. The container had --memory=256m and no --max-old-space-size. Node, believing it had the host's 32 GB available, let the heap grow to 300 MB while parsing a 40 MB supplier feed with JSON.parse on the full string. The kernel killed it at 256 MB, before V8 had run a major GC. The fix was three parts: --max-old-space-size=192, streaming the feed with a SAX-style parser, and an alert on RSS ratio. The heap limit alone would have converted the silent kill into an explicit heap out of memory error with a stack trace, which is worth a lot at 2 a.m.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Page cache counts. Reading a 300 MB file counts toward the memory cgroup as page cache; the kernel reclaims it under pressure, but a tight limit plus large file I/O can still trigger OOM.
  • Worker threads and child processes share the cgroup; a worker_threads pool with 4 workers each with a 200 MB heap needs a limit sized for all of them.
  • CPU throttling without CPU-bound code. GC and the libuv pool consume quota; throttling manifests as p99 spikes. Check nr_throttled in cpu.stat.
  • docker stop grace of 10 s is shorter than many drain sequences; pass -t 30 or configure the orchestrator.
  • Logs filling the disk. json-file without rotation on a busy service writes gigabytes; set max-size=50m max-file=5 in the daemon config.
  • Paused containers still hold memory and connections; PostgreSQL sees the sessions as idle.
  • Exit code 0 on failure. A worker that catches all errors and exits 0 never triggers on-failure restarts; exit non-zero on unrecoverable errors.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They set memory limits and the heap flag together, always, in the base image or the deployment template so nobody can forget one. They export process memory metrics and alert on ratio-to-limit, so the team sees pressure minutes before the kernel acts. They keep stdout as the only log destination. And they check OOMKilled and the exit code before reading a single line of application logs, because the kernel's verdict is the ground truth.

Common mistakes

  • Memory limit with no --max-old-space-size.
  • Heap flag larger than the container limit.
  • Logging to files inside the container.
  • docker rm -f in scripts, guaranteeing an unclean stop.
  • Ignoring restart counts because "it comes back up".

Interview questions

  1. Your container has a 512 MB limit and no Node flags. What can go wrong and how do you fix it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: V8 may grow past the limit and get SIGKILLed with no log; set --max-old-space-size to ~75% and monitor RSS.
  2. What is the difference between exit codes 134, 137 and 143?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: V8 heap OOM abort, SIGKILL (cgroup OOM or forced stop), SIGTERM.
  3. Why can a container with a CPU limit show latency spikes when the CPU is not busy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CFS quota throttling within 100 ms periods; GC and thread pool consume quota.
  4. Where should a containerised service write logs and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: stdout/stderr; runtime captures; agents ship; no disk growth; no rotation logic in the app.

Practical exercise

Run the orders API with --memory=256m and a request that builds a 300 MB array. Observe the kill with docker inspect and dmesg (or docker events). Add --max-old-space-size=192 and observe the V8 error instead. Add a /metrics gauge for RSS and a readiness check at 90%. Acceptance criteria: the process fails with a logged heap error rather than a silent 137, the readiness endpoint returns 503 before the crash, and docker logs shows structured JSON with no writes to the container filesystem.

44.11 Container security

Concept

Container security is a set of layered defaults that limit what an attacker gains if your application is compromised: the process runs as an unprivileged user, on a read-only filesystem, with no Linux capabilities it does not need, from an image that contains no secrets and as few packages as possible, scanned for known vulnerabilities, with a record of what is inside (SBOM) and a signature proving who built it.

Why does it exist?

A NestJS API has a large attack surface: HTTP parsing, JSON, dozens of dependencies, database drivers. Remote code execution vulnerabilities in the Node ecosystem appear every year. When one is exploited, the question is what the attacker can do next. Root inside a container with all capabilities on a node with a kernel bug is root on the node and, from there, on the cluster. A non-root process on a read-only filesystem with dropped capabilities can do very little beyond what the application itself could do. Image scanning and minimal bases reduce the number of exploitable holes in the first place.

Mental model

Imagine the difference between a hotel guest and a hotel manager. Both are inside the building. A guest has a key to one room, cannot enter the kitchen, cannot change the locks, cannot access the safe. A manager can do all of that. If a thief steals a guest's key, they get a room. If they steal the manager's, they get the hotel. Run your application as a guest.

How it works

The layers, from the image up:

  1. Minimal base. Fewer packages, fewer CVEs. Alpine, slim or distroless (44.2). No curl, wget, compilers or package managers in the runtime image.
  2. Non-root user. USER node in the Dockerfile. Verify with docker run --rm image id -u printing 1000. In Kubernetes, enforce with runAsNonRoot: true.
  3. Read-only root filesystem. docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp or Kubernetes readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. An attacker cannot drop a binary, modify dist, or persist. Your app needs explicit writable paths (/tmp for uploads in flight, a cache dir if any).
  4. Drop capabilities. --cap-drop=ALL. A Node API binding to port 3000 needs none. If you must bind to port 80 as non-root, use --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE or, better, bind to 3000 and let the load balancer handle 80/443.
  5. No privilege escalation. --security-opt=no-new-privileges so setuid binaries cannot elevate.
  6. Seccomp and AppArmor defaults. Keep Docker's default seccomp profile; never --privileged.
  7. No secrets in layers. Secrets arrive at run time (44.9). Build secrets use RUN --mount=type=secret. Scan images for accidental secrets with trivy image --scanners secret.
  8. Vulnerability scanning. Trivy or Grype in CI on every build, failing on high/critical with a fix available:
Shell
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 \
  registry.internal/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2
  1. Keep bases fresh. A pinned digest is reproducible but ages. Rebuild weekly against the newest upstream digest, scan, and roll out. Dependabot or Renovate can bump the FROM digest automatically.
  2. SBOM. A Software Bill of Materials lists every package in the image so that when the next openssl or undici CVE lands you can answer "which of our 60 images are affected" in seconds instead of rebuilding everything to find out. BuildKit can attach one at build time (docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true), or generate it with syft.
  3. Signing. cosign signs the image digest with a key or, in CI, with a short-lived keyless certificate tied to the GitHub Actions identity. The cluster's admission controller (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) refuses to run unsigned images. This closes the "someone pushed a tag from a laptop" hole.

Run-time flags for a hardened container, all together:

Shell
docker run -d --name orders-api \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  --memory=512m --cpus=1 --pids-limit=256 \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  -e NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=384 \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  registry.internal/orders-api@sha256:9f3c...

Practical example

Your CI pipeline for orders-api: build (multi-stage, non-root, pinned base), trivy image gate, syft SBOM attached to the release, cosign sign keyless, push by digest. Kubernetes admission policy: only images from registry.internal with a valid signature, runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities.drop: [ALL]. A pull request that adds USER root is rejected by hadolint before a human sees it.

NestJS example

Applications must cooperate with a read-only filesystem. The usual offenders are libraries writing caches or temp files. Make writable paths explicit and configurable:

TypeScript
// src/uploads/multer.config.ts
import { diskStorage } from 'multer';
import { mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';

// /tmp is a tmpfs mount; everything else is read-only
const tmpDir = process.env.UPLOAD_TMP_DIR ?? '/tmp/uploads';
mkdirSync(tmpDir, { recursive: true });

export const multerOptions = {
  storage: diskStorage({ destination: tmpDir }),
  limits: { fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 }, // 10 MB, one file per request
};

And a startup self-check that fails fast if the process is unexpectedly root:

TypeScript
// src/main.ts (excerpt, before NestFactory.create)
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' && process.getuid?.() === 0) {
  console.error('Refusing to start as root in production');
  process.exit(1);
}

PostgreSQL example

Least privilege extends to the database. The API's role should own nothing it does not need:

SQL
-- Migrations run as the owner role; the API runs as a restricted role
CREATE ROLE orders_migrator LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
CREATE ROLE orders_api LOGIN PASSWORD '...';

ALTER SCHEMA public OWNER TO orders_migrator;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO orders_api;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO orders_api;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE orders_migrator IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO orders_api;

-- No DDL, no superuser, no COPY to files for the API role
REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM orders_api;
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET statement_timeout = '10s';

A compromised API container can then read and write order rows, but cannot drop tables, read pg_authid, or write to the server's filesystem.

Production scenario

A fintech runs 80 services with the hardened defaults above. In a year, Trivy blocked 140 builds, most fixed by bumping a dependency the same day. During a widely reported undici vulnerability, the SBOM index answered "23 images affected" in under a minute and all were rebuilt within 3 hours. A penetration test that achieved code execution through a deserialisation bug in one service reported "contained: non-root, read-only filesystem, no lateral movement possible", which is the sentence you want in that report.

Failure scenario

An e-commerce company ran its catalogue API as root with a writable filesystem. A vulnerable image-processing library allowed a crafted PNG to execute a shell command. The attacker wrote a crypto miner to /usr/local/bin, used CAP_NET_RAW to scan the pod network, found a Redis with no password, and read session tokens. Detection took 9 days, by which time the cloud bill had doubled. Every step after the initial exploit would have been blocked by non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, and a Redis password. The initial exploit would have been blocked by the Trivy gate; the CVE had been public for 3 weeks.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Read-only breaks libraries that write caches (sharp, some font libraries, npm itself). Find them in staging with --read-only; give them a tmpfs.
  • Non-root cannot bind below 1024. Bind to 3000; do not add capabilities.
  • Scanner noise. Unfixed CVEs in the base OS produce permanent findings; use --ignore-unfixed and a reviewed .trivyignore with expiry dates.
  • Secrets in build logs. echo $NPM_TOKEN in a RUN line prints it into CI logs; use secret mounts and never echo.
  • Signing without verification is theatre; the admission controller must enforce it.
  • Base image republished with the same tag silently reintroduces an old vulnerability; the digest pin plus scheduled rebuild handles it.
  • docker.sock mounted into a container (for CI-in-Docker) grants root on the host; use rootless builders or Kaniko/BuildKit in a dedicated runner.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume the application will be compromised eventually and design the blast radius to be small. They make the secure path the default path: a base image and deployment template that are already hardened, with linting and admission policy to keep it that way, so that a developer would have to work hard to be insecure. They measure "time from CVE publication to all images rebuilt" as a team metric. And they keep humans out of the push path: images come from CI, signed, or they do not run.

Common mistakes

  • USER root to fix a permission error.
  • --privileged or mounting /var/run/docker.sock in application containers.
  • Scanning only once, at project creation.
  • Treating a scanner pass as "secure" while running with all capabilities and a writable filesystem.
  • Sharing one database superuser between migrations and the API.

Interview questions

  1. Name six hardening measures for a container running a Node API and what each prevents.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: non-root (privilege), read-only fs (persistence), cap-drop (kernel-level abuse), no secrets in layers (credential theft), minimal base plus scanning (fewer exploitable CVEs), signing plus admission policy (supply chain).
  2. What is an SBOM and when does it pay off?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inventory of packages per image; answers "which images contain X" instantly when a CVE lands.
  3. Why is "root inside a container" dangerous when namespaces exist?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no user namespace by default, kernel exploits, mounted sockets and volumes; uid 0 is uid 0 on the host.
  4. How do you use a private npm token during docker build without leaking it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: BuildKit --mount=type=secret; never ARG/ENV; verify with docker history.
  5. What does image signing protect against and what does it not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: unauthorised or tampered images reaching the cluster; not vulnerabilities in legitimately built images.

Practical exercise

Harden the orders API image and run it with --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges --user 1000:1000. Fix every failure (writable paths, port binding). Add a Trivy gate and generate an SBOM with syft. Acceptance criteria: the container serves traffic and passes health checks under all flags, trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed returns zero findings, the SBOM lists @nestjs/core with its exact version, and docker history shows no secret values.

44.12 Docker Compose for local development

Concept

Docker Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file: services, their images or build instructions, networks, volumes, environment, health checks and start-up ordering. docker compose up creates everything; docker compose down removes it. For a backend team it replaces the "install PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Kafka, Jaeger, Prometheus and Grafana on your laptop" onboarding document with one command that works the same on every machine.

Why does it exist?

A NestJS API depends on at least a database and usually a cache, a broker and observability tools. Installing them natively means version drift between developers (PostgreSQL 14 on one laptop, 16 on another), port conflicts, forgotten background services, and "works for me" bugs. Compose pins every dependency's version, isolates them on a private network, gives them persistent volumes, and encodes the start-up order so the API does not try to connect before PostgreSQL accepts connections.

Mental model

Imagine a theatre production. Compose is the stage manager's call sheet: which actors (services) are in the show, what costume (image) each wears, where they stand (network), what props they keep between performances (volumes), who must be in position before the curtain rises (depends_on with health conditions), and how to check that they are ready (health checks). One call sheet, same show every night.

How it works

  1. Compose reads docker-compose.yml (and any -f overrides, merged in order), substituting ${VARS} from the shell and the .env file next to it.
  2. It creates a project network (<dir>_default) and named volumes.
  3. It resolves depends_on. With condition: service_healthy, a service starts only after its dependency's healthcheck passes; with condition: service_completed_successfully, only after a one-shot dependency exits 0.
  4. It builds images for services with build: (using BuildKit and the layer cache), pulls the rest.
  5. It creates and starts containers, attaching them to the network with their service names as DNS names.
  6. docker compose logs -f multiplexes stdout from every container with a colour per service. docker compose ps shows state and health.

Key features that matter for a backend stack:

Feature Syntax Why you need it
Health check healthcheck: { test: [...], interval, timeout, retries, start_period } Ordering on real readiness, not on "container started"
Ordered start depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy } } No ECONNREFUSED storms at boot
One-shot job restart: "no" plus depends_on: ... condition: service_completed_successfully on consumers Migrations run once before the API starts
Hot reload bind mount ./src:/app/src plus nest start --watch Edit on host, container reloads
Profiles profiles: ["observability"] Start heavy optional services only when needed
Override files docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up Same base, different environment
Resource hints deploy.resources.limits (honoured by docker compose v2) Reproduce memory limits locally

Practical example

A full local stack for the orders API: PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Kafka (KRaft, no ZooKeeper), Jaeger for traces, Prometheus and Grafana, a migration runner, and the API with hot reload. Observability is behind a profile so the default up is fast.

YAML
# docker-compose.yml
name: orders

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: orders
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: orders
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"                 # for a GUI on the laptop; the API uses the service name
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U orders -d orders"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s

  redis:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "128mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 10

  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093,EXTERNAL://:29092
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092,EXTERNAL://localhost:29092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "true"
    ports:
      - "29092:29092"               # laptop clients use localhost:29092; containers use kafka:9092
    volumes:
      - kafkadata:/var/lib/kafka/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 > /dev/null 2>&1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 20s

  migrate:
    build:
      context: .
      target: build                 # has compiled dist and the TypeORM CLI
    command: ["node", "node_modules/typeorm/cli.js", "migration:run", "-d", "dist/database/data-source.js"]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: deps                  # full toolchain for nest start --watch
    command: ["npx", "nest", "start", "--watch", "--preserveWatchOutput"]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      DB_HOST: postgres
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      KAFKA_BROKERS: kafka:9092
      OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://jaeger:4318
      CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING: "true"
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
      - "9229:9229"                 # node --inspect for the debugger
    volumes:
      - ./src:/app/src
      - ./tsconfig.json:/app/tsconfig.json:ro
      - /app/node_modules
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 512M              # feel the production limit locally

  jaeger:
    image: jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.60
    profiles: ["observability"]
    ports:
      - "16686:16686"               # UI
      - "4318:4318"                 # OTLP HTTP
    environment:
      COLLECTOR_OTLP_ENABLED: "true"

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.54.1
    profiles: ["observability"]
    volumes:
      - ./observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:11.2.0
    profiles: ["observability"]
    environment:
      GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD: admin
    volumes:
      - grafanadata:/var/lib/grafana
      - ./observability/grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro
    ports:
      - "3001:3000"

volumes:
  pgdata:
  kafkadata:
  grafanadata:

Everyday commands:

Shell
docker compose up -d                              # core stack
docker compose --profile observability up -d      # plus Jaeger, Prometheus, Grafana
docker compose logs -f api migrate                # follow two services
docker compose exec postgres psql -U orders       # shell into the database
docker compose run --rm migrate node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:revert -d dist/database/data-source.js
docker compose down                               # keep volumes
docker compose down -v                            # destroy data, fresh start

If you prefer RabbitMQ to Kafka locally, the service is simpler: image: rabbitmq:3.13-management-alpine, ports 5672:5672 and 15672:15672, healthcheck ["CMD", "rabbitmq-diagnostics", "-q", "ping"], and the API's RABBITMQ_URL=amqp://guest:guest@rabbitmq:5672.

NestJS example

The API should start cleanly against this stack and be debuggable. nest start --watch --debug 0.0.0.0:9229 exposes the inspector on all interfaces inside the container so the published port works:

JSON
{
  "scripts": {
    "start:dev": "nest start --watch --preserveWatchOutput",
    "start:debug": "nest start --watch --debug 0.0.0.0:9229 --preserveWatchOutput",
    "build": "nest build",
    "migration:run": "node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:run -d dist/database/data-source.js",
    "migration:generate": "npm run build && node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:generate -d dist/database/data-source.js"
  }
}

A VS Code launch.json attach configuration then points at localhost:9229 with remoteRoot: /app and localRoot: ${workspaceFolder} so breakpoints in src map to the container's files.

PostgreSQL example

The health check pg_isready answers "is the server accepting connections", which is what the migration runner needs. The init script directory sets up extensions and, for local dev only, a second database for integration tests so that Jest does not truncate your manual test data:

SQL
-- db/init/02-test-db.sql (runs once, on an empty volume)
CREATE DATABASE orders_test OWNER orders;
\connect orders_test
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto";

TypeORM example

The migration runner in Compose is the same command CI runs before deploying, and the same command the Kubernetes Job runs in production (Part 45). One command, three places:

Shell
node node_modules/typeorm/cli.js migration:run -d dist/database/data-source.js

Because dist/database/data-source.js reads the environment (44.9), DB_HOST=postgres locally and an RDS hostname in production need no code change.

Sequelize example

With sequelize-cli, the migration service becomes:

YAML
  migrate:
    build: { context: ., target: build }
    command: ["npx", "sequelize-cli", "db:migrate", "--config", "dist/config/sequelize-cli.js", "--migrations-path", "dist/migrations"]
    env_file: .env
    environment: { DB_HOST: postgres }
    restart: "no"
    depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy } }

Production scenario

Compose is a development and single-host tool. Some teams run small internal services with docker compose on one VM plus restart: unless-stopped, and that is fine for a service with no availability requirement. For anything customer-facing with more than one replica, use ECS, Kubernetes or a managed platform (see Part 45 and the cloud deployment discussion in Part 64). The value Compose keeps delivering in production teams is the parity: the same images, migration command and environment variable names on a laptop, in CI, and in the cluster.

Failure scenario

A new hire runs docker compose up and the API crashes in a loop with ECONNREFUSED postgres:5432. The Compose file has depends_on: [postgres] in the old list form, which only orders container start, not readiness. PostgreSQL takes 6 seconds to initialise on first run; the API tries at second 1. The fix is the healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy. A related trap: the API itself should still retry database connections at startup (TypeORM retryAttempts/retryDelay), because in production a database failover can produce the same window.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Old depends_on list form orders start only; use the map form with conditions.
  • Health check commands must exist in the image. curl is absent in Alpine and distroless; use wget -qO-, pg_isready, redis-cli, or node -e.
  • Hot reload across the Desktop VM needs polling (CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING) and can be slow with large trees; bind-mount src only.
  • Port collisions between projects; use name: and different host ports, or no published ports.
  • .env precedence. Shell variables override .env; a stale DB_HOST exported in your shell profile wins silently.
  • Kafka advertised listeners. Clients inside the network must use kafka:9092, clients on the laptop localhost:29092; mixing them produces "connected then metadata failed" errors.
  • Migration service re-runs on every up. Fine (migrations are idempotent by design) but slow; use docker compose up api to skip it when nothing changed.
  • Data left in volumes makes "fresh clone works?" tests lie; run down -v before testing onboarding.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see Compose as documentation that executes: the file is the list of dependencies and their versions. They keep it honest with health checks and one-shot migrations so that up either works or fails loudly. They keep it fast with profiles. And they make sure the images and commands in it are the same ones production uses, because parity is where the bugs are found early.

Common mistakes

  • List-form depends_on and startup crash loops.
  • Publishing every port and colliding across projects.
  • Running migrations inside the API's startup (slow boots, races between replicas; see Part 24 and Part 25 on migrations and zero-downtime releases).
  • Committing .env with real credentials.
  • Bind-mounting node_modules.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make the API wait for PostgreSQL in Compose, and why is that not enough on its own?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: healthcheck plus condition: service_healthy; the app still needs connection retries for production failovers.
  2. How do you run migrations exactly once before the API starts locally?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one-shot service with restart: "no" and condition: service_completed_successfully.
  3. Why should the Compose migration command match the production one?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: parity; the same dist/data-source.js and environment contract; bugs surface locally.
  4. When is Compose appropriate in production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: single host, low availability needs, internal tools; otherwise an orchestrator.

Practical exercise

Build the Compose stack above for your service. Run docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d and time it until curl localhost:3000/health/ready returns 200. Break the migration (a bad SQL statement) and confirm the API does not start. Acceptance criteria: a clean start completes in under 90 seconds on a warm image cache, the API never logs ECONNREFUSED during boot, a failing migration blocks the API with a clear log line, and a colleague can run the stack from a fresh clone with only cp .env.example .env && docker compose up.

44.13 Containerizing a NestJS + PostgreSQL application

This section is the whole part applied to one service, end to end: the orders API (NestJS 10, TypeORM, PostgreSQL 16, Redis for caching and BullMQ). The goal is a production image under 250 MB, non-root, signal-safe, with a health check, plus Compose files for development and for a single-host production-like run, an image tagging strategy, and the exact build and push commands.

44.13.1 The production Dockerfile

Dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
# ---------- deps: full install (dev deps included) for build and test ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:2d07db07a2df6830718ae2a47db6fedce6745f5bcd174c398f2acdda90a11c03 AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
# Cache mount keeps the npm cache across builds so the second install below is fast
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

# ---------- build: compile TypeScript to dist ----------
FROM deps AS build
COPY tsconfig.json tsconfig.build.json nest-cli.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# ---------- prod-deps: runtime dependencies only ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:2d07db07a2df6830718ae2a47db6fedce6745f5bcd174c398f2acdda90a11c03 AS prod-deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev \
 && npm cache clean --force

# ---------- runtime: minimal, non-root, signal-safe ----------
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20@sha256:2d07db07a2df6830718ae2a47db6fedce6745f5bcd174c398f2acdda90a11c03 AS runtime
RUN apk add --no-cache tini tzdata

ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    TZ=UTC \
    PORT=3000 \
    NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=384 --enable-source-maps"

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=node:node --from=prod-deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --chown=node:node --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./

USER node
EXPOSE 3000

# Used by Compose and standalone Docker; ignored by Kubernetes (kubelet probes replace it)
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/live').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"]

ARG GIT_SHA=unknown
ARG VERSION=0.0.0
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.title="orders-api" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="${VERSION}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/acme/orders-api"

ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

Why each choice was made:

  • Digest-pinned base on all three FROM lines: reproducible; the sha256 is the same string, so it is easy to bump with Renovate.
  • tini so that SIGTERM is forwarded and zombies reaped; CMD in exec form so node is the direct child.
  • --max-old-space-size=384 assumes a 512 MB limit in production; if the deployment sets 1 GB, override NODE_OPTIONS there.
  • --enable-source-maps so stack traces point at src/orders/orders.service.ts:42, not dist/orders/orders.service.js:17.
  • USER node after all copies; files are already owned by node via --chown, so no extra layer.
  • Labels last so the volatile GIT_SHA never invalidates the cache.
  • The HEALTHCHECK uses node -e because Alpine's busybox wget works but curl does not exist, and a distroless variant would have neither.

44.13.2 .dockerignore

Text
node_modules
dist
coverage
.git
.github
.vscode
.idea
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
*.md
test
**/*.spec.ts
**/*.e2e-spec.ts
Dockerfile*
docker-compose*.yml
observability
db/init
npm-debug.log*

The build context for the orders API drops from 480 MB (with node_modules) to 1.9 MB.

44.13.3 The application side

Three things in the code make the image behave: shutdown hooks, health endpoints and a config schema. The main.ts from 44.1 (enableShutdownHooks, bind 0.0.0.0), the HealthController from 44.5 (/health/live without the database, /health/ready with it) and the Joi schema from 44.9 are exactly what this image expects. The only addition is the TypeORM connection retry so that a database restart during boot does not crash the container:

TypeScript
// src/app.module.ts (excerpt)
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    ...dataSourceOptions,
    host: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_HOST'),
    // Retry for ~30 s at boot instead of exiting on the first ECONNREFUSED
    retryAttempts: 10,
    retryDelay: 3_000,
    autoLoadEntities: true,
  }),
}),

44.13.4 Development Compose

The development file is the one shown in 44.12: PostgreSQL 16 on a named volume, Redis, the migration runner as a one-shot service, and the API built to the deps target running nest start --watch with src bind-mounted. Nothing in it is repeated here; the point is that the same Dockerfile serves both (target: deps for dev, the default final stage for production).

44.13.5 Production-like Compose

For a staging box or a single-host deployment, an override file changes only what must differ: the final image from the registry instead of a local build, no bind mounts, no published database port, resource limits, restart policies, log rotation and file-mounted secrets.

YAML
# docker-compose.prod.yml  (use with: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d)
services:
  postgres:
    ports: !reset []                     # not reachable from outside the host
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]
    restart: unless-stopped
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { memory: 2G }

  redis:
    ports: !reset []
    restart: unless-stopped

  migrate:
    image: registry.internal/orders-api:${IMAGE_TAG}
    build: !reset null
    command: ["node", "node_modules/typeorm/cli.js", "migration:run", "-d", "dist/database/data-source.js"]
    environment:
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets: [db_password]

  api:
    image: registry.internal/orders-api:${IMAGE_TAG}
    build: !reset null
    command: !reset []                   # fall back to the image CMD: tini + node dist/main.js
    volumes: !reset []                   # no bind mounts; the image is the code
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
      CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING: !reset null
    secrets: [db_password]
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: ["/tmp:size=64m"]
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { memory: 512M, cpus: "1.0" }
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options: { max-size: "50m", max-file: "5" }

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt      # outside Git; on a real host, from a secret store

The !reset tag is Compose's way to remove a key inherited from the base file. The DB_PASSWORD_FILE variable requires a tiny addition to the config loader: if DB_PASSWORD is unset and DB_PASSWORD_FILE is set, read the file. Do that once in database.config.ts and both Compose and Kubernetes secret volumes work.

44.13.6 Build, tag and push

Shell
# Local build of the production image
docker build \
  --build-arg GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  --build-arg VERSION=$(node -p "require('./package.json').version") \
  -t orders-api:local .

# Verify the essentials before pushing anything
docker run --rm orders-api:local id -u                              # 1000
docker run --rm orders-api:local node -e "console.log(process.version)"
docker inspect orders-api:local --format '{{.Config.Entrypoint}} {{.Config.Cmd}}'
docker history --format "table {{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}" orders-api:local | head -20

# Tag and push (CI does this; see 26.15 for the buildx version with cache)
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
VERSION=1.4.2
REG=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ${REG%%/*}
docker tag orders-api:local $REG:sha-$SHA
docker tag orders-api:local $REG:$VERSION
docker tag orders-api:local $REG:1.4
docker push $REG:sha-$SHA && docker push $REG:$VERSION && docker push $REG:1.4
docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' $REG:sha-$SHA   # the digest to deploy

44.13.7 Tagging strategy

Tag Example Who moves it Used by
Git SHA sha-3f9a1c2 Never (immutable) Deployments; every rollout references one
Semver 1.4.2 Never after release Changelogs, support, customers of an internal library
Floating minor 1.4 Each patch release Humans browsing the registry; never deployments
Digest @sha256:9f3c... Never Signed, verified production references
latest Every push Nothing; do not push it from CI at all

CI produces sha-* on every main-branch build and adds x.y.z and x.y on a tagged release. The Kubernetes manifest (or Helm value) is updated with the sha-* tag or the digest by the pipeline. A rollback is a change of that one string back to the previous SHA.

44.13.8 Size before and after

Measured on the orders API (52 runtime dependencies including typeorm, pg, ioredis, bullmq, kafkajs, @nestjs/swagger, @opentelemetry/sdk-node):

Stage of improvement Image size Build (warm cache, source change) Pull on a fresh node Trivy high/critical
Original: node:20, single stage, COPY . ., npm install 1.38 GB 6 min 40 s 48 s 61
Layer order fixed, .dockerignore, npm ci 1.31 GB 58 s 46 s 61
Multi-stage on node:20-slim 296 MB 62 s 9 s 7
Multi-stage on node:20-alpine with tini and tzdata 221 MB 61 s 6 s 2
Same, base digest bumped after the scan 221 MB 61 s 6 s 0

The 6-second pull is what makes autoscaling useful: a new replica is serving traffic 12 seconds after the scheduler places it, instead of a minute.

44.13.9 Verifying the contract

Before the image is allowed into production, run the checks a senior engineer runs by hand the first time and CI runs forever after:

Shell
# 1. Starts, becomes healthy, serves
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
until [ "$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' orders-api-1)" = "healthy" ]; do sleep 1; done
curl -fsS localhost:3000/health/ready

# 2. Stops cleanly under load
autocannon -c 20 -d 15 localhost:3000/orders &  sleep 5
time docker compose stop -t 30 api                 # should be ~3 s, exit code 0
docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' orders-api-1

# 3. Runs as non-root on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities
docker compose exec api sh -c 'id -u; touch /app/x 2>&1; touch /tmp/x && echo tmp-ok'

# 4. No secrets in the image
docker history --no-trunc registry.internal/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2 | grep -i -E 'password|token|secret' || echo clean
trivy image --scanners secret registry.internal/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2

Expected results: healthy within 20 seconds, stop in about 3 seconds with exit code 0 and zero failed requests during the drain, uid 1000, touch /app/x denied, /tmp writable, no secrets found.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the Dockerfile, .dockerignore, Compose files and the main.ts bootstrap as one unit with one contract: bind 0.0.0.0, read config from the environment, log to stdout, expose /health/live and /health/ready, exit cleanly on SIGTERM, run as uid 1000 on a read-only filesystem, fit in 512 MB. Every service in the company follows the same contract, which is what allows a platform team to operate 60 services with a single deployment template. When a new service is created, the contract is copied, not reinvented.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through a production Dockerfile for a NestJS API and justify each stage and flag.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the four stages, digest pins, tini, USER node, NODE_OPTIONS, labels last, exec-form CMD.
  2. How do you run database migrations in a containerised deployment locally and in production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one-shot container using the same image and command; Compose service_completed_successfully; Kubernetes Job; never at API startup.
  3. What is your image tagging strategy and how does rollback work?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: immutable sha-*, semver on releases, deploy by SHA or digest, rollback by changing one reference.
  4. What would you check before trusting an image in production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: non-root, clean stop under load, read-only filesystem works, no secrets in layers, scanner pass, size and pull time.

Practical exercise

Containerise one of your own NestJS services using the Dockerfile, .dockerignore, development Compose and production override from this section. Fill in the size-before-and-after table with your own numbers. Acceptance criteria: the production image is under 260 MB on Alpine, runs as uid 1000 with read_only: true, stops within 5 seconds under load with zero failed requests, the migration runner gates the API start, and docker history contains no secrets.

44.14 Debugging containers

Concept

Debugging a container means answering four questions in order: is the process running and why did it stop (docker inspect, exit code), what did it say (docker logs), what is it doing now (docker exec, docker stats, node --inspect), and what is the environment it sees (docker inspect config, docker exec env). The same four questions apply on Kubernetes with kubectl (Part 45); the mechanics below are the foundation.

Why does it exist?

A process inside a container is one step removed from you: you cannot attach a debugger to it by default, its filesystem is not your filesystem, its logs are not in a file you can open, and its death is often decided by the kernel rather than by your code. Without a repeatable method, engineers guess, restart, and hope. With one, most container problems are diagnosed in minutes.

Mental model

Imagine a black-box flight recorder. After an incident you do not start by interviewing the pilot's colleagues; you read the recorder: what was the last state, what were the instruments showing, what was said in the cockpit. docker inspect is the state, docker stats is the instruments, docker logs is the cockpit voice recorder, docker exec is climbing into the cockpit while it is still flying.

How it works

The commands, what they show, and what to look for:

Shell
# 1. State and cause of death
docker inspect orders-api --format '{{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}} started={{.State.StartedAt}} finished={{.State.FinishedAt}}'
# running exit=0 oom=false ...     -> alive
# exited exit=137 oom=true ...     -> killed by the memory cgroup
# exited exit=137 oom=false ...    -> SIGKILL after stop grace period (or docker kill)
# exited exit=1 ...                -> the app threw; read the logs
# restarting ...                   -> restart policy loop; check RestartCount

docker inspect orders-api --format '{{.RestartCount}} {{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}'

# 2. Logs, with time filters so you are not scrolling through a day of JSON
docker logs --since 15m --timestamps orders-api 2>&1 | tail -200
docker logs -f orders-api                  # follow
docker logs orders-api 2>&1 | grep -E '"level":"(error|fatal)"' | tail -50

# 3. Live resource usage: CPU %, memory used / limit, network, block I/O, PIDs
docker stats --no-stream orders-api
# If MEM USAGE is within 10% of LIMIT, an OOM kill is coming

# 4. Inside the container
docker exec -it orders-api sh                      # Alpine; bash on Debian; nothing on distroless
docker exec orders-api env | sort                  # what config does the process actually see
docker exec orders-api cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max
docker exec orders-api cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat | grep throttled   # CPU throttling counters
docker exec orders-api ls -la /app/dist
docker exec orders-api node -e "console.log(process.memoryUsage())"

# 5. Networking from inside
docker exec orders-api getent hosts postgres
docker exec orders-api nc -zv postgres 5432
docker exec orders-api cat /etc/resolv.conf

# 6. Host-side evidence of OOM kills (Linux hosts)
dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'killed process|out of memory' | tail -5
docker events --since 30m --filter event=oom --filter event=die

Distroless images have no shell. The options are docker debug (Docker Desktop feature), running a second container that shares the namespaces (docker run --rm -it --pid=container:orders-api --network=container:orders-api nicolaka/netshoot), or, in Kubernetes, kubectl debug with an ephemeral container. Plan for this before choosing distroless.

Attaching the Node inspector to a running container:

  1. Start the container with the inspector listening on all interfaces and the port published: docker run -p 9229:9229 ... node --inspect=0.0.0.0:9229 dist/main.js. In Compose this is the start:debug script from 44.12.
  2. For an already running process, send SIGUSR1: docker kill --signal=SIGUSR1 orders-api. Node opens the inspector on 127.0.0.1:9229, which is reachable only from inside the container; forward it with docker exec orders-api socat TCP-LISTEN:9230,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:9229 if socat is available, or plan ahead with a published port in development only.
  3. Attach from VS Code or chrome://inspect. Take a heap snapshot or a CPU profile. Do this in staging with production-like data before you need it in production; never leave the inspector port published in production.

Reading an OOM kill: the tell-tale triad is exit code 137, OOMKilled: true, and no shutdown log lines from the app (it never had a chance). If OOMKilled is false but the code is 137, the runtime killed it after the grace period, which means SIGTERM was ignored or shutdown took too long. If the last log line is FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit, V8 hit --max-old-space-size and aborted with 134, which is a different, more informative failure.

Practical example

docker stats on the orders API shows MEM USAGE / LIMIT 470MiB / 512MiB and climbing 2 MB per minute. docker exec orders-api node -e "console.log(process.memoryUsage())" shows heapUsed at 150 MB but external at 280 MB: a Buffer leak, not a heap leak. A heap snapshot would not show it; the culprit is a Kafka consumer accumulating unacknowledged message payloads. The metric that would have caught it earlier is process.memoryUsage().external exported to Prometheus.

NestJS example

Make the process debuggable from the outside without a shell: a diagnostics endpoint on a separate, unpublished port that reports memory, event loop lag, pool usage and config (redacted). Bind it to the pod network only, never behind the public ingress.

TypeScript
// src/diagnostics/diagnostics.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { monitorEventLoopDelay } from 'node:perf_hooks';

const loopDelay = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 });
loopDelay.enable();

@Controller('internal/diagnostics')
export class DiagnosticsController {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  @Get()
  snapshot() {
    const mem = process.memoryUsage();
    const pool = (this.dataSource.driver as any).master; // pg Pool instance
    return {
      pid: process.pid,
      uptimeSec: Math.round(process.uptime()),
      memoryMb: {
        rss: Math.round(mem.rss / 1_048_576),
        heapUsed: Math.round(mem.heapUsed / 1_048_576),
        external: Math.round(mem.external / 1_048_576),
      },
      eventLoopLagMs: { p50: loopDelay.percentile(50) / 1e6, p99: loopDelay.percentile(99) / 1e6 },
      pgPool: { total: pool?.totalCount, idle: pool?.idleCount, waiting: pool?.waitingCount },
      config: { nodeEnv: process.env.NODE_ENV, dbHost: process.env.DB_HOST, poolMax: process.env.DB_POOL_MAX },
    };
  }
}

curl this from docker exec (or kubectl port-forward) to see what the process believes about itself.

Production scenario

An SRE team documents a five-minute triage for any restarting container: inspect for exit code and OOM, logs for the last 200 lines, stats for headroom, exec for config, then decide between "fix config and redeploy", "raise limit and investigate leak", or "rollback". Median time from page to diagnosis fell from 25 minutes to 6 after the runbook was written and rehearsed.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 checkout-api is restarting. The engineer reads application logs for 20 minutes and finds nothing unusual: the last line is a normal request log. Only then do they run docker inspect and see OOMKilled: true. The application logs were never going to explain it. The runbook order (inspect first) exists so that this 20 minutes is never lost again.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Logs lost on docker rm. Removing a container deletes its json-file logs; ship logs off the host before cleanup scripts run.
  • docker logs on a container with millions of lines is slow; always use --since or --tail.
  • docker exec as root when the container runs as node can create root-owned files that break the app later; use docker exec -u node.
  • Inspector left enabled is remote code execution for anyone who can reach the port.
  • docker stats memory includes page cache and can look higher than RSS; compare with process.memoryUsage().
  • Clock differences between docker logs --timestamps (host clock) and application timestamps (container's view of the same clock, but possibly a different TZ) confuse timelines; log in UTC.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They debug in a fixed order: state, logs, stats, exec. They build observability into the service so that most questions are answered by a metric or a diagnostics endpoint rather than a shell. They rehearse the inspector attach in staging so that under pressure it is muscle memory. And they never trust "the logs show nothing" until they have read the exit code.

Common mistakes

  • Reading application logs before checking the exit code and OOMKilled.
  • Choosing distroless without a plan for shell-less debugging.
  • Leaving --inspect on in production images.
  • docker logs without --since on a busy service.

Interview questions

  1. A container restarts every minute. Walk me through your first five commands.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inspect (exit code, OOM, restart count), logs --since, stats, exec env, then hypothesis.
  2. How do you attach a debugger to a Node process in a container?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: --inspect=0.0.0.0:9229 with a published port in dev; SIGUSR1 for a running process; never in production.
  3. Exit code 137, OOMKilled: false. What happened?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: killed after the stop grace period; SIGTERM ignored or slow shutdown.
  4. How would you debug a container built from a distroless image?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sidecar sharing namespaces, kubectl debug ephemeral container, diagnostics endpoint, metrics.

Practical exercise

Deliberately break the orders API three ways: a memory leak (accumulate Buffers per request), a missing environment variable, and a SIGTERM handler that never resolves. For each, use only docker inspect, docker logs, docker stats and docker exec to diagnose, and write down the exact evidence that identified the cause. Acceptance criteria: each diagnosis under 5 minutes, the evidence for each names the distinguishing signal (OOM flag, config error line, exit 137 with OOM false), and a heap snapshot taken through the inspector shows the leaked Buffers.

44.15 Building in CI

Concept

CI builds the image, tests it, scans it, signs it and pushes it. Two things distinguish a good CI build from a laptop build: it starts from an empty cache on every run unless you bring the cache with you, and it must produce the same image for every platform your nodes run on (x86 and ARM). BuildKit's registry cache and buildx multi-platform builds solve both.

Why does it exist?

Ephemeral CI runners have no layer cache. Without a remote cache, every build reinstalls dependencies (2 to 6 minutes) even when only a controller changed. Without multi-arch, moving to Graviton nodes (30 to 40% cheaper for the same throughput) means a second pipeline. Without reproducibility, the image built for a hotfix differs from the one tested. And without signing in CI, "built by CI" is a claim nobody can verify.

Mental model

Imagine a bakery that opens a new kitchen every morning with empty shelves. Bringing yesterday's prepared dough (the cache) from cold storage means the first loaf is ready in minutes. Baking the same recipe in two oven types (amd64 and arm64) at the same time means every customer gets bread that fits their toaster.

How it works

  1. Remote cache. --cache-from type=registry,ref=REPO:buildcache imports layer metadata and pulls only the layers that hit. --cache-to type=registry,ref=REPO:buildcache,mode=max exports all intermediate stages (not just the final one), so the deps and prod-deps layers are reusable. On GitHub Actions, type=gha uses the Actions cache instead (10 GB limit per repo; fine for a few services).
  2. Multi-arch. docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 builds both, either with QEMU emulation (slow: 3 to 8 times) or with native runners per architecture and a manifest merge. Native ARM runners are worth it once you have more than a handful of services.
  3. Reproducibility. Same base digest, same lockfile, npm ci, no network access during the build except to the npm registry (--network=none for later stages if possible), SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH set to the commit time so layer timestamps are stable. The result: two builds of the same commit produce identical layer digests, which makes "did anything change" a comparison rather than an investigation.
  4. Tests against the image. Run unit tests in the build target (same dependencies as the artefact) and integration tests against the runtime image with Compose services.
  5. Gate, then push, then sign. Scan before push so a vulnerable image never lands in the registry. Sign the digest, not the tag.

A GitHub Actions workflow that does all of it:

YAML
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: build-and-push
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write        # OIDC for AWS and for keyless cosign
  packages: write

env:
  REGISTRY: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
  IMAGE: orders-api

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-ecr-push
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - name: Compute tags
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}
          tags: |
            type=sha,prefix=sha-,format=short
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}}

      - name: Unit tests in the build stage
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          target: build
          load: true
          tags: ${{ env.IMAGE }}:test
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}:buildcache
      - run: docker run --rm ${{ env.IMAGE }}:test npm test -- --ci

      - name: Build runtime image (multi-arch) without pushing
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: false
          load: false
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          build-args: |
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}
            VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}:buildcache
