          cache-to: type=registry,ref=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}:buildcache,mode=max
          outputs: type=oci,dest=/tmp/image.tar

      - name: Scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          input: /tmp/image.tar
          severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"

      - name: Push
        id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          build-args: |
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}
            VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}:buildcache
          sbom: true
          provenance: mode=max

      - name: Sign the digest (keyless, tied to this workflow identity)
        run: cosign sign --yes ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}

The second build step is a cache hit for everything the first one already produced, so "build, scan, push" costs one build in practice. steps.push.outputs.digest is the value the deploy step writes into the Kubernetes manifest or Helm values.

Practical example

A team moves the orders API from x86 m6i nodes to Graviton m7g nodes. Because CI already produced a multi-arch manifest, the change is a node pool swap; the kubelet on an ARM node pulls the arm64 manifest automatically. Throughput per dollar improves 35%. The one surprise: a native module (sharp) had a prebuilt for linux-arm64-musl but an older transitive dependency did not; the build stage compiled it under QEMU, taking 9 minutes until they added a native ARM runner.

Production scenario

Across 60 services, registry-backed caching brought the median CI build from 5 min 10 s to 1 min 25 s. Multi-arch builds with QEMU added 2 minutes each until native ARM runners were introduced. Signing and SBOMs added 15 seconds. The registry's buildcache tags are cleaned by a lifecycle rule after 14 days.

Failure scenario

A hotfix is built on an engineer's laptop with docker build and pushed as sha-abc1234 because CI was "too slow". The laptop is an M2 Mac; the image is arm64 only. Production nodes are amd64. Every pod goes to CrashLoopBackOff with exec /sbin/tini: exec format error. The rollback takes 4 minutes; the post-mortem takes an hour and ends with an admission policy that rejects unsigned images, which removes the laptop path entirely.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cache poisoning across branches. A shared buildcache tag means a feature branch can export layers that main imports; acceptable for dependency layers, but keep secrets out of build args.
  • mode=max cache size grows with every stage; set a registry lifecycle rule.
  • QEMU and native modules. Emulated compiles are slow and occasionally miscompile; use native runners for ARM.
  • load: true with multi-platform is not supported; test on the runner's platform and build the multi-arch image separately.
  • Docker Hub rate limits on base image pulls from CI IP ranges; mirror bases into your registry.
  • Provenance attestations change the manifest type to an index even for single-arch images; older tooling that expects a plain manifest may choke.
  • Clock and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. Without it, RUN layers get build-time timestamps and digests differ per build.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make CI the only path to the registry and the registry the only path to the cluster. They spend an afternoon on caching because it pays back every day. They build multi-arch from day one so that a cheaper node type is a configuration change. And they sign what they build, because a supply-chain incident is the kind that ends careers.

Common mistakes

  • No remote cache, so every CI build is a cold build.
  • Building on laptops and pushing.
  • Single-arch images discovered when switching node types.
  • Scanning after pushing.
  • Tag-based deploys instead of digest-based.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make CI builds fast when runners are ephemeral?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: BuildKit registry or GHA cache with mode=max, correct layer order, cache mounts for npm.
  2. Explain multi-arch images and how you would build them.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: manifest index per platform, buildx --platform, QEMU versus native runners, exec format error symptom.
  3. What makes a container build reproducible?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: digest-pinned base, lockfile plus npm ci, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, no network variance, same build args.
  4. Where do scanning and signing sit in the pipeline and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scan before push, sign the digest after push, verify at admission.

Practical exercise

Add the workflow above to a NestJS repository (adapt the registry). Measure a cold build, then a build after a source-only change. Switch a Kubernetes node pool or a local docker run --platform linux/arm64 to prove the ARM image works. Acceptance criteria: the warm build finishes in under 2 minutes, both architectures run and pass /health/ready, Trivy blocks a deliberately added vulnerable dependency, and cosign verify succeeds for the pushed digest.

44.16 Edge cases and failure modes

Every item below is a real incident pattern. For each: what happens, why, how you notice it, and the fix.

  • SIGTERM ignored, SIGKILL after 10 seconds, in-flight requests lost. npm start, shell-form CMD, or no shutdown hooks. Notice: exit code 137 with OOMKilled: false, a burst of 502/ECONNRESET on every deploy. Fix: tini, exec-form CMD, enableShutdownHooks(), a grace period longer than the drain (44.4).
  • OOM because Node does not respect the container memory limit. Heap grows past the cgroup line; kernel kills it silently. Notice: exit 137, OOMKilled: true, no shutdown logs. Fix: --max-old-space-size at ~75% of the limit, RSS metrics and alerts, streaming instead of loading whole payloads (44.10).
  • npm install instead of npm ci, dependencies drift. Different transitive versions in different builds; a bug that reproduces only in one environment. Notice: lockfile modified in CI, package-lock.json diff in the image. Fix: npm ci, committed lockfile, CI fails if the lockfile changes (44.3).
  • Secrets baked into a layer. .env copied, ARG NPM_TOKEN, a private key COPYed then deleted. Notice: docker history, trivy --scanners secret, or a breach. Fix: .dockerignore, BuildKit secret mounts, run-time injection, rotate everything that was exposed (44.9, 44.11).
  • Running as root. A compromise becomes a host compromise. Notice: docker exec id -u prints 0; admission policy flags it. Fix: USER node, runAsNonRoot, fix permissions with --chown rather than privilege (44.11).
  • latest tag rollouts. Two nodes pull latest an hour apart and run different code; rollback is impossible because the previous image has no name. Notice: replicas behaving differently, RepoDigests differ between pods. Fix: immutable sha-* tags or digests; never push latest from CI (44.2, 44.13).
  • Time zone or locale missing on Alpine. TZ ignored because tzdata is absent; dates rendered in UTC for a report that promised local time. Notice: date in the container prints UTC despite TZ. Fix: apk add --no-cache tzdata, or better, keep servers in UTC and convert at the edge (44.5).
  • Native module build failures on Alpine. bcrypt, sharp, argon2 fail with gyp ERR! or crash with Error loading shared library. Notice: build logs, or a runtime ELF error. Fix: -slim base, prebuilt-compatible module versions, build tools in the build stage only, runtime shared libs (libstdc++) in the runtime stage (44.2, 44.6).
  • DNS resolution differences. Intermittent ENOTFOUND on Alpine under Kubernetes ndots:5 with many search domains; localhost resolving to ::1. Notice: resolver errors that never reproduce on Debian; EAI_AGAIN under load. Fix: glibc base, FQDNs with a trailing dot for external hosts, dnsConfig with lower ndots, bind to :: or connect to 127.0.0.1 explicitly (44.7).
  • Huge images slowing deploys and autoscaling. A 1.3 GB image takes 45 seconds to pull; the HPA adds replicas that are not ready for a minute; the spike is over before they help. Notice: ContainerCreating durations, image pull events. Fix: multi-stage, prod deps only, .dockerignore, base image mirrored close to the nodes (44.6, 44.13).
  • Log output blocking when stdout is not drained. Node writes to a pipe synchronously on Linux; a blocked logging driver blocks the event loop. Notice: latency spikes correlated with log volume, docker stats showing low CPU while requests hang. Fix: --log-opt mode=non-blocking, a log agent with buffering, sane log volume (44.10).
  • File permission errors on bind mounts. Container uid 1000 versus host uid 501 or 1001; EACCES on ./uploads or PostgreSQL refusing its data directory. Notice: EACCES/EPERM in logs on Linux hosts only. Fix: named volumes for data the container owns, matching uids for shared directories, never USER root (44.8).
  • Container clock skew. The container has no clock of its own; a host with broken NTP (or a Docker Desktop VM that slept) is minutes off. JWTs are rejected as "not yet valid", TLS handshakes fail, distributed locks expire early. Notice: date inside the container versus a trusted source; auth errors that appear on one node only. Fix: NTP/chrony on hosts, restart the Desktop VM, never trust wall-clock differences across machines for ordering (see Part 11 and Part 31).
  • HEALTHCHECK assumed to drive Kubernetes. The pod has no probes; a wedged process keeps receiving traffic. Notice: kubectl describe pod shows no probes. Fix: define liveness/readiness probes in the pod spec (Part 45).
  • Restart loop hiding a config error. restart: always masks a service that exits in 200 ms because DATABASE_URL is missing. Notice: RestartCount in the hundreds; CPU spent on booting. Fix: config validation with a clear error, alert on restart count, CrashLoopBackOff visibility in Kubernetes.
  • Pool multiplied by replicas exhausts PostgreSQL. 30 containers with max: 20 want 600 connections; max_connections is 200. Notice: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already during a scale-out. Fix: size pools per replica count, PgBouncer, or a lower max (see Part 19 — PostgreSQL Internals).
  • Zombie processes from spawned children. Puppeteer or ImageMagick children never reaped because node is PID 1 without tini. Notice: ps inside the container shows <defunct> entries; pids.max reached. Fix: tini (with -g for process groups) (44.4).
  • Build context includes .git. Slow builds, and the whole repository history in a layer if COPY . . runs. Notice: "Sending build context" measured in hundreds of MB. Fix: .dockerignore (44.3).

Senior Checklist — Part 44

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain namespaces, cgroups and OverlayFS in plain language and say what each one does for a NestJS process
  • I can order a Dockerfile so that a source-only change rebuilds in under 90 seconds
  • I can write a four-stage multi-stage build that produces a non-root image under 260 MB
  • I can prove a container stops cleanly under load with exit code 0 and no failed requests
  • I can size --max-old-space-size against a container memory limit and explain exit codes 134, 137 and 143
  • I can connect a container to PostgreSQL by service name and explain why localhost fails
  • I can write a Compose stack with health checks, a one-shot migration runner and hot reload
  • I can validate configuration at startup with Joi or zod and keep secrets out of images
  • I can run a container read-only, non-root, with all capabilities dropped, and fix what breaks
  • I can diagnose a restarting container with inspect, logs, stats and exec in under five minutes
  • I can set up a CI build with a registry cache, multi-arch output, a scan gate and a signature

Part 44 — Key Takeaways

  • A container is a normal process the kernel isolates with namespaces, limits with cgroups and roots in a layered filesystem; it shares the host kernel and has no clock, disk or memory of its own.
  • The image is a content-addressed snapshot; deploy by digest or immutable sha- tag, never by latest, and pin the base image by digest.
  • Layer order decides build time: manifests, then npm ci, then source; .dockerignore is part of the build, not an afterthought.
  • PID 1 does not get default signal handling: use tini plus exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"] and enableShutdownHooks(), and never npm start.
  • Multi-stage builds ship only dist and production node_modules; a NestJS API lands at about 200 MB on Alpine or slim, and that size is mostly Node itself.
  • Inside a container, localhost is the container; talk to dependencies by service name and bind your server to 0.0.0.0.
  • Application containers are stateless: data lives in named volumes locally and in managed services in production; bind mounts are for source code in development only.
  • Configuration comes from the environment and is validated at boot; secrets are injected at run time, preferably as files, and never appear in a layer.
  • Set the memory limit and --max-old-space-size together; exit 137 with OOMKilled: true means the kernel killed you and the logs will not explain it.
  • Non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, minimal base, scanning, SBOM and signing turn a compromise into a contained event instead of a cluster-wide one.
  • Compose is executable documentation: health checks, service_healthy, a one-shot migration runner and the same image and commands you use in production.
  • Debug in order: inspect for the exit code, logs with --since, stats for headroom, exec for the environment; the kernel's verdict comes before the application's story.
  • CI is the only path to the registry: remote layer cache, multi-arch, scan before push, sign the digest, and verify at admission.

What you will learn

Kubernetes is where your container goes to become a service. Part 44 gave you an image that starts in two seconds, stops cleanly and fits in 512 MB. Kubernetes decides which machine runs it, how many copies, what happens when one dies, how traffic finds it, how it gets its configuration, and how a new version replaces the old without anyone noticing. It does this with a small set of objects described in YAML and a control loop that never stops comparing what you asked for with what exists.

Most backend engineers meet Kubernetes through a wall of YAML and a pod in CrashLoopBackOff. This part takes the other route: the problem each object solves, the mechanism underneath, the exact manifest for a NestJS API, the numbers that matter (probe timings, resource sizes, grace periods), and the failure modes that page you. By the end you should be able to deploy an API and its BullMQ workers to a cluster, watch a rollout, roll it back, and debug the six pod states that account for nearly every incident.

45.1 Why Kubernetes exists and what it costs

Concept

Kubernetes is a cluster operating system for containers. You describe the desired state ("three replicas of orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2, each with 512 MB, reachable on port 80 as orders-api, scaled between 3 and 20 on CPU"), and the cluster continuously works to make reality match. It schedules containers onto machines, restarts them when they die, replaces machines that fail, rolls out new versions gradually, gives every service a stable name, injects configuration and secrets, and scales replicas up and down.

Why does it exist?

Run one containerised NestJS service on one VM with docker compose and you are fine. Run forty services on thirty VMs and the questions pile up: which VM has room for this container? What restarts it when it crashes at 3 a.m.? How does orders-api find inventory-api when the latter moves to a different VM? How do you deploy a new version without downtime? How do you add ten replicas for the Black Friday spike and remove them after? How do you rotate a database password across all replicas? Every one of those has a hand-written answer (scripts, Ansible, cron jobs, a spreadsheet of IPs), and every hand-written answer is a future incident. Kubernetes is one consistent set of answers, tested by thousands of companies.

Mental model

Imagine a large hotel with a very disciplined operations manager. You hand her a card: "I need three identical rooms set up for the Orders team, each with a desk, a 512 MB safe, and a phone that answers to 'orders'. If a room becomes unusable, set up another one somewhere else. If more Orders guests arrive, open more rooms, up to twenty." She never sleeps, never forgets, and every minute she walks the building comparing the cards to the rooms and fixing any difference. You do not tell her how to do it; you tell her what you want. That is the desired-state model. The cost is that she is very literal: if your card is wrong, she will diligently create the wrong thing, three times, forever.

How it works

What Kubernetes gives you, in the order you will feel it:

  1. Scheduling. The scheduler places each pod on a node with enough free CPU and memory (based on your requests), respecting constraints you set (spread across availability zones, avoid certain nodes).
  2. Self-healing. If a container exits, the kubelet restarts it. If a node dies, the controller recreates its pods elsewhere. If a pod fails its liveness probe, it is restarted. If it fails readiness, it stops receiving traffic.
  3. Scaling. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the replica count from metrics; the Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled.
  4. Rolling updates. A Deployment replaces pods gradually, only proceeding while new pods report ready, and can be rolled back with one command.
  5. Service discovery. A Service gives a stable name and virtual IP to a changing set of pods; DNS resolves orders-api.shop.svc.cluster.local to it.
  6. Configuration and secrets. ConfigMaps and Secrets are injected as environment variables or files, versioned with the rest of your manifests.
  7. Declarative everything. Every object is YAML in Git; the cluster state is reproducible, reviewable and auditable.

What it costs:

  • Concepts. Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes, requests and limits, HPA, PDB, RBAC, NetworkPolicy. Around fifteen objects to know well before you can operate a service safely.
  • Operations. Cluster upgrades every 4 to 6 months (versions are supported for about 14 months), node image patching, add-on management (ingress controller, cert-manager, metrics server, log agent, CNI), capacity planning, cost allocation.
  • A platform team. Below roughly 10 services or 5 engineers, the people cost of running Kubernetes well usually exceeds the benefit. Managed control planes (EKS, GKE, AKS) remove the hardest 40%; they do not remove the rest.
  • Failure modes you did not have before. Evictions, CrashLoopBackOff from a typo, DNS ndots surprises, PDBs blocking upgrades, HPA flapping, cross-zone data-transfer bills.

The decision table a senior engineer uses before recommending Kubernetes (the cloud-side detail is in Part 64, which covers AWS deployment options):

Option You manage Good fit Poor fit Rough cost of operation
Single VM with Compose Everything on one host Internal tools, prototypes, one service with no HA requirement Anything customer-facing that must survive a host failure Very low, until it fails
AWS App Runner / Google Cloud Run Nothing but the container Stateless HTTP APIs, bursty traffic, small teams Long-lived WebSockets, background workers, custom networking, GPU Low; pay per request/CPU-second
AWS ECS on Fargate Task definitions, services, ALB 5 to 50 services on AWS, teams without a platform team, workers and APIs Multi-cloud, complex scheduling needs, operator-based databases Low to medium
Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) Cluster add-ons, upgrades, manifests, policies 20+ services, a platform team, workers plus APIs plus cron plus stateful add-ons, portable tooling (Helm, ArgoCD, KEDA) Small teams; a single monolith; teams unwilling to own upgrades Medium to high; 1 to 3 engineers
Self-managed Kubernetes Everything including the control plane and etcd Regulated on-premises, edge Almost everyone else High

Practical example

A food-delivery company has 35 services: 20 NestJS APIs, 10 BullMQ and Kafka workers, 5 cron-style jobs, plus an ingress layer with TLS, per-service autoscaling, and a requirement to deploy 40 times a day with zero downtime. They started on ECS, which handled the APIs well; what pushed them to EKS was the operational toolkit: KEDA for queue-based worker scaling, ArgoCD for GitOps, a shared ingress with cert-manager, Prometheus Operator, and the ability to hire engineers who already knew it. Two platform engineers run the cluster for 60 developers.

Production scenario

The same cluster during a promotional campaign: orders-api scales from 4 to 22 pods over 3 minutes as CPU crosses 65%; the Cluster Autoscaler adds 5 nodes in about 90 seconds; notifications-worker scales from 2 to 15 on queue depth via KEDA; a node fails mid-campaign and its 11 pods are rescheduled within 40 seconds with no customer-visible errors because the PodDisruptionBudget and anti-affinity had spread replicas. Nobody did anything by hand. That is the payoff; the cost was three months of platform work to get there.

Failure scenario

A four-person startup with one NestJS monolith adopts Kubernetes "for scale". Six months later: two cluster upgrades consumed a week each; an expired ingress certificate caused an outage because nobody owned cert-manager; the cluster's fixed cost (control plane plus three nodes) is triple what App Runner would charge for their traffic; and the one engineer who understood the manifests left. The honest architecture would have been App Runner or ECS Fargate with RDS. Kubernetes did not fail; it was the wrong tool for the team size.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Version support windows. A cluster left on an unsupported version becomes expensive to upgrade (multiple hops, removed APIs; see 45.21).
  • Add-ons are your problem. Ingress controller, CNI, DNS, metrics server and log agent all need upgrades and can all break the cluster.
  • Cost visibility. Requests, not usage, drive node count; over-requesting doubles the bill silently.
  • Multi-tenancy is weak by default. Without NetworkPolicy, RBAC and quotas, every team can reach and starve every other team.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "what would this look like on the simplest platform that works?" before saying Kubernetes. They count the operational surface, not the feature list. They insist on a managed control plane and on a named owner for every add-on. If the answer is Kubernetes, they adopt it fully: GitOps, policies, autoscaling, observability; a half-adopted Kubernetes is worse than ECS.

To a product manager: "Kubernetes is a very capable operations team in software. It is worth it when we have enough services that a human operations team would be more expensive. Until then it is overhead."

Common mistakes

  • Choosing Kubernetes for a monolith and a team of four.
  • Treating a managed control plane as "managed Kubernetes"; nodes and add-ons are still yours.
  • Skipping the platform basics (ingress, TLS, metrics, logs, policies) and running bare Deployments.
  • Never upgrading.

Interview questions

  1. What problems does Kubernetes solve that Docker alone does not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery, scaling, config and secrets across many hosts.
  2. When would you recommend ECS or Cloud Run over Kubernetes?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: small team, few services, stateless HTTP, no platform team; Kubernetes when the ecosystem (KEDA, ArgoCD, operators) and portability pay for the operations.
  3. What are the ongoing costs of running Kubernetes?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: upgrades every few months, add-on ownership, capacity and cost management, policies, on-call knowledge.
  4. Explain desired state versus imperative deployment to a junior.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: you declare the end state; controllers reconcile; no scripts that "do steps".

Practical exercise

Write a one-page recommendation for your own organisation: number of services, team size, traffic shape, workers and cron needs, compliance. Score Compose, App Runner or Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, and EKS against those needs with the table above. Acceptance criteria: a clear recommendation, the top three operational costs of the chosen option, and the trigger that would make you move to the next option up.

45.2 Architecture in simple terms

Concept

A Kubernetes cluster has two kinds of machines. The control plane holds the desired state and runs the controllers that make decisions. The nodes (workers) run your containers. Everything communicates through one component, the API server, and everything is stored in one database, etcd. Every other component is a loop: read desired state, observe actual state, act to close the gap, repeat.

Why does it exist?

Separating "what should exist" (control plane) from "what is running" (nodes) makes the system resilient: nodes can die and the desired state survives in etcd; the control plane can restart and pods keep running on the nodes. The single API server gives one place for authentication, authorisation, validation and audit. The controller-loop design means no component holds a to-do list that can be lost; every loop re-derives its work from the current state.

Mental model

Imagine the hotel again. The front desk (API server) is the only place anyone talks to; it writes every request into the ledger (etcd). A rooms planner (scheduler) reads the ledger for rooms that have no floor assigned and picks a floor with space. A set of supervisors (controller manager) each watch one kind of card: the "three rooms for Orders" supervisor keeps counting Orders rooms and asking the front desk to create or remove them. On each floor, a floor manager (kubelet) reads the front desk's instructions for that floor and actually sets up the rooms, checks on them and reports back. A switchboard operator on each floor (kube-proxy) makes sure calls to "orders" reach an Orders room.

How it works

The components:

Component Where What it does What breaks if it is down
kube-apiserver Control plane REST API for every object; authn/authz; validation; admission webhooks; writes to etcd No changes possible; running pods keep running
etcd Control plane Strongly consistent key-value store (Raft); the only state Everything; back it up; managed offerings hide it
kube-scheduler Control plane Watches unscheduled pods; scores nodes by resources, affinity, taints, spread; sets nodeName New pods stay Pending
kube-controller-manager Control plane Dozens of controllers: ReplicaSet keeps replica counts, Deployment drives rollouts, Node marks dead nodes, Job tracks completions, EndpointSlice tracks pod IPs No self-healing, no rollouts, no scaling
cloud-controller-manager Control plane Talks to the cloud: LoadBalancer Services, node lifecycle, volumes LoadBalancers not created; dead cloud instances not detected
kubelet Every node Watches pods assigned to its node; pulls images; starts containers via the runtime; runs probes; enforces limits; reports status Node goes NotReady after 40 s; pods evicted after 5 min
kube-proxy Every node Programs iptables or IPVS so that Service virtual IPs reach pod IPs New Services and endpoint changes not routed
Container runtime (containerd) Every node Pulls images, creates containers with namespaces and cgroups (Part 44) Nothing starts
CoreDNS Runs as pods Resolves Service and pod names Every name lookup fails
CNI plugin (VPC CNI, Calico, Cilium) Every node Gives pods IPs and connectivity; enforces NetworkPolicy Pods stuck ContainerCreating without IPs

The reconciliation loop, applied to kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml with three replicas:

Nothing calls anything directly except through the API server, and every arrow labelled "watch event" is a controller noticing a difference between desired and observed state. If a node dies, the Node controller marks it, the pods are marked for deletion, the ReplicaSet controller sees 2 of 3, creates one more, the scheduler places it, the kubelet starts it. Same loop, no special code path.

Desired versus observed state lives in the same object: spec is what you want, status is what the controllers report. kubectl get deployment orders-api shows READY 2/3 when spec says 3 and status says 2 are ready.

Practical example

Your CI pipeline runs kubectl set image deployment/orders-api api=registry/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2. That is one PATCH to the API server changing one field in spec.template. Everything after that (new ReplicaSet, gradual pod replacement, endpoint updates) is controllers reconciling. If CI dies one second after the patch, the rollout still completes; there was no script driving it.

Production scenario

On EKS the control plane is managed and multi-AZ; you never see etcd. What you do operate: node groups (or Karpenter), the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, the metrics server, and any add-ons. A cluster of 40 nodes runs around 900 pods; the API server handles a few hundred requests per second, mostly watches from kubelets and controllers. Control-plane outages on managed offerings are rare but do happen; the important property is that running workloads are unaffected, only changes stall.

Failure scenario

At 09:30 the platform team upgrades CoreDNS. The new version's ConfigMap has a typo; CoreDNS pods crash. Within a minute every service in the cluster fails DNS lookups: orders-api cannot resolve inventory-api, connection pools to RDS (by hostname) fail to reconnect, error rate hits 40%. Pods themselves are healthy; the cluster's name resolution is down. Rollback takes 3 minutes. The lesson: cluster add-ons are part of your application's availability, and DNS in particular deserves a canary and an alert on CoreDNS error rate.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • API server unavailable. Existing pods run; kubelets keep applying last-known state; no scaling, no rollouts, HPA stalls.
  • etcd latency. Slow disks on self-managed etcd make every kubectl slow and controllers lag; managed offerings handle this.
  • Node NotReady. Pods are evicted after pod-eviction-timeout (5 minutes default via taints); a network partition between a node and the API server evicts healthy pods that are still serving.
  • Controller lag at scale. Thousands of pods churning make the EndpointSlice controller lag, so a Service points at deleted pods for seconds.
  • Clock skew across nodes affects certificate validation and log ordering; run NTP everywhere.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that "the cluster is down" almost never means their pods are down; it means changes are blocked. They know DNS, the CNI and the ingress controller are the add-ons most likely to take the application down and treat them as tier-one dependencies. They read status before spec when debugging, because status is what the controllers actually saw.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a control-plane outage stops traffic.
  • Editing pods directly (kubectl edit pod) and being surprised when the ReplicaSet reverts the change.
  • Ignoring add-on upgrades until they are three versions behind.
  • Not knowing which CNI the cluster runs and therefore whether NetworkPolicy is enforced.

Interview questions

  1. Describe what happens between kubectl apply of a Deployment and a pod serving traffic.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: API server validates and stores; Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet; ReplicaSet controller creates pods; scheduler binds; kubelet pulls and starts; probes; EndpointSlice updated; kube-proxy routes.
  2. If the API server goes down, what happens to running pods?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: they keep running; no changes or scaling; kubelets continue with last state.
  3. What is a controller, in one sentence?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a loop that observes state, compares with desired state, and acts to reconcile.
  4. Which cluster components can take your application down even when your pods are healthy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CoreDNS, CNI, ingress controller, kube-proxy, node problems.

Practical exercise

On a local cluster (kind or minikube), apply a Deployment with 3 replicas, then kubectl delete pod one of them and kubectl get pods -w to watch the ReplicaSet recreate it. Then kubectl scale --replicas=0 deployment/coredns -n kube-system and observe what happens to a curl orders-api from another pod; restore it. Acceptance criteria: a written timeline of the recreate (with timestamps from kubectl get events), the exact DNS error the application logged, and the time to recover after CoreDNS was restored.

45.3 Pod

Concept

A pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, one port space, localhost between them), share storage volumes, and are scheduled, started and stopped together on one node. Almost always, a pod is one application container plus, optionally, helpers: an init container that runs before it, or a sidecar that runs beside it. Pods are ephemeral: they are created and destroyed freely, their IPs change, and you never repair one; you replace it.

Why does it exist?

Containers are single-process by design, but some deployment units need a small group of tightly coupled processes: your API plus a log forwarder, or your API plus a proxy that terminates mTLS. Putting them in one pod gives them what separate containers cannot easily share: the same IP and localhost, and the same volumes. Making the pod (not the container) the unit of scheduling means those helpers always land on the same node as the application.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel room booked for a small team. Everyone in the room shares the same phone line (pod IP) and can talk to each other by shouting across the room (localhost). They share the room's desk (volumes). Housekeeping prepares the room before they arrive (init containers). When the booking ends, everyone leaves together and the room is reset; next time they may get a different room number (new pod IP). You never "fix" a room; you get a new one.

How it works

  1. The scheduler binds the pod to a node. The kubelet asks the runtime to create a "pause" container that holds the pod's network namespace and IP (from the CNI).
  2. Init containers run one at a time, in order, each to completion. If one fails, the pod restarts it (subject to restartPolicy). They are for one-off preparation: waiting for a dependency, fetching a config file, warming a cache.
  3. App containers (and sidecars) start. Each gets its own filesystem from its image, its own cgroup limits, but joins the pod's network namespace. Two containers in a pod cannot both listen on port 3000.
  4. Kubernetes 1.29+ has native sidecars: an init container with restartPolicy: Always that starts before app containers, stays running, and is stopped after them. Before that, sidecars were ordinary containers with racy ordering (see 45.21).
  5. The kubelet runs probes per container, restarts containers per restartPolicy (Always for Deployments, Never/OnFailure for Jobs), and reports status.phase (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed) and per-container states.
  6. When the pod is deleted, all containers receive SIGTERM (after preStop), the grace period applies to the pod as a whole, and the IP is released.

A minimal but realistic pod spec for a NestJS API (you will almost never write a bare Pod; a Deployment wraps this template):

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: orders-api-debug
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
spec:
  serviceAccountName: orders-api
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-postgres
      image: postgres:16.4-alpine
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until pg_isready -h $DB_HOST -p 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
      env:
        - name: DB_HOST
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef: { name: orders-api-config, key: DB_HOST }
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2
      ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 3000
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef: { name: orders-api-config }
        - secretRef: { name: orders-api-secrets }
      resources:
        requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
        limits: { memory: 512Mi }
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 64Mi }
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Why not two NestJS processes in one pod: they would share one IP and could not both use port 3000; they would be scaled, scheduled and restarted as a unit even if only one needed it; their resource limits are per container but the HPA sees pod-level metrics; and a liveness failure in one restarts only that container while traffic keeps arriving at the pod. Scale replicas, not containers. The one-process-per-container, one-app-per-pod rule keeps every Kubernetes feature meaningful.

Init containers for migrations: tempting, and wrong for multi-replica Deployments. Three replicas starting at once would run the migration three times concurrently (TypeORM takes an advisory lock in recent versions, but the others still wait and the rollout blocks), a failed migration puts every pod in Init:Error, and a rollback of the Deployment does not roll back the schema. Run migrations as a Job before the rollout (45.10, 45.19). An init container that waits for the database (as above) is fine; one that changes it is not.

Practical example

The orders-api pod is one container. The payments-api pod has two: the NestJS app and a Vault agent sidecar that renews a database credential and writes it to a shared emptyDir; the app watches that file. They share the pod so that the file never crosses the network and the credential lives only in memory (emptyDir with medium: Memory).

NestJS example

Pods know their identity through the Downward API, which is how you get a pod name into logs and traces without a library:

YAML
env:
  - name: POD_NAME
    valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
  - name: POD_IP
    valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: status.podIP } }
  - name: NODE_NAME
    valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: spec.nodeName } }
  - name: MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES
    valueFrom: { resourceFieldRef: { containerName: api, resource: limits.memory } }
TypeScript
// src/logging/logger.factory.ts
import { LoggerService } from '@nestjs/common';
import pino from 'pino';

export function createLogger(): LoggerService & { pino: pino.Logger } {
  const base = pino({
    level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info',
    base: {
      service: 'orders-api',
      pod: process.env.POD_NAME,      // which replica said this
      node: process.env.NODE_NAME,    // which machine it was on
      version: process.env.APP_VERSION,
    },
  });
  return {
    pino: base,
    log: (msg, ctx) => base.info({ ctx }, msg),
    warn: (msg, ctx) => base.warn({ ctx }, msg),
    error: (msg, trace, ctx) => base.error({ ctx, trace }, msg),
    debug: (msg, ctx) => base.debug({ ctx }, msg),
    verbose: (msg, ctx) => base.trace({ ctx }, msg),
  };
}

With pod in every log line, "which replica is slow" is a filter, not an investigation.

PostgreSQL example

Pods are ephemeral; their IPs change. If you use pg_hba.conf rules by IP, or pg_stat_activity.client_addr to identify clients, you will chase ghosts. Instead identify by application_name, which the driver sets from the connection string:

SQL
-- Which pods hold connections right now
SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'orders'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 4 DESC;

Set application_name to the pod name in TypeORM via extra: { application_name: process.env.POD_NAME } so the output reads orders-api-7d9f6b4c8-x2k9p rather than an IP that will be reused by a different pod tomorrow.

Production scenario

A cluster of 40 nodes runs 900 pods, of which 600 are single-container application pods, 200 include a log or metrics sidecar, and 100 are DaemonSet pods (one per node: log agent, CNI, node exporter). Pod churn is around 2,000 creations a day from rollouts and autoscaling. Pod IP reuse within minutes is normal; anything that caches a pod IP (a client without DNS re-resolution, an old kube-proxy rule) will misroute.

Failure scenario

A team puts typeorm migration:run in an init container. A Friday deploy includes a migration adding an index to a 200 million row table without CONCURRENTLY. Six replicas roll out; six init containers start the migration; the first takes the lock and runs for 25 minutes; the other five block. The Deployment's rollout stalls at zero new ready pods; the old pods keep serving, which is the only good news. The on-call cannot roll back cleanly because the half-built index must be handled by hand. Migrations moved to a Job with a CONCURRENTLY policy and a review checklist (Part 24 and Part 25 cover safe migrations and zero-downtime schema changes).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Port collision in a pod. Two containers listening on the same port; the second fails with EADDRINUSE.
  • Sidecar not ready when the app starts (pre-1.29): the app's first database connection goes through a proxy that is not up yet; add startup retries and use native sidecars.
  • Init container hangs waiting for a dependency that never appears; the pod stays Init:0/1 forever; add a timeout and an alert on pods stuck in init.
  • emptyDir on disk counts toward ephemeral storage; large temporary files evict the pod (45.21).
  • Pod IP reused by a different pod; clients that cached the IP send traffic to the wrong service.
  • fsGroup on large volumes makes the kubelet chown every file at mount time; slow starts.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

One process per container, one application per pod, replicas for scale. Sidecars only for cross-cutting infrastructure (proxy, secrets agent, log shipper) and only when a DaemonSet or a library cannot do the job. Init containers wait; Jobs change. Every pod carries its name into logs, traces and application_name.

Common mistakes

  • Running migrations in init containers.
  • Bundling two services in one pod "because they talk a lot".
  • Treating pods as pets: kubectl exec to fix a file, which the next rollout erases.
  • Relying on pod IPs anywhere.

Interview questions

  1. What do containers in a pod share and what do they not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: share network namespace and IP, volumes, lifecycle and scheduling; do not share filesystem roots, cgroup limits or process namespace by default.
  2. Why not run migrations in an init container?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: concurrent execution across replicas, rollout blocked on failure, schema not rolled back with the Deployment; use a Job.
  3. When is a sidecar justified?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: infrastructure concerns that need the pod's network or filesystem (mTLS proxy, secret agent); otherwise a DaemonSet or library.
  4. A pod is Pending. What are the usual causes?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: insufficient requests capacity, unsatisfiable affinity or taints, PVC not bound, image pull not yet started (see 45.20).

Practical exercise

Deploy the pod above (adjusting the image) with a wait-for-postgres init container. Observe kubectl get pod -w through Init:0/1, PodInitializing, Running, Ready. Then add a second container that also listens on 3000 and observe the failure. Finally replace the init container with a native sidecar (restartPolicy: Always) that tails a shared emptyDir file the app writes to. Acceptance criteria: a written timeline of pod phases, the EADDRINUSE error captured, and kubectl logs pod -c sidecar showing the app's file contents.

45.4 Deployment

Concept

A Deployment is the object you use to run a stateless service. It says: run N identical pods from this template, and when the template changes, replace the old pods with new ones gradually. Under it sits a ReplicaSet, which does one thing: keep exactly N pods matching a label selector alive. A Deployment manages a series of ReplicaSets, one per template version, and moves replicas from the old to the new during a rollout. Roll back, and it moves them back.

Why does it exist?

Replacing a running version by hand means stopping old containers and starting new ones in the right order, checking each is healthy, stopping if something breaks, and remembering how to undo it. A Deployment encodes that procedure with two numbers (maxSurge, maxUnavailable), uses readiness probes as the "is it healthy" signal, keeps a history of previous versions, and exposes rollback as one command.

Mental model

Imagine replacing the tyres on a moving bus. You cannot stop the bus (traffic keeps coming). A Deployment adds a fifth wheel (surge), waits until it is turning smoothly (ready), removes one old wheel (unavailable), and repeats. If a new wheel wobbles, it stops swapping and the bus keeps rolling on the old wheels. If you say "put the old wheels back", it runs the same procedure in reverse.

How it works

  1. You change spec.template (usually the image tag). The Deployment controller hashes the template; the hash becomes the pod-template-hash label and part of the ReplicaSet name (orders-api-b41c...).
  2. A new ReplicaSet is created with 0 replicas. The rollout begins.
  3. With strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0 on 3 replicas: scale new RS to 1 (4 pods total). Wait for that pod's readiness probe to pass. Scale old RS to 2. Scale new to 2. Wait. Scale old to 1. Scale new to 3. Wait. Scale old to 0. Done.
  4. minReadySeconds (for example 10) makes the controller wait that long after readiness before counting a pod as available, so a pod that passes readiness and crashes 3 seconds later does not advance the rollout.
  5. progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) marks the rollout as failed if it makes no progress for that long; the Deployment condition Progressing=False, reason=ProgressDeadlineExceeded is what CI should check.
  6. Old ReplicaSets are kept (scaled to 0) up to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10). kubectl rollout undo scales a previous one back up using the same rolling procedure.

The two rollout parameters:

Setting Meaning Effect on 3 replicas Choose when
maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25% (defaults) Up to 1 extra, up to 1 down Can dip to 2 serving Capacity headroom exists; fastest
maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 Never below desired Always 3 serving, briefly 4 Latency-sensitive APIs; the usual choice
maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 No extra capacity used Dips to 2 Cluster is tight on resources; slower
strategy.type: Recreate Kill all, then start all Downtime Singleton workers that cannot run two versions at once

A production Deployment for the orders API (probes, resources and security context are explained in 45.12 to 45.16; here the focus is the rollout fields):

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  minReadySeconds: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "8f4e2a"          # bumped when ConfigMap changes; forces a rollout
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 3000 }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }

The commands you will use daily:

Shell
kubectl -n shop set image deployment/orders-api api=REG/orders-api:sha-b41c9d2   # trigger rollout
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=300s              # block until done or failed
kubectl -n shop rollout history deployment/orders-api                            # revisions
kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/orders-api                               # previous revision
kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/orders-api --to-revision=4               # specific revision
kubectl -n shop rollout pause deployment/orders-api                              # stop mid-rollout (canary by hand)
kubectl -n shop rollout restart deployment/orders-api                            # new pods, same template
kubectl -n shop get rs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api                      # ReplicaSets and their hashes

rollout restart works by adding an annotation with a timestamp to the template, which changes the hash. It is the right way to pick up a rotated Secret or a new ConfigMap (45.7).

Practical example

CI deploys sha-b41c9d2. With maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, minReadySeconds: 10 and a readiness probe every 5 seconds, each pod swap takes about 25 seconds (pull 6 s, boot 4 s, probe 5 s, minReady 10 s). A 3-replica rollout completes in around 80 seconds; a 20-replica one in 8 minutes. If that is too slow, raise maxSurge to 25% or 50%; capacity permitting, rollouts parallelise.

NestJS example

A version endpoint makes rollouts observable from the outside. Watching it during a rollout shows the mix of versions serving, which is how you confirm a canary or spot a stuck rollout:

TypeScript
// src/version/version.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('internal/version')
export class VersionController {
  @Get()
  version() {
    return {
      version: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? 'unknown',   // semver from the image label, injected as env
      commit: process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'unknown',
      pod: process.env.POD_NAME,
      startedAt: new Date(Date.now() - process.uptime() * 1000).toISOString(),
    };
  }
}

for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s orders-api.shop/internal/version | jq -r .commit; done | sort | uniq -c from inside the cluster shows, for example, 13 sha-3f9a1c2 and 7 sha-b41c9d2 mid-rollout.

PostgreSQL example

During a rolling update, both versions run against the same database for a minute or more. Every schema change must be compatible with the old and the new code at once. Adding a NOT NULL column without a default breaks the old version's inserts the moment the migration runs; renaming a column breaks one version or the other. The expand-and-contract pattern (add the new column nullable, deploy code that writes both, backfill, deploy code that reads the new one, then drop the old) is the only safe way. Part 24 and Part 25 cover this in depth; the Deployment's job is only to make the overlap window explicit.

Production scenario

An e-commerce platform performs 200 rollouts a day across 60 Deployments. Their standard: maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0, minReadySeconds: 15, progressDeadlineSeconds: 600, CI runs rollout status and on failure runs rollout undo automatically, and a rollout that fails twice pages the owning team. Median rollout of a 6-replica API is 2 minutes. Automated rollbacks fire about twice a week, nearly always for a readiness failure caused by a config or dependency problem, and the customer-visible impact is zero because old pods never left.

Failure scenario

At 14:05 a rollout of catalog-api stalls: rollout status shows 1 of 6 updated replicas available for 10 minutes, then ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The new pod's readiness probe fails because the new version requires SEARCH_URL, which was added to the ConfigMap in a different pull request that had not merged. Old pods kept serving; customers saw nothing. CI rolled back. The engineer merged the ConfigMap change and redeployed. Without maxUnavailable: 0 and readiness gating, the old strategy of "stop all, start all" would have been a 10-minute outage.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Readiness probe too lenient (or absent) lets a broken version roll out completely; readiness is the gate.
  • Two versions serving at once breaks clients that assume a single API version; the overlap window is real (see WebSockets in 45.21).
  • maxUnavailable: 25% on 2 replicas rounds down to 0 unavailable but maxSurge rounds up to 1, which is fine; on 1 replica with maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable must be at least 1 or the rollout deadlocks.
  • Selector immutability. You cannot change spec.selector on a Deployment; changing labels requires a new Deployment.
  • HPA and replicas conflict. If the manifest sets replicas: 3 and the HPA has scaled to 12, kubectl apply resets to 3 and the HPA scales back up; omit replicas from the manifest when an HPA owns it (or use server-side apply with field ownership).
  • revisionHistoryLimit: 0 deletes rollback targets.
  • Recreate strategy is downtime; only for workloads that cannot overlap.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They set maxUnavailable: 0 for anything customer-facing and accept the extra capacity cost during rollouts. They make readiness honest so that rollouts self-gate. They wire rollout status into CI with automatic undo. They treat the overlap window as a design constraint on API and schema changes. And they use rollout pause for a manual canary before investing in Argo Rollouts or Flagger.

Common mistakes

  • No readiness probe, so rollouts replace healthy pods with broken ones at full speed.
  • Deploying with kubectl apply of a manifest that pins replicas while an HPA is active.
  • Not checking rollout status in CI; the pipeline goes green while the rollout is stuck.
  • Assuming rollback reverts the database.
  • Editing the ReplicaSet directly.

Interview questions

  1. Explain maxSurge and maxUnavailable and choose values for a latency-sensitive API.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: extra pods allowed and pods allowed down; 1/0 or 25%/0; readiness gates progress.
  2. How does kubectl rollout undo work?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scales a retained ReplicaSet back up with the same rolling procedure; template hash identifies revisions; the database is not reverted.
  3. A rollout is stuck at 1 of 6. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: new pod's readiness, describe pod, logs, ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition, ConfigMap/Secret changes; roll back if needed.
  4. Why must schema changes be backward compatible during a rolling update?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: old and new versions run concurrently against one schema; expand-and-contract.
  5. How do you restart pods to pick up a new Secret?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rollout restart or a checksum annotation on the template.

Practical exercise

Deploy the orders API with 3 replicas and the strategy above. Trigger a rollout to a version whose readiness fails (point it at a wrong DB_HOST). Observe rollout status, get rs, and describe deployment conditions. Roll back. Then perform a manual canary with rollout pause after one new pod is ready and use the version endpoint to measure the traffic split. Acceptance criteria: zero failed requests from a load generator during both the failed rollout and the rollback, the ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition captured, and the observed canary split within 10% of 1-in-4.

45.5 Service

Concept

A Service gives a stable name and a virtual IP (the ClusterIP) to a set of pods selected by labels. Pods come and go; the Service stays. Kubernetes keeps an EndpointSlice listing the IPs of the currently ready pods behind the Service, and kube-proxy programs every node so that a connection to the ClusterIP is forwarded to one of those pods. CoreDNS gives the Service a name: orders-api.shop.svc.cluster.local.

Why does it exist?

Pod IPs are unstable and unknowable in advance. Without a Service, every client would need to discover pod IPs, watch for changes, and balance across them. A Service moves that problem into the platform: clients connect to one name, and the platform sends each new connection to a ready pod.

Mental model

Imagine a company's main phone number. Callers dial one number; the switchboard connects each call to whichever agent is currently at their desk and not on a break (ready). Agents change shifts all day; the number never changes. The switchboard does not move a call once connected: if you are talking to an agent for an hour, you keep talking to that agent even if ten new agents arrive. That last property is the gRPC and WebSocket caveat.

How it works

  1. You create a Service with selector: app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api, port: 80, targetPort: http.
  2. The EndpointSlice controller watches pods matching the selector and lists the IPs of those with Ready=true. Readiness (45.12) is therefore what adds and removes a pod from traffic.
  3. kube-proxy on every node watches EndpointSlices and writes iptables rules (or IPVS entries): packets to 10.96.12.7:80 are DNAT-ed to one endpoint, chosen randomly (iptables) or round-robin (IPVS), per new connection. There is no process behind the ClusterIP; it exists only as rules.
  4. CoreDNS answers orders-api.shop.svc.cluster.local with the ClusterIP. Inside the same namespace, orders-api alone resolves through the search path; from another namespace, orders-api.shop.
  5. Some CNIs (Cilium) replace kube-proxy with eBPF; the behaviour is the same from the application's view.

Service types:

Type What you get Reachable from Use for
ClusterIP (default) Virtual IP inside the cluster Pods only Every internal service; the API behind an Ingress
NodePort ClusterIP plus a port (30000 to 32767) on every node Anything that can reach a node Rarely; ingress controllers on bare metal
LoadBalancer NodePort plus a cloud load balancer (NLB/ALB) The internet or VPC One per public entry point; usually the ingress controller, not each app
ExternalName A DNS CNAME to an external host Pods Pointing postgres at an RDS hostname so config looks uniform
Headless (clusterIP: None) No VIP; DNS returns the pod IPs directly Pods StatefulSets, client-side load balancing, gRPC
YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80            # what clients connect to
      targetPort: http    # container port by name (3000)
      protocol: TCP

The long-lived connection problem: load balancing happens at connection time. HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive from a Node client (undici or axios with an agent) opens a handful of connections and reuses them for minutes; those connections all go to whichever pods existed when they were opened. Scale from 3 to 10 pods and the new 7 receive almost nothing from existing clients. gRPC (one HTTP/2 connection multiplexing thousands of requests) and WebSockets make it worse: one connection, one pod, forever. Fixes, in increasing effort: client-side keep-alive with a short max age (close and reopen connections every 30 to 60 seconds); a headless Service plus client-side load balancing (gRPC's dns:/// resolver with round-robin); an L7 proxy in the path (the Ingress controller, Envoy, a service mesh) that balances requests rather than connections.

Practical example

orders-api calls inventory-api at http://inventory-api.shop/reserve. Both run as Deployments with ClusterIP Services. orders-api uses an undici Agent with keepAliveTimeout: 30_000 and keepAliveMaxTimeout: 60_000 so connections are recycled within a minute and new inventory-api pods receive traffic within a minute of becoming ready. External clients never see either Service; they enter through the Ingress (45.6).

NestJS example

The outbound client is where the load-balancing caveat is handled. A NestJS provider wrapping undici with connection recycling and per-request timeouts:

TypeScript
// src/inventory/inventory.client.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Agent, request } from 'undici';

@Injectable()
export class InventoryClient implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly agent = new Agent({
    connections: 20,
    keepAliveTimeout: 30_000,        // idle connections are closed after 30 s
    keepAliveMaxTimeout: 60_000,     // no connection lives longer than 60 s: new pods get traffic
    connect: { timeout: 1_000 },
  });
  private readonly baseUrl = process.env.INVENTORY_URL ?? 'http://inventory-api.shop';

  async reserve(orderId: string, items: { sku: string; qty: number }[]): Promise<void> {
    const res = await request(`${this.baseUrl}/reserve`, {
      method: 'POST',
      dispatcher: this.agent,
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'idempotency-key': orderId },
      body: JSON.stringify({ orderId, items }),
      headersTimeout: 2_000,
      bodyTimeout: 2_000,
    });
    if (res.statusCode >= 500) {
      await res.body.dump();
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('inventory unavailable');
    }
    await res.body.json();
  }

  async onModuleDestroy(): Promise<void> {
    await this.agent.close();
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The database usually lives outside the cluster (RDS). An ExternalName Service keeps the configuration uniform so that DB_HOST=postgres works in every environment, and a later move (to a read replica endpoint, to a proxy) is a Service change rather than a config change on every app:

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: shop
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: orders-prod.cluster-abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com

The connection string then uses postgres.shop.svc.cluster.local (or postgres inside the namespace). Note that TLS certificate validation must still match the RDS hostname; use sslmode=verify-full with the RDS CA bundle and set the servername explicitly if your driver checks the connected hostname.

Production scenario

A cluster with 400 Services and 3,000 endpoints: iptables mode handles it, but rule updates on endpoint churn take hundreds of milliseconds per node; IPVS or eBPF is preferred beyond a few thousand endpoints. During a rollout of a 20-replica API, endpoint changes propagate to all nodes within 1 to 3 seconds, which is the window that preStop sleeps cover (45.14).

Failure scenario

At 19:20 notifications-api scales from 4 to 16 pods under load, but p99 latency does not improve and the 4 original pods stay at 90% CPU while the 12 new ones idle at 3%. All callers are Node services with default keep-alive agents; their connections were opened an hour ago and pinned to the original 4 pods. The fix that night was rollout restart of the callers (forcing new connections); the fix that week was keepAliveMaxTimeout in the shared HTTP client library.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Selector mismatch. A typo in labels gives a Service with zero endpoints; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders-api is empty; every request times out.
  • targetPort mismatch. Service points at 8080, container listens on 3000; connection refused.
  • Readiness removes all pods (dependency down) and the Service has no endpoints; see 45.21.
  • Session affinity (sessionAffinity: ClientIP) pins by source IP, which behind a NAT is one IP; avoid; use Redis for sessions.
  • DNS ndots:5. Resolving api.stripe.com from a pod tries api.stripe.com.shop.svc.cluster.local, .svc.cluster.local, .cluster.local, then the real name: four extra lookups. Use a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.) or dnsConfig: { options: [{ name: ndots, value: "2" }] }.
  • Cross-namespace access requires the name.namespace form; NetworkPolicy may block it.
  • LoadBalancer per app creates one cloud load balancer per Service; expensive; put an Ingress in front instead.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that a Service balances connections, not requests, and design clients accordingly. They put an L7 proxy in front of anything with long-lived connections. They keep exactly one LoadBalancer (the ingress controller) and everything else ClusterIP. They check endpoints before they check code when "the service is unreachable".

Common mistakes

  • Expecting new replicas to receive traffic from clients with persistent connections.
  • One LoadBalancer Service per application.
  • Selector and label typos.
  • Hardcoding pod IPs or ClusterIPs anywhere.
  • Ignoring ndots and paying 4x DNS latency on every external call.

Interview questions

  1. How does a ClusterIP work if nothing listens on it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: kube-proxy DNAT rules per node; per-connection selection among ready endpoints.
  2. Why did scaling an API not reduce latency for existing callers?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: keep-alive connections pinned to old pods; recycle connections or use an L7 proxy.
  3. What is a headless Service and when do you use it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no VIP, DNS returns pod IPs; StatefulSets, client-side load balancing, gRPC.
  4. What determines whether a pod is in a Service's endpoints?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: label selector match plus readiness.
  5. Explain the ndots problem.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: search-path expansion on external names; trailing dot or lower ndots.

Practical exercise

Create the Service above and, from a debug pod, run nslookup orders-api.shop.svc.cluster.local, kubectl get endpointslices, and 100 curl requests printing the pod name from the version endpoint. Then open 10 keep-alive connections with a small Node script, scale the Deployment from 3 to 6, and count which pods answer over the next 60 requests. Fix the client with keepAliveMaxTimeout and repeat. Acceptance criteria: a table of pod hit counts before and after, showing the new pods receiving traffic only after the fix, and the ndots behaviour demonstrated with tcpdump or CoreDNS logs on an external lookup.

45.6 Ingress

Concept

An Ingress is the HTTP entry point to the cluster: rules that map hostnames and paths to Services, plus TLS termination. The Ingress object is just configuration; an ingress controller (NGINX, AWS Load Balancer Controller for ALB, Traefik, HAProxy) reads it and does the actual proxying. One controller with one cloud load balancer serves hundreds of Ingress rules, which is why you do not create a LoadBalancer Service per app.

Why does it exist?

External traffic needs a public IP, TLS certificates, host and path routing, and often rate limits, body-size limits, timeouts and WebSocket support. Doing that per Service would be expensive (a load balancer each) and inconsistent. Ingress centralises it: one place for certificates, one place for routing, one place for edge policies.

Mental model

Imagine the building's reception desk with a directory. A visitor asks for "orders, second floor" (host and path); reception checks their ID at the door (TLS), applies house rules (max parcel size, how long they may wait), and sends them to the right floor (Service), where any available agent (pod) takes them.

How it works

  1. The ingress controller runs as a Deployment (or DaemonSet) with one LoadBalancer Service. The cloud provisions an NLB or ALB pointing at it.
  2. The controller watches Ingress objects (filtered by ingressClassName) and Services, and builds its proxy configuration: for NGINX, an nginx.conf regenerated on changes; for ALB, listener rules and target groups pointing directly at pod IPs (target-type: ip).
  3. A request for https://api.shop.example.com/orders hits the load balancer, reaches the controller, matches the host and path rule, and is proxied to the Service's endpoints (NGINX resolves endpoints itself and balances requests, which solves the long-connection problem for external traffic).
  4. TLS: the controller terminates HTTPS using a certificate stored in a Secret; cert-manager can obtain and renew it from Let's Encrypt automatically.
  5. Annotations tune per-Ingress behaviour: timeouts, body size, WebSocket, CORS, rate limits, sticky sessions.

An Ingress for the orders API with NGINX and cert-manager:

YAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"          # file uploads up to 10 MB
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "60"        # seconds; raise for long polls/WebSockets
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "60"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-connect-timeout: "5"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "50"                 # per client IP, coarse protection
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.shop.example.com]
      secretName: api-shop-example-com-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: orders-api, port: { name: http } }
          - path: /inventory
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: inventory-api, port: { name: http } }

The same for an AWS ALB, where annotations configure the load balancer itself:

YAML
metadata:
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip                   # route to pod IPs, not NodePorts
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abcd
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /health/ready
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-attributes: idle_timeout.timeout_seconds=120
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-group-attributes: deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds=15
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb

WebSockets: NGINX ingress proxies them without special flags, but proxy-read-timeout (default 60 s) closes idle sockets; set it to the client's ping interval times a margin (for example 3600 for hourly reconnects, with application-level pings every 30 s). ALB supports WebSockets natively; idle_timeout plays the same role.

Gateway API is the successor to Ingress: Gateway (the listener, owned by the platform team) and HTTPRoute (routing rules, owned by application teams), with typed fields for timeouts, header matching and traffic splitting instead of vendor annotations. New clusters increasingly use it; the concepts are identical.

Practical example

api.shop.example.com is one ALB serving 22 Ingress rules across 6 namespaces. Certificates come from ACM. Each team owns its Ingress; the platform team owns the controller. Adding a new API is a 15-line Ingress in the team's Helm chart.

NestJS example

Behind a proxy, the app must trust the proxy's headers to see the real client IP (for rate limiting and audit logs) and the original protocol. In NestJS with Express:

TypeScript
// src/main.ts (excerpt)
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
// Trust exactly one hop (the ingress controller), not arbitrary X-Forwarded-For chains
app.set('trust proxy', 1);

And a ThrottlerGuard that keys on the forwarded IP rather than the ingress controller's pod IP:

TypeScript
// src/common/throttler-behind-proxy.guard.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';

@Injectable()
export class ThrottlerBehindProxyGuard extends ThrottlerGuard {
  protected async getTracker(req: Record<string, any>): Promise<string> {
    // req.ips is populated by Express when trust proxy is set; first entry is the client
    return req.ips?.length ? req.ips[0] : req.ip;
  }
}

Without trust proxy, every request appears to come from 10.244.x.x (the controller), and a per-IP rate limit throttles the whole world as one client.

Production scenario

An ingress layer handling 4,000 RPS on 3 NGINX controller pods (each at 40% CPU), TLS terminated at the controller, p50 added latency 0.8 ms, p99 3 ms. cert-manager renews 40 certificates automatically; an alert fires if any certificate has under 14 days left. Body size limits stop a 2 GB upload at the edge before it reaches a NestJS pod.

Failure scenario

At 03:00 on a Sunday, api.shop.example.com starts failing TLS handshakes: the certificate expired. cert-manager had been failing to renew for 30 days because a NetworkPolicy added in a security hardening sprint blocked its HTTP-01 challenge traffic; nobody had alerted on certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds. The fix was a NetworkPolicy exception and an alert. The senior lesson: automation without an alert on its failure is a delayed outage.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Default body size on NGINX ingress is 1 MB; uploads fail with 413 at the edge while the app never sees them.
  • Timeout mismatches. Ingress read timeout 60 s, app timeout 30 s, ALB idle 60 s, Node keepAliveTimeout 5 s: the last one causes intermittent 502 because the proxy reuses a connection Node just closed. Set Node's keepAliveTimeout above the proxy's idle timeout (for example 65 s versus 60 s) and headersTimeout above that.
  • Path rewrites. A Prefix path of /orders forwards /orders/123 unchanged; if the app expects /123, you need a rewrite annotation, which is a common source of 404s.
  • Multiple controllers. Without ingressClassName, an Ingress may be picked up by none or by both.
  • WebSocket idle timeout dropping connections every 60 s.
  • Health check path on ALB must return 200 during rollouts; pointing it at /health/live (which does not check dependencies) masks dependency failures; point it at /health/ready.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

One ingress controller, one load balancer, certificates automated and alerted. They align every timeout along the path (client, load balancer, ingress, app, database) so the outermost is longest. They put body-size and rate limits at the edge and treat annotations as production configuration under review. They plan for Gateway API on new clusters.

Common mistakes

  • A LoadBalancer Service per application.
  • Forgetting trust proxy and rate-limiting the ingress controller instead of clients.
  • Node keepAliveTimeout shorter than the proxy's idle timeout.
  • Certificates without expiry alerts.
  • Default 1 MB body limit surprising an upload feature.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between an Ingress and an ingress controller?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the object is configuration; the controller is the proxy that implements it.
  2. How do you support WebSockets behind NGINX ingress or ALB?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: raise read/idle timeouts; keep application pings; expect reconnects on rollout.
  3. Why do you see intermittent 502 between a proxy and Node?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: keep-alive timeout race; set Node's above the proxy's.
  4. Where should rate limiting and body-size limits live?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: coarse limits at the edge, precise per-user limits in the app with Redis.
  5. What is Gateway API and why does it exist?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: typed, role-separated successor to Ingress; portable configuration instead of annotations.

Practical exercise

Expose the orders API through NGINX ingress with TLS from cert-manager (staging issuer). Upload a 5 MB file and observe the 413; fix it with the annotation. Set Node's keepAliveTimeout to 2 s, run a 60-second load test, count 502s, then set it to 65 s and repeat. Acceptance criteria: a valid certificate, uploads up to 10 MB succeeding, 502 count dropping to zero after the keep-alive fix, and the client IP appearing correctly in the app's request logs.

45.7 ConfigMap and Secret

Concept

A ConfigMap is a named bag of key/value pairs stored in the cluster. A Secret is the same thing with two differences: the values are base64-encoded in the API, and Kubernetes treats the object as sensitive (it can be encrypted at rest in etcd, kept out of kubectl describe output, and restricted by RBAC). Both are injected into a pod in one of two ways: as environment variables, or as files in a mounted volume.

That is the whole object model. Everything interesting about ConfigMaps and Secrets is in the consequences of that model: what happens when a value changes, who can read it, what happens when the value is wrong, and whether "Secret" means anything at all from a security point of view.

Why does it exist?

Configuration must vary per environment while the image stays identical. Part 44 established the rule: one image, promoted from staging to production unchanged. If the database host is baked into the image, you need a different image per environment, and the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

ConfigMaps and Secrets are the mechanism that keeps the image constant. They also give you three properties you would otherwise build yourself: the values live in the cluster's API (so they are auditable and RBAC-controlled), they can be mounted as files (so a 40 KB TLS certificate or a pino transport config does not have to become an environment variable), and they can be updated without rebuilding anything.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel room (the pod) that is identical in every branch of the chain. What differs is the little card in the room: the local emergency number, the Wi-Fi name, the manager's name. Housekeeping (the kubelet) puts the right card in the room when the room is prepared. The safe combination (the Secret) is delivered on a separate card, handled by staff with higher clearance, but it is still a card in the room: anyone who gets into the room can read it. "Secret" describes who is allowed to hand it out, not how hard it is to read once delivered.

How it works

  1. You create a ConfigMap or Secret. The API server stores it in etcd. Secrets are stored base64-encoded; if the cluster has encryption at rest configured, the value is encrypted with a KMS key before it reaches disk.
  2. A pod references it. The kubelet fetches the object before starting the container.
  3. Environment variables are set once, at process start. The container's environment is fixed for the life of the container. If you change the ConfigMap, running pods keep the old value forever. There is no reload.
