  • Missing zone labels on nodes (some bare-metal or older setups) make zone-based rules no-ops that silently do nothing.
  • PDB on a single-replica Deployment blocks every node drain; kubectl drain hangs and eventually times out.
  • PDB does not protect against node failure, only against voluntary eviction.
  • Anti-affinity is evaluated at scheduling time only (IgnoredDuringExecution); pods already placed are not moved when the rule would now be violated. Use the descheduler if you need rebalancing.
  • Taint without toleration on a DaemonSet means your log agent or CNI does not run on those nodes, so they have no logs and possibly no networking.
  • Node affinity plus cluster autoscaler: the autoscaler must be able to model your constraints, or it adds nodes in the wrong zone and the pods stay Pending.
  • Scheduling constraints make evictions slower, which lengthens node drains and cluster upgrades; budget for it.
  • Cost. Spreading across zones means cross-AZ traffic between your pods and their dependencies, which is billed (see 45.21).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They name the failure domains first: process, pod, node, zone, region. Then they ask, for each customer-facing service, "which of these can I lose without an incident?" and set constraints that make the answer true. Zone spread with DoNotSchedule for anything user-facing; node spread as ScheduleAnyway so autoscaling still works; a PDB that permits maintenance while guaranteeing capacity.

They keep noisy or greedy workloads on their own node pools with taints, because "it only affects the batch job" stops being true the moment it shares a node with your API. And they test their constraints by actually draining a node in staging, because a constraint you have never exercised is a hypothesis.

Common mistakes

  • Three replicas, one node, and calling it high availability.
  • required anti-affinity on an autoscaled service.
  • No PDB, so a routine upgrade takes out every replica.
  • A PDB that makes drains impossible, which gets deleted by an administrator during an incident.
  • Tolerations without a nodeSelector, so pods "allowed" on a dedicated pool run everywhere.
  • Assuming a PDB protects against node crashes.

Interview questions

  1. How do you guarantee replicas are spread across availability zones?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: topology spread constraints with maxSkew: 1 and DoNotSchedule on the zone key; matchLabelKeys with pod-template-hash during rollouts; anti-affinity as the older alternative.
  2. What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against, and what does it not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: voluntary disruptions (drains, autoscaler scale-down, upgrades) versus involuntary (node failure, OOMKill, unnotified spot reclamation).
  3. Why can required anti-affinity break autoscaling?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one pod per node; replicas capped at node count; Pending pods.
  4. How do you dedicate nodes to a workload?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: taint the nodes, tolerate the taint, and add a nodeSelector or node affinity so the pod actually goes there.
  5. A node drain hangs. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: PDBs blocking eviction, pods without controllers, long grace periods, unready replacements; kubectl get pdb and its ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column.

Practical exercise

Deploy orders-api with 6 replicas and no constraints on a 3-node, 3-zone cluster, then record the distribution across kubectl get pods -o wide. Repeat with the topology spread constraints above. Add the PDB, then run kubectl drain on the node with the most pods and time the drain in both configurations. Finally set minAvailable equal to the replica count and observe the drain blocking, and read what kubectl get pdb reports for allowed disruptions. Acceptance criteria: the pod distribution recorded for all cases, the drain duration compared, and the blocked drain reproduced and explained.

45.16 Security in the cluster

Concept

Cluster security for a backend engineer comes down to five questions with concrete answers: what can this pod talk to (NetworkPolicy), what can it do to the cluster (ServiceAccount and RBAC), what can it do in AWS (IRSA), what can it do inside its own container (security context and Pod Security Standards), and where does its image come from (registry credentials and image provenance).

Why does it exist?

The default posture of a Kubernetes cluster is wide open. Every pod can reach every other pod, in every namespace, on every port. Every pod gets a ServiceAccount token mounted into it. Containers run as root unless told otherwise, with a writable filesystem and a default set of Linux capabilities. That is fine for a demo and unacceptable in production, because an application vulnerability (an SSRF, a dependency compromise, a leaked deserialisation bug) becomes lateral movement across your entire estate.

Mental model

Imagine an office where every door is unlocked, every desk has a master key in the drawer, and every employee is an administrator. Security work is not adding a firewall at the front door; it is making each room open only for the people who need it, taking the master keys out of the drawers, and giving each employee exactly the permissions their job requires.

How it works

NetworkPolicy: default deny, then explicit allow. A NetworkPolicy is enforced by your CNI (Calico, Cilium; note that some CNIs ignore them entirely, which is a nasty surprise). The rule is simple: a pod selected by any policy is deny-by-default for the directions that policy mentions.

YAML
# 1. Default deny everything in and out of the namespace.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}                 # every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
# 2. DNS must be allowed or nothing resolves. This is the step everyone forgets.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }
---
# 3. orders-api: accept traffic only from the ingress controller.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-api-ingress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 3000 }
---
# 4. orders-api egress: PostgreSQL (outside the cluster), Redis and Kafka only.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-api-egress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.0.32.0/20        # the RDS subnet
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-redis
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 6379 }
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: kafka
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 9092 }

Two things that trip everyone up. DNS: without the allow-dns policy, every hostname lookup fails and your app reports getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND postgres while you stare at a perfectly correct database policy. External services: NetworkPolicy works on IP addresses, not DNS names, so allowing api.stripe.com means allowing an IP range that changes. In practice teams allow egress to 0.0.0.0/0 minus the internal RFC1918 ranges for internet access, or route external calls through an egress gateway, or use Cilium's DNS-aware policies.

ServiceAccount and RBAC least privilege. Most application pods need zero Kubernetes API access. Say so:

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: false     # the app never calls the Kubernetes API
YAML
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: orders-api
      automountServiceAccountToken: false

Without this, every pod carries a token for the namespace's default ServiceAccount at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. If an attacker gets code execution or a file-read primitive in your pod, that token is the first thing they take. Removing it costs nothing and closes a real path.

When a pod does need API access (a controller, a leader-election lock), give it a Role with the specific verbs on the specific resources, ideally with resourceNames:

YAML
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: orders-leader-election
  namespace: shop
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["leases"]
    resourceNames: ["orders-scheduler-lock"]     # one specific lease, nothing else
    verbs: ["get", "update"]
  - apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["leases"]
    verbs: ["create"]                            # create cannot be name-scoped

IRSA: AWS access without keys. IAM Roles for Service Accounts lets a pod assume an IAM role using a projected OIDC token, so there are no AWS access keys anywhere: not in a Secret, not in an env var, not in the image.

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/orders-api-prod

The trust policy on the IAM role restricts it to exactly this ServiceAccount in exactly this namespace:

JSON
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "oidc.eks.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE:sub": "system:serviceaccount:shop:orders-api",
        "oidc.eks.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLED539D4633E53DE1B71EXAMPLE:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
      }
    }
  }]
}

The AWS SDK v3 picks this up automatically through the default credential chain; no code change. Credentials are short-lived and rotated by the SDK. The permission policy attached to that role should be scoped to specific resources (one S3 prefix, one Secrets Manager path), because "the pod can read every bucket in the account" is the failure this feature exists to prevent. EKS Pod Identity is the newer equivalent with simpler setup and the same model.

Pod Security Standards and the security context. PSS replaced PodSecurityPolicy; it is enforced by an admission controller configured per namespace with three levels: privileged, baseline, restricted.

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted        # warn on kubectl apply
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted       # audit log entries

And the pod-level settings that satisfy restricted:

YAML
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1001                 # matches the USER in the Dockerfile
        runAsGroup: 1001
        fsGroup: 1001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault          # blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls
      containers:
        - name: api
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]             # a Node process on port 3000 needs none
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }              # writable scratch
            - { name: cache, mountPath: /app/.cache }
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 256Mi }
        - name: cache
          emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 128Mi }

Each line earns its place. runAsNonRoot means a container escape lands as an unprivileged user rather than as root on the node. readOnlyRootFilesystem means an attacker cannot drop a binary or modify your code in place; it requires emptyDir mounts for anything that writes (/tmp for uploads, sharp's cache, some npm tooling). drop: ["ALL"] removes capabilities like NET_RAW (used for packet crafting and ARP spoofing) and CHOWN; a web API needs none of them. allowPrivilegeEscalation: false blocks setuid binaries from gaining privileges.

Image pull secrets and provenance. For a private registry that is not ECR-with-IRSA:

Shell
kubectl -n shop create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=deploy \
  --docker-password="$TOKEN" \
  --docker-email=devops@example.com
YAML
    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: regcred
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/orders-api@sha256:9f2b1c...   # digest, not tag
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

Pinning by digest rather than tag makes the deployed artifact immutable and verifiable; a tag can be repointed at different content. On EKS with ECR, the node's instance role usually grants pull access and no pull secret is needed at all, which is one fewer credential to rotate. Beyond that: scan images in CI (Trivy, Grype) and fail the build on fixable criticals, and consider signing with cosign and enforcing signatures with a policy controller (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) so only images your pipeline built can run.

Practical example

orders-api in production: dedicated ServiceAccount with automountServiceAccountToken: false and an IRSA annotation for one S3 prefix and one Secrets Manager path; restricted Pod Security on the namespace; non-root UID 1001, read-only root filesystem with two emptyDir mounts; all capabilities dropped; default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allows for DNS, RDS, Redis, Kafka and the ingress controller; images pulled from ECR by digest, scanned in CI, and signed.

NestJS example

Application-level security must line up with the pod's constraints, or the pod will not start:

TypeScript
// src/main.ts (excerpt)
import helmet from 'helmet';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

app.use(helmet());                      // security headers at the app layer
app.useGlobalPipes(
  new ValidationPipe({
    whitelist: true,                    // strip unknown properties
    forbidNonWhitelisted: true,         // reject requests that send them
    transform: true,
  }),
);

// Bind on 3000, not 80: a non-root user cannot bind ports below 1024,
// and runAsNonRoot means the container would crash on startup.
await app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0');

And the Dockerfile side must agree with runAsUser:

Dockerfile
# Part 44 covers this in depth; the numeric UID must match the securityContext.
RUN addgroup -g 1001 -S nodejs && adduser -u 1001 -S nestjs -G nodejs
USER 1001
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

If the image's USER is root and the pod says runAsNonRoot: true, the kubelet refuses to start the container with CreateContainerConfigError: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root. That error message is exact and is the fastest security feedback loop you will get.

PostgreSQL example

Defence in depth from the database's side, so that a compromised pod is still limited:

SQL
-- Application role cannot change the schema (see 27.7) and cannot read other databases.
REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE orders FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE orders TO orders_app;

-- Restrict where the app role may connect from (RDS parameter groups and security
-- groups do the network half; this is the credential half).
ALTER ROLE orders_app CONNECTION LIMIT 240;   -- matches maxReplicas * pool size

-- Row level security for a multi-tenant table, so an SQL injection in one tenant's
-- request cannot read another tenant's rows.
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

The security group on RDS should allow 5432 only from the cluster's node subnets, so even a NetworkPolicy bypass does not reach the database from elsewhere in the VPC.

Production scenario

A platform enforces this with policy rather than review: a Kyverno cluster policy rejects any pod without runAsNonRoot, with privileged: true, mounting hostPath, using the default ServiceAccount, or referencing an image by tag rather than digest in production namespaces. Violations fail at kubectl apply time with a message naming the rule, so developers find out in CI rather than in a quarterly audit. Rolling this out took three months, mostly spent fixing images that wrote to their root filesystem.

Failure scenario

A dependency in an internal admin service has a server-side request forgery bug. An attacker uses it to reach 169.254.169.254, the EC2 instance metadata service, and retrieves credentials for the node's IAM role, which has broad permissions because it was created before IRSA and was never trimmed. From there they list S3 buckets across the account.

The three controls that would each have stopped it: IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1 (so a pod cannot reach the node's metadata service at all), a NetworkPolicy denying egress to the link-local range, and a node role with no application permissions because every application uses IRSA. All three were implemented afterwards. The general lesson: the blast radius of an application bug is decided by the cluster's configuration, before the bug exists.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy. Policies apply cleanly and do nothing. Verify with an actual connection test, not by reading YAML.
  • Forgetting DNS egress in a default-deny namespace: everything fails with ENOTFOUND and the cause is not obvious.
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem without emptyDir for /tmp: uploads, sharp, and some npm tooling fail with EROFS.
  • runAsNonRoot with a root image: CreateContainerConfigError.
  • Binding to port 80 as non-root: EACCES; use 3000 and let the Service map 80.
  • A wide IRSA policy ("s3:" on "") is only marginally better than static keys.
  • The default ServiceAccount token mounted everywhere because nobody set automountServiceAccountToken: false.
  • Secrets readable via exec by anyone with debug permissions (45.8).
  • hostNetwork or hostPID in a pod spec bypasses most isolation.
  • NetworkPolicy and health probes. Probes come from the kubelet on the node, not from a pod; policies that only allow pod sources can break them on some CNIs.
  • Image pull secrets per namespace. They are namespaced; a new namespace silently gets ImagePullBackOff.
  • Egress policies and third-party IPs that change without notice, causing intermittent failures nobody attributes to the network policy.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume the application will be compromised eventually, and they design so that the compromise is boring: a pod that cannot become root, cannot write to its filesystem, cannot reach anything but its three dependencies, holds no Kubernetes token, and has AWS permissions covering one bucket prefix. They implement it once in the shared Helm chart so every service gets it by default, and they enforce it with admission policy rather than review, because review does not scale and does not run at 2 a.m.

They pin images by digest so the deployed artifact is the audited artifact. They keep the network policy for DNS in the base chart because everyone forgets it. And they measure this work in blast radius, not in checkbox counts: "if this pod is owned, what exactly can the attacker reach?" is the only question that matters.

Common mistakes

  • No NetworkPolicy at all, so any compromised pod can scan the whole cluster.
  • Default-deny without allowing DNS, then reverting the whole policy in frustration.
  • Running containers as root because "it was easier".
  • Using the default ServiceAccount with an auto-mounted token.
  • Static AWS keys in a Secret instead of IRSA.
  • Deploying by mutable tag, so what runs is not necessarily what was scanned.
  • Treating cluster security as the platform team's problem while writing the pod spec yourself.

Interview questions

  1. Describe a default-deny NetworkPolicy and what you must explicitly allow.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: empty podSelector with both policy types, then DNS to kube-dns, then the specific dependencies; IP-based rules for external services; the CNI must support it.
  2. How does a pod get AWS permissions without access keys?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: IRSA (or EKS Pod Identity): OIDC provider, ServiceAccount annotation, trust policy conditioned on system:serviceaccount:ns:name, SDK default credential chain, short-lived credentials.
  3. What does readOnlyRootFilesystem break and how do you fix it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: temp writes; mount emptyDir at /tmp and any cache path; verify the app's write paths.
  4. Why is automountServiceAccountToken: false worth setting?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: removes a cluster credential from the container filesystem; most apps never call the API; limits post-exploitation.
  5. What are Pod Security Standards and how are they applied?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: privileged, baseline, restricted; namespace labels for enforce, audit and warn; replacement for PodSecurityPolicy.
  6. An attacker gets code execution in a pod. Walk through what they can reach in a well-configured cluster.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no root, read-only filesystem, no capabilities, no cluster token, NetworkPolicy limits to three dependencies, IRSA scoped to one prefix, IMDSv2 hop limit blocks node credentials.

Practical exercise

Apply the default-deny plus allow policies to the shop namespace and verify from a debug pod that PostgreSQL is reachable, api.github.com is not, and DNS works. Then remove the DNS policy and observe the failure mode from the application's logs. Add the restricted security context and fix whatever breaks (expect at least EROFS on /tmp). Finally, set up IRSA for a bucket read, then try to read a different bucket and capture the AccessDenied. Acceptance criteria: a written table of allowed and denied connections tested from inside a pod, the app running as UID 1001 with a read-only root filesystem, and the scoped IRSA denial captured.

45.17 Observability in Kubernetes

Concept

Observability in Kubernetes has two layers, and confusing them wastes hours during incidents. The application layer is your logs, metrics and traces, which are the same as anywhere else except that they must go to stdout and carry pod identity. The platform layer is what Kubernetes itself knows: events, pod states, restart counts, resource usage, scheduling decisions. Most incidents are diagnosed by looking at the platform layer first (why is this pod not running?) and the application layer second (why is this code slow?).

Why does it exist?

Pods are ephemeral. A crashed pod's filesystem is gone, its logs with it. There is no server to SSH into, no /var/log/app.log that persists, and the thing you want to look at was deleted 30 seconds ago by the controller that replaced it. Everything you will need must be shipped off the node before the pod dies.

Mental model

Imagine a courier company where vans are constantly replaced. You cannot inspect a van after it breaks down, because it has already been scrapped. So every van transmits its telemetry continuously to a central system, and the depot keeps a log of every event it ever caused: dispatched, refused entry, sent for repair. Debugging is reading those two streams, never examining the van.

How it works

Logs: stdout, structured, shipped. The container writes JSON lines to stdout. The container runtime writes them to /var/log/pods/... on the node. A DaemonSet agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Promtail) reads those files, adds Kubernetes metadata (namespace, pod, container, labels) and ships them to Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch.

The rules that follow from that pipeline:

  • Never write to a file inside the container. It fills ephemeral storage, gets the pod evicted, and nobody can read it.
  • One JSON object per line. A multi-line stack trace becomes ten unrelated log entries unless your agent is configured to join them, so serialise errors into a single line with the stack as a field.
  • Node-level rotation is real. The kubelet rotates container logs at 10 MB by default and keeps 5 files; kubectl logs can only show what is still on disk.
  • Log volume costs money and CPU. At 800 RPS, one access-log line per request is 69 million lines a day. Sample successful requests, keep all errors.
TypeScript
// src/observability/http-logger.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { logger } from '../logging/logger.config';

@Injectable()
export class HttpLoggerMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
    const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
    res.on('finish', () => {
      const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6;
      // Sample: all errors and slow requests, 1 in 20 of the rest.
      const interesting = res.statusCode >= 400 || ms > 500;
      if (!interesting && Math.random() > 0.05) return;
      logger.info({
        method: req.method,
        route: (req as any).route?.path ?? req.path,
        status: res.statusCode,
        duration_ms: Math.round(ms),
        trace_id: req.header('x-request-id'),
        // pod, namespace, node and version come from the logger base (27.8)
      });
    });
    next();
  }
}

Metrics: ServiceMonitor. With the Prometheus Operator, you do not edit Prometheus configuration; you create a ServiceMonitor and the operator generates the scrape config:

YAML
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack     # must match the Prometheus instance's selector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api    # selects the SERVICE, not the pods
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames: [shop]
  endpoints:
    - port: http                            # the NAMED port on the Service
      path: /internal/metrics
      interval: 30s
      scrapeTimeout: 10s
      relabelings:
        - sourceLabels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_name]
          targetLabel: pod

The two failures here are always the same: the release label does not match what the Prometheus instance selects (so the ServiceMonitor is ignored and no error appears anywhere), and port refers to a port name on the Service that does not exist. Check Status -> Targets in the Prometheus UI; a missing target is the symptom.

kubectl describe and events are first-class debugging tools. Events are the cluster telling you what it did and why it could not do something. They are, more often than not, the answer:

Shell
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p     # events at the bottom: scheduling, pulls, probes, kills
kubectl -n shop get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -40
kubectl -n shop get events --field-selector type=Warning,involvedObject.name=orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p

Events you should be able to recognise on sight: FailedScheduling (with the reason: insufficient cpu, node affinity, taints), Failed with ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff, BackOff (restarting failed container), Unhealthy (a probe failed, with the probe's response), Killing, Evicted, FailedMount, FailedCreate (quota). Note the trap: events expire after one hour by default. The event explaining last night's incident is gone by morning unless you ship events to your log store, which every mature platform does (Fluent Bit's kubernetes_events input, or the event-exporter project).

kubectl logs --previous after a crash. When a container restarts, its old logs are still on the node for one generation:

Shell
kubectl -n shop logs orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p --previous          # the CRASHED container's output
kubectl -n shop logs orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p -c api --previous --tail=200
kubectl -n shop logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api --tail=50 --max-log-requests=10   # all pods
kubectl -n shop logs -f deployment/orders-api --since=10m         # follow one pod of a Deployment

--previous is the single most useful flag in kubectl logs, because the pod you are looking at is the new one and its logs are clean; the reason for the crash is in the previous container.

kubectl top for a quick answer:

Shell
kubectl -n shop top pods --sort-by=memory
kubectl top nodes
kubectl -n shop top pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p --containers

It reads Metrics Server, so it shows a smoothed 15-second-resolution value: good for "which pod is huge right now", useless for a 2-second spike that caused an OOMKill.

The metrics that matter, with the queries and the reason each one earns a dashboard panel:

Signal Query (kube-state-metrics / cAdvisor) Why it matters
Restarts increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m]) > 0 Any restart is either a crash or a liveness kill; both need explaining
OOMKills kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"} Memory is being exceeded; sizing or unbounded work (45.12)
CPU throttling rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]) / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]) Explains p99 latency that has no cause in the code
Pending pods kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"} > 0 for 5m Capacity, quota, affinity or volume problem; the autoscaler is stuck
Ready endpoints kube_endpoint_address_available{endpoint="orders-api"} The number that says whether anyone can reach you at all
Replicas versus desired kube_deployment_status_replicas_available < kube_deployment_spec_replicas A rollout is stuck or pods are failing
HPA at max kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_status_current_replicas == kube_horizontalpodautoscaler_spec_max_replicas You are capacity-limited and nobody was told
Memory working set versus limit container_memory_working_set_bytes / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes > 0.9 An OOMKill you can see coming
Node conditions kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 Node problems before they become pod problems
PVC usage kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes / kubelet_volume_stats_capacity_bytes < 0.15 Disk full is a slow, entirely predictable outage

If you can only have five alerts, take: restarts, OOMKills, pending pods for over 5 minutes, available endpoints below expected, and available replicas below desired for over 10 minutes. Those five catch the overwhelming majority of Kubernetes-caused incidents.

Production scenario

A platform ships stdout to Loki via Fluent Bit (roughly 40 GB a day across 620 pods after sampling), scrapes 180 ServiceMonitors into Prometheus with 15-day local retention and a year in Thanos, exports Kubernetes events into Loki so post-mortems can look back past the one-hour window, and traces with OpenTelemetry to Tempo. The on-call dashboard for a service has exactly six panels: RPS and error rate, p50/p95/p99, pod count versus HPA bounds, restarts and OOMKills, CPU throttling, and ready endpoints. Mean time to identify a Kubernetes-level cause is under 4 minutes, because the first three questions (is it running, is it ready, is it being throttled or killed) are all on one screen.

Failure scenario

At 08:50 an API is slow: p99 has gone from 150 ms to 2.4 s. Application traces show the time is inside the service, not in the database. CPU is at 40%, memory is fine, no restarts, no errors in logs. Twenty minutes of dead ends.

The answer was on a panel nobody had: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total showed 34% of periods throttled. A limits.cpu: 500m had been added two days earlier by a well-meaning cleanup pull request that "added missing resource limits everywhere". CPU utilisation looked innocent at 40% because the average includes all the periods where the container was stopped and using nothing. Removing the CPU limit restored p99 within a minute.

The lesson: the platform can degrade your application in ways that are invisible in application metrics. Throttling, evictions, node pressure and network policy drops all produce symptoms that look like application problems. That is why the platform-layer panels sit on the same dashboard as the application ones.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Events expire after an hour, so the explanation for a nightly failure is gone by 09:00 unless exported.
  • kubectl logs only shows what is on the node. After a pod is deleted and its node reclaimed, the logs exist only in your log store.
  • --previous fails if the container has never restarted, or if two restarts have happened (only one generation is kept).
  • Logging to a file fills ephemeral storage and gets the pod evicted with The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage.
  • High-cardinality metric labels (user id, order id, raw URL) will slowly kill Prometheus; the failure looks like a monitoring outage during an incident.
  • ServiceMonitor label mismatch: no target, no error, no metrics, no alert.
  • kubectl top unavailable because Metrics Server is not installed, which also means no CPU-based HPA.
  • Sidecar log duplication: a mesh proxy logs every request too, doubling volume.
  • Timestamps. Container logs carry the node's clock; clock skew across nodes makes cross-pod correlation confusing without a trace id.
  • Log agents lose data on node loss. Buffered lines that were not yet shipped are gone with the node; for audit-critical events, write to the database, not to a log.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They instrument at both layers and put them on the same dashboard, because during an incident nobody has time to correlate two tools. They ship events and logs off the node immediately, and they treat "I could not find out what happened" as a bug to fix in the platform, not as bad luck.

Their debugging order is fixed and platform-first: is the pod running, is it ready, has it restarted, was it OOMKilled, is it throttled, is it scheduled at all. Only then do they open application logs. They keep cardinality under control deliberately, sample logs so the bill is proportional to value, and they alert on the small set of platform signals that are always actionable rather than on everything the cluster emits.

Common mistakes

  • Writing logs to a file inside the container.
  • Multi-line stack traces shipped as separate log entries.
  • No structured logging, so you cannot filter by pod, route or trace id.
  • Never looking at events, and debugging application code when the answer was FailedScheduling.
  • Forgetting --previous and reading the healthy new container's logs after a crash.
  • Unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus metrics.
  • No alert on restarts or OOMKills, so pods flap for weeks unnoticed.

Interview questions

  1. A pod restarted an hour ago. How do you find out why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: describe pod last state and reason, logs --previous, events (and whether they have expired), OOMKill and exit code 137, restart count metric.
  2. Why must application logs go to stdout?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the runtime captures stdout; agents ship from the node; files inside containers are lost and fill ephemeral storage.
  3. How does Prometheus discover your pods?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor selecting a Service by label, named port, operator-generated scrape config, label matching the Prometheus instance.
  4. Which platform metrics do you alert on?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: restarts, OOMKills, pending pods, available endpoints, available versus desired replicas, throttling, node conditions; each with a reason.
  5. p99 is bad but CPU looks fine. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CFS throttling ratio, event loop lag, GC pauses, neighbour pressure on the node, network policy drops; average CPU hides throttled periods.
  6. How do you keep observability costs sane?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sample successful requests, keep errors, control label cardinality, tiered retention, drop noisy sidecar logs.

Practical exercise

Instrument orders-api with structured JSON logs including pod, namespace and node, plus Prometheus metrics with a route-pattern label. Create the ServiceMonitor and confirm the target appears in Prometheus. Then cause four failures and diagnose each using only kubectl and your dashboards, writing down the first command that revealed the cause: (1) a bad env var causing a boot crash, (2) a memory limit that OOMKills under load, (3) a CPU limit that throttles, (4) a readiness probe pointing at a wrong path. Finally set the log level to debug under load and measure the log volume per hour. Acceptance criteria: four causes each identified in under three commands, the throttling ratio graphed, and a log-volume estimate in GB per day at both log levels.

45.18 How a NestJS API actually gets deployed to Kubernetes

Concept

Everything in this part now goes into one place. This section is the complete production manifest set for orders-api: an HTTP API with 3 to 24 replicas, a BullMQ worker Deployment scaled on queue depth, a migration Job, and the objects that make them safe (Service, Ingress, HPA, PDB, NetworkPolicy). Every field is one you have already met; what follows is why each one is set the way it is, and then how CI drives it.

Why does it exist?

A manifest that omits probes, resources, a preStop hook, a PDB or an anti-affinity rule will work perfectly in staging and fail on the first node drain, the first deploy under load, or the first zone incident. This is the baseline that a senior engineer applies to every customer-facing service without being asked.

Mental model

Imagine a shop opening in a mall. The Deployment is the staff roster and the shop's fit-out. The Service is the unit number on the directory. The Ingress is the mall's main entrance and the sign pointing to you. The HPA is the rule for calling in extra staff. The PDB is your agreement with mall management about maintenance. The NetworkPolicy is which back corridors you are allowed to use. Miss one and the shop still opens, but something goes wrong the first busy weekend.

How it works

The Deployment. Every field annotated with its reason:

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
    app.kubernetes.io/component: api
    app.kubernetes.io/version: "1.42.0"
spec:
  # replicas is deliberately ABSENT: the HPA owns it (27.14).
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5              # five rollback targets, not the default ten
  minReadySeconds: 10                  # a pod must stay ready 10 s before the rollout advances
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600         # CI fails the deploy if no progress for 10 minutes
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1                      # one extra pod during the rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0                # never drop below the desired count: no capacity dip
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
        app.kubernetes.io/component: api
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "9c1f7a3e5b2d48c0a7e6f1b3d9c8e2a4"    # config change triggers a rollout (27.7)
        checksum/secret: "3b8d2f0a7c6e4915b2d8f1a0c7e39b46"
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: orders-api                 # IRSA-annotated (27.16)
      automountServiceAccountToken: false            # the app never calls the Kubernetes API
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60              # 15 s preStop + up to 45 s of draining (27.13)
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1001
        runAsGroup: 1001
        fsGroup: 1001
        seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
      topologySpreadConstraints:                     # 27.15: survive a zone loss
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api }
          matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:                             # prefer separate nodes, do not require it
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api }
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api@sha256:9f2b1c4e7a08d3f6b5c2e9a1d7f40b83c6e5a294f1d8b70e3c9a5f26d1b48e07
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 3000 }    # non-privileged port: non-root cannot bind 80
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: orders-api-config }
          env:
            - name: DB_PASSWORD
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: orders-api-secrets, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
            - name: JWT_SIGNING_KEY
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: orders-api-secrets, key: JWT_SIGNING_KEY } }
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
            - name: K8S_NAMESPACE
              valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.namespace } }
            - name: NODE_NAME
              valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: spec.nodeName } }
            - name: NODE_OPTIONS
              value: "--max-old-space-size=384"      # ~75% of the 512Mi limit (27.12)
            - name: GIT_SHA
              value: "3f9a1c2"
          startupProbe:                              # 120 s of boot grace, then liveness takes over
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 24
          livenessProbe:                             # cheap, no dependencies (27.11)
            httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
          readinessProbe:                            # own pool and Redis only
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 3
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }                # no CPU limit: avoid CFS throttling (27.12)
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"] }   # endpoint propagation (27.13)
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 256Mi }

Two decisions worth defending out loud in a review. No replicas field, because the HPA owns it and an apply would otherwise reset the count on every deploy. No CPU limit, because the request already guarantees a share and a limit only buys throttling; if your platform policy requires one, set it to 1000m, four times the request.

The Service. Nothing surprising, and that is the point:

YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api          # the ServiceMonitor selects on this (27.17)
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
  ports:
    - { name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http, protocol: TCP }

The Ingress, with the annotations that actually matter in production:

YAML
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip                    # straight to pod IPs, no NodePort hop
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443},{"HTTP":80}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abcd-1234
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /health/ready    # ready, not live
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-interval-seconds: "10"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthy-threshold-count: "2"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/unhealthy-threshold-count: "3"
    # Idle timeout above Node's keepAliveTimeout would cause 502s; Node is set to 65 s,
    # so the ALB must be BELOW that: 60 s. See 27.6.
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-attributes: idle_timeout.timeout_seconds=60
    # Deregistration delay must be covered by the preStop sleep (15 s).
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-group-attributes: deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds=15
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/wafv2-acl-arn: arn:aws:wafv2:eu-west-1:123456789012:regional/webacl/prod/abcd
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: api.shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: orders-api, port: { name: http } }

Body size on an ALB is fixed at 1 MB for the request line and headers but the body is unbounded, so upload limits belong in the app (bodyParser limits) or in NGINX ingress via proxy-body-size. With NGINX instead of ALB, the equivalent annotations are nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m", proxy-read-timeout: "60" and proxy-connect-timeout: "5".

The HPA:

YAML
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: orders-api }
  minReplicas: 3                        # one per zone; absorbs load while nodes are added
  maxReplicas: 24                       # 24 * DB_POOL_MAX 10 = 240 connections of 500 (27.14)
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_requests_per_second }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "120" }
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 75 }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }
        - { type: Pods, value: 4, periodSeconds: 30 }
      selectPolicy: Max
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - { type: Percent, value: 25, periodSeconds: 60 }

The migration Job, run as a Helm pre-upgrade hook so the schema is ready before new pods start (45.10). The worker Deployment is the same shape as the API with three differences: no Service or Ingress, no HTTP probes (use an exec liveness that touches a heartbeat file the worker writes), and a much longer grace period:

YAML
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-worker
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-worker
spec:
  # replicas absent: KEDA owns it.
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-worker }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-worker }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: orders-worker
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300            # longest job is 4 minutes (27.13)
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1001
        seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
      tolerations:
        - { key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: workers, effect: NoSchedule }
      nodeSelector:
        workload: workers                           # dedicated node pool (27.15)
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api@sha256:9f2b1c4e7a08d3f6b5c2e9a1d7f40b83c6e5a294f1d8b70e3c9a5f26d1b48e07
          command: ["node", "dist/worker.js"]       # same image, different entrypoint
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: orders-api-config }
          env:
            - name: DB_PASSWORD
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: orders-api-secrets, key: DB_PASSWORD } }
            - name: NODE_OPTIONS
              value: "--max-old-space-size=768"
          livenessProbe:
            exec:
              # The worker touches this file on every event loop tick group; if it stops,
              # the process is wedged and a restart is the right remedy.
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "test $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y /tmp/heartbeat) )) -lt 60"]
            periodSeconds: 30
            failureThreshold: 3
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi }
            limits: { memory: 1Gi }
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 512Mi }

Its KEDA ScaledObject (45.14) scales it from 1 to 25 on bull:orders:wait length. The PodDisruptionBudget for each:

YAML
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1                     # not minAvailable: works at any replica count
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api }

The NetworkPolicy is the default-deny plus explicit allows from 45.16. That is the complete set: Deployment, Service, Ingress, HPA, PDB, NetworkPolicy, ConfigMap, ExternalSecret, ServiceAccount, ServiceMonitor, migration Job, worker Deployment, ScaledObject, worker PDB. Fourteen objects, all of them generated from one Helm chart with about 60 lines of values per environment.

Practical example

The CI/CD flow from a merged pull request to serving traffic:

YAML
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt)
      - name: Build and push
        run: |
          IMAGE="$ECR/orders-api"
          docker build -t "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" .
          docker push "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
          DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}")
          echo "digest=$DIGEST" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Deploy
        run: |
          helm upgrade --install orders-api ./charts/orders-api \
            --namespace shop \
            --values ./charts/orders-api/values-prod.yaml \
            --set image.digest="${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}" \
            --set version="${GITHUB_SHA::7}" \
            --wait --timeout 10m --atomic          # --atomic rolls back automatically on failure

      - name: Verify
        run: |
          kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=600s
          kubectl -n shop get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api

The commands you use to watch a rollout, in the order you reach for them:

Shell
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=600s     # blocks; the CI gate
kubectl -n shop get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api -w        # live pod states
kubectl -n shop get rs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api             # old and new ReplicaSets
kubectl -n shop describe deployment orders-api | tail -20               # conditions and events
kubectl -n shop get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30
kubectl -n shop logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api --tail=50 --max-log-requests=10
watch -n2 'kubectl -n shop get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders-api -o wide'

A full rollback walkthrough. At 15:12 a deploy goes out; at 15:14 the error rate rises from 0.1% to 6%. Not a crash, not a probe failure: a logic bug producing 500s on one endpoint, so the rollout completed successfully and Kubernetes is perfectly happy.

Shell
# 1. Confirm what is running and since when.
kubectl -n shop rollout history deployment/orders-api
# REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
# 12        image sha-3f9a1c2
# 13        image sha-b41c9d2   <- current, bad

kubectl -n shop describe deployment orders-api | grep -i image

# 2. Roll back. This scales revision 12's ReplicaSet up and 13 down, with the same
#    rolling strategy: maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0, readiness gated. No downtime.
kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/orders-api
# or, to a specific revision:
kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/orders-api --to-revision=12

# 3. Watch it complete.
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=300s

# 4. Confirm the version actually serving.
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/orders-api -- wget -qO- localhost:3000/internal/version

# With Helm, the equivalent, which also reverts ConfigMaps and every other object:
helm -n shop history orders-api
helm -n shop rollback orders-api 12 --wait --timeout 5m

Elapsed time from decision to healthy: about 90 seconds for 6 replicas. Three things this walkthrough assumes, and each is a prerequisite you must have arranged in advance: revisionHistoryLimit above 0 so a rollback target exists; the previous image still present in the registry (never delete tags that are still in a rollout history); and the database schema still compatible with the old code, which is the one Kubernetes cannot help with. rollout undo reverts pods, never data. If revision 13 ran a migration that dropped a column, rolling back the pods gives you the old code against a schema it cannot use, and you have turned a 6% error rate into a 100% one. That is why migrations are expand-only and why Parts 24, 25 matter more than this chapter for deploy safety.

Production scenario

This exact setup at a mid-sized retailer: 6 to 18 API pods, 2 to 20 worker pods, 40 deploys a week, median rollout 2 minutes 10 seconds, zero-downtime by measurement (a synthetic checker at 5 RPS records no failures across deploys for 14 months). Automatic Helm rollbacks fire roughly twice a month, always for readiness failures caused by config. Manual rollbacks (like the one above, for a logic bug) happen about once a quarter and take under two minutes because the runbook is four commands.

Failure scenario

At 11:40 a deploy hangs: rollout status prints Waiting for deployment "orders-api" rollout to finish: 1 out of 6 new replicas have been updated for eight minutes, then --atomic rolls it back. kubectl describe pod on the new pod shows Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503, and kubectl logs shows RedisConnectionError: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND orders-redis-primary. The values file for production had been updated with a Redis hostname from a planned migration that had not happened yet. Old pods served throughout; customers saw nothing; the fix was a one-line revert. This is what a correctly configured rollout is supposed to feel like: a failed pipeline, not an incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • replicas present in the chart while an HPA exists: every deploy resets the count and the HPA scales back, a sawtooth under load.
  • --atomic without --timeout waits the default 5 minutes, which is shorter than some rollouts.
  • Image by tag rather than digest makes rollbacks and audits unreliable (45.21).
  • Migration hook that fails leaves the release in a pending-upgrade state; helm rollback is needed before the next deploy.
  • rollout undo after two rapid deploys may go back to a revision you did not expect; check history first.
  • A missing ImagePullSecret in a new namespace looks like a broken deploy but is a credentials problem.
  • Smoke tests that hit the load balancer may reach old pods mid-rollout; test the version endpoint, not just a 200.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They keep one chart and one deploy path for every service, so the twelfth service inherits every lesson from the first eleven. They gate CI on rollout status and make failure automatic (--atomic), because a human deciding whether to roll back at 15:14 is slower and worse than a pipeline that already did.

They rehearse rollback. A rollback command nobody has run is not a rollback plan. And they know exactly which failures Kubernetes can fix (a crashing pod, a failing probe, a bad config) and which it cannot (a schema change, a corrupted cache, a message published in a new format), and they make the second category impossible by design rather than recoverable by heroics.

Common mistakes

  • Deploying with kubectl apply from a laptop instead of a pipeline.
  • No rollout status gate, so CI is green while the rollout is stuck.
  • Rolling back pods and assuming the database came with them.
  • Deleting old image tags, so rollback targets do not exist.
  • Copying a manifest without probes, resources, preStop or a PDB.
  • One giant manifest file per service instead of a templated chart.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through deploying a NestJS API to Kubernetes with zero downtime.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: image by digest, migrations as a pre-upgrade Job, rolling update with maxUnavailable: 0, readiness gating, preStop and grace period, PDB, topology spread, rollout status in CI with automatic rollback.
  2. Where does the HPA fit and what must the manifest omit?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: HPA owns replicas; omit it from the chart or the apply fights the autoscaler.
  3. A rollout is stuck at 1 of 6. Give me your first five commands.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rollout status, get pods, describe pod, logs (and --previous), get events.
  4. How do you roll back, and what does rollback not cover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rollout undo or helm rollback; scales the previous ReplicaSet with the same strategy; does not revert schema, data, or messages already published.
  5. Why pin an image by digest?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: immutability, reproducibility, the artifact scanned is the artifact deployed, tags can be repointed.

Practical exercise

Assemble the full object set for orders-api in a chart and deploy it to a test cluster. Run a load generator at 50 RPS with a synthetic checker recording every failure. Then perform, in order: a normal deploy, a deploy with a broken readiness probe (confirm automatic rollback), a kubectl rollout undo after a successful deploy, a node drain of the node hosting two pods, and a KEDA-driven worker scale-up by pushing 3,000 jobs. Acceptance criteria: zero failed requests across all five events, the automatic rollback triggered by --atomic, the drain respecting the PDB (visible in kubectl get pdb), and the worker replica count graphed against queue depth.

45.19 Helm and GitOps in practice

Concept

Helm is a templating and release system: a chart is a set of templated manifests plus a values.yaml, and helm upgrade renders them and applies the result as a versioned release. GitOps inverts the direction of deployment: instead of CI pushing to the cluster, an in-cluster agent (ArgoCD or Flux) pulls the desired state from Git and continuously reconciles the cluster towards it.

Why does it exist?

Fourteen objects per service times forty services is 560 YAML files, 90% identical. Templating removes the duplication and makes "every service gets a PDB" enforceable rather than aspirational. GitOps removes the other problem: a cluster whose actual state has drifted from what anyone believes is deployed, because six people ran kubectl apply from six laptops.

Mental model

Helm is a mail-merge: one letter template, many recipients, one variable list per recipient. GitOps is a thermostat: you set the target temperature in Git, and a device in the room continuously compares and corrects, whether or not anyone is watching.

How it works

The chart layout for this application:

Text
charts/orders-api/
  Chart.yaml                 # name, version, appVersion
  values.yaml                # defaults: the safe, production-shaped baseline
  values-dev.yaml            # 1 replica, debug logs, no HPA, relaxed resources
  values-staging.yaml        # 2 replicas, real probes, staging hostnames
  values-prod.yaml           # HPA 3 to 24, prod hostnames, strict policies
  templates/
    _helpers.tpl             # name, fullname, common labels
    deployment.yaml
    deployment-worker.yaml
    service.yaml
    ingress.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    scaledobject.yaml
    pdb.yaml
    configmap.yaml
    externalsecret.yaml
    serviceaccount.yaml
    servicemonitor.yaml
    networkpolicy.yaml
    job-migrate.yaml         # helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade
    NOTES.txt
YAML
# values-prod.yaml (excerpt): only what differs from the safe defaults
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api
  digest: ""                       # injected by CI, never a floating tag
replicaCount: null                 # HPA owns it
autoscaling:
  enabled: true
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 24                  # 24 * dbPoolMax(10) = 240 of RDS max_connections 500
  targetRps: 120
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
  limits: { memory: 512Mi }
nodeOptions: "--max-old-space-size=384"
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: api.shop.example.com
  certificateArn: arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abcd-1234
config:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  DB_HOST: orders-prod.cluster-abc123.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com
  DB_POOL_MAX: "10"
worker:
  enabled: true
  keda: { minReplicas: 1, maxReplicas: 25, listLength: 50 }

The discipline that makes this work: defaults in values.yaml are the production-safe values, and per-environment files only override what genuinely differs. The opposite (permissive defaults, hardened prod) means every new service ships insecure until someone remembers to harden it.

Two Helm behaviours worth knowing. helm upgrade --atomic rolls the release back automatically if it does not become ready within --timeout. And Helm does not delete objects that a previous chart version created but the new one does not render, unless the object is still tracked in the release; orphaned objects from a renamed template are a real source of confusion.

ArgoCD in one page. ArgoCD runs in the cluster, watches a Git repository, renders the chart, compares the result with live state, and either reports drift or corrects it.

YAML
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: orders-api-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: shop
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/k8s-manifests.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: charts/orders-api
    helm:
      valueFiles: [values-prod.yaml]
      parameters:
        - name: image.digest
          value: sha256:9f2b1c4e7a08d3f6b5c2e9a1d7f40b83c6e5a294f1d8b70e3c9a5f26d1b48e07
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true                    # delete objects removed from Git
      selfHeal: true                 # revert manual kubectl changes
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=false
      - PruneLast=true
    retry:
      limit: 3
      backoff: { duration: 30s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 5m }

The flow becomes: CI builds and pushes the image, then commits the new digest to the manifests repository. ArgoCD notices within seconds (or immediately via webhook), renders, syncs, and reports health. What you gain: the repository is the single source of truth, drift is visible and auto-corrected (selfHeal), rollback is git revert, the audit trail is the Git history, and CI no longer needs cluster credentials, which removes the most dangerous secret in your pipeline.

What it costs: an extra system to run and upgrade, a slightly indirect debugging path ("why is this not deploying?" is now an ArgoCD question), and the need for discipline about selfHeal, which will cheerfully undo an emergency manual fix 30 seconds after you make it. During an incident, pause auto-sync before hand-editing anything.

Kustomize as the alternative. Kustomize takes plain YAML and applies overlays: a base/ with real manifests, and overlays/prod/ with patches. It is built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k), has no templating language and no release state, and produces manifests that are readable as YAML rather than as a template.

Helm Kustomize
Mechanism Go templates plus values Strategic-merge and JSON patches on plain YAML
Learning curve Template syntax, _helpers.tpl, quoting Patch semantics, less to learn
Third-party software The standard: most vendors ship charts Awkward; usually wrap a rendered chart
Release state and rollback helm history, helm rollback None; rollback is git revert plus apply
Conditionals and loops Yes, and easily overused Deliberately absent
Best for Reusable, parameterised, distributable apps A handful of your own apps across environments

The common production answer: Helm for third-party components (ingress controller, cert-manager, kube-prometheus-stack, KEDA) because that is how they are distributed, and either tool for your own services. Many teams end up with one shared internal chart used by every service, which is Helm's real value here: not templating, but standardisation.

Production scenario

A k8s-manifests repository holds one ArgoCD Application per service per environment, generated by an ApplicationSet from a list. Forty services, three environments, 120 Applications. CI's only cluster interaction is committing an image digest; it holds no kubeconfig. A production deploy is a commit, visible and revertable. Drift detection catches roughly two manual changes a month, auto-reverts them, and posts to Slack, which has ended the "who changed this?" genre of conversation entirely.

Failure scenario

At 22:30 an engineer fixes an incident by editing a ConfigMap directly and restarting the Deployment. Service recovers. Forty seconds later ArgoCD's selfHeal reverts the ConfigMap to the Git version and the incident returns, now more confusing because the engineer knows they fixed it. Ten minutes are lost before someone notices the ArgoCD sync events. The fix, added to the runbook: pause auto-sync (argocd app set orders-api --sync-policy none) before manual changes, and always follow an emergency change with a Git commit within the hour. GitOps is a strong guarantee, and strong guarantees are inconvenient exactly when you want to break the rules.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • selfHeal reverting emergency fixes, as above.
  • prune: true deleting an object you created out of band and depended on.
  • Helm release stuck in pending-upgrade after a failed hook; helm rollback is required before the next attempt.
  • Values drift between environments: staging works, production does not, because a key was added to only one file. Schema-validate values (values.schema.json).
  • Chart version and app version confusion in Chart.yaml, so nobody can tell what is deployed.
  • Secrets in values files committed to Git; use ESO or SOPS.
  • ArgoCD out of sync forever because a mutating webhook or a controller changes a field the chart also sets (a classic with replicas and HPAs; use ignoreDifferences).
  • Rendered manifests that differ from what you reviewed; always run helm template in CI and diff it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They standardise once: one internal chart with production-safe defaults, so every new service is born with probes, resources, a PDB, a NetworkPolicy and a ServiceMonitor. They keep values files small and reviewable and put the reasoning for numbers (maxReplicas and connection budget) in comments next to them.

They prefer GitOps because it removes cluster credentials from CI and makes drift visible, and they accept its inconvenience during incidents by writing the pause step into the runbook. They diff rendered manifests in CI, because a template change that quietly drops a securityContext is invisible in a values diff.

Common mistakes

  • Charts with permissive defaults so every new service ships insecure.
  • Secrets in values.yaml.
  • helm upgrade without --wait or --atomic, so a broken release is "successful".
  • Manual kubectl edit in a GitOps cluster.
  • Overusing template conditionals until nobody can predict the output.
  • Not pinning chart versions of third-party components, so an upgrade arrives by surprise.

Interview questions

  1. Helm or Kustomize?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: mechanism, release state and rollback, third-party distribution, complexity; a defensible either-way answer with reasons.
  2. What does GitOps change about your CI pipeline?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CI stops needing cluster credentials; it commits a digest; the in-cluster agent reconciles; rollback is a revert; drift is detected and healed.
  3. selfHeal fought your emergency fix. What is the process?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pause auto-sync, fix, commit, resume; runbook step; why the guarantee is worth the inconvenience.
  4. How do you keep environments from drifting?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: production-safe defaults, minimal overrides, values schema validation, rendered-manifest diffs in CI, one chart per service family.
  5. How do you manage secrets with GitOps?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: never in Git; External Secrets Operator or SOPS/Sealed Secrets; the tradeoffs of each.

Practical exercise

Convert the manifests from 45.18 into a chart with values.yaml, values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml, and verify with helm template ... | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -. Add a values.schema.json requiring image.digest and resources.requests.memory, and confirm a deploy fails without them. Then install ArgoCD in a test cluster, create an Application with selfHeal: true, edit a live ConfigMap with kubectl, and time how long until it is reverted. Acceptance criteria: three environments rendering correctly from one chart, the schema rejecting an incomplete values file, and the self-heal reversion timed and explained.

45.20 A debugging runbook

Concept

Nearly every Kubernetes incident a backend engineer meets is one of about ten states. This is the table you memorise, followed by the walkthrough for each.

Symptom Most likely cause First command Usual fix
Pending No node with enough free requests; affinity or taint; PVC zone; quota kubectl describe pod (Events) Lower requests, add nodes, fix constraints, raise quota
ContainerCreating (stuck) Volume attach, image pull, CNI IP exhaustion, secret missing kubectl describe pod Fix mount, subnet IPs, secret name
CrashLoopBackOff App exits at boot: bad env var, missing config, port in use kubectl logs --previous Fix config, then redeploy
OOMKilled / exit 137 Memory limit exceeded; no --max-old-space-size kubectl describe pod (Last State) Fix unbounded work, set the flag, size correctly
ImagePullBackOff Wrong tag, wrong registry, missing pull secret, no ECR permission kubectl describe pod (Events) Fix reference or credentials
Running but 0/1 READY Readiness failing: dependency, wrong path or port, auth on probe kubectl describe pod + logs Fix the check or the dependency
Evicted Node memory or ephemeral-storage pressure kubectl describe pod + describe node Set requests, stop writing files, add capacity
Error / Completed on a Job Non-zero or zero exit from a batch task kubectl logs job/<name> Fix the script
Terminating (stuck) Long grace period, finalizer, unresponsive node kubectl describe pod Wait, remove finalizer, --force last
High p99, CPU looks fine CFS throttling, event loop lag, noisy neighbour Throttling metric Raise or remove the CPU limit

Pending. The scheduler could not place the pod. The reason is always in the events:

Shell
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p | tail -20
# Warning  FailedScheduling  0/12 nodes are available:
#   5 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: workers},
#   4 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints.

Read the sentence literally: it counts nodes per reason and they sum to your cluster size. Insufficient cpu means no node has that much unreserved request free, regardless of actual usage. Check the arithmetic and the autoscaler:

Shell
kubectl describe node ip-10-0-3-14 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu,MEM:.status.allocatable.memory'
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler --tail=50 | grep -i "scale.up\|no.scale"
kubectl -n shop describe resourcequota                # quota rejection looks similar

Fixes, in order of preference: lower an inflated request (most common real cause), let the autoscaler add a node (check its logs to see why it did not), relax a required anti-affinity to preferred, or add a toleration. For a PVC-related volume node affinity conflict, see 45.9.

CrashLoopBackOff from a bad env var. The container starts, exits non-zero, and the kubelet backs off (10 s, 20 s, 40 s, doubling to 5 minutes). The exact sequence:

Shell
kubectl -n shop get pods                                   # RESTARTS climbing
kubectl -n shop logs orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p --previous   # the CRASHED container's output
# Error: Config validation error: "DB_HOST" is not allowed to be empty

kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p      # Last State, Exit Code, Events
kubectl -n shop get configmap orders-api-config -o yaml | grep DB_HOST
kubectl -n shop get secret orders-api-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data}' | tr ',' '\n'   # KEYS only

# Verify what the pod actually received, without a shell in the app container:
kubectl -n shop debug orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p -it --image=busybox --target=api -- env | sort

Exit codes tell you a lot: 1 is a generic application error (read the logs), 137 is SIGKILL (OOM or grace-period expiry), 139 is a segfault (a native module), 143 is SIGTERM handled correctly, and 127 is "command not found" (a wrong command: or a missing binary in a distroless image). Note the pod-level distinction: a missing ConfigMap key gives CreateContainerConfigError, not CrashLoopBackOff, and the container never starts at all.

OOMKilled and exit code 137:

Shell
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p | grep -A6 "Last State"
#     Last State:     Terminated
#       Reason:       OOMKilled
#       Exit Code:    137
kubectl -n shop top pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=orders-api --containers
kubectl -n shop get pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'

There will be no application error and no stack trace: the process was killed between two instructions. Ask three questions in order: is --max-old-space-size set to about 75% of the limit (45.12); is there an unbounded operation (a query without LIMIT, a file read into a Buffer, an in-memory cache with no eviction); and is the limit simply too small for the real working set? Raise the limit only after answering the first two.

ImagePullBackOff:

Shell
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p | grep -A5 Events
# Failed to pull image "...:sha-b41c9d2": not found
# or: pull access denied, repository does not exist or may require authorization
aws ecr describe-images --repository-name orders-api --image-ids imageTag=sha-b41c9d2
kubectl -n shop get sa orders-api -o yaml | grep -A3 imagePullSecrets

Causes ranked by frequency: the tag does not exist (a CI push failed but the deploy ran anyway), the pull secret is missing in this namespace, the node role lacks ECR permissions, or a registry rate limit (Docker Hub's anonymous limit is the classic). ErrImagePull is the first attempt; ImagePullBackOff is the retry state.

Readiness failing and traffic disappearing:

Shell
kubectl -n shop get pods                    # 1/1 vs 0/1 in the READY column
kubectl -n shop get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=orders-api -o yaml | grep -c 'ready: true'
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p | grep -A3 "Readiness probe"
# Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

# Ask the pod directly, bypassing the Service and the Ingress:
kubectl -n shop port-forward pod/orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p 3000:3000 &
curl -s localhost:3000/health/ready | jq .
# {"status":"error","error":{"redis":{"status":"down","message":"timeout"}}}

The error object names the failing check, which is the entire reason for using Terminus rather than a bare return 'ok'. Zero ready endpoints means the ingress has nothing to route to and everything returns 503; see the incident in 45.11.

Evicted under node pressure:

Shell
kubectl -n shop get pods --field-selector status.phase=Failed
kubectl -n shop describe pod orders-api-old-xxxxx | head -20
# Status: Failed   Reason: Evicted
# Message: The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage.
#          Container api was using 4.2Gi, request is 0.
kubectl describe node ip-10-0-3-14 | grep -A5 Conditions      # MemoryPressure, DiskPressure

Evicted pods stay in the list as Failed objects until cleaned up. The two common causes: memory pressure evicting BestEffort or over-request pods (fix by setting requests, which also improves your QoS class), and ephemeral storage from logging to a file or writing large temporary uploads (fix by logging to stdout and setting sizeLimit on emptyDir).

CPU throttling:

PromQL
rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{pod=~"orders-api.*"}[5m])
  / rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{pod=~"orders-api.*"}[5m])

Above 0.25 and your latency graph is a picture of the CPU limit, not of your code. See 45.12 and the incident in 45.17.

DNS failures inside the cluster:

Shell
kubectl -n shop run dnsutils --rm -it --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.7 -- bash
  nslookup orders-api                          # same namespace, via search path
  nslookup orders-api.shop.svc.cluster.local   # fully qualified
  nslookup api.stripe.com.                     # trailing dot: skips the search path
  cat /etc/resolv.conf                         # nameserver, search list, ndots:5

kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=100 | grep -i error
kubectl -n kube-system top pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns

Ranked causes: a NetworkPolicy blocking UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system (45.16), a missing .namespace suffix in a cross-namespace name, CoreDNS overloaded or under-replicated (scale it, or deploy NodeLocal DNSCache), and the ndots:5 search-path tax on external names, which turns one lookup into five and shows up as mysterious 20 ms of added latency on every outbound call.

kubectl exec and port-forward techniques:

Shell
kubectl -n shop exec -it deploy/orders-api -- sh                        # a shell in one pod
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/orders-api -- node -e "console.log(process.memoryUsage())"
kubectl -n shop port-forward svc/orders-api 8080:80                     # through the Service
