kubectl -n shop port-forward pod/orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p 3000:3000     # one specific pod
kubectl -n shop port-forward svc/orders-redis 6379:6379                 # then redis-cli locally

# Distroless image with no shell: attach a debug container sharing its namespaces.
kubectl -n shop debug -it orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api
  # inside: curl localhost:3000/health/ready, dig, ss -tulpen, tcpdump

# Copy a heap snapshot out before the pod dies:
kubectl -n shop exec orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p -- \
  node -e "require('v8').writeHeapSnapshot('/tmp/heap.heapsnapshot')"
kubectl -n shop cp orders-api-b41c9d2-x7k2p:/tmp/heap.heapsnapshot ./heap.heapsnapshot

kubectl debug with an ephemeral container is the modern answer to "I cannot exec because the image has no shell", and it does not require rebuilding the image or weakening it. Remember that exec grants Secret access (45.8), so it should be an audited, break-glass permission rather than a daily one.

Practical exercise

Deliberately create all ten states above in a test namespace: a pod requesting 40 CPUs, a missing env var, a memory limit of 64Mi with a big query, a nonexistent image tag, a readiness probe on a wrong path, a pod writing 5 GB to /tmp, a Job exiting 1, a pod with a 600-second grace period, a CPU limit of 100m under load, and a NetworkPolicy blocking DNS. For each, record the first command that revealed the cause and the exact log or event line that named it. Acceptance criteria: a ten-row table of symptom, command, evidence and fix, produced without looking back at this section.

45.21 Edge cases and failure modes

  • A rolling update deploying a schema-incompatible version. Old and new pods run together for minutes against one database. A migration that renames or drops a column breaks whichever version does not expect it, and a rollback then breaks the other one. Expand and contract: add nullable, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, deploy, then drop in a later release. See Part 24 and Part 25.
  • Liveness restarting healthy but GC-paused pods. A major V8 GC on a large heap can pause 200 to 800 ms; with timeoutSeconds: 1 and failureThreshold: 3 on a busy pod, three unlucky pauses restart a healthy process, dropping in-flight requests and cold-starting caches. Use timeoutSeconds: 2 to 3, failureThreshold of 3 to 6, and keep /health/live free of any await.
  • Readiness dependency checks cascading an outage. Every replica checks the same dependency, so a slow dependency empties the Service in one probe cycle and the ingress returns 503 for endpoints that never needed it. Check only per-pod state; alert on available endpoints; consider serving degraded responses instead of leaving the load balancer.
  • Node drain without a PDB. kubectl drain evicts every pod on the node at once. Three replicas on two nodes with no PDB can go to one replica instantly, which then falls over under full load. A PDB with maxUnavailable: 1 makes the drain serial and slow, which is correct.
  • Long-lived WebSocket connections severed during a rollout. Endpoint removal does not close established connections, and preStop plus grace period only delays the inevitable: at exit, every socket on that pod drops. With 6 pods and a rollout, 100% of connections reconnect within a few minutes, all at once. Mitigations: send a server-initiated close with a reason during preStop, reconnect on the client with exponential backoff and jitter, keep session state in Redis so a reconnect lands anywhere, and consider a longer grace period so reconnects spread out.
  • Secrets rotated but pods not restarted. Environment variables are frozen at container start (45.7). A rotated database password takes effect only for new connections after a restart, producing intermittent authentication failures as pooled connections are recycled. Rotate with a dual-password window, then rollout restart, then retire the old credential; or use Reloader/checksum annotations to automate it.
  • A cluster upgrade removing a deprecated API version. Kubernetes removes APIs on a schedule (extensions/v1beta1 Ingress, policy/v1beta1 PDB, autoscaling/v2beta2 HPA are past examples). Manifests using a removed version fail to apply after the upgrade, and Helm releases whose stored manifests reference them can fail to upgrade at all. Run kubectl deprecations tooling (pluto, kubent) before every upgrade, and read the release notes for removals rather than features.
  • Ephemeral storage filling from logs. A container logging 3 GB a day to a file, or writing uploads to /tmp without cleanup, triggers DiskPressure and eviction, and it takes neighbouring pods with it. Log to stdout, set sizeLimit on every emptyDir, set ephemeral-storage requests and limits, and alert on node disk usage.
  • Sidecar startup ordering. A classic with service meshes: the app container starts before the proxy is ready, its first outbound calls fail, and the app crashes at boot. In the other direction, at shutdown the proxy exits first and the app's final calls fail. Kubernetes 1.29+ native sidecars (init containers with restartPolicy: Always) fix the ordering properly; before that, the workarounds are startup retries in the app and holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts.
  • Cross-AZ latency and its data-transfer bill. Spreading pods across three zones for availability means most calls between your services cross a zone: about 0.5 to 1.5 ms extra per hop, and in AWS roughly 0.01 USD per GB in each direction. A chatty service pair exchanging 10 TB a month across zones costs around 200 USD a month in transfer alone, and a chain of five services multiplies the latency. Mitigate with spec.trafficDistribution: PreferClose (or topology-aware routing) for services that do not need cross-zone balancing, while keeping the spread that protects you from a zone loss. This is a real tradeoff, not a bug: pay it deliberately.
  • HPA thrashing. Scaling up on a spiky metric, then down as soon as the spike passes, then up again, costs pod startups, cold caches and node churn, and each new pod's cold start temporarily raises the very metric driving the decision. Fix with scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, percentage policies, longer metric windows (a 2-minute rate, not 30 seconds), and a higher minReplicas.
  • Image tag latest making rollbacks meaningless. With latest, rollout undo restores a pod template whose image reference now resolves to different content, and two pods created a minute apart can run different code. imagePullPolicy: Always masks it further. Deploy by immutable digest, keep every deployed tag in the registry for at least the rollback window, and never use latest outside a laptop.
  • Zombie pods on an unresponsive node. When a node stops reporting, its pods are marked for deletion but the kubelet is not there to stop the containers. For a Deployment, replacements start after the eviction timeout (about 5 minutes by default) while the originals may still be running and writing. Anything that must be a singleton needs a lease or a database-level lock, not a replica count of 1.
  • kubectl apply fighting controllers. An HPA sets replicas, a mutating webhook injects a sidecar, a controller adds annotations; an apply that includes those fields flips them back and forth. Omit fields another controller owns, or use server-side apply with field ownership.
  • DNS ndots:5 on external calls. Every external hostname lookup tries four cluster-internal suffixes first, adding latency and CoreDNS load to every outbound HTTP call. Use a trailing dot in the hostname or set dnsConfig.options with ndots: 2.
  • Init containers holding the pod hostage. An init container that waits for a dependency ("wait until the database answers") stops the pod from ever starting when that dependency is slow, and it is not covered by a startup probe. Prefer handling the wait in the application, where you can log it, time-box it, and serve a not-ready status.

Senior Checklist — Part 45

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can decide honestly whether a team should use Kubernetes at all
  • I can write a production Deployment with probes, resources, preStop, security context and spread constraints from memory
  • I can explain what liveness, readiness and startup probes each do to traffic, and why liveness must never check a dependency
  • I can explain CPU throttling with cgroup quota arithmetic and why a CPU limit can worsen p99
  • I know why --max-old-space-size must be about 75% of the memory limit, and what happens when it is not set
  • I can describe the shutdown sequence exactly, including why a preStop sleep is required
  • I can size an HPA, including the database connection arithmetic behind maxReplicas
  • I can scale workers on queue depth or consumer lag with KEDA, and I know the partition-count ceiling
  • I can write a default-deny NetworkPolicy that does not break DNS
  • I can grant AWS access with IRSA instead of static keys
  • I can diagnose Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff, Evicted and readiness failures from kubectl alone
  • I can perform and have rehearsed a rollback, and I know what a rollback does not revert
  • I can explain why a rolling update forces backward-compatible schema changes

Part 45 — Key Takeaways

  • Kubernetes is a desired-state control loop, not a deployment tool; you describe what you want and controllers work continuously to make reality match. Its cost is real and a small team is often better served by ECS, Cloud Run or App Runner.
  • Readiness gates rollouts, controls traffic and is the most powerful lever in the system. Liveness restarts. Never let liveness depend on anything outside the process, and never let readiness depend on something every replica shares.
  • Requests decide scheduling; limits decide throttling and killing. CPU limits throttle in 100 ms windows and damage p99; memory limits kill instantly with exit code 137 and no stack trace.
  • Set --max-old-space-size to roughly 75% of the memory limit, or V8 will happily let the kernel kill your process before it bothers to collect garbage.
  • Graceful shutdown needs a preStop sleep because endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, plus enableShutdownHooks(), a grace period sized from the longest unit of work, and draining in the right order. It reduces how often you need idempotency; it never replaces it.
  • Configuration is part of the deployment artifact: validate it at boot with a schema, hash it into the pod template, and roll it out the way you roll out code. A Secret is base64, not encryption.
  • Spread replicas across zones with topology spread constraints and protect them with a PodDisruptionBudget, or your replica count is decoration during a node drain or a zone incident.
  • Autoscale on what describes the work: RPS or event loop lag for APIs, queue depth or consumer lag for workers. CPU is a poor proxy for I/O-bound Node.js. Scale up fast, scale down slowly, and always check what is downstream of the autoscaler.
  • Security is decided before the bug exists: non-root, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, no ServiceAccount token, default-deny NetworkPolicy, IRSA scoped to one prefix. Enforce it with admission policy, not with code review.
  • Debug platform-first: is it scheduled, is it running, is it ready, did it restart, was it OOMKilled, is it throttled. kubectl describe pod, events and kubectl logs --previous answer most incidents in three commands.
  • Deploy by immutable digest, gate CI on rollout status, roll back automatically, and rehearse the manual rollback. A rollback restores pods, never data, which is why every schema change must be backward compatible.
  • Run stateless workloads in Kubernetes and buy your databases managed, unless you can name the person who handles failover at 3 a.m. and you have restored a backup from scratch at least once.

  15. 46.15The Well-Architected pillars applied
  16. 46.16Infrastructure as code
  17. 46.17Edge cases and failure modes

The cloud is not a different discipline. It is the same engineering you already know (compute, storage, networking, failure) rented by the hour, with someone else's hands on the hardware. What changes is where the boundaries sit: which failures are yours to handle, which knobs exist, and what every decision costs per month. This part teaches the architectural concepts first and uses AWS as the concrete mapping because it is the platform you are most likely to meet. Every concept here has an equivalent on GCP and Azure; the names differ, the physics does not.

46.1 The cloud mental model

Concept

A cloud provider runs data centers around the world and sells slices of them through APIs. You describe what you want (a virtual machine with 4 vCPUs, a PostgreSQL database with a standby, a queue), the provider creates it in minutes, and you pay for what you use while it runs. The three ideas that shape every architecture on top of this are regions and availability zones (where things physically live), shared responsibility (which failures are yours), and managed versus self-managed (how much operations work you keep).

Why does it exist?

Before the cloud, adding a server meant a purchase order, a rack, a six-week lead time, and a capacity plan made a year in advance. You over-provisioned for the Diwali or Black Friday peak and paid for idle hardware the other eleven months. Failure handling was a second data center that half the companies never finished wiring. The cloud turns capacity into an API call with a per-hour price, which makes elasticity (grow for the peak, shrink after) and redundancy (a copy in another building) affordable for a five-person team.

Mental model

Imagine a region as a city and each availability zone as a separate power station district inside it. The districts are far enough apart that a fire or flood in one does not touch the others, but close enough that a phone call between them is instant. A region-wide event is something like a city-wide blackout: rare, but not impossible. Building in two districts protects you against the common failure (one building goes dark). Building in two cities protects you against the rare one, at several times the cost and complexity.

How it works

Regions. A region is a geographic area with its own independent set of services: us-east-1 (N. Virginia), eu-west-1 (Ireland), ap-south-1 (Mumbai), ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) and about thirty more. Resources are regional by default; an RDS instance in Mumbai does not exist in Ireland. Data does not leave a region unless you move it, which is why regions matter for data-residency law as much as for latency.

Availability zones (AZs). Each region has several AZs, typically three or more. An AZ is one or more data centers with independent power, cooling and network, physically separated from the other AZs by kilometers but linked by private fiber. The numbers that matter:

Path Typical round-trip latency
Same AZ 0.1 to 0.3 ms
Cross-AZ, same region 0.5 to 2 ms
Cross-region, same continent (Virginia to Ohio) 10 to 15 ms
Cross-region, transatlantic (Virginia to Ireland) 75 to 90 ms
Cross-region, Virginia to Mumbai 180 to 200 ms

AZ names (ap-south-1a) are shuffled per account, so your 1a may be someone else's 1c; use AZ IDs (aps1-az1) when coordinating with another account.

Shared responsibility. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical buildings, the hypervisor, the hardware, the managed service software. You are responsible for security in the cloud: your data, your IAM policies, your security groups, your operating system patches on EC2, your application code, your encryption choices. The line moves with how managed the service is. On EC2 you patch the OS; on RDS AWS patches PostgreSQL but you choose the maintenance window and the parameter values; on Lambda you only own the code.

Layer EC2 ECS on Fargate RDS Lambda
Hardware, network, facilities AWS AWS AWS AWS
OS and runtime patches You AWS AWS AWS
Database engine upgrades You n/a AWS, you schedule n/a
Application code and dependencies You You n/a You
IAM, encryption keys, network rules You You You You
Backups You n/a AWS, you configure retention n/a

Managed versus self-managed. For almost every component there is a ladder. PostgreSQL: run it yourself on EC2 (full control, full ops burden), RDS (AWS handles backups, patching, failover; you lose superuser and filesystem access), Aurora (AWS rewrote the storage layer; faster failover, more expensive per instance), Aurora Serverless v2 (capacity scales automatically; highest cost per unit at steady load). Each step up removes an operational chore and a knob, and raises the unit price. The senior question is not "which is best" but "which chores does my team have the skill and the headcount to own".

Pay-per-use and elasticity. Compute is billed per second (EC2, Fargate) or per request and millisecond (Lambda). Storage is billed per GB-month. Network is billed per GB moved, with the rules that surprise people: traffic into AWS is free, traffic out to the internet costs about $0.09/GB, and traffic between AZs costs $0.01/GB in each direction. Elasticity is the ability to add capacity when load rises and remove it when load falls. Stateless things (API containers) are elastic in minutes; stateful things (an RDS instance) resize with a restart and cannot shrink their disk at all.

The concept-to-service map. Learn the concept, then look up the name.

Concept AWS service Notes
Virtual machines EC2 Instance families, auto scaling groups, spot
Container orchestration ECS, EKS ECS is AWS-native and simpler; EKS is Kubernetes
Serverless functions Lambda Event-driven, 15-minute limit
Relational database RDS PostgreSQL, Aurora PostgreSQL Multi-AZ, replicas, PITR
Key-value or wide-column DB DynamoDB Partition-key design, single-digit ms
Cache ElastiCache for Redis or Valkey Cluster mode, Multi-AZ
Queue SQS Standard and FIFO, DLQ
Pub/sub SNS Fan-out to SQS, Lambda, HTTP
Event bus EventBridge Rules, schema registry, scheduler
Log or stream MSK (Kafka), Kinesis Ordered, replayable
Object storage S3 Unlimited, eleven nines durability
CDN CloudFront Edge caching, signed URLs
DNS Route 53 Routing policies, health checks
Identity IAM, STS, Cognito Roles over keys
Secrets Secrets Manager, Parameter Store Rotation, KMS-encrypted
Encryption keys KMS Envelope encryption
Network VPC Subnets, route tables, security groups
Load balancing ALB (L7), NLB (L4) Target groups, health checks
API edge API Gateway Throttling, auth, WebSocket
Monitoring CloudWatch, X-Ray Metrics, logs, alarms, traces
Web firewall WAF, Shield Rate rules, managed rule sets

Practical example

An e-commerce backend written in NestJS needs, at minimum: something to run the API containers (ECS on Fargate), a PostgreSQL database that survives a data-center failure (RDS Multi-AZ), a cache (ElastiCache Redis), a queue for order-confirmation emails and inventory updates (SQS), a place for product images (S3 behind CloudFront), DNS and TLS (Route 53 and ACM), and monitoring (CloudWatch). Every one of these is a regional resource placed in two or three AZs. The bill for a modest deployment of this shape is a few hundred dollars a month; at 1,000 requests per second it is a few thousand (we size it precisely in section 46.13).

Production scenario

A food-delivery platform runs eight NestJS API tasks on Fargate at a normal 300 RPS. Friday at 19:00 the traffic climbs toward 1,800 RPS. Target-tracking auto scaling on ALBRequestCountPerTarget adds tasks every minute until 36 are running by 19:20; the scale-out takes about 90 seconds per step (task pull, start, health check, register). The RDS instance does not scale; its 4 vCPUs handle the load only because 85% of reads hit Redis. At 23:30 the tasks scale back in and the platform pays for the extra capacity for roughly four hours instead of all week. That difference (paying for 36 tasks for 4 hours versus 168 hours) is the entire economic argument for the cloud, and it only works because the API tier was designed stateless.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call was paged: 33% of API requests were failing with connection timeouts. One AZ in the region had lost network connectivity. The API tasks were spread over three AZs and the ALB stopped routing to the dark one within 30 seconds, so the API itself recovered on its own. But the Redis cluster had been created single-AZ, in the AZ that failed, to save $75 a month. Every cache read timed out, every request fell through to PostgreSQL, and the database hit 100% CPU inside two minutes. The fix during the incident was to fail over to a new Redis node in another AZ (12 minutes, cache cold). The permanent fix was Multi-AZ Redis with automatic failover and a load test that proves the database survives a cold cache. Lesson: an architecture is only as multi-AZ as its least redundant component.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A single-AZ resource inside a multi-AZ design: one NAT gateway, one Redis node, one EFS mount target, one bastion. The AZ failure takes it and everything that depends on it.
  • Cross-AZ traffic surprise: a chatty service that calls a database in another AZ pays $0.02/GB round trip. At 1 TB/day that is $600/month you did not plan.
  • Region-wide service degradation: rare (a few times a year across all regions), but real. Regional control-plane APIs (launching new instances, updating IAM) fail while already-running resources keep working. Your architecture must not need to create things to survive.
  • Quotas: every service has soft limits (EC2 vCPUs per family, Lambda concurrency 1,000, ENIs per region). Auto scaling silently stops at the quota. Request increases before the sale, not during.
  • Elasticity lag: a Fargate task takes 60 to 120 seconds to become healthy; a traffic spike that doubles in 30 seconds arrives before the capacity does. Keep headroom or scale on a leading indicator.
  • Clock skew: instance clocks drift; AWS provides the Time Sync service (169.254.169.123), and signed requests fail if your clock is more than 5 minutes off.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, for every component, "which AZ is this in, and what happens to the user if that AZ disappears?" They treat the managed-service ladder as a staffing decision: a team without a DBA does not self-host PostgreSQL. They know the three prices that dominate a bill (compute-hours, database instance, data transfer) and can estimate a design's monthly cost before drawing it. They refuse to build multi-region until someone can state the revenue lost per hour of regional outage, because multi-region roughly doubles cost and triples complexity. To a product manager they explain: "Multi-AZ means we survive a building failure automatically. Multi-region means we survive a city failure, and it costs this much more."

Common mistakes

  • Treating the cloud as "someone else's computer" and copying an on-prem design onto EC2, losing every benefit of managed services.
  • Choosing a region by habit (us-east-1) when the users are in India, adding 200 ms to every request.
  • Assuming AWS backs up your data. RDS snapshots are on by default, but S3 versioning, DynamoDB PITR and EBS snapshots are not.
  • Forgetting the account and region quotas until the auto-scaler stalls at peak.
  • Reading "99.99% SLA" as a promise about your app. The SLA credits you a few percent of the bill; it does not restore your orders table.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a region and an availability zone, and which one does Multi-AZ RDS protect you from?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: AZ is an isolated data-center group inside a region; Multi-AZ protects against an AZ failure, not a regional one. Follow-up: what does a regional failure look like in practice?
  2. Explain shared responsibility for an RDS instance.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: AWS patches the engine and manages storage; you own parameter tuning, IAM, security groups, encryption choice, backup retention, and the schema.
  3. Why is cross-AZ traffic a cost concern and how do you reduce it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: $0.01/GB each direction; AZ-aware routing, keeping chatty pairs in the same AZ, compressing payloads, caching.
  4. When would you pick a self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2 over RDS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rarely; needs like custom extensions not on RDS, filesystem-level access, extreme cost sensitivity with an experienced DBA on staff.
  5. A traffic spike doubles load in 20 seconds. Will auto scaling save you?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: not by itself; 60 to 120 second lead time; keep headroom, use predictive or scheduled scaling, protect the database with a cache and admission control.

Practical exercise

Take the architecture of a system you know and draw it as an AZ map like the diagram above. For each box write its AZ count. Acceptance criteria: every stateful component is in at least two AZs or has a documented recovery time; you can list the three most expensive line items and estimate the monthly cost within 30%; you can name the one component whose failure would take the whole system down.

46.2 Compute: EC2, ECS and EKS

Concept

Compute is where your NestJS process runs. On AWS you choose the level at which you want to think: a virtual machine you manage (EC2), a container you hand to an orchestrator (ECS or EKS), or a function that runs only when an event arrives (Lambda, covered in 46.3). Each level trades control for less operational work.

Why does it exist?

A single machine cannot be patched, replaced or scaled without downtime. Orchestration exists so that a fleet of identical containers can be rolled out, health-checked, scaled and replaced automatically, and so that the machine underneath becomes disposable. AWS offers two orchestrators because Kubernetes (EKS) is the portable industry standard with a huge ecosystem, while ECS is the AWS-native option with far fewer moving parts.

Mental model

Imagine renting space for a restaurant. EC2 is renting the whole building: you install the kitchen, fix the plumbing, and decide when to renovate. ECS on Fargate is renting a furnished kitchen by the hour: you bring the recipes (container images) and the staff show up where told. EKS is joining a franchise with a thick operations manual: enormous flexibility, a global community of franchisees, and a manual you must actually read. Lambda is a food stall you only pay for while a customer stands in front of it.

How it works

EC2 instances. An instance is a virtual machine from a family sized for a workload. General purpose (m7g, m7i; burstable t3, t4g) for API servers; compute optimized (c7g, c7i) for CPU-bound work such as image resizing; memory optimized (r7g, r7i) for databases and caches; storage optimized (i4i) for local NVMe throughput. The letter after the family number tells you the processor: g is Graviton (arm64), about 20% cheaper per unit of work than the equivalent Intel instance. Node.js runs natively on arm64; the only thing you must do is build multi-architecture Docker images. Burstable t instances earn CPU credits while idle and spend them under load; a NestJS API on a t3.medium that runs at 40% CPU all day will exhaust credits and throttle to baseline, which looks like a mysterious afternoon slowdown.

Auto Scaling Groups (ASG). An ASG owns a launch template (AMI, instance type, user data, IAM instance profile) and maintains a desired count between a minimum and a maximum across chosen subnets. Scaling policies: target tracking ("keep average CPU at 60%"), step scaling (add 2 instances when CPU is above 70% for 3 minutes), scheduled (30 instances at 18:00 on Fridays). Health checks can be EC2-level (the VM responds) or ELB-level (the load balancer's health check passes), and you almost always want ELB-level, because a VM that is up with a crashed process is not healthy. Instance refresh rolls out a new AMI in batches.

Spot instances. Spare capacity sold at up to 90% discount, with a two-minute interruption notice when AWS wants it back. Excellent for stateless workers, batch jobs, CI runners and even API capacity if you mix on-demand and spot (a mixed-instances policy with, say, 40% on-demand base). Never for the database, never for anything that cannot lose a node with two minutes' warning. Diversify across several instance types; a single-type spot pool is the one that runs dry.

ECS. Amazon's own orchestrator. The objects: a cluster (a logical group), a task definition (a versioned recipe: containers, CPU and memory, ports, environment, secrets, log driver, health check), a task (one running copy of a task definition) and a service (keeps N tasks running, registers them with a load balancer target group, and manages deployments). Deployments are rolling by default, controlled by minimumHealthyPercent (how many old tasks must stay during the rollout, typically 100) and maximumPercent (how many total tasks may exist, typically 200, meaning new tasks start before old ones stop). The deployment circuit breaker watches for tasks that fail to become healthy and rolls back automatically. Blue/green is available through CodeDeploy integration. Scaling uses Application Auto Scaling on CPU, memory or ALBRequestCountPerTarget.

Fargate versus EC2 launch type. With Fargate you never see a VM: you declare cpu: 1024 (1 vCPU) and memory: 2048 (MB) per task and pay per vCPU-second and GB-second, about $0.040 per vCPU-hour and $0.0044 per GB-hour in us-east-1. A 1 vCPU, 2 GB task costs about $36 per month. With the EC2 launch type you run an ASG of instances with the ECS agent and pack tasks onto them; it is cheaper at scale (better bin-packing, reserved pricing, spot) and needed for GPUs or privileged containers, but you patch and right-size the instances. Most teams start with Fargate and move hot services to EC2 capacity when the bill justifies the ops.

EKS. Managed Kubernetes. AWS runs the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) across three AZs for about $73 per month per cluster; you run the worker nodes. Node options: managed node groups (ASG-backed, AWS handles the AMI and drain on upgrade), self-managed nodes, Fargate profiles (pods without nodes, with restrictions), or Karpenter for just-in-time node provisioning. Networking uses the VPC CNI, which gives every pod a real VPC IP address; a /24 subnet with 251 IPs fills up faster than you expect. Kubernetes versions are supported for about 14 months and then you pay for extended support, so a cluster upgrade every year is mandatory operations work.

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). The clean way for a pod to get AWS permissions. The cluster has an OIDC identity provider; a Kubernetes service account is annotated with an IAM role ARN; the pod receives a projected service-account token; the AWS SDK exchanges it through sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for temporary credentials. No access keys in the pod, no shared node role. The newer EKS Pod Identity feature achieves the same with an agent and simpler setup. Either way the rule is the same: one role per workload, least privilege.

When ECS is simpler than EKS. ECS has no control plane to upgrade, no CRDs, no Helm charts, no ingress controllers to choose, no CNI IP arithmetic, and IAM is native. A team of six running twelve NestJS services will ship faster on ECS. Choose EKS when you already have Kubernetes expertise, need operators (a PostgreSQL operator, Argo Rollouts, cert-manager), need portability across clouds, or run hundreds of services where the Kubernetes ecosystem pays for its weight. Kubernetes concepts themselves are covered in Part 45 — Kubernetes.

Practical example

A trimmed task definition for the NestJS orders API on Fargate. The important choices: secrets come from Secrets Manager by ARN and are injected as environment variables at start; the container health check is the readiness endpoint; logs go to CloudWatch; the task role (what the app may call) is separate from the execution role (what ECS needs to pull the image and read the secret).

JSON
{
  "family": "orders-api",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "1024",
  "memory": "2048",
  "runtimePlatform": { "cpuArchitecture": "ARM64", "operatingSystemFamily": "LINUX" },
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/orders-api-task",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/orders-api-exec",
  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "api",
      "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:9f3c2ab",
      "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 3000, "protocol": "tcp" }],
      "environment": [
        { "name": "NODE_ENV", "value": "production" },
        { "name": "PORT", "value": "3000" }
      ],
      "secrets": [
        { "name": "DATABASE_URL", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456789012:secret:prod/orders/db-Ab12Cd" },
        { "name": "JWT_SECRET", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456789012:secret:prod/orders/jwt-Ef34Gh" }
      ],
      "healthCheck": {
        "command": ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health/ready || exit 1"],
        "interval": 15, "timeout": 5, "retries": 3, "startPeriod": 30
      },
      "stopTimeout": 30,
      "logConfiguration": {
        "logDriver": "awslogs",
        "options": { "awslogs-group": "/ecs/orders-api", "awslogs-region": "ap-south-1", "awslogs-stream-prefix": "api" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The image tag is a git SHA, never latest (see Part 47 — CI/CD). stopTimeout: 30 is how long ECS waits after SIGTERM before SIGKILL; your NestJS shutdown must finish inside it.

NestJS example

Two things every container behind an ALB must do: drain gracefully on SIGTERM, and keep HTTP keep-alive connections open longer than the load balancer's idle timeout (the reason is in section 46.7; the short version is that if Node closes an idle connection at the same moment the ALB reuses it, the ALB returns a 502).

TypeScript
// src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { Logger, ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Server } from 'node:http';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap(): Promise<void> {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true });
  app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));
  app.set('trust proxy', 1); // ALB sets X-Forwarded-For; needed for correct client IP and rate limits

  // Lets OnModuleDestroy / OnApplicationShutdown hooks run on SIGTERM
  // (close DB pools, stop SQS consumers, finish in-flight work).
  app.enableShutdownHooks();

  const server = app.getHttpServer() as Server;
  // ALB idle timeout is 60 s by default; backend keep-alive must be longer.
  server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;
  server.headersTimeout = 66_000; // must be greater than keepAliveTimeout

  await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), '0.0.0.0');
  new Logger('Bootstrap').log(`orders-api listening, pid ${process.pid}`);
}
bootstrap();

And the readiness endpoint the ALB and the ECS health check both call, using @nestjs/terminus:

TypeScript
// src/health/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator, MemoryHealthIndicator } from '@nestjs/terminus';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly memory: MemoryHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  // Liveness: is the process alive? Never touch dependencies here.
  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([]);
  }

  // Readiness: can this task serve traffic right now?
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 }), // SELECT 1 through the pool
      () => this.memory.checkHeap('heap', 1_500 * 1024 * 1024), // fail before OOMKill
    ]);
  }
}

The 1.5 GB heap threshold matches a 2 GB task with --max-old-space-size=1536 set in the Dockerfile CMD; a task that exceeds its memory is killed by ECS with exit code 137 and no log line, which is the container equivalent of OOMKilled (see Part 44 — Docker).

Production scenario

The orders API at 1,000 RPS peak runs eight Fargate tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB across three AZs, each handling around 150 RPS at 35% CPU with p95 of 60 ms; the headroom is deliberate so that losing one AZ (three tasks) leaves the remaining five at about 60% CPU. Auto scaling targets 200 requests per target and adds up to four tasks per minute. A deploy replaces the eight tasks in about six minutes with minimumHealthyPercent: 100 and maximumPercent: 150. The four background workers (SQS consumers) run on a separate service with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB each, because their scaling signal is queue depth, not HTTP request count.

Failure scenario

A team moved the orders API from t3.large EC2 instances to Fargate and, to save money, set the task to 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. Load tests passed at 300 RPS. In production, every deploy caused two minutes of 5xx errors. The cause: with 0.5 vCPU, the NestJS bootstrap (TypeORM metadata build, 40 modules, connection pool warm-up) took 45 seconds, but startPeriod in the health check was 10 seconds, so ECS marked new tasks unhealthy, killed them, started replacements, and the circuit breaker eventually rolled back. Meanwhile the ALB had already deregistered old tasks. The fix was startPeriod: 60, a 1 vCPU task (bootstrap dropped to 12 seconds), and a rule: measure cold start on the production task size before setting health-check timers.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Task cannot pull image: ECR permission missing on the execution role, or no route to ECR from a private subnet without a NAT or VPC endpoint. Symptom: CannotPullContainerError, service stuck at 0 running.
  • ENI exhaustion: awsvpc mode gives every task its own network interface and IP. A /26 subnet runs out at about 59 tasks.
  • Spot interruption during deploy: capacity vanishes mid-rollout; keep an on-demand base and use capacity-provider strategies that fall back.
  • SIGTERM ignored: Node started via a shell (sh -c node main.js) does not receive the signal; use exec form in the Dockerfile CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"].
  • Deregistration delay: ALB keeps sending in-flight requests to a task for up to 300 seconds (default) after deregistration begins; set it to 30 seconds for APIs and make sure the app keeps serving during that window.
  • EKS IP exhaustion: pods fail to schedule with failed to assign an IP address; fix with larger subnets, prefix delegation, or custom networking.
  • Burstable credit exhaustion: t3 instances silently throttle; the metric CPUCreditBalance at zero is the tell.
  • Node group upgrade drains pods too fast: without a PodDisruptionBudget, the upgrade evicts every replica at once.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick the simplest orchestrator the team can operate, which for most teams under fifty engineers is ECS on Fargate, and they say so plainly even when Kubernetes is fashionable. They size tasks by measuring, not guessing: cold-start time, steady-state CPU at target RPS, heap under load. They ask "what happens during a deploy" and "what happens when an AZ dies" before "how many tasks". They insist that scaling signals match the workload: request count for APIs, queue depth for workers, never CPU alone for a Node process that is I/O bound. They put a PodDisruptionBudget or minimumHealthyPercent in place before the first production deploy, because the first deploy is when it matters.

Common mistakes

  • Running a single task or a single replica in production "for now".
  • Using latest image tags so that a scale-out event silently deploys a new version.
  • Setting CPU-based scaling for a Node API, which sits at 25% CPU while its event loop is saturated by I/O waits.
  • Sharing one IAM role across every service on the cluster.
  • Choosing EKS for three services because a blog post said Kubernetes is the standard.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between an ECS task role and an execution role.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and read secrets; task role is assumed by your code to call AWS APIs. Follow-up: what breaks if you swap them?
  2. How does a rolling deployment on ECS avoid downtime, and what settings control it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: minimumHealthyPercent, maximumPercent, ALB health checks, deregistration delay, circuit breaker.
  3. When would you choose EKS over ECS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: existing Kubernetes skills, need for operators or Helm ecosystem, portability, large scale; otherwise ECS is simpler.
  4. How does a pod on EKS get AWS credentials safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: IRSA or Pod Identity, OIDC token exchanged via STS for temporary credentials, one role per workload.
  5. What is spot capacity good for and what is it dangerous for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: stateless workers, batch, CI; dangerous for databases and anything unable to tolerate two-minute eviction.

Practical exercise

Deploy a NestJS service to ECS Fargate behind an ALB across two AZs with a task definition that injects a Secrets Manager secret. Acceptance criteria: a deploy of a new image tag completes with zero failed requests under a 100 RPS load test; killing one task by hand is invisible to the load test; the task role can read only its own S3 prefix and nothing else; SIGTERM handling is proven by watching the pool close in the logs during a deploy.

46.3 Compute: Lambda and serverless functions

Concept

Lambda runs a function in response to an event: an HTTP request through API Gateway, a message in SQS, an object landing in S3, a schedule, a change in DynamoDB. You upload code, choose memory, and pay per request and per millisecond. There is no server to size, patch or scale; there is also no process that stays alive between events unless AWS decides to keep it warm.

Why does it exist?

Many workloads are bursty or rare: a webhook that arrives three times a minute, an image thumbnail job that runs when a product photo is uploaded, a nightly report. Paying for a container 24 hours a day to handle three events per minute wastes 99% of the money. Lambda makes idle time free and scaling automatic, and for event glue between AWS services it removes almost all operational work.

Mental model

Imagine a call center that hires a new agent for every incoming call, trains them in a few hundred milliseconds, lets them handle the call, and then keeps them at their desk for a while in case another call arrives. If a thousand calls arrive at once, a thousand agents are hired. Each one opens their own line to the database.

How it works

  1. Execution environment. On the first invocation Lambda creates a micro-VM, downloads your code, starts the Node runtime, and runs your module's top-level code. This is the cold start. For a plain Node handler it is 100 to 250 ms; for a NestJS application that builds a dependency graph of forty modules and initialises TypeORM it is commonly 800 ms to 3 seconds. The environment is then reused for subsequent invocations (warm), and frozen when idle; after some minutes of inactivity it is destroyed.
  2. Concurrency. Each in-flight invocation needs its own environment. 500 simultaneous requests means 500 environments, each with its own cold start if not already warm. The account default limit is 1,000 concurrent executions per region (a soft limit). Reserved concurrency caps one function; provisioned concurrency keeps N environments pre-warmed, at a price.
  3. Limits. 15-minute maximum duration, 128 MB to 10 GB memory (CPU scales with memory; below about 1,769 MB you get less than one full vCPU), 512 MB to 10 GB of /tmp, 6 MB synchronous payload, 250 MB unzipped deployment package (10 GB with container images).
  4. Triggers. Synchronous (API Gateway, ALB, function URL: the caller waits), asynchronous (S3, SNS, EventBridge: Lambda queues internally and retries twice), and poll-based (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams: Lambda polls and invokes with batches, respecting a maximumConcurrency).
  5. The connection-pooling problem. A container-based API holds a pool of 10 connections and serves thousands of requests through it. A Lambda fleet holds one connection per environment, and the fleet can be 1,000 environments wide. A traffic spike therefore opens hundreds of new PostgreSQL connections at once. PostgreSQL forks a process per connection and RDS max_connections for a db.t3.medium is about 400. The result is FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved and a database that spends its CPU on connection setup instead of queries.
  6. RDS Proxy. A managed connection pooler that sits between Lambda and RDS. Lambdas connect to the proxy (cheap, fast), and the proxy multiplexes them onto a small warm pool of real database connections. It also survives failover with less disruption (it re-routes to the new primary without the client seeing DNS delays) and supports IAM authentication so no password is needed. Caveat: pinning. If a session does something the proxy cannot safely share (a SET statement, an advisory lock, LISTEN, a temporary table), the proxy pins that client to a dedicated connection and the multiplexing benefit disappears. Some ORMs run SET statements on connect; check yours. Pricing is about $0.015 per vCPU-hour of the target instance, minimum 2 vCPUs, roughly $22 per month.

When to use Lambda. Webhook receivers (Stripe, Razorpay, Shopify) that validate a signature and drop a message on SQS. S3-triggered processing (thumbnails, virus scan, CSV import). EventBridge glue that transforms one event into another. Scheduled jobs. Low-traffic internal APIs. Anything where the code runs for under a minute, a few times a minute.

When not to use Lambda. Long-lived connections (WebSocket servers, Kafka consumers, database LISTEN): the environment freezes between events. Latency-critical hot paths with a strict p99, because cold starts land on real users. Sustained high throughput: at a steady 1,000 RPS with 100 ms at 512 MB, Lambda costs about $2,700 per month (2.6 billion requests at $0.20 per million plus 130 million GB-seconds at $0.0000167) versus about $300 for the equivalent Fargate tasks. Jobs longer than 15 minutes. Anything that needs a warm in-process cache to be fast.

Practical example

A Razorpay payment webhook arrives at API Gateway. The Lambda verifies the HMAC signature with the secret from Secrets Manager, writes an idempotent record keyed by the event id, publishes payment.captured to SQS, and returns 200 within 50 ms. The heavy work (updating the order, notifying the warehouse, sending email) happens in the ECS workers that consume the queue. The Lambda is tiny, has no ORM, and its cold start is 120 ms. This is Lambda at its best: an always-available front door that does almost nothing.

NestJS example

If you do run NestJS on Lambda (a reasonable choice for a low-traffic admin API), bootstrap once per environment and keep the app in module scope. Use @codegenie/serverless-express to translate API Gateway events into Express requests.

TypeScript
// src/lambda.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ExpressAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import serverlessExpress from '@codegenie/serverless-express';
import express from 'express';
import type { APIGatewayProxyEvent, Context, Handler } from 'aws-lambda';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

let cachedHandler: Handler | undefined; // survives across warm invocations

async function bootstrap(): Promise<Handler> {
  const expressApp = express();
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, new ExpressAdapter(expressApp), {
    logger: ['error', 'warn'], // less startup logging shaves cold start
  });
  await app.init(); // no listen(): API Gateway hands us each request
  return serverlessExpress({ app: expressApp });
}

export const handler: Handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEvent, context: Context, callback) => {
  // Return as soon as the response is ready; do not wait for the pool's idle sockets.
  context.callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop = false;
  cachedHandler ??= await bootstrap(); // cold start pays this once per environment
  return cachedHandler(event, context, callback);
};

And the TypeORM configuration that goes with it: a pool of one, connecting to RDS Proxy, with short timeouts so a frozen environment does not hold a dead socket.

TypeScript
// src/database/typeorm.config.ts
import { TypeOrmModuleOptions } from '@nestjs/typeorm';

export const lambdaTypeOrmConfig = (): TypeOrmModuleOptions => ({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.DB_PROXY_HOST, // orders-proxy.proxy-abc.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com
  port: 5432,
  username: process.env.DB_USER,
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD, // or an IAM auth token generated per invocation
  database: 'orders',
  ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true },
  autoLoadEntities: true,
  synchronize: false,
  extra: {
    max: 1,                       // one environment, one connection
    idleTimeoutMillis: 5_000,     // drop idle sockets quickly; the proxy holds the real pool
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
  },
});

Bundle with esbuild into a single file: Lambda cold start is dominated by the number of files it must read, and a NestJS node_modules tree has tens of thousands.

Production scenario

An image-processing pipeline: product photos land in s3://shop-uploads/, an S3 event notification invokes a 1,769 MB Lambda (one full vCPU) that produces three sizes with sharp and writes them to s3://shop-images/. At 20,000 uploads a day, each taking 900 ms, the monthly cost is under $2. The same job on a permanently running Fargate task would cost $36 and require a queue and a consumer. This is the shape where Lambda wins without argument.

Failure scenario

At 11:00 a marketing email went out and 3,000 users opened the "track my order" page within a minute. The page was served by a NestJS Lambda talking directly to RDS. Lambda scaled to 700 environments, each opening a connection. RDS max_connections was 420. Two-thirds of the environments failed with too many connections, retried, and made it worse; the database's CPU went to 100% on connection handling, and the ECS-based checkout API (sharing the same database) started timing out. Orders were lost for eleven minutes. The fixes: RDS Proxy in front (connections capped at the proxy's pool), reserved concurrency of 100 on the tracking function so it cannot swamp shared resources, and a Redis cache for tracking lookups. The general lesson: a Lambda fleet is an unbounded client; every shared dependency behind it needs a bound.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cold start on the critical path: p50 of 40 ms and p99 of 2,500 ms because 1% of requests hit a new environment. Provisioned concurrency fixes it for a fixed cost.
  • Connection storm as above; also seen with Redis (ECONNRESET under 1,000 clients) and third-party APIs with per-client rate limits.
  • Frozen environment with an open socket: the DB server times out the idle connection while the environment is frozen; the next invocation gets ECONNRESET. Short idle timeouts and a retry-on-first-query fix it.
  • Async retries produce duplicates: asynchronous invocations retry twice on error; without idempotency the S3 event processes three times.
  • SQS partial batch failure: return batchItemFailures or the whole batch is retried, including the messages that succeeded.
  • 15-minute timeout mid-transaction: the transaction is rolled back by the server; the function has no chance to clean up.
  • Throttling (429 TooManyRequestsException) when regional concurrency is exhausted by another team's function.
  • Deployment package too large after adding sharp or a headless browser; use layers or container images.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see Lambda as a tool for events, not as a replacement for the API tier. The question they ask is "what is the invocation pattern?": bursty and rare means Lambda; steady and hot means containers. They bound every Lambda with reserved concurrency when it touches a shared database. They refuse to put a NestJS monolith on Lambda for a 1,000 RPS API, because the cold-start tail and the cost curve both punish it. They explain to a product manager: "Serverless is cheapest when idle and most expensive when busy; our checkout is busy all day."

Common mistakes

  • Creating the NestJS app inside the handler on every invocation.
  • Opening a TypeORM pool of 10 per environment "for performance", multiplying the connection storm by ten.
  • Forgetting callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop = false, so every invocation waits for the idle socket timeout.
  • Treating Lambda logs in CloudWatch as free; at scale they cost more than the compute.
  • No dead-letter queue on asynchronous triggers, so failed events vanish after two retries.

Interview questions

  1. Why does Lambda cause database connection exhaustion and how do you fix it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one connection per environment, unbounded fleet; RDS Proxy, reserved concurrency, cache, or move the hot path to containers.
  2. What is a cold start, what makes it slow for NestJS, and how do you reduce it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: environment creation plus module init; DI graph and ORM setup; bundle, lazy modules, smaller apps, provisioned concurrency.
  3. When is Lambda more expensive than containers?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: sustained load; give the crossover intuition with numbers.
  4. How do asynchronous Lambda invocations retry, and what does that imply for your handler?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: two retries then DLQ or destination; handler must be idempotent.
  5. What is RDS Proxy pinning?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: session-state statements force a dedicated connection, losing multiplexing; audit SET statements from the ORM.

Practical exercise

Build a payment-webhook receiver on Lambda that validates a signature, stores the event id in PostgreSQL through RDS Proxy with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and enqueues to SQS. Acceptance criteria: replaying the same webhook 50 times creates one row and one queue message; a load test of 500 concurrent webhooks shows database connections staying under 30 in pg_stat_activity; a forced Lambda error lands the event in a DLQ that an alarm watches.

46.4 Relational data: RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL

Concept

RDS is PostgreSQL (or MySQL, and others) installed, patched, backed up and failed over by AWS. You get an endpoint, a parameter group, and a console; you do not get ssh, superuser, or the filesystem. Aurora is AWS's own storage engine underneath a PostgreSQL-compatible front end; it changes how replication and failover behave, and it costs more per instance. Everything you learned about PostgreSQL internals in Parts 19–23 still applies; what changes is the operational envelope around it.

Why does it exist?

Running PostgreSQL well means WAL archiving, base backups tested by restore, streaming replication, failover with fencing, minor-version patching, monitoring for disk and connections, and a person who wakes up when it breaks. RDS packages all of that behind an API so that a team without a database administrator can have a Multi-AZ PostgreSQL with point-in-time recovery in fifteen minutes. The price is loss of low-level control and a higher hourly rate than raw EC2.

Mental model

Imagine a serviced office versus an empty warehouse. In the serviced office the landlord handles power, cleaning, security, and will move you to an identical office next door if yours floods (Multi-AZ), but you cannot knock down a wall (no superuser, no custom kernel). Aurora is the same office, but the filing cabinets are in a vault shared with your neighbours in three buildings; any of you can read the same files instantly (shared storage replicas), and moving offices takes seconds because the files never move.

How it works

Instance classes. db.t4g burstable for dev and small workloads; db.m7g and db.m6g general purpose; db.r7g and db.r6g memory optimized, which is what production PostgreSQL usually wants because shared_buffers and the OS page cache are what make queries fast. A db.r6g.xlarge has 4 vCPUs and 32 GB and costs about $0.48 per hour single-AZ in us-east-1.

Multi-AZ instance deployment. A synchronous standby in a second AZ receives every WAL record before the primary acknowledges the commit (adding about 1 to 3 ms per commit). The standby is not readable. On failure of the primary (or its AZ, or during your patch window) RDS promotes the standby and repoints the DNS endpoint. Failover takes 60 to 120 seconds, during which writes fail. The cost is exactly double the instance price. The newer Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment uses one writer and two readable standbys with semi-synchronous replication, fails over in about 35 seconds, and exposes a reader endpoint; it is the better default when the budget allows three instances.

Read replicas. Asynchronous streaming replicas (up to 15, in-region or cross-region) with their own endpoints. Lag is normally tens of milliseconds, but a long-running report query on the replica or a burst of writes on the primary can push it to seconds or minutes (the mechanics and hot_standby_feedback are in Part 23 — Database Scaling). Replicas can be promoted to standalone instances, which is a manual disaster-recovery path, not automatic failover.

Parameter groups. The RDS way to edit postgresql.conf. A parameter group is attached to an instance; dynamic parameters apply immediately, static ones (shared_buffers, max_connections, wal_level) need a reboot. Defaults worth knowing: shared_buffers is 25% of memory, max_connections is derived from memory as LEAST(DBInstanceClassMemory / 9531392, 5000) (about 1,700 for 16 GB, about 400 for 4 GB), rds.force_ssl forces TLS, and log_min_duration_statement is off by default, so slow-query logging must be turned on by you.

Performance Insights. A dashboard of database load measured in average active sessions, broken down by wait event and by SQL. It answers "what was the database doing at 14:05" better than any ad hoc query, and the seven-day retention tier is free. Enhanced Monitoring adds OS-level metrics (per-process CPU, actual free memory) at one-second granularity.

Backups and PITR. RDS takes a daily snapshot and ships transaction logs to S3 every five minutes. With a retention of 1 to 35 days you can restore to any second within that window (the latest restorable time is usually about five minutes behind now). A restore creates a new instance with a new endpoint; it does not roll the existing one back, and it takes from ten minutes to well over an hour depending on data size. Manual snapshots persist until deleted and can be copied cross-region. Practice a restore quarterly; a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.

Storage and IOPS. gp3 storage gives a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s below 400 GiB, and 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s at 400 GiB and above; more can be provisioned. io2 goes far higher for the money. Storage autoscaling grows the volume when free space drops below 10% (it cannot shrink). The classic surprise: a 200 GiB database with a write-heavy batch job pins WriteIOPS + ReadIOPS at 3,000 and every query queues behind the disk.

Aurora PostgreSQL. Aurora replaces the storage layer with a distributed, log-structured volume spread as six copies across three AZs; a write is durable when four of six copies acknowledge. The database instance ships only redo log records, not full pages, so write amplification drops. Consequences:

  • Up to 15 replicas read the same storage volume, so replica lag is typically under 20 ms and does not grow with write volume the way streaming-replica lag does.
  • Failover to a replica takes roughly 30 seconds, sometimes less, because no data needs to catch up. A reader endpoint load-balances across replicas.
  • Storage grows automatically to 128 TiB and is billed per GB used; I/O is billed per request in the standard tier, or included in the I/O-Optimized tier which is cheaper above roughly 25% I/O share of the bill.
  • Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in units of ACUs within seconds; Aurora Global Database replicates to another region with typical lag under a second.

Aurora is not always the right choice: instance prices are about 20% higher, I/O charges can surprise write-heavy workloads on the standard tier, and some PostgreSQL extensions and features lag behind RDS. Pick Aurora when failover time and replica lag matter, or when read scaling is the bottleneck; pick RDS PostgreSQL when you want the closest thing to vanilla PostgreSQL.

RDS Proxy. A managed pooler in front of either engine (section 46.3 covered the Lambda motivation). It also helps container fleets: 40 tasks with a pool of 10 each is 400 connections; through the proxy the database sees perhaps 60. It shortens failover disruption because the proxy tracks the new primary itself. PgBouncer on your own cluster is cheaper and more configurable (see Part 19 — PostgreSQL Internals); RDS Proxy is the answer when you would rather not run PgBouncer.

Practical example

The orders database for the 1,000 RPS platform: db.r6g.xlarge Multi-AZ (writes, about 2,000 queries per second at peak), one db.r6g.large read replica for product-catalogue and order-history reads, 500 GiB gp3 (past the 400 GiB threshold on purpose for the 12,000 IOPS baseline), 14-day backup retention, Performance Insights on, log_min_duration_statement = 500, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 30000, statement_timeout set per role rather than globally so migrations can run long.

NestJS example

Reading from the replica is a deliberate decision per query, not a global switch, because a user who just placed an order must see it on the next request (read-your-writes). TypeORM's replication support sends find and select query-builder queries to a replica by default and everything else to the master; you force the master where consistency matters.

TypeScript
// src/database/database.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        type: 'postgres',
        replication: {
          master: {
            host: config.getOrThrow('DB_WRITER_HOST'), // orders.cluster-xyz.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com
            port: 5432,
            username: config.getOrThrow('DB_USER'),
            password: config.getOrThrow('DB_PASSWORD'),
            database: 'orders',
          },
          slaves: [
            { host: config.getOrThrow('DB_READER_HOST'), port: 5432,
              username: config.getOrThrow('DB_USER'), password: config.getOrThrow('DB_PASSWORD'), database: 'orders' },
          ],
        },
        ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true },
        autoLoadEntities: true,
        synchronize: false,
        extra: {
          max: 10,                      // per task; 8 tasks = 80 connections on the writer
          idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,    // recycle so DNS is re-resolved after failover
          connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
          keepAlive: true,
          keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 10_000,
          statement_timeout: 5_000,     // applied on connect by node-postgres
        },
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class DatabaseModule {}

TypeORM example

TypeScript
// src/orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  // Order history: replica lag of a few hundred ms is acceptable.
  async listHistory(userId: string): Promise<Order[]> {
    return this.dataSource.getRepository(Order).find({
      where: { userId }, order: { createdAt: 'DESC' }, take: 50,
    }); // find() goes to a slave under replication config
  }

  // Just-placed order confirmation: must read the primary.
  async getForConfirmation(orderId: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner('master');
    try {
      return await runner.manager.findOne(Order, { where: { id: orderId } });
    } finally {
      await runner.release();
    }
  }
}

Sequelize example

Sequelize has the same split: a replication block with write and read, and useMaster: true on any query that must not see replica lag.

TypeScript
// src/database/sequelize.config.ts
import { Sequelize } from 'sequelize';

export const sequelize = new Sequelize('orders', undefined, undefined, {
  dialect: 'postgres',
  replication: {
    write: { host: process.env.DB_WRITER_HOST, username: process.env.DB_USER, password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD },
    read: [{ host: process.env.DB_READER_HOST, username: process.env.DB_USER, password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD }],
  },
  pool: { max: 10, idle: 30_000, acquire: 3_000 },
  dialectOptions: { ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true }, statement_timeout: 5_000 },
  logging: false,
});

// Elsewhere: a read that must reflect a write from the same request.
// const order = await Order.findByPk(orderId, { useMaster: true });

PostgreSQL example

What you actually run on RDS to see the state of replication and connections, because the console shows averages and you need the current truth.

SQL
-- On the primary: who is replicating and how far behind, in bytes.
SELECT client_addr, state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(sent_lsn, replay_lsn) AS bytes_behind,
       replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On a replica: lag in wall-clock terms (NULL means idle primary, not zero lag).
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replica_lag;

-- Connection budget: RDS derives max_connections from memory.
SHOW max_connections;
SELECT usename, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY usename, state
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

-- Per-role safety limits instead of a global parameter-group change:
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET statement_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE orders_api SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE reporting SET statement_timeout = '5min';

Typical output of the first query on a healthy replica: bytes_behind = 0 to a few kilobytes and replay_lag of 00:00:00.02. During a bulk import, bytes_behind climbs into the hundreds of megabytes and replay_lag into seconds; that is when your read-from-replica paths start showing stale orders.

Production scenario

The daily "reconcile inventory" job runs at 03:00 and rewrites 8 million stock_levels rows. On RDS with a streaming replica, the replica lags 40 seconds during the job and product pages served from the replica show yesterday's stock for that window; the team accepts it because the job runs at night. When the business asked for the job to run hourly, the team moved to Aurora, where the replica lag during the same job stayed under 30 ms because replicas read the shared volume. That is a concrete reason to pay the Aurora premium; "it is newer" is not.

Failure scenario

At 14:05 the on-call saw write latency jump from 2 ms to 80 ms and the API p95 climb past 2 seconds. CPU on the db.r6g.large was 30%. CloudWatch showed ReadIOPS + WriteIOPS flat at exactly 3,000 and DiskQueueDepth at 45. The database was 180 GiB on gp3, so its IOPS baseline was 3,000, and a new "recently viewed products" feature had started writing one row per page view, about 900 writes per second with index updates. Every other query queued behind the disk. The immediate fix was to provision 12,000 IOPS on the volume (applied online, took 20 minutes to take effect). The real fix was moving page-view tracking to Redis with batched flushes. Lesson: on RDS, disk is a quota you chose, and CPU at 30% tells you nothing about it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Failover DNS and stale connections: the endpoint CNAME flips, but a pool that never recycles keeps sockets to the old primary (now standby, read-only) and every write fails with cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Idle timeouts and TCP keepalives fix it; details in Part 23.
  • Replica lag exposed to users: an order placed then not visible on refresh. Route read-your-writes queries to the primary.
  • Storage full: without autoscaling the instance goes to storage-full status and refuses writes; with autoscaling there is a cooldown of six hours between increases, so a runaway job can still fill it.
  • Long transaction blocking a minor-version upgrade: the maintenance window fails and retries next week; your logs show nothing.
  • max_connections hit from too many tasks: every new task adds a pool; use RDS Proxy or PgBouncer, or lower per-task max.
  • PITR restores to a new endpoint: the runbook must include repointing secrets and restarting tasks; the old instance keeps taking writes until you stop it.
  • Aurora I/O bill surprise: a write-heavy workload on the standard tier pays per I/O; switch to I/O-Optimized.
  • Parameter change needing a reboot applied "immediately" restarts the instance during business hours.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat Multi-AZ as non-negotiable for any database whose loss costs money, and they know its failover time to the second because they have tested it. They put the replica lag metric on the same dashboard as API latency. They resist "just add a bigger instance" until Performance Insights shows the load is CPU and not a missing index. They keep the backup retention at 14 to 35 days and schedule a restore drill. When asked "RDS or Aurora", they answer with the failover and replica-lag requirements, then the I/O profile, then the price.

Common mistakes

  • Single-AZ production database to save $300 a month on a system earning $50,000 a day.
  • Reading everything from the replica, including the confirmation page after checkout.
  • Global statement_timeout in the parameter group that kills the nightly migration.
  • Leaving log_min_duration_statement off and debugging slow queries blind.
  • Never running a restore, then discovering the backup retention was set to zero days by a Terraform default.

Interview questions

  1. What does Multi-AZ RDS protect against and what does it not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: instance and AZ failure with automatic promotion; not bad deploys, not deleted rows, not regional outage. Follow-up: how does PITR fit in?
  2. Why is Aurora replica lag so much lower than an RDS read replica's?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: replicas read shared distributed storage instead of replaying WAL over a stream.
  3. A restore from PITR completed. Are you done?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; new endpoint, repoint app, verify data, consider the writes that landed on the old instance since.
  4. Your write latency spiked with CPU at 30%. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: IOPS versus baseline, queue depth, lock waits in Performance Insights, checkpoint activity.
  5. When would you send a query to a read replica and when not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: lag-tolerant reads (history, catalogue); never read-your-writes or anything feeding a decision that writes.

Practical exercise

Stand up an RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ instance and one read replica. Point a NestJS service at both using the replication config above. Run 200 RPS of mixed traffic and trigger a reboot with failover from the console. Acceptance criteria: writes recover within 120 seconds with no manual action; the replica-lag chart shows the failover; a PITR restore to five minutes earlier is completed and the app repointed within 30 minutes, following a written runbook.

46.5 DynamoDB and ElastiCache Redis

Concept

DynamoDB is a managed key-value and wide-column database: you fetch items by a partition key (and optionally a sort key), it scales horizontally without you thinking about it, and it answers in single-digit milliseconds at any size. ElastiCache is managed Redis (or the Redis-compatible Valkey), the cache and data-structure server you met in Part 27 — Caching, with replication and failover handled by AWS.

Why does it exist?

PostgreSQL scales writes vertically; past a point you shard by hand. DynamoDB exists for workloads with simple access patterns and enormous or spiky write volume where that hand-sharding is not worth it. ElastiCache exists because running Redis with replication and failover yourself is another operations job, and because a cache in a different AZ from its replica is what survives an AZ loss.

Mental model

Imagine DynamoDB as a vast wall of numbered lockers. If you know the locker number (partition key) you get your item instantly, and adding a million more lockers is free of thought. But asking "which lockers contain a red jacket" means opening every locker (a scan), and the wall does not know that two lockers relate to each other (no joins). ElastiCache Redis is the whiteboard next to your desk: fastest thing in the building, wiped if the building loses power, so you keep a copy on the whiteboard next door.

How it works

DynamoDB basics. A table has a partition key (hash key) and optionally a sort key (range key). Items are up to 400 KB. Data is spread across partitions by the hash of the partition key; each physical partition serves up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second and holds up to 10 GB. Reads are eventually consistent by default (a few hundred ms window) or strongly consistent on request at double the cost. Secondary indexes: a GSI has its own keys and capacity and is eventually consistent; an LSI shares the partition key, must be created with the table, and caps the total size per partition-key value at 10 GB. Capacity is on-demand (pay per request; writes cost about five times reads) or provisioned (cheaper at steady load, throttles above the number). Extras: TTL for automatic expiry, Streams for change capture, transactions across up to 100 items at double cost, PITR, and global tables for multi-region active-active.

Partition-key design. Everything about DynamoDB performance is "how evenly are requests spread across partition keys". A key like date puts every write of the day into one partition and throttles at 1,000 writes per second no matter how big the table is. A key like userId spreads writes well but makes "all orders today" a scan. Adaptive capacity moves throughput toward hot partitions, but it cannot exceed the per-partition ceiling.

Single-table design. The idiomatic pattern: one table with generic PK and SK attributes, where a user, their orders, and each order's items share the same PK (USER#42) with different SK prefixes (PROFILE, ORDER#2025-09-01#abc, ORDER#...#ITEM#1). One Query on PK = USER#42 AND SK BEGINS_WITH ORDER# returns the user's orders without a join. The design starts from the list of access patterns, not from the entities; adding a new access pattern later may require a new GSI or a data migration. That rigidity is the price of the speed.

When DynamoDB beats PostgreSQL. Sessions and carts (get and put by id), idempotency keys with TTL, device state, activity feeds, rate-limit counters, anything with hundreds of thousands of writes per second and key-shaped access, and workloads that must be serverless from top to bottom.

When DynamoDB is a mistake. Reporting and analytics, ad hoc queries, anything with joins or aggregates, evolving access patterns in a young product, uniqueness constraints across non-key attributes, and multi-row invariants that need real transactions with isolation levels. The classic failure is a team that models an e-commerce catalogue with filters ("size 42, colour red, price under 3,000, in stock") in DynamoDB and ends up building a search index anyway.

ElastiCache Redis topologies. Cluster mode disabled: one shard, a primary and up to five replicas, a primary endpoint for writes and a reader endpoint for reads, everything fits in one node's memory. Cluster mode enabled: data is split across up to 500 shards by the 16,384 hash slots, each shard with its own replicas, and clients use the configuration endpoint and must be cluster-aware (multi-key commands only work when keys share a hash tag {userId}). Multi-AZ with automatic failover promotes a replica in another AZ when the primary fails and updates DNS; it typically completes in well under a minute, during which writes fail and reads may continue from replicas. Persistence is by RDB snapshot only; treat ElastiCache as a cache or a rebuildable store, not a system of record. maxmemory-policy defaults to volatile-lru, meaning only keys with a TTL are evicted; a cache full of keys without TTL fails writes with OOM command not allowed.

Client behaviour during failover. ioredis reconnects on ECONNRESET, follows MOVED redirects in cluster mode, and can be told how many times to retry a command (maxRetriesPerRequest). The two knobs that matter: a short connectTimeout (a few seconds) and a per-command timeout in your code, so a Redis failover degrades to "cache miss, go to PostgreSQL" instead of "every request hangs for 30 seconds".

Practical example

An idempotency store for the payments API in DynamoDB: PK = IDEMPOTENCY#<key>, attributes status, responseBody, expiresAt (TTL 24 hours). A conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists(PK) is the atomic "claim this key" operation: the first request wins, a concurrent duplicate gets ConditionalCheckFailedException and returns the stored response. This is the same pattern as the PostgreSQL INSERT ... ON CONFLICT version in Part 15 — API Design, but it costs nothing when idle and scales to any burst.

NestJS example

A cache-aside read for product details against ElastiCache with a hard per-command timeout, so a Redis failover cannot take the product page down.

TypeScript
// src/products/product-cache.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class ProductCacheService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ProductCacheService.name);
  private readonly redis = new Redis({
    host: process.env.REDIS_PRIMARY_HOST, // cluster-mode-disabled primary endpoint
    port: 6379,
    tls: {},                              // in-transit encryption enabled on the cluster
    connectTimeout: 2_000,
    maxRetriesPerRequest: 1,              // fail fast during failover
    enableOfflineQueue: false,            // do not buffer commands while disconnected
    commandTimeout: 150,                  // a cache slower than the DB is not a cache
  });

  async getOrLoad<T>(key: string, ttlSeconds: number, loader: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    try {
      const hit = await this.redis.get(key);
      if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit) as T;
    } catch (err) {
