      this.logger.warn(`redis get failed for ${key}: ${(err as Error).message}`); // degrade, do not fail
    }
    const value = await loader(); // PostgreSQL, ~2 ms local
    this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), 'EX', ttlSeconds).catch(() => undefined); // fire and forget
    return value;
  }
}

Production scenario

A ride-booking platform stores live driver locations in ElastiCache (GEOADD per driver every 4 seconds, 50,000 drivers, about 12,000 writes per second on a cache.r7g.large) and ride records in PostgreSQL. Trip state that must survive anything goes to PostgreSQL; the location grid is rebuilt in under a minute from the drivers' next updates if Redis is lost. The team chose cluster mode disabled with two replicas across AZs because the working set is 3 GB and one shard's throughput is enough; cluster mode would only add client complexity.

Failure scenario

A notifications team stored "notifications per user per day" in DynamoDB with PK = <date> and SK = <userId> so that a nightly job could query one day cheaply. At 09:00 every weekday a batch of 400,000 push notifications was recorded within five minutes. All of them hit the single partition for that date, which caps at 1,000 writes per second. Writes throttled (ProvisionedThroughputExceededException even on on-demand), the SDK retried with backoff, the Lambda writers scaled to 900 concurrent, and the batch that should have taken five minutes took forty while burning ten times the write cost in retries. The fix was PK = <userId>, SK = <date>#<notificationId>, with a GSI on a sharded date key (<date>#<random 0-9>) for the nightly job. Lesson: in DynamoDB the partition key is the throughput plan.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Hot partition from a low-cardinality key; symptom is throttling with plenty of total capacity.
  • Eventually consistent read after write returns the old item; use ConsistentRead: true where it matters.
  • Item over 400 KB fails; move blobs to S3 and store the key.
  • GSI throttling back-pressures the base table: an under-provisioned index throttles writes to the table itself.
  • Redis eviction with volatile-lru and no TTLs: writes fail with OOM while memory sits at 100%.
  • Redis failover mid-pipeline: READONLY You can't write against a read only replica from a client still talking to the demoted node; reconnect on that error.
  • Cluster-mode CROSSSLOT error for multi-key operations without hash tags.
  • Cache stampede after failover: an empty cache sends every request to PostgreSQL; request coalescing and warming are covered in Part 27.
  • Reserved memory (reserved-memory-percent 25%) is needed for replication buffers; set it to zero and a full sync can crash the node.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start every DynamoDB conversation with "list the access patterns", and if the list is unstable they choose PostgreSQL. They keep Redis as a cache or rebuildable state, never the only copy of anything, and they can say how long the system limps without it. They pick cluster mode disabled until a single shard's memory or throughput is actually exceeded. They put a timeout on every cache call because a slow cache is worse than no cache.

Common mistakes

  • Using DynamoDB because it is "web scale" for a system with 50 writes per second and evolving requirements.
  • Modelling DynamoDB like a relational schema: one table per entity, then trying to join in application code.
  • Single-node Redis in production as the session store; a failover logs everyone out.
  • No command timeout on Redis, so a failover becomes a full outage.
  • Storing sessions in Redis without a TTL and being surprised by OOM six months later.

Interview questions

  1. How do you choose a DynamoDB partition key?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: high cardinality, evenly spread by access, matches the dominant query; sharded keys for time series.
  2. When is DynamoDB the wrong choice?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ad hoc queries, joins, reporting, unstable access patterns, cross-attribute uniqueness.
  3. What happens to your app during an ElastiCache Multi-AZ failover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: writes fail for tens of seconds, DNS flips, clients must reconnect; design for cache-miss degradation.
  4. Cluster mode enabled or disabled?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: disabled until one shard's memory or throughput is exceeded; enabled brings hash slots and client constraints.
  5. Explain single-table design in two sentences.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one table, generic PK/SK, items co-located by access pattern so one Query returns a whole aggregate.

Practical exercise

Implement the idempotency store twice: in DynamoDB with a conditional put and TTL, and in PostgreSQL with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Fire 1,000 concurrent duplicate requests at each. Acceptance criteria: exactly one side effect per key in both; p99 latency of the claim operation recorded for both; a written half-page on which you would ship and why, including the monthly cost at 10 million requests.

46.6 Messaging: SQS, SNS and EventBridge

Concept

SQS is a queue: a producer puts a message in, one consumer takes it out, and if the consumer crashes the message comes back. SNS is a publisher: one message goes in, every subscriber gets a copy. EventBridge is an event bus with routing rules: events go in, rules match on content, and matching events are delivered to targets, with a schema registry and a scheduler on the side. The messaging patterns themselves (outbox, idempotent consumers, ordering, DLQs) are in Part 28 — Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS; this section is about what the AWS services guarantee and cost.

Why does it exist?

Kafka is a powerful log, and it is also a cluster you operate (or pay MSK to operate) with partitions, consumer groups and rebalancing to understand. Most backends have a dozen places that need "do this later, reliably" or "tell everyone this happened" and none of the properties that justify a log. SQS and SNS give you those two things with zero servers, per-request pricing, and at-least-once delivery. EventBridge exists for the routing problem: many producers, many consumers, and rules in the middle so that producers do not know who listens.

Mental model

Imagine SQS as a restaurant's order rail: tickets go up, any free cook takes one, and if a cook drops it the ticket goes back up after a while. SNS is the kitchen bell: everyone who cares hears it, and each takes their own copy of what it means. EventBridge is a receptionist with a rule book: "if the letter mentions a refund, copy it to finance and support; if it is from a partner, forward to integrations".

How it works

SQS standard queues. At-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering, effectively unlimited throughput. A consumer calls ReceiveMessage (use long polling with WaitTimeSeconds: 20 to avoid empty responses and cost); the message becomes invisible for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours); the consumer must DeleteMessage after success or the message reappears. If work takes longer than the timeout, extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility (a heartbeat). After maxReceiveCount failed receives, the redrive policy moves the message to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), which you alarm on and can redrive back. Messages are up to 256 KB (larger payloads go through S3 with the extended client library), retained 4 days by default (up to 14), and can be delayed up to 15 minutes. Price: $0.40 per million requests after the first million, and a batch of ten messages counts as one request.

SQS FIFO queues. Ordered within a MessageGroupId, deduplicated by MessageDeduplicationId (or a content hash) for five minutes, delivered exactly once to the consumer (you still need idempotency if your side effect can fail after delete). Throughput is 300 messages per second per API action without batching, 3,000 with batching, and much higher in high-throughput mode where ordering is per message group. Use FIFO when order per entity matters (events for one order) and the volume is moderate.

SNS. A topic with subscriptions: SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS, Firehose. Publishing once delivers to all; this is fan-out. Filter policies on message attributes (or on the body) let each subscription receive only what it wants, so the orders topic can feed the warehouse queue only order.paid and the analytics queue everything. Subscribing an SQS queue to a topic is the standard durable fan-out: SNS retries HTTP endpoints for a while and gives up; an SQS subscriber holds the message until the consumer is back. Turn on raw message delivery, or the SQS body arrives wrapped in an SNS JSON envelope with your payload as a string inside Message. FIFO topics deliver in order to FIFO queues.

EventBridge. An event bus (the default bus receives AWS service events; you create custom buses for your domain) with rules: JSON patterns that match on any field of the event ("detail-type": ["OrderPaid"], "detail": {"amount": [{"numeric": [">", 50000]}]}) and route to up to five targets each (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, ECS tasks, another bus in another account or region, API destinations with stored credentials). The schema registry stores event schemas, can discover them from traffic, and generates code bindings. The Scheduler runs cron and rate schedules at scale, including one-time schedules ("cancel this reservation at 18:30 if unpaid"), replacing home-made cron tables. Archive and replay let you re-deliver past events to a rule after a bug fix. Pipes connect a source (SQS, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis) to a target with optional filtering and enrichment. Delivery is at-least-once with retries for up to 24 hours and a DLQ per target. Price: about $1 per million custom events. Latency is typically around half a second, and PutEvents throughput is a soft limit in the thousands per second per region.

Choosing between them.

Need SQS SNS EventBridge Kafka / MSK
One consumer does the work later Yes Possible, heavier
Fan-out to several consumers via SNS to SQS Yes Yes Consumer groups
Content-based routing, many producers Attributes only Yes In consumers
Ordering per entity FIFO FIFO topics No Per partition
Replay history No No Archive, coarse Yes, native
Throughput 100k+ msg/s sustained Yes, standard Yes No Yes
Retention beyond 14 days No No Archive Yes
Cross-account, cross-region routing Manual Manual Native MirrorMaker
Ops burden None None None Cluster to run
Cost at 100M msg/month About $40 About $50 About $100 About $500 plus

The rule of thumb: SQS for work queues, SNS plus SQS for fan-out of the same event to several workers, EventBridge for a domain event bus with routing and scheduling across services and accounts, Kafka when you need replay, strict ordering at high volume, or stream processing. Do not run Kafka to send emails.

Practical example

Order placement: the API writes the order and an outbox row in one transaction (the outbox pattern, Part 28 — Messaging). A relay publishes OrderPaid to the orders SNS topic with attributes eventType=order.paid, amount=7200. Three SQS queues are subscribed with filters: fulfilment, analytics, fraud review (only above 50,000). Each queue has a DLQ with maxReceiveCount: 5 and an alarm on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0 in the DLQ. The fulfilment consumers are ECS tasks scaling on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible of their queue. The whole thing costs a few dollars a month at a million orders.

NestJS example

A long-polling SQS consumer with a visibility heartbeat and no-delete-on-failure, so a crashed worker's message comes back and a poison message reaches the DLQ.

TypeScript
// src/fulfilment/order-paid.consumer.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { SQSClient, ReceiveMessageCommand, DeleteMessageCommand, ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand, Message } from '@aws-sdk/client-sqs';
import { FulfilmentService } from './fulfilment.service';

@Injectable()
export class OrderPaidConsumer implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderPaidConsumer.name);
  private readonly sqs = new SQSClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION }); // credentials from the task role
  private readonly queueUrl = this.config.getOrThrow<string>('FULFILMENT_QUEUE_URL');
  private running = false;

  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService, private readonly fulfilment: FulfilmentService) {}

  onModuleInit() { this.running = true; void this.loop(); }
  async onModuleDestroy() { this.running = false; } // SIGTERM: stop receiving; in-flight messages finish

  private async loop(): Promise<void> {
    while (this.running) {
      try {
        const { Messages = [] } = await this.sqs.send(new ReceiveMessageCommand({
          QueueUrl: this.queueUrl, MaxNumberOfMessages: 10, WaitTimeSeconds: 20, VisibilityTimeout: 60,
        }));
        await Promise.all(Messages.map((m) => this.handle(m)));
      } catch (err) {
        this.logger.error(`receive failed: ${(err as Error).message}`);
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2_000)); // do not hot-loop on an SQS outage
      }
    }
  }

  private async handle(m: Message): Promise<void> {
    const heartbeat = setInterval(() => {
      this.sqs.send(new ChangeMessageVisibilityCommand({
        QueueUrl: this.queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: m.ReceiptHandle!, VisibilityTimeout: 60,
      })).catch(() => undefined);
    }, 30_000); // extend while a slow fulfilment call runs
    try {
      const event = JSON.parse(m.Body!) as { eventId: string; orderId: string };
      await this.fulfilment.reserveAndShip(event); // idempotent on eventId (Part 28 — Messaging)
      await this.sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: this.queueUrl, ReceiptHandle: m.ReceiptHandle! }));
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn(`message ${m.MessageId} failed, will retry: ${(err as Error).message}`);
      // no delete: SQS redelivers after the visibility timeout; DLQ after maxReceiveCount
    } finally {
      clearInterval(heartbeat);
    }
  }
}

Production scenario

The notifications platform pushes 30 million messages a month through one SNS topic to four SQS queues (email, push, SMS, audit). The SMS consumer talks to a provider limited to 100 requests per second, so its ECS service is capped at two tasks and the queue simply grows during a campaign and drains over an hour; the email consumer scales to twenty tasks and drains in minutes. Same event, different back-pressure per consumer, and nobody had to size a Kafka cluster. Monthly messaging cost: under $60.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 finance reported customers receiving two invoices for one order. The invoice worker called a PDF service that had slowed from 3 seconds to 45 seconds per document. The SQS visibility timeout was 30 seconds. Each message became visible again while the first worker was still generating the PDF; a second worker picked it up, and both emailed the customer. Nothing had "failed", so no alarm fired. Fixes: a visibility heartbeat as in the example above; an idempotency check on invoiceGeneratedFor(orderId) before the slow call and a conditional update after; and an alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, which had been climbing for half an hour. At-least-once delivery is not a corner case; it is the normal behaviour under slowness.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Duplicate delivery from redelivery, from producer retries, and from SNS retries to SQS; the consumer must be idempotent by event id.
  • Visibility timeout shorter than processing produces duplicates as above; heartbeat or set it to six times the p99 processing time.
  • Poison message without a DLQ cycles forever, consuming a worker slot each time.
  • DLQ with no alarm is a black hole; messages expire after 14 days unseen.
  • FIFO throughput ceiling hit during a campaign; one message group per entity, or standard queue plus idempotency.
  • SNS envelope surprise: consumer JSON-parses the body and finds Type, MessageId, Message; enable raw delivery.
  • EventBridge rule pattern silently matching nothing after a producer renames a field; test patterns with test-event-pattern and alarm on FailedInvocations and on zero MatchedEvents.
  • Consumer crash after side effect, before delete: the message returns; idempotency is the only defence.
  • Large payload: a 300 KB event fails to publish; send a reference (S3 key or order id) instead of the document.
  • Queue growing while workers are healthy: the downstream dependency is slow; scale on oldest-message age, not just depth.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "does this need ordering, replay, or more than 3,000 messages per second?" and if the answer is no three times, Kafka is not on the table. They insist every queue has a DLQ, every DLQ has an alarm, and every consumer is idempotent, before a single message flows. They scale consumers on queue age, because depth is fine and age is what the customer feels. They keep events small and self-describing (eventId, eventType, occurredAt, orderId) and put the schema in a registry once more than two teams consume it.

Common mistakes

  • Deleting the message before processing it "so it is not processed twice".
  • No visibility heartbeat on a consumer that calls a slow third party.
  • One giant queue for every job type, so a slow job type starves the fast ones.
  • Fan-out by publishing to three queues from application code instead of one SNS topic, and forgetting the third one in the retry path.
  • Using EventBridge as a work queue and being surprised by 24-hour retry semantics and half-second latency.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the SQS visibility timeout and what goes wrong when it is too short or too long.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: duplicates when too short, slow recovery from crashes when too long; heartbeat for variable work.
  2. How do you implement fan-out with at-least-once durability on AWS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: SNS topic with SQS subscribers, filter policies, DLQs per queue.
  3. SQS FIFO promises exactly-once processing. Do you still need idempotency?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: yes; exactly-once covers delivery to the consumer, not your side effects after a partial failure.
  4. When would you pick EventBridge over SNS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: content-based routing, many producers and consumers, cross-account, schema registry, scheduler; SNS for simple high-throughput fan-out.
  5. Where does Kafka earn its cost over SQS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: replay, ordering at high volume, stream processing, long retention.

Practical exercise

Build the orders fan-out: one SNS topic, three filtered SQS queues with DLQs, one NestJS consumer per queue. Publish 10,000 events with 5% forced failures in one consumer. Acceptance criteria: the failed messages land in that queue's DLQ after five attempts and an alarm fires; replaying the DLQ after a fix processes them exactly once (verified by a database count); slowing the consumer to 50 seconds per message produces zero duplicates thanks to the heartbeat.

46.7 Load balancing and the API edge: ALB, NLB and API Gateway

Concept

A load balancer is the one stable address in front of a fleet of replaceable containers. AWS gives you two: the Application Load Balancer (ALB) understands HTTP (layer 7) and routes by host, path and headers; the Network Load Balancer (NLB) forwards TCP and UDP connections (layer 4) at very high speed without reading them. API Gateway is a third kind of front door: a managed API layer with authentication, throttling per client, request validation and WebSocket support, designed mostly for Lambda backends but able to front containers too.

Why does it exist?

Containers come and go: deploys replace them, auto scaling adds and removes them, an AZ failure kills a third of them. Clients need one DNS name, one TLS certificate and one place where unhealthy targets are removed from rotation within seconds. Beyond that, an API edge needs cross-cutting features (TLS termination, WAF, rate limiting, routing between services) that you do not want to build into every NestJS application.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel. The ALB is the concierge who reads your booking (host, path, headers) and sends you to the right desk, and who quietly stops sending guests to a desk whose clerk has stepped away. The NLB is the revolving door: it moves people through as fast as physically possible and reads nothing. API Gateway is a front desk with a guest register: it checks ID, counts how many times each guest has asked for something today, and can call room service (Lambda) without any clerk being on shift.

How it works

ALB. A listener on 443 terminates TLS with an ACM certificate and evaluates rules in priority order: host header, path pattern, HTTP method, headers, query string, source IP. Each rule forwards to one or more target groups, optionally weighted (95% to orders-v41, 5% to orders-v42 is a canary). Targets are instances, IP addresses (what Fargate tasks register as) or Lambda functions. The ALB runs health checks against each target (path /health/ready, interval 30 s default, timeout 5 s, healthy after 5 successes and unhealthy after 2 failures by default; production settings are usually interval 10, healthy 2, unhealthy 2, so a dead task leaves rotation within 20 s). Targets being removed enter draining for the deregistration delay (300 s default; set 30 s for APIs), during which in-flight requests finish and no new ones arrive. ALB speaks HTTP/2 and gRPC to clients and to targets (gRPC target groups), supports WebSocket upgrades, sticky sessions by cookie (avoid; keep state in Redis), and attaches to WAF. Cross-zone load balancing is always on, which means every target receives an equal share regardless of AZ. Access logs go to S3. Pricing is about $16 per month plus $0.008 per load-balancer capacity unit hour; an LCU is 25 new connections per second, 3,000 active connections per minute, 1 GB per hour processed, or 1,000 rule evaluations per second, whichever is highest.

NLB. Forwards TCP, UDP and TLS connections with sub-millisecond added latency and millions of requests per second. It offers one static IP per AZ (or your own Elastic IPs), preserves the client's source IP to the target, and has a fixed 350 s TCP idle timeout. It does not see HTTP, so no path routing, no header-based rules, no WAF. Choose it for non-HTTP protocols (a PostgreSQL proxy, MQTT, Kafka brokers exposed to a partner), when a partner must allow-list fixed IPs, for PrivateLink endpoint services (which require an NLB or a Gateway Load Balancer), and when you need raw throughput with a stable IP.

The keep-alive timeout rule. The ALB keeps connections to your targets open and reuses them. Its idle timeout is 60 s by default. Node's HTTP server closes an idle keep-alive connection after server.keepAliveTimeout, which defaults to 5 s. Picture the race: a connection has been idle for 5.000 s; Node decides to close it; at 5.001 s the ALB picks that same connection for a new request. The request hits a closing socket, the ALB gets a reset, and the client receives 502 Bad Gateway with nothing in your application logs. The fix is a rule you will apply everywhere: the backend's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the proxy's idle timeout. For ALB set keepAliveTimeout = 65_000 and headersTimeout = 66_000 (Node requires headers timeout to exceed keep-alive timeout). The same rule applies to NLB (350 s), to an Nginx ingress (keepalive_timeout upstream, 60 s default), and to CloudFront's origin keep-alive (5 s default, raise it to 60 s at the origin setting and keep Node above that).

API Gateway. Three products under one name.

  • REST API: the full-featured one. Request validation against JSON schemas, mapping templates to reshape requests, usage plans with API keys and per-client quotas, response caching, canary stages, WAF, private APIs inside a VPC, direct integrations with AWS services (write to SQS or DynamoDB with no Lambda). About $3.50 per million requests plus data, and it adds tens of milliseconds.
  • HTTP API: the lighter, cheaper one. About $1.00 per million, lower latency, built-in JWT authorizer (perfect for Cognito or any OIDC issuer), CORS handling, and integration with a private ALB or NLB through a VPC link. No usage plans, no caching, no request validation, no WAF attachment.
  • WebSocket API: manages persistent client connections for you. Routes $connect, $disconnect, $default and custom routes to Lambda or HTTP backends; your backend pushes to a client by calling the @connections management API with the connection id. Connections last at most two hours with a ten-minute idle timeout. This is how you do WebSockets without running a WebSocket server.

Throttling: an account-level default of 10,000 requests per second with a burst of 5,000 per region, overridable per stage and per route, and per client through usage plans. Exceeding it returns 429 Too Many Requests; your clients must retry with backoff. The integration timeout is 29 s by default (raisable for regional REST APIs on request) and the payload limit is 10 MB. Authorizers: IAM (SigV4-signed requests), Cognito user pools, Lambda authorizers (custom logic, cacheable), JWT (HTTP API).

API Gateway versus ALB.

Question ALB API Gateway
Backend is containers at high, steady RPS Yes; $50 to $150 per month at 1,000 RPS Expensive: $2,600 to $9,000 per month at 1,000 RPS
Backend is Lambda Possible (Lambda target) Native, better fit
Per-client API keys, quotas, plans No (build it in the app) REST API usage plans
Request schema validation at the edge No REST API
JWT validation at the edge No (use the app or Cognito with ALB auth action) HTTP API built in
WebSockets Pass-through to your servers Managed, serverless
WAF Yes REST API only
Path and host routing across services Yes, rich Per route
Added latency About 1 ms 5 to 30 ms

Most container platforms run CloudFront in front of an ALB and use API Gateway only for Lambda-backed pieces (webhooks, a WebSocket notification channel).

Practical example

The listener rules for the e-commerce ALB, in priority order: host api.shop.example and path /v1/orders* to target group orders-api; /v1/catalog* to catalog-api; /v1/payments/webhooks/* to a Lambda target group; a default rule that returns a fixed 404 JSON response so that unknown paths never reach any service. During a canary, the orders rule forwards to two target groups weighted 95 and 5. WAF in front applies a rate-based rule (2,000 requests per 5 minutes per IP) and the AWS managed core rule set.

NestJS example

A WebSocket gateway that lives behind an ALB. Two things matter: the ALB idle timeout (60 s) also applies to WebSocket frames, so the server must send a ping more often than that; and horizontal scaling needs shared state, so the gateway publishes through Redis rather than holding rooms in memory.

TypeScript
// src/notifications/notifications.gateway.ts
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect, WebSocketGateway, WebSocketServer } from '@nestjs/websockets';
import type { Server, WebSocket } from 'ws';

@WebSocketGateway({ path: '/ws' }) // @nestjs/platform-ws adapter registered in main.ts
export class NotificationsGateway implements OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect {
  @WebSocketServer() server!: Server;
  private readonly logger = new Logger(NotificationsGateway.name);
  private readonly heartbeats = new Map<WebSocket, NodeJS.Timeout>();

  handleConnection(client: WebSocket) {
    // ALB idle timeout is 60 s; a frame every 25 s keeps the connection alive
    // and detects dead clients (a phone that lost signal never sends close).
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      if (client.readyState !== client.OPEN) return;
      client.ping();
    }, 25_000);
    this.heartbeats.set(client, timer);
  }

  handleDisconnect(client: WebSocket) {
    clearInterval(this.heartbeats.get(client));
    this.heartbeats.delete(client);
  }

  // Called by a Redis subscriber: any task can fan out to its own clients.
  broadcastOrderUpdate(payload: { orderId: string; status: string }) {
    const frame = JSON.stringify({ type: 'order.updated', ...payload });
    for (const client of this.server.clients) {
      if (client.readyState === client.OPEN) client.send(frame);
    }
  }
}

Set the keepAliveTimeout from section 46.2 as well; it protects the plain HTTP requests on the same ALB.

Production scenario

At 1,000 RPS the ALB for the platform handles roughly 6 GB per hour of traffic, a few hundred new connections per second (CloudFront reuses connections, so far fewer than the client count), and one or two rule evaluations per request. That is about 7 LCUs, or $40 per month on top of the $16 base. Target groups use interval 10, healthy 2, unhealthy 2, timeout 4 and a 30 s deregistration delay. A deploy of the orders service therefore shows a target leaving rotation within 20 s of failing and joining within 20 s of passing, and a rollout of 8 tasks takes about 6 minutes end to end.

Failure scenario

For three weeks the orders API showed a steady 0.04% rate of 502s: about 35 per hour at peak. Application logs showed nothing; every request the app saw was answered. The ALB metric HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count (errors generated by the load balancer, distinct from HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count) matched the number exactly. Access logs showed the 502s had a target processing time of -1: the ALB never got a response. The service had been migrated from an EC2 host with Nginx in front (whose upstream keep-alive was tuned) to Fargate with Node directly behind the ALB and the default 5 s keepAliveTimeout. Setting it to 65 s dropped the 502s to zero the same afternoon. The senior lesson is not the number; it is the diagnostic habit of separating "errors the load balancer made" from "errors the target made".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Health check hitting a heavy endpoint: a readiness check that runs three database queries at interval 10 across 8 tasks and 3 AZ checkers is 7 queries per second of pure overhead; keep it to SELECT 1.
  • Health check passing while the app is broken: /health/live returns 200 but every real endpoint 500s; smoke tests after deploy catch it (Part 47 — CI/CD).
  • Deregistration delay longer than task stop timeout: ECS kills the task while the ALB still routes to it; align stopTimeout and the delay.
  • Sticky sessions with auto scaling: scale-in logs out a share of users; keep sessions in Redis.
  • Idle timeout during a long request: an export endpoint that takes 90 s gets a 504 from the ALB at 60 s; make it asynchronous or raise the idle timeout for that listener.
  • Cross-zone data charges: ALB-to-target traffic across AZs is not charged for ALB, but your target-to-database traffic is.
  • API Gateway 429s during a burst because the stage limit is below the account limit; Retry-After is not sent, so clients need jittered backoff.
  • API Gateway 29 s timeout killing a slow report; the Lambda keeps running and the client retries, doubling the load.
  • WebSocket behind ALB without pings silently dropped at 60 s of idle.
  • NLB and security groups: NLB (newer ones) supports security groups; older setups saw the client IP directly at the target, so the target's security group had to allow the whole internet.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They put every service behind a target group with an honest readiness check and a short deregistration delay before the first deploy. They know the keep-alive rule cold and apply it to every proxy layer in the path. They choose ALB for container APIs by default and reach for API Gateway when the backend is Lambda or the requirement is per-client quotas. They read HTTPCode_ELB_5XX and HTTPCode_Target_5XX as two different alarms with two different owners.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving the Node default keepAliveTimeout of 5 s behind any proxy.
  • Using the ALB's 60 s idle timeout as the request timeout for the whole system, so a slow database query fails at the edge while the server keeps working.
  • Fronting a 1,000 RPS container API with API Gateway REST and discovering a $9,000 line item.
  • One target group for all services with path routing done in the app, which makes canaries and per-service scaling impossible.
  • Health checks with a 30 s interval and 5 healthy threshold, so a new task takes two and a half minutes to receive traffic.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a Node service behind an ALB return sporadic 502s, and what is the fix?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: keep-alive race; backend timeout longer than the ALB idle timeout, plus headers timeout above it.
  2. ALB or NLB for a gRPC service? For a PostgreSQL proxy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ALB supports gRPC natively at L7; a PostgreSQL proxy is raw TCP, so NLB.
  3. How do you run a canary with an ALB?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: weighted target groups on the listener rule, metrics per target group, automated promotion (Part 47).
  4. When is API Gateway worth its price?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: Lambda backends, per-client keys and quotas, edge validation, managed WebSockets; not for high-RPS container APIs.
  5. What does HTTPCode_ELB_5XX tell you that HTTPCode_Target_5XX does not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the load balancer generated the error (no healthy targets, keep-alive resets, timeouts) versus your app returned it.

Practical exercise

Put a NestJS service behind an ALB with the default Node settings and run a 200 RPS load test for ten minutes with a mix of request sizes. Acceptance criteria: you observe a non-zero HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count; you find the matching access-log lines with target processing time -1; applying the keep-alive rule brings the count to zero over a second ten-minute run; a weighted target group canary at 10% is demonstrated with per-target-group latency graphs.

46.8 CloudFront and Route 53

Concept

CloudFront is the content delivery network: several hundred edge locations that cache your responses close to users and carry uncached traffic to your origin over AWS's backbone. Route 53 is DNS with routing policies and health checks, which makes it the tool for sending users to the nearest, healthiest, or chosen endpoint.

Why does it exist?

A user in Mumbai calling an origin in Virginia pays 200 ms of physics per round trip before any work happens; a cached product image served from the Mumbai edge arrives in 10 ms. Even for uncacheable API calls, terminating TLS at the edge and reusing warm backbone connections to the origin saves two to three round trips. Route 53 exists because "which IP should this name resolve to" is a decision (nearest region, healthy endpoint, 5% to the new stack) rather than a static fact.

Mental model

Imagine CloudFront as a chain of neighbourhood shops stocked from one central warehouse. Popular items sit on local shelves (cached); rare items are fetched from the warehouse on request (origin fetch); and a regional depot (Origin Shield) sits between the shops and the warehouse so that a thousand shops asking for the same new item send one request, not a thousand. Route 53 is the phone book that gives a different warehouse address depending on who is asking and which warehouses are open.

How it works

CloudFront distributions. A distribution has one or more origins (an S3 bucket with Origin Access Control so the bucket stays private, an ALB, an API Gateway, any HTTPS host) and behaviors matched by path pattern (/static/* to S3, /api/* to the ALB, default to S3). Each behavior has a cache policy (what forms the cache key: which headers, cookies and query strings; minimum, default and maximum TTL), an origin request policy (what is forwarded to the origin beyond the cache key) and optionally a response headers policy. The origin's Cache-Control header drives TTL: s-maxage=86400 caches a day at the edge, no-store or private is never cached (as long as the cache policy respects it, which the managed CachingDisabled policy does). Cached objects live first at the edge, then at a regional edge cache. Origin Shield adds one more layer in a region of your choice, collapsing requests from all edges into a single origin fetch per object; it costs about $0.0075 per 10,000 requests and is worth it when origin load or cost matters.

Dynamic content. With CachingDisabled, CloudFront still adds value for an API: TLS terminates at the edge (saving round trips on the handshake), HTTP/3 to the client, persistent warm connections to the origin, and WAF and DDoS protection at the edge. The cost is per request (about $0.01 per 10,000 HTTPS requests) plus data transfer (around $0.085 per GB out in North America and Europe, more in India and South America), so at 900 million requests a month the request cost is about $900, which is a real line item to weigh against a direct ALB.

Signed URLs and signed cookies. A key group (public key registered in CloudFront, private key kept in Secrets Manager) lets your backend mint a URL that works for one object until an expiry time (and optionally only from one IP range), or a set of cookies that grant access to a whole path pattern. Use signed URLs for "download this invoice"; use signed cookies for "stream any file of this video course". This is separate from S3 pre-signed URLs (section 46.10): a CloudFront signed URL serves from the cache, an S3 pre-signed URL goes straight to the bucket.

Invalidation and versioning. Invalidating /static/app.js at every deploy costs money after the first thousand paths per month and takes a minute to propagate. Versioned file names (app.3f9a2c.js with a one-year TTL) and short TTLs for HTML avoid invalidations entirely.

Edge compute. CloudFront Functions run tiny JavaScript (sub-millisecond, no network) for header rewrites, redirects and A/B cookie assignment; Lambda@Edge runs full Lambda at regional edges for heavier work like authentication against a token service.

Route 53 routing policies.

Policy Answer depends on Use
Simple Nothing One endpoint
Weighted Weights 0 to 255 Canary a new stack at 5%, migrate gradually
Latency Resolver's measured latency to each region Multi-region active-active
Failover Health check of primary Active-passive DR
Geolocation User's country or continent Data residency, localized content
Geoproximity Distance with bias Shift load between regions
Multivalue answer Up to 8 healthy records Cheap client-side load balancing
IP-based Client CIDR Partner-specific routing

Health checks. Route 53 checkers in several regions probe an endpoint every 30 s (10 s optional) and mark it unhealthy when a threshold of consecutive failures is reached (3 by default), so detection takes 30 to 90 s. Checks can be HTTP with string matching, TCP, calculated (aggregate of others) or based on a CloudWatch alarm (the way to health-check a private resource). Failover records only work with health checks attached.

TTL reality. You set 60 s on a failover record. Route 53 honours it, but the user's operating system, browser and corporate resolver may not. Some clients keep the old answer for minutes. Failover via DNS is therefore "most clients within a couple of minutes", never "everyone in 60 seconds"; for the rest you rely on the old endpoint returning errors quickly so clients retry and re-resolve.

Practical example

The storefront: shop.example is a CloudFront distribution. /static/* and /images/* go to S3 with a one-year TTL and versioned names; /api/* goes to the ALB with CachingDisabled and an origin request policy that forwards Authorization, Accept-Language and all query strings; /api/catalog/products/* has its own behavior with a 60 s TTL and a cache key that includes the Accept-Language header but no cookies, because the catalogue is public and identical for every user. Invoice downloads are CloudFront signed URLs valid for 15 minutes, minted by the NestJS orders service.

NestJS example

Minting a CloudFront signed URL for a private invoice PDF stored in S3 behind the distribution.

TypeScript
// src/invoices/invoice-link.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { getSignedUrl } from '@aws-sdk/cloudfront-signer';

@Injectable()
export class InvoiceLinkService {
  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  // Returns a URL that serves from the edge cache and expires in 15 minutes.
  signedInvoiceUrl(orderId: string, invoiceKey: string): string {
    const url = `https://cdn.shop.example/invoices/${encodeURIComponent(invoiceKey)}`;
    return getSignedUrl({
      url,
      keyPairId: this.config.getOrThrow('CF_KEY_PAIR_ID'),          // public key id from the key group
      privateKey: this.config.getOrThrow('CF_PRIVATE_KEY'),         // loaded from Secrets Manager at boot
      dateLessThan: new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 60 * 1000).toISOString(),
    });
  }
}

The object itself is stored with Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 so that an edge never serves it to a request without a valid signature, and the behavior for /invoices/* has "restrict viewer access" enabled with the key group.

Production scenario

During a flash sale the product page is requested 4,000 times per second. The catalogue behavior with a 60 s TTL and Origin Shield means the ALB sees about 15 requests per second per distinct product-and-language pair instead of thousands, and the origin CPU barely moves. The API behavior (/api/cart, /api/checkout) is uncached and sees the real 1,000 RPS. When the on-call watches the sale, the CloudFront cache hit ratio (above 95% on the catalogue behavior) is the number that tells them the origin is safe.

Failure scenario

At 10:22 support received three tickets within a minute: users saw someone else's name and address in the account header. The team had added a /api/* behavior the previous evening using the managed CachingOptimized policy "to make things faster". That policy builds the cache key from the URL only, ignoring cookies and the Authorization header, and the /api/me endpoint returned Cache-Control: max-age=60 from an old interceptor. For 60 seconds after the first user in each edge location loaded the page, every other user at that edge got that user's profile. The distribution was switched to CachingDisabled for /api/* within ten minutes and an invalidation of /api/* issued. The permanent fix: Cache-Control: private, no-store as the default for every authenticated response in the NestJS global interceptor, and a rule that a cache policy for any authenticated path must include the Authorization header in the cache key. This is the most expensive kind of caching bug: not slow, but wrong.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Private response cached at the edge as above; defence in depth: no-store from the app and a cache policy that respects it.
  • Vary ignored: CloudFront only varies on what is in the cache key; a response that differs by Accept-Encoding or Accept-Language needs those in the key.
  • Stale after overwrite: S3 is strongly consistent, but CloudFront serves the old object until TTL or invalidation; use versioned names.
  • Origin timeout at 30 s (default, raisable to 60 s) kills long API requests before the ALB's 60 s.
  • Origin keep-alive: CloudFront's origin keep-alive of 5 s with Node's 5 s default is the same 502 race as the ALB.
  • Signed URL clock skew: a URL minted with a 1-minute expiry fails for clients whose clocks drift; use 10 minutes or more.
  • DNS failover flapping when a health check threshold is too tight; a 1-in-3 packet loss toggles the primary every minute.
  • Health check probing a cached path returns 200 from the edge while the origin is down; probe an uncacheable path.
  • Resolvers ignoring TTL keep users on a dead primary for minutes.
  • Route 53 hosted-zone deletion or NS record change takes down everything with a TTL of two days on the NS records at the registrar.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate content by cacheability before touching CloudFront: static and versioned, public and short-lived, private and never. They default every authenticated response to no-store and treat any exception as a reviewed decision. They use Route 53 failover only where a real, tested secondary exists, because a failover record pointing at an unscaled stack is a promise the system cannot keep. They explain to a product manager: "The CDN makes public pages fast and cheap; personal pages get faster TLS but are never cached, on purpose."

Common mistakes

  • Putting /api/* behind a caching policy that ignores Authorization.
  • Invalidating the whole distribution at every deploy instead of versioning file names.
  • Health checks hitting an endpoint that succeeds without touching the origin.
  • Assuming a 60 s TTL means a 60 s failover.
  • Serving user uploads straight from S3 public URLs instead of signed CloudFront URLs, exposing the bucket.

Interview questions

  1. How would you cache a public product endpoint at the edge without ever caching a user's cart?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: separate behaviors, cache key design, Cache-Control from the app, CachingDisabled for authenticated paths.
  2. CloudFront signed URL or S3 pre-signed URL?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: CloudFront for cached, edge-served, path-scoped access; S3 for direct upload or download to the bucket.
  3. What is Origin Shield and when is it worth paying for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a collapsing layer between edges and origin; worth it for expensive origins or many edges requesting the same objects.
  4. Design DNS failover for an API and state its real recovery time.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: failover policy, health checks on an uncacheable path, 60 to 90 s detection plus TTL and resolver behaviour, so two to five minutes for most clients.
  5. Why can a 60 s DNS TTL still leave users on a dead endpoint?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: OS, browser and corporate resolvers cache beyond TTL; rely on fast failure and client retries.

Practical exercise

Put a NestJS catalogue API and an S3 bucket behind one CloudFront distribution with three behaviors (static, public catalogue with a 60 s TTL, authenticated API uncached). Acceptance criteria: curl -I shows x-cache: Hit from cloudfront on the catalogue and Miss or RefreshHit never on /api/me; two different users fetching /api/me through the same edge never see each other's data (verify with a script); a Route 53 failover record with a health check flips to a secondary within three minutes when you stop the primary's tasks.

46.9 VPC networking

Concept

A VPC is your private network inside AWS: an IP address range you choose, cut into subnets placed in specific AZs, with route tables that decide where packets go, and two kinds of firewall. Every EC2 instance, Fargate task, RDS instance and ElastiCache node lives in a subnet and gets a private IP from it. Nothing reaches the internet, and nothing reaches your resources, unless a route and a firewall rule say so.

Why does it exist?

Without a private network, every database would need a public IP and a password as its only defence. The VPC makes "the database is reachable only from the API's security group" a fact of the network rather than a hope about configuration. It also determines the two most surprising line items on a bill: NAT gateway processing and cross-AZ traffic.

Mental model

Imagine an office building you designed. Floors are AZs; rooms are subnets. Some rooms have windows to the street (public subnets with a route to the internet gateway); most do not (private subnets). To send mail out from an inner room you use the mail room (NAT gateway), which charges per letter. The badge on each door (security group) remembers who it let in and lets them back out; the guard at the stairwell (network ACL) checks every person in both directions and remembers nothing. A pneumatic tube straight to the archive (VPC endpoint) means you never pay the mail room to fetch a document from S3.

How it works

Address space and subnets. Choose a CIDR that will not collide with an office or partner network you may peer with later; 10.0.0.0/16 gives 65,536 addresses. Cut it per AZ and per tier: in each of three AZs a public /24 (load balancer nodes, NAT gateway), a private application /20 (ECS tasks and EKS pods, which consume an IP each, so be generous) and a private data /24 (RDS, ElastiCache) with no route to the internet at all. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet.

Routing. Each subnet is associated with a route table. A public subnet's table has 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway (free, highly available). A private subnet's table has 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway that sits in a public subnet of the same AZ. A data subnet's table has no default route. Inbound from the internet to a private subnet is impossible regardless of security groups, because there is no route back.

NAT gateways and their cost. A NAT gateway costs about $0.045 per hour (around $33 per month) plus $0.045 per GB processed in both directions. Pulling a 2 GB container image from ECR through the NAT costs 9 cents each time; a fleet pulling 1 TB of images and S3 objects a month through the NAT pays $45 for the privilege, and an app that fetches 20 TB of S3 data pays $900. The other trap: one NAT gateway in one AZ. Tasks in the other AZs route through it (paying cross-AZ charges) and lose all outbound connectivity when that AZ fails. Production means one NAT gateway per AZ and per-AZ route tables.

Security groups versus network ACLs.

Security group Network ACL
Attached to Elastic network interface (instance, task, RDS, ALB) Subnet
State Stateful: reply traffic is automatically allowed Stateless: you must allow ephemeral return ports
Rules Allow only Allow and deny, evaluated by number
Can reference Other security groups, CIDRs, prefix lists CIDRs only
Typical use Everything Block a hostile CIDR at the subnet edge

The idiom that makes security groups powerful is referencing: the RDS security group allows port 5432 from sg-orders-api, not from an IP range. Tasks come and go with new IPs; the rule still holds. Chain it: sg-alb allows 443 from the internet; sg-api allows 3000 from sg-alb; sg-db allows 5432 from sg-api and sg-workers; sg-redis allows 6379 from sg-api and sg-workers. Nothing else can reach the database, including a developer's laptop, which is the point.

VPC endpoints. A gateway endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB adds a route-table entry so traffic to those services stays inside AWS; it is free and should exist in every VPC. An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) places an elastic network interface with a private IP in your subnets, with private DNS so sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com resolves to it; about $0.01 per hour per AZ plus $0.01 per GB. Create them for the services your private tasks call constantly: ECR (ecr.api and ecr.dkr, plus the S3 gateway endpoint for image layers), CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, STS, SQS, SNS, KMS. With those in place, a private subnet may need no NAT gateway at all. PrivateLink in the other direction lets you expose your own service (through an NLB) to another VPC or account as an endpoint, without peering and without public IPs.

Connecting VPCs. Peering is point-to-point and not transitive (A to B and B to C does not give A to C); Transit Gateway is a regional hub that scales to dozens of VPCs and on-premises links. Both charge per GB.

Flow logs. VPC Flow Logs record accepted and rejected connections per interface; they are how you answer "who tried to reach the database on 5432 last night".

Practical example

Debugging production data without a bastion host or a public database: SSM Session Manager port forwarding through a small private instance (or an ECS task with the SSM agent) whose security group is allowed by sg-db. No inbound ports, no SSH keys, every session logged to CloudTrail.

Shell
# Forward local 5433 to the RDS endpoint through an SSM-managed instance.
aws ssm start-session \
  --target i-0abc123def456 \
  --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost \
  --parameters '{"host":["orders.cluster-xyz.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com"],"portNumber":["5432"],"localPortNumber":["5433"]}'

# In another terminal, an ordinary psql session (read-only role, statement_timeout set on the role).
psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=5433 dbname=orders user=readonly sslmode=require"

Expected output of the first command: Starting session with SessionId: praveen-0f1e... followed by Port 5433 opened for sessionId ...; the session ends when you press Ctrl+C, and the tunnel is gone.

Production scenario

The platform VPC is 10.20.0.0/16 in three AZs with the layout above. The ECS API tasks run in the private app subnets and reach ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, SQS and S3 through endpoints; the only traffic through the NAT gateways is calls to third-party APIs (payment provider, SMS gateway), about 40 GB a month, so NAT processing costs under $2 and the three gateways' hourly charge (about $100) is the whole NAT bill. Before the endpoints existed, image pulls and S3 traffic through a single NAT gateway cost $260 a month and the NAT's AZ was a single point of failure for every outbound call.

Failure scenario

At 06:30 an AZ lost power. The API tasks in the other two AZs kept serving. But every payment failed: the payment provider is called over the internet, and the VPC had one NAT gateway, in the dark AZ. The route tables of all private subnets pointed at it, so outbound traffic from the healthy AZs went nowhere. The fix under pressure was creating a NAT gateway in a healthy AZ and rewriting the route tables (25 minutes, during which no order could be paid). The permanent fix: one NAT gateway per AZ, one route table per AZ, and a Terraform module that makes it impossible to build it any other way. Cost of the fix: $66 a month. Cost of the incident: 25 minutes of checkout.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NAT gateway as a bottleneck: it scales to 100 Gbps but has a limit of 55,000 simultaneous connections per destination; a worker fleet hammering one third-party IP hits ErrorPortAllocation.
  • Subnet exhaustion: /24 app subnets fill up at 251 tasks or pods; scale-out fails with an ENI allocation error and nothing obvious in the app logs.
  • Security group rule to a CIDR that changes: the "office IP" changes and every developer is locked out, or worse, a stale CIDR now belongs to someone else.
  • NACL without ephemeral ports: outbound allowed, but the reply on ports 1024 to 65535 is denied; connections hang.
  • Cross-AZ database traffic when the pool always talks to the primary in AZ a from tasks in AZ b; unavoidable for writes, but reads can prefer a same-AZ replica.
  • Endpoint policy too tight blocks ECR pulls with a misleading CannotPullContainerError.
  • Private DNS for an interface endpoint disabled, so the SDK still resolves the public IP and goes through the NAT.
  • RDS in a public subnet with PubliclyAccessible: true and a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0; scanners find it within hours.
  • Peering CIDR overlap: two VPCs with 10.0.0.0/16 can never be peered; choose distinct ranges from day one.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the VPC once, with three AZs, three tiers, per-AZ NAT and endpoints for every AWS service the app calls, and they codify it so no environment drifts. They can draw the security-group chain from memory and use it as the access-control model instead of IP lists. They look at the NAT gateway processing metric when a bill surprises them, because that is where it hides. They refuse a public database or a bastion with SSH keys when SSM exists.

Common mistakes

  • One NAT gateway for the whole VPC.
  • No S3 gateway endpoint, paying NAT fees for every image layer and every upload.
  • Security groups allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432 "temporarily".
  • /24 subnets for a Kubernetes cluster.
  • Ignoring the difference between the ALB's security group and the tasks' security group, so tasks accept traffic from anywhere.

Interview questions

  1. Explain how a request from the internet reaches a Fargate task in a private subnet and how the reply gets back.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: internet gateway to ALB in a public subnet, ALB to task over the VPC, reply through the stateful security group and the same path; no NAT involved.
  2. Stateful versus stateless firewall, with the concrete consequence for outbound HTTPS.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: security group allows the reply automatically; a NACL needs an ephemeral port allow rule.
  3. Why does a single NAT gateway violate multi-AZ design and what does it cost to fix?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: outbound single point of failure plus cross-AZ charges; one per AZ, about $33 each.
  4. Your bill shows $700 of NAT processing. First three things you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints, ECR and Logs interface endpoints, which workload is pulling data from the internet.
  5. How do you give a developer read access to production PostgreSQL safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: SSM port forwarding, a read-only role with timeouts, no public endpoint, audit logging.

Practical exercise

Build the three-tier, three-AZ VPC above in Terraform or CDK. Deploy a NestJS task in a private subnet that pulls from ECR, writes logs, reads a secret and uploads to S3 with the NAT gateway routes removed. Acceptance criteria: the task starts and works using only endpoints; VPC Flow Logs show zero traffic to the NAT; the RDS security group has exactly one inbound rule and it references a security group, not a CIDR; a psql session through SSM port forwarding succeeds while a direct connection from your laptop times out.

46.10 Object storage: S3

Concept

S3 stores objects (any bytes, up to 5 TB each) under a key in a bucket, replicated across at least three AZs, addressable over HTTPS, and billed per GB-month and per request. It is not a filesystem: there are no directories, no partial updates, no appends and no locks. It is the place where product images, invoices, exports, backups, logs and uploaded files live, and it is the origin behind CloudFront. The upload mechanics from the application's point of view (multipart, validation, virus scanning, resumable uploads) are in Part 33 — File Storage and Uploads; this section covers what S3 itself guarantees and costs.

Why does it exist?

Files do not belong in PostgreSQL (bloat, backup size, no CDN) or on a container's disk (gone at the next deploy). S3 gives unlimited capacity with eleven nines of durability, a permission model that lets a browser upload directly without touching your API, and events that trigger processing when an object lands.

Mental model

Imagine a valet lot of infinite size. You hand over an item, get a claim ticket (the key), and can get it back from any window in the region. The valets keep three copies in three buildings. You can ask for "all tickets starting with invoices/2025/09/" and get them in order, but asking "find all red items" means reading every ticket. Overwriting means handing in a new item under the same ticket; the old one is gone unless you turned on versioning.

How it works

Buckets and keys. Bucket names are globally unique and DNS-compatible; buckets are regional. Keys are strings; the / is a convention that the console renders as folders, and a prefix is any leading substring. Throughput scales per prefix: at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix, and S3 partitions further automatically. Spread hot workloads across prefixes (uploads/<userIdHash>/...) rather than one prefix per day.

Consistency. Since December 2020 S3 is strongly consistent for every operation: a GET or LIST after a PUT, overwrite or DELETE reflects the change. What is not consistent is everything you put in front of it: CloudFront caches by TTL, your application may cache metadata, a client may cache by ETag. "S3 is eventually consistent" is now false; "the path to S3 has caches" is still true.

Durability and availability. Designed for 99.999999999% durability (across AZs) and 99.99% availability for Standard (the SLA credits at 99.9%). An AZ loss is invisible; a regional S3 event, rare as it is, means writes fail and your app must degrade (queue the upload, show a fallback image).

Storage classes.

Class Per GB-month (us-east-1, approximate) Retrieval Use
Standard $0.023 Immediate, free Active data, images served by CDN
Intelligent-Tiering $0.023 plus monitoring Immediate Unknown access patterns
Standard-IA $0.0125 Immediate, $0.01/GB, 30-day minimum Old invoices, backups read rarely
One Zone-IA $0.01 Immediate, one AZ only Re-creatable derived data
Glacier Instant Retrieval $0.004 Milliseconds, $0.03/GB, 90-day minimum Archives read a few times a year
Glacier Flexible Retrieval $0.0036 Minutes to hours Compliance archives
Glacier Deep Archive $0.00099 12 hours Seven-year retention
Express One Zone Higher Single-digit ms, directory buckets Latency-sensitive hot data

Lifecycle rules move objects between classes after N days, expire them, delete old versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads (which otherwise sit invisibly and cost money forever). Versioning keeps every overwritten and deleted version (a delete becomes a delete marker), which is the only protection against an application bug that overwrites a thousand images; pair it with a lifecycle rule that expires non-current versions after 30 days.

Pre-signed URLs. Your backend, holding credentials, signs a URL that lets anyone with the URL perform one operation (GET or PUT) on one key until an expiry. The browser uploads straight to S3; your API never sees the bytes. A pre-signed POST adds conditions (content-length-range, content-type, key prefix), which a pre-signed PUT cannot enforce. The expiry you set is capped by the lifetime of the credentials that signed it: an IAM user's long-lived keys can sign for up to seven days, but an ECS task role's temporary credentials expire (and rotate) within hours, so a "7-day" URL signed by a task dies early. Keep pre-signed URLs to minutes for uploads and an hour or so for downloads, and use CloudFront signed URLs (section 46.8) for long-lived access.

Event notifications. s3:ObjectCreated:*, s3:ObjectRemoved:* and others can invoke Lambda or land in SQS, SNS or EventBridge, filtered by prefix and suffix. Delivery is at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent by key and version id. EventBridge gives richer filtering and many rules per bucket; the classic notification configuration allows only one target per event type and prefix.

Encryption and access. Every object is encrypted at rest by default with SSE-S3; SSE-KMS adds per-key policies and CloudTrail audit of each decrypt at the cost of KMS requests (turn on bucket keys so a hot bucket does not throttle KMS). Block Public Access at the account level, then grant access through bucket policies and IAM roles; ACLs are disabled by default and should stay that way. Object Lock provides write-once-read-many for compliance. Cross-region replication copies new objects asynchronously (minutes typically, 15 minutes with Replication Time Control) for disaster recovery.

Practical example

Product images: the seller's browser asks the NestJS API for an upload ticket; the API creates a files row with status pending, returns a pre-signed POST for key uploads/<sellerId>/<uuid>.jpg limited to 8 MB and image/jpeg; the browser uploads; an S3 event invokes a Lambda that validates the image, produces three sizes into images/..., and publishes image.ready; a worker marks the row ready. A nightly job expires pending rows (and their orphan objects) older than 24 hours.

NestJS example

Issuing the pre-signed POST with size and type constraints.

TypeScript
// src/uploads/upload-ticket.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
import { createPresignedPost } from '@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

@Injectable()
export class UploadTicketService {
  private readonly s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION }); // task role credentials
  private readonly bucket = this.config.getOrThrow<string>('UPLOADS_BUCKET');

  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  async createImageTicket(sellerId: string) {
    const key = `uploads/${sellerId}/${randomUUID()}.jpg`;
    const { url, fields } = await createPresignedPost(this.s3, {
      Bucket: this.bucket,
      Key: key,
      Conditions: [
        ['content-length-range', 1, 8 * 1024 * 1024], // 1 byte to 8 MB, enforced by S3
        ['eq', '$Content-Type', 'image/jpeg'],
      ],
      Fields: { 'Content-Type': 'image/jpeg' },
      Expires: 300, // 5 minutes; well inside the task role credential lifetime
    });
    return { key, url, fields }; // the browser POSTs a multipart form with these fields plus the file
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The files table that keeps S3 honest: the database is the source of truth about which objects exist and belong to whom; S3 holds the bytes.

SQL
CREATE TABLE files (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  owner_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  s3_key      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  status      text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'ready', 'rejected')),
  size_bytes  bigint,
  sha256      bytea,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  ready_at    timestamptz
);

-- Cleanup job: pending tickets never completed. Partial index keeps it cheap
-- even when the table holds 50 million ready files.
CREATE INDEX files_pending_created_idx ON files (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Nightly: select orphans, delete the S3 object (if any), then the row.
SELECT id, s3_key FROM files
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '24 hours'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 1000;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on that query with 50 million rows and a few thousand pending shows an Index Scan using files_pending_created_idx reading a handful of buffers in under a millisecond; without the partial index it is a full-table scan of several gigabytes.

Production scenario

The catalogue bucket holds 20 million images, about 4 TB. Storage in Standard costs about $92 a month; the request bill is negligible because CloudFront absorbs the reads; the lifecycle rule moves originals older than 90 days to Standard-IA (derived sizes stay hot), saving about $30 a month, and aborts incomplete multipart uploads after two days, which recovered 300 GB of invisible garbage the first time it ran. Versioning is on with non-current versions expiring after 30 days; that policy saved the catalogue once when a migration script overwrote 40,000 images with zero-byte files.

Failure scenario

Invoice download links began failing with 403 Forbidden around 55 minutes after being emailed, although the API signed them with expiresIn: 7 * 24 * 3600. The API ran on ECS with a task role. Task role credentials are temporary and rotate roughly every hour; a pre-signed URL is only valid while the credentials that signed it are, and the SDK had silently signed with a session token that expired. Nobody had tested a link older than a few minutes. The fix: invoices moved behind CloudFront with signed URLs from a long-lived key pair, and the API's pre-signed S3 URLs were limited to 15 minutes by policy. Lesson: the expiry you type is an upper bound, not a promise.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CloudFront serving a stale object after overwrite; versioned keys or invalidation.
  • 503 SlowDown on a hot prefix during a bulk import; back off, spread prefixes.
  • Duplicate event notifications; idempotent consumers keyed by key + versionId + sequencer.
  • Overwrite without versioning is silent data loss.
  • Abandoned multipart uploads accumulate cost; lifecycle abort rule.
  • 403 instead of 404 for a missing object when the caller lacks s3:ListBucket; confusing but correct.
  • KMS throttling on an SSE-KMS bucket at thousands of GETs per second; bucket keys.
  • Pre-signed URL signed with expiring credentials as above.
  • Public bucket through a bucket policy typo; account-level Block Public Access prevents it.
  • Cross-region replication lag during a regional failover: the last minutes of uploads are missing in the secondary region.
  • Object key with unusual characters (+, spaces, unicode) encoded differently by two SDKs, producing "not found" for an object that exists.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never let the API proxy file bytes when a pre-signed URL can do it. They turn on versioning, Block Public Access, and an abort-multipart lifecycle rule before the first object lands. They treat the database as the index of what exists and S3 as dumb storage, so a lost row is an orphan object, not a lost file. They know the expiry rule for pre-signed URLs and the cache rule for CloudFront because they have been bitten by both.

Common mistakes

  • Streaming uploads through the NestJS process, then wondering why 20 uploads saturate the task.
  • Sequential or date-based prefixes for a write-hot workload.
  • Assuming a DELETE frees storage when versioning is on.
  • Long pre-signed expiries from a task role.
  • Serving private files from public object URLs "because it is easier".

Interview questions

  1. Is S3 eventually consistent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no, strongly consistent since 2020 for all operations; caches in front of it are not.
  2. Design an upload flow that never sends file bytes through your API.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pre-signed POST with conditions, database ticket, event-driven processing, cleanup of orphans.
  3. Why did a 7-day pre-signed URL expire in an hour?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: temporary credentials from a role; use CloudFront signed URLs or short expiries.
  4. When would you use SSE-KMS over SSE-S3?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: per-key access control, audit of decrypts, compliance; mind the request cost and bucket keys.
  5. How do you protect against an application bug that overwrites a million objects?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: versioning with non-current expiry, least-privilege write roles, Object Lock for the truly critical.

Practical exercise

Implement the upload ticket flow end to end with a NestJS API, a bucket with versioning and Block Public Access, an S3 event to SQS, and a consumer that marks files ready. Acceptance criteria: an upload larger than 8 MB or of the wrong type is rejected by S3, not by your code; killing the consumer mid-batch produces no duplicate ready transitions; the cleanup job removes an orphan object from a pending ticket; overwriting an object and restoring the previous version is demonstrated with the CLI.

46.11 Identity and secrets: IAM, STS, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and KMS

Concept

IAM decides which principal (a person, a role assumed by a workload) may call which API on which resource. STS hands out short-lived credentials so that workloads never hold permanent keys. Secrets Manager and Parameter Store hold configuration your code needs at runtime (database passwords, API keys, feature settings); KMS holds the encryption keys that protect them and everything else at rest.

Why does it exist?

An access key pasted into an environment variable is a permanent password to your cloud account, copied into CI logs, laptops and git history. A role is a costume a workload puts on: the credentials last an hour, are minted by AWS, and are tied to a policy that names exactly what the workload may do. Without least privilege, a bug in the image resizer can delete the orders bucket; with it, the resizer can only write to images/.

Mental model

Imagine a building where nobody owns a key. Each job (API server, worker, deploy pipeline) has a badge (role) that opens only the doors its policy lists, and the badge expires every hour and is reissued automatically by the front desk (STS). Secrets Manager is the safe where the database combination is kept, and the safe itself is locked by a key that lives in a vault nobody can enter (KMS).

How it works

Principals and policies. Users (for humans, ideally federated through an identity provider and SSO rather than IAM users at all), groups, and roles (for workloads and cross-account access). A policy is JSON: Effect, Action, Resource, optional Condition. Identity-based policies attach to principals; resource-based policies attach to buckets, queues, topics, secrets and KMS keys and can grant other accounts. Evaluation: everything is denied by default; an explicit Deny anywhere wins; an Allow in an identity or resource policy grants; permission boundaries and service control policies (in Organizations) cap what an allow can ever give. Changes propagate in seconds but not instantly.

Roles for workloads. EC2 uses an instance profile and fetches credentials from the instance metadata service (require IMDSv2, which defeats SSRF theft of credentials). ECS has the task role (your code) and the execution role (the agent). EKS uses IRSA or Pod Identity (section 46.2). Lambda has an execution role. In all cases the AWS SDK finds credentials through its default chain (environment, then the role endpoint) so your code never mentions them.

STS. AssumeRole returns temporary credentials (15 minutes to 12 hours) for a role, possibly in another account; AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchanges an OIDC token (from EKS, from GitHub Actions in Part 47 — CI/CD, from Cognito) for credentials; GetCallerIdentity is the first command you run when something says AccessDenied ("who am I right now?"). Role chaining (assuming a role from assumed-role credentials) is capped at one hour.

Never long-lived keys in applications. If you find AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in a task definition, treat it as an incident: rotate it, replace with a role. Detect the rest with the IAM credential report and IAM Access Analyzer (unused keys, public resources, cross-account grants).

Secrets Manager. Stores a secret string or binary, versioned with staging labels (AWSCURRENT, AWSPREVIOUS, AWSPENDING), encrypted with KMS, replicated to other regions if asked, and rotated on a schedule by a Lambda you own or an AWS-provided one for RDS. About $0.40 per secret per month and $0.05 per 10,000 API calls, so cache it in the process and refresh on failure rather than fetching per request. Two rotation strategies for databases: single user (change the password of the one user; anything holding the old password fails at the instant of rotation) and alternating users (two users, rotate the inactive one, swap labels; the old credentials keep working until the next rotation, which is what you want).

Parameter Store (in Systems Manager). Hierarchical parameters (/prod/orders/db/host), plain or SecureString via KMS, standard tier free up to 10,000 parameters of 4 KB, advanced tier for larger values and policies. No built-in rotation. Default throughput is 40 requests per second unless you enable the higher tier. Use it for configuration; use Secrets Manager for things that rotate.

KMS. Customer-managed keys cost $1 per month plus $0.03 per 10,000 requests; AWS-managed keys are free. Keys never leave KMS. Data is protected with envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext data key and the same key encrypted under the KMS key; you encrypt the data with the plaintext key, throw it away, and store the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext; Decrypt on the encrypted data key gets it back. S3, RDS, EBS, Secrets Manager and SQS do this for you. Key policies are the root of access to a key (an IAM allow is not enough if the key policy does not permit the principal), which is a common source of AccessDenied on an SSE-KMS bucket. Request quotas are thousands per second per region; a hot S3 bucket without bucket keys can exhaust them. Automatic yearly rotation keeps old material to decrypt old data.

Practical example

The orders API task role policy: read one secret, consume one queue, publish to one topic, write to one S3 prefix. Everything else is denied by absence.

JSON
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "ReadDbSecret", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456789012:secret:prod/orders/db-*" },
    { "Sid": "ConsumeFulfilmentQueue", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility", "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:123456789012:prod-fulfilment" },
    { "Sid": "PublishOrderEvents", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["sns:Publish"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sns:ap-south-1:123456789012:prod-orders" },
    { "Sid": "WriteInvoices", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::shop-documents/invoices/*" },
    { "Sid": "DecryptWithAppKey", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:GenerateDataKey"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:123456789012:key/2f1a...",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": ["secretsmanager.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com", "s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com"] } } }
  ]
}

Note the S3 resource is the object ARN (bucket/prefix/*); a policy on arn:aws:s3:::shop-documents alone grants bucket-level actions like listing, and PutObject fails with AccessDenied at runtime. That single asterisk is the most common IAM bug in application roles.

NestJS example

Loading the database secret at bootstrap through @nestjs/config, caching it, and refreshing when PostgreSQL rejects the password, which is what happens the moment a single-user rotation runs.

TypeScript
// src/config/secrets.loader.ts
import { SecretsManagerClient, GetSecretValueCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager';

const client = new SecretsManagerClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });

export interface DbSecret { username: string; password: string; host: string; port: number; dbname: string }

export async function loadDbSecret(secretId = process.env.DB_SECRET_ID!): Promise<DbSecret> {
  const out = await client.send(new GetSecretValueCommand({ SecretId: secretId })); // AWSCURRENT
  return JSON.parse(out.SecretString!) as DbSecret;
}

// Registered with ConfigModule.forRoot({ load: [dbConfig] }) so the value is
// resolved once at boot; nothing hits Secrets Manager per request.
export const dbConfig = async () => ({ db: await loadDbSecret() });
TypeScript
// src/database/database.module.ts (relevant part)
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => {
    const db = config.getOrThrow<DbSecret>('db');
    return {
      type: 'postgres', host: db.host, port: db.port, database: db.dbname,
      username: db.username,
      // node-postgres accepts a function: it is called for every NEW connection,
      // so a rotated password is picked up without restarting the task.
      password: async () => (await loadDbSecret()).password,
      autoLoadEntities: true, synchronize: false,
      extra: { max: 10, idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000, connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000 },
    };
  },
}),
