A password function on every new connection costs one Secrets Manager call per connection (a few per minute in steady state), which is cheap insurance against the failure story below. Cache it for 60 seconds if the fleet is large.

Production scenario

The platform has 24 secrets in Secrets Manager (databases, payment provider keys, JWT signing keys, CloudFront key pair), rotated quarterly except the RDS credentials, which rotate every 30 days with the alternating-users strategy. Total cost under $15 a month. Every workload has its own role; a quarterly Access Analyzer review flags unused permissions, and the last one removed s3:* from a worker that had been granted it during an incident two years earlier.

Failure scenario

At 03:00 the scheduled rotation of the orders database secret ran with the single-user strategy. The rotation Lambda changed the password in PostgreSQL and updated AWSCURRENT. The API tasks had received the password as an environment variable at start-up, eight days earlier. For one minute nothing happened: existing pooled connections kept working. Then idle connections recycled and new ones failed with password authentication failed for user "orders_api". Readiness checks began failing; ECS replaced tasks; the replacements received the new secret and worked. Total: seven minutes of rising 5xx as tasks cycled, and a 03:07 page. The team switched to the alternating-users strategy (old credentials valid until the next rotation) and to the password function above, so a rotation is now invisible. Secrets injected as environment variables are a snapshot; rotation is a stream.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • AccessDenied at runtime on an action that worked in staging: different role, missing /*, a KMS key policy, an SCP, or a resource policy in another account; GetCallerIdentity first, then the policy simulator.
  • Secret cached forever in a module-level variable; rotation breaks the app hours later.
  • Rotation Lambda cannot reach the database (no VPC config or security group); the secret is updated in one place and not the other.
  • Secrets Manager throttling when 500 Lambdas cold-start at once; use the caching client library or provisioned concurrency.
  • Parameter Store 40 TPS default exceeded by a fleet that reads per request.
  • STS credentials expiring mid-job in a 9-hour batch; refresh through the SDK provider, not a one-time AssumeRole.
  • IMDSv1 enabled and an SSRF in an image fetcher leaks the instance role.
  • Access key committed to git: scanners find it in minutes; rotate first, ask questions later; rewriting history is in Part 48 — Git.
  • KMS key deleted (7 to 30 day pending window): every object encrypted with it is unrecoverable once deletion completes.
  • Secrets in Terraform state or CloudFormation outputs readable by anyone with state access.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat roles as the unit of identity and a long-lived key as a defect. They write the task role policy before the code and expand it only with a reviewed pull request. They design for rotation from the first day: fetch on connect, refresh on failure, alternating users. They put kms:ViaService and resource ARNs on everything, because "the API can read any secret in the account" is one SSRF away from a breach. They can explain to a product manager why the deploy pipeline uses OIDC instead of a shared key: "a leaked key is a permanent break-in; a role is a one-hour badge".

Common mistakes

  • "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*" on an application role.
  • Secrets as build-time environment variables baked into the image.
  • One role shared by the API, the workers and the deploy pipeline.
  • Single-user rotation with credentials injected at start-up.
  • Reading Parameter Store on every request.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a role safer than an access key even if both have the same policy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: temporary, auto-rotated, no secret to leak, tied to a workload identity, revocable centrally.
  2. An app gets AccessDenied on s3:PutObject although the policy allows it on the bucket ARN. Why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: object actions need the bucket/* resource; also check the KMS key policy for SSE-KMS.
  3. Design database credential rotation that never breaks running services.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: alternating users, fetch on connect, refresh on auth failure, or IAM database authentication.
  4. Explain envelope encryption in two sentences.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a data key encrypts the data, KMS encrypts the data key; you store the encrypted key with the data and ask KMS to unwrap it.
  5. What is a permission boundary and when do you use it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a cap on the maximum permissions an identity policy can grant; delegating role creation to teams safely.

Practical exercise

Give a NestJS service a task role with the least-privilege policy above and run it against Secrets Manager with 30-day rotation enabled using the alternating-users strategy. Acceptance criteria: forcing a rotation from the console produces zero errors in a 50 RPS load test; removing kms:Decrypt from the policy produces a clear AccessDenied at boot that names the key; aws sts get-caller-identity from inside the task shows the task role, not the execution role; the IAM Access Analyzer report for the role shows no unused actions after a week.

46.12 Observability on AWS: CloudWatch, X-Ray and OpenTelemetry

Concept

CloudWatch is where AWS services put their metrics and where your logs land by default; it also runs alarms and dashboards. X-Ray is AWS's distributed tracing backend. OpenTelemetry (Part 43 — Observability: Logs, Metrics and Traces) is the vendor-neutral way to instrument your NestJS code and ship traces and metrics to X-Ray, CloudWatch, Prometheus or any vendor. This section is about what the AWS pieces cost, what they do well, and what they do badly.

Why does it exist?

Every AWS service emits metrics you did not have to write (ALB request counts and 5xx, RDS IOPS and connections, SQS oldest-message age, Lambda throttles). Your alarms on those metrics are the difference between a page at 02:14 and a customer complaint at 09:00. Logs and traces answer the follow-up: which request, which query, which dependency.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital ward. Metrics are the monitors at every bed: a number per second, cheap to keep, easy to alarm on. Logs are the nurses' notes: detailed, expensive to store, and you must know which patient to read about. Traces are one patient's complete chart across every department they visited. CloudWatch is the ward; OpenTelemetry is the standard chart format any hospital can read.

How it works

Metrics. Namespaced (AWS/ApplicationELB, AWS/RDS, your own) with dimensions (load balancer name, target group). Standard resolution is one minute (EC2 basic monitoring is five unless detailed monitoring is enabled); high-resolution custom metrics go down to one second. Custom metrics cost about $0.30 per metric per month, where a "metric" is every unique combination of name and dimension values, so latency with a userId dimension is a cardinality bomb. Embedded Metric Format (EMF) lets you write a JSON log line that CloudWatch turns into metrics asynchronously, with no PutMetricData calls and no rate limits in your request path. Percentiles (p99) are available on any metric where you sent raw values, not pre-aggregated ones.

Logs. Log groups (per service) contain streams (per task). Ingestion costs about $0.50 per GB, storage $0.03 per GB-month, and the default retention is never expire; set it (30 days for application logs, 1 year for audit) or the storage line grows forever. Logs Insights queries structured JSON logs with a SQL-like language at $0.005 per GB scanned, so scoping the time range matters. The Infrequent Access log class halves ingestion cost for logs you rarely query. Subscription filters stream logs to Kinesis, Lambda or OpenSearch.

Alarms. Static thresholds, anomaly-detection bands, and composite alarms that page only when several conditions hold ("5xx rate high AND healthy hosts below 3"), which cuts noise. The TreatMissingData setting matters for sparse metrics: an alarm on the DLQ depth must treat missing as notBreaching, and an alarm on "requests per second" must treat missing as breaching (no data means the service is gone). Alarm actions go to SNS, then to PagerDuty, Slack or an auto-scaling policy. About $0.10 per alarm per month.

Container Insights. Per-task and per-pod CPU, memory, network and restart metrics for ECS and EKS, plus performance logs. Useful, and billed as custom metrics, so a cluster with 500 containers can cost a few hundred dollars a month in Insights alone.

X-Ray versus OpenTelemetry. X-Ray stores traces (segments and subsegments), draws a service map, and samples by default at one request per second plus 5% of the rest, at about $5 per million traces recorded. The AWS SDK and Lambda integrate with it natively. OpenTelemetry is the instrumentation standard: the NestJS process runs the OTel SDK with auto-instrumentation for HTTP, pg, ioredis and the AWS SDK, exports OTLP to a collector (the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry, ADOT, as a sidecar or daemon), and the collector exports to X-Ray, CloudWatch metrics, Amazon Managed Prometheus, or a vendor. Instrument with OpenTelemetry, choose X-Ray as a backend; never instrument with the X-Ray SDK directly in new code, because you would be re-instrumenting the day you change vendors.

Practical example

The orders API logs one JSON line per request (requestId, traceId, route, status, durationMs, userId hashed) at about 400 bytes; at 350 RPS average that is about 360 GB a month, roughly $180 in ingestion and $11 in storage with 30-day retention. Debug logging is off in production and can be enabled per request with a header for ten minutes. Metrics come from EMF lines (orders placed, payment failures by provider, checkout latency) and from ALB, RDS, SQS and ElastiCache namespaces. Four composite alarms page; twenty simple alarms only post to Slack.

NestJS example

Emitting a business metric through EMF from an interceptor, so the checkout latency percentile exists without any metrics API call in the request path.

TypeScript
// src/observability/checkout-metrics.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';
import { createMetricsLogger, Unit } from 'aws-embedded-metrics';

@Injectable()
export class CheckoutMetricsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const started = Date.now();
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<{ route?: { path: string } }>();
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap({
        next: () => this.emit(req.route?.path ?? 'unknown', Date.now() - started, 'ok'),
        error: () => this.emit(req.route?.path ?? 'unknown', Date.now() - started, 'error'),
      }),
    );
  }

  private emit(route: string, ms: number, outcome: 'ok' | 'error'): void {
    const metrics = createMetricsLogger();          // one EMF JSON line to stdout per call
    metrics.setNamespace('Shop/Checkout');
    metrics.setDimensions({ Route: route, Outcome: outcome }); // low cardinality on purpose
    metrics.putMetric('Latency', ms, Unit.Milliseconds);
    metrics.putMetric('Count', 1, Unit.Count);
    metrics.flush().catch(() => undefined);         // never fail a request over telemetry
  }
}

And the Logs Insights query the on-call runs when the p99 alarm fires, against the structured request logs:

Text
fields @timestamp, requestId, route, status, durationMs, dbMs, redisMs
| filter route = "/v1/checkout" and durationMs > 2000
| sort durationMs desc
| limit 50

Followed by the aggregate that tells you whether the slowness is in the database or somewhere else:

Text
filter route = "/v1/checkout"
| stats pct(durationMs, 99) as p99, pct(dbMs, 99) as dbP99, count() as n by bin(1m)

Production scenario

The 02:14 page from section 46.1 was a composite alarm: ALB 5xx rate > 2% for 3 minutes AND ElastiCache CurrConnections dropped to 0. The on-call opened the dashboard where API latency, Redis connections, RDS CPU and the AZ health of ECS tasks sit on one screen, saw the Redis line flat, and did not need Logs Insights at all. That is the goal: the alarm names the cause, the dashboard confirms it, and the logs are for the 20% of incidents that are new.

Failure scenario

A developer set LOG_LEVEL=debug in the production task definition to chase a bug at 17:00 and forgot it. The debug logger printed every SQL statement with parameters and every Redis command. Ingestion went from 12 GB a day to 2.1 TB a day. The Cost Anomaly Detection alert arrived 30 hours later: the log bill for those hours was about $1,300, and the storage line would have kept growing because retention was set to never expire. Fixes: log retention set on every group by Terraform; a budget alarm at 20% above the monthly forecast; debug logging only via a per-request header with a ten-minute expiry stored in Redis; and a code review rule that a task definition change to LOG_LEVEL needs an expiry date in the description.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Alarm stays OK on missing data while the service is dead; set TreatMissingData deliberately per alarm.
  • Retention never set; the storage bill compounds quietly.
  • Metric cardinality from a per-user or per-order dimension; hundreds of thousands of metrics at $0.30 each.
  • Logs Insights over 90 days scans terabytes and costs real money; scope the range.
  • Trace sampling hides the rare error; sample 100% of errors with a tail-sampling collector, or at least of 5xx responses.
  • PutMetricData rate limits hit by a fleet calling per request; use EMF.
  • Timestamps rejected when a metric is more than two weeks in the past or two hours in the future; clock skew on a host makes its metrics vanish.
  • Log delivery lag of a minute or two during regional trouble, exactly when you need it.
  • One-minute granularity on ALB metrics smooths a ten-second outage into a small bump.
  • Container Insights cost surprising a cluster with many small tasks.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They alarm on symptoms customers feel (error rate, latency, queue age) and put causes on the dashboard. They instrument with OpenTelemetry once and treat the backend as a replaceable choice. They review the observability bill with the same rigour as the RDS bill, because logs are the line item that grows without a decision. They make sure every alarm has a runbook link in its description, because an alarm without a next step is noise.

Common mistakes

  • Logging full request and response bodies in production.
  • No retention policy on log groups.
  • Alarming on CPU for a Node service instead of latency and error rate.
  • Instrumenting with the X-Ray SDK and having to redo it for a vendor.
  • Dashboards with forty panels and no alarm.

Interview questions

  1. Which three alarms would you set first on a new NestJS service on ECS, and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ALB 5xx rate, p99 latency, healthy target count (plus DLQ depth for workers); symptoms, not causes.
  2. What is EMF and why use it over PutMetricData?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: metrics from log lines, asynchronous, no API limits or latency in the request path.
  3. How does OpenTelemetry relate to X-Ray?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: OTel instruments and exports; X-Ray is one backend via the ADOT collector.
  4. What does TreatMissingData control and give an example where the wrong setting hides an outage.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: how absent data is evaluated; a request-count alarm treating missing as OK while the service is down.
  5. Your CloudWatch bill tripled this month. Where do you look?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: log ingestion by group, custom metric count, Logs Insights scanned bytes, Container Insights.

Practical exercise

Instrument a NestJS service with OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation and an ADOT sidecar on ECS exporting traces to X-Ray and metrics via EMF. Acceptance criteria: a trace of a checkout request shows the HTTP span, the PostgreSQL query spans and the Redis spans with realistic durations; a composite alarm pages only when error rate and latency both breach; every log group has a retention policy verified by a script; the monthly observability cost is estimated from actual ingestion after one day of load.

46.13 A reference architecture for the NestJS platform on AWS

Concept

Everything in Part 46 so far has been a service at a time. This section assembles them into one architecture that a real team can run: a NestJS API and its workers on ECS Fargate, PostgreSQL on RDS, Redis on ElastiCache, a queue, object storage, secrets, and observability, fronted by Route 53, CloudFront, WAF and an ALB. Then it does the part most architecture diagrams skip: it sizes each component for a specific load, explains the arithmetic behind each number, and puts an indicative price on it.

Why does it exist?

Because "we'll use ECS and RDS" is not an architecture, it is a shopping list. The design decisions that matter are how many tasks of what size, which database instance class and why, what is synchronous and what is queued, where the network boundaries are, and what each choice costs per month. A senior engineer is expected to produce those numbers in a design review and defend them, and to be able to say which of them are guesses that need a load test.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. Route 53 is the address on the map, CloudFront is the takeaway window that serves the popular items without bothering the kitchen, WAF is the doorman, the ALB is the host who seats people at whichever table is free, the Fargate tasks are the cooks, RDS is the pantry where everything is really kept, ElastiCache is the counter of prepared items within arm's reach, the queue is the ticket rail for things that do not need to be done while the customer stands there, and CloudWatch is the manager watching how long each order takes.

How it works

Component by component, with the decision behind each:

Route 53. The hosted zone for shop.example.com, an alias record to the CloudFront distribution. Health checks are configured but do nothing yet; they become the failover mechanism in 46.14. TTLs of 60 seconds on records you might need to move.

CloudFront. In front of everything, not only static assets. It terminates TLS at the edge (so the handshake happens 20 ms from the user instead of 180 ms away), it caches product images and the built frontend bundle, and it passes API calls through to the ALB over AWS's backbone, which is measurably more reliable than the public internet for the long haul. The cache policy for /api/* forwards Authorization and sets TTL 0, because caching an authenticated response is one of the worst bugs in this part (46.17).

WAF. Attached to the CloudFront distribution, not the ALB, so bad traffic is dropped at the edge and never costs you an ALB LCU or a Fargate CPU cycle. Managed rule groups (core rule set, known bad inputs, IP reputation), a rate-based rule at 2,000 requests per 5 minutes per IP, and a size-constraint rule on request bodies. Every custom rule starts in count mode for a week before it blocks anything.

ALB. Public subnets across three AZs, listener on 443 with an ACM certificate, target group of ECS tasks with /health/ready as the health check path, deregistration_delay of 30 seconds so draining tasks finish their requests, and an idle timeout of 60 seconds that must be less than the Node server's keepAliveTimeout (46.17 explains what happens when it is not).

ECS Fargate: the API service. Private subnets, no public IP, egress through NAT gateways. One task definition, one container plus the ADOT sidecar, a task role scoped to exactly the S3 prefix, SQS queues, and secrets it needs. Autoscaling on ALB request count per target with a target of 120 RPS per task, plus a scheduled minimum before known peaks.

ECS Fargate: the worker services. Separate services and separate task definitions from the API, deliberately. Workers doing 20-second jobs must not share an event loop, a deploy cadence or a scaling policy with a latency-sensitive API, and a blocked worker must not fail an API health check (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure).

RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ, plus a read replica. The primary and its standby are in different AZs with synchronous replication; the read replica is asynchronous and serves reports and the heavier read paths. RDS Proxy sits in front if Lambda functions also connect. Automated backups with a 7-day window, performance_insights_enabled = true, and a parameter group in Terraform (19.13).

ElastiCache Redis. Cluster mode disabled, primary plus one replica in another AZ, automatic failover on, maxmemory-policy = allkeys-lru for the cache instance. If sessions and rate limits also live in Redis, they belong on a separate instance from the cache, because a cache eviction storm should not delete anyone's session.

SQS (or MSK). SQS standard queues with a dead-letter queue after 5 receives, a visibility timeout of 6x the p99 job duration, and long polling. MSK only if you need replay, ordering per key, or fan-out to multiple independent consumer groups (Part 28 — Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS).

S3. One bucket for user uploads (presigned PUT, block public access, versioning, lifecycle to Intelligent-Tiering at 30 days), one for exports with a 7-day expiry lifecycle rule, one for logs.

Secrets Manager and Parameter Store. Database credentials with rotation in Secrets Manager; non-secret configuration in Parameter Store as it is roughly free. Injected into the task definition as secrets, which means they arrive as environment variables at task start and are not re-read when rotated (46.17).

CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry. The ADOT collector sidecar receives OTLP from the NestJS process, exports traces to X-Ray and metrics to CloudWatch; structured JSON logs go to CloudWatch Logs with a retention policy set in Terraform.

Sizing for 1,000 RPS

The load: an e-commerce API at 1,000 RPS peak and about 350 RPS daily average, p50 25 ms, p99 target 250 ms, read/write ratio about 9:1, roughly 3 database queries per request, 40 percent of reads served from Redis.

Component Size Reasoning
API tasks 8 minimum, 24 maximum, 1 vCPU / 2 GB each A NestJS process doing I/O-bound JSON work handles 120–180 RPS per vCPU before event-loop lag rises. At 150 RPS per task, peak needs 7 tasks; 8 minimum gives AZ spread and headroom, 24 maximum covers a 3x flash sale. 2 GB because Node's default old-space plus the sidecar fits comfortably and OOM is worse than the extra $0.004/hour
Worker tasks 4, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB Queue depth, not RPS, sizes these. 200 jobs/s at 40 ms each needs 8 concurrent slots; 4 tasks with a concurrency of 4 gives 16 with headroom for retries
RDS instance db.r6g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GB), Multi-AZ 3,000 queries/s at p99 8 ms needs roughly 24 concurrently active backends; 8 vCPU handles that with room. 64 GB lets shared_buffers be 16 GB and effective_cache_size 48 GB, which holds a 40 GB hot working set in memory. Memory, not CPU, is the sizing driver for OLTP PostgreSQL
RDS storage 500 GB gp3, 12,000 IOPS, 500 MB/s gp3 decouples IOPS from size, so you do not over-provision storage to buy IOPS. 12,000 IOPS covers checkpoint bursts with margin
Read replica 1 × db.r6g.xlarge Reports and heavy list endpoints only, about 15 percent of query volume. Half the primary's size because it does not carry the write path
ElastiCache cache.r7g.large primary + 1 replica 40 percent of reads at 350 RPS average is a few thousand operations/s, far below a single node's 100k+. Sized by memory: 13 GB holds the product and session working set. The replica is for failover, not throughput
Messaging SQS standard, 3 queues + 3 DLQs About 200 events/s. SQS is serverless, needs no capacity decision, and is one tenth the cost of a 3-broker MSK cluster at this volume
MSK alternative 3 × kafka.m3.small or m5.large, 3 AZs Only if replay, per-key ordering or multiple independent consumer groups are required
NAT gateways 2 (one per AZ used for egress) Three would be more available and 50 percent more expensive; two is the common compromise. VPC endpoints for S3, ECR, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch remove most of the traffic that would otherwise cross them
ALB 1, 3 AZs Scales itself; you size nothing, you only pay LCUs

Indicative monthly cost

Prices move, differ by region, and drop substantially with Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. Treat this as the shape of the bill, not a quote. On-demand, one production environment, a mid-size region:

Line item Monthly (USD) Note
ECS Fargate, API (avg 10 tasks) 360 Autoscaled; Compute Savings Plan cuts this ~20 percent
ECS Fargate, workers (4 tasks) 75 Fargate Spot for workers can halve it
ALB 130 Fixed hourly plus LCUs
CloudFront 320 Egress dominates; depends entirely on response sizes
WAF 560 $0.60 per million requests plus rules; the surprise line for most teams
RDS primary, Multi-AZ 1,410 Doubled for the standby; this is the price of a 60-second RTO
RDS read replica 355
RDS storage and backups 90 500 GB gp3 plus snapshot storage
ElastiCache (2 nodes) 330
SQS 120 Batching by 10 cuts request count 10x
NAT gateways plus data processing 290 Cut sharply by VPC endpoints
S3 storage and requests 130
CloudWatch logs, metrics, alarms, X-Ray 310 Grows silently; set retention
Secrets Manager, KMS, Route 53 25
Total ≈ 4,500 Plus a staging environment at roughly 25 percent of this

Two observations a senior engineer makes about this table. First, the database is a third of the bill and Multi-AZ is half of the database, so "do we need Multi-AZ" is a real question with a real answer (yes, for a production e-commerce system, because the alternative is a 20-minute restore). Second, WAF and CloudWatch together cost more than the entire compute fleet, which is not intuitive and is why per-request and per-GB pricing deserves the same review as instance sizing.

Production scenario

A team ran exactly this architecture for eighteen months at growing load. The changes they made, in order: added VPC endpoints (NAT bill fell 60 percent), moved workers to Fargate Spot (worker cost halved, with interruption handling already in place because the jobs were idempotent), bought a one-year Compute Savings Plan (compute down 24 percent), set CloudWatch retention to 30 days (log storage stopped compounding), and moved from db.r6g.2xlarge to db.r7g.2xlarge (about 15 percent more throughput for a similar price). Nothing in that list was an architecture change; all of it was operations, and it cut the bill by about 30 percent.

Failure scenario

The first version of this architecture put the NestJS API and the Kafka consumers in the same ECS service to "save a task definition". A poison message caused the consumer to block for 40 seconds on every retry; the shared event loop stopped serving HTTP; the ALB health check failed; ECS killed the task; the replacement task picked up the same message and did it again. Six tasks entered a restart loop and the API was down for eleven minutes because of a message that had nothing to do with any HTTP request. Splitting the services was a thirty-minute change that permanently removed a class of outage.

46.14 Multi-AZ and multi-region

What Multi-AZ actually protects against. An availability zone is one or more physically separate data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, a few kilometres apart, connected by low-latency fibre (typically under 2 ms round trip). Multi-AZ protects against the loss of one building: a power event, a network device failure, a flood, a fire. It does not protect against a bad deploy, a dropped table, an expired certificate, an IAM misconfiguration, a corrupted schema migration, or a region-wide control-plane failure. Those are the majority of real outages, and no amount of zone redundancy touches them.

Synchronous within a zone pair, asynchronous across regions. RDS Multi-AZ replicates synchronously: a commit is not acknowledged until the standby has the WAL record. At 1–2 ms of inter-AZ latency this costs a couple of milliseconds per commit, which is affordable. Across regions the round trip is 60–200 ms, so synchronous replication would make every write unusably slow; cross-region replicas are asynchronous, and asynchronous means a non-zero RPO by definition. Aurora Global Database narrows the window (typically under a second) with storage-level replication, but the window still exists.

Active-passive versus active-active. Active-passive means one region serves traffic and another is warm, with data replicating one way. Failover is a decision (usually human-approved) plus a DNS change plus promoting the database. Active-active means both regions accept writes, which requires you to answer one question that has no general answer: what happens when the same order, the same inventory row or the same user profile is written in both regions at the same time? The options are all uncomfortable: partition the data by region so each key has one writer (works well for user-scoped data, badly for global inventory), use last-write-wins and accept silent data loss, use CRDTs (which constrain what operations you may express), or route all writes to one region and only reads locally, which is active-passive for writes and honest about it. DynamoDB Global Tables give you last-write-wins across regions; PostgreSQL gives you nothing multi-master out of the box, and the third-party options are heavy operational commitments.

Posture Protects against RPO RTO Cost delta Complexity
Single AZ Nothing structural Last backup, hours Hours (restore) Baseline Low
Multi-AZ Loss of one data centre 0 (synchronous) 60–120 s automatic +100 percent on the database Low; managed
Multi-AZ + cross-region read replica Data centre loss, plus a manual regional escape Seconds to minutes 30–60 min (manual promote, DNS, config) +30–50 percent overall Medium
Active-passive multi-region, warm standby Region loss Seconds 10–30 min, mostly rehearsal-dependent +60–90 percent High
Active-active multi-region Region loss with no failover step Depends on conflict strategy Near zero +100 percent or more Very high; a permanent design tax

The honest recommendation for most teams. Run Multi-AZ for the database, the cache and the compute, spread across three AZs, and stop there. Add automated cross-region backup copies so a region loss is recoverable, and write down and rehearse the restore. Multi-region active-passive is worth building when you have a contractual RTO measured in minutes, a regulatory requirement, or genuine users on another continent whose latency justifies it. Multi-region active-active is worth building when you have a business that loses more money in an hour of downtime than a dedicated platform team costs in a year, and even then you should expect the conflict-resolution design to be the hardest thing your team does. Most teams that build multi-region before they have mastered Multi-AZ end up with two regions that both fail, because the complexity itself became the outage cause. Part 50 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery covers RTO/RPO targets, backup verification and the failover runbook in depth.

The dotted lines are the ones that fail in a real disaster, because they are the ones nobody exercises. Rehearse them quarterly or assume they do not work.

46.15 The Well-Architected pillars applied

Operational excellence. Everything in the reference architecture is defined in Terraform, deployed by a pipeline, and observable before it is released. Deploys are rolling with an ECS deployment circuit breaker that rolls back automatically when new tasks fail health checks. Every alarm has a runbook link in its description. The questions a senior asks: Can we deploy on a Friday afternoon without discussion, and if not, what specifically stops us? When this alarm fires at 02:14, what is the first command the on-call runs? How do we know a change worked, other than the absence of complaints?

Security. Private subnets for everything except the ALB, security groups referencing each other rather than CIDR ranges, one task role per service with least-privilege policies, secrets in Secrets Manager with rotation, KMS customer-managed keys for RDS and S3, TLS everywhere including in-VPC to RDS, S3 buckets with public access blocked at the account level, and WAF at the edge. The questions: If one task's credentials leak, what exactly can the attacker reach? Which of our resources would be exposed if someone made a bucket public tomorrow, and what stops that? When did we last rotate the database password, and did anything break?

Reliability. Three AZs, Multi-AZ RDS with automatic failover, ElastiCache with automatic failover, ECS spreading tasks across AZs, queues with dead-letter queues, health checks that reflect the pod's real ability to serve, graceful shutdown with deregistration_delay, and backups tested by restoring them. The questions: What is our RTO and RPO, and when did we last measure them rather than assume them? Which single resource, if it disappeared, would take the whole system down? What happens to in-flight requests during a deploy?

Performance efficiency. Sizing derived from measured RPS per task rather than from a guess, autoscaling on a metric that leads rather than lags (request count per target, not CPU), CloudFront doing the work the origin does not need to do, a read replica for the read-heavy paths, and Redis in front of the hot reads. The questions: What is the p99 and where does it go: network, application, database, or waiting for a connection? What is the cheapest component we could remove without the user noticing? Are we scaling on the metric that actually predicts saturation for a single-threaded runtime?

Cost optimisation. Savings Plans for the steady-state compute, Spot for interruption-tolerant workers, VPC endpoints to avoid NAT data-processing charges, gp3 rather than provisioned IOPS, S3 lifecycle rules, CloudWatch log retention, and a monthly review of Cost Explorer grouped by tag. Every resource carries Service, Environment and Owner tags, enforced by a tag policy, because untagged cost is unattributable cost. The questions: Which three line items are the biggest, and does each one buy something the business asked for? What would this cost at 3x traffic, and does that scale linearly? What are we paying for in staging that could be turned off at night?

Sustainability. Fewer, better-utilised resources; Graviton (ARM) instance families, which do more work per watt and usually cost less; right-sized tasks rather than generous ones; lifecycle policies so cold data moves to colder storage; and turning non-production environments off outside working hours. The questions: Are we running anything only because nobody remembers what it does? Could this workload run on Graviton, and have we tested it? What is the utilisation of our largest instances, honestly measured?

46.16 Infrastructure as code

Why clicking in the console is a production incident waiting to happen. A console change has no review, no history, no reproducibility and no rollback. Six months later nobody can say why that security group has a rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 5432, whether the staging environment has it too, or what breaks if it is removed. When the region has an incident and you must rebuild, the console-created resources are the ones you cannot recreate. And the most common real-world outage from console work is subtler: someone fixes a problem by hand, the fix is not in code, the next terraform apply reverts it, and the incident happens again with everyone confused.

Terraform and CDK, positioned honestly. Terraform is declarative HCL with a mature provider ecosystem, a plan output that is readable by people who do not write the code, and portability across clouds and SaaS providers (you can manage Datadog monitors and GitHub repositories in the same run). Its weakness is that HCL is not a programming language: loops and conditionals are awkward and complex abstractions get ugly. AWS CDK is TypeScript (which your team already writes) compiled to CloudFormation, with high-level constructs that encode good defaults and remove enormous amounts of boilerplate. Its weaknesses are that you inherit CloudFormation's slow, sometimes stuck deployments and its resource coverage gaps, that a cdk diff is far less readable than a terraform plan, and that it is AWS-only. Neither is wrong. Pick Terraform if your team values explicit, reviewable plans and multi-provider reach; pick CDK if your team is TypeScript-first and wants the abstractions. Do not pick both.

Module and environment layout. Keep composition separate from implementation:

Text
infra/
  modules/
    ecs-service/        # one reusable module: task def, service, ALB target group, autoscaling, alarms
    rds-postgres/
    redis/
    network/
  envs/
    staging/
      main.tf           # calls the modules with staging-sized inputs
      backend.tf        # its own state file
      terraform.tfvars
    production/
      main.tf           # same modules, production-sized inputs
      backend.tf
      terraform.tfvars

The rule that makes this work: staging and production call the same modules with different variables. If staging has a hand-written resource that production does not, staging has stopped being a test of production. Differences should be values (task count, instance class, whether Multi-AZ is on), never structure.

State and drift. Terraform state is the map from your code to real resource ids, and it is sensitive (it can contain secrets) and concurrency-critical. Store it in S3 with versioning and encryption, with DynamoDB or S3-native locking so two engineers cannot apply at once. Never edit it by hand; use terraform import to adopt an existing resource and terraform state mv to rename. Drift is reality diverging from code, and it always happens: an emergency console fix, an AWS-side default change, a service that mutates its own tags. Detect it by running terraform plan -detailed-exitcode on a schedule in CI and alerting when the exit code is 2; a scheduled drift check is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort pipeline jobs you can add.

Reviewing infrastructure changes like code. A pull request that changes infrastructure gets the same treatment as one that changes the order service, plus the plan:

Shell
terraform init -backend-config=envs/production/backend.tf
terraform plan -var-file=envs/production/terraform.tfvars -out=tfplan
terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt   # posted as a PR comment by the pipeline

The reviewer reads plan.txt for one thing above all others: the word destroy. A plan that says 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy is routine. A plan that says must be replaced next to an RDS instance, a security group referenced by others, or anything holding data is a conversation before it is an approval, because Terraform will happily delete and recreate a database to satisfy a changed field. Also check: does this widen any security group or IAM policy, does it change a subnet or route table, does it touch a resource shared by other services, and is the same change queued for staging first?

The plan-before-apply discipline. The pipeline runs plan on the pull request and posts the output; a human approves; apply runs from the merge commit using the saved plan file, not a fresh plan, so what was reviewed is exactly what is executed. Applies happen only from CI, never from a laptop, and the CI role is the only principal with write permissions in production. Engineers get read-only production credentials for investigation. This is the same discipline as database migrations: the change is reviewed as a diff, applied by a machine, and recorded in history.

46.17 Edge cases and failure modes

  • An availability zone outage exposing a single-AZ resource. Everything is Multi-AZ except the one NAT gateway, the one ElastiCache node, or the EBS volume of a legacy EC2 instance. AZ 1b degrades and that single resource takes the system with it. Find them before the outage: audit every resource for a subnet or AZ attribute, and make "which AZ is this in, and what happens if that AZ is gone" a required question in design review.

  • RDS failover with stale connections held by the pool. RDS failover swaps the DNS record for the endpoint, typically in 60–120 seconds. Your Node process resolved that DNS at startup and cached it (Node caches DNS for the life of a socket, and the pool holds sockets open indefinitely). The pool keeps sending queries to the old primary's IP, which is now the standby and rejects writes, or simply blackholes. Mitigations: keep connections short-lived (idleTimeoutMillis and a maxLifetime so sockets are recycled every few minutes), handle 57P01 and ECONNRESET by discarding the connection rather than retrying on it, use RDS Proxy which handles failover on your behalf, and never set a DNS TTL override longer than the RDS endpoint's own (5 seconds).

  • Lambda connection storms exhausting max_connections. Each concurrent Lambda execution environment opens its own database connection and holds it while warm. A traffic spike to 800 concurrent executions is 800 connections against a max_connections of 500, and the API tasks that share the database are the ones that get FATAL: too many clients. The fix is RDS Proxy, which multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a small warm pool; the second fix is reserved concurrency on the function so it cannot exceed a number you chose.

  • A NAT gateway becoming a throughput and cost bottleneck. A NAT gateway handles up to about 100 Gbps but charges roughly $0.045 per GB processed on top of the hourly rate, and every byte your tasks pull from S3, ECR, Secrets Manager or CloudWatch crosses it unless you have VPC endpoints. A worker fleet pulling 40 TB a month from S3 through NAT costs about $1,800 a month for traffic that a free S3 gateway endpoint would carry for nothing. Add gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free) and interface endpoints for the services you use heavily.

  • ALB 502s from a keep-alive timeout mismatch. The ALB's idle timeout is 60 seconds by default and Node's server.keepAliveTimeout is 5 seconds. The ALB reuses a connection at second 6; Node has already closed it; the ALB reports 502 Bad Gateway for a request the application never saw. The rule is that the application's keep-alive timeout must be greater than the load balancer's: set server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000 and server.headersTimeout = 66_000 in main.ts. This produces a low but persistent 502 rate that is very hard to diagnose from application logs, because there are none.

  • CloudFront caching an authenticated response. A cache policy that does not include Authorization in the cache key will serve user A's /api/me to user B. This is a data breach, not a bug. For any authenticated path, set the cache policy to CachingDisabled or include Authorization in the key, and add Cache-Control: private, no-store from the application as a second line of defence. Test it explicitly: two users, two tokens, same path, different responses.

  • IAM permission denied only at runtime in production. The task role is missing s3:PutObject on one prefix, or kms:Decrypt on the key the bucket uses (a very common one: S3 access granted, KMS access forgotten). It works in staging because staging's role is broader. The error surfaces the first time a real user uploads a file. Prevention: identical role structure across environments with different resource ARNs, iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy in CI for the critical actions, and a smoke test after deploy that exercises each external permission once.

  • Secret rotation not picked up by running tasks. ECS injects secrets as environment variables at task start. When Secrets Manager rotates the database password, running tasks keep the old value and start failing authentication at the next reconnect, while a freshly deployed task works fine, which makes the symptom look like a code problem. Either fetch secrets at runtime through the SDK with a short cache, or make rotation trigger a service deployment, and use RDS's two-password rotation strategy so both old and new credentials work during the overlap.

  • API Gateway throttling returning 429 to your own service. The default account-level limit is 10,000 requests per second with a 5,000 burst, and per-stage or usage-plan limits are often set much lower during a proof of concept and never raised. A legitimate traffic increase produces 429 Too Many Requests from your own infrastructure, which your client retries, which makes it worse. Set the limits deliberately, alarm on ThrottleCount, and make sure your clients honour Retry-After with backoff and jitter.

  • SQS duplicate delivery. Standard queues are at-least-once, and even FIFO queues deduplicate only within a 5-minute window. A visibility timeout shorter than the job's p99 duration guarantees duplicates: the job is still running when the message becomes visible again and a second worker picks it up. Set the visibility timeout to at least 6x the p99, extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility for long jobs, and make every handler idempotent on the message's business key.

  • A cost explosion from log volume or cross-AZ traffic. Two silent line items. Debug logging left on turns 12 GB a day into 2 TB a day and $1,300 before anyone notices. Cross-AZ data transfer at $0.01 per GB in each direction is invisible until a chatty service pair lands in different zones and moves 50 TB a month. Defences: log retention set in Terraform, a budget alarm at 20 percent above forecast, Cost Anomaly Detection enabled, and awareness that AZ-aware routing (or simply keeping chatty pairs together) is a real optimisation.

  • CloudFormation or Terraform stuck mid-apply. A CDK deployment that fails during UPDATE_ROLLBACK can leave a stack in a state that needs manual intervention; a Terraform apply killed halfway leaves state locked and resources created but untracked. Prevention: apply only from CI so there is one actor, keep state locking on, and know the recovery commands (terraform force-unlock with the lock id, continue-update-rollback for CloudFormation) before you need them at 02:14.

Senior Checklist — Part 46

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain the region, AZ and edge model and say which of my resources live in exactly one AZ
  • I can choose between EC2, ECS Fargate, EKS and Lambda for a given workload and defend the choice on operational cost, not fashion
  • I know when Lambda is wrong (long-lived connections, strict p99, sustained high throughput) and what it costs at 1,000 RPS versus Fargate
  • I can size an RDS instance from working-set memory and concurrent active backends, and I know why Multi-AZ doubles the price
  • I know when DynamoDB beats PostgreSQL and when it is a trap, and how ElastiCache is sized by memory rather than throughput
  • I can choose between SQS, SNS, EventBridge and MSK, and I know what each costs at my message volume
  • I can explain ALB versus NLB versus API Gateway and configure health checks, deregistration delay and keep-alive timeouts correctly
  • I can configure CloudFront for a mixed static and authenticated API origin without ever caching a private response
  • I can design a VPC with public and private subnets, security groups that reference each other, and VPC endpoints that keep traffic off the NAT gateway
  • I use presigned URLs, block public access, versioning and lifecycle rules on every S3 bucket
  • I can write a least-privilege task role, explain how IRSA or task roles deliver credentials, and handle secret rotation without breaking running tasks
  • I instrument with OpenTelemetry, alarm on symptoms rather than causes, and set log retention on every log group in code
  • I can draw the full reference architecture and justify every component, its size and its monthly cost
  • I can state the RTO and RPO of my architecture and say what Multi-AZ does and does not protect against
  • I can explain why active-active multi-region is hard and what specific write-conflict question it forces me to answer
  • I can apply the six Well-Architected pillars to a concrete architecture with two or three real questions per pillar
  • All my infrastructure is in code, applied only from CI from a reviewed plan, with state locking and a scheduled drift check
  • I read a terraform plan for the word "destroy" before anything else

Part 46 — Key Takeaways

  • The cloud is someone else's data centre with an API. The API is the product; the leverage is that capacity becomes a code change instead of a purchase order.
  • Managed services trade money and flexibility for operational hours you do not have. That is usually a good trade, and it is always a trade you should be able to price.
  • Size compute from measured throughput per task, not from a guess: a NestJS process handles roughly 120–180 RPS per vCPU for I/O-bound work, and it is single-threaded, so scale on request count per target rather than CPU.
  • Size PostgreSQL from working-set memory first and CPU second. Multi-AZ doubles the database bill and buys a 60–120 second automatic failover; that is the actual price of your RTO.
  • Per-request and per-GB pricing outgrows instance pricing quietly. WAF, CloudWatch Logs, NAT data processing and CloudFront egress can together exceed the entire compute bill.
  • VPC endpoints, Savings Plans, Spot for idempotent workers, gp3, and log retention are five changes that cut 30 percent off a typical bill without touching the architecture.
  • Multi-AZ protects against losing a building. It does not protect against a bad deploy, a dropped table or an expired certificate, which is what actually causes most outages.
  • Cross-region replication is asynchronous, therefore your RPO is not zero. Write the number down and rehearse the restore, or assume the failover path does not work.
  • Active-active multi-region forces you to answer "what happens when both regions write the same row", and there is no general answer. Most teams should master Multi-AZ instead.
  • Separate the API and the workers into different services. A blocked consumer must never be able to fail an HTTP health check.
  • The keep-alive timeout of your Node server must exceed the ALB's idle timeout, or you will serve mysterious 502s that appear in no application log.
  • Never let CloudFront cache an authenticated response. Include Authorization in the cache key or disable caching on those paths, and test it with two users.
  • Console changes are undocumented, unreviewable and reverted by the next apply. Everything in code, applied from CI, from a plan a human read.
  • Read every infrastructure plan for "destroy" and "must be replaced" before you read anything else.
  • Run a scheduled drift check. Reality and code diverge continuously, and finding out during an incident is the expensive way.

Part 47 — CI/CD and Deployment Strategies

  • 2 h 26 min read

What you will learn

  1. 47.1Continuous integration
  2. 47.2Continuous delivery and deployment
  3. 47.3Artifacts and supply chain
  4. 47.4Secrets in CI
  5. 47.5Testing stages in the pipeline
  6. 47.6Security scanning
  7. 47.7Deployment strategies
  8. 47.8Feature flags
  9. 47.9Rollbacks
  10. 47.10Smoke tests and post-deploy verification
  11. 47.11A complete GitHub Actions setup
  12. 47.12DORA metrics
  13. 47.13Edge cases and failure modes

There is a moment in every engineer's career when deployment stops being someone else's job. You have written the service, tested it, containerised it, and now the question is not "does it work?" but "how does it get from my laptop to a machine serving real customers, safely, twenty times a day, at 4 p.m. on a Friday, without anyone holding their breath?"

That question is what CI/CD answers. Continuous integration is the machine that tells you within minutes whether your change is safe to merge. Continuous delivery is the machine that turns a merged commit into a deployable artifact and puts it in front of an approval gate. Continuous deployment is what happens when you trust that machine enough to remove the gate. The whole discipline exists to shrink one number: the time between "I wrote a line of code" and "I know whether that line is good", and then the time between "it is good" and "it is live".

This part builds the pipeline from the first push to the last smoke test. It covers what belongs in CI and what does not, why you must promote the same immutable artifact rather than rebuild it per environment, how to get secrets into a runner without ever storing a long-lived key, the five deployment strategies and what each one really costs, feature flags as the thing that separates deploy from release, and the honest truth about rollbacks (the image rolls back easily; the database usually does not). The centrepiece is three complete GitHub Actions workflows with every meaningful step explained. Then DORA metrics, and a long catalogue of the failure modes that turn a routine deploy into an incident.

The pipeline this part builds looks like this:

Text
Git Push -> Build -> Unit Tests -> Integration Tests -> Security Scan -> Docker Build -> Push Image -> Deploy -> Smoke Tests -> Production

Note one thing about that diagram before we go further: the same artifact flows all the way through. There is exactly one docker build in the whole pipeline. Everything after it moves bytes that already exist. That single property is what makes staging a meaningful test of production, and it is the property most teams get wrong first.

47.1 Continuous integration

Concept

Continuous integration is the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared main branch frequently (at least daily), with an automated build and test run on every change, so that integration problems surface in minutes instead of at the end of a release cycle.

The word people forget is integration. CI is not "we have a pipeline". CI is "we integrate constantly, and a machine proves the integration is sound". A team with a beautiful pipeline and three-week feature branches is not doing continuous integration; they are doing automated testing on a batch of divergence that will hurt when it lands.

Why does it exist?

Before CI, teams did "integration weeks". Everybody worked in isolation for a month, then spent a week merging, and the merge exposed every conflicting assumption at once: two people renamed the same column, one team's DTO change broke another team's consumer, a dependency bump changed behaviour nobody noticed. The cost of a bug rises steeply with the time between writing it and finding it. A type error found by CI in 90 seconds costs 90 seconds. The same error found by a customer costs an incident, a rollback, a postmortem, and trust.

CI attacks that curve directly. Small change, fast feedback, merged immediately. The main branch is always in a known state, so anyone can cut a release from it at any time.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. Continuous integration is the head chef tasting every sauce as it is made, not the whole dish at service time. If the sauce is too salty, you find out with 200 ml of sauce in the pan, not with forty plates going out.

The other half of the analogy matters too: tasting is only useful if it is fast. If tasting took twenty minutes, the chef would stop doing it. A CI pipeline that takes 45 minutes will be worked around: people will push and go to lunch, batch three changes into one push, or merge on red "because it's probably that flaky test again". Speed is not a nice-to-have; it is what keeps the practice alive.

How it works

A push triggers a workflow. The workflow runs a sequence of jobs on ephemeral machines (runners), each starting from a clean image. The essential shape:

  1. Checkout. Fetch the commit. For most jobs a shallow clone (fetch-depth: 1) is enough and saves 10 to 30 seconds on a repo with long history. Jobs that need history (changelog generation, git describe, SonarQube blame) need full depth.
  2. Restore toolchain. Install the exact Node version from .nvmrc or package.json engines. Never "whatever the runner has".
  3. Restore cache. Dependencies, build outputs, Docker layers.
  4. Install deterministically. npm ci, not npm install. npm ci deletes node_modules, installs exactly what package-lock.json says, and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree. npm install is allowed to update the lockfile, which means two runs of your pipeline can install different code.
  5. Static checks. Lint, format check, TypeScript tsc --noEmit. These are cheap (10 to 40 seconds) and catch a surprising share of review comments before a human sees the diff.
  6. Unit tests. Fast, isolated, no network, no database. Target: under 3 minutes.
  7. Integration tests. Real PostgreSQL and Redis, started as service containers. Target: under 8 minutes.
  8. Report. Coverage, test results, artifacts. Post a summary on the PR.

What belongs in CI: anything that is deterministic, fast, and can fail the change. Compilation, type checking, linting, unit tests, integration tests against real ephemeral dependencies, database migration dry-runs, dependency audit, secret scanning, license checks, contract tests, build of the Docker image.

What does not belong in CI: anything slow, flaky, or environment-dependent that does not gate correctness of this change. A full 40-minute load test on every PR. End-to-end tests against a shared staging environment that three other teams are also deploying to. Long-running security scans that take 20 minutes. Manual QA steps. These belong on a schedule (nightly), on the merge to main, or on the pre-production stage. The rule: if a failure would not clearly mean "this PR is wrong", it does not gate the PR.

Reproducible builds. A build is reproducible when the same inputs give the same output. In practice this means: pin the Node version, commit the lockfile and use npm ci, pin the base image by digest, do not fetch anything from the internet at build time that is not pinned, and never let the build read the current time or a random value into the artifact. When a build is not reproducible, "it passed yesterday and fails today with no code change" becomes a normal event, and people stop believing the pipeline.

Caching, with real numbers. For a NestJS monorepo package with roughly 900 direct plus transitive dependencies:

Step Cold Cached How
npm ci 95–140 s 22–35 s actions/setup-node with cache: npm (caches the npm download cache, still unpacks)
npm ci 95–140 s 10–18 s actions/cache on node_modules keyed by hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') (skips install entirely on hit)
tsc build 45 s 12 s tsBuildInfoFile incremental cache
Jest 6 min 5 min Jest cache helps transform, not execution
Docker build (4-stage) 6–8 min 50–90 s BuildKit cache-from/cache-to against a registry cache tag

The Docker number is the big one. A registry-backed BuildKit cache turns a 7-minute image build into 70 seconds when only src/ changed, because the npm ci layer is a cache hit. On a team doing 30 merges a day that is roughly three hours of runner time saved daily, and, more importantly, it is the difference between a hotfix reaching production in 9 minutes and in 25.

Caching node_modules directly is faster but riskier: the cache key must include the lockfile hash and the Node version and the OS, because native modules compiled against Node 20 will crash under Node 22. Get the key wrong and you have a cache-poisoning bug that is very hard to see.

Matrix and parallel jobs. Two different uses. A matrix runs the same job across several dimensions (Node 20 and 22; PostgreSQL 15 and 16) to prove compatibility. Sharding splits one slow suite across N runners to cut wall-clock time. Jest supports this natively with --shard=1/4. A 12-minute suite on four shards lands at about 3.5 minutes (never exactly a quarter, because setup cost is paid per shard). Beyond 4 to 6 shards you usually stop winning: the fixed cost of checkout, install and database startup dominates.

Required status checks. Branch protection on main lists which checks must pass before merge. Two rules senior engineers insist on: (1) the list must be exactly the checks that mean correctness, no more, or people will beg for exceptions; (2) "require branches to be up to date before merging" must be considered carefully. It prevents semantic conflicts (your PR is green, my PR is green, together they break) but it serialises merges: every merge invalidates every other open PR, which on a busy repo means constant rebasing. The middle ground most teams land on is a merge queue, which tests the combined result of the queued PRs and merges them in order.

The flaky-test policy. This is where seniority shows. A flaky test is one that passes and fails on the same code. It is not a minor annoyance; it is an active attack on the pipeline's authority. Once people learn that red might mean nothing, red always means nothing.

The policy that actually works:

  1. Never blanket-retry. jest --retries=3 on the whole suite is how you hide a real race condition for eight months and then meet it in production. Retrying is not a fix; it is a way to stop measuring.
  2. Detect flakiness explicitly. Run the suite against main on a schedule (say hourly). Any failure there, where the code did not change, is by definition flaky. Record it.
  3. Quarantine within an hour. Move the test to a non-blocking suite with an owner and a ticket. It still runs; it just does not block merges. The quarantine list is visible on a dashboard and reviewed in standup.
  4. Fix within a sprint or delete. A quarantined test that nobody fixes in two weeks is dead weight pretending to be coverage. Delete it and write the ticket for the real gap.
  5. Cap the quarantine. If more than about 1% of tests are quarantined, stop feature work and fix the suite. That number is a canary for test design problems: shared state, real timers, sleep, order dependence, unseeded randomness.

The common root causes, in the order you will meet them: unmocked time (Date.now() and real setTimeout), tests sharing a database without truncation between them, tests depending on execution order, a race between an async write and a read, an external network call, and unseeded random data that collides once every few hundred runs (see Part 41 — Testing Backend Systems with Jest and NestJS for the mechanics of fixing each).

Practical example

An orders API. The CI contract is written into package.json so the same commands run locally and in CI:

JSON
{
  "scripts": {
    "lint": "eslint \"src/**/*.ts\" --max-warnings=0",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json",
    "test:unit": "jest --config jest.unit.config.js --ci",
    "test:int": "jest --config jest.int.config.js --ci --runInBand",
    "test:cov": "jest --config jest.unit.config.js --coverage --ci",
    "build": "nest build",
    "migration:dry": "typeorm-ts-node-commonjs migration:show -d src/data-source.ts"
  },
  "engines": { "node": ">=20.18 <21" }
}

Two Jest configs, not one. Unit tests have no globalSetup and no database; integration tests do, and run with --runInBand because they share a PostgreSQL instance and parallel workers would fight over the same tables unless each worker gets its own schema.

NestJS example

The one piece of application code CI depends on is configuration validation, because a service that boots with a missing variable will fail in the integration job in a confusing way:

TypeScript
// src/config/config.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule } from '@nestjs/config';
import * as Joi from 'joi';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({
      isGlobal: true,
      // Fail fast and loudly. In CI this turns a mysterious timeout into
      // a one-line error naming the missing variable.
      validationSchema: Joi.object({
        NODE_ENV: Joi.string().valid('development', 'test', 'production').required(),
        DATABASE_URL: Joi.string().uri().required(),
        REDIS_URL: Joi.string().uri().required(),
        JWT_SECRET: Joi.string().min(32).required(),
        PORT: Joi.number().default(3000),
      }),
      validationOptions: { abortEarly: false },
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppConfigModule {}

Production scenario

A team of 22 engineers on a food-delivery platform, 8 services, roughly 40 merges to main per day. Their PR pipeline takes 7 minutes p50 and 11 minutes p95: 70 seconds of lint and typecheck, 3.5 minutes of sharded unit tests, 6 minutes of integration tests running in parallel with the unit shards. Docker build runs only on merge to main, not on the PR, because a PR does not need an image. Cache hit rate on npm ci sits around 92%; the misses are lockfile changes.

They measure one number weekly: time from push to first red signal. It is 95 seconds, because lint and typecheck run first and independently. That number matters more than total pipeline time, because most failures are caught by the cheap checks and the developer can start fixing while the rest still runs.

Failure scenario

At 16:40 on a Thursday a payments bug is found: refunds above 10,000 currency units are rejected by a validation rule that should have been removed. The fix is four characters. The engineer pushes the hotfix and CI goes red on notifications.e2e.spec.ts, a test unrelated to payments that has been flaky for three months and is "usually fine on a re-run".

They re-run. Red again, different test. They re-run again. Twelve minutes per attempt. At 17:25 someone suggests merging with admin override; the tech lead refuses because the last time that happened it shipped a broken migration. At 17:50 the fix goes out, 70 minutes after it was ready, and roughly 400 refunds failed in that window.

The postmortem action was not "make the pipeline faster". It was the flaky-test policy above: quarantine within an hour, owner assigned, fixed or deleted in a sprint. Nine tests moved to quarantine that week; six were fixed (all shared-state bugs), three were deleted. The suite has been trustworthy since, which means that when it is red, people believe it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The green pipeline that tests nothing. Coverage thresholds are met by tests that assert expect(service).toBeDefined(). See 47.5 for gates that actually mean something.
  • Cache key too loose. node_modules cached without the Node version in the key; a runner image upgrade changes Node and native modules segfault with no useful message.
  • Cache key too tight. Keyed on the commit SHA, so it never hits. Silent, and costs you 90 seconds every run forever.
  • Secrets unavailable on fork PRs. GitHub does not give repository secrets to workflows triggered by a fork's pull request. A job that needs a token will fail on every external contribution. Split it: run the secret-needing job only on push to internal branches.
  • Runner disk exhaustion. GitHub-hosted runners have around 14 GB free. A Docker build with several large stages plus a node_modules cache plus test containers can hit no space left on device intermittently, which reads exactly like flakiness.
  • Concurrent runs on the same PR. Push three times in a minute and you have three runs competing for cache and CI minutes. Use a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: true.
  • Time-dependent tests. Anything asserting on "today" breaks at midnight UTC, at month boundaries, and on 29 February.
  • Order-dependent tests. Pass locally where Jest picks one order, fail in CI where it picks another after sharding.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat CI as a product with users (the engineers) and an SLO (p95 under 10 minutes). When it degrades, that is a real ticket, not background noise.

They ask three questions of any proposed CI step: Does a failure here unambiguously mean the change is wrong? Is it deterministic? Does it cost less time than the bugs it catches? A step that fails "sometimes" is worse than no step, because it teaches people to ignore red.

They refuse two things absolutely: blanket test retries, and admin merge overrides as a routine tool. Both trade a small amount of short-term pain for the permanent loss of the pipeline's authority.

Explained to a product manager: "CI is the smoke alarm. If it goes off for burnt toast twice a week, someone takes the battery out, and then it does not help during a real fire. Keeping it accurate is why we spend time on test quality."

Common mistakes

  • Using npm install in CI, so builds are not reproducible.
  • Running everything sequentially in one job, so a lint error is discovered at minute 11.
  • Adding a retry wrapper instead of fixing a race condition.
  • Making every check "required", including optional ones, then routinely bypassing branch protection.
  • Building the Docker image on every PR push when nothing consumes it.
  • Long-lived feature branches with a beautiful pipeline, and calling it continuous integration.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between npm ci and npm install, and why does CI care?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: ci is deterministic from the lockfile, wipes node_modules, fails on lockfile/manifest mismatch; install may mutate the lockfile, so two runs can differ. Follow-up: what else makes a build non-reproducible?
  2. A test fails 1 in 20 runs. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: quarantine immediately so it stops blocking, assign an owner, find the root cause (shared state, time, ordering, async race), fix or delete within a sprint; never blanket-retry. Follow-up: how would you detect flakiness systematically?
  3. How would you get a 22-minute pipeline under 10 minutes?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: measure stage times first; parallelise independent jobs; shard the slow suite; cache dependencies and Docker layers; move slow non-gating checks off the PR path; fail fast on cheap checks.
  4. What should not run in CI on every PR?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: load tests, long security scans, E2E against a shared environment, anything non-deterministic or slow whose failure does not clearly indict the PR.
  5. You cache node_modules keyed by the lockfile hash. What can go wrong?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: native modules compiled for a different Node/OS/arch; cache poisoning across branches; key must include runner OS, arch and Node version.

Practical exercise

Take an existing service pipeline and instrument it. Record the duration of every step for 20 runs and build a table of p50 and p95. Then make three changes: split lint/typecheck into their own fast job, shard the unit suite four ways, and add a dependency cache with a correct key. Acceptance criteria: p95 total time reduced by at least 40%, time-to-first-red-signal under 2 minutes, and a written note explaining why your cache key includes each of its components.

47.2 Continuous delivery and deployment

Concept

Continuous delivery means every commit that passes the pipeline produces an artifact that could be released to production at the push of a button. The gate is a human decision, not a technical obstacle.

Continuous deployment removes the button. Every commit that passes goes to production automatically.

The distinction is one of policy, not capability. A team practising continuous delivery has already done all the engineering; they have simply decided that a human should look before the last step. That decision is legitimate for a payments core, a medical records system, or anything with a regulator. It is usually not legitimate for an internal admin API, and teams that keep the gate out of habit rather than reason pay for it in batch size: gates encourage waiting, waiting encourages batching, and a deploy of 14 commits is far harder to debug than a deploy of one.

Why does it exist?

Because the alternative is the release train, and the release train has a specific failure mode. When you deploy once a fortnight, each deploy contains 60 changes. When something breaks, you have 60 suspects, the rollback reverts 59 innocent changes along with the guilty one, and nobody remembers the context of the code they wrote nine days ago. Risk per deploy scales with batch size, which is why deploying more often makes each deploy safer, which is the counter-intuitive result at the heart of the DORA research (47.12).

Mental model

Imagine a bakery. Continuous delivery is having bread cooling on the rack, ready to sell, and a manager who decides when to open the shop door. Continuous deployment is the door opening by itself as each loaf is ready. Either way the bread is baked, wrapped and priced. The argument is only about the door.

Now the important part of the analogy: the loaf on the rack must be the same loaf that goes into the bag. You do not bake a "test loaf" and then bake a fresh one for the customer, because the second one might come out different. That is the immutable artifact rule, and it is the single most important idea in this section.

How it works

Environments are stages that an artifact passes through, each closer to production:

Environment Purpose Data Who deploys Typical gate
CI ephemeral Prove the change is correct Throwaway containers Automatic All checks green
Development / integration Services talk to each other Synthetic, resettable Automatic on merge Deploy succeeds
Staging / pre-production Production-shaped rehearsal Anonymised copy or realistic synthetic Automatic E2E + smoke pass
Production Real customers Real Automatic or approved Approval, change window, SLO health

The rule that matters: promote the same immutable artifact. Build once, in one place, from one commit. Everything downstream references that artifact by digest. You do not run docker build again for staging and again for production. Ever.

Why so strict? Because if you rebuild per environment, the thing you tested in staging is not the thing you shipped. A transitive dependency published a patch between the two builds. The base image tag moved. A build-time environment variable differed. Now your staging test result is an opinion about production rather than evidence, and you have reintroduced exactly the class of bug containers were supposed to eliminate.

What does change per environment is configuration, injected at run time: database URLs, feature flag defaults, log level, replica counts, resource limits, secret references. This is the twelve-factor separation of config from code, and it has a practical test: if you cannot take the production image, point it at staging config, and have it work, your artifact is not really immutable.

Approvals and environment protection. GitHub Actions models this with environments: a named environment can require specific reviewers, enforce a wait timer, restrict which branches may deploy to it, and hold environment-scoped secrets. The important design points:

  • Required reviewers should be a team, not a person, or the deploy blocks when that person is on holiday.
  • A wait timer (say 5 minutes) between staging and production is sometimes more useful than a human approval: it gives monitoring time to react while requiring nobody to be awake.
  • Restrict the production environment to the main branch and to tags. Otherwise a feature branch can reach production secrets.
  • The approver should see what they are approving: the commit range, the image digest, and the migration plan. An approval button with no context is theatre.

Where the database migration goes. This is the question that separates people who have deployed a schema change from people who have not. The short answer: the migration runs before the new code, and the migration must be safe for the old code that is still running.

During the rolling update, old pods and new pods run simultaneously against one schema. That schema must satisfy both. This is why migrations are restricted to additive (expand) operations at deploy time: add a nullable column, add a new table, add an index concurrently, add a constraint as NOT VALID and validate later. The destructive half (drop the old column, drop the old table, add NOT NULL) happens in a later deploy, after all code that referenced the old shape is gone. The full mechanics, including backfills, dual writes and the exact lock behaviour of each DDL statement, are in Part 24 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes, and the compatibility rules that make it work are in Part 25 — Backward Compatibility.

Running the migration as a separate step before the rollout (a Kubernetes Job, not an init container on every pod, and never on application boot) matters for three reasons: it runs exactly once rather than once per replica; a failure stops the pipeline before any new code is live; and you can see it as a discrete, timed, logged event when you are reading a timeline at 3 a.m.

Practical example

An e-commerce platform ships orders-api roughly 12 times a day. Merge to main triggers: build image tagged sha-3f9a1c2, push to ECR, deploy to staging automatically, run 40 E2E tests (4 minutes), then the workflow pauses on the production environment which requires one reviewer from the @acme/backend team. Median time in the approval queue is 6 minutes during working hours. Outside working hours the pipeline stops there and the deploy happens the next morning, which the team accepts because their change failure rate does not justify waking anyone.

The migration step is a separate Job executed against the production database before the kubectl set image, with statement_timeout and lock_timeout set so a blocked DDL fails in 5 seconds instead of queueing behind a long report query and locking the orders table.

Failure scenario

A team rebuilt their image per environment. Staging built at 14:05, production at 14:40. Between those two builds, a transitive dependency (fast-json-stringify, pulled in by their logger) published a patch release that changed how it serialised BigInt. Their package-lock.json pinned direct dependencies but a ^ range in a sub-dependency allowed the drift, and they used npm install rather than npm ci.

Staging was fine. Production started throwing TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt on the order-total field, which is a bigint column mapped to a JavaScript BigInt. It affected 100% of order responses. The rollback worked (the previous image was intact), but the debugging took 40 minutes because the code was byte-identical and everyone was looking for a config difference.

Two fixes went in: npm ci with a fully resolved lockfile, and build-once-promote-everywhere. The second fix would have prevented it on its own.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Config drift between environments. Staging has POOL_MAX=5, production has 50; a connection-pool bug never appears until production. Diff environment config in the pipeline and alert on unexpected keys.
