  • Staging data is nothing like production. 500 orders in staging, 40 million in production. A query with a missing index passes staging in 3 ms and takes 9 seconds in production.
  • Approval that never comes. The workflow sits pending for 6 hours and expires; the deploy silently never happened. Alert on deploys stuck in approval for more than N minutes.
  • The environment allows any branch. Someone deploys a feature branch to production because the environment protection rule was never set.
  • Migration and deploy in the wrong order. New code deployed first, reads a column that does not exist yet, every request 500s (47.13).
  • Two pipelines deploying at once. Two merges within a minute; both run kubectl set image; the second overwrites the first mid-rollout. Use a concurrency group per environment.
  • A "config-only" deploy that rebuilds. Changing a ConfigMap should not require a new image; if it does, your config is baked in.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask: what is the smallest thing we can ship, and how quickly can we un-ship it? Everything else follows. Small batches make failures obvious and rollbacks cheap. They would rather deploy 12 times a day with a 5% change failure rate than once a fortnight with 2%, because the first team restores service in 8 minutes and the second takes 4 hours to find which of 60 changes did it.

On the delivery-versus-deployment question they are pragmatic. They will argue for removing the approval gate only after the team can show: reliable smoke tests, automated rollback, feature flags for risky changes, and a change failure rate under about 10%. Removing the gate before those exist is not maturity, it is optimism.

They also treat "promote the artifact" as non-negotiable and will block a design review over it, because every environment-specific build quietly converts your test results into guesses.

Explained to a product manager: "We bake the software once and move that exact copy through testing to production. If we baked it again for production, we would be shipping something nobody tested."

Common mistakes

  • Rebuilding the image for each environment, or building from a branch name rather than a commit SHA.
  • Running migrations on application startup, so ten replicas race to run the same DDL.
  • Putting the approval gate on staging rather than production, where it slows learning and protects nothing.
  • Baking environment config into the image, then needing a rebuild to change a log level.
  • Treating "continuous deployment" as a goal in itself rather than as the result of trustworthy automation.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: both produce a deployable artifact automatically; deployment removes the human gate. Follow-up: what must be true before you would remove the gate?
  2. Why must the same artifact be promoted across environments?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rebuilding introduces dependency drift, base image drift, build-env differences; staging results stop being evidence about production. Follow-up: what differs between environments, then?
  3. Where does a database migration run relative to the deploy, and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: before the rollout, as a separate one-shot job, and it must be backward compatible because old and new pods coexist. Follow-up: what do you do about dropping a column?
  4. How do you prevent two deploys colliding?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: concurrency group per environment, queue rather than cancel for production, deploy locks, or a merge queue.
  5. Your approval gate adds 6 hours of latency at night. Is that a problem?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: depends on lead time targets and incident risk; discuss automated rollback plus canary as the alternative to a human.

Practical exercise

Take a service that currently builds per environment. Restructure the pipeline so the image is built once on merge, tagged sha-<short>, pushed, and then referenced by digest in staging and production deploys. Add an environment protection rule requiring a team review for production and restricting it to main. Acceptance criteria: docker inspect on a staging pod and a production pod shows the same RepoDigest; the pipeline contains exactly one docker build; and a deploy from a feature branch to production is rejected by the platform, not by convention.

47.3 Artifacts and supply chain

Concept

An artifact is the immutable output of your build: for a backend service, a container image. Supply chain security is the practice of knowing exactly what is inside that artifact, where each piece came from, and being able to prove it later.

Why does it exist?

Two forces. The first is operational: you cannot roll back to a version you cannot name. The second is security: modern attacks target the build pipeline rather than the running system, because a compromised build injects code into an artifact that everyone already trusts. The event-stream npm incident, the xz backdoor and the SolarWinds compromise all worked this way. When a CVE lands on a Friday, the only question that matters is "which of our 60 services contain this package, at which version?" and you can only answer it in minutes if you recorded the answer at build time.

How it works

Tagging. Every image gets at least two tags plus its digest:

  • orders-api:sha-3f9a1c2 — the immutable identity. Points at exactly one commit, forever. This is what deployment manifests reference.
  • orders-api:1.14.3 — the semantic version, for humans, release notes and support conversations.
  • orders-api@sha256:9f3c... — the digest, which the registry computes. This is the only reference that cannot be moved.

You may also push a floating 1.14 or an environment pointer like production-current, but nothing in a deployment manifest should reference a moving tag.

Why latest makes rollbacks meaningless. latest is a mutable pointer, and it points at whatever was pushed most recently. Three concrete consequences: two nodes that pull at different times run different code with no way to tell from the manifest; a rollback has no target, because the previous image has no name you can reference; and imagePullPolicy: Always combined with latest means a pod restart at 3 a.m. silently upgrades to code nobody deployed. Configure the registry to reject pushes to immutable tags after the first (ECR supports tag immutability per repository), and never let a manifest contain a moving tag.

SBOM (Software Bill of Materials). A machine-readable list of every package in the image with name, version, license and, ideally, its source. Generate it at build time with Syft or docker buildx --sbom=true, in SPDX or CycloneDX format, and store it as an artifact attached to the image. It costs about 10 seconds per build. When the next log4shell-class vulnerability drops, you query SBOMs and know your exposure in two minutes instead of grepping 60 repositories for a day.

Build provenance (attestations). A signed statement describing how the artifact was produced: which source commit, which builder, which parameters, at what time. The SLSA framework defines levels; the practical target for most teams is provenance generated by the CI platform itself (GitHub's actions/attest-build-provenance, or docker buildx --provenance=mode=max) and verified at deploy time. This is what lets you answer "was this image built from our repository by our pipeline, or did someone push it from a laptop?" — a question that has an uncomfortable answer in most organisations.

Signing. Cosign signs an image digest with a key or, better, with keyless OIDC identity tied to the workflow. An admission controller in the cluster (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) refuses to run images without a valid signature from your CI identity. That single control turns "an attacker with registry write access owns production" into "an attacker with registry write access owns nothing".

Retention. Storage is cheap until it is not; more importantly, an unbounded registry makes it hard to find anything. A workable policy for ECR lifecycle rules:

Tag pattern Keep Reason
sha-* Last 50 images per repository Rollback targets for recent history
Semver v* All, or last 2 years Support, audit, reproducing old bugs
Untagged manifests Delete after 7 days Build cache and orphaned layers
cache-* (BuildKit cache) Delete after 14 days Regenerated on demand

Keep at least the last 10 deployable images. A team that keeps 3 discovers, during a bad week with three consecutive rollbacks, that there is nothing left to roll back to.

Production scenario

A platform with 60 services, 200 deploys a day, ECR in eu-west-1. Each image build produces: the image (about 210 MB, of which 130 MB is the shared base layer), a CycloneDX SBOM (roughly 400 KB), a provenance attestation, and a Trivy scan report stored as a workflow artifact for 90 days. Storage sits around 900 GB after lifecycle rules, costing roughly 90 USD a month, which is one hour of engineer time. The SBOM index is queryable: when a critical CVE in undici was announced, the security team produced the list of 23 affected services in under 5 minutes and the platform team shipped base image bumps the same afternoon.

Failure scenario

A team deployed with imagePullPolicy: Always and the tag orders-api:production. During a node autoscaling event at 02:50, three new pods started and pulled production — which had been overwritten 20 minutes earlier by a broken build from a developer testing the pipeline locally with their own credentials. The cluster now ran two versions simultaneously: seven pods on the good code and three on code that had never passed CI. Requests failed for roughly 30% of users, and kubectl get deployment showed everything healthy because the tag matched.

The fix took three changes: tag immutability enabled in ECR, deployments referencing sha-* tags only, and registry write permission restricted to the CI role via OIDC (47.4). None of these are expensive; all of them were "we'll do it later" items on a backlog.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Tag reuse. Someone force-pushes a tag; two nodes now differ. Enable tag immutability.
  • Registry garbage collection deletes a layer still referenced. Rare, but it makes an old image unpullable exactly when you need it for a rollback.
  • Dirty build tree. An image built from a working directory with uncommitted changes has a sha- tag that lies. Fail the build if git status --porcelain is non-empty (47.13).
  • Multi-arch confusion. An arm64-only image deployed to amd64 nodes fails with exec format error at pod start, after the deploy has been declared successful by the pipeline.
  • SBOM generated from the source tree rather than the image. It then misses OS packages, which is where a large share of CVEs live. Scan the built image.
  • Provenance that nobody verifies. Generating attestations without an admission policy is documentation, not a control.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask one question about every artifact: can I name it, find it, and prove where it came from, in six months, during an incident, at 3 a.m.? If yes, the supply chain hygiene is adequate. If not, everything else is decoration.

They also weigh cost honestly. Full SLSA level 3 with hermetic builds is real work; SBOM generation, digest-pinned deploys, tag immutability and Trivy in the pipeline take an afternoon and remove most of the risk. Do the afternoon's work first, and add the rest when a customer questionnaire or a regulator asks.

Common mistakes

  • Deploying latest or an environment-named tag.
  • Keeping only 3 images and losing rollback targets.
  • Generating an SBOM and never storing or querying it.
  • Allowing developer credentials to push to the production registry.
  • Tagging by branch name, so two branches with the same name collide.

Interview questions

  1. Why is latest dangerous in production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: mutable pointer, nodes diverge, no rollback target, silent upgrade on restart. Follow-up: what would you tag instead, and what enforces it?
  2. What is an SBOM and when has it saved you time?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: package inventory per image; answers "am I affected by CVE-X" in minutes across all services.
  3. What does build provenance prove that a signature alone does not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: not just "signed by us" but "built from commit X by workflow Y with these inputs"; ties artifact to source.
  4. How do you stop an image that did not come from CI from running in the cluster?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: keyless signing in CI plus an admission policy verifying the signer identity.

Practical exercise

Add three things to an existing build workflow: SBOM generation with Syft attached as a workflow artifact, tag immutability on the registry repository, and a build step that fails if the working tree is dirty or the commit is not on main. Then write an ECR lifecycle policy implementing the retention table above. Acceptance criteria: a pushed image cannot be overwritten; an SBOM can be downloaded for any image from the last 90 days; and you can answer "which services contain axios@1.6.0?" from stored SBOMs without cloning any repository.

47.4 Secrets in CI

Concept

Your pipeline needs credentials: to push to a registry, to deploy to a cluster, to run migrations against a database. The naive approach is to store an AWS access key ID and secret in the CI system's secret store. The senior approach is to store nothing long-lived at all, and instead have the CI platform prove its identity to AWS at run time, receiving credentials that expire in an hour.

Why does it exist?

A long-lived AWS access key in CI is a permanent, exfiltratable, often over-privileged credential sitting in a system that runs arbitrary code from pull requests. It does not rotate. It does not expire. If it leaks, it works from anywhere on the internet until a human notices and revokes it, and the leak paths are numerous: an echo $AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in a debug line, a dependency with a postinstall script, a compromised third-party Action, a fork PR that a maintainer approved without reading.

OIDC federation removes the credential entirely. There is nothing to leak.

Mental model

Imagine a courier who needs to enter your office building. The old way is to give the courier company a permanent master key. Anyone who steals it walks in, forever, and you would not know.

OIDC is a different arrangement. The courier arrives, shows a badge issued by their employer that says "this is courier #42, working job #9981, today". Your security desk trusts that employer's badge system, checks that the job number matches an expected delivery, and issues a visitor pass valid for one hour, for floor 3 only. Nothing permanent changes hands.

How it works

Step by step:

  1. You register GitHub's OIDC issuer (https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com) as an identity provider in your AWS account. This is a one-time setup that stores the issuer URL, the audience, and lets AWS fetch GitHub's public keys.
  2. A workflow with permissions: id-token: write asks the GitHub runtime for a signed JWT. That token contains claims describing exactly what is running: repository, ref, sha, workflow, environment, job_workflow_ref, and a composite sub.
  3. The workflow calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with that token and a role ARN.
  4. AWS verifies the signature against GitHub's published keys, then evaluates the role's trust policy against the token claims.
  5. If the conditions match, STS returns temporary credentials, typically valid for one hour.

The trust policy is where the security actually lives:

JSON
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
        },
        "StringLike": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:acme/orders-api:environment:production"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Read every line of that, because each one blocks a real attack:

  • Principal.Federated names the specific OIDC provider in your account. Without it any identity provider could be used.
  • aud StringEquals sts.amazonaws.com ensures the token was minted for AWS, not for some other service that also accepts GitHub OIDC tokens. A token issued for a different audience cannot be replayed here.
  • sub StringLike is the critical one. repo:acme/orders-api:environment:production means: only a job in that repository, running in the production environment, can assume this role. Because GitHub environments can require reviewers and restrict branches, this transitively enforces "only approved deploys from main".

The condition patterns you will actually use:

sub pattern Grants access to
repo:acme/orders-api:ref:refs/heads/main Jobs on the main branch only
repo:acme/orders-api:environment:production Jobs targeting the production environment (best for deploy roles)
repo:acme/orders-api:pull_request Jobs triggered by a PR (use only for read-only roles)
repo:acme/* Any repository in the org (too broad; avoid)
repo:acme/orders-api:* Any workflow, branch, or fork-triggered event in the repo (too broad)

The two mistakes that make OIDC useless: using StringLike with a trailing * on the repo (repo:acme/*), which lets any repository in the organisation deploy anything; and omitting the sub condition entirely, which lets any GitHub repository in the world assume your role. That last one has happened to real companies. If your condition block does not name your repository, you have published a role to the internet.

Least-privilege deploy roles. Separate the roles by what they do, and never merge them into one "CI role":

Role Permissions Trusted sub
ci-read ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, pull only pull_request
ci-build-push ECR push to specific repositories ref:refs/heads/main
deploy-staging EKS describe, assume the staging cluster role environment:staging
deploy-production EKS describe on one cluster, one namespace environment:production

Constrain resources, not just actions: ecr:PutImage on arn:aws:ecr:eu-west-1:123456789012:repository/orders-api, not *. A deploy role that can write to every repository lets a compromised orders pipeline poison the payments image.

The blast radius of a compromised CI runner. Be honest about this, because it is the strongest argument for short-lived credentials. A runner executes code from your repository, your dependencies (including postinstall scripts), and third-party Actions. Any of those can read the runner's environment, memory and filesystem. So a compromised runner can:

  • Read every secret and token the job was given, including the OIDC-derived credentials for their remaining lifetime.
  • Push an image (if the job has push rights) containing arbitrary code, which then flows through your normal, trusted deploy path.
  • Modify the artifact after tests pass but before push, if build and test are in the same job.
  • Reach anything network-reachable from the runner, including self-hosted runners inside your VPC. This is why self-hosted runners must live in an isolated subnet with no route to production databases.
  • With contents: write, push commits or move tags.

The mitigations that follow directly: default permissions: contents: read at workflow level and grant more only per job; pin third-party Actions to a full commit SHA (actions/checkout@8ade135a41bc03ea155e62e844d188df1ea18608) rather than a tag, because tags move; keep production deploy credentials in a separate job gated by an environment, so the code-execution-heavy jobs (tests, builds) never hold them; use ephemeral runners that are destroyed after one job; and never run untrusted fork PR code with pull_request_target, which gives it the base repository's secrets.

Preventing secrets in logs. GitHub masks known secret values in output, but only exact matches: a base64-encoded or JSON-embedded secret is not masked. Never echo a variable you have not verified, disable set -x in scripts that touch secrets, and add secret scanning (47.6) on both the repository and the CI logs. If a secret does appear in a log, treat it as compromised: rotate first, then delete the log. Deleting the log without rotating is the mistake, because the log may already have been read, cached, or replicated.

Production scenario

A company with 60 repositories has zero AWS access keys in GitHub. One OIDC provider, and roughly 120 roles generated by Terraform from a module that takes repo, environment and a policy document. The deploy-production roles are all scoped to environment:production, which requires two reviewers. Credential lifetime is one hour. When a third-party Action was compromised in a widely-reported incident, their exposure assessment took 20 minutes: the Action was used in a test job with contents: read and no cloud role, so nothing needed rotating. The team that had static keys in the same Action rotated 40 credentials over two days.

Failure scenario

At 09:12 a security alert fires: an AWS access key belonging to ci-deploy-user was used from an IP in a country the company does not operate in. The key had been in GitHub secrets for two years, had AdministratorAccess because "it needed to do a lot of things", and had been printed once into a workflow log in 2023 by a debug line that was reverted the same day. The log was public because the repository was open source for four months.

Containment took six hours: revoke the key, audit CloudTrail for every action it performed, rotate every downstream credential it could have read from Secrets Manager, and rebuild two EC2 instances it had touched. The remediation was OIDC, per-environment roles and resource-scoped policies — about two days of work that would have prevented the whole event.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Trust policy too broad. repo:acme/* or a missing sub condition; any repo, or any repo on GitHub, can assume the role.
  • Job longer than the credential lifetime. A 90-minute deploy fails at minute 61 with ExpiredToken. Either shorten the job or refresh credentials.
  • Fork PRs get no secrets. Correct and intentional, but it means a job written to always need a token will always fail for external contributors.
  • pull_request_target misuse. Runs the workflow from the base branch with full secrets, but people then check out the fork's code, which executes untrusted code with secrets. This is the single most exploited GitHub Actions pattern.
  • Self-hosted runner reuse. A non-ephemeral runner keeps files, caches and credentials from the previous job. One malicious PR poisons every job after it.
  • Action tag mutation. some-action@v3 is a tag the maintainer (or an attacker with their credentials) can move. Pin by SHA.
  • Secrets in the build context. An .env copied into the Docker build context ends up in a layer and is shipped to the registry (Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers).
  • Environment secrets on the wrong environment. Staging secrets available to a production job, or the reverse, because the job did not declare environment:.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start from the assumption that the runner will be compromised eventually, and design so that the compromise is boring. Short-lived credentials, narrow trust conditions, resource-scoped policies, separation between jobs that run untrusted code and jobs that hold deploy rights.

They ask of every secret: what is the worst thing that can be done with this, from anywhere on the internet, for as long as it exists? A long-lived admin key scores catastrophically on all three axes. An OIDC-derived, environment-scoped, one-hour credential scores badly on none.

They also insist that rotation be routine rather than heroic. If rotating a credential requires a maintenance window and a wiki page, it will not happen after a suspected leak, which is exactly when it must.

Explained to a product manager: "Instead of giving the build system a permanent master key, we give it a way to prove who it is each time, and it gets a pass that expires in an hour and only opens one door."

Common mistakes

  • Storing long-lived cloud access keys in CI secrets.
  • A trust policy without a sub condition, or with an over-broad wildcard.
  • One AdministratorAccess role used by every workflow.
  • Third-party Actions pinned to tags rather than commit SHAs.
  • pull_request_target combined with checking out the PR head.
  • Deleting a leaked log without rotating the secret.
  • Self-hosted runners on a network that can reach the production database.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through how OIDC federation replaces an AWS access key in CI.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: workflow requests a signed ID token, calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AWS verifies signature and trust policy conditions, returns 1-hour credentials. Follow-up: which claim stops another repository using your role?
  2. What is wrong with "sub": "repo:acme/*" in a trust policy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: any repository in the org, including a new low-trust one, can assume the role; scope to repo plus branch or environment.
  3. A CI runner is compromised. What can the attacker reach?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: all job secrets, live cloud credentials for their remaining TTL, the ability to push artifacts through the trusted path, network reach from the runner. Follow-up: how do you shrink each of those?
  4. Why pin Actions to a commit SHA?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: tags are mutable; a moved tag executes new code with your secrets.
  5. A secret was printed into a build log. What is your order of operations?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rotate first, then revoke downstream, then delete the log and audit usage; assume it has been read.

Practical exercise

Replace a static AWS key in one workflow with OIDC. Create the identity provider, a role whose trust policy is scoped to repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:staging, and a permissions policy limited to ecr:PutImage on one repository plus ecr:GetAuthorizationToken. Then prove the controls work: run the same workflow from a feature branch without the environment and confirm the role assumption is denied, and try assuming the role from a second repository and confirm it is denied. Acceptance criteria: no long-lived credential exists anywhere in the repository settings, both negative tests fail as expected, and the workflow's permissions block grants contents: read and id-token: write and nothing else.

47.5 Testing stages in the pipeline

Concept

A pipeline is a sequence of increasingly expensive, increasingly realistic filters. Each stage catches a class of bug the previous one could not, and costs more to run. The design goal is to catch each bug at the cheapest stage that can catch it, and to fail as early as possible so nobody waits 20 minutes to learn about a typo.

Why does it exist?

Because you cannot afford to run everything on every push, and you cannot afford to run nothing. A full end-to-end suite against a production-shaped environment might take 25 minutes and need a database seeded with 2 million rows. Running that on every push means a 25-minute feedback loop and an environment permanently occupied. Running only unit tests means you ship a query that works against a mock and deadlocks against real PostgreSQL.

Staging solves this: cheap deterministic tests gate every push, expensive realistic tests gate the release.

Mental model

Imagine airport security. The metal detector is fast, everyone goes through it, and it catches the obvious. The bag scanner is slower and catches more. A hand search is slow, invasive and reserved for the small number of cases that reach it. You would never hand-search every passenger, and you would never let someone board on the strength of the metal detector alone.

Your pipeline is the same shape. Unit tests are the metal detector: 40,000 of them, 3 minutes, every push. E2E is the hand search: 40 of them, 6 minutes, once per release candidate.

How it works

Unit tests: every push. No network, no database, no filesystem, no real timers. In a NestJS service these test services, domain logic, pipes, guards, mappers and pure functions, with repositories replaced by test doubles. Budget: 40,000 tests in under 3 minutes with four shards. They should be so fast that developers run them on save.

Integration tests: every push, with service containers. These are the tests that earn their keep, because most backend bugs live at the boundary: a unique constraint you forgot, a transaction that does not roll back the way you assumed, a ON CONFLICT clause that silently updates the wrong row, a Redis key that never expires. GitHub Actions services: starts real containers on the runner network:

YAML
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.4-alpine
    env:
      POSTGRES_USER: test
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
      POSTGRES_DB: orders_test
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    # Without a health check the job races the database and fails
    # intermittently with ECONNREFUSED on the first test.
    options: >-
      --health-cmd "pg_isready -U test"
      --health-interval 5s
      --health-timeout 5s
      --health-retries 10
  redis:
    image: redis:7.4-alpine
    ports: ["6379:6379"]
    options: >-
      --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
      --health-interval 5s
      --health-retries 10

Two details that cause most of the pain here. First, the health check is not optional: without it the job starts running tests while PostgreSQL is still initialising, and you get an ECONNREFUSED that looks exactly like flakiness and occurs on maybe one run in eight. Second, services: containers are only reachable on localhost when the job runs directly on the runner; if the job itself runs in a container, you address them by service name instead. That difference has cost more engineering hours than it should.

Isolation between tests is the other half. Three workable strategies:

Strategy Speed Isolation Notes
Truncate all tables between tests Fast (5–15 ms) Good Must respect FK order or use TRUNCATE ... CASCADE
Wrap each test in a transaction and roll back Fastest (1–3 ms) Good Breaks if the code under test manages its own transactions
A schema per Jest worker Fast Excellent Enables parallel workers; costs a migration run per schema

For a NestJS service with TypeORM, the schema-per-worker approach lets you drop --runInBand and run integration tests on four workers, which typically takes a 9-minute suite to 3 minutes.

Contract tests. When orders-api calls payments-api, integration tests in the orders repository usually mock the payments HTTP client. That mock encodes an assumption about the payments API, and nothing checks that the assumption stays true. Contract testing (Pact is the common tool) makes the assumption executable: the consumer's tests generate a contract file describing the requests it makes and the responses it expects; the provider's pipeline replays that contract against the real provider and fails if it no longer satisfies it. The provider learns it broke a consumer in its own pipeline, before deploying.

This is the cheapest way to get most of the value of end-to-end testing without an end-to-end environment. It scales: 12 consumers times 8 providers is 96 relationships that would be impossible to cover with E2E but are perfectly manageable as contracts. See Part 25 — Backward Compatibility for what the contracts should assert.

E2E before production. A small number (20 to 60) of tests that drive real HTTP against a deployed stack, covering the critical user journeys end to end: register, log in, browse products, add to cart, checkout with a sandbox payment provider, receive the confirmation. They run against staging after the image is deployed there, and they are the last gate before production.

Keep them few and keep them about journeys, not details. Every E2E test you add is a test that will eventually be flaky, because it depends on a network, a deployed environment, external sandboxes and timing. Sixty E2E tests with a 0.5% flake rate each means roughly a 26% chance that any given run is red for no reason. That is how teams end up ignoring E2E failures.

Sharding. For a suite of N tests across M runners, Jest's --shard=i/M partitions deterministically by file. Real numbers from a mid-size NestJS service: 4,100 unit tests, 11 min 40 s on one runner, 3 min 25 s on four shards, 2 min 40 s on eight. The eighth shard costs twice the runner minutes for 45 seconds of wall clock, because each shard pays about 80 seconds of fixed cost (checkout, npm ci from cache, Jest startup). Choose the point where the curve flattens, not the maximum.

Integration tests shard differently: each shard needs its own database, so you either run schema-per-shard against one PostgreSQL service or accept fewer shards. Two to four is usually right.

Coverage gates that mean something. A global "80% line coverage" threshold is nearly useless. It can be satisfied by tests that execute code without asserting anything, it says nothing about which 80%, and it creates an incentive to write tests for trivial getters while the payment reconciliation logic stays uncovered.

What works instead:

  1. Coverage on the diff, not the repository. Require that lines added or changed in this PR are covered at, say, 85%. New code is where new bugs are. Tools: jest --changedSince, or a coverage service that computes patch coverage.
  2. Per-path thresholds. Jest supports coverageThreshold per glob. Set 95% on src/domain/** and src/payments/**, 70% on src/**, and exempt generated code and DTOs.
  3. Ratchet, never lower. Coverage may not decrease. If the number drops, the build fails; if it rises, the floor rises with it.
  4. Branch coverage, not just lines. A try/catch where the catch is never executed shows 100% line coverage on the happy path and zero knowledge of the error path.
JavaScript
// jest.unit.config.js
module.exports = {
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/src/**/*.spec.ts'],
  collectCoverageFrom: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.module.ts', '!src/**/*.dto.ts'],
  coverageThreshold: {
    // Repository floor: low, and only there to catch collapse.
    global: { lines: 70, branches: 60 },
    // The code where a bug costs money gets a real gate.
    './src/payments/': { lines: 95, branches: 90 },
    './src/domain/': { lines: 92, branches: 85 },
  },
};

The deeper treatment of what to test and how to write tests that survive refactoring is in Part 41 — Testing Backend Systems with Jest and NestJS. This section is only about where in the pipeline each kind runs and what gates on it.

Practical example

orders-api, stage by stage, with real budgets:

Stage Trigger Runs Duration Gates
Lint + typecheck Every push 1 job 70 s Merge
Unit Every push 4 shards 3 min 25 s Merge
Integration (pg + redis) Every push 2 shards 5 min 50 s Merge
Consumer contract publish Merge to main 1 job 40 s Nothing (publishes)
Provider contract verify Merge to main of provider 1 job 2 min Provider deploy
Migration dry-run Every push touching migrations 1 job 45 s Merge
E2E on staging After staging deploy 1 job 6 min Production deploy
Smoke on production After production deploy 1 job 30 s Rollback trigger
Load test Nightly on main 1 job 22 min Nothing (alerts)

NestJS example

An integration test that would be impossible to write meaningfully with a mocked repository, because the behaviour under test belongs to PostgreSQL:

TypeScript
// src/orders/orders.service.int-spec.ts
import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { TypeOrmModule, getDataSourceToken } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource, QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';
import { OrdersModule } from './orders.module';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

describe('OrdersService (integration)', () => {
  let service: OrdersService;
  let dataSource: DataSource;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
      imports: [
        TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
          type: 'postgres',
          url: process.env.DATABASE_URL, // points at the services: container
          autoLoadEntities: true,
          synchronize: false,             // migrations run first, like production
        }),
        OrdersModule,
      ],
    }).compile();

    service = moduleRef.get(OrdersService);
    dataSource = moduleRef.get(getDataSourceToken());
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    await dataSource.query('TRUNCATE orders, order_items RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE');
  });

  afterAll(async () => dataSource.destroy());

  it('rejects a duplicate idempotency key with the real unique constraint', async () => {
    const key = 'idem-9f3c-0001';
    await service.placeOrder({ customerId: 'c-1', items: [], idempotencyKey: key });

    // A mocked repository would happily accept this. PostgreSQL will not.
    await expect(
      service.placeOrder({ customerId: 'c-1', items: [], idempotencyKey: key }),
    ).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(QueryFailedError);
  });
});

Production scenario

A payments team runs 6,200 unit tests, 480 integration tests and 28 E2E tests. Over one quarter, the bugs caught by each stage were: unit 61%, integration 31%, E2E 6%, production 2%. The integration tests, which cost the most runner minutes of the three gating stages, caught almost a third of everything and nearly all of the expensive class (constraint violations, transaction boundaries, lock ordering). The E2E stage caught only six bugs but two of them were configuration problems in the deployed environment that no other stage could have found: a missing environment variable and a service-to-service network policy.

That distribution is the argument for keeping all three, and for keeping the E2E suite small.

Failure scenario

A team's integration job started failing on 1 run in 6, always with a different test, always ECONNREFUSED on PostgreSQL. Two engineers spent three days chasing a suspected connection-pool leak. The actual cause: they had recently switched the job to run inside a container (container: node:20), and in that mode services: containers are addressed by hostname, not localhost. Their DATABASE_URL still said localhost, and it sometimes worked because a leftover port mapping was reachable on some runner images and not others.

The fix was one line. The lesson recorded in the postmortem was better: when a CI failure is intermittent and infrastructural, stop debugging the application. Print the resolved connection target, the container network, and the health-check status at the start of the job. Ten lines of diagnostics would have saved three days.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Service container race. No health check, tests start before PostgreSQL accepts connections.
  • Localhost vs service name. Job in a container addresses services differently; see above.
  • Shared database between parallel workers. Two workers truncate each other's rows mid-test.
  • Migrations not run in the test database. Tests pass against synchronize: true and fail in production, because synchronize generates a schema your migrations never produce.
  • E2E against a shared staging environment. Another team deploys mid-run; your tests fail for their reason.
  • Sandbox provider outage. The payment sandbox is down; your E2E gate blocks all deploys including the fix for an unrelated incident. Have a documented, audited bypass.
  • Coverage gate satisfied by assertion-free tests. 100% coverage, zero expect calls.
  • Coverage collapse hidden by a global threshold. Payments drops from 96% to 40% while the global number stays above 70%.
  • Test data that grows. A test that inserts and never cleans up makes the suite slower every week until someone notices at 40 minutes.
  • Sharding with unbalanced files. One shard holds the 90-second file and finishes 4 minutes after the others.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, for every proposed test: what class of bug does this catch, and is there a cheaper stage that could catch it? A test that mocks the database to check that a query "was called" catches nothing; the same test written against a real PostgreSQL catches constraint and transaction bugs and belongs in the integration stage.

They watch the ratio, not the count. If integration tests take 20 minutes, that usually means someone is writing integration tests for logic that is pure and should be a unit test. If production keeps finding bugs that integration tests should have caught, the mocks are too generous.

They defend the E2E suite's small size against pressure to add "just one more", because they know the flake maths. And they treat coverage as a conversation starter rather than a target: they will happily merge a PR at 68% coverage that tests the two things that can lose money, and reject one at 94% that asserts nothing.

Explained to a product manager: "We test in layers. Cheap tests run on every change and catch most things in three minutes. Expensive, realistic tests run before release and catch the rest. Adding more expensive tests everywhere would make every change slower without catching much more."

Common mistakes

  • Mocking the database in tests whose entire purpose is database behaviour.
  • Using synchronize: true in test setup so the tested schema differs from the migrated one.
  • A single global coverage threshold, treated as the goal.
  • Growing the E2E suite to hundreds of tests and then disabling it because it is flaky.
  • Running integration tests against a shared, long-lived database instead of ephemeral containers.
  • Sharding without measuring, and paying for eight runners to save 45 seconds.

Interview questions

  1. Which tests would you run on every push and which only before release, and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: deterministic and fast gate the push (unit, integration, contract); slow and environment-dependent gate the release (E2E, load); reasoning about feedback time and flake risk.
  2. Why run integration tests against a real PostgreSQL instead of a mock?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: constraints, transactions, isolation levels, lock behaviour, SQL correctness, JSON/type coercion — none of which a mock reproduces.
  3. What makes a coverage gate meaningful?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: patch coverage, per-path thresholds on critical code, branch coverage, ratchet; and the acknowledgement that coverage measures execution, not assertion.
  4. Your integration job fails 1 in 6 runs with ECONNREFUSED. How do you debug it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: check service health checks, connection target resolution, container networking mode, startup ordering; add diagnostics rather than retries.
  5. How do contract tests reduce the need for end-to-end tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: they verify the consumer-provider agreement in each side's own pipeline, catching breaking changes before deploy, without needing all services running together.

Practical exercise

Add an integration job to a service pipeline with services: containers for PostgreSQL and Redis, health checks, and migrations run before the tests. Then convert three existing unit tests that mock the repository into integration tests, and confirm at least one of them now catches a real behaviour the mock hid (a constraint, a cascade, an isolation effect). Finally, replace the global coverage threshold with a per-path configuration plus a patch-coverage check. Acceptance criteria: the integration job is green ten times in a row; one converted test fails when you deliberately drop a database constraint; and a PR that adds uncovered code to src/payments/ is blocked while one that adds uncovered code to a DTO is not.

47.6 Security scanning

Concept

Security scanning in CI is a set of automated checks that look for known-vulnerable dependencies, vulnerable OS packages in the image, hardcoded secrets, insecure code patterns, and license violations, before the artifact reaches a registry or a cluster.

Why does it exist?

Because the majority of exploitable vulnerabilities in a typical backend service are not in code you wrote. They are in the 900 packages you depend on, and in the 120 OS packages in your base image. Nobody reads those changelogs. A scanner does, continuously, against a database of published CVEs, and it costs about 40 seconds per build.

The second reason is secrets. A leaked AWS key, database password or Stripe secret in a repository is exploited fast: public GitHub repositories are scanned by attackers continuously, and the observed time-to-abuse for an exposed AWS key is often measured in minutes. A pre-push hook plus a CI check plus provider-side push protection is a layered defence against a mistake that everyone eventually makes.

Mental model

Imagine a building inspection. Some findings mean the building cannot open today: no fire exit, live wiring exposed. Some mean a work order within a month: a cracked tile, a flickering light. If the inspector treated every finding as "cannot open", the building would never open and people would start forging inspection reports.

Your scanner is that inspector. The engineering is not in running the scan; it is in deciding which findings stop the world.

How it works

Five distinct scan types, each looking at something different:

Scan What it inspects Tools Typical duration
Dependency audit (SCA) package-lock.json against CVE databases npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot, Trivy fs 10–30 s
Container image scan OS packages and app libraries in the built image Trivy, Grype, ECR scanning 20–60 s
Secret scanning Repository history and working tree for credential patterns Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitHub push protection 15–90 s
SAST Your source code for insecure patterns CodeQL, Semgrep, eslint-plugin-security 3–12 min
License check Dependency licenses against an allowlist license-checker, FOSSA, Trivy 10–20 s

Dependency audit. Runs against the lockfile, matches package versions to advisories. The signal problem is severe here: npm audit on a typical NestJS project reports 30 to 80 findings, and most are transitive dev dependencies in the build toolchain that never execute in production. A "high severity ReDoS in a package used only by the linter" is not a production risk.

The discipline that fixes this:

  • Audit production dependencies separately: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high. That is the gate. Dev dependencies get a warning-only run.
  • Use reachability information where a tool provides it (Snyk, Semgrep supply-chain): a CVE in a code path you never call is a different risk from one in your HTTP parser.
  • Maintain an expiring allowlist. If you must accept a finding, record it with an owner, a reason and an expiry date (30 days). When it expires, the build fails again. An allowlist without expiry becomes permanent silence.

Container image scanning. Scans the built image before push. Most findings are OS packages in the base image, which means the fix is usually not yours: bump the base image. This is why a weekly automated base image bump plus rebuild of all services is worth more than any individual scan finding. Fail the build on CRITICAL and HIGH with a fix available; warn on everything else. Trivy's --ignore-unfixed is the key flag: failing on a vulnerability with no available patch just blocks you from shipping with no way to comply.

Secret scanning. Three layers, and you want all three:

  1. Pre-commit, via a gitleaks hook, so the secret never enters your local history.
  2. Push protection at the platform, which rejects the push server-side. This is the only layer that stops a secret from becoming public.
  3. CI scan of history, which catches secrets committed before the other layers existed.

A secret found in history is not fixed by deleting the file in a new commit. The blob is still reachable. The response order is always: rotate the credential first, then rewrite history, then coordinate the force-push (the full procedure is in Part 48 — Git, section 48.14).

SAST. Static analysis for injection, unsafe deserialisation, path traversal, weak crypto, hardcoded credentials, SSRF patterns. CodeQL is the practical default for TypeScript on GitHub, and Semgrep is excellent for custom organisational rules ("never call createQueryBuilder().where() with a template literal", "every controller must have a guard"). SAST is slow (3 to 12 minutes on a large repo) and has a real false-positive rate, so run it on merge to main and on a schedule rather than on every PR push, and gate on a curated subset of rules rather than everything.

License checks. Fast, boring and occasionally career-saving. A copyleft license (AGPL, GPL) pulled in as a transitive dependency can create a genuine legal obligation for a commercial product. Maintain an allowlist of permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC), fail on anything not on it, and route exceptions to legal rather than to a developer's judgement.

Which findings fail the build. This table is the actual policy, and it should live in the repository:

Finding Action Reason
Verified secret in the diff Block push, page security Time-to-abuse is minutes
Critical CVE, production dependency, fix available Fail build Exploitable, and fixable now
High CVE, production dependency, fix available Fail build (grace: 7 days via allowlist) Exploitable, fixable, some coordination needed
High CVE, no fix available Warn, create ticket, consider mitigation Blocking helps nobody
Any CVE, dev dependency only Warn Does not run in production
Critical/High in base image OS packages Fail if fixed upstream; else warn and bump on schedule Base image bump is the fix
SAST high-confidence rule (SQL injection, SSRF) Fail build Direct exploitability
SAST medium/low confidence Comment on PR False-positive rate too high to gate
Non-allowlisted license Fail build Legal exposure, needs a human decision
Medium/low CVE anywhere Report to dashboard Noise if gated

Keeping the signal-to-noise ratio survivable. This is the part that decides whether security scanning helps or becomes decoration. The techniques that work:

  • Gate on a small, high-confidence set; report the rest. A gate that fires falsely once a week will be disabled within a month.
  • Separate production from development dependency findings, always.
  • Deduplicate: one dashboard, not five bots commenting on every PR.
  • Batch dependency updates. Dependabot configured to open one grouped PR per week for patch and minor updates, and individual PRs only for security fixes, turns 40 PRs a week into 1 plus exceptions.
  • Every allowlist entry has an owner and an expiry.
  • Measure the false-positive rate. If more than about 1 in 10 gate failures is dismissed as noise, the gate is miscalibrated and you fix the gate, not the people.
  • Fix the base image once a week for everyone rather than asking 60 teams to triage the same OS CVE.

Practical example

An orders service pipeline runs, in parallel with the tests: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high (12 s), Gitleaks on the diff (8 s), and a license check against an allowlist (14 s). After the image is built, Trivy scans it with --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 (35 s) before the push step, so a vulnerable image never reaches the registry. CodeQL runs on merge to main and nightly. Total added time on the PR path: about 35 seconds, because everything runs in parallel with a 6-minute integration job.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 a developer pushed a branch containing a .env.staging file with a real database password, added by accident because their .dockerignore covered it but their .gitignore did not. Push protection was not enabled. Gitleaks was in the pipeline but configured to scan only the working tree of the default branch, so it did not run on the feature branch.

The password was rotated 4 hours later when a colleague noticed it during review. The staging database was internet-reachable through a bastion whose security group had been widened for a demo two weeks earlier. Access logs showed no unauthorised connections, but nobody could prove it conclusively because the log retention was 24 hours and the window had partly rolled off.

The three fixes: push protection enabled organisation-wide (server-side, cannot be skipped), Gitleaks running on every push against the diff, and staging credentials moved to a secret manager with 24-hour rotation. The cheapest of these — push protection — is a checkbox.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Scanner database outage. Trivy cannot fetch its vulnerability DB and exits non-zero; every build fails for a reason unrelated to your code. Cache the DB and treat a fetch failure as a warning, not a gate.
  • New CVE published overnight. Yesterday's green build is today's red build with no code change. This is correct behaviour, and it surprises people. Communicate it.
  • A CVE with no fix. Blocking builds on an unfixable finding stops all work including the mitigation. Warn and mitigate.
  • False positive in a critical gate. A HIGH in a package that is bundled but never imported. Allowlist with expiry, and record why.
  • Secrets in build logs rather than code. Scanners look at the repository, not the logs. Scan logs too, or better, never print them.
  • Scan runs after push. A vulnerable image is already in the registry and pullable. Scan before push, always.
  • License check that only sees direct dependencies. The AGPL package is three levels down.
  • Alert fatigue. 200 open findings, none triaged, everyone has muted the channel. This is the most common end state and the one to design against.
  • Fork PRs cannot upload SARIF results without elevated permissions, so security results silently disappear for external contributions.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They optimise for the number of acted-upon findings, not the number of findings. A scanner producing 400 alerts that nobody reads has negative value: it consumes attention and provides false assurance.

They ask of every gate: if this fires at 4 p.m. on a Friday during a hotfix, is blocking the deploy the right outcome? For a verified secret, yes. For a medium CVE in a dev dependency, obviously not. That question calibrates the policy better than any severity matrix.

They also push the fix upstream. Sixty services each triaging the same openssl CVE is sixty times the work of one platform team bumping the golden base image (Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers) and triggering rebuilds. Centralising the fix is the highest-leverage security work available in most organisations.

Explained to a product manager: "We check every build for known security holes. We stop the build only for the ones that are both dangerous and fixable right now; the rest become tickets. Otherwise we would block releases on problems we cannot solve."

Common mistakes

  • Failing the build on every npm audit finding, then adding || true two weeks later.
  • Scanning the image after pushing it.
  • Treating dev and production dependencies identically.
  • An allowlist with no expiry dates, which grows monotonically.
  • Running SAST on every push and adding 10 minutes to the feedback loop.
  • Relying only on CI secret scanning, with no server-side push protection.
  • Ignoring license findings until an acquisition due-diligence process finds them.

Interview questions

  1. Which security findings should fail a build, and which should not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: verified secrets and fixable critical/high in production dependencies fail; unfixable, dev-only, and low-confidence findings warn. Reasoning about actionability.
  2. npm audit reports 60 vulnerabilities. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: split prod from dev, gate on prod high/critical with a fix, batch updates, allowlist with expiry, and fix the base image centrally.
  3. A secret was committed and pushed. Walk me through your response.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rotate first, assess exposure from access logs, then rewrite history with git filter-repo, coordinate force-push, add push protection.
  4. Why scan the image rather than only the lockfile?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: OS packages, base image libraries and anything installed at build time are invisible to a lockfile scan, and are a large share of findings.
  5. How do you keep security scanning from becoming noise people ignore?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: gate narrowly, report broadly, single dashboard, expiring exceptions, measure false-positive rate, centralise base image fixes.

Practical exercise

Configure a full scanning layer on one service: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high as a gate with a separate warning-only dev run; Gitleaks on every push; a license allowlist; and Trivy on the built image with --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 placed before the push step. Then write the policy table above into SECURITY.md in the repository, including the allowlist format with mandatory owner and expiry fields. Acceptance criteria: deliberately introducing a known-vulnerable dependency version fails the build; introducing the same one as a dev dependency does not; a fake AWS key in a commit is blocked before it reaches the remote; and every current allowlist entry has an owner and a date under 30 days away.

47.7 Deployment strategies

Concept

A deployment strategy is the answer to one question: how do you replace running version A with version B while requests keep arriving? The five common answers differ in how much capacity you must pay for, how fast you can undo the change, how much traffic a bad version touches before you notice, and what they demand of the database.

Why does it exist?

Because "stop the old one, start the new one" means downtime, and because the moment of replacement is when almost all deploy-related incidents happen. The strategies exist to trade money and complexity for either less downtime, less blast radius, or a faster undo.

Mental model

Imagine replacing the tyres on a car. Recreate is stopping the car, changing all four, and driving on: simple, cheap, and you were parked for ten minutes. Rolling is changing one tyre at a time while three keep turning: no stop, but for a while you are driving on a mix of old and new tyres, and they had better be compatible. Blue/green is having a second identical car waiting; you step out of one and into the other, and if the new one makes a noise you step back. Canary is putting the new tyre on and driving slowly around the block before committing to the motorway. Shadow is towing the new car behind, spinning its wheels against the same road, measuring, but never steering with it.

How it works

Rolling update. Replace instances in small batches. Kubernetes does this natively: maxSurge controls how many extra pods may exist above the desired count, maxUnavailable how many may be missing. With maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 on 12 replicas, Kubernetes starts 3 new pods, waits for them to pass readiness, terminates 3 old ones, and repeats.

Rollback speed: a rollback is another rolling update in reverse, so it takes as long as a deploy, typically 2 to 6 minutes for a 12-replica service with a 30-second readiness ramp. Database requirement: strict N-1 compatibility, because old and new pods serve traffic simultaneously for the whole window. Traffic shifting: implicit, via the service's endpoint list as pods become ready and unready. Cost: near zero extra capacity (only maxSurge worth). Choose it when: this is your default. It is what Kubernetes does out of the box and it is correct for the large majority of stateless services.

Blue/green. Run two complete environments. Blue serves production. Deploy the new version to green at full capacity, test it, then switch the router from blue to green in one action. Keep blue running for a while as the rollback target.

Rollback speed: seconds, and this is the whole point. Flip the router back. Database requirement: still N-1 compatible, because during the switch in-flight requests exist on both sides, and because your rollback target (blue) must work against the schema the new version created. Traffic shifting: a single atomic change (a Kubernetes Service selector change, an ALB target group swap, a DNS change — though DNS is a poor choice because of TTL caching and client-side pinning). Cost: 2x compute during the deploy window, which on a 12-pod service with 1 vCPU and 2 GB each is real money if the window lasts hours. Choose it when: rollback speed matters more than cost, the release is risky, or you need a full-capacity rehearsal before taking traffic.

The subtlety people miss: blue/green gives you a fast rollback of code, not of data. Green has been writing to the shared database. Flipping back to blue leaves those writes in place, and blue must tolerate them.

Canary. Send a small fraction of traffic to the new version, watch the metrics, and increase the fraction in steps if the metrics stay healthy.

Rollback speed: seconds for the traffic shift; and crucially, only 5% of users saw the problem. Database requirement: N-1 compatible, and for a longer period than a rolling update because canary analysis takes 10 to 60 minutes. Traffic shifting: weighted routing at the ingress (NGINX canary annotations), a service mesh (Istio VirtualService weights), an ALB with weighted target groups, or a progressive delivery controller (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) that automates the steps and the analysis. Cost: modest extra capacity plus significant setup complexity plus the metrics infrastructure to judge it. Choose it when: the change is risky, traffic is high enough for 5% to be statistically meaningful, and you have per-version metrics.

The statistical requirement is the one people skip. At 10 requests per second, 5% of traffic is 0.5 rps; over 15 minutes that is 450 requests, and a failure rate change from 0.1% to 0.4% is invisible in that sample. Canary needs volume. Below roughly 100 rps on the canary slice, you are watching noise.

Recreate. Stop all old instances, then start all new ones.

Rollback speed: another full recreate, so another outage window (1 to 5 minutes). Database requirement: none — this is its one genuine advantage. Because no two versions ever run at once, a migration can be destructive and the code can assume the new schema exclusively. Traffic shifting: none; there is downtime equal to shutdown plus startup, typically 30 to 120 seconds for a NestJS service. Cost: zero extra capacity. Choose it when: the workload cannot tolerate two versions running (a singleton scheduler, a stateful consumer holding an exclusive lock, a migration that genuinely cannot be made backward compatible), or it is a low-traffic internal tool where a 60-second maintenance window costs nothing. Also the right default for local development and CI environments.

Shadow (traffic mirroring). Send a copy of production traffic to the new version. Its responses are discarded. Compare behaviour, latency and errors against the live version.

Rollback speed: not applicable, because shadow traffic never serves users; you simply stop mirroring. Database requirement: the shadow must not write to production data. This is the hard part and the reason shadow deployments are rare: any write path must be routed to a copy, stubbed, or made a no-op, and every outbound side effect (charging a card, sending an email, publishing a Kafka event) must be blocked. Traffic shifting: mirroring at the proxy (Istio mirror with mirrorPercentage, NGINX mirror directive, Envoy request shadowing). Cost: full extra capacity for the shadow plus the isolation engineering plus doubled load on any shared read-only dependency. Choose it when: you are rewriting a critical service and want production-realistic validation with zero user risk — a database engine migration, a framework rewrite, a new pricing engine you need to prove matches the old one on real inputs.

The comparison table. This is the one to memorise:

Strategy Downtime Rollback speed Blast radius of a bad version DB compatibility needed Traffic mechanism Extra capacity Complexity Choose when
Recreate 30–120 s Full redeploy (minutes, with downtime) 100% after switch None (versions never overlap) None 0% Very low Singletons, exclusive locks, unavoidable breaking migration, dev environments
Rolling None Reverse rollout, 2–6 min 100% by the end N-1 required Readiness gates on the Service +25% during window Low Default for stateless services
Blue/green None Seconds (router flip) 100% after switch, until you flip back N-1 required Atomic router/selector switch +100% during window Medium Risky releases, fast rollback mandated, full-capacity rehearsal
Canary None Seconds, and only a slice was exposed 5–10% initially N-1 required, for a longer window Weighted routing / mesh +5–20% High High-traffic risky changes with good per-version metrics
Shadow None N/A (never serves) 0% Writes must be isolated Request mirroring +100% Very high Rewrites and engine swaps needing production-realistic proof

Practical example

An e-commerce platform uses three strategies deliberately:

  • orders-api, catalog-api, notifications-worker: rolling, maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0, 12 to 40 replicas. This covers about 90% of deploys.
  • payments-api: canary via Argo Rollouts. Steps at 5% for 10 minutes, 25% for 10 minutes, 50% for 5 minutes, then 100%, with automated analysis on error rate, p99 latency and the payment-authorisation success rate. A regression aborts the rollout automatically.
  • scheduler, a singleton that holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock and must never have two instances: recreate, with a 40-second window at 03:00.

NestJS example

Rolling and blue/green both depend on your application handling readiness and shutdown correctly, or every deploy drops requests. This is the code that makes the strategy work:

TypeScript
// src/health/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator, HttpHealthIndicator,
} from '@nestjs/terminus';

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  private shuttingDown = false;

  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly http: HttpHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  // Liveness: is the process wedged? Keep it trivial. A dependency check here
  // means a database blip restarts every pod at once.
  @Get('live')
  live() {
    return { status: 'ok' };
  }

  // Readiness: should this pod receive traffic right now? Checks dependencies,
  // and reports NOT ready as soon as SIGTERM arrives so the Service removes
  // this pod from its endpoints before the process stops accepting sockets.
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    if (this.shuttingDown) {
      throw new Error('shutting down');
    }
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 }),
      () => this.http.pingCheck('payments', 'http://payments-api/health/live', { timeout: 1000 }),
    ]);
  }

  markShuttingDown(): void {
    this.shuttingDown = true;
  }
}

The shutdown sequence that pairs with it: on SIGTERM, flip readiness to failing, wait about 10 seconds (long enough for the load balancer to notice, typically 2 to 3 failed probes), then stop accepting new connections, drain in-flight requests with a timeout, close the database pool, exit 0. terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed that total or Kubernetes sends SIGKILL mid-request. The mechanics of preStop, signal handling and exit codes are in Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers and Part 45 — Kubernetes for Backend Engineers.

Production scenario

A canary rollout of payments-api at 14:00 on a Tuesday. Traffic is 1,800 rps, so the 5% slice is 90 rps — enough for statistics. The analysis window is 10 minutes: 54,000 requests through the canary. Baseline error rate is 0.08%; the abort threshold is 0.25% sustained over 3 minutes, or p99 latency above 1.4x baseline.

At 14:06 the canary's p99 rises from 190 ms to 340 ms. The analysis job flags it at 14:08 and Argo Rollouts aborts, shifting traffic back to stable in 4 seconds. Total user impact: about 90 rps experiencing elevated latency for 8 minutes, roughly 0.3% of requests in that window, no errors. The cause was a missing index on a new payment_attempts.idempotency_key column, which only mattered under real cardinality. Staging had 400 rows; production had 60 million.

Note what the canary bought: not the discovery of the bug (a load test might have found it), but the fact that 95% of customers never experienced it and nobody had to be paged.

Failure scenario

A team ran blue/green on a service with a shared database. The new version (green) added a NOT NULL column with a default and started writing a new status value, PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, that the old code did not know about. They switched to green at 10:00. At 10:25 an unrelated bug in green caused 500s on the refund endpoint, so they flipped back to blue in 6 seconds — exactly the fast rollback blue/green promises.

Then blue started throwing Unhandled enum value: PARTIALLY_REFUNDED on every order-listing request, because 340 orders written in those 25 minutes had a status the old code's exhaustive switch did not handle. The fast rollback rolled back the code and could not roll back the data. They spent 50 minutes writing and running a data patch under pressure.

The lesson is the one this part keeps returning to: rollback speed is a property of the deployment strategy; rollback safety is a property of your compatibility discipline. New enum values, like new columns, must be readable by the previous version before the version that writes them ships. See Part 25 — Backward Compatibility for the general rule and Part 24 for the schema mechanics.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Readiness probe that always passes. A return 'ok' readiness endpoint means a rolling update replaces every pod with a broken one, cheerfully, in 90 seconds.
  • maxUnavailable > 0 on a service at capacity. You remove 25% of capacity during the rollout and the remaining pods saturate.
  • Sticky sessions across a blue/green switch. Users mid-session get inconsistent behaviour, or the switch does not actually move them.
  • Canary without per-version metrics. You cannot tell whether the error rate rose because of the canary or in general. Label every metric with the version.
  • Canary at low traffic. 3 requests per minute through the canary proves nothing; you promote a broken version with a green analysis.
  • Canary that passes at low traffic and fails at peak. The 5% slice never triggers the connection-pool exhaustion that 100% will. Include a load-proportional step or hold at 50% through a peak.
  • Shadow traffic writing to production. Duplicate orders, duplicate emails, double charges. This has happened, more than once, at well-known companies.
  • Shadow doubling load on a shared dependency. The mirrored traffic hits the same third-party API and you exhaust its rate limit.
  • Blue/green with connection-limited dependencies. Both environments hold full connection pools; 24 pods times 20 connections exceeds max_connections (Part 19 — PostgreSQL Internals).
  • Long-running requests during a switch. A 90-second report request is killed mid-flight when blue scales down 30 seconds later.
  • In-flight Kafka messages. A consumer group rebalance during a rolling update pauses consumption; with a large partition count the rebalance can take longer than the rollout.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick rolling by default and justify anything else. The question they ask is what does this change actually risk, and what would we need to see to know it is going wrong? If the answer is "we would see it in the error rate within two minutes", rolling with automated rollback is sufficient. If the answer is "we would only see it in the refund reconciliation report tomorrow", no deployment strategy saves you and the work belongs in feature flags and better observability instead.

They are sceptical of canary as a default, because it costs real complexity and demands per-version metrics that many teams do not have. A canary you cannot judge is just a slow rolling update with extra YAML.

They also separate the two rollback questions explicitly: how fast can we get the old code back? (a strategy question) and will the old code work? (a compatibility question). Teams that only answer the first one get the blue/green incident described above.

Explained to a product manager: "We usually replace servers a few at a time so there is no downtime. For risky changes we send a small slice of customers to the new version first and watch. And for anything that touches money, we ship the code turned off and turn it on separately."

Common mistakes

  • Choosing canary because it sounds advanced, without per-version metrics or enough traffic.
  • Assuming blue/green makes a bad migration safe.
  • Readiness probes that do not check dependencies, or that check too many.
  • Not testing the rollback path, so the first time you use it is during an incident.
  • Mirroring traffic to a shadow that shares the production database.
  • Setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than the drain time.

Interview questions

  1. Compare rolling, blue/green and canary on rollback speed, cost and blast radius.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the table above, with reasoning. Follow-up: which would you pick for a payments service at 2,000 rps, and why?
  2. What must be true of your database schema for a rolling update to be safe?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: N-1 compatibility; old and new code share one schema; only additive changes at deploy time; destructive changes in a later release.
  3. Blue/green gives a 5-second rollback. What does it not roll back?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: data written by the new version, external side effects, messages published, cache entries; hence compatibility still required.
  4. When is Recreate the right choice?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: singletons with exclusive locks, workloads that cannot tolerate two versions, genuinely non-backward-compatible migrations, low-traffic internal tools.
  5. Your canary passes at 5% and the service falls over at 100%. What happened and how do you prevent it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: load-dependent failure (pool exhaustion, cache miss storm, lock contention, GC); mitigate with load-proportional steps, holding at 50% through peak, and load testing.
  6. What is required to make shadow traffic safe?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: complete write isolation, side-effect suppression, separate data store, awareness of doubled load on shared dependencies.

Practical exercise

Take a service currently deployed with a rolling update and implement blue/green using two Deployments and a Service selector switch. Measure three things: time to switch (should be under 5 seconds), peak resource consumption during the window, and requests lost during the switch under a 200 rps load generator. Then deliberately break the new version's readiness probe and confirm the switch does not happen. Acceptance criteria: zero failed requests during a successful switch, a documented rollback command that takes under 10 seconds, and a written statement of what the switch does not protect you from.

47.8 Feature flags

Concept

A feature flag is a runtime switch that changes application behaviour without changing the deployed artifact. The code for both paths ships together; a configuration value decides which path runs, and for whom.

Why does it exist?

To decouple deploy from release. Deploying is a technical event: new bytes are running. Releasing is a product event: customers can see a change. Tying them together means every product decision requires a deploy, every deploy carries product risk, and turning something off requires a rollback.

Separate them and everything gets easier. You merge to main daily even though the feature is half-finished, because it is behind a flag that is off. You ship the risky refactor and turn it on for 1% of users. When it misbehaves at 02:00, the on-call flips a switch in 10 seconds instead of running a deploy pipeline. And you stop needing long-lived feature branches, which is the single biggest cause of painful merges (Part 48 — Git).

Mental model

Imagine a new wing of a hospital. You build it, wire it, furnish it, and inspect it, all while the old wing operates normally. The doors stay locked. Then one morning you unlock one door for the outpatient clinic and watch. Then another. If something is wrong with the ventilation, you lock the doors again — you do not demolish the wing.

The flag is the door. Building the wing is the deploy; unlocking the door is the release.

How it works

Four types, with genuinely different lifecycles. Confusing them is the root of most feature-flag mess:

Type Purpose Lifetime Who changes it Removal
Release flag Hide unfinished work; gradual rollout Days to weeks Engineering Mandatory once at 100%
Ops / kill switch Disable an expensive or fragile subsystem under load Permanent On-call, at 3 a.m. Never; it is infrastructure
Experiment flag A/B test, measure variants Length of the experiment Product/data Mandatory when the experiment concludes
Permission / entitlement Gate by plan, role or tenant Permanent Product, billing Never; it is a business rule

Only two of the four are temporary, and those two are the ones that rot.

The lifecycle and the discipline of deletion. A release flag has a defined life: created with an owner and an expiry date, rolled out in steps (internal users, 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%), soaked at 100% for a week, then the flag and the dead branch are deleted from the code. That last step is the one teams skip, and the cost compounds: every unremoved flag doubles the number of code paths, and ten flags create up to 1,024 theoretical combinations, of which you test one. Bugs then appear only for the users whose flag combination nobody has ever exercised.

Enforce it mechanically, not by good intentions: every flag has an owner and an expiry in the flag system; a scheduled job opens a ticket (or fails a build) when a flag is past expiry; and a lint rule forbids adding a flag without registering it. A reasonable steady state for a service is under 15 active flags, most of them permanent ops and permission flags.

Flag-driven read switches during migrations. This is the highest-value use of flags for backend engineers. During an expand/contract schema migration you have a moment where both the old column and the new column exist and are being written, and you need to switch reads from one to the other — reversibly, instantly, without a deploy.

TypeScript
// src/orders/order-total.reader.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { FeatureFlagService } from '../flags/feature-flag.service';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrderTotalReader {
  constructor(private readonly flags: FeatureFlagService) {}

  // During the migration both columns are populated by dual writes.
