  // The flag decides which one is authoritative for reads, so switching
  // back after a bad result takes seconds, not a deploy.
  async read(order: Order): Promise<bigint> {
    const useNewColumn = await this.flags.isEnabled('orders.read_total_minor_units', {
      tenantId: order.tenantId,
    });
    return useNewColumn ? order.totalMinorUnits : BigInt(Math.round(order.total * 100));
  }
}

The full migration pattern — add column, dual write, backfill, verify, switch reads by flag, stop writing the old column, drop it — is in Part 24 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes. The flag is what makes the "switch reads" step reversible.

The evaluation-consistency problem. This is the failure mode that catches people. Your service runs 24 pods. Each pod evaluates flags locally against a cached ruleset, refreshed by polling or streaming. That cache does not update everywhere at the same instant.

Consequences, concretely:

  • A user's first request hits pod 7 (flag on, new checkout page) and their next request hits pod 12 (flag off, old checkout page). The session breaks.
  • A kill switch flipped during an incident takes effect over 30 seconds as pods poll, so the graph does not drop instantly and someone flips it twice.
  • A canary pod and a stable pod disagree about a flag, contaminating your canary analysis.

The mitigations:

  1. Deterministic bucketing. Percentage rollouts must hash a stable identifier (userId, tenantId), not a random number: hash(flagKey + userId) % 100 < rolloutPercentage. Every pod computes the same answer for the same user with no coordination. Never use Math.random() for a rollout.
  2. Evaluate once per request, at the edge of the request. Resolve all flags in a middleware or interceptor, attach the resolved set to the request context, and pass it down. Do not re-evaluate deep in a service, where a mid-request refresh can flip the value between two steps of the same transaction.
  3. Streaming updates over polling where the provider supports it, cutting propagation from 30–60 seconds to under 1 second.
  4. Accept eventual consistency and design for it. For anything where mid-flight inconsistency is unacceptable (a multi-step checkout), pin the resolved value into the session or the order record at the start.

OpenFeature in one paragraph. OpenFeature is a vendor-neutral specification and SDK for feature flag evaluation, with a stable API (getBooleanValue, getStringValue, evaluation context, hooks) and pluggable providers for LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, Unleash, GrowthBook, ConfigCat or an in-house service. You write against the OpenFeature client once; swapping the backing provider becomes a configuration change instead of a refactor across 200 call sites. It also standardises evaluation hooks, which is how you get flag evaluations onto your traces and metrics automatically — genuinely useful when debugging "why did this user see the old page?". For a NestJS service, wrap the OpenFeature client in an injectable provider so tests can supply an in-memory provider with fixed values.

Production scenario

A ride-booking platform runs 9 services with 47 active flags: 6 release flags (each with an owner and an expiry under 30 days), 12 kill switches (surge pricing recalculation, driver ETA prediction model, promotional engine, real-time map updates), 21 entitlement flags (feature tiers per city and per partner), and 8 experiment flags. Flag evaluation is local and in-memory, refreshed by a streaming connection; p99 evaluation latency is under 0.1 ms because there is no network call in the request path.

During a Kafka partition incident, the on-call disabled the ETA prediction subsystem with a kill switch. Latency recovered in 20 seconds. The alternative — a deploy of a version without that call — would have taken 11 minutes.

Failure scenario

A team added a release flag, checkout.new_tax_engine, in March. It reached 100% in April. Nobody removed it. In September a config cleanup script "tidied up" flags with no recent changes and set several to their default value, which for this flag was false. The old tax engine had not been exercised in five months and had since drifted: a currency added in June was not handled by it. Checkout began throwing Unsupported currency: RON for Romanian customers.

It took 35 minutes to diagnose, because the deployed code had not changed and everyone was looking at the deploy log. The postmortem produced two rules the team now enforces: a release flag past its expiry fails the nightly build, and any code path behind a flag at 100% for more than 30 days is deleted along with the flag.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Flag provider outage. If your SDK fails open or closed at the wrong moment, a vendor incident becomes your incident. Always configure explicit defaults in code, cache the last known ruleset to disk, and test the provider-unavailable path.
  • Math.random() bucketing. Users flip between variants on every request.
  • Flag read inside a loop. 10,000 evaluations per request; even at 0.05 ms each that is half a second.
  • Flags controlling database writes. Turning a flag off mid-transaction leaves half-written state.
  • Combinatorial explosion. 12 boolean flags, 4,096 combinations, 1 tested.
  • A flag left on forever. The dead path rots and eventually gets executed (see the story above).
  • Flag state not in the incident timeline. You cannot correlate a spike with a flag change if flag changes are not an audited, timestamped event stream. Emit them like deploys.
  • Flags used as configuration. Connection pool sizes and timeouts belong in config management, not the flag system.
  • Permission flags implemented as release flags. Someone "cleans up" a flag and every customer gets the enterprise tier.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat flags as code with a shorter half-life. Every flag is technical debt with a due date; the discipline is not "have fewer flags" but "have an expiry on every temporary one and honour it".

They insist that risky changes ship behind a flag and that the off path is exercised. A rollback path nobody has run is not a rollback path.

They also draw a firm line: flags control behaviour, not infrastructure. Pool sizes, timeouts and endpoints belong to configuration management. Mixing them means the flag system becomes a second, unaudited config system, and eventually the thing that takes production down.

Explained to a product manager: "We can put the code in production with the feature switched off, then turn it on for a small group and watch. If it misbehaves we switch it off in seconds instead of doing an emergency release."

Common mistakes

  • Never deleting flags, so the codebase accumulates untested branches.
  • Random rather than deterministic bucketing.
  • Evaluating flags deep in the call stack instead of once per request.
  • No owner or expiry, so nobody knows if a flag is safe to remove.
  • Using flags to hide a missing rollback plan rather than as a deliberate release control.
  • Flag changes that are not audited, so they are invisible during incident review.

Interview questions

  1. What problem do feature flags solve that deployment strategies do not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: decoupling deploy from release; per-user targeting; sub-second reversal without a pipeline; merging unfinished work safely.
  2. Name the flag types and their lifecycles.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: release (temporary, must be deleted), ops kill switch (permanent), experiment (until concluded), permission (permanent business rule).
  3. How do you keep 24 pods agreeing on a percentage rollout?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: deterministic hashing of a stable id, evaluate once per request, streaming updates, accept eventual consistency and pin where needed.
  4. How do flags help during a schema migration?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a reversible read switch between old and new columns during expand/contract, without a deploy.
  5. What happens when your flag provider is unavailable?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: in-code defaults, cached rulesets, fail to a known-safe value, and having tested that path.

Practical exercise

Introduce a flag-driven read switch for a field you are migrating. Implement deterministic bucketing by tenantId, resolve all flags in a NestJS interceptor and attach them to the request context, and emit a metric labelled with the resolved variant. Then simulate a provider outage by blocking the SDK's network access and confirm the service serves the in-code default without added latency. Acceptance criteria: the same tenant always gets the same variant across all pods; flag evaluation adds under 1 ms at p99; the provider-down path is covered by a test; and the flag is registered with an owner and an expiry date.

47.9 Rollbacks

Concept

A rollback is returning production to a previously known-good state. In practice it means two very different things: rolling back the image, which is fast and reliable, and rolling back the database, which usually is not possible at all.

Why does it exist?

Because your ability to recover matters more than your ability to avoid failure. Time to restore service is one of the four DORA metrics precisely because it is the one you control on your worst day. A team that deploys carefully but cannot undo is more fragile than a team that deploys casually and recovers in 90 seconds.

Mental model

Imagine a document with version history. Rolling back the code is pressing undo on the text: instant, complete. Rolling back the database is trying to un-send the emails that the document generated while it existed. The text goes back. The consequences do not.

How it works

Image rollback is easy. Your previous image still exists in the registry with an immutable tag. kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api or helm rollback orders-api 41 or, better, re-running your deploy pipeline pinned to the previous SHA. Two to six minutes for a rolling update; seconds for blue/green or a canary abort. This works because containers are immutable and the registry is durable — which is exactly why 47.3 insists on immutable tags and retention. latest breaks this completely: there is nothing to roll back to.

Database rollback usually is not. A "down migration" that reverses a schema change is a comforting fiction in most real cases:

  • DROP COLUMN cannot be undone. The data is gone. A down migration that re-adds the column gives you an empty column.
  • A backfill that transformed 40 million rows cannot be reversed unless you kept the original values.
  • A migration that ran halfway and failed leaves the schema in a state neither version expects.
  • The old code may not tolerate rows the new code wrote, even with the schema unchanged (the enum story in 47.7).

This is why the professional default is roll forward, not back. Fix the problem in a new commit, ship it through the normal pipeline (which for a hotfix should take under 15 minutes), and reserve true rollback for the case where the new code is catastrophically broken and the schema change was purely additive.

The decision, as an algorithm:

Keeping N-1 compatibility so rollback is even possible. The rule: version N must be able to run against the schema and data produced by version N+1. Concretely, that means every release must satisfy:

  • Only additive DDL at deploy time: new nullable columns, new tables, new indexes (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), constraints added NOT VALID then validated.
  • No column, table or enum value removed until the release after the last code that referenced it.
  • New enum values, new event types and new status codes must be tolerated by the previous version — usually meaning the previous version must already have a default branch that ignores unknown values. This is why "accept unknown values gracefully" ships one release before the values themselves (Part 25 — Backward Compatibility).
  • API responses may add fields but not remove or retype them.

Enforce it, do not hope for it. A CI check that inspects migration files and fails on DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE, ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE or ALTER TABLE ... SET NOT NULL unless the file carries an explicit, reviewed -- destructive: approved-by marker costs an afternoon and prevents the whole class.

Automated rollback on SLO breach. The pipeline should not need a human. After a deploy, watch a small set of signals for a defined window and roll back automatically if they breach:

Signal Threshold Window
HTTP 5xx rate > 2x the 1-hour baseline, or > 1% absolute 3 min sustained
p99 latency > 1.5x baseline 5 min sustained
Pod restarts / CrashLoopBackOff Any new pod restarting more than twice 2 min
Readiness failures More than 25% of new pods unready 3 min
Domain metric (orders/min, payment success) > 3 standard deviations below forecast 5 min

The domain metric is the one that catches the failures technical metrics miss: a deploy where every request returns 200 OK and every order silently fails validation shows a perfect error rate and a cliff in orders per minute.

Argo Rollouts and Flagger implement this as AnalysisTemplate resources querying Prometheus. In a plain GitHub Actions pipeline you can do a simpler version: after kubectl rollout status succeeds, poll your metrics endpoint for 5 minutes and call kubectl rollout undo on breach. The mechanics of defining the SLOs and the queries are in Part 43 — Observability.

Practising rollbacks deliberately. A rollback path that has never been executed is a hypothesis. Run a game day: pick a low-traffic hour, deploy a deliberately broken version to production behind a canary, and let the automation catch it. Measure time to detect and time to restore. The first time a team does this they usually discover something concrete and embarrassing — the previous image was garbage-collected, the rollback script referenced a tag that no longer exists, the on-call did not have permission to run it, or kubectl rollout undo restored the deployment but not the ConfigMap.

Production scenario

A team deploys 12 times a day with a 4% change failure rate, so roughly one bad deploy every two days. Their automated analysis catches 80% of those within 4 minutes and rolls back without human involvement; median time to restore is 3 minutes 40 seconds. The remaining 20% are subtler (a report that produces wrong numbers, a webhook that stops firing) and are caught by alerting within 20 to 90 minutes, then fixed by rolling forward. Their migration policy is strictly expand-only at deploy time, with contractions batched into a monthly cleanup release, which is what makes the automated rollback safe to run without a human judging the schema question.

Failure scenario

At 21:40 a deploy of inventory-api included a migration that renamed stock_count to available_quantity — done "properly", they thought, with a down migration that renamed it back. At 21:52 an unrelated bug in the same release caused 500s and the on-call ran helm rollback.

The old image came back in 90 seconds and immediately failed on every query: column "stock_count" does not exist. The rename had not been reverted, because helm rollback rolls back Kubernetes resources, not database state. The on-call then ran the down migration manually. It renamed the column back — and dropped the 3,100 rows that the new code had inserted using a column list that included two new columns, because the down migration also dropped those columns.

Total outage: 41 minutes. The two lessons: never rename in a single step (add, dual write, backfill, switch reads, drop later), and never assume a deployment tool's rollback touches the database.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Previous image deleted by a retention policy. Rollback target does not exist. Keep at least 10.
  • Registry outage during a rollback. Nodes cannot pull the old image. Mitigate by keeping the previous image on nodes (do not aggressively prune), or by rolling back to a running replica set that has not been scaled to zero.
  • Rollback to an image incompatible with the new schema. The central problem of this section.
  • Config not rolled back with the code. ConfigMaps, secrets and feature flags are separate objects with their own history.
  • Rollback during an in-progress rollout. Kubernetes handles it, but you can end up with three replica sets alive at once; verify the final state explicitly.
  • Messages already published. Events with a new schema are in Kafka and the old consumer cannot parse them (Part 25).
  • Cache poisoned by the bad version. Rolling back the code leaves wrong values in Redis with a 24-hour TTL. Include a targeted cache invalidation in the runbook.
  • Rollback that succeeds technically and fails operationally. The deployment reports Available with the old image while a sidecar or an init container still runs the new one.
  • Nobody has permission. The person on call at 03:00 cannot run the rollback because production access requires an approval from someone asleep.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design every release around the question how do we undo this? before the question how do we ship this? If the honest answer is "we cannot", the release gets restructured until it can be — usually by splitting it into an additive schema change, a flag-gated behaviour change, and a later cleanup.

They prefer roll-forward as the stated default, because it is honest: it acknowledges that state is not reversible and directs energy at making the hotfix path fast (which is the same investment that makes ordinary deploys fast).

They also treat the rollback runbook as production code: version controlled, reviewed, and executed on a schedule. A rollback that is only ever run during an incident is run for the first time by a stressed person at 3 a.m.

Explained to a product manager: "We can always put yesterday's software back in minutes. We usually cannot put yesterday's data back, so we design changes so that today's data still works with yesterday's software."

Common mistakes

  • Believing a down migration is a rollback plan.
  • Retention policies that delete the images you would roll back to.
  • Rolling back code without rolling back configuration or flags.
  • No automated rollback, so recovery depends on someone being awake.
  • Never practising, so the runbook is fiction.
  • Destructive migrations shipped in the same release as the code that stops using the old shape.

Interview questions

  1. Why is rolling back the database harder than rolling back the code?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: state is not reversible, dropped data is gone, backfills are one-way, partial migrations leave unexpected states; hence expand/contract and roll-forward.
  2. What is N-1 compatibility and how do you enforce it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: version N runs against version N+1's schema and data; enforced by additive-only DDL at deploy time, deferred contractions, tolerant readers, and a CI check on migration files.
  3. When would you roll back instead of rolling forward?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: catastrophic breakage, no schema change or purely additive, hotfix would take longer than the rollback, blast radius growing.
  4. Design an automated rollback trigger.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: small set of signals (5xx rate, p99, restarts, a domain metric), thresholds relative to baseline, sustained windows to avoid flapping, and a manual override.
  5. Your rollback fails because the previous image is gone. What went wrong upstream?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: retention policy too aggressive, or mutable tags, or building per environment; fix at the artifact layer.

Practical exercise

Run a rollback game day on a staging environment that mirrors production. Deploy a version that returns 500 on 30% of requests, and measure: time until your automated analysis detects it, time until traffic is fully back on the good version, and whether configuration and flags returned to their previous state. Then repeat with a release that included an additive migration, and confirm the old code runs correctly against the new schema. Acceptance criteria: detection under 4 minutes, restore under 6 minutes, a written runbook that a new team member could execute, and evidence that the previous 10 images are retained and pullable.

47.10 Smoke tests and post-deploy verification

Concept

A smoke test is a very small set of checks run immediately after a deploy against the real environment, answering one question: is this thing actually working? Not "is it correct in every detail" — that is what the test suite was for — but "is it up, connected, and serving the critical path".

The name comes from hardware: power it on and see if smoke comes out.

Why does it exist?

Because kubectl rollout status returning success means "the pods are running and their readiness probes passed". It does not mean the application can reach the database, that the new configuration is valid, that the certificate is trusted, or that an order can be placed. The gap between "deployment succeeded" and "the product works" is where a specific and painful class of incident lives: the deploy is green, the dashboards are green, and orders quietly stopped 20 minutes ago.

Mental model

Imagine a pilot's pre-taxi checklist. It is not a full inspection of the aircraft; that happened in the hangar. It is six things checked in ninety seconds: controls free, instruments alive, fuel sufficient, doors closed. Short enough to be done every single time, specific enough that failing one means you do not take off.

How it works

The handful of checks that must pass. Keep it under ten, keep it under 60 seconds, and make every one of them prove a dependency is genuinely working end to end:

Check Proves Fails when
GET /health/live returns 200 Process is up Crash loop, bad image
GET /health/ready returns 200 on all pods Dependencies reachable from this environment Wrong DB URL, network policy, secret missing
GET /version returns the expected git SHA The intended artifact is actually serving Rollout stalled, old replica set still up, wrong tag
Authenticated GET /orders?limit=1 returns 200 Auth, database read path, serialisation Migration missing, JWT secret rotated wrongly
POST /orders with a synthetic payload returns 201 The full write path: validation, transaction, constraints Broken migration, constraint violation, pool exhausted
Read back the synthetic order Write actually persisted and is visible Replica lag, wrong connection routing
A queue publish and consume round trip Broker connectivity and consumer liveness Broker credentials, topic missing, consumer not started
Outbound dependency ping (payments sandbox) Egress and credentials Egress firewall, expired API key

The synthetic checkout. The single most valuable post-deploy check for an e-commerce system is a scripted end-to-end purchase against production, using a dedicated test account, a test payment method and a product flagged as synthetic:

  1. Authenticate as synthetic-monitor@internal.
  2. Add a specific SKU (SYNTHETIC-TEST-001, stock 999,999, price 1 minor unit) to a cart.
  3. Check out with a sandbox card token that always succeeds.
  4. Assert the order reaches CONFIRMED within 15 seconds.
  5. Assert the confirmation event appears on the Kafka topic.
  6. Cancel and refund the order, so it does not pollute reporting.

Every synthetic record must be tagged (is_synthetic = true) and excluded from analytics, revenue reporting and inventory. Getting that wrong produces a different and very awkward incident: a finance team reconciling 4,000 one-cent orders.

Run it after every production deploy and on a schedule (every 2 to 5 minutes) as an ongoing monitor. Then a deploy failure and a Tuesday-afternoon outage are found by the same mechanism, which means the mechanism is well tested.

The alert watch window. After the smoke tests pass, the deploy is not finished. Hold the pipeline for a defined window — 5 to 15 minutes is typical — and watch. Two reasons: some failures need traffic to appear (a memory leak, a slow query under real cardinality, a connection pool that exhausts after 8 minutes), and some need the next scheduled job to run.

During the window the pipeline should: keep the deploy job open so it is obvious a deploy is in progress, suppress unrelated deploys to the same service via a concurrency lock, and evaluate the automated rollback signals from 47.9. Annotate your dashboards with the deploy marker — a vertical line at the deploy time on every graph turns "when did this start?" from a 10-minute investigation into a glance.

What to do when they fail. The order matters, and it should be written down before you need it:

  1. Stop the rollout immediately. For a canary or progressive rollout, abort. For a rolling update in progress, kubectl rollout pause to freeze the blast radius while you decide.
  2. Decide roll back or roll forward using the schema question from 47.9. If the release was additive-only, roll back; the decision should take seconds because the answer was determined at merge time.
  3. Verify the rollback with the same smoke tests. A rollback that has not been smoke tested is an assumption. This is the step people skip under pressure and regret.
  4. Preserve evidence before it disappears. Grab logs from the failing pods (kubectl logs --previous), a heap snapshot if it is a memory issue, and the exact image digest. A rollback deletes the pods and, with them, the evidence.
  5. Communicate. Post in the incident channel what failed, what you did, and current status. The smoke test failure message should already name the check and include the failing response body.
  6. Do not retry the same deploy hoping it was transient. If a smoke test is flaky enough that re-running fixes it, that flakiness is itself a defect: it means you cannot distinguish a broken deploy from a broken test at the exact moment you most need to.

Practical example

A NestJS /version endpoint that makes step 1 of the checklist possible, populated at build time:

TypeScript
// src/version/version.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('version')
export class VersionController {
  // GIT_SHA and BUILD_TIME are injected as env vars by the deploy manifest,
  // sourced from the CI workflow. They are not baked into the image, so the
  // same artifact is still promotable across environments.
  @Get()
  version() {
    return {
      sha: process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'unknown',
      builtAt: process.env.BUILD_TIME ?? 'unknown',
      startedAt: new Date(Date.now() - Math.floor(process.uptime() * 1000)).toISOString(),
      env: process.env.NODE_ENV,
    };
  }
}

The smoke script asserts that every pod reports the expected SHA, not just the one the load balancer happened to route to. A rollout that stalled at 60% will pass a single-request check and fail this one.

Failure scenario

At 15:20 a deploy of checkout-api completed. kubectl rollout status reported success in 2 minutes 10 seconds. The team's smoke test was curl -f https://api.example.com/health/live, which returned 200. The pipeline went green and everyone moved on.

At 16:05 support escalated: customers could not complete checkout. The new release had a typo in the Kafka topic name for order-confirmation events. The health endpoint did not touch Kafka. Orders were being created and then never confirmed, sitting in PENDING. 2,300 orders were affected over 45 minutes, and reconciling them took two engineers most of the next day.

The fix was the synthetic checkout: a single test that places a real order and asserts the confirmation event arrives would have failed in 15 seconds and rolled the deploy back automatically. The team's rule since: a smoke test that only checks liveness is not a smoke test. It must exercise the business-critical path through every dependency the service owns.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Smoke tests hitting only one pod. The load balancer routes to a healthy pod; the broken one is never sampled. Address pods directly, or run enough requests.
  • Health check that passes while the app is broken. return 'ok' with no dependency check. The most common version of this failure.
  • Synthetic data polluting production. Orders in revenue reports, inventory decremented, marketing emails sent to the test account.
  • Smoke test credentials expiring. The monitor account's password rotates and every deploy fails for 40 minutes until someone realises the deploy was fine.
  • Smoke tests that are slow. A 5-minute suite delays the rollback decision by 5 minutes.
  • Testing through a cache. A CDN serves the previous version's response and the smoke test passes against code that is not running.
  • Watch window too short. A memory leak OOMs at minute 14 of a 10-minute window and the pipeline has already reported success.
  • No deploy annotation on dashboards. Nobody can correlate a metric change with the deploy.
  • Alerting suppressed during deploys. Someone silenced alerts "because deploys are noisy", so the real breakage is invisible.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask: if this deploy were subtly broken, which single request would tell me? That request is the smoke test. Everything else is padding.

They insist that smoke tests exercise real dependencies, because the entire class of bug they exist to catch is environmental — configuration, credentials, network policy, migration state — and none of those are visible to a mocked check.

They also treat the post-deploy watch window as part of the deploy, not as an afterthought. A deploy is not finished when the pipeline is green; it is finished when the service has served real traffic on the new version for long enough to trust it. In practice that means the engineer who merged the change is still around and paying attention.

Explained to a product manager: "After every release we automatically place a test order end to end. If it does not go through, we put the previous version back before customers notice."

Common mistakes

  • Smoke tests that only check /health.
  • Running smoke tests through a cache or CDN.
  • Synthetic orders that reach real reports and real inventory.
  • No /version endpoint, so you cannot prove what is running.
  • Declaring the deploy done the moment the rollout completes.
  • Retrying a failed smoke test instead of investigating it.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between rollout status: success and "the deploy worked"?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: rollout status proves pods are running and ready; it proves nothing about configuration, downstream connectivity, migrations or the business path.
  2. Design a smoke test suite for an orders service.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: under 10 checks, under 60 seconds, version assertion across all pods, an authenticated read, a synthetic write, a queue round trip, an egress check; synthetic data tagged and cleaned up.
  3. Your smoke test passed but customers are broken. What was missing?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the check did not exercise the failing dependency; add a synthetic transaction covering the critical path.
  4. How long should the post-deploy watch window be, and what happens during it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 5–15 minutes; automated SLO evaluation, deploy concurrency lock, dashboard annotation, human attention; long enough for load-dependent failures to surface.
  5. A smoke test fails. Walk me through the next five minutes.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pause or abort the rollout, decide roll back vs forward from the schema question, verify with the same smoke tests, preserve logs and digest, communicate; do not blindly retry.

Practical exercise

Write a smoke test script for one service containing at most eight checks, including a /version assertion against every pod and one synthetic write that is tagged and cleaned up. Wire it into the deploy workflow so a failure triggers kubectl rollout undo and a notification naming the failed check. Then prove it works: deploy a version with an intentionally wrong database password and confirm the pipeline rolls back automatically. Acceptance criteria: total smoke duration under 60 seconds, automatic rollback triggered within 90 seconds of the bad deploy, synthetic records excluded from reporting queries, and the notification message identifying which check failed and why.

47.11 A complete GitHub Actions setup

Everything so far has been principles. This section is the implementation: three workflows that together take a commit from a pull request to production, with an explanation of every step that does real work. They are written for a NestJS service called orders-api deployed to Amazon EKS, with images in ECR and credentials obtained through OIDC. Nothing here is pseudocode; the mechanics are the ones you will actually type.

47.11.1 ci.yml — the gate on every pull request

YAML
name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# Only one CI run per branch. A new push cancels the previous run, which on a
# busy repo saves a large share of runner minutes and stops stale red checks
# from confusing reviewers.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# Least privilege by default. Any job needing more must ask for it explicitly.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  static:
    name: Lint and typecheck
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
          cache: npm
      # npm ci, never npm install: deterministic, and it fails if
      # package.json and package-lock.json disagree.
      - run: npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit --fund=false
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck

  unit:
    name: Unit tests (shard ${{ matrix.shard }} of 4)
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      # Without fail-fast: false, one failing shard cancels the other three
      # and you only learn about one failure per run.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit --fund=false
      - name: Jest shard
        run: npm run test:unit -- --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4 --coverage --coverageReporters=json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-unit-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: coverage/coverage-final.json
          retention-days: 1

  integration:
    name: Integration tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 25
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16.4-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: test
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: orders_test
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        # Without the health check the job starts running tests while
        # PostgreSQL is still initialising and fails roughly 1 run in 8
        # with ECONNREFUSED, which reads exactly like a flaky test.
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U test"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
      redis:
        image: redis:7.4-alpine
        ports: ['6379:6379']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 10
    env:
      NODE_ENV: test
      # localhost works because this job runs directly on the runner. If the
      # job itself ran in a container, these would be postgres:5432 and
      # redis:6379 on the job's Docker network instead.
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://test:test@localhost:5432/orders_test
      REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
      JWT_SECRET: ci-only-secret-at-least-32-characters
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit --fund=false
      # Migrations run first so the test schema is the migrated schema, not
      # one produced by synchronize: true. Those two drift apart silently.
      - name: Run migrations
        run: npm run migration:run
      - name: Integration tests
        run: npm run test:int -- --coverage --coverageReporters=json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-int
          path: coverage/coverage-final.json
          retention-days: 1

  coverage:
    name: Coverage gate
    needs: [unit, integration]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit --fund=false
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: coverage-*
          path: coverage-parts
          merge-multiple: false
      # Shards each produce partial coverage. Merged, they are the real number;
      # judged separately, every shard looks catastrophically low.
      - name: Merge coverage from all shards
        run: npx nyc merge coverage-parts coverage/merged.json
      - name: Enforce thresholds
        run: npx nyc report --temp-dir coverage --check-coverage --lines 70 --branches 60

  security:
    name: Security checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # Gitleaks needs history to scan commits added by this PR.
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit --fund=false
      # Production dependencies only, high and above: this is the gate.
      - name: Audit production dependencies
        run: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high
      # Dev dependencies are reported but never block a merge.
      - name: Audit dev dependencies (report only)
        run: npm audit --audit-level=moderate || true
      - name: Secret scan
        uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - name: License allowlist
        run: npx license-checker --production --onlyAllow "MIT;Apache-2.0;BSD-2-Clause;BSD-3-Clause;ISC;0BSD;Unlicense"

  ci-complete:
    # A single required status check. Branch protection points at this job
    # only, so adding or renaming a job never means editing branch protection
    # (and never leaves a required check that no longer runs, which blocks
    # every PR forever).
    name: CI complete
    if: always()
    needs: [static, unit, integration, coverage, security]
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - name: Fail if any dependency failed
        if: contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1
      - run: echo "All CI checks passed"

The design decisions worth calling out. concurrency with cancel-in-progress: true is right for CI and wrong for deploys (47.13). fail-fast: false on the matrix means one broken shard does not hide the other three. Coverage is merged across shards before it is judged, because a shard on its own covers a quarter of the code. Migrations run before integration tests so the schema under test is the migrated schema. And ci-complete exists so branch protection has exactly one required check to name, which removes an entire category of "the required check never ran and now nothing can merge" incidents.

Note what is not here: no Docker build, no deploy, no E2E. A pull request does not need an image, and E2E belongs after a deploy to staging.

47.11.2 build-and-push.yml — build once, scan, push, attest

YAML
name: Build and push

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  # Deliberately NOT cancel-in-progress. Cancelling a build mid-push can leave
  # a partially uploaded manifest, and we want every commit on main to produce
  # an artifact so every commit is a rollback target.
  group: build-main
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write        # required to request the OIDC token
  attestations: write    # required to publish build provenance
  packages: read

env:
  AWS_REGION: eu-west-1
  ECR_REPOSITORY: orders-api

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 30
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
      image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # An image tagged sha-abc1234 must contain exactly the code at abc1234.
      # A dirty tree produces an artifact whose name is a lie, and that lie is
      # discovered during an incident when the rollback behaves unexpectedly.
      - name: Refuse to build from a dirty tree
        run: |
          if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
            echo "::error::Working tree is dirty; refusing to build a mislabelled artifact"
            exit 1
          fi

      # No access keys anywhere. The runner proves its identity with a signed
      # OIDC token; AWS returns credentials valid for one hour.
      - name: Assume AWS role via OIDC
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-orders-api-build
          aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}

      - id: ecr
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - id: meta
        name: Compute tags
        run: |
          SHORT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short=7 HEAD)
          echo "tag=sha-${SHORT_SHA}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "image=${{ steps.ecr.outputs.registry }}/${{ env.ECR_REPOSITORY }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      # Build and load locally so we can scan the real image before it is
      # published. cache-from/cache-to against a registry cache tag turns a
      # 7-minute cold build into roughly 70 seconds when only src/ changed.
      - name: Build image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          push: false
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:buildcache
          cache-to: type=registry,ref=${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:buildcache,mode=max
          build-args: |
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}

      # Scan BEFORE the push. Scanning afterwards means a vulnerable image is
      # already pullable by anything with registry access.
      - name: Trivy image scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          image-ref: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
          ignore-unfixed: true      # do not block on findings with no patch
          exit-code: '1'
          format: 'table'

      - name: Generate SBOM
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
        with:
          image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
          format: cyclonedx-json
          artifact-name: sbom-${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}.json

      # Second build call. Every layer is a cache hit, so this takes seconds.
      # It runs with the OCI exporter, which is what makes provenance and SBOM
      # attestations possible; the local docker exporter cannot carry them.
      - id: push
        name: Push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
            ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:main
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}:buildcache
          provenance: mode=max
          sbom: true
          build-args: |
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}

      # A signed statement binding this digest to this commit, this workflow
      # and this runner. An admission policy in the cluster verifies it, which
      # is what stops an image pushed from a laptop from ever running.
      - name: Attest build provenance
        uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v1
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    with:
      image_tag: ${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
      environment: staging
    secrets: inherit

  deploy-production:
    needs: [build, deploy-staging]
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    with:
      image_tag: ${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
      environment: production
    secrets: inherit

The two-call build pattern deserves a note because it looks wasteful and is not. The first call loads the image into the runner's local Docker daemon so Trivy can scan the exact bytes that will be published. The second call pushes with the OCI exporter, which supports provenance and SBOM attestations that the local exporter does not. Because the first call populated the cache, the second is entirely cache hits and takes a few seconds.

Also note :main as a secondary tag. It is a convenience pointer for humans and for the BuildKit cache; nothing in a deployment manifest ever references it.

47.11.3 deploy.yml — approve, migrate, roll out, verify, roll back

YAML
name: Deploy

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      image_tag: { required: true, type: string }
      environment: { required: true, type: string }
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      image_tag:
        description: 'Image tag, e.g. sha-3f9a1c2'
        required: true
        type: string
      environment:
        required: true
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]

# One deploy per service per environment at a time, and queued rather than
# cancelled: two concurrent kubectl set image calls are how you get a rollout
# that reverts itself halfway through (29.13).
concurrency:
  group: deploy-orders-api-${{ inputs.environment }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 30
    # This is where approvals live. The production environment requires two
    # reviewers from a team and is restricted to the main branch. It also
    # scopes the OIDC subject claim, so the deploy role can only be assumed
    # by an approved production job.
    environment:
      name: ${{ inputs.environment }}
      url: https://${{ inputs.environment == 'production' && 'api' || 'staging-api' }}.example.com
    env:
      NAMESPACE: orders
      DEPLOYMENT: orders-api
      CLUSTER: ${{ inputs.environment }}-eks
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Assume deploy role via OIDC
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-orders-api-deploy-${{ inputs.environment }}
          aws-region: eu-west-1

      - name: Configure kubectl
        run: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$CLUSTER" --region eu-west-1

      - name: Resolve image digest
        id: img
        run: |
          # Deploy by digest, not by tag. Even an immutable tag is a name;
          # the digest is the artifact.
          DIGEST=$(aws ecr describe-images \
            --repository-name orders-api \
            --image-ids imageTag=${{ inputs.image_tag }} \
            --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text)
          REGISTRY=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
          echo "ref=${REGISTRY}/orders-api@${DIGEST}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      # The migration runs as a one-shot Job: exactly once, before any new
      # code is live, with its own logs and its own timing in the timeline.
      # Never as an init container (once per replica) and never on app boot.
      - name: Run database migration
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ steps.img.outputs.ref }}
        run: |
          export JOB_NAME="migrate-${{ inputs.image_tag }}-${{ github.run_id }}"
          envsubst < k8s/migration-job.yaml | kubectl apply -n "$NAMESPACE" -f -
          if ! kubectl wait -n "$NAMESPACE" --for=condition=complete \
                 "job/$JOB_NAME" --timeout=600s; then
            echo "::error::Migration failed or timed out"
            kubectl logs -n "$NAMESPACE" "job/$JOB_NAME" --tail=300
            exit 1
          fi
          kubectl logs -n "$NAMESPACE" "job/$JOB_NAME" --tail=100

      - name: Roll out
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ steps.img.outputs.ref }}
        run: |
          # Helm keeps release history, which makes `helm rollback` possible.
          helm upgrade --install "$DEPLOYMENT" ./charts/orders-api \
            --namespace "$NAMESPACE" \
            --set image.repository="${IMAGE%@*}" \
            --set image.digest="${IMAGE#*@}" \
            --set gitSha="${{ github.sha }}" \
            --values "charts/orders-api/values.${{ inputs.environment }}.yaml" \
            --wait --timeout 10m
          # The plain-kubectl equivalent, if you are not using Helm:
          #   kubectl set image -n "$NAMESPACE" \
          #     deployment/"$DEPLOYMENT" api="$IMAGE" --record=false

      - name: Wait for rollout
        run: kubectl rollout status -n "$NAMESPACE" "deployment/$DEPLOYMENT" --timeout=600s

      # rollout status only proves pods are ready. Smoke tests prove the
      # product works: version on every pod, an authenticated read, a
      # synthetic write, and a queue round trip. Under 60 seconds.
      - name: Smoke tests
        env:
          BASE_URL: https://${{ inputs.environment == 'production' && 'api' || 'staging-api' }}.example.com
          EXPECTED_SHA: ${{ github.sha }}
          SMOKE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SMOKE_TOKEN }}
        run: ./scripts/smoke.sh

      # Any failure above this point rolls back automatically. `if: failure()`
      # runs even when an earlier step aborted the job.
      - name: Automatic rollback
        if: failure()
        run: |
          echo "::warning::Deploy failed, rolling back"
          helm rollback "$DEPLOYMENT" -n "$NAMESPACE" --wait --timeout 5m
          kubectl rollout status -n "$NAMESPACE" "deployment/$DEPLOYMENT" --timeout=300s
          # Verify the rollback with the same checks. An unverified rollback
          # is an assumption, and this is the step people skip under pressure.
          ./scripts/smoke.sh || echo "::error::Rollback did not pass smoke tests. Escalate."

      - name: Notify
        if: always()
        uses: slackapi/slack-github-action@v1
        with:
          payload: |
            {
              "text": "orders-api ${{ inputs.image_tag }} -> ${{ inputs.environment }}: ${{ job.status }} (${{ github.actor }})"
            }
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_DEPLOY_WEBHOOK }}

Read the order of operations once more, because it is the whole point: migrate, roll out, wait, verify, roll back on any failure, always notify. The migration is separate and first because it must run once and because its failure must stop the deploy before new code is live. The rollback step verifies itself. And the notification runs if: always() so a failed deploy is as visible as a successful one — a silent failure is worse than a loud one.

Two things this workflow deliberately does not do. It does not roll back the migration, because as 47.9 explained, that is usually impossible and often destructive; the migration was additive, so the old code still works. And it does not retry the smoke tests, because a smoke test that passes on the second attempt has told you nothing.

47.11.4 The GitLab CI equivalents

The concepts map one to one; only the syntax differs. If your organisation uses GitLab, this is the translation table:

GitHub Actions GitLab CI Notes
jobs: in a workflow file stages: plus jobs in .gitlab-ci.yml GitLab orders by stage; use needs: for a DAG
needs: [build] needs: [build] Same semantics, same DAG behaviour
strategy.matrix parallel.matrix Same purpose
strategy.matrix for sharding parallel: 4 with CI_NODE_INDEX / CI_NODE_TOTAL GitLab injects the shard index as variables
services: containers services: Nearly identical; GitLab addresses them by service alias
actions/cache cache: with key: files: [package-lock.json] Built into the job definition
environment: production with reviewers environment: name: production plus when: manual and protected environments Approvals come from protected environments
permissions: id-token: write id_tokens: with an aud GitLab issues OIDC JWTs the same way
OIDC to AWS Same IAM trust policy, issuer gitlab.com (or your instance) The sub claim format differs: project_path:group/repo:ref_type:branch:ref:main
concurrency group resource_group: Serialises deploys to one environment
if: failure() when: on_failure Rollback jobs use this
GitHub Packages / ECR login action docker login $CI_REGISTRY or the same AWS ECR login GitLab has a built-in container registry
actions/upload-artifact artifacts: paths: Plus reports: for native coverage and JUnit integration

A compact GitLab equivalent of the integration job:

YAML
integration:
  stage: test
  image: node:20.18.1
  services:
    - name: postgres:16.4-alpine
      alias: postgres
    - name: redis:7.4-alpine
      alias: redis
  variables:
    POSTGRES_USER: test
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
    POSTGRES_DB: orders_test
    # The job runs in a container here, so services are addressed by alias,
    # not localhost. This is the single most common GitLab CI mistake.
    DATABASE_URL: postgres://test:test@postgres:5432/orders_test
    REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
  cache:
    key:
      files: [package-lock.json]
    paths: [.npm/]
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm run migration:run
    - npm run test:int
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml

The one real behavioural difference to remember: in GitLab the job itself normally runs inside a container, so services: are reachable by alias and never on localhost. In GitHub Actions the job usually runs directly on the runner, so services: are reachable on localhost through published ports — unless you set container:, in which case the rule flips. Getting this backwards produces intermittent ECONNREFUSED that people spend days blaming on the application.

47.12 DORA metrics

Concept

DORA (the DevOps Research and Assessment program) identified four measurements that together predict both software delivery performance and organisational performance:

  1. Deployment frequency — how often you deploy to production.
  2. Lead time for change — from commit to running in production.
  3. Change failure rate — the percentage of deployments causing a degradation requiring a fix.
  4. Time to restore service — how long from detection to recovery.

The first two measure speed. The last two measure stability. The central finding, which surprises people every time, is that these do not trade off: teams that deploy more often are also more stable, because small batches are easier to verify, easier to diagnose and easier to undo.

Why does it exist?

Because engineering organisations otherwise measure the wrong things: story points, lines of code, number of PRs. Those measure activity. DORA measures the delivery system's actual behaviour, and every one of the four is directly influenced by decisions in this part.

Mental model

Imagine a kitchen. Deployment frequency is how many plates leave per hour. Lead time is how long a single order takes from ticket to table. Change failure rate is what fraction come back. Time to restore is how fast you replace a returned plate. A kitchen that sends out plates in huge batches every two hours has a terrible lead time, and when a batch is wrong, forty customers are wrong at once.

How it works

How each pipeline decision moves the numbers:

Decision Deploy frequency Lead time Change failure rate Time to restore
Cut CI from 22 min to 8 min Up Down sharply Neutral Down (hotfixes ship faster)
Trunk-based development, small PRs Up Down Down (smaller batches) Down (fewer suspects)
Build once, promote the artifact Neutral Slightly down Down (no drift) Neutral
Automated rollback on SLO breach Neutral Neutral Neutral (same failures) Down sharply
Feature flags for risky changes Up (merge without releasing) Down Down Down sharply (flip, do not deploy)
Canary with automated analysis Slightly down (slower rollout) Slightly up Down (caught before 100%) Down
Expand/contract migrations Neutral Neutral Down Down (rollback stays possible)
Manual approval gate at night Down Up sharply Neutral Up (nobody to approve the fix)
Flaky tests tolerated Down Up Up (people bypass checks) Up
Removing the E2E suite entirely Up Down Up sharply Neutral

Note the last two rows: not every change that raises speed is good, and DORA is only useful when you read all four together. A team that deletes its tests will show wonderful frequency and lead time, and a change failure rate that makes the point.

What "elite" actually looks like day to day. The published thresholds are roughly:

Metric Elite High Medium Low
Deployment frequency On demand, multiple per day Weekly to monthly Monthly to every 6 months Less than every 6 months
Lead time for change Under 1 hour 1 day to 1 week 1 week to 1 month 1 to 6 months
Change failure rate 5–10% 10–15% 10–15% 40–60%
Time to restore Under 1 hour Under 1 day 1 day to 1 week Over 6 months

Numbers are abstract. Here is what an elite team's Tuesday actually looks like:

  • 09:20 An engineer opens a PR with 140 changed lines. CI is green in 7 minutes. A colleague reviews in 15 minutes because the diff is small enough to read properly.
  • 09:50 Merged. The build workflow produces sha-a71c33f and deploys it to staging automatically.
  • 10:02 E2E passes on staging. The production deploy runs; nobody approves anything, because the gate was removed once change failure rate stayed under 8% for a quarter.
  • 10:09 Rolled out, smoke tests pass, the deploy is annotated on the dashboards. Lead time: 49 minutes.
  • 14:30 A different deploy trips the automated analysis: 5xx rate doubled. Rollback is automatic, complete at 14:33. Time to restore: 3 minutes. The engineer who merged it is still at their desk and starts the fix immediately.
  • 16:00 That fix ships as a normal deploy. Nobody was paged. Nobody wrote an incident report, because service was never meaningfully degraded.

Twelve deploys that day, one failure, three minutes of recovery. The remarkable part is how boring it is — which is exactly the point. Elite delivery performance does not feel heroic; it feels routine.

Measuring honestly. Two traps. First, deployment frequency counted per service rather than per team rewards splitting services rather than shipping. Second, change failure rate depends on what you count as a failure; if only paging incidents count, teams stop paging. Define it once, write it down (any deploy requiring a rollback, hotfix or flag flip within 24 hours), and hold the definition steady even when the number is embarrassing.

You can compute all four from data you already have: deployment frequency and lead time from the deploy pipeline's own event log joined to commit timestamps; change failure rate from deploys tagged as rollbacks or followed by a hotfix; time to restore from incident open and close timestamps. This is a day of work, and it turns arguments about process into arguments about data.

Common mistakes

  • Treating DORA as a performance review tool. The moment individuals are measured, the numbers are gamed and become useless.
  • Optimising one metric alone. High frequency with a 40% failure rate is chaos, not maturity.
  • Measuring lead time from "ticket created" rather than "commit pushed". That measures product prioritisation, not delivery.
  • Comparing teams with different risk profiles. A payments core and an internal dashboard should not have identical targets.

Interview questions

  1. Name the four DORA metrics and say which measure speed and which measure stability.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: frequency and lead time (speed); change failure rate and time to restore (stability).
  2. Why do teams that deploy more often tend to be more stable?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: smaller batches, fewer suspects per failure, faster diagnosis, cheaper rollback, more practised recovery.
  3. Your change failure rate is 4% and deployment frequency is once a month. Where do you start?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: batch size is the problem; low failure rate reflects small sample and heavy pre-release process; work on CI speed, trunk-based development and flags.
  4. How would you instrument these four metrics with what you already have?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pipeline event log plus git timestamps plus incident timestamps; define change failure explicitly.

47.13 Edge cases and failure modes

Each of these is a real pattern. For each: what happens, why, how you notice, and the fix.

  • Deploy succeeds but the migration failed halfway. A multi-statement migration adds a column, backfills 40 million rows, then adds an index and times out. The transaction rolls back the DDL but the migration tracking table may or may not record it, and some engines cannot run all DDL transactionally. Notice: migration Job exits non-zero, or the schema does not match either version. Fix: one logical change per migration file, short transactions, lock_timeout and statement_timeout set, backfills as separate batched jobs rather than inside the migration, and an idempotent design so re-running is safe (Part 24).

  • The migration ran before old pods drained. A destructive migration (drop column, rename) executes while old pods are still serving. Every request from those pods 500s until the rollout completes. Notice: a burst of column ... does not exist errors exactly at the migration timestamp, ending when the rollout finishes. Fix: additive-only at deploy time; destructive changes in a later release when no code references the old shape.

  • Two pipelines deploying concurrently. Two merges 40 seconds apart. Both jobs run helm upgrade. The second starts while the first is mid-rollout; pods from three replica sets exist at once and the final state depends on timing. Notice: kubectl get rs shows three sets with non-zero replicas; the running SHA is neither of the deployed ones. Fix: a concurrency group per service per environment with cancel-in-progress: false so deploys queue, and a check that the rollout is settled before starting.

  • CI cache poisoning. A node_modules cache keyed only on the lockfile hash is written by a job running on a different Node version or architecture. Every subsequent job restores native modules built for the wrong ABI. Notice: segfaults or invalid ELF header with no code change; works when the cache is cleared. Fix: include OS, arch and Node version in the cache key; never let a fork PR write to a cache branch protection would not trust; prefer the npm download cache over caching node_modules outright.

  • A flaky test blocking a hotfix. Described fully in 47.1. Notice: repeated re-runs, rising pressure, someone reaching for admin merge. Fix: the quarantine policy, plus a documented, audited emergency path (a labelled hotfix workflow that skips non-gating checks, requires two approvers, and files a ticket automatically) so the bypass is designed rather than improvised.

  • A secret printed in logs. A debug line, a set -x in a shell script, or a tool that dumps its environment on error. Masking only catches exact string matches, so base64 or JSON-wrapped values pass straight through. Notice: a scanner, a colleague, or an abuse alert. Fix: rotate first, then delete the log, then audit usage; disable command tracing around secret-handling steps; never echo an environment variable you have not verified.

  • An image built from a dirty tree. A self-hosted runner with leftover files, or a build that patches a file before building. The sha- tag names a commit whose contents are not what shipped. Notice: the image behaves differently from a rebuild of the same SHA; docker history shows unexpected content. Fix: fail the build if git status --porcelain is non-empty; use ephemeral runners; never modify files in the build job.

  • Rolling back to an image incompatible with the new schema. The central hazard of 47.9. Notice: the rollback completes and the old version immediately errors on missing columns or unknown enum values. Fix: N-1 compatibility enforced by a CI check on migration files; expand/contract; tolerant readers shipped one release ahead.

  • A canary that passes at low traffic and fails at peak. 5% of off-peak traffic never exhausts the connection pool, never triggers the cache stampede, never contends on the hot row. Promoted to 100% at peak, it falls over. Notice: green canary analysis followed by a full outage minutes after promotion. Fix: hold a step through a real peak; make one step proportional to load rather than time; load-test the new version at expected peak concurrency before the canary; alert on saturation metrics (pool utilisation, queue depth), not only errors and latency.

  • A feature flag left on forever. The dead code path rots and is eventually executed by a cleanup, a default reset or a provider outage. Notice: an error in code nobody has deployed for months. Fix: an owner and expiry on every temporary flag, a nightly job that fails the build on expired flags, and deletion of the branch when the flag reaches 100% and soaks for a week.

  • Environment drift between staging and production. Different instance sizes, different pool limits, different PostgreSQL minor versions, an extra sidecar in production, a feature flag defaulted differently. Notice: "works in staging" incidents that repeat with different specifics. Fix: generate both environments from the same IaC modules with a small, reviewed diff; run a config-diff job in the pipeline and fail on unexpected keys; test with production-shaped data volumes for the queries that matter.

  • A registry outage blocking rollback. The rollback pulls an image the nodes no longer have cached and the registry is down. Notice: ImagePullBackOff on the rollback, during an incident. Fix: do not aggressively prune node images; prefer a rollback to an existing replica set that is still scaled above zero, which requires no pull at all; keep a pull-through cache or a mirror in a second region; and treat "can we roll back with the registry down?" as a game-day scenario.

  • A health check that passes while the app is broken. The liveness endpoint returns a static 200 and readiness does not check dependencies. Every pod is "healthy" while every request fails. Notice: green dashboards, red customers. Fix: readiness checks real dependencies with short timeouts; liveness stays trivial (a dependency check in liveness restarts every pod during a database blip); and smoke tests exercise the business path, not the health path.

  • imagePullPolicy: Always with a moving tag. A node autoscaling event at 03:00 pulls whatever the tag points at now. Notice: pods running code nobody deployed. Fix: immutable tags, digest references, registry tag immutability.

  • Deploy annotations missing from dashboards. Every incident starts with ten minutes of "when did this begin, and did we deploy?" Fix: emit a deploy event to your metrics backend from the pipeline and render it as an annotation on every dashboard.

  • The approval that expires. A production deploy sits pending overnight, expires, and silently never happens. The team believes the fix is live. Notice: the running SHA is not the expected one. Fix: alert on deploys pending longer than N minutes; assert the deployed SHA in the smoke tests.

  • Runner disk exhaustion. Docker builds plus caches plus service containers exceed the runner's free space intermittently. Notice: no space left on device on some runs. Fix: prune between steps, use a larger runner class for build jobs, keep build and test in separate jobs.

  • Third-party Action tag moved. some/action@v3 is repointed by a compromised maintainer account and runs with your secrets. Notice: usually nobody notices, which is the problem. Fix: pin every third-party Action to a full commit SHA, and review the dependency list like any other supply chain.

Senior Checklist — Part 47

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can get a PR pipeline under 10 minutes at p95 and explain where every second goes
  • I can write a flaky-test policy and enforce it without blanket retries
  • I can explain why the same artifact must be promoted, and prove two environments run the same digest
  • I can set up OIDC federation to AWS and write a trust policy scoped to one repository and environment
  • I can describe the blast radius of a compromised CI runner and the controls that shrink it
  • I can start PostgreSQL and Redis as CI service containers with working health checks
  • I can design coverage gates that catch real regressions instead of rewarding trivial tests
  • I can state which security findings fail the build and defend the line
  • I can compare rolling, blue/green, canary, recreate and shadow on rollback speed, cost and database requirements
  • I can explain what blue/green does not roll back
  • I can implement a flag-driven read switch during a migration with deterministic bucketing
  • I can explain why roll-forward is the default and when rollback is safe
  • I can write smoke tests that would have caught a broken Kafka topic name
  • I can build the three workflows in 47.11 from scratch and explain every step
  • I can compute the four DORA metrics from data my organisation already has

Part 47 — Key Takeaways

  • CI's job is fast, trustworthy feedback; the moment red might mean nothing, the pipeline has stopped working regardless of how much it runs.
  • Never blanket-retry tests. Quarantine within an hour, fix within a sprint, delete if nobody will.
  • Build the artifact once and promote that exact digest through every environment; a rebuild per environment turns your staging results into guesses.
  • latest and moving tags make rollback impossible and let nodes silently diverge; deploy by digest or an immutable sha- tag, with registry tag immutability enforced.
  • Replace long-lived cloud keys with OIDC federation, and scope the trust policy to your repository and environment; a sub condition of repo:org/* is a role published to the internet.
  • Gate on deterministic, high-confidence checks and report everything else; a security gate that fires falsely once a week will be disabled within a month.
  • Rolling is the correct default. Blue/green buys seconds of rollback for 100% extra capacity. Canary needs volume and per-version metrics or it is theatre.
  • Deployment strategy controls how fast you get the old code back; only compatibility discipline controls whether the old code still works.
  • The database migration runs before the rollout, once, as its own job, and is additive-only, because old and new pods share one schema.
  • Roll forward by default. A down migration is not a rollback plan, and a rollback path you have never executed is a hypothesis.
  • Feature flags decouple deploy from release and give you a ten-second undo; every temporary flag needs an owner, an expiry, and eventual deletion.
  • rollout status: success is not "it works". Smoke tests must place a synthetic order through every dependency the service owns, in under 60 seconds.
  • Automate rollback on SLO breach, including one domain metric, because a deploy can return 200 on every request while orders quietly stop.
  • Deploy frequency and stability rise together; small batches are the mechanism, and everything in this part exists to make small batches cheap.

Volume 5: Production Engineering

Part 48 — Git from Intermediate to Senior

  • 2 h 2 min read
  • 15 sections
  • 14 diagrams
  • 102 code examples

What you will learn

  1. 48.1Git internals first
  2. 48.2Commits
  3. 48.3Branches
  4. 48.4Merge
  5. 48.5Rebase
  6. 48.6Cherry-pick
  7. 48.7Reset
  8. 48.8Revert
  9. 48.9Stash, tag, bisect, reflog, detached HEAD
  10. 48.10The senior's toolbox
  11. 48.11Merge vs rebase, reset vs revert, merge vs cherry-pick
  12. 48.12Branching strategies
  13. 48.13The pull request workflow at senior level
  14. 48.14Recovery scenarios
  15. 48.15Edge cases and failure modes

Most engineers learn Git as a list of spells. git commit, git push, git pull, and when something goes wrong, git reset --hard or a fresh clone. That works until the day it does not: a rebase leaves you in a state no tutorial mentioned, a force-push erases a colleague's afternoon, a revert of a merge quietly drops a feature that everyone believed was released, or a secret ends up in history and someone asks whether deleting the file is enough. (It is not.)

The difference between an intermediate and a senior user of Git is not knowing more commands. It is knowing the object model. Once you understand that Git stores snapshots as content-addressed objects, that branches are 41-byte files containing a hash, and that almost nothing is ever really deleted until garbage collection runs, every command stops being a spell and becomes an obvious consequence. reset moves a pointer. rebase replays commits as new objects. cherry-pick applies a diff and creates a new commit. reflog is a log of where your pointers used to be, which is why "lost" work is almost never lost.

This part starts with the object model, because everything after it is downstream. Then commits, branches, merge, rebase, cherry-pick, reset and revert — each with the mechanics, realistic command output, and the specific traps. Then the senior's toolbox: bisect, blame -w -C, the pickaxe, worktrees, hooks. Then branching strategies, the pull request workflow as it is actually practised at senior level, a set of step-by-step recovery procedures for the situations that cause real panic, and a catalogue of failure modes.

48.1 Git internals first

Concept

Git is a content-addressed key/value store with a version control interface on top. It stores four kinds of objects. Every object is identified by the SHA-1 (or SHA-256, in newer repositories) hash of its content, so the identifier is a fingerprint of what is inside.

  • Blob — the raw contents of a file. No name, no permissions, no history. Just bytes.
  • Tree — a directory listing: a set of entries, each with a mode, a type, a hash and a name. Trees point at blobs and at other trees.
  • Commit — a snapshot pointer: one tree (the whole project state), zero or more parents, an author, a committer, timestamps, and a message.
  • Tag (annotated) — a named pointer to an object with its own message and optional signature.

Around the objects sit refs: human-readable names that hold an object hash. A branch is a ref. A tag is a ref. HEAD is a special ref pointing at the branch you are on.

Why does it exist?

Because the alternative — storing diffs and reconstructing state by replaying them — is what older systems did, and it makes several important operations slow or impossible. Reconstructing a five-year-old file means applying 4,000 patches in order. Verifying that history has not been tampered with is hard. Deduplicating identical files across branches is hard.

Content addressing solves all three at once. Every object's name is its hash, so identical content is stored once no matter how many commits or branches reference it. A commit's hash covers its tree and its parents, so it transitively covers the entire history: change one byte in a five-year-old file and every commit hash after it changes. That is why Git history is tamper-evident, and it is also why rewriting history produces new commits rather than modifying old ones — a fact that explains rebase, amend, filter-repo and force-push in one sentence.

Mental model

Imagine a library where every book is filed by a fingerprint of its own text rather than by a shelf number. Two identical books get one copy. A "commit" is a card that says: here is the fingerprint of the complete catalogue of the library at this moment, here is the card that came before, and here is why I changed things. A "branch" is a sticky note on one card saying main. Moving the sticky note to a different card does not change any book or any card; it changes what main means.

That is the whole model. reset moves a sticky note. checkout/switch changes which note you are standing next to. commit writes a new card and drags your note forward. Nothing else is happening.

How it works

Commits are snapshots, not diffs. Every commit references a complete tree describing the entire project at that moment. When you see a diff in git log -p, Git computed it on the fly by comparing two trees. Storage does not suffer, because unchanged subtrees and unchanged files are the same objects reused — a 100 MB repository with one changed file adds one blob, a handful of trees and one commit.

Let us look at a real object graph. Start from HEAD:

Shell
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 8f94139338f9404f26296befa88755fc2598c289
parent 4a1c2b9e3d5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b
author Priya Nair <priya@example.com> 1757328041 +0100
committer Priya Nair <priya@example.com> 1757328041 +0100

feat(orders): reject duplicate idempotency keys with a unique index

Six lines. That is a commit: a tree, a parent, who wrote it, who committed it, and why. Note there is no diff and no file list. Now the tree:

Shell
$ git cat-file -p 8f94139
100644 blob a906cb2a4a904a152e80877d4088654daad0c859    .gitignore
100644 blob 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad    README.md
100644 blob c1f2a8d34e5b6079a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2    package.json
040000 tree 4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6f70    src

Four entries. 100644 is a regular file, 100755 an executable, 040000 a directory (which points at another tree), 120000 a symlink, 160000 a submodule commit. Descend one level:

Shell
$ git cat-file -p 4d5e6f7
040000 tree 9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b    orders
100644 blob 5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6    main.ts

And finally a blob, which is just content:

Shell
$ git cat-file -p a906cb2
node_modules
dist
.env
coverage

You can inspect any object's type and size:

Shell
$ git cat-file -t 8f94139
tree
$ git cat-file -s 8f94139
239

Content addressing, demonstrated. Git hashes the content plus a small header of the form <type> <length>\0:

Shell
$ echo -n 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin
b6fc4c620b67d95f953a5c1c1230aaab5db5a1b0

$ echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a

Two different hashes, because the second string has a trailing newline. That one-byte difference is why line-ending configuration matters so much (48.10 and 48.15): a file converted from LF to CRLF is, to Git, a completely different blob.
