Notice that both commits point at the same .gitignore blob. That is deduplication falling out of content addressing for free.

Refs, branches and HEAD. A branch is a file containing a hash:

Shell
$ cat .git/refs/heads/main
9f3c1a2b8e7d6c5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a7b6c5d4e3f

$ cat .git/HEAD
ref: refs/heads/main

That is it. main is 41 bytes. Creating a branch writes 41 bytes; that is why git switch -c feature/x is instantaneous even in a 4 GB repository. HEAD normally holds a symbolic reference to a branch. When it holds a raw hash instead, you are in detached HEAD (48.9): commits you make have no branch pointing at them, so when you leave, nothing references them.

The three areas. Git has three places your files exist, and almost every confusing message is about the boundary between two of them:

Text
Working tree          Index (staging area)        HEAD commit
   your files    -->     .git/index          -->   the last snapshot
                 git add                 git commit

The index is a binary file (.git/index) listing every tracked path with its mode, its blob hash and cached stat information. It is not "a list of changes"; it is a complete proposed next tree. git add writes a blob and updates the index entry. git commit turns the index into trees and writes a commit. git status is a three-way comparison: working tree vs index (unstaged changes), index vs HEAD (staged changes).

Shell
$ git ls-files --stage src/orders/orders.service.ts
100644 5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6 0	src/orders/orders.service.ts

The 0 is the merge stage. During a conflict, the same path appears at stages 1 (common ancestor), 2 (ours) and 3 (theirs), which is exactly how git checkout --ours and --theirs know what to pick (48.4).

The .git layout.

Text
.git/
├── HEAD                     ref: refs/heads/main
├── config                   repository-local config
├── index                    the staging area (binary)
├── objects/
│   ├── 8f/94139338f940...   a loose object, zlib-compressed
│   ├── info/
│   └── pack/
│       ├── pack-3a9f.idx    index into the packfile
│       └── pack-3a9f.pack   many objects, delta-compressed
├── refs/
│   ├── heads/main           41 bytes: a commit hash
│   ├── tags/v1.4.2
│   └── remotes/origin/main
├── packed-refs              refs collapsed into one file after gc
├── logs/
│   ├── HEAD                 the reflog
│   └── refs/heads/main
└── hooks/                   sample hooks, plus yours

Packfiles. Loose objects are one file each, zlib-compressed but stored whole. That is fine for a hundred objects and terrible for a million. git gc (run automatically) packs them: many objects into one .pack file, with similar objects stored as deltas against each other, plus an .idx for random access. This is the one place Git does store diffs — as a storage optimisation, below the object model, invisible to it. A repository with 300,000 loose objects can pack down by 10x or more.

Shell
$ git count-objects -vH
count: 412
size: 2.31 MiB
in-pack: 284917
packs: 2
size-pack: 189.44 MiB

Reachability and garbage collection. An object is reachable if you can get to it by starting from any ref (branches, tags, remote-tracking refs, the reflog, the index, stashes) and following pointers. Unreachable objects are candidates for deletion by git gc, but not immediately: the default gc.pruneExpire is two weeks, and the reflog keeps its own entries for 90 days (30 for unreachable ones).

This is the single most reassuring fact in Git. When you "lose" commits with a bad reset or rebase, the commits still exist as objects; only the ref that pointed at them moved. The reflog records where every ref used to point, so recovery is usually one command (48.9, 48.14). The window is generous, but it is not infinite, and an explicit git gc --prune=now closes it immediately.

Shell
$ git fsck --lost-found
Checking object directories: 100% (256/256), done.
dangling commit 7b2e5d1a9c8f4e3b2a1d0c9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a
dangling blob   c4d3e2f1a0b9c8d7e6f5a4b3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5

Practical example

A team is debugging why a 2.4 GB clone takes eleven minutes on a new laptop. git count-objects -vH shows size-pack: 2.28 GiB for 41,000 commits — far too much for a TypeScript codebase. git rev-list --objects --all piped through git cat-file --batch-check and sorted by size reveals the cause: 340 versions of a 6 MB test-fixtures.sqlite file committed over three years, totalling roughly 1.9 GB.

The objects are reachable from history, so no amount of gc removes them. Deleting the file today does nothing: every historical commit still references its blob. The only fixes are to rewrite history (48.14) or to move the file to Git LFS going forward and accept the existing weight. This is why "giant binaries bloat the repository forever" is in the failure-modes list: the object model that makes Git fast is the same one that makes this permanent.

Production scenario

A monorepo with 180,000 commits, 24,000 files and a 1.1 GB packfile. git switch between branches takes about 400 ms, because switching writes only the files that differ between two trees; Git compares tree hashes and skips whole subtrees that are identical. git log --oneline -20 returns in 30 ms because it walks 20 commit objects and never touches a blob. git blame on a 3,000-line file takes 4 seconds because it must walk history for every line. Understanding which operations touch the object graph and which touch the working tree is what lets you predict performance instead of being surprised by it.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 an engineer runs git reset --hard origin/main to "clean up", not realising they had three days of local commits on a branch they had never pushed. The working tree is replaced and the branch pointer moves back to origin/main. They report that three days of work is gone.

It is not. The commits are unreachable but not collected. git reflog shows every position HEAD held:

Shell
$ git reflog
9f3c1a2 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to origin/main
7b2e5d1 HEAD@{1}: commit: feat(orders): add partial refund handling
a3c9f04 HEAD@{2}: commit: test(orders): cover refund edge cases
5e1d8b7 HEAD@{3}: commit: refactor(orders): extract RefundCalculator

git branch recovered 7b2e5d1 recreates a branch at the tip and all three commits are back. Total recovery: 40 seconds. The only work genuinely lost was uncommitted changes in the working tree, which the reflog does not cover, because they were never objects in the first place. That is the practical rule: commit early, and Git can almost always save you; leave work uncommitted, and it cannot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Uncommitted changes are not in the object store. reset --hard, checkout -- . and clean -fd destroy them permanently. git stash at least creates objects.
  • gc --prune=now closes the recovery window immediately. Never run it while trying to recover something.
  • Detached HEAD commits are unreachable the moment you switch away, though the reflog remembers them for 30 days.
  • SHA-1 collisions are theoretically constructible (SHAttered). Git added collision detection, and new repositories can use SHA-256. Not a practical risk, but worth knowing when someone asks.
  • The index can hold content that exists in no commit. git add then delete the file: the blob exists, the working tree does not have it.
  • Large loose object counts slow everything. Thousands of small commits without gc degrade status and log.
  • .git on a case-insensitive filesystem creates rename problems (48.15).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They reason about Git in terms of objects and pointers, never in terms of "what does this command do to my files". Asked what git reset --hard HEAD~2 does, they answer: "moves the current branch ref back two commits, makes the index match, makes the working tree match; the two commits still exist and the reflog knows where they were." That framing makes the risk obvious (the working tree is overwritten) and the recovery obvious (reflog).

They also treat "commit often, locally" as a safety practice rather than a style preference, because an object in the store is recoverable and a working-tree change is not. History gets tidied later with interactive rebase (48.5).

Explained to a product manager: "Git keeps a complete photo of the project at every save point, and names each photo by its contents. Branches are just labels stuck on photos. Almost nothing is ever really thrown away, which is why we can usually recover from mistakes."

Common mistakes

  • Believing commits store diffs, which makes rebase and cherry-pick seem mysterious.
  • Believing a branch "contains" commits. It points at one commit; the rest is reachability.
  • Thinking git rm on a large file shrinks the repository.
  • Running gc --prune=now or a fresh clone during a recovery attempt, destroying the evidence.
  • Confusing the index with "changes" rather than a complete proposed snapshot.

Interview questions

  1. What are Git's object types and how do they relate?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: blob (content), tree (directory listing pointing at blobs and trees), commit (one tree plus parents plus metadata), annotated tag. Follow-up: what exactly is in a commit object? (No diff, no filenames.)
  2. Are commits snapshots or diffs?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: snapshots at the model level; packfiles use deltas as a storage optimisation underneath. Follow-up: why does that make branching cheap?
  3. What is a branch, physically?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a file under .git/refs/heads containing a commit hash; creating one is 41 bytes.
  4. What is detached HEAD and why is it risky?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: HEAD holds a hash instead of a symbolic ref; new commits have no branch pointing at them and become unreachable when you leave.
  5. How would you recover from reset --hard that discarded three commits?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: git reflog, find the old HEAD, git branch recovered <sha> or git reset --hard <sha>; note that uncommitted changes are not recoverable.
  6. Why does deleting a large file not shrink the clone?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: historical commits still reference the blob, so it stays reachable; only history rewriting or LFS changes that.

Practical exercise

In a scratch repository, create one file and commit it. Then use only plumbing commands to walk the graph: git cat-file -p HEAD to get the tree, git cat-file -p <tree> to list entries, git cat-file -p <blob> to print content. Add a second file, commit again, and confirm that the first file's blob hash is unchanged and reused by the second commit's tree. Then run git hash-object on the file's content by hand and confirm it matches the blob hash in the tree. Acceptance criteria: a diagram of your repository's object graph with real hashes, and a written explanation of exactly which objects the second commit created and which it reused.

48.2 Commits

Concept

A commit is one atomic unit of change: a complete snapshot, a link to its parents, and a message explaining why the change exists. Everything senior engineers care about here comes from treating the commit as a communication artifact and a recovery unit, not merely as a save button.

Why does it exist?

Because you will read this history under pressure. When git bisect narrows an incident to one commit at 03:00, the value of that commit being small, self-contained and well-described is enormous. When you git revert a bad change, an atomic commit reverts cleanly; a commit that mixed a refactor, a dependency bump and a bug fix does not.

Mental model

Imagine a lab notebook. Each entry should be one experiment, with a note saying what you were testing and why. An entry that says "stuff" and contains three unrelated experiments is worthless six months later, when the only person who can interpret it has left.

How it works

Atomic commits. One logical change per commit. The test: can this commit be reverted on its own without breaking anything, and does the test suite pass at this commit? If reverting it would also remove an unrelated fix, it is not atomic.

In practice this means splitting work as you go, using git add -p to stage hunks selectively:

Shell
$ git add -p src/orders/orders.service.ts
diff --git a/src/orders/orders.service.ts b/src/orders/orders.service.ts
@@ -42,7 +42,7 @@ export class OrdersService {
-    const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
+    const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.priceMinor * i.qty, 0);
(1/3) Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]? y

s splits a hunk into smaller ones, e opens an editor to stage individual lines. This is the everyday tool for keeping a messy working session from becoming a messy history.

Message quality. The structure that has become standard:

Text
<type>(<scope>): <subject in the imperative, under 72 chars>

Explain WHY this change exists. What was broken or missing, what
approach you chose, and what you deliberately did not do. Wrap at
72 columns so `git log` reads well in a terminal.

Refs: ORD-4182

Three rules that matter more than the format:

  1. Imperative mood. "Add rate limiting", not "Added" or "Adds". The convention exists because Git's own generated messages are imperative ("Merge branch...", "Revert..."), so the whole log reads consistently as instructions: apply this commit and it will add rate limiting.
  2. Why over what. The diff already says what changed. It cannot say that you chose a database-level unique index instead of an application check because the application check had a race window under concurrent requests. That sentence saves the next engineer an hour.
  3. Subject under about 72 characters, blank line, then the body. Tools truncate the subject; a run-on first line becomes unreadable in --oneline.

A bad message and a good one on the same change:

Text
fix bug
Text
fix(orders): prevent duplicate orders from concurrent retries

Clients retry POST /orders on timeout. The previous check did a SELECT
for an existing idempotency key and then an INSERT, which has a race
window: two concurrent requests both see no row and both insert.

Adds a unique index on orders(idempotency_key) and catches 23505 to
return the original order. The application-level check stays as a fast
path so the common case does not rely on an exception.

Refs: ORD-4182

Conventional Commits, and what they actually buy you. The format is type(scope): subject, with types like feat, fix, refactor, perf, test, docs, build, ci, chore, and BREAKING CHANGE: in the footer or a ! after the type.

The concrete payoffs, in order of value:

  • Automated semantic versioning and changelogs. semantic-release or changesets reads the commits since the last tag: any feat bumps the minor version, any fix bumps the patch, any BREAKING CHANGE bumps the major, and the changelog writes itself. This is the main reason to adopt it, and it only works if the discipline is enforced (a commitlint hook).
  • Filterable history. git log --oneline --grep '^fix(payments)' gives you every payment bug fix in seconds.
  • Reviewer routing and risk signalling. A feat! in payments can require an extra approver automatically.

What it does not buy you: better messages. A feat(orders): stuff is still worthless. The type is metadata; the body is the communication.

--amend. Rewrites the most recent commit, producing a new commit object with a new hash. The old one becomes unreachable (and recoverable through the reflog).

Shell
$ git commit --amend                      # edit the message and add staged changes
$ git commit --amend --no-edit            # add staged changes, keep the message
$ git commit --amend --author="Priya Nair <priya@example.com>"

The rule follows from the object model: because it creates a new hash, amending a commit you have already pushed requires a force-push, which rewrites shared history. Safe on your own unmerged branch; a problem on a shared one (48.5, 48.15).

Signing. A signature proves that a commit came from the key holder. Without it, user.name and user.email are just strings anyone can set, so a commit can claim any author.

Shell
$ git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
$ git config --global gpg.format ssh
$ git config --global commit.gpgsign true

$ git log --show-signature -1
commit 9f3c1a2b8e7d6c5f4a3b2c1d0e9f8a7b6c5d4e3f
Good "git" signature for priya@example.com with ED25519 key SHA256:8kP2...
Author: Priya Nair <priya@example.com>
Date:   Sun Sep 8 10:20:41 2025 +0100

    feat(orders): reject duplicate idempotency keys

SSH signing (gpg.format ssh) is far easier to adopt than GPG because engineers already have SSH keys. Combined with a branch protection rule requiring signed commits, and with build provenance in CI (Part 47, section 47.3), it closes the "who actually wrote this code" question that supply chain attacks exploit.

Practical example

A pull request that changes a query, adds an index migration and bumps a dependency arrives as one commit titled "fixes". A reviewer cannot separate the risky part from the trivial part, and a revert would undo all three. Split into three commits — perf(orders): add index on orders(customer_id, created_at), fix(orders): use the new index in the listing query, build(deps): bump pg to 8.13.1 — the review takes half the time and, six weeks later when the dependency bump turns out to be the problem, git revert touches exactly one commit.

Production scenario

A payments team requires signed commits and Conventional Commits on main, enforced by branch protection plus a commitlint hook. Releases are fully automated: merging a fix produces 1.14.4 with a changelog entry, a Git tag, and a deploy through the pipeline in Part 47. Over a year they cut release preparation from about 90 minutes of manual changelog writing per release to zero, and increased release frequency from weekly to daily, because the cost of a release stopped being a reason to batch.

Failure scenario

An engineer amended a commit that had already been pushed and reviewed, then force-pushed. Two reviewers had approved the previous version; GitHub dismissed the approvals, which was fine. What was not fine: a colleague had already branched off that commit for dependent work. Their branch now had the old commit as an ancestor. When both merged, the change appeared twice — once from the amended commit and once from the original — and the second application conflicted in a way that produced a silently broken merge resolution.

The rule that would have prevented it: rewrite only history that nobody else has based work on. For a shared branch, use a new commit (or a revert) instead of an amend.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Amending after push requires force-push and breaks anyone who branched off.
  • Empty commits (--allow-empty) are legitimate for triggering CI, but confusing in a log.
  • Author vs committer. A rebase or cherry-pick preserves the author and sets you as committer. git log shows the author by default, which is why rebased history can look like someone committed on a date they were on holiday.
  • Commits with wrong identity. A work laptop configured with a personal email; the commits do not link to the corporate account and may fail a CLA check.
  • Enormous commits. A 4,000-line commit is unreviewable and unbisectable; it will be approved unread.
  • Secrets in an amended commit. Amending removes it from the tip but the old object remains until gc, and it is already on the remote if you pushed (48.14).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write commit messages for the person debugging an incident in eighteen months, who might be themselves. They ask: if git bisect lands on this commit, will the message alone tell me what it was trying to do?

They keep local history messy while working and clean it before review with interactive rebase, because those are different activities: local commits are save points, published commits are documentation.

They also insist on the atomicity test — "would reverting this commit alone be safe and meaningful?" — because it is the property that makes every recovery tool in this part work.

Common mistakes

  • "fix", "wip", "update", "changes" as messages.
  • Mixing formatting, refactoring and behaviour change in one commit, which hides the real diff in noise.
  • Describing what the diff already shows instead of why.
  • Amending or force-pushing shared branches.
  • Committing generated files, lockfile churn and .env alongside real changes.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a commit atomic and why does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one logical change, tests pass at that commit, revertible in isolation; matters for bisect, revert, review and cherry-pick.
  2. Why imperative mood in commit messages?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: consistency with Git's own generated messages; the log reads as instructions describing what applying the commit does.
  3. What does Conventional Commits actually give you?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: automated semver and changelogs, filterable history, risk routing; not better content.
  4. What does --amend do at the object level, and when is it unsafe?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: creates a new commit object, old becomes unreachable; unsafe once pushed and others have based work on it.
  5. Why sign commits?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: author fields are unauthenticated strings; signing plus branch protection proves provenance and blocks impersonation.

Practical exercise

Take a branch where you have three unrelated changes mixed in your working tree. Using git add -p, produce three atomic commits, each with a Conventional Commits subject and a body explaining why. Verify each commit independently: check it out and run the test suite. Then enable SSH commit signing and confirm git log --show-signature reports a good signature. Acceptance criteria: three commits that each pass tests in isolation, each revertible without touching the others, all signed, and a message body that a stranger could act on.

48.3 Branches

Concept

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, plus one automatic behaviour: when you commit while HEAD points at that branch, the branch pointer moves forward to the new commit.

Why does it exist?

To let several lines of work exist at once without copying the repository. Because a branch is 41 bytes and commits are shared objects, having 200 branches costs essentially nothing. This is a genuine architectural difference from older systems where a branch meant a server-side copy of the tree.

Mental model

Imagine a row of stepping stones (commits) across a river. A branch is a coloured flag placed on one stone. Standing on a stone with your flag and adding a new stone moves your flag onto it. Other flags do not move. Switching branches is walking to a different flag, and the stones between the two are untouched.

How it works

Creating and switching. Modern Git splits the overloaded git checkout into two clearer commands, and you should use them:

Shell
$ git switch -c feature/idempotent-orders          # create and switch
Switched to a new branch 'feature/idempotent-orders'

$ git switch main                                   # switch to an existing branch
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

$ git switch -                                      # switch back to the previous branch
$ git switch --detach v1.4.2                        # explicit detached HEAD at a tag

git switch only changes branches. git restore only restores file content. git checkout still does both, which is precisely why it confused a generation of engineers: git checkout main and git checkout main -- src/file.ts do completely different things.

Tracking remotes. A remote-tracking ref (refs/remotes/origin/main) is your local record of where the remote's branch was at your last fetch. It is not live; it updates only on fetch or pull. An upstream is a configured link between your local branch and a remote branch, which is what makes bare git push and git pull work and what produces "ahead 2, behind 1".

Shell
$ git push -u origin feature/idempotent-orders
$ git branch -vv
* feature/idempotent-orders 7b2e5d1 [origin/feature/idempotent-orders] feat(orders): add idempotency key
  main                      9f3c1a2 [origin/main: behind 3] chore: bump deps

git fetch updates remote-tracking refs and touches nothing else — it is always safe. git pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase with --rebase), and it is the one that can surprise you. Configuring pull.rebase=true and pull.ff=only prevents the accidental merge commits that clutter feature branches:

Shell
$ git config --global pull.ff only        # refuse to create a merge commit implicitly
$ git config --global fetch.prune true    # delete local refs for deleted remote branches

Restoring files. git restore is the safe, explicit replacement for the destructive half of checkout:

Shell
$ git restore src/orders/orders.service.ts            # discard working-tree changes (DESTRUCTIVE)
$ git restore --staged src/orders/orders.service.ts   # unstage, keep working-tree changes
$ git restore --source=HEAD~2 src/orders/orders.service.ts  # bring back an older version

The first form permanently discards uncommitted work with no reflog entry. It is the second most common way engineers lose work, after reset --hard.

Naming and hygiene. Conventions that pay off: a type prefix and a ticket (feat/ORD-4182-idempotent-orders, fix/ORD-4199-refund-rounding), lowercase with hyphens, and no slashes that collide (feature and feature/x cannot both exist, because refs are files and a file cannot also be a directory). Delete merged branches promptly — git branch --merged main lists candidates — and set fetch.prune so remote deletions clean up locally.

The most important branch hygiene rule is not naming, though. It is lifetime. A branch that lives three weeks accumulates divergence, and the merge cost grows superlinearly with the number of commits on both sides. Keep branches under two days where you can, which is a statement about how you slice work, not about Git (48.12).

Practical example

An engineer starts feat/ORD-4182-idempotent-orders from main, pushes with -u, and opens a draft PR immediately so CI runs on every push. main receives 6 commits over the next day. Rather than merging main in repeatedly and producing a tangled history, they rebase once before requesting review:

Shell
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/ORD-4182-idempotent-orders.
$ git push --force-with-lease

--force-with-lease rather than --force is the important detail: it refuses the push if the remote branch has moved since your last fetch, which is what protects a colleague who pushed to the same branch (48.15).

Failure scenario

A team kept a develop branch and a release/2.0 branch that diverged for four months. When the time came to merge release/2.0 into develop, there were 340 commits on one side, 510 on the other, and 62 conflicting files including a lockfile and a generated API client. The merge took two engineers three days, produced a broken build for two more, and one conflict was resolved incorrectly — reintroducing a bug that had been fixed on develop in month two.

Nothing about Git caused this. The branching strategy did (48.12). The cost of integration is a function of how long you defer it, and Git only makes deferral possible, not free.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • git restore <file> discards uncommitted work permanently, with no reflog entry.
  • Branch name collisions with directory structure. feature and feature/x cannot coexist as refs.
  • Stale remote-tracking refs. origin/main is a cached value; "up to date" after a week means nothing without a fetch.
  • Detached HEAD from git checkout <sha>. Commits there vanish from view when you switch away.
  • Case-only renames (Orders.ts to orders.ts) on macOS or Windows appear to do nothing (48.15).
  • git pull creating surprise merge commits on a feature branch. Set pull.ff only or pull.rebase true.
  • Deleting an unmerged branch. git branch -D succeeds silently; recovery is via reflog only.
  • Branch protection bypassed by admins, so main receives an unreviewed force-push.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see branches as cheap and branch lifetime as expensive. The question is never "should I branch?" but "how do I get this merged today?" — which leads to smaller slices, feature flags (Part 47, section 47.8), and expand/contract migrations (Part 24).

They standardise the safe commands across the team: switch and restore over checkout, push --force-with-lease over --force, pull.ff only, fetch.prune true. These are small settings that remove entire categories of accident.

Explained to a product manager: "A branch is a label, and making one is free. What costs us is keeping work separate for weeks; the longer two versions drift apart, the more expensive and risky it is to bring them together."

Common mistakes

  • Using git checkout for everything and eventually running the destructive form by accident.
  • Long-lived branches, then blaming Git for the merge pain.
  • git push --force on a shared branch instead of --force-with-lease.
  • Never pruning, so git branch -a lists 400 dead branches.
  • Assuming origin/main is current without fetching.

Interview questions

  1. What physically happens when you create a branch and commit on it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a 41-byte ref file is written; committing creates objects and moves that ref; other refs are untouched.
  2. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: fetch updates remote-tracking refs only and is always safe; pull also merges or rebases into your branch.
  3. Why prefer switch and restore over checkout?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: checkout conflates branch switching and file restoration; the split is explicit and the destructive operation is named.
  4. What does "ahead 2, behind 3" mean and against what?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: compared to the remote-tracking ref as of the last fetch, which may be stale.
  5. Why is --force-with-lease safer than --force?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it refuses if the remote moved since your last fetch, protecting a colleague's push.

Practical exercise

Configure pull.ff only, fetch.prune true and an alias for push --force-with-lease. Then create a feature branch, have a colleague (or a second clone) push a commit to main, and bring your branch up to date with a rebase rather than a merge. Deliberately attempt a --force-with-lease push after simulating a colleague pushing to your branch from the second clone, and confirm it is rejected. Acceptance criteria: a linear feature branch history, an explanation of what the rejected force-push protected, and a git branch -vv output you can read aloud and interpret.

48.4 Merge

Concept

Merging combines two lines of history into one. Git finds the best common ancestor of the two branches, computes what each side changed since that ancestor, and produces a result containing both sets of changes — recorded as a new commit with two parents.

Why does it exist?

Because parallel work is the normal state of a team, and the history must record that it happened. A merge commit is not clutter; it is a factual statement that two independent lines of development were brought together at a specific point, by a specific person, and here is the result they verified.

Mental model

Imagine two people editing copies of the same document from a shared starting version. Merging is a third person comparing both copies against the original and producing one document containing both sets of edits. Where the two edited the same sentence, the third person cannot decide — that is a conflict, and a human must choose.

How it works

Fast-forward. If the target branch has no commits since the branch point, there is nothing to combine. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is created, and history stays linear.

Shell
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature/idempotent-orders
Updating 9f3c1a2..7b2e5d1
Fast-forward
 src/orders/orders.service.ts | 24 ++++++++++++++++++------
 src/migrations/1725870000-add-idempotency-index.ts | 18 ++++++++++++++++++
 2 files changed, 36 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)

Three-way merge. If both branches have moved since the common ancestor, Git performs a three-way merge using the merge base, and records a commit with two parents:

Shell
$ git merge feature/refunds
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 src/orders/refunds.service.ts | 61 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 61 insertions(+)

The default strategy is ort ("ostensibly recursive's twin"), which replaced recursive in Git 2.34. It handles the case of multiple merge bases (criss-cross merges) by merging the bases first, and it is substantially faster on large repositories.

--no-ff. Forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible:

Shell
$ git merge --no-ff feature/idempotent-orders

Why you would want that: the merge commit is a record that these five commits belong to one unit of work, which makes git log --first-parent a clean list of features rather than a list of individual commits, and makes reverting the whole feature one command (48.8). Why you might not: on a busy repository it produces a merge commit for every trivial branch, and the graph becomes hard to read.

The practical policy most teams land on: --no-ff for feature branches merged into main (so each feature is one node), fast-forward for trivial single-commit branches, and never a merge commit produced accidentally by git pull (set pull.ff only).

Conflict resolution workflow. A conflict occurs when both sides changed the same region of the same file, or when one side edited a file the other deleted. Git stops and leaves the repository in a merging state:

Shell
$ git merge feature/refunds
Auto-merging src/orders/orders.service.ts
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/orders/orders.service.ts
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

$ git status --short
UU src/orders/orders.service.ts
M  src/orders/refunds.service.ts

UU means both sides modified it. Other codes you will meet: AA both added, DU deleted by us and modified by them, UD the reverse.

The file contains conflict markers:

TypeScript
<<<<<<< HEAD
    const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.priceMinor * i.qty, 0);
=======
    const total = calculateTotal(items, { includeTax: true });
>>>>>>> feature/refunds

Turning on merge.conflictstyle=zdiff3 adds the common ancestor, which is the single highest-value Git configuration change most engineers can make:

TypeScript
<<<<<<< HEAD
    const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.priceMinor * i.qty, 0);
||||||| merge base
    const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
=======
    const total = calculateTotal(items, { includeTax: true });
>>>>>>> feature/refunds

Now you can see that one side renamed a field and the other extracted a function — so the correct resolution is neither side verbatim, it is calculateTotal using priceMinor. Without the base, you would have picked one and silently reverted the other's change.

The workflow:

  1. git status to list conflicted paths.
  2. Resolve each file. Understand both intents; do not pick a side to make it compile.
  3. git add <file> for each resolved file, which sets the merge stage to 0.
  4. Run the tests. A merge that compiles is not a merge that works.
  5. git commit (the message is pre-filled) or git merge --continue.
  6. git merge --abort at any point returns you to exactly where you started.

ours and theirs. During a merge, "ours" is the branch you are on and "theirs" is the branch being merged in:

Shell
$ git checkout --ours package-lock.json     # take our version entirely
$ git checkout --theirs docs/api.md         # take their version entirely
$ git add package-lock.json docs/api.md

Two warnings. First, during a rebase the meanings invert, because rebase replays your commits on top of the target: "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto, "theirs" is your own work. This reversal catches everyone once. Second, --ours on a lockfile is almost always wrong; the correct fix is to regenerate it (48.14).

There is also git merge -X ours / -X theirs, a strategy option that auto-resolves conflicting hunks in favour of one side while still merging non-conflicting changes normally. Different from -s ours, which discards the other side's changes entirely and keeps only the merge record — occasionally useful to mark a branch as merged without taking its content, and dangerous if used by accident.

rerere. "Reuse recorded resolution". When enabled, Git records how you resolved each conflict hunk and replays that resolution automatically the next time it sees the same conflict:

Shell
$ git config --global rerere.enabled true
$ git config --global rerere.autoupdate true
Shell
$ git rebase origin/main
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/orders/orders.service.ts
Resolved 'src/orders/orders.service.ts' using previous resolution.

This is transformative in exactly one situation: a long-lived branch that you rebase repeatedly, or a release branch you merge forward every day, hitting the same conflicts each time. Without rerere you resolve them again on every attempt. With it, you resolve once. It is also useful during a difficult rebase you abort and retry.

The caveat: rerere replays a resolution that was correct then. If the surrounding code has changed meaning, it will confidently apply a stale resolution. Review what it did (git rerere diff) rather than trusting it blindly, and git rerere forget <path> to drop a bad recording.

Practical example

Two engineers work on orders.service.ts for two days. One extracts a RefundCalculator; the other renames price to priceMinor throughout for a currency-precision fix. Merging produces four conflicts. With zdiff3 the resolution is mechanical, because in each hunk the base shows exactly which side introduced which change and the correct result combines both. It takes 15 minutes. Without the base, the reviewer of a similar merge the previous month had picked "theirs" wholesale and silently reverted a currency fix, which surfaced three weeks later as a rounding discrepancy in a reconciliation report.

Production scenario

A monorepo with 40 engineers takes about 55 merges into main per day through a merge queue. Merges are --no-ff squash-free merges of already-rebased branches, so conflicts at merge time are rare (the rebase happened in the PR). git log --first-parent --oneline gives a clean, readable feature-level history that release notes are generated from. Average time from "approved" to "on main" is 9 minutes, dominated by the queue re-running CI on the combined result.

Failure scenario

At 14:50 a merge of a four-week branch produced 31 conflicting files. The engineer worked through them quickly under release pressure, resolving several with --theirs "because the branch is newer". Tests passed, because the tests for the reverted code lived on the other side of the merge and had been resolved away too.

Three days later, rate limiting was found to be disabled in production. The merge had silently reverted a ThrottlerGuard registration and its test. git log -S 'ThrottlerGuard' --oneline found the commit that added it and the merge commit that removed it in about a minute — but the three days had already happened.

The postmortem produced three rules: branches live under three days; zdiff3 is set globally; and a conflict resolution that deletes lines from either side gets a second reviewer. That last one is the sharpest, because a merge diff against both parents (git show -m <merge>) reveals exactly this class of error and almost nobody looks at it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Silent revert during conflict resolution. The most dangerous merge failure, because tests can pass. Review git show -m or git diff HEAD^1 HEAD^2 on a big merge.
  • Semantic conflict with no textual conflict. One side renames a method, the other adds a call to the old name in a different file. Git merges cleanly; the build breaks. Only CI on the merged result catches this — which is what a merge queue is for.
  • Lockfile conflicts. Never resolve by hand (48.14).
  • Generated files committed. Every merge conflicts on them. Do not commit build output.
  • Criss-cross merges. Multiple merge bases; ort handles them, but the result can be surprising. Prefer rebasing feature branches to keep the graph simple.
  • -s ours used by mistake, silently discarding a whole branch's changes while claiming it was merged.
  • Merging with a dirty working tree. Git refuses if the merge would overwrite local changes; commit or stash first.
  • Line-ending conflicts. A whole file conflicts because one side has CRLF (48.15).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They optimise for the size of the merge, not the technique. A one-day branch merges cleanly with any strategy; a four-week branch is dangerous no matter how skilled the resolver.

When resolving, they reconstruct intent before touching the file: what was each side trying to do? The zdiff3 base makes that mechanical. They refuse to resolve a large conflict at the end of a long day under release pressure, because that is precisely when silent reverts happen.

They also treat "tests pass after the merge" as necessary and not sufficient, because a resolution can delete both the code and its test.

Explained to a product manager: "Combining two weeks of separate work is where mistakes hide. Merging small pieces daily is not bureaucracy; it is how we avoid quietly deleting each other's work."

Common mistakes

  • Resolving conflicts by picking whichever side compiles.
  • Leaving conflict markers in the file and committing them.
  • git checkout --ours on a lockfile.
  • Not running tests after resolving.
  • Merging main into a feature branch repeatedly, producing a tangled graph that nobody can read.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a fast-forward and a three-way merge?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: fast-forward moves a pointer when the target has not diverged; three-way creates a commit with two parents using the merge base.
  2. When would you use --no-ff and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: to record a feature as one unit, enabling log --first-parent and a single-command revert of the whole feature.
  3. What is zdiff3 and why does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: shows the merge base in conflict markers, revealing which side changed what, preventing silent reverts.
  4. During a rebase, what do "ours" and "theirs" refer to?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inverted relative to merge — "ours" is the upstream you are replaying onto, "theirs" is your commit being applied.
  5. What is rerere and what is its risk?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: records and replays conflict resolutions; risk is applying a stale resolution when surrounding code changed meaning.
  6. A merge had no conflicts and the build broke. How?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: semantic conflict; textual merge cannot see meaning; CI on the merged result is the defence.

Practical exercise

Create a conflict deliberately: two branches, both editing the same function, one renaming a field and one extracting a helper. Resolve it twice — once with the default conflict style and once with zdiff3 — and write down which resolution you would have got wrong without the base. Then enable rerere, abort the merge, redo it, and confirm the resolution is replayed. Acceptance criteria: a correct resolution combining both intents, tests passing, and a git show -m review of your merge commit showing no accidental deletions.

48.5 Rebase

Concept

Rebase replays your commits on top of a different base commit. Because a commit's hash covers its parent, replaying a commit onto a new parent necessarily produces a new commit object with a different hash. The original commits are not modified; they are abandoned, and remain reachable through the reflog.

Why does it exist?

To keep history linear and readable, and to let you tidy your work before others read it. A feature branch rebased onto the current main looks as though you wrote it against the latest code, which is exactly the history a reviewer and a future bisect want.

Mental model

Imagine you wrote three pages of a report based on version 4 of a shared document, and meanwhile the shared document reached version 9. Merging staples your pages on and adds a note explaining the two versions came together. Rebasing rewrites your three pages as if you had written them against version 9 — the same ideas, freshly typed, and if a paragraph you edited was changed in version 9, you must decide what the merged paragraph should say.

The key insight: rebasing produces new pages. Anyone holding the old pages now has documents that do not exist in your version.

How it works

After git switch feature && git rebase main, commits C and D are replayed onto F as new commits C' and D'. The branch becomes A-B-E-F-C'-D', and the original C and D are unreachable.

Shell
$ git switch feature/idempotent-orders
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/idempotent-orders.

Interactive rebase is where most of the value is:

Shell
$ git rebase -i origin/main
Text
pick 5e1d8b7 feat(orders): add idempotency key column
pick a3c9f04 wip
pick 7b2e5d1 fix typo
pick c8f1a92 feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
pick 2d4e6f8 fix review comments

# Commands:
# p, pick   = use commit
# r, reword = use commit, but edit the message
# e, edit   = use commit, but stop for amending
# s, squash = meld into previous commit, combine messages
# f, fixup  = like squash, but discard this commit's message
# d, drop   = remove commit
# b, break  = stop here (continue with git rebase --continue)

Rewritten into three meaningful commits:

Text
pick 5e1d8b7 feat(orders): add idempotency key column
fixup a3c9f04 wip
fixup 7b2e5d1 fix typo
pick c8f1a92 feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
fixup 2d4e6f8 fix review comments

Reordering lines reorders commits. Deleting a line drops that commit entirely — which is also the easiest way to lose work by accident, so read the list before saving.

edit stops the rebase at that commit so you can amend it, or split it (48.14). break stops at a point without modifying anything, useful for running tests mid-history.

--autosquash. Rather than editing the todo list by hand, mark the fixups when you create them:

Shell
$ git commit --fixup 5e1d8b7          # message becomes "fixup! feat(orders): add idempotency key column"
$ git commit --squash c8f1a92         # combines and lets you edit the message
$ git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main

Git reorders the todo list automatically, placing each fixup! immediately after its target with the fixup action pre-selected. Set rebase.autosquash=true globally and it applies to every interactive rebase. This is the fastest way to respond to review comments without polluting history with "fix review comments" commits.

--onto. The precise form. git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> replays the commits in <upstream>..<branch> onto <newbase>. It is the tool for moving a branch that was based on the wrong thing:

Shell
# feature-b was branched from feature-a, but feature-a is being abandoned.
# Move only feature-b's own commits onto main.
$ git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b

Without --onto, a plain git rebase main feature-b would also try to replay all of feature-a's commits, which is almost never what you want.

Another common use: dropping a range of commits from the middle of a branch.

Shell
# Drop the three commits between HEAD~5 and HEAD~2
$ git rebase --onto HEAD~5 HEAD~2 feature/x

The golden rule. Do not rebase commits that exist in a repository others have based work on.

The reason is now obvious from the object model: rebase creates new commits and abandons old ones. A colleague whose branch descends from your old commits will, when they pull, see both the old and the new versions of every commit. Merging then applies the same changes twice, producing spurious conflicts and, worse, resolutions that silently drop code.

The practical boundary:

Branch Rebase? Why
Your unpushed local branch Freely Nobody has seen it
Your pushed feature branch, no other contributors Yes, with --force-with-lease Only you build on it; PR history is not sacred
A shared feature branch two people push to Only with explicit coordination Both will have divergent copies
main, develop, a release branch Never Everyone's history breaks

Conflicts mid-rebase. A rebase applies commits one at a time, so you may hit a conflict at each one:

Shell
$ git rebase origin/main
Auto-merging src/orders/orders.service.ts
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/orders/orders.service.ts
error: could not apply c8f1a92... feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
Resolve all conflicts manually, mark them as resolved with
"git add/rm <conflicted_files>", then run "git rebase --continue".
You can instead skip this commit: run "git rebase --skip".
To abort and get back to the state before "git rebase", run "git rebase --abort".

Three exits, and knowing which to use matters:

  • git rebase --continue after git adding your resolution. The normal path.
  • git rebase --skip drops the current commit entirely. Correct only when the commit's change is already present upstream. Used carelessly, it silently deletes your work.
  • git rebase --abort restores the branch exactly as it was. Always safe. When a rebase is going badly, abort, do not push through.

Remember the inverted ours/theirs here. And git status during a rebase tells you where you are:

Shell
$ git status
interactive rebase in progress; onto 9f3c1a2
Last commands done (3 commands done):
   pick 5e1d8b7 feat(orders): add idempotency key column
   pick c8f1a92 feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
Next command to do (1 remaining command):
   pick 2d4e6f8 fix review comments

Practical example

A pull request receives eight review comments over two days. The engineer fixes each with git commit --fixup <target>, pushing after each so reviewers see incremental changes. When approved, one git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main collapses the eight fixups into the three original commits, and git push --force-with-lease publishes a clean, reviewable, bisectable history. The reviewers saw the increments; main gets the finished product.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 an engineer rebased a shared feature/checkout-v2 branch that two colleagues were also pushing to, then force-pushed. Both colleagues had local commits based on the old versions. When they pulled, Git merged the old and new histories: every commit appeared twice, 40 conflicts appeared, and one colleague resolved them by taking "theirs" everywhere, which discarded a day of the other colleague's work.

Recovery took two hours: git reflog on each machine to find each person's pre-pull tip, cherry-picking the genuinely missing commits onto a fresh branch from the rebased base, and verifying with git log --oneline --graph plus a careful diff against the pre-incident state.

The team's rule since: shared branches are never rebased. If a shared branch must be updated from main, it is merged. Only single-owner branches are rebased, and --force-with-lease is mandatory so an unexpected colleague push aborts the push instead of destroying it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rebasing a shared branch. The scenario above.
  • --skip used to escape a conflict. Silently drops the commit.
  • Long rebase with many conflicts. Twelve commits each conflicting is twelve resolutions; rerere helps, and so does squashing first, then rebasing.
  • Rebase changes committer date but keeps author date. History looks like commits made on days people were away.
  • Signatures are lost. Rebasing produces new commits that are unsigned unless you use -S or set commit.gpgsign.
  • --force instead of --force-with-lease destroys a colleague's push with no warning.
  • CI results become stale. After a rebase, the SHAs reviewers approved no longer exist; approvals may auto-dismiss.
  • Rebasing merge commits. By default they are flattened; --rebase-merges preserves the structure, and is fiddly.
  • Very long rebase on a big repository can take minutes and leave you mid-operation if interrupted; git rebase --abort recovers.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate two questions: what history do reviewers need? (incremental, showing responses to feedback) and what history does main need? (atomic, bisectable, each commit passing tests). Interactive rebase with --autosquash is how they get both from the same branch.

They apply the golden rule mechanically rather than by judgement, because the cost of getting it wrong falls on colleagues rather than on themselves. A shared branch gets merges; a personal branch gets rebases.

They also treat --abort as the default response to a rebase going wrong. There is no prize for pushing through a twelve-conflict rebase at 18:00.

Explained to a product manager: "Rebasing rewrites our local history so it reads cleanly. We only do it on work nobody else has built on, because rewriting shared history creates duplicate versions of the same change and people lose work."

Common mistakes

  • Rebasing main or a shared branch.
  • git push --force rather than --force-with-lease.
  • Using --skip to make a conflict go away.
  • Squashing a whole feature into one commit before review, so reviewers cannot follow the reasoning.
  • Rebasing when the branch has a merge commit in it and being surprised the merge disappeared.

Interview questions

  1. What does rebase do at the object level?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: replays commits as new objects with new hashes onto a new base; originals become unreachable but remain in the reflog.
  2. State the golden rule and explain why it exists.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: never rebase history others have based work on; duplicated commits, spurious conflicts, silent loss.
  3. What is --onto for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: replaying a precise range onto a new base, e.g. moving a branch off an abandoned parent branch or dropping a middle range.
  4. How do you respond to review comments without polluting history?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: --fixup commits during review, then rebase -i --autosquash before merge.
  5. You are mid-rebase with a conflict and unsure. What are your options?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: continue after resolving, skip (drops the commit — dangerous), abort (always safe); prefer abort when unsure.
  6. Why did a colleague's work disappear after your rebase and force-push?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: they had commits on the old objects; force-push replaced the ref; recovery through their reflog.

Practical exercise

Create a branch with six messy commits including two "wip" and one "fix typo". Use git commit --fixup for two further changes, then run git rebase -i --autosquash main to produce three clean, atomic commits. Verify each of the three passes tests independently. Then deliberately create a conflict during a rebase and practise all three exits: continue, skip (observe what is lost), and abort. Acceptance criteria: a three-commit linear branch, a written note describing exactly what --skip discarded, and a demonstration that --abort returned you to the exact pre-rebase state (compare git rev-parse HEAD before and after).

48.6 Cherry-pick

Concept

git cherry-pick takes the change introduced by one commit and applies it as a new commit on your current branch. It computes the diff between that commit and its parent, applies it, and commits the result with a new hash.

Why does it exist?

Because sometimes you need one specific change somewhere else, without the rest of the branch it came from. The canonical case is a hotfix: a bug is fixed on main, and the same fix must go onto release/2.4 which is running in production and must not receive the twenty other commits main has accumulated.

Mental model

Imagine copying one paragraph from one document into another. The words are the same; the paragraph is not the same object — it has a different position, a different surrounding context, and it exists twice.

How it works

Shell
$ git switch release/2.4
$ git cherry-pick 7b2e5d1
[release/2.4 e4a9c02] fix(payments): reject refunds above the original charge
 Date: Sun Sep 8 11:04:12 2025 +0100
 2 files changed, 18 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

Note the new hash e4a9c02. The change is the same; the commit is not.

-x. Appends a line to the message recording where the change came from:

Shell
$ git cherry-pick -x 7b2e5d1
Text
fix(payments): reject refunds above the original charge

(cherry picked from commit 7b2e5d1a9c8f4e3b2a1d0c9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a)

Always use -x when picking between long-lived branches. It is the only durable record of the relationship, and it lets you answer "is this fix on the release branch?" with a grep instead of a diff review. Many teams alias cherry-pick to always include it.

Ranges.

Shell
$ git cherry-pick 5e1d8b7^..c8f1a92     # inclusive range: 5e1d8b7 through c8f1a92
$ git cherry-pick 5e1d8b7..c8f1a92      # exclusive of 5e1d8b7
$ git cherry-pick -n 7b2e5d1            # apply to the index without committing
$ git cherry-pick -m 1 3a9f04c          # pick a merge commit, taking parent 1's line as the base

The ^.. form catches people: A..B in Git range syntax excludes A itself, so A^..B is how you include it. During a range pick, --continue, --skip and --abort work as they do in rebase.

When it creates duplicate commits. This is the part that matters at senior level. If you cherry-pick a commit from main onto release/2.4, and later merge release/2.4 back into main, the same change now exists as two different commits with different hashes.

Usually this is fine: Git's ort strategy notices that the content is already present ("patch already applied") and the merge is clean. But it breaks down in three situations:

  1. The picked commit was modified during the pick (conflicts resolved differently, or the surrounding code differed). Now the two commits are not equivalent, and merging produces a real conflict or applies a partial duplicate.
  2. The original was later amended or rebased on the source branch, so the two diverge.
  3. The change is not idempotent in effect — a migration that adds a column, an append to a changelog, an increment. Applying it twice is not the same as applying it once, even when Git merges the text cleanly.

git cherry tells you what has and has not been ported:

Shell
$ git cherry -v release/2.4 main
+ 7b2e5d1 feat(orders): add partial refund support
- a3c9f04 fix(payments): reject refunds above the original charge

- means an equivalent change is already in release/2.4 (matched by patch id, so hash differences do not matter); + means it is not.

The alternative that avoids the whole problem. Fix the bug on the oldest branch that needs it — the release branch — and then merge that branch forward into main. Now there is one commit, one hash, and no duplication. This is the discipline used by projects with many maintained versions (Linux, PostgreSQL), and it is strictly better than cherry-picking backwards when your branching model allows it. Cherry-picking is the pragmatic tool when it does not.

Practical example

A production incident at 22:10: refunds above the original charge amount are accepted. The fix is on main as 7b2e5d1, alongside 22 other commits including a schema change that is not ready for release.

Shell
$ git switch release/2.4
$ git pull
$ git cherry-pick -x 7b2e5d1
$ npm run test:unit && npm run test:int
$ git push
$ git tag -a v2.4.7 -m "Hotfix: reject over-refunds"
$ git push origin v2.4.7

The pipeline (Part 47) builds and deploys v2.4.7. Total time from decision to production: 14 minutes. Later, release/2.4 is merged back into main; the ort strategy recognises the change is already there and the merge is clean.

Failure scenario

An engineer cherry-picked a three-commit fix onto a release branch. The second commit conflicted, and they resolved it differently from the original because the release branch lacked a refactor that main had. Three weeks later release/2.4 was merged into main. The merge appeared clean. In fact the resolution on the release branch had dropped a null check that existed in the original, and the merge preferred the release branch's version of that hunk.

Production then threw TypeError: Cannot read properties of null on a code path exercised once every few thousand requests. Finding it required git log --oneline --graph around the merge, git show -m on the merge commit, and a comparison of the cherry-picked commit against its original — about 90 minutes.

The lesson: a cherry-pick that required conflict resolution is not the same change any more. Record that fact (the -x line plus a note in the message), and diff the picked commit against the original before merging branches back together.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Conflict during the pick produces a different change under the same message.
  • Picking a merge commit requires -m to choose which parent's line is the baseline; getting it wrong applies a huge unintended diff.
  • Picking a range that includes merges fails unless handled explicitly.
  • Dependent commits. Picking commit 3 without 1 and 2 compiles but is semantically wrong.
  • Migrations. Cherry-picking a migration onto a branch with a different migration history produces out-of-order timestamps and a broken sequence.
  • Duplicate history noise. Frequent cherry-picking makes git log show every fix twice, which confuses release notes and git bisect.
  • Forgetting -x so nobody can trace where a commit came from.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat cherry-pick as a controlled exception, not a workflow. Routine cherry-picking between long-lived branches is a signal that the branching strategy is wrong (48.12) — usually too many maintained lines, or a develop branch that should not exist.

Before picking, they ask: is this commit self-contained? Does it depend on anything not present on the target? Will the pick conflict, and if it does, is the resolved change still the same change? If the answers are uncomfortable, they write the fix directly against the release branch and merge forward instead.

Explained to a product manager: "We can copy a single fix onto the released version without shipping everything else we have been building. It is a copy, though, not the same change, so we verify it separately on that branch."

Common mistakes

  • Omitting -x, losing all traceability.
  • Cherry-picking a commit whose dependencies are absent.
  • Resolving a conflict during a pick and assuming the result is identical to the original.
  • Using cherry-pick as the normal way to move work between long-lived branches.
  • Cherry-picking migrations without checking migration ordering.

Interview questions

  1. What does cherry-pick do and how does the result differ from the original?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: applies the commit's diff as a new commit with a new hash; same content, different object and parent.
  2. Why use -x?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: records the source commit in the message; the only durable trace of the relationship across branches.
  3. When does cherry-picking create problems on a later merge?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when the pick was modified by conflict resolution, when the original was amended, or when the change is not idempotent in effect.
  4. How do you check whether a fix has already been ported to a release branch?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: git cherry -v release main, which matches by patch id rather than hash.
  5. What is the alternative to cherry-picking backwards?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: fix on the oldest supported branch and merge forward, so one commit exists.

Practical exercise

Set up main and release/1.0 diverged by several commits. Cherry-pick a fix from main onto the release branch with -x, tag a patch release, then merge release/1.0 back into main and confirm the merge is clean. Then repeat with a fix that conflicts during the pick, resolve it differently, and observe what the later merge does. Acceptance criteria: git cherry -v release/1.0 main correctly reports which commits are ported, a written explanation of what changed between the original and the picked commit in the conflicting case, and a note on how you would have detected it before the merge.

48.7 Reset

Concept

git reset moves the current branch ref to a specified commit, and — depending on the mode — optionally updates the index and the working tree to match.

Three modes, three levels of destruction:

Mode Moves branch ref Resets index Resets working tree Destroys uncommitted work
--soft Yes No No No
--mixed (default) Yes Yes No No
--hard Yes Yes Yes Yes

Why does it exist?

Because you will frequently want to undo something locally: uncommit but keep the changes staged, unstage a file, or discard everything and start over. Each of those is a different combination of "which of the three areas do I want to move?"

Mental model

Imagine three shelves stacked vertically: the top is your desk (working tree), the middle is the outbox (index), the bottom is the filing cabinet (HEAD commit). reset always moves the cabinet's pointer. --soft stops there. --mixed also empties the outbox to match. --hard also clears your desk — and your desk is the only one of the three that Git was never keeping copies of.

How it works

--soft: uncommit, keep everything staged.

Shell
$ git reset --soft HEAD~3
$ git status --short
M  src/orders/orders.service.ts
A  src/migrations/1725870000-add-idempotency-index.ts

The three commits are gone from the branch; all their changes are staged, ready to be recommitted as one. This is the simplest way to squash the last N commits without an interactive rebase.

--mixed: uncommit and unstage.

Shell
$ git reset HEAD~1
Unstaged changes after reset:
M	src/orders/orders.service.ts

$ git reset -- src/config/database.ts    # unstage one file, keep its changes

The default. Changes remain in your working tree but are no longer staged, so you can restage them selectively with git add -p.

--hard: uncommit, unstage, and overwrite the working tree.

Shell
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
HEAD is now at 9f3c1a2 chore: bump dependencies

Nothing warns you. Uncommitted changes are gone and are not in the reflog, because they were never objects. Committed changes are recoverable.

Reset vs restore. reset operates on the branch ref and (optionally) the index and tree wholesale. restore operates on specific files. Use git restore --staged <file> to unstage rather than git reset -- <file>; it says what it does.

Recovery through the reflog. The reflog records every position HEAD and each branch has held, with a timestamp and the command that moved it:

Shell
$ git reflog
9f3c1a2 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
c8f1a92 HEAD@{1}: commit: feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
a3c9f04 HEAD@{2}: commit: test(orders): cover duplicate key path
5e1d8b7 HEAD@{3}: commit: feat(orders): add idempotency key column
9f3c1a2 HEAD@{4}: checkout: moving from main to feature/idempotent-orders
Shell
$ git reset --hard c8f1a92        # back to where you were
# or, non-destructively:
$ git branch rescue c8f1a92

Per-branch reflogs also exist (git reflog show feature/idempotent-orders), which is useful when HEAD's log is noisy. Reflog entries expire after 90 days by default (30 days for entries whose commits are unreachable), and git gc --prune=now clears them immediately — which is why you must never run it while recovering.

Practical example

An engineer has made five commits on a local branch. Three are "wip". Before pushing, they collapse the lot:

Shell
$ git reset --soft origin/main
$ git status --short
M  src/orders/orders.service.ts
M  src/orders/orders.controller.ts
A  src/migrations/1725870000-add-idempotency-index.ts
$ git commit -m "feat(orders): make order creation idempotent

Adds a unique index on orders(idempotency_key) and returns the existing
order on a duplicate key rather than creating a second one.

Refs: ORD-4182"

One clean commit, no interactive rebase needed. --soft to the merge base is the fastest squash there is.

Failure scenario

At 17:50 an engineer with two hours of uncommitted work ran git reset --hard origin/main intending to update a different branch. The working tree was replaced instantly. There was no reflog entry that could help, because the changes had never been committed or stashed and therefore had never become objects.

Partial recovery came from two accidents: the IDE's local history had most of one file, and a node_modules-adjacent build output contained a compiled version of another. About 40 minutes of work was genuinely lost, plus 90 minutes of recovery.

Two habits prevent this entirely. First, commit early and often locally — a "wip" commit costs nothing and is fully recoverable, and interactive rebase cleans it up later. Second, git stash before any destructive operation; a stash is a real commit object and appears in git fsck --lost-found even after stash drop.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • --hard destroys uncommitted work permanently. The single most common way engineers lose work.
  • reset on a shared branch, then force-push. Rewrites public history for everyone (48.15).
  • Untracked files survive --hard but are destroyed by git clean -fd, which people often run next.
  • reset --hard <remote> on the wrong branch, as above.
  • Reflog expiry. 90 days, or immediately after gc --prune=now.
  • reset after a merge conflict abandons the merge state; use git merge --abort instead, which is purpose-built.
  • Submodule contents are not reset by default, leaving a confusing mixed state.
  • Confusing reset with revert. reset rewrites history and is for local work; revert adds a commit and is for shared history (48.8).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask one question before any reset: is anything here uncommitted? If yes, stash or commit first, always. Everything committed is recoverable through the reflog; nothing uncommitted is.

They use --soft routinely (squashing), --mixed occasionally (restaging), and --hard rarely and deliberately, having checked git status first.

They also know that on a shared branch the answer is never reset. It is revert.

Common mistakes

  • reset --hard with uncommitted changes present.
  • Using reset to undo a pushed commit on a shared branch.
  • Not knowing the reflog exists, and re-cloning after a mistake — which destroys the reflog and any hope of recovery.
  • Running git gc --prune=now while trying to recover.
  • Using reset -- <file> when restore --staged <file> is clearer.

Interview questions

  1. Explain --soft, --mixed and --hard in terms of HEAD, index and working tree.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the table above, precisely.
  2. You committed three times and want one commit. Two ways?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: reset --soft to the base then commit, or rebase -i with squash/fixup.
  3. What does the reflog recover, and what can it never recover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: recovers anything that was ever a commit; cannot recover changes that were never committed or stashed.
  4. When would you never use reset?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: on a branch others have pulled; use revert.
  5. Someone ran reset --hard and lost three commits. Walk me through recovery.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: git reflog, identify the pre-reset SHA, git branch rescue <sha> or reset --hard <sha>; do not gc, do not re-clone.

Practical exercise

In a scratch repository, make three commits and one uncommitted edit. Run git reset --soft HEAD~3, inspect git status, then recover with the reflog. Repeat with --mixed, then with --hard, and document precisely what survived each time — paying attention to the uncommitted edit. Then simulate the disaster: make uncommitted changes, reset --hard, and attempt recovery. Acceptance criteria: a table of what each mode did to HEAD, index, working tree and untracked files, and a written statement of exactly which state is unrecoverable and why.

48.8 Revert

Concept

git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an existing commit. History is not rewritten; it is extended with an explicit "undo this" entry.

Why does it exist?

Because you cannot rewrite history that other people have. reset plus force-push works on your own branch and destroys everyone else's. Revert is the safe undo: it is a normal commit, it merges normally, it pulls normally, and it leaves an auditable record that says a change was deliberately backed out and by whom.

Mental model

Imagine a ledger. You cannot erase an entry, because others have copies and audits depend on them. Instead you write a correcting entry: "reverses entry 4182". The original stays, the correction is visible, and the balance is right.

How it works

Shell
$ git revert 7b2e5d1
[main 3d8f0a1] Revert "feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key"
 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+), 18 deletions(-)

The generated message is Revert "<original subject>" plus This reverts commit <sha>. Add why to the body — "reverted because it caused a 12% error rate spike, see INC-2291" — because a revert with no reason invites someone to reapply the change next week.

Shell
$ git revert --no-commit 7b2e5d1 a3c9f04   # stage several reverts, commit once
$ git revert 5e1d8b7..c8f1a92               # revert a range (newest applied first)
$ git revert --no-edit 7b2e5d1              # accept the generated message

Reverting a merge. A merge commit has two parents, so "the inverse of this commit" is ambiguous: relative to which parent? -m selects the mainline, the parent whose line of history you want to keep.

Shell
$ git revert -m 1 3a9f04c

For a merge of a feature branch into main, parent 1 is main and parent 2 is the feature branch. -m 1 therefore means "keep the mainline, undo everything the feature branch brought in", which is almost always what you want. Confirm before running:

Shell
$ git log --oneline -1 --parents 3a9f04c
3a9f04c 9f3c1a2 c8f1a92 Merge pull request #412 from acme/feature/refunds

The first hash after the merge's own is parent 1 (9f3c1a2, the main tip), the second is parent 2 (c8f1a92, the feature tip). Getting -m wrong reverts all of main instead of the feature, which produces a spectacular and immediately obvious diff.

The revert-of-a-revert trap. This is the sharpest edge in everyday Git, and it catches senior engineers.

You merge feature/refunds into main. It causes an incident. You revert the merge with -m 1. main no longer has the feature. Good.

The team then fixes the feature and merges the branch again — and nothing appears. The build succeeds, the merge is clean, and the feature is still missing.

Why: merging is based on reachability, not on file content. After M1, every commit on feature is already an ancestor of main. The revert R1 changed the files but did not change reachability. When you merge feature again, Git computes the merge base — which is the tip of feature, already merged — sees nothing new to bring in, and produces an empty or near-empty merge. The revert's deletion stands.

Three correct ways out:

  1. Revert the revert, then continue. git revert R1 restores the feature's content, and further work continues on top. Cleanest when the original feature was fine and only needed a small fix.

    Shell
    $ git revert 3d8f0a1          # 3d8f0a1 is the revert commit
$ git switch -c fix/refunds-null-check

  2. Rebase the feature branch onto the post-revert main, so its commits become new objects that are not yet ancestors, then merge. This gives clean history but rewrites the branch, so it must be a branch you own.

  3. Start a fresh branch from the current main and reapply the work (cherry-pick the original commits, which creates new hashes). Slower, but unambiguous.

The rule to remember: after reverting a merge, you cannot simply re-merge the same branch. Write it in the revert commit's message so the next person does not lose an afternoon.

Practical example

At 15:40 a merge introduces a memory leak. The on-call reverts:

Shell
$ git log --oneline -1 --parents 3a9f04c
3a9f04c 9f3c1a2 c8f1a92 Merge pull request #412 from acme/feature/refunds

$ git revert -m 1 3a9f04c
$ git commit --amend

with the message:

Text
Revert "Merge pull request #412 from acme/feature/refunds"

This reverts commit 3a9f04c, reversing changes made to 9f3c1a2.

Reverted because the refund reconciliation job leaked ~40 MB per run,
OOM-killing pods after roughly 90 minutes. See INC-2291.

NOTE: do not simply re-merge feature/refunds. Because the merge is
already an ancestor of main, a second merge brings in nothing. Either
revert this revert first, or rebase the branch onto main.

Deploy takes 6 minutes through the pipeline (Part 47). The feature returns two days later by reverting this revert, then merging the fix.

Failure scenario

A team reverted a merge on a Friday. The following Wednesday, after fixing the bug on the feature branch, they merged it again. The PR showed a small diff (just the fix). CI passed. It deployed.

The feature was still missing in production. QA raised it as a new bug; two engineers spent a day investigating "why is the code not running", checking feature flags, deployment digests and configuration, before someone ran git log --oneline -- src/orders/refunds.service.ts and saw the revert.

Total cost: about 14 engineer-hours, entirely avoidable with one sentence in the revert message and one line in the team's runbook.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Revert-of-a-revert trap. As above.
  • Wrong -m value. Reverts the mainline instead of the feature; enormous diff, usually caught immediately.
  • Reverting a commit whose changes were built upon. Conflicts, or a clean revert that breaks later code.
  • Reverting a migration commit does not undo the migration. The code reverts; the schema does not (Part 24).
  • Range direction. git revert A..B applies reverts from newest to oldest; getting the range backwards produces conflicts.
  • Revert with no explanation, so the change is reapplied next sprint by someone who assumes it was an accident.
  • Reverting a squash-merged PR. One revert undoes the whole PR, which is convenient, but you cannot revert just one commit inside it because they no longer exist (48.13).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Their decision rule is simple and mechanical: has this been pushed to a branch others use? If yes, revert. If no, reset or rebase. There is no judgement call.

They treat the revert commit message as an incident artifact: what broke, what the evidence was, the incident ID, and explicit instructions about re-merging. During an incident, the revert is the fastest safe action — faster than a fix, and reversible.
