They also check what the revert does not undo: database migrations, published events, cache state, external side effects. Reverting code is one step of recovery, not all of it (Part 47, section 47.9).

Explained to a product manager: "We add a change that undoes the previous one, rather than pretending it never happened. Everyone's copy stays consistent, and we keep the record of what we tried."

Common mistakes

  • Using reset plus force-push on a shared branch instead of revert.
  • Forgetting -m 1 when reverting a merge, or guessing the parent number.
  • Re-merging a branch whose merge was reverted, and shipping nothing.
  • Reverting a commit and assuming the database change went with it.
  • Empty revert messages.

Interview questions

  1. When do you revert and when do you reset?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: revert for shared/pushed history (adds a commit); reset for local, unpublished work (rewrites).
  2. How do you revert a merge commit, and what does -m 1 mean?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: -m selects the mainline parent; parent 1 is normally the branch you merged into.
  3. You reverted a merge, fixed the branch, re-merged, and the feature is missing. Explain and fix.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the branch's commits are already ancestors so the merge brings nothing; revert the revert, or rebase the branch, or reapply on a fresh branch.
  4. What does reverting a commit that added a migration actually undo?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: only the code; the schema change persists and needs its own forward migration.
  5. Why does a revert commit message matter more than most?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it is read during incidents; it must record why and warn about re-merging.

Practical exercise

Build the trap end to end. Create a feature branch with two commits, merge it into main with --no-ff, then revert the merge with -m 1. Add a fix commit on the feature branch and merge again; confirm the feature is still absent and explain why using git log --graph --oneline and git merge-base. Then recover using each of the three approaches (revert the revert, rebase the branch, fresh branch with cherry-picks) and compare the resulting histories. Acceptance criteria: a graph for each approach, a statement of which you would use in an incident and why, and a revert message template your team could adopt.

48.9 Stash, tag, bisect, reflog, detached HEAD

These five are grouped because they share a theme: they are the tools you reach for when something is unexpected — an urgent interruption, a release that needs naming, a bug with no obvious cause, work that seems to have vanished, or a state you did not intend to be in.

48.9.1 Stash

Concept

git stash takes your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged), saves them as real commit objects, and restores your working tree to a clean state.

Why does it exist?

Because interruptions are real. You are halfway through a refactor when a production incident needs a one-line fix on main. Git refuses to switch branches when the switch would overwrite modified files, and committing half a refactor pollutes history.

How it works

Under the hood a stash is two or three commits: one for the index state, one for the working tree, and optionally one for untracked files, all pointed at by the refs/stash ref with its own reflog. That is why a stash is recoverable even after git stash drop — the objects survive until garbage collection.

Shell
$ git stash push -m "wip: extracting RefundCalculator"
Saved working directory and index state On feature/refunds: wip: extracting RefundCalculator

$ git stash list
stash@{0}: On feature/refunds: wip: extracting RefundCalculator
stash@{1}: On main: debugging pool exhaustion

$ git stash show -p stash@{0}          # view the diff
$ git stash pop                        # apply and remove from the list
$ git stash apply stash@{1}            # apply and keep it in the list
$ git stash push -u -m "with untracked"  # include untracked files
$ git stash push -m "just this file" -- src/orders/orders.service.ts
$ git stash branch fix/refunds stash@{0} # create a branch and apply the stash there

Two flags that matter. -u includes untracked files, which the default does not — the most common stash surprise is a brand-new file left behind and then destroyed by a later git clean. -p stages hunks interactively so you can stash only part of your work.

git stash pop can conflict. If it does, the stash is not dropped (Git is careful here), so you can resolve, git add, and then git stash drop manually.

Recovering a dropped stash:

Shell
$ git fsck --no-reflog | awk '/dangling commit/ {print $3}'
c4d3e2f1a0b9c8d7e6f5a4b3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5
$ git stash apply c4d3e2f1

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Untracked files not stashed by default, then deleted by git clean -fd.
  • Stash stack forgotten. Twelve stashes from six months ago, none with useful messages. Always use -m.
  • pop conflicts leave you mid-resolution with the stash still present; people then pop again and duplicate the changes.
  • Stashes are local. They do not push, and they are lost with the clone.
  • Stashing during a merge or rebase produces a confusing state; abort the operation first.

The senior habit: prefer a wip commit on a throwaway branch over a stash for anything you might not return to within the hour. A commit has a message, a branch name, and shows up in git log; a stash is invisible until you remember it exists.

48.9.2 Tag

Concept

A tag is a named pointer to a commit. Lightweight tags are just a ref file containing a hash. Annotated tags are full objects with a tagger, date, message and optional signature.

Why does it exist?

To name releases immutably. v2.4.7 should mean one exact commit forever, so that "which code is running in production?" and "what changed between v2.4.6 and v2.4.7?" have precise answers.

How it works

Shell
$ git tag -a v2.4.7 -m "Hotfix: reject over-refunds"      # annotated (use this)
$ git tag v2.4.7-rc1                                       # lightweight
$ git tag -s v2.4.7 -m "Release 2.4.7"                     # signed
$ git push origin v2.4.7                                   # tags are NOT pushed by default
$ git push origin --tags                                   # push all tags
$ git tag -l 'v2.4.*'
$ git show v2.4.7
$ git describe --tags                                      # v2.4.7-12-g9f3c1a2

git describe output reads as: 12 commits after v2.4.7, currently at 9f3c1a2. Build tooling uses this to produce version strings, which is why a shallow clone (which may not fetch tags) breaks versioning in CI (48.15).

Always use annotated tags for releases: they carry who tagged, when, and why, they can be signed, and git describe prefers them.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Moving a tag after release. git tag -f plus a force-push makes v2.4.7 mean two different commits for different people. Never move a release tag; cut v2.4.8.
  • Tags not pushed. A local-only release tag that CI cannot see.
  • Tags not fetched. git fetch --tags or fetch.tags=true; shallow clones and --filter clones often omit them.
  • Lightweight tags for releases, losing the tagger and message.
  • Deleting a tag locally does not delete it on the remote (git push origin :refs/tags/v2.4.7 does).

48.9.3 Bisect

Concept

git bisect performs a binary search over history to find the commit that introduced a behaviour change. You mark one commit as good and one as bad; Git checks out the midpoint; you test and mark it; repeat. n commits take about log2(n) steps.

Why does it exist?

Because "when did this break?" is often the hardest question in an incident, and reading 400 commit diffs is not a strategy. Bisect turns it into eight or nine tests.

An incident story

At 08:50 on a Monday, a report lands: order totals on invoices are off by one cent for about 3% of orders. Nobody knows when it started. The last release everyone trusts is v2.3.0, tagged eleven weeks ago. Since then there are 412 commits on main.

The engineer writes a test script first, because a manual bisect over nine steps invites human error:

Shell
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/bisect-test.sh
# Exit 0 = good, 1 = bad, 125 = skip (cannot test this commit).
set -e

# The build must succeed for the test to mean anything. If it does not,
# skip rather than marking bad, or we will blame an unrelated broken commit.
npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 125
npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 125

# One focused test that reproduces the defect and nothing else.
npx jest --config jest.unit.config.js -t 'invoice total rounding' --silent

Then the crucial optimisation: the defect is in invoice totals, so only commits touching that area can be responsible. Bisect accepts a path filter, which restricts the candidate set:

Shell
$ chmod +x scripts/bisect-test.sh
$ git bisect start -- src/invoices src/orders/pricing
$ git bisect bad HEAD
$ git bisect good v2.3.0
Bisecting: 31 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)

412 commits became 63 candidates, because only those touched the relevant paths. Then:

Shell
$ git bisect run ./scripts/bisect-test.sh
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'
Bisecting: 15 revisions left to test after this (roughly 4 steps)
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'
Bisecting: 7 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'
Bisecting: 3 revisions left to test after this (roughly 2 steps)
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'
Bisecting: 1 revision left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'
Bisecting: 0 revisions left to test after this (roughly 0 steps)
running './scripts/bisect-test.sh'

a3c9f04e2b1d7c6f5a4b3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5e4f is the first bad commit
commit a3c9f04e2b1d7c6f5a4b3c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5e4f
Author: Sam Okafor <sam@example.com>
Date:   Thu Jul 24 16:12:03 2025 +0100

    refactor(pricing): centralise tax calculation in PricingService

 src/orders/pricing/pricing.service.ts | 42 +++++++++++++-----------
 1 file changed, 23 insertions(+), 19 deletions(-)

bisect run success

Six automated steps, four minutes of wall clock, and a 42-line diff to read. The refactor had replaced a Math.round(x * 100) / 100 on a decimal string with floating-point arithmetic on a number, which is correct for 97% of values and wrong for the rest.

Shell
$ git bisect reset          # return to where you started

How it works

Details that make bisect work in practice:

  • Exit code 125 means skip. Use it for commits that will not build; marking them bad blames the wrong change.
  • Path filters (git bisect start -- <paths>) can cut the candidate set dramatically.
  • git bisect log records the session; git bisect replay <file> reruns it. Save it before doing anything risky.
  • Bisect requires that the property is monotonic. If the bug was introduced, fixed, and reintroduced, bisect finds a transition, not necessarily the interesting one.
  • Merge commits complicate it. The build may be broken on one side of a merge; use --first-parent (Git 2.29+) to bisect only mainline commits, which is much more reliable when the history is full of feature merges.

This is also the strongest practical argument for atomic commits, small PRs, and against squash-merging everything (48.13): bisect's resolution is exactly your commit granularity. Landing a 4,000-line squashed commit means the best bisect can tell you is "it is somewhere in these 4,000 lines".

48.9.4 Reflog

Concept

The reflog is a per-ref journal of every value that ref has held, local to your clone. It is how you find commits that no branch points at any more.

How it works

Shell
$ git reflog                            # HEAD's history
$ git reflog show main                  # one branch's history
$ git reflog show --date=iso stash

$ git reflog
9f3c1a2 HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature/refunds
9f3c1a2 HEAD@{1}: rebase (pick): feat(orders): add partial refund support
4a1c2b9 HEAD@{2}: rebase (start): checkout origin/main
7b2e5d1 HEAD@{3}: commit: feat(orders): add partial refund support

HEAD@{3} is the pre-rebase tip. git branch pre-rebase 7b2e5d1 recreates it. You can also use time syntax: git show 'main@{2 days ago}', git diff 'HEAD@{yesterday}'.

The three facts to internalise: it is local only (a fresh clone has none), it expires (90 days, 30 for unreachable entries), and git gc --prune=now clears it immediately. Which means: never re-clone and never gc while recovering.

48.9.5 Detached HEAD

Concept

HEAD normally contains a symbolic ref (ref: refs/heads/main). In detached HEAD it contains a commit hash directly. You are on a commit, not on a branch. Commits you make advance HEAD but no branch follows, so when you switch away, nothing points at them.

When you meet it

Shell
$ git switch --detach v2.4.7
$ git checkout 9f3c1a2
$ git rebase -i main            # detached for the duration
$ git bisect start             # detached at each tested commit
Shell
$ git status
HEAD detached at v2.4.7
nothing to commit, working tree clean

Legitimate uses: inspecting an old release, testing a specific commit, building a tagged version, and every rebase and bisect (which is why understanding it matters even if you never detach deliberately).

The danger, and the fix:

Shell
$ git switch main
Warning: you are leaving 2 commits behind, not connected to
any of your branches:

  c8f1a92 experiment: try batching the pricing calls
  a3c9f04 experiment: measure with 500 concurrent orders

If you want to keep them by creating a new branch, this may be a good time
to do so with:

 git branch <new-branch-name> c8f1a92

Git warns you. If you miss the warning, the reflog still has them for 30 days:

Shell
$ git reflog | head -5
$ git branch experiments c8f1a92

The habit: the moment you make a commit in detached HEAD, create a branch. It costs 41 bytes and removes the entire class of problem.

48.10 The senior's toolbox

These are the commands that separate someone who uses Git from someone who investigates with it.

git log --oneline --graph --decorate. The single most useful log invocation. --graph draws the branch topology, --decorate shows which refs point where, --oneline keeps it readable.

Shell
$ git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all -12
*   3a9f04c (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Merge pull request #412 from acme/feature/refunds
|\
| * c8f1a92 (origin/feature/refunds) feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate key
| * a3c9f04 test(orders): cover duplicate key path
| * 5e1d8b7 feat(orders): add idempotency key column
|/
* 9f3c1a2 (tag: v2.4.6) chore: bump dependencies
* 4a1c2b9 fix(payments): reject refunds above the original charge

Add --first-parent to collapse merged branches and see only the mainline — the fastest way to answer "what features landed this week?" Alias it:

Shell
$ git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
$ git config --global alias.lgm "log --oneline --graph --decorate --first-parent"

git blame -w -C. Blame answers "who last touched this line, and in which commit?" The flags are what make it usable:

  • -w ignores whitespace changes, so a reformatting commit does not claim every line.
  • -C detects lines moved or copied within the same commit from other files. -C -C also looks at files the commit modified; -C -C -C searches all files in the parent commit.
  • -M detects moves within the same file.
  • -L 40,80 limits to a line range.
Shell
$ git blame -w -C -L 42,48 src/orders/pricing/pricing.service.ts
a3c9f04e (Sam Okafor 2025-07-24 16:12:03 +0100 42)   const subtotal = items.reduce(
5e1d8b7c (Priya Nair 2025-06-02 09:41:55 +0100 43)     (sum, i) => sum + i.priceMinor * i.qty, 0);
a3c9f04e (Sam Okafor 2025-07-24 16:12:03 +0100 44)   const tax = subtotal * rate;

Without -w -C, a file that was moved and reformatted shows one commit for every line and tells you nothing. Blame is a starting point, not an accusation: the commit it names is where the line arrived, and the message is what you actually wanted.

The pickaxe: log -S and log -G. Blame finds who last touched a line that exists. The pickaxe finds when a string appeared or disappeared anywhere in history — including in code that has since been deleted.

Shell
# Commits where the NUMBER OF OCCURRENCES of the string changed.
# This is how you find where something was introduced or removed.
$ git log -S 'ThrottlerGuard' --oneline
c8f1a92 feat(api): add rate limiting to public endpoints
3a9f04c Merge pull request #412 from acme/feature/refunds

# Commits whose diff MATCHES a regex (more matches, noisier).
$ git log -G 'Math\.round\(.*\* 100\)' --oneline -p

# Restrict to a path, and follow renames.
$ git log -S 'idempotencyKey' --oneline -- src/orders/
$ git log --follow --oneline -- src/orders/pricing/pricing.service.ts

-S is the one to reach for first. "When did this configuration value disappear?", "Which commit removed this guard?", "When was this feature flag introduced?" are all one command. It is the tool that found the silently-reverted rate limiter in 48.4.

git worktree. Multiple working directories from one repository, sharing the object store.

Shell
$ git worktree add ../orders-hotfix release/2.4
Preparing worktree (checking out 'release/2.4')

$ git worktree list
/home/priya/orders           9f3c1a2 [feature/refunds]
/home/priya/orders-hotfix    e4a9c02 [release/2.4]

$ git worktree remove ../orders-hotfix

Why this beats stashing: you keep your in-progress refactor untouched in one directory, fix the incident in another, and each has its own node_modules, its own running dev server and its own IDE window. On a large monorepo where a fresh clone takes eleven minutes and npm ci takes three, a worktree takes seconds because the objects are already there. The one rule: two worktrees cannot have the same branch checked out.

git sparse-checkout. Check out only part of the tree. Essential in a monorepo where you work on one service out of forty.

Shell
$ git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse git@github.com:acme/platform.git
$ cd platform
$ git sparse-checkout set services/orders libs/shared
$ git sparse-checkout list
services/orders
libs/shared

--filter=blob:none makes a partial clone: commit and tree objects are fetched, blobs only on demand. On a repository with ten years of history this can cut a 4 GB clone to 400 MB and eleven minutes to ninety seconds. The tradeoff is that operations needing historical file content (log -p, blame on old ranges) fetch blobs on demand and are slower offline.

Hooks, husky and lint-staged. Hooks are scripts in .git/hooks that Git runs at defined points. They are not versioned and not installed by clone, which is what husky solves: it stores hooks in the repository and points core.hooksPath at them on npm install.

JSON
{
  "scripts": { "prepare": "husky" },
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.ts": ["eslint --fix --max-warnings=0", "prettier --write"],
    "*.{json,md,yml}": ["prettier --write"]
  }
}
Shell
# .husky/pre-commit
npx lint-staged

# .husky/commit-msg
npx commitlint --edit "$1"

lint-staged runs tools only on staged files, so a pre-commit hook takes 2 seconds instead of 40. The discipline:

  • Hooks are a convenience, not a control. They run on developer machines, can be skipped with --no-verify, and do not run in CI. Every rule that matters must also be enforced in the pipeline (Part 47).
  • Keep pre-commit under about 3 seconds. A slow hook gets bypassed, and then it protects nothing.
  • Put lint and format in pre-commit, message validation in commit-msg, and anything slow (typecheck, tests) in pre-push at most — or better, only in CI.

.gitattributes and line endings. Windows uses CRLF, Linux and macOS use LF. Without configuration, the same file gets different blob hashes on different machines, producing phantom whole-file diffs and unresolvable conflicts.

The robust setup is a committed .gitattributes, because it applies to everyone regardless of their local config:

Text
# Normalise: LF in the repository, native on checkout where it matters.
* text=auto eol=lf

# Files that must stay LF even on Windows.
*.sh text eol=lf
Dockerfile text eol=lf

# Files that must be CRLF.
*.bat text eol=crlf

# Binary: never convert, never diff as text.
*.png binary
*.pdf binary
*.woff2 binary

# Generated: collapse in diffs and mark for review tooling.
package-lock.json linguist-generated=true -diff
dist/** linguist-generated=true

# Custom merge driver for lockfiles (see 30.14).
package-lock.json merge=ours

.gitattributes also controls export filtering (export-ignore), diff drivers per language, and LFS tracking.

Git LFS. Large File Storage replaces large binaries with small text pointers in Git, storing the real bytes on a separate server fetched on checkout.

Shell
$ git lfs install
$ git lfs track "*.psd" "*.mp4" "fixtures/*.sqlite"
$ git add .gitattributes

Use it for assets you genuinely must version: design files, video fixtures, ML model weights, large test fixtures. Do not use it as a general dumping ground — LFS storage costs money, git lfs pull is a new failure mode in CI, and not every host supports it identically. And critically: LFS only helps for files added after you enable it. Existing history keeps its blobs (48.1).

.gitignore patterns. The rules people get wrong:

Text
node_modules/          # trailing slash: directories only
dist/
*.log
.env                   # but NOT .env.example
.env.*
!.env.example          # negation re-includes
coverage/
*.tsbuildinfo

/build                 # leading slash: only at repository root
build/                 # anywhere in the tree
docs/**/tmp/           # ** matches across directories

Three facts that cause most confusion:

  1. .gitignore only affects untracked files. Adding config/local.json to .gitignore after committing it changes nothing. Use git rm --cached config/local.json to untrack it.
  2. A negation cannot re-include a file inside an excluded directory. logs/ followed by !logs/keep.txt does not work, because Git never descends into logs/. Write logs/* then !logs/keep.txt.
  3. .gitignore is not security. A file being ignored does not stop git add -f. Secrets are prevented by scanning and push protection (Part 47, section 47.6), not by ignore rules.

git check-ignore -v <path> tells you exactly which rule in which file matched.

Submodules versus subtrees versus a package. A submodule is a pointer from your repository to a specific commit in another repository. It sounds like the right answer for shared code and usually is not.

Approach Clone experience Update flow Failure mode
Submodule --recurse-submodules or an empty directory Enter submodule, commit, return, commit the pointer Detached HEAD inside; forgotten pointer commits; CI clones without --recurse-submodules and the build fails mysteriously; every engineer must learn a second workflow
Subtree Normal clone, files just there git subtree pull --prefix=libs/shared <remote> main --squash History gets noisy; pushing changes upstream is awkward
Published package Normal clone plus npm ci Version bump in package.json Requires a registry and a release process — which you already have

For a Node.js backend, the package almost always wins. You already run a registry (npm, GitHub Packages, Verdaccio, CodeArtifact), you already have semantic versioning, and consumers get an explicit version pin rather than an implicit commit pointer that half the team forgets to commit. Submodules earn their place for vendored third-party source you must build from, or for genuinely separate deliverables with independent lifecycles — not for "our shared types library".

48.11 Merge vs rebase, reset vs revert, merge vs cherry-pick

48.11.1 Merge versus rebase

Both integrate main into your feature branch. They differ in what history records.

Merge preserves the actual sequence of events and adds a commit with two parents:

Rebase replays your commits on top of main, producing new commits and a straight line:

Merge Rebase
History shape Branched graph, records reality Linear, records intent
Commit hashes Preserved New objects for every replayed commit
Safe on shared branches Yes No
Conflict resolution Once, at the merge Potentially once per commit (mitigate with rerere)
git bisect Works; merges can complicate it (use --first-parent) Cleanest possible
git log readability Noisy on busy repositories Very readable
Records "when this was integrated" Yes, explicitly No, that fact is erased
Recovery if it goes wrong git merge --abort git rebase --abort, or reflog

Decision guidance:

  • Updating your own unmerged feature branch from main: rebase. It keeps the PR diff clean and avoids "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commits that reviewers must scroll past.
  • A branch two or more people push to: merge. Rebasing rewrites objects others hold.
  • Integrating a finished feature into main: merge (usually --no-ff, or a squash — see 48.13). Never rebase main itself.
  • Tidying your own commits before review: interactive rebase.
  • Anything already released or tagged: never rebase.

The one-sentence rule: rebase your work onto other people's; merge other people's work into shared branches.

48.11.2 Reset versus revert

Both undo. They differ in whether history is rewritten.

Text
reset:   A - B - C - D          becomes   A - B          (C, D unreachable; force-push needed)
                     ^                        ^
                    main                     main

revert:  A - B - C - D          becomes   A - B - C - D - D' - C'
                     ^                                        ^
                    main                                     main
reset revert
Effect on history Rewrites: moves the branch pointer Extends: adds new commits
Safe after pushing to a shared branch No Yes
Requires force-push Yes No
Auditability The change vanishes from the branch Explicit record of what was undone and why
Can destroy uncommitted work Yes (--hard) No
Recovery Reflog Revert the revert
Typical use Cleaning up local commits, squashing Backing out a bad change from main during an incident

Decision guidance: ask one question — has anyone else pulled this? If no, reset is fine and often cleaner. If yes, revert, without exception. On main, develop or a release branch, the answer is always yes.

48.11.3 Merge versus cherry-pick

Both bring changes from one branch to another. They differ in whether the source history comes along.

Merge brings the whole branch and records the relationship, so the source commits become ancestors:

Cherry-pick copies one commit's change as a new commit; the source stays unrelated:

Merge Cherry-pick
What moves Every commit on the branch One commit's diff (or a range)
Hashes Preserved; source commits become ancestors New commits, unrelated to the source
Relationship recorded Yes, by the merge commit Only if you use -x
Duplicate changes later No Possible, especially if the pick conflicted
Typical use Integrating a finished feature Hotfix onto a release branch
Effect on git cherry Nothing to report Reports equivalence by patch id

Decision guidance:

  • You want everything from the branch: merge.
  • You want exactly one fix on a different line of development: cherry-pick with -x.
  • You find yourself cherry-picking routinely between long-lived branches: the branching strategy is wrong (48.12). Prefer fixing on the oldest supported branch and merging forward, which keeps one commit instead of two.
  • You want a subset of a branch because the rest is not ready: that is a signal the branch is doing too much. Split the work instead; a subset picked out of a coherent branch is rarely coherent on its own.

The one-sentence rule: merge moves history, cherry-pick copies a change. Everything surprising about cherry-pick follows from the word "copies".

48.12 Branching strategies

Concept

A branching strategy is a team agreement about which branches exist, what each one means, how work flows between them, and what triggers a release. Git supports any strategy; the strategy is a people decision, and it is where most teams' Git pain actually originates.

Why does it exist?

Because without an agreement, everyone invents their own, and the repository becomes a set of long-lived branches nobody dares merge. The strategy determines your integration frequency, and integration frequency determines merge cost, which is superlinear in divergence.

Mental model

Imagine a river system. Trunk-based development is one wide river: everyone paddles in the same water and any obstruction is immediately visible. Git Flow is a canal network with locks: safe, controlled, and every boat spends time waiting at gates. GitHub Flow is a river with short side channels that rejoin within a day.

The right answer depends on one thing: how many versions of your software are alive at once? A SaaS backend has one. A shipped on-premises product has several. Almost every argument about branching strategies is really an argument about that question with the question left unstated.

48.12.1 Git Flow

Five branch types: main (released code, tagged), develop (integration), feature/* (branched from and merged to develop), release/* (stabilisation, branched from develop, merged to both main and develop), hotfix/* (branched from main, merged to both).

Fits: teams shipping versioned software on a schedule to customers who install it — desktop applications, mobile releases tied to app store review, on-premises enterprise products, firmware. Anything where several versions are supported simultaneously and a release must be stabilised for days.

Cadence: weeks to months.

Failure mode: applied to a web backend that deploys continuously, it is pure overhead. develop and main diverge, every change is merged two or three times, hotfixes must be merged to both branches and someone always forgets one — so a bug fixed in production reappears in the next release. The double bookkeeping produces the classic symptom: "the fix is in main but not in develop", found weeks later by a customer. If you deploy main on every merge, develop has no purpose except to delay integration.

48.12.2 GitHub Flow

One long-lived branch: main, always deployable. Short-lived branches off main, a pull request, review, CI, merge, deploy. That is the whole model.

Fits: web services and SaaS backends with one live version, continuous deployment, and a team that can review quickly. This is the correct default for the stack this book targets.

Cadence: several times a day.

Failure mode: it depends entirely on branches being short-lived and main genuinely being deployable. A team that lets branches live two weeks has invented Git Flow's problems without Git Flow's release branch to contain them. It also has no answer for "we need to patch version 2.3 for a customer still on it" — if that requirement appears, you need release branches.

48.12.3 Trunk-based development

Everyone commits to main (the trunk), either directly or through branches that live hours, not days. Unfinished work ships behind feature flags (Part 47, section 47.8). Releases are cut as tags on main, or as short-lived release branches that receive only cherry-picked fixes.

Fits: teams with strong CI, comprehensive tests, feature flags and a culture of small changes. It is the model most strongly associated with elite DORA performance (Part 47, section 47.12), and the mechanism is simple: integration cost is near zero when the integration interval is four hours.

Cadence: continuous, many merges a day.

Failure mode: without the supporting practices it is chaos. Trunk-based development requires that main is never broken, which requires fast reliable tests, a merge queue or pre-merge CI on the combined result, and flags for anything incomplete. A team that adopts "commit to main" without those breaks main daily and blocks everyone.

48.12.4 Release branches, hotfixes and monorepos

Release branches. Even in GitHub Flow or trunk-based development, you need one the moment you must support a version that is not the tip of main. The pattern:

Shell
# Cut the release branch at the commit you are releasing.
$ git switch -c release/2.4 v2.4.0
$ git push -u origin release/2.4

Rules that keep release branches from becoming Git Flow by accident:

  • A release branch receives only fixes, never features.
  • Fix on the oldest supported branch, then merge forward: release/2.3 into release/2.4 into main. This produces one commit and avoids the cherry-pick duplication of 48.6. Cherry-pick backwards only when merging forward is impossible.
  • Every release branch has an end-of-life date, published. Without one, you accumulate seven supported versions and a permanent merge burden.
  • Protect release branches like main: reviews, CI, no force-push.

Hotfix flow, end to end:

Shell
$ git switch release/2.4 && git pull
$ git switch -c hotfix/ORD-4402-over-refund
# fix, with a regression test
$ git commit -m "fix(payments): reject refunds above the original charge"
$ git push -u origin hotfix/ORD-4402-over-refund
# PR into release/2.4, expedited review, CI green
$ git switch release/2.4 && git pull
$ git tag -a v2.4.7 -m "Hotfix: reject over-refunds"
$ git push origin v2.4.7
# then merge forward so the fix is not lost in the next release
$ git switch main && git pull
$ git merge release/2.4
$ git push

The merge-forward step is the one people skip at 23:00, and it is how a fixed bug returns in the next release. Automate it: a scheduled job that opens a PR merging each release branch forward, failing loudly if it conflicts.

Monorepo considerations. One repository holding many services changes several things:

  • Branch naming needs a scope, because fix/timeout is ambiguous across 40 services: fix/orders/ORD-4402-timeout.
  • CI must be path-filtered. Running all 40 services' tests on every PR is unaffordable. Use paths: filters or a build graph tool (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel) to test only what changed and what depends on it.
  • CODEOWNERS per directory routes review to the owning team automatically.
  • Merge queues become essential, because 40 engineers merging into one branch means constant "required branches to be up to date" churn without one.
  • Sparse checkout and partial clone (48.10) keep local working copies manageable.
  • Tags need prefixes: orders-api/v2.4.7, not v2.4.7, or two services cannot both release.
  • git log -- services/orders becomes the default way to read history; teach it early.

48.12.5 Choosing

Git Flow GitHub Flow Trunk-based
Long-lived branches main, develop, releases main main
Branch lifetime Days to weeks Hours to days Hours
Live versions supported Many One One (plus release tags)
Deploy cadence Scheduled, weeks On merge, daily Continuous
Requires feature flags No Helpful Yes
Requires fast reliable CI Helpful Yes Absolutely
Merge pain High Low Very low
Hotfix complexity Defined but heavy Needs a release branch bolted on Cherry-pick or merge forward
Best for Installed/versioned products SaaS backends, most web teams High-performing teams with flags and strong CI

How a senior engineer decides: start from how many versions must be alive. One version and continuous deployment means GitHub Flow, moving toward trunk-based as CI and flags mature. Multiple supported versions means release branches, regardless of what you call the rest. develop is only justified when there is a genuine stabilisation phase that main cannot host — and for a service that deploys on every merge, there is not.

The strategy also has to match the tests. Trunk-based development with a 40-minute flaky suite is a broken main every afternoon. Fix the pipeline first (Part 47), then shorten the branches.

48.13 The pull request workflow at senior level

Concept

A pull request is a proposal to merge, plus the review conversation and the automated checks around it. Everything in this section is about making that proposal easy to say yes or no to.

Why small PRs get better reviews

This is not a style preference; it is a measurable effect. Review effectiveness collapses as diff size grows. Reviewers reliably find defects in changes up to roughly 200–400 lines; beyond that, comments shift from logic to naming and formatting, and above about 1,000 lines most reviews become an approval with a "looks good".

The mechanism is simple: a reviewer holds the change in working memory to reason about it. When it no longer fits, they stop reasoning and start skimming. A 900-line PR does not get 3x the scrutiny of a 300-line one; it gets less scrutiny in total, because the reviewer gives up.

Concretely, small PRs also: get reviewed sooner (a 60-line diff gets picked up in minutes, a 900-line one waits for someone to find an hour), conflict less, bisect better, and revert cleanly. If a change is genuinely large, split it: interface first, then implementation, then the call sites; or ship it behind a flag in three PRs.

Stacked PRs are how you keep them small without blocking: PR 2 targets PR 1's branch rather than main, and its diff shows only the increment. When PR 1 merges, PR 2 retargets to main. It costs some rebasing discipline and pays for itself immediately on any change over about 400 lines.

Description templates

The description is where the author does the reviewer's work for them. A template in .github/pull_request_template.md:

Markdown
## What and why
<!-- What changes, and what problem it solves. Link the ticket. -->

## Approach
<!-- Why this design. What alternatives you rejected and why. -->

## Risk
<!-- What could break. Blast radius. Is it behind a flag? -->

## Database
<!-- Migrations? Backward compatible? Expand/contract stage? -->

## Rollback
<!-- How do we undo this if it goes wrong in production? -->

## How to verify
<!-- Exact steps or commands a reviewer can run. -->

## Screenshots / output

The Rollback and Database sections are the senior additions, and they change behaviour before review even starts. An author who cannot fill in "how do we undo this" usually discovers the design problem themselves and restructures the change. That is the template earning its keep.

Draft PRs

Open a draft the moment you push the first commit. It costs nothing and buys three things: CI runs on every push so you find breakage early; colleagues can see direction before you have spent three days on it; and the PR body becomes the place you accumulate context while it is fresh, instead of reconstructing it at the end.

Mark it ready for review only when CI is green and you would be comfortable with it merging as-is. "Ready for review" with failing checks wastes a reviewer's time and trains people to ignore your notifications.

Review etiquette

For the reviewer:

  • Review within four hours during working hours. A PR waiting a day is a branch diverging, an author context-switching, and a queue forming behind it. Fast review is the highest-leverage thing a senior can do for team throughput.
  • Distinguish blocking from non-blocking. Prefix: blocking: for correctness, security or data-loss issues; nit: for preferences; question: when you genuinely do not know; praise: when something is good, which costs nothing and makes the rest land better.
  • Comment on the code, not the person. "This query has no index on customer_id and will sequential-scan at 40M rows" rather than "you forgot the index again".
  • Give the reason, not just the instruction. A review comment is teaching material.
  • Approve with comments when the remaining points are nits. Blocking a PR over naming is a tax on the whole team.
  • If you cannot review it properly, say so. "This is 1,400 lines and I cannot review it meaningfully; can we split it?" is a legitimate and useful review.

For the author:

  • Respond to every comment, even with "done" or "disagree, because X".
  • Push fixes as --fixup commits during review (48.5) so reviewers see increments, then autosquash before merge.
  • Do not force-push mid-review unless you must; it destroys the reviewer's "changes since my last review" view. If you must, say so in a comment.
  • Never merge over an unresolved blocking comment.

Squash vs merge vs rebase-merge

Three merge strategies, three different histories, and a real consequence for git bisect.

Strategy What lands on main History Effect on bisect Effect on revert
Merge commit (--no-ff) Every branch commit, plus a merge commit Branched graph; --first-parent shows features Full granularity; merges need --first-parent to be reliable revert -m 1 undoes the whole feature in one command
Squash merge One commit containing the whole PR Perfectly linear Resolution is the whole PR; a 900-line PR is one bisect step One revert undoes the whole PR; cannot revert part of it
Rebase merge Every branch commit, replayed, no merge commit Perfectly linear Best possible: every commit, no merge complications Revert individual commits; no single "undo the feature" commit

Policy in practice:

  • Squash merge is the pragmatic default for most teams, because it makes branch hygiene irrelevant: authors can commit "wip" freely and main stays clean. The price is bisect granularity. It is a good trade if PRs are small. It is a bad trade if PRs are 900 lines, because you have converted a fine-grained history into a coarse one exactly where you needed detail. Squash merge and large PRs are the combination to avoid.
  • Rebase merge gives the best history and the best bisect, but requires that authors curate their commits (interactive rebase before merge) and that every commit builds. Worth it for teams that will do that; frustrating for teams that will not.
  • Merge commits preserve the most information and make feature-level revert trivial. On a busy repository the graph gets dense, though --first-parent largely solves that.

Whichever you pick, pick one and configure the repository to allow only that. A repository where all three are enabled produces a history nobody can reason about.

Protecting main

The rules worth enforcing on main:

  • Require a pull request; no direct pushes.
  • Require at least one approval, two for high-risk paths (payments, auth, migrations) via CODEOWNERS.
  • Require status checks: point at the single ci-complete job (Part 47, section 47.11) rather than listing every job.
  • Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed.
  • Require conversation resolution before merge.
  • Require signed commits (48.2).
  • Block force-push and deletion.
  • Include administrators. A protection that admins can bypass is a protection that gets bypassed at 17:55 on a Friday.
  • Use a merge queue on busy repositories, so CI runs on the actual combined result rather than on each PR in isolation. This is the only defence against semantic conflicts (48.4).

CODEOWNERS

A .github/CODEOWNERS file maps paths to owning teams and auto-requests their review:

Text
# Default owners for everything.
*                             @acme/backend

# High-risk areas need their owners, and two approvals via branch protection.
/src/payments/                @acme/payments @acme/security
/src/auth/                    @acme/security
/src/migrations/              @acme/dba @acme/backend

# Infrastructure and pipeline changes.
/.github/workflows/           @acme/platform
/charts/                      @acme/platform
/terraform/                   @acme/platform

# Generated code: nobody needs to review it, but flag changes.
/src/generated/               @acme/backend

Two cautions. First, CODEOWNERS creates bottlenecks: if one small team owns a path every other team touches daily, that team becomes a queue. Review ownership boundaries when review latency rises. Second, a CODEOWNERS entry on /.github/workflows/ is genuinely important — a PR that edits the pipeline can disable the checks that gate it, which is a privilege escalation path (Part 47, section 47.4).

48.14 Recovery scenarios

Seven procedures, step by step. Print them; you will need them under pressure, and under pressure is exactly when people improvise badly.

48.14.1 A secret was pushed

Order of operations matters more than the commands.

Step 1 — Rotate first. Before touching Git, invalidate the credential. Rewriting history does not un-read the secret: it was on the remote, in CI logs, in forks, in clones, in caches, and possibly in an attacker's hands. Time-to-abuse for a leaked cloud key is measured in minutes.

Shell
# Example: AWS. Create a new key, deploy it, then delete the old one.
$ aws iam create-access-key --user-name svc-orders
# update the secret store and redeploy, verify, then:
$ aws iam delete-access-key --user-name svc-orders --access-key-id AKIA...

Step 2 — Assess exposure. Check provider access logs (CloudTrail, database audit logs) for use of the credential from unexpected sources, and record the exposure window: first push time to revocation time.

Step 3 — Rewrite history. Use git filter-repo (BFG is an alternative; filter-branch is deprecated and dangerously slow).

Shell
$ pip install git-filter-repo

# Work on a mirror so you never damage anyone's working copy.
$ git clone --mirror git@github.com:acme/orders-api.git orders-api-mirror
$ cd orders-api-mirror

# Option A: remove a file from all history.
$ git filter-repo --invert-paths --path config/production.env

# Option B: redact a string but keep the file.
$ printf 'AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE==>REDACTED\n' > /tmp/replacements.txt
$ git filter-repo --replace-text /tmp/replacements.txt

# filter-repo removes the remote to prevent accidental pushes. Re-add it.
$ git remote add origin git@github.com:acme/orders-api.git

Step 4 — Coordinate the force-push. This rewrites every commit hash after the earliest affected commit, so every open branch and every clone is affected. Do it deliberately:

  1. Announce a freeze. Ask everyone to push work and stop.

  2. Temporarily disable branch protection on the affected branches (an admin action, logged).

  3. Push:

    Shell
    $ git push --force --all
$ git push --force --tags

  4. Re-enable branch protection immediately.

  5. Tell everyone to re-clone. Do not tell them to pull: pulling merges the old and new histories and reintroduces the secret.

  6. Ask the hosting provider to garbage-collect and to expire cached views of the old commits. On GitHub, old commits can remain reachable via the API by SHA and in forks; open a support request, and remember that any fork is a separate repository you cannot rewrite.

Step 5 — Prevent recurrence. Enable server-side push protection, add Gitleaks pre-commit and CI (Part 47, section 47.6), and move the credential to a secret manager.

48.14.2 A force-push overwrote a teammate

Their commits are unreachable on the remote but still exist in their local reflog, and often in the remote's reflog too.

Shell
# On the teammate's machine, or any clone that had fetched the old state:
$ git reflog show origin/feature/checkout
7b2e5d1 refs/remotes/origin/feature/checkout@{0}: fetch: forced-update
c8f1a92 refs/remotes/origin/feature/checkout@{1}: fetch: fast-forward

# c8f1a92 is the pre-force-push tip. Recreate it.
$ git branch rescue/checkout c8f1a92

# Find what was lost relative to the current remote state.
$ git log --oneline origin/feature/checkout..rescue/checkout

# Reapply onto the current branch.
$ git switch feature/checkout
$ git cherry-pick <each missing sha>
$ git push

If no local clone has it, check whether the host does: GitHub's Events API and the branch's activity log often retain the overwritten SHA, and a commit can be fetched by SHA even when no ref points at it (git fetch origin <sha>).

Prevention: --force-with-lease instead of --force, and branch protection blocking force-push on shared branches.

48.14.3 Committed to the wrong branch

You made three commits on main that belong on a feature branch, and you have not pushed.

Shell
# 1. Create the branch here, capturing the commits.
$ git branch feature/refunds

# 2. Move main back to where it should be.
$ git reset --hard origin/main

# 3. Continue on the feature branch.
$ git switch feature/refunds

If you already pushed to main and it is protected/shared, do not reset. Revert on main and cherry-pick onto the feature branch:

Shell
$ git switch feature/refunds
$ git cherry-pick <sha1> <sha2> <sha3>
$ git switch main
$ git revert --no-commit <sha3> <sha2> <sha1>     # newest first
$ git commit -m "Revert: move refund work to feature/refunds (pushed to main in error)"

If only the last, unpushed commit is on the wrong branch, the quick form is:

Shell
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1        # uncommit, keep changes staged
$ git switch -c feature/refunds  # take the staged changes with you
$ git commit -c ORIG_HEAD        # reuse the original message

48.14.4 Splitting one commit into three

Shell
$ git rebase -i HEAD~4
# mark the target commit with `edit`, save.

Stopped at 7b2e5d1... feat(orders): idempotency, logging and a dependency bump

# Undo the commit, keeping the changes in the working tree, unstaged.
$ git reset HEAD^

$ git status --short
 M src/orders/orders.service.ts
 M package.json
 M package-lock.json
 M src/common/logging.interceptor.ts

# Stage and commit each logical piece. Use -p to split within a file.
$ git add -p src/orders/orders.service.ts
$ git commit -m "feat(orders): return existing order on duplicate idempotency key"

$ git add src/common/logging.interceptor.ts
$ git commit -m "feat(observability): log idempotency key on order creation"

$ git add package.json package-lock.json
$ git commit -m "build(deps): bump pg to 8.13.1"

$ git rebase --continue
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/refunds.

Verify each commit builds and tests independently before continuing — that is the whole point of splitting.

48.14.5 Moving commits to a new branch

Five commits on feature/a; the last two belong on feature/b.

Shell
# 1. Branch at the current tip, capturing all five.
$ git branch feature/b

# 2. Drop the last two from feature/a.
$ git switch feature/a
$ git reset --hard HEAD~2

# 3. feature/b has all five; replay only its own two onto main.
$ git rebase --onto main feature/a feature/b

--onto (48.5) is what makes step 3 precise: replay the commits in feature/a..feature/b — exactly the two — onto main.

If either branch was pushed, --force-with-lease and tell anyone who might have pulled.

48.14.6 A package-lock.json conflict

Never resolve a lockfile by hand and never take one side wholesale. The lockfile is a derived artifact: resolve the source of truth (package.json) and regenerate.

Shell
$ git status --short
UU package.json
UU package-lock.json

# 1. Resolve package.json manually. Keep BOTH sides' dependency additions
#    unless they genuinely conflict on the same package.
$ git checkout --conflict=diff3 package.json
# edit, remove markers
$ git add package.json

# 2. Regenerate the lockfile from the resolved package.json.
$ git checkout --theirs package-lock.json     # any valid starting point
$ npm install --package-lock-only             # rewrites the lock to match package.json
$ git add package-lock.json

# 3. Prove it actually installs and the app still works.
$ rm -rf node_modules && npm ci
$ npm run build && npm run test:unit

$ git merge --continue

If npm install --package-lock-only produces a large unexpected diff, delete the lockfile and run npm install fresh, then review the diff for unintended major version jumps.

You can reduce the frequency of these conflicts with a .gitattributes entry marking the lockfile as generated (package-lock.json -diff linguist-generated=true), which does not prevent the conflict but stops it from dominating the PR diff. Some teams go further with a custom merge driver that always regenerates; that is a per-team decision.

48.14.7 Work "lost" after a bad rebase

Shell
# 1. Find where the branch was before the rebase started.
$ git reflog show feature/refunds
9f3c1a2 feature/refunds@{0}: rebase (finish): refs/heads/feature/refunds onto 4a1c2b9
c8f1a92 feature/refunds@{1}: rebase (start): checkout origin/main
7b2e5d1 feature/refunds@{2}: commit: feat(orders): add partial refund support

feature/refunds@{2} (or the entry immediately before rebase (start)) is the pre-rebase state.

Shell
# 2. Recover non-destructively into a new branch first. Never reset --hard
#    as your first move during a recovery.
$ git branch rescue/pre-rebase 7b2e5d1

# 3. Compare and confirm before doing anything else.
$ git log --oneline feature/refunds..rescue/pre-rebase
$ git diff feature/refunds rescue/pre-rebase

# 4. Either reset the branch back, or cherry-pick the missing commits.
$ git switch feature/refunds
$ git reset --hard rescue/pre-rebase
# or
$ git cherry-pick <missing shas>

If the reflog has been pruned or you are on a fresh clone, git fsck finds unreachable objects directly:

Shell
$ git fsck --lost-found --no-reflog
dangling commit 7b2e5d1a9c8f4e3b2a1d0c9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a
$ git show 7b2e5d1
$ git branch rescue 7b2e5d1

The two rules for any recovery: do not gc, do not re-clone. Both destroy the evidence you are trying to recover.

48.15 Edge cases and failure modes

  • Force-push to a shared branch. Everyone's history diverges; commits based on the old tip are orphaned and pulls produce duplicated changes. Notice: colleagues report "my commits are gone" or a pull that produces dozens of conflicts. Fix: --force-with-lease by default, block force-push in branch protection, and recover through the remote-tracking reflog (48.14.2).

  • Rebasing published history. The same damage as above, arrived at differently. Notice: a PR whose commit count doubles after someone pulls. Fix: the golden rule — merge into shared branches, rebase only your own.

  • Giant binaries bloating the repository forever. A 6 MB fixture committed 340 times is 1.9 GB in the packfile, permanently, because every historical commit references its blob. Notice: clone time, git count-objects -vH. Fix: LFS or an artifact store going forward; history rewriting with filter-repo if it is worth the coordination cost. Prevention: a pre-commit hook or a CI check rejecting files over, say, 5 MB.

  • Line-ending chaos across operating systems. Without normalisation, a Windows checkout writes CRLF, the file is committed with CRLF, and Linux engineers see the entire file as changed. Notice: whole-file diffs with no visible change; git diff showing ^M; unresolvable conflicts. Fix: commit .gitattributes with * text=auto eol=lf (48.10); normalise once with git add --renormalize . and commit; note that shell scripts with CRLF fail in containers with a confusing bad interpreter error.

  • reset --hard destroying uncommitted work. No reflog entry exists because the changes were never objects. Notice: immediate and irreversible. Fix: none after the fact beyond IDE local history. Prevention: git stash -u or a wip commit before any destructive operation.

  • The reverted-merge trap. After reverting a merge, re-merging the same branch brings in nothing, because its commits are already ancestors (48.8). Notice: a clean merge with an empty or tiny diff and a missing feature. Fix: revert the revert, rebase the branch, or reapply on a fresh branch. Prevention: state the warning in the revert commit message.

  • Commits orphaned in detached HEAD. Committing on a checked-out SHA and switching away leaves them unreferenced. Notice: Git's "you are leaving N commits behind" warning, which is easy to scroll past. Fix: git reflog, then git branch <name> <sha>, within 30 days. Prevention: create a branch as soon as you commit while detached.

  • Long-lived branches and integration hell. Divergence cost grows superlinearly. Notice: a merge with 60 conflicting files. Fix: nothing good at that point; merge in stages, from the merge base forward, with tests between stages. Prevention: branches under two days, feature flags for incomplete work, expand/contract for schema changes.

  • Squash merges destroying bisect granularity. A 900-line PR becomes one commit; bisect narrows to it and stops. Notice: bisect "finds" a commit whose diff is unreviewable. Fix: none retroactively. Prevention: small PRs, or rebase-merge for large ones.

  • Moved tags after a release. git tag -f v2.4.7 && git push --force origin v2.4.7. Anyone who fetched before sees the old commit; anyone after sees the new one, and git describe-based version strings become ambiguous. Notice: two builds claiming the same version with different content. Fix: never move a release tag; cut v2.4.8. Enforce with protected tags on the host.

  • Hooks that do not run in CI. Client-side hooks live on developer machines and are skippable with --no-verify. A team that enforces lint only through husky ships unlinted code the moment someone clones without running npm install. Notice: main failing checks that "always pass locally". Fix: every hook-enforced rule must also be a CI job (Part 47). Hooks are for fast feedback, not enforcement.

  • Case-insensitive filesystem rename problems. On Windows and macOS (default settings), git mv Orders.ts orders.ts appears to do nothing, because the filesystem considers them the same file. Later, a Linux CI runner or a colleague on a case-sensitive filesystem sees two files, or an import fails with a name that resolves locally and not in the container. Notice: "module not found" only in Docker or CI. Fix: rename in two steps (git mv Orders.ts tmp.ts && git mv tmp.ts orders.ts), or git config core.ignorecase false with care. Prevention: a CI check for paths differing only by case (git ls-files | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -d).

  • Shallow clones breaking version tooling. git clone --depth 1 or actions/checkout with the default fetch-depth: 1 fetches no tags and one commit, so git describe --tags fails and semantic-release cannot determine the last release. Notice: version strings like 0.0.0-development, or "fatal: No names found". Fix: fetch-depth: 0 (and fetch-tags: true) for jobs that need history; keep depth 1 for jobs that do not, because full history costs real time on a large repository.

  • git pull creating surprise merge commits. A feature branch with "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commits interleaved through it, making the PR diff unreadable. Fix: git config --global pull.ff only so a non-fast-forward pull fails and you decide explicitly.

  • Submodule pointer not committed. You update the submodule but forget to commit the new pointer in the parent; CI builds the old version. Notice: works locally, fails in CI, with no diff explaining why. Fix: prefer a published package (48.10); if you must use submodules, add a CI check that the submodule pointer matches an expected ref.

  • .gitignore added after the file was committed. The file stays tracked and keeps being committed. Notice: .env changes appearing in diffs despite being "ignored". Fix: git rm --cached <file>, commit, and treat any secret in it as leaked (48.14.1).

  • Committer identity wrong. A personal email on a work laptop; commits do not attribute to the corporate account and may fail a CLA or a signed-commit policy. Fix: per-directory config with includeIf "gitdir:~/work/" in ~/.gitconfig.

  • Merge queue absent on a busy repository. Two independently green PRs break main together (a semantic conflict). Notice: main red immediately after two rapid merges. Fix: a merge queue that tests the combined result before merging.

Senior Checklist — Part 48

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can walk an object graph with git cat-file -p and explain what each object contains
  • I can explain why commits are snapshots and why rebase produces new hashes
  • I can describe exactly what reset --soft, --mixed and --hard move, and what is unrecoverable
  • I can recover lost commits from the reflog and from git fsck without re-cloning
  • I can resolve a conflict correctly using zdiff3 and prove I did not silently revert either side
  • I can run an interactive rebase with --autosquash and produce atomic, individually testable commits
  • I can state the golden rule of rebasing and say exactly why it matters
  • I can revert a merge with the correct -m value and explain the revert-of-a-revert trap
  • I can find the commit that introduced a bug with git bisect run and a test script
  • I can use git log -S to find when code was added or removed, including code since deleted
  • I can choose a branching strategy from the number of live versions and the deploy cadence
  • I can explain what squash merging does to git bisect and when that trade is acceptable
  • I can execute the leaked-secret procedure in the right order, starting with rotation
  • I can set up .gitattributes, hooks and branch protection so a team avoids whole categories of accident

Part 48 — Key Takeaways

  • Git is a content-addressed object store: blobs, trees, commits and tags, named by the hash of their content. Every command makes sense once that does.
  • Commits are snapshots with parents, not diffs; packfiles use deltas only as a storage detail below the model.
  • A branch is a 41-byte file holding a commit hash. Creating one is free; keeping one alive for three weeks is not.
  • Anything that was ever committed is recoverable through the reflog for weeks; anything never committed is gone the instant reset --hard runs.
  • Rebase and amend create new commit objects and abandon the old ones, which is the entire reason the golden rule about shared branches exists.
  • Rebase your work onto other people's; merge other people's work into shared branches. Revert on anything published, reset only on what is still yours.
  • Turn on merge.conflictstyle=zdiff3: seeing the merge base is what stops you silently reverting a colleague's change while resolving a conflict.
  • Reverting a merge does not un-merge the branch. Re-merging afterwards brings in nothing, so revert the revert or rebase the branch.
  • Cherry-pick copies a change into a new commit; always use -x, and treat a pick that needed conflict resolution as a different change.
  • git bisect run with a test script and a path filter turns "somewhere in 400 commits" into six automated steps and a 40-line diff.
  • git log -S finds when a string appeared or disappeared anywhere in history, including in code that no longer exists. It is the most underused command in Git.
  • Choose a branching strategy from how many versions are live, not from fashion; develop earns its place only when there is a real stabilisation phase.
  • Small pull requests get genuinely better reviews; above roughly 400 lines reviewers stop reasoning and start skimming.
  • Squash merging keeps history tidy and destroys bisect granularity; it is a good trade only while PRs stay small.
  • When a secret is pushed, rotate first. History rewriting is cleanup, not containment, and it never un-reads what was already public.

49.1 The SRE mindset

49.1.1 Reliability is a feature with a price

Concept

Site Reliability Engineering is what you get when you treat operations as a software problem and reliability as a product feature that has a cost. Not a virtue. Not a moral position. A feature, with a price tag, that competes for engineering time against every other feature.

That single reframing changes every conversation. "Should we be more reliable?" has only one answer and it is useless. "Is the checkout API's 99.9 percent worth spending two engineer-months to make it 99.99 percent, given that the last six months of outages cost us 41 lakh rupees in lost orders?" is a question a business can actually answer.

Everything else in this part — SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, incident process, postmortems — is machinery for having that conversation with data.

Why does it exist?

Because without it, two failure modes dominate, and both are expensive.

Under-investment. Nobody owns reliability. The team ships features. Outages are treated as bad luck. The same incident happens four times because nothing forced a fix. Customers leave quietly.

Over-investment. A team traumatized by one outage builds five nines of infrastructure for an internal admin tool used by nine people. Every deploy needs three approvals. Shipping slows to a crawl. The company loses to a competitor who shipped.

The right amount of reliability is the least that keeps users happy and the business safe, because every increment beyond that is engineering time not spent on something users would rather have. Going from 99.9 percent to 99.99 percent typically means multi-region, active-active data, automated failover, and a large increase in on-call load. If your users cannot tell the difference, you paid for nothing.

Mental model

Imagine a courier company. Nobody promises every parcel arrives. They promise a rate — "98 percent of next-day parcels arrive next day" — and they design the network, the depots and the staffing to hit that rate at a cost that still leaves a margin. Promising 100 percent would mean a van per parcel. The promise is a business decision; the operations are how you keep it.

Your API is the courier. The SLO is the promise. The error budget is the parcels you are allowed to be late with.

49.1.2 Toil

Concept

Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and grows linearly with the size of the service. Restarting a stuck pod every Tuesday. Manually clearing a queue. Running the same five kubectl commands to onboard a customer. Copying numbers into a spreadsheet for the weekly report.

Toil is not "work I dislike". Debugging a novel outage is unpleasant and is not toil, because it produces understanding. Toil produces nothing that lasts.

Why it matters

Toil scales with your system and your engineers do not. A team spending 15 percent of its time on toil at 20 services will spend 45 percent at 60 services, and then it stops shipping anything. Google's classic guidance — cap toil at 50 percent of an SRE's time — exists because teams reliably drift past it without noticing.

The discipline: measure it, then delete it. In every retro, name the top toil item. Every quarter, one engineer's time goes to eliminating it. Concretely, in a NestJS shop, this looks like:

Toil Elimination
Manually replaying failed jobs from Redis with a CLI An admin endpoint with filtering, caps and spacing (Part 36)
Restarting a pod when the event loop wedges A liveness probe that detects it, plus fixing the blocking code
Running a migration by hand at 2 a.m. Expand-contract migrations in CI (Part 24)
Answering "is the site up?" in Slack A status page and a public dashboard
Granting a customer a refund by SQL A support tool with an audit log
Copying incident timelines into a doc An incident bot that timestamps every command

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They notice the second time they do something manually, and they say so out loud. They also resist the opposite failure: automating a three-times-a-year task with a framework nobody maintains. The test is frequency x time x risk versus the cost of automation plus its own maintenance.

49.1.3 Error budgets as the arbitration mechanism

Concept

If the SLO is 99.9 percent successful requests over 30 days, then 0.1 percent of requests are allowed to fail. That allowance is the error budget. It is not a target to hit; it is a resource to spend.

This is the piece that makes SRE work as an organizational practice rather than a set of dashboards. Before error budgets, the argument goes:

Product: "Ship the new checkout on Friday." Engineering: "It feels risky." Product: "Everything feels risky to you."

That argument is settled by seniority and volume. After error budgets:

Engineering: "We have 8 percent of the month's error budget left with 11 days to go. Our policy says feature freeze below 10 percent. The checkout change ships after we land the two reliability fixes, or we agree to burn the rest of the budget and accept a possible SLA breach."

Same disagreement. Now it is arithmetic, agreed in advance, and both sides can read the same graph. The budget converts an argument about feelings into an argument about a number, and — this is the part people miss — it gives product the right to spend it. A team sitting at 97 percent of its budget unspent every month is over-invested in reliability and should be shipping faster.

49.2 SLI: what to actually measure

49.2.1 The four kinds that matter

Concept

A Service Level Indicator is a number, between 0 and 1, that says what fraction of something was good. Always a ratio. Always "good events divided by valid events". If you cannot express it that way, it is a diagnostic metric, not an SLI.

CPU is not an SLI. Memory is not an SLI. Pod count is not an SLI. Users do not experience CPU.

Four families cover almost everything:

Availability — the fraction of requests that succeeded.

Text
good  = requests that returned a non-5xx response
valid = all requests that reached us, excluding client errors we consider the client's fault
SLI   = good / valid

Latency — the fraction of requests served faster than a threshold. Note the shape: it is a ratio, not a percentile. "99 percent of checkout requests complete in under 800 ms" is an SLI. "p99 is 800 ms" is the same statement viewed sideways, but the ratio form composes with error budgets and the percentile form does not.

Correctness — the fraction of outputs that were right. Harder to measure and often the one that matters most. For checkout: the fraction of orders whose total equals the sum of their lines, or the fraction of paid orders that have a matching payment record.

Freshness — the fraction of data younger than some age. For a search index: the fraction of product updates visible in search within 60 seconds. For a queue (Part 36): the fraction of jobs started within 5 minutes of enqueue.

49.2.2 Measure from the user's side

Why does it exist?

This is the single most common SLI mistake, and it is worth stating bluntly: if you measure inside your service, you will miss the outages your users actually saw.

A NestJS pod that has crashed emits no metrics. Its request counter simply stops. Your sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) drops, and your error ratio — errors divided by requests — looks fine, because both numerator and denominator went to zero. Meanwhile the load balancer is returning 502 to every customer.

The same blindness hides: TLS handshake failures, ingress misconfiguration, DNS problems, connection-pool exhaustion at the proxy, requests killed by a timeout at the gateway before your handler returned, and every request that never reached a pod because there were no healthy pods.

Order of preference:

  1. Real user monitoring in the browser or mobile app. It includes DNS, TLS, network and client rendering. It is also noisy, includes users on trains, and is hard to alert on. Use it to validate, not usually to page.
  2. The load balancer or ingress. ALB access logs, nginx-ingress metrics, Envoy stats. This sees every request that reached your infrastructure, including the ones your pods never answered. This is where your availability SLI should come from.
  3. The service itself. Rich, cheap, well-labelled by route. Excellent for diagnostics and for latency distributions. Use it, but know it is blind to your own absence.
  4. Black-box probes. A synthetic request every 30 seconds from outside. Catches total outages fast, catches nothing partial, and gives a tiny sample. A good complement, a poor primary.

The practical answer for most teams: compute availability from ingress metrics, compute latency from service histograms, and keep a black-box probe as a canary. Then reconcile them monthly; a persistent gap between ingress and service error rates is itself a finding.

49.2.3 Real PromQL

Assume nginx-ingress exposes nginx_ingress_controller_requests with status, ingress and path labels, and your NestJS service exposes http_request_duration_seconds as a histogram with a route label (Part 43 — Observability).

Availability SLI at the edge, over 30 days:

PromQL
# Fraction of checkout requests that did not return 5xx, measured at the ingress.
sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="checkout", status!~"5.."}[30d]))
/
sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="checkout"}[30d]))

Note what is excluded and what is not. 4xx stays in the denominator but counts as good: a 400 Bad Request for a malformed payload is the client's problem, not an availability failure. But be careful — 429 Too Many Requests because you under-provisioned is your failure, and 401 storms because your token service is down are your failure. Decide these deliberately and write them in the SLO document, because this line is where teams accidentally define away their own outages.

Latency SLI as a ratio:

PromQL
# Fraction of checkout requests served in under 800 ms.
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/checkout",le="0.8"}[30d]))
/
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{route="/checkout"}[30d]))

The le="0.8" bucket must actually exist. Histogram buckets are chosen at instrumentation time, so define your buckets around your SLO thresholds. If your SLO is 800 ms and your buckets are [0.5, 1, 2.5], you cannot compute this SLI without interpolation error. Add 0.8.

TypeScript
// Buckets chosen to bracket the SLO thresholds we actually promise.
new Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'HTTP request duration',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'] as const,
  buckets: [0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.5, 3, 8],  // 0.8 and 1.5 are SLO edges
});

Correctness SLI, exported by a checker job rather than by the request path:

PromQL
# Fraction of paid orders in the last hour that have a matching payment record.
sum(rate(order_payment_reconciled_total{result="matched"}[30d]))
/
sum(rate(order_payment_reconciled_total[30d]))

Freshness SLI for the search index:

PromQL
# Fraction of product updates indexed within 60 seconds.
sum(rate(search_index_lag_seconds_bucket{le="60"}[30d]))
/
sum(rate(search_index_lag_seconds_count[30d]))

Recording rules, because a [30d] range query over raw series will time out and hammer Prometheus. Pre-compute the ratio at short intervals and aggregate the recorded series:

YAML
groups:
  - name: slo-checkout
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - record: sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="checkout", status!~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{ingress="checkout"}[5m]))

      - record: sli:checkout_latency:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/checkout",le="0.8"}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{route="/checkout"}[5m]))

Common mistakes

  • Measuring availability with up{job="orders-api"}. That says a scrape succeeded, not that users were served.
  • Averaging SLIs across all endpoints, so a broken checkout is hidden by a healthy /health.
  • Putting userId or orderId in metric labels and destroying Prometheus.
  • Excluding requests that timed out at the gateway because your service never saw them. Those are exactly the ones that matter.
  • Counting 4xx as failures wholesale, so a bot scanning for /wp-admin ruins your SLI.
  • Choosing a threshold by looking at current p99 and rounding up. That measures what you do, not what users need.

49.3 SLO: the internal target

49.3.1 Per journey, not per service

Concept

A Service Level Objective is a target value for an SLI over a window. "99.95 percent of checkout requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 days."

The critical design choice: write SLOs for user journeys, not for services. Users do not experience payment-service. They experience "I could pay for my basket". A journey crosses several services, and its SLO is what the business cares about.

For an e-commerce checkout, the journey SLOs look like this:

Journey SLI Target Window Why this number
Browse and search availability 99.9 % 30d rolling Users retry; brief blips are tolerable
Add to cart availability 99.95 % 30d rolling Losing a cart loses the session
Checkout submit availability 99.95 % 30d rolling Direct revenue; every failure is a lost order
Checkout submit latency < 800 ms 99 % 30d rolling Above ~1 s, abandonment rises measurably
Payment capture correctness 99.99 % 30d rolling Money. A wrong capture is worse than a slow one
Order confirmation email freshness < 5 min 99 % 30d rolling Beyond 5 min, support tickets start
Order history page availability 99.5 % 30d rolling Annoying, not revenue-critical

Notice 99.5 on order history. Deliberately lower. A team that gives everything the same target is not making choices; it is copying a number. The point of an SLO is that some things are allowed to be worse so that other things can be better.

Choosing an achievable target

Three inputs, in this order:

  1. What do users need? Ask support: at what point do tickets spike? Ask analytics: at what latency does conversion drop? For checkout at one retailer the answer was clear — conversion fell about 1.5 percent per extra 100 ms above 700 ms, and support volume tripled when the failure rate crossed 0.1 percent.
  2. What can you actually do? Look at the last 90 days of measured SLI. If you have been running at 99.7 percent, an SLO of 99.99 percent is a fiction that will be permanently breached and therefore permanently ignored. Set 99.9 percent, meet it for a quarter, then tighten.
  3. What do your dependencies allow? If your managed PostgreSQL has a 99.95 percent SLA and every checkout request touches it synchronously, your ceiling is 99.95 percent. Promising more is arithmetic you cannot win (49.6).

Start slightly looser than you think, and tighten over time. An SLO that is breached every month teaches everyone to ignore SLOs. An SLO that is never breached teaches nobody anything and probably means you are over-invested.

Dependency SLOs

Every internal dependency should have its own SLO, and yours should be built on theirs. Write them down as a table, because this is where fantasy targets get exposed:

Dependency Their SLO Synchronous in checkout? Effect on our ceiling
PostgreSQL primary (managed) 99.95 % Yes Hard ceiling 99.95 %
Redis (cache) 99.9 % No — we degrade to the database None if degradation works
Payment gateway 99.9 % Yes Hard ceiling; we mitigate with a second provider
Inventory service (internal) 99.95 % Yes Hard ceiling
Email provider 99.5 % No — queued None on checkout; affects the freshness SLO

That table is the single most useful artefact in an SLO document, because it turns "we want four nines" into "we would need to remove three synchronous dependencies first".

49.3.2 Writing an SLO document a product manager can read

Keep it to one page per journey. Real structure, real language:

Text
SLO: Checkout Submit
Owner: Orders team (Slack #orders, on-call rota "orders-primary")
Reviewed: 2026-09-01. Next review: 2026-12-01.

What it measures
  When a customer presses "Place order", we either create the order or tell them
  clearly why we could not.

SLI
  Availability = non-5xx responses / all responses for POST /api/orders,
  measured at the ingress. 429 counts as a failure (it means we ran out of capacity).
  Latency = fraction of those requests completing in under 800 ms.

Targets over a rolling 30 days
  Availability: 99.95 %   (allowed: ~21.6 minutes of full outage, or ~600 failed
                           orders out of 1.2 million)
  Latency:      99.0 % under 800 ms

Why these numbers
