  Analytics shows conversion falls about 1.5 % per 100 ms above 700 ms.
  Support volume triples above a 0.1 % failure rate.
  Our managed database's own SLA is 99.95 %, so we cannot promise more without
  removing it from the synchronous path.

What is excluded
  Planned maintenance announced 7 days ahead (max 2 windows per quarter, max 30 min each).
  Requests rejected as malformed (400/422).
  Traffic from known scrapers, identified by user agent and rate.

What happens when the budget runs out
  See the Error Budget Policy. Short version: feature releases to checkout pause
  and reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers above 20 %.

Dashboards
  grafana.internal/d/checkout-slo

Every sentence in that document is designed to be read by someone who does not know what a histogram is. If a product manager cannot read your SLO document and tell you what happens when it is breached, it is not finished.

49.4 SLA: the external promise

Concept

A Service Level Agreement is a contract with a customer that says what you promise and what you owe them if you break it. Service credits, refunds, a right to terminate. It is a legal and commercial document, not an engineering one.

The relationship between the three, and it matters:

Text
SLI  = the measurement          "99.973 % of checkout requests succeeded this month"
SLO  = the internal target      "we aim for 99.95 %"   -> triggers engineering action
SLA  = the external promise     "we guarantee 99.9 %"  -> triggers money

The rule: the SLA is always looser than the SLO

Always. Never equal. The gap is your safety margin, and it is the difference between "we had a bad month and paused feature work" and "we had a bad month and owe forty customers a 10 percent credit".

A typical spread: SLA 99.9 percent, SLO 99.95 percent. That means by the time you breach the contract, your own alerting has been shouting for a while and your budget policy has already changed the team's behaviour. If SLO and SLA are the same number, your first warning is a lawyer's email.

Internal SLO External SLA
Audience Your engineers and product Customers, procurement, legal
Target 99.95 % 99.9 %
Measurement Rolling 30 days, ingress metrics Calendar month, often a coarser definition
Consequence Budget policy: freeze features, prioritize reliability Service credits, contract remedies
Who changes it The team, quarterly Sales and legal, per contract
Exclusions Few, documented Many: maintenance, force majeure, customer misuse

Practical notes from the field

  • Define measurement precisely in the contract. "Availability" without a definition is a dispute waiting to happen. Say which endpoints, measured where, at what granularity, with what exclusions, and who provides the data. Ambiguity is always resolved in favour of the party with more lawyers.
  • Calendar month versus rolling window. SLAs almost always use calendar months because billing does. Your SLO should use a rolling window because reliability does not reset on the first of the month. Expect them to disagree; that is normal and fine.
  • Internal SLAs are usually a bad idea. Between two internal teams, an SLA with "consequences" produces defensive behaviour and gaming. Use SLOs between teams, and escalate through management if one is chronically missed.
  • You cannot promise more than your dependencies. If you resell on top of a cloud provider with a 99.9 percent SLA and you offer 99.99 percent, you have written a cheque your infrastructure cannot cash. Either add redundancy that genuinely removes the dependency, or lower the promise.
  • Someone must actually compute it. More SLAs are breached un-noticed than are breached and paid. A monthly automated report per contracted customer, generated from the same recording rules as your SLO dashboard, is thirty lines of code and prevents a class of embarrassment.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They are in the room when sales proposes an SLA number, or they make sure someone technical is. They ask: what is the measurement definition, what are the exclusions, what does it cost us if we breach, and what would we have to build to make this achievable? Then they check it against the last 90 days of measured SLI, and if the answer is "we have never once hit that", they say so before the contract is signed rather than after.

Interview questions

  1. Define SLI, SLO and SLA and give a checkout example of each.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: measurement, internal target, external contract with consequences; SLA looser than SLO. Follow-up: why must the SLA be looser?
  2. Why measure availability at the load balancer rather than in the service?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a crashed service emits no metrics, so the error ratio looks fine while users get 502s; the edge also sees TLS, ingress and no-healthy-pod failures.
  3. Write the PromQL for "99 percent of checkout requests under 800 ms".
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the le="0.8" bucket over the total count, plus the point that the bucket must exist and buckets should bracket SLO thresholds.
  4. Should 429 responses count against your availability SLI?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it depends on why — self-inflicted capacity shortfall counts as a failure, deliberate abuse protection does not; the decision belongs in the SLO document.
  5. How do you choose an SLO target?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: user need from support and conversion data, historical achievability, and the ceiling imposed by synchronous dependencies.
  6. Your team wants a 99.99 percent SLO and the managed database offers 99.95 percent. What do you say?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it is arithmetically impossible while the database is synchronous; options are removing it from the path, adding redundancy that survives its failure, or lowering the target.

Practical exercise

Pick a real endpoint in a service you own and write its SLO document using the template above.

Acceptance criteria: the SLI is a ratio of good to valid events; the availability measurement comes from ingress or load-balancer metrics, not from inside the service; the latency histogram has a bucket exactly at your threshold; you have recording rules for both SLIs; you have computed the last 90 days of achieved SLI and your target is achievable but not already free; the exclusions are written down; and a non-engineer on your team can read the document and correctly answer "what happens if we miss it?"

49.5 Error budgets

49.5.1 The arithmetic

Concept

The error budget is simply 1 - SLO, expressed over your window. It is the amount of failure you are permitted. Two useful units: time (how many minutes of total outage) and requests (how many individual failures).

For a 30-day rolling window:

SLO Budget as a fraction Budget in minutes / 30 days Budget in failed requests, at 1.2 M requests / 30 days
99 % 1 % 432 min (14.2 h) 12,000
99.5 % 0.5 % 216 min (10.6 h) 6,000
99.9 % 0.1 % 43.2 min 1,200
99.95 % 0.05 % 21.6 min 600
99.99 % 0.01 % 4.32 min 120
99.999 % 0.001 % 0.43 min (26 s) 12

The request-based column is the one to show a product manager. "We are allowed 600 failed checkouts a month; we have used 410 of them and it is the 12th" is a sentence anyone understands. "We are at 99.966 percent" is not.

Two ways to count, and they are not equivalent:

  • Time-based: count minutes where the service was "down" by some definition. Simple, matches how SLAs are written, and terrible at partial failures. A bug affecting 3 percent of users costs you nothing in a time-based budget because no minute was fully down.
  • Request-based: count failed requests over total requests. Captures partial failures properly and is what you should use internally.

Prefer request-based for your SLO. Expect your SLA to be time-based because contracts are. Compute both; they will disagree, and knowing by how much is useful.

The budget as a graph

The one graph every team should have on the wall:

PromQL
# Remaining error budget as a fraction, over a rolling 30 days.
# 1 - (observed error ratio / allowed error ratio)
1 - (
  (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate5m_30d)
  /
  (1 - 0.9995)
)

It starts each window at 1.0 and walks down. When it hits zero you have spent the month's allowance. When it goes negative you have breached the SLO. Plot it with a straight line from 1.0 to 0.0 across the window as the "spending at exactly the allowed rate" reference; being above the line is healthy, below it is a warning.

49.5.2 Burn rate

Concept

Burn rate is how fast you are consuming the budget, relative to consuming it exactly evenly over the window.

  • Burn rate 1 means you will spend exactly the whole budget by the end of the window. Sustainable, by definition.
  • Burn rate 2 means you will spend it in half the window: 15 days.
  • Burn rate 14.4 means you will spend it in about 50 hours.
  • Burn rate 1440 means you spend the whole 30-day budget in 30 minutes. That is a total outage of a 99.9 percent service.

The formula:

Text
burn rate = observed error ratio / allowed error ratio
          = observed error ratio / (1 - SLO)

For a 99.9 percent SLO, allowed error ratio is 0.001. If you are currently failing 1.44 percent of requests, burn rate is 0.0144 / 0.001 = 14.4.

And the time to exhaustion:

Text
hours to exhaust = (window in hours) x (budget remaining fraction) / burn rate

At burn rate 14.4 with a full budget and a 30-day window: 720 x 1.0 / 14.4 = 50 hours.

Mental model

Imagine a monthly data plan of 100 GB. Burn rate 1 is streaming at exactly the pace that uses it up on the last day of the month. Burn rate 14.4 is someone downloading a game: you will be out of data by Wednesday. Burn rate 1440 is a device stuck in a loop: gone before lunch.

You want a text message for the game download (act today) and a phone call for the loop (act now). You do not want a notification every time someone opens a web page. That is exactly what multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting gives you.

49.5.3 Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting

Why does it exist?

Two naive alerting strategies both fail.

Alert on a fixed error-rate threshold ("page if error rate > 1 percent for 5 minutes"). It fires on a 90-second blip that consumed 0.2 percent of the budget, and it stays silent through a two-week slow bleed at 0.4 percent that consumes the entire budget. It is disconnected from what you actually promised.

Alert when the budget is exhausted. Too late by definition. The month is already lost.

The fix is to alert on burn rate, at several rates, each paired with a window sized to that rate. High burn rates get short windows so you are paged fast; low burn rates get long windows so noise is filtered out.

And each alert uses two windows: a long one that establishes the burn rate, and a short one (typically one twelfth of the long one) that must also be burning. The short window is what makes the alert stop firing quickly once the problem is fixed — without it, a 5-minute outage keeps a 1-hour-window alert firing for an hour after recovery.

The standard configuration

The widely used four-alert setup, for a 30-day window:

Burn rate Long window Short window Budget consumed when it fires Severity Time to exhaustion
14.4 1 hour 5 min 2 % Page ~2 days
6 6 hours 30 min 5 % Page ~5 days
3 1 day 2 hours 10 % Ticket ~10 days
1 3 days 6 hours 10 % Ticket 30 days
YAML
groups:
  - name: checkout-slo-burn
    rules:
      # Fast burn: 2 percent of the 30-day budget in one hour. Wake someone up.
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
        expr: |
          (
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate1h) > (14.4 * 0.0005)
            and
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate5m) > (14.4 * 0.0005)
          )
        labels:
          severity: page
          journey: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout burning error budget at 14.4x; budget gone in ~2 days"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.internal/checkout/slo-burn"

      # Medium burn: 5 percent in six hours. Still a page, but you have hours.
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetMediumBurn
        expr: |
          (
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate6h) > (6 * 0.0005)
            and
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate30m) > (6 * 0.0005)
          )
        labels: { severity: page, journey: checkout }

      # Slow burn: a persistent bleed. A ticket, not a page. Nobody wakes for this.
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetSlowBurn
        expr: |
          (
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate1d) > (3 * 0.0005)
            and
            (1 - sli:checkout_availability:ratio_rate2h) > (3 * 0.0005)
          )
        labels: { severity: ticket, journey: checkout }

0.0005 is 1 - 0.9995, the allowed error ratio for the 99.95 percent SLO. Keep that number in exactly one place per SLO; a copy-paste with a stale target is a classic source of alerts that fire at the wrong level.

A worked example

Checkout SLO is 99.95 percent over 30 days. Traffic is 1.2 million requests per 30 days, so about 1,667 requests per hour. The budget is 600 failed requests.

Scenario A — a bad deploy at 14:00. A regression makes 12 percent of checkouts fail.

  • Observed error ratio: 0.12. Allowed: 0.0005. Burn rate: 0.12 / 0.0005 = 240.
  • Time to exhaust the full budget: 720 hours / 240 = 3 hours.
  • The fast-burn alert threshold is 14.4 x 0.0005 = 0.0072, i.e. 0.72 percent. At 12 percent we are far above it. But the alert uses a 1-hour window and a 5-minute window; the 5-minute rate crosses within about 5 minutes, and the 1-hour rate crosses once roughly 6 percent of the hour's requests have failed — about 4 to 6 minutes in. On-call is paged at roughly 14:06.
  • They roll back at 14:14. Total failures: about 14 minutes at 12 percent of 1,667/hour, so 1667 x (14/60) x 0.12 = 47 failed checkouts. That is 7.8 percent of the month's budget, spent in 14 minutes.
  • The 5-minute window drops below threshold within 5 minutes of the rollback, so the alert resolves at about 14:19 rather than at 15:14. That is the whole point of the short window.

Scenario B — a slow bleed. A retry bug makes 0.2 percent of checkouts fail intermittently, starting Monday.

  • Burn rate: 0.002 / 0.0005 = 4.
  • Time to exhaust: 720 / 4 = 180 hours = 7.5 days.
  • The fast-burn threshold (0.72 percent) never fires. The medium threshold (6 x 0.0005 = 0.3 percent) never fires. The slow-burn threshold (3 x 0.0005 = 0.15 percent) fires once the 1-day and 2-hour windows both exceed it — on Tuesday.
  • It creates a ticket, not a page. Nobody's sleep is disturbed for a bug that gives you a week to fix it. By Friday the team has landed the fix having spent about 45 percent of the budget.

That contrast is the value of the whole scheme. The same alerting philosophy caught both a 14-minute catastrophe and a week-long bleed, paged for exactly one of them, and both times the number in the alert directly answered "how urgent is this?"

49.5.4 The error budget policy

Concept

The policy is the written, pre-agreed answer to "what happens when the budget runs out". It must be agreed by engineering and product and management before an incident, because during an incident everyone's incentives change.

A real, workable policy:

Text
Error Budget Policy — Checkout journey
Agreed by: Head of Engineering, Head of Product, Orders team lead. Review: quarterly.

Budget remaining > 50 %
  Normal operation. Ship freely. Consider raising risk appetite: run more
  experiments, deploy more often, tighten the SLO next review if we are
  never below 80 %.

Budget remaining 20 % to 50 %
  Caution. Deploys continue. No large migrations or infrastructure changes
  without a rollback plan reviewed by a second engineer.

Budget remaining 0 % to 20 %
  Feature freeze on this journey. Only reliability fixes, security fixes and
  P0 customer-blocking bugs ship to checkout. The team's next sprint is
  reliability work drawn from open postmortem action items.

Budget exhausted (below 0 %)
  As above, plus: a written report to the Head of Engineering within 2 business
  days naming the top three contributors and the work that will prevent a repeat.
  Product may request an exception in writing, accepting the SLA risk.

Repeated exhaustion (2 of 3 consecutive windows)
  The SLO is wrong or the system is. Mandatory review: either the target comes
  down (with the SLA re-examined) or reliability work is staffed properly.

The last clause is the honest one. An SLO breached every single month is not motivating anyone; it is decoration. Either fix the system or fix the number, and say which out loud.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They notice that an unspent budget is also a signal. A team that ends every month at 95 percent budget remaining is being too careful: it could deploy more often, run chaos experiments, take on more ambitious changes. Reliability that exceeds the target is not free virtue, it is unspent capital.

They also refuse to let the budget become a stick. The policy pauses features, it does not punish people. The moment a team hides failures to protect its budget, the SLI is corrupted and the whole system is worthless.

Common mistakes

  • Alerting on burn rate without recording rules, so the alert query itself times out and never fires.
  • Copying the 14.4 / 6 / 3 / 1 numbers without adjusting for a different window length.
  • One SLO for an entire service instead of per journey, so a broken checkout is diluted by healthy static assets.
  • A policy nobody signed, which is therefore renegotiated during every incident.
  • Resetting the budget after an incident "because it was not our fault". If users experienced it, it counts. Exclusions belong in the SLO document, agreed in advance, not applied retroactively.

49.6 Availability maths

49.6.1 The nines

Concept

"Nines" is shorthand for an availability target. What matters is the allowed downtime it implies, and how quickly that becomes implausible.

Availability Per day Per week Per 30 days Per year
99 % 14.4 min 1.68 h 7.2 h 3.65 days
99.5 % 7.2 min 50.4 min 3.6 h 1.83 days
99.9 % 1.44 min 10.1 min 43.2 min 8.77 h
99.95 % 43 s 5 min 21.6 min 4.38 h
99.99 % 8.6 s 1 min 4.32 min 52.6 min
99.999 % 0.86 s 6 s 26 s 5.26 min

Read the 99.99 percent row carefully. 4.32 minutes per month. A single Kubernetes rolling deploy that goes wrong and takes six minutes to roll back has blown the month. A PostgreSQL failover takes 30 to 90 seconds if it is automated and well-tested; three of those in a month and you are done.

This is why the honest question is never "how many nines do we want" but "what is our mean time to recovery, and how many incidents do we have per month". Availability is 1 - (incidents x MTTR / window). Improving MTTR from 40 minutes to 8 minutes does more for your availability than any amount of extra redundancy, and it is usually cheaper: better alerts, a rollback button, a documented kill switch, a runbook.

49.6.2 Serial dependencies multiply

Concept

If a request must pass through several components, and any one failing fails the request, the availabilities multiply.

Text
A_total = A1 x A2 x A3 x ... x An

Four services at 99.9 percent each:

Text
0.999 ^ 4 = 0.996006  ->  99.6 %  ->  about 2.9 hours of downtime per 30 days

You built four highly reliable services and shipped a mediocre one. This is the most under-appreciated fact in distributed systems and it is why "microservices improve reliability" is, on its own, false. Splitting a monolith into six services that all sit in the checkout path makes checkout less available unless you also add isolation, fallbacks and asynchrony.

A realistic checkout chain:

Component Availability Running product
CDN / edge 99.99 % 99.99 %
Load balancer 99.99 % 99.98 %
API pods (3 replicas, 2 AZ) 99.95 % 99.93 %
Auth service 99.95 % 99.88 %
Inventory service 99.95 % 99.83 %
PostgreSQL (managed, multi-AZ) 99.95 % 99.78 %
Payment gateway 99.9 % 99.68 %

99.68 percent. That is 2.3 hours of expected downtime per 30 days, from components that individually look excellent. And your SLO says 99.95 percent.

49.6.3 What actually fixes it

Three levers, in order of effectiveness.

1. Remove the dependency from the synchronous path. This is the biggest win and it is an architecture decision, not an infrastructure purchase. The email provider was in the chain until we queued it (Part 36); now its availability does not appear in the product at all. Ask of every box in the diagram: does the response depend on it?

2. Make failure non-fatal. A dependency you can degrade around drops out of the multiplication. If Redis being down means you read from PostgreSQL more slowly instead of returning 500, Redis contributes nothing to your unavailability. If the recommendation service being down means the recommendations panel is empty rather than the page failing, same. This is graceful degradation (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure) and it is worth more than another nine on any single component.

3. Add real redundancy. For components in parallel, where either one serving the request is enough, unavailabilities multiply instead:

Text
A_parallel = 1 - (1 - A1) x (1 - A2)

Two payment gateways at 99.9 percent each, with automatic failover:

Text
1 - (0.001 x 0.001) = 0.999999  ->  99.9999 %

That looks magical, and here is the catch that catches everyone: the formula assumes independent failures and instant, correct failover. In reality:

  • The failover logic is itself a component with its own availability, and it is the least-tested code you own.
  • Failures correlate. Both gateways sit behind the same DNS provider, the same TLS library, the same cloud region, the same expired CA bundle.
  • A failover that takes 90 seconds to detect and switch contributes 90 seconds of downtime per event regardless of the maths.
  • The standby path is often broken and nobody knows, because it is never exercised. This is why game days exist (49.12).

A realistic figure for two-provider redundancy with tested automatic failover is not six nines. It is roughly one extra nine, maybe a bit more. Claim that, not the theoretical number.

49.6.4 Why 99.99 percent on a 99.9 percent database is a fantasy

Concept

If every request touches a managed PostgreSQL whose provider offers 99.9 percent, your ceiling is 99.9 percent. You cannot be more available than the thing you must call. Promising 99.99 percent means promising to be up during 43 minutes a month when your database is, by contract, allowed to be down.

This is not pedantry; it is the arithmetic that will be quoted back to you after the incident.

There are only four honest responses:

  1. Lower the target to 99.9 percent or slightly below, and be right.
  2. Remove the database from the critical path for that journey. Serve reads from a cache with a documented staleness bound. Accept writes into a durable queue and confirm asynchronously. Both are real designs with real trade-offs, and both change the product contract.
  3. Add genuine redundancy: a multi-AZ primary with automatic failover (which most managed offerings already include in that 99.95 percent figure), a cross-region replica with tested promotion, or a second write path. Each adds cost, complexity and new failure modes — split brain, replication lag, and the failover that does not fire.
  4. Change the definition so the promise is meetable: promise availability on reads but not writes, or exclude the provider's maintenance windows explicitly in the SLA. This is legitimate if it is honest and written down, and dishonest if it is a trick to make a dashboard green.

What you must not do is set the number because a competitor's marketing page says four nines.

Production scenario

A team promised 99.99 percent to an enterprise customer. Their stack: one managed PostgreSQL (99.95 percent), one Redis (99.9 percent, in the synchronous path because sessions lived there), one payment gateway (99.9 percent), one Kubernetes cluster in a single region. Serial product: 0.9995 x 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 = 99.68 percent. Their allowed downtime under the contract was 4.32 minutes a month; their expected downtime was 2.3 hours.

They breached in month one, month two and month four. The fixes that actually moved the number were not exotic: move sessions out of the synchronous Redis path to signed tokens (removed 0.1 percent), add a second payment provider with tested failover (removed most of 0.1 percent), and — biggest of all — cut MTTR from 35 minutes to 6 by adding a one-click rollback and three runbooks. They landed at about 99.94 percent and renegotiated the SLA to 99.9 percent with a straight face.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They draw the dependency chain before they agree to a number, and they multiply. They know that MTTR is usually the cheapest lever and redundancy is usually the most expensive. They are deeply suspicious of parallel-redundancy arithmetic that assumes independence, and they insist the failover path is exercised on a schedule, because an untested failover is not redundancy, it is a story you tell yourself.

And they say the uncomfortable sentence out loud in the meeting: "We cannot promise that. Here is the arithmetic. Here is what it would cost to make it true."

Interview questions

  1. What is an error budget and how do you compute it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 1 - SLO over the window, expressed in minutes and in failed requests; request-based preferred internally. Follow-up: why is request-based better than time-based?
  2. Explain burn-rate alerting to someone who only knows threshold alerts.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: burn rate is observed error ratio over allowed error ratio; multiple rates with paired long and short windows page for fast burns and ticket for slow bleeds; the short window makes alerts resolve quickly.
  3. Four services at 99.9 percent in series. What is the result and what do you do about it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 99.6 percent; remove dependencies from the synchronous path, degrade gracefully, then add redundancy; and improve MTTR.
  4. Why is two-provider redundancy not really six nines?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: correlated failures, the failover mechanism's own reliability, detection and switch time, untested standby paths.
  5. Your database provider promises 99.95 percent and product wants a 99.99 percent SLO. What do you say?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it is arithmetically impossible synchronously; the four honest options.
  6. What should happen when the error budget is exhausted?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the pre-agreed budget policy — feature freeze on that journey, reliability work prioritized, a written report, and a review if it recurs.

Practical exercise

Compute your own numbers rather than reading someone else's.

  1. Draw the full synchronous dependency chain for your most important journey. Put each component's stated or measured availability on it and multiply.
  2. Compare the result to your current SLO. If the product is lower than the target, list what you would remove from the synchronous path to close the gap.
  3. Build the burn-rate alerts for that journey with recording rules, all four rates.
  4. Simulate a 12 percent error rate for 15 minutes with a feature flag in staging and measure how long the fast-burn alert takes to fire and to resolve.

Acceptance criteria: the fast-burn alert fires within 10 minutes of the fault starting and resolves within 10 minutes of it stopping; the slow-burn alert does not fire; you can state your journey's budget in both minutes and failed requests; and you have a written budget policy with at least two named signatures.

49.7 Incident management

49.7.1 What an incident is, and severity levels

Concept

An incident is any unplanned event that degrades a service below its expected level and requires a coordinated response. The word "coordinated" is doing the work: a bug one engineer fixes in ten minutes is not an incident. A bug that needs three people, a customer communication and a decision about rolling back is.

The purpose of severity levels is not to rank how bad you feel. It is to answer three operational questions instantly: who gets woken up, how often do we communicate, and does this need a postmortem.

Sev Definition Concrete examples Response Comms Postmortem
SEV1 Complete outage of a critical journey, or data loss, or a security breach Checkout returns 500 for everyone; the orders table was truncated; customer data exposed Page immediately, 24x7, wake whoever is needed, exec notified Status page within 15 min, updates every 30 min Mandatory, within 5 business days
SEV2 Major degradation of a critical journey, or complete outage of a non-critical one Checkout p99 at 12 s and 8 % failing; payments work for cards but not UPI; the entire admin panel is down Page immediately, 24x7 Status page within 30 min, updates hourly Mandatory
SEV3 Partial or minor degradation with a workaround, or a non-critical outage Order confirmation emails delayed 40 min; search is stale by an hour; one merchant's exports fail Page during business hours; ticket out of hours Internal only unless a customer asks Recommended
SEV4 Cosmetic, or affecting a small number of users with no revenue impact A label is wrong; one legacy integration times out; a dashboard panel is broken Ticket None No

Two rules that make severity levels work in practice:

  1. Start high and downgrade. It is easy to say "actually this is a SEV3" fifteen minutes in. It is very hard to catch up when you started at SEV3 and it was always a SEV1. Anyone may declare; nobody is criticized for over-declaring.
  2. Severity is about impact, not about cause. "It is only a config typo" is not a severity. If checkout is down, it is a SEV1 whether the cause is a typo or a datacentre fire.

49.7.2 The roles

Concept

Three distinct jobs, and in anything above a SEV3 they must be three different people.

Incident Commander (IC). Owns the incident, not the fix. Decides. Delegates. Keeps the timeline. Asks "what do we know, what are we doing, who is doing it, when do we next check in". Explicitly does not type into a terminal. The IC is the only person who can declare severity changes and resolution.

Communications Lead. Owns everything outside the war room: the status page, the internal Slack channel, the message to support, the update to the executive who is asking. Translates "the Kafka consumer group is rebalancing continuously" into "some order confirmation emails are delayed; orders are unaffected".

Operations Lead. Owns the hands on keyboard. Runs commands, reads dashboards, proposes and executes mitigations. Reports findings to the IC. May have helpers (a database expert, a network expert) whom the IC assigns.

Why one person cannot hold all three

Because the modes are incompatible, and I have watched this fail every time it is attempted.

The Operations Lead is deep in a terminal reading a query plan. That requires uninterrupted focus. Meanwhile the VP of Sales is asking in Slack whether to call the customer, support wants a line for the ticket queue, and someone needs to decide whether to roll back. If those are the same person, one of two things happens: either they stop debugging to answer messages, and the incident lasts three times longer, or they ignore the messages, and the company finds out about a two-hour outage from Twitter.

The IC exists because decisions and diagnosis compete for the same brain. The Comms Lead exists because communication is a full-time job during an incident and it is the part engineers are worst at.

For a small team where three people is not realistic at 03:00: the on-call is the IC and the Operations Lead initially, and their first action after acknowledging is to pull in a second person for comms if severity is 1 or 2. "I am the IC, you are ops, I will handle comms" is a valid three-role split across two people. One person doing all three alone for a SEV1 is not a staffing plan, it is a hope.

49.7.3 Declaring, the war room, the status page

Declaring should take one command and no permission. A Slack command that creates a dedicated channel, a video bridge link, an incident record with a timestamp, and pages the IC rotation. The friction of declaring is directly proportional to how long your incidents last, because engineers who must ask permission will instead "just have a quick look" for forty minutes.

The war room is a dedicated channel plus a voice bridge. Rules that make it work:

  • All decisions and findings go in the channel, not only the voice call. The channel is the timeline and the record for the postmortem. If it was only said on the call, it did not happen.
  • Anyone not actively working the incident stays out of the voice call and reads the channel. An executive on the bridge asking for updates costs you an engineer.
  • The IC posts a structured update at a fixed cadence, even when the update is "no change":
Text
[14:32] SEV2 checkout-latency
Impact: ~8 % of checkouts failing, p99 11 s. Started 14:02.
Current theory: connection pool exhaustion after the 13:58 deploy.
Actions: Priya rolling back to 2.14.2 (ETA 14:38). Arun checking pg_stat_activity.
Next update: 14:45.

Four lines: impact, theory, actions with owners, next update time. That format survives handoffs, feeds the postmortem timeline directly, and answers every question an observer would otherwise ask.

The status page. Publish before you are certain, in plain language, without causes. "We are investigating reports of errors during checkout" at 14:15 is infinitely better than a precise explanation at 16:00. Customers forgive outages; they do not forgive silence. Update on a schedule even when there is nothing new, and post a resolution note plus a link to the public postmortem if you write one.

Never put an internal cause on a public status page. "A Kafka consumer group rebalance caused duplicate deliveries" tells attackers about your stack and tells customers nothing. "Some customers received duplicate order confirmation emails. Orders and payments were not affected." is what they need.

Escalation. Every rotation needs a written escalation path with time bounds: primary has 5 minutes to acknowledge, then secondary is paged, then the engineering manager, then the head of engineering. And a subject-matter escalation list: who to call for PostgreSQL, for Kafka, for the payment integration, for the cloud account. At 03:00 nobody should be searching a wiki for a phone number.

49.7.4 The first ten minutes

This is the most important section in this part, and its entire content is one instruction.

Mitigate first. Diagnose later.

The natural engineering instinct is to understand the problem before acting. That instinct is correct in every context except an active incident. During an incident, every minute of understanding costs real money and real customers. Understanding is what the postmortem is for. Your job right now is to make the bleeding stop.

The first-ten-minutes checklist:

Text
FIRST TEN MINUTES — do these before diagnosing

[ ] 1. Acknowledge the page. Say in the channel that you have it.
[ ] 2. Confirm the impact in 60 seconds. Which journey, what fraction of users,
       since when. One dashboard. Do not go deeper yet.
[ ] 3. Declare the incident and severity. Start the channel and the timeline.
[ ] 4. DID ANYTHING CHANGE? Check the deploy log, the feature-flag log, the
       config/migration log, and the cloud provider's status page. Last 2 hours.
[ ] 5. If yes: ROLL IT BACK NOW. Do not verify the theory first. Rolling back
       a good deploy costs 5 minutes. Not rolling back a bad one costs an hour.
[ ] 6. If no change: try the standard mitigations, in this order.
       [ ] Scale out. More replicas is cheap and instant.
       [ ] Shed load. Turn on aggressive rate limiting; protect the core journey
           by rejecting the periphery.
       [ ] Disable the feature. Kill switches for non-essential paths:
           recommendations, personalization, the new checkout variant.
       [ ] Fail over. Switch provider, promote the replica, drain the AZ.
       [ ] Restart the sick component. Crude, often effective, buys time.
[ ] 7. Confirm the mitigation worked by looking at the user-facing SLI,
       not at the thing you changed.
[ ] 8. Only now: start diagnosing. Preserve evidence first — take a heap dump,
       copy the logs, screenshot the dashboards, note the pod names.
       Rolling back destroys the evidence you will want tomorrow.
[ ] 9. Post an update every 15 to 30 minutes whether or not anything changed.

Step 5 deserves its own paragraph, because it is where teams lose hours. Roll back before you know it was the deploy. The cost matrix is completely lopsided: rolling back an innocent deploy costs a few minutes and some mild embarrassment; failing to roll back a guilty one costs the whole incident. If a deploy went out in the two hours before the symptoms started, it is the most likely cause by a large margin, and you can prove or disprove it far more comfortably once customers are being served again.

The same applies to step 8's evidence note, which is the one thing people forget under pressure. A pod that is restarted is a pod whose heap you cannot inspect. Thirty seconds of kubectl logs --previous > incident.log and a screenshot will save your postmortem.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call is paged: checkout error rate 22 percent. She spends 35 minutes reading logs and tracing a suspicious query, builds a solid theory about lock contention, and is preparing a hotfix when a colleague asks whether anything deployed. A feature flag had been enabled at 02:09 by a scheduled rollout. Turning it off took eleven seconds. Total impact: 47 minutes and roughly 900 failed orders, of which 46 minutes and 880 orders were avoidable.

Nothing she did was incompetent. The theory was even partly right — the flag caused the lock contention. The process was wrong: she diagnosed before she mitigated, and there was no checklist telling her not to.

49.8 On-call

49.8.1 Designing a rotation

Concept

On-call is a system with humans in it, and like any system it can be designed well or badly. Badly designed on-call does not fail loudly; it fails by attrition, and by the time you notice, your two most experienced engineers have resigned.

The design parameters:

Parameter Reasonable Why
Rotation size 6 to 8 people minimum Fewer than 6 means one week in five or worse, which is unsustainable
Shift length 1 week, handing over midweek Weekly is long enough for context, short enough to survive. Midweek handover avoids ruining two weekends for the same person
Layers Primary plus secondary The secondary catches missed pages and provides a second brain for SEV1s
Follow-the-sun Only if you genuinely have teams in two timezones Better than night shifts; do not fake it with one person in another country
Out-of-hours pages Target fewer than 2 per week Above this, the rotation is a burnout machine and alert quality is the bug
Compensation Paid, at a rate people notice Unpaid on-call is a tax on the conscientious

Handover is a five-minute conversation and a written note, not a calendar change. The outgoing engineer states: what fired this week, what is still degraded, what is deliberately silenced and until when, what is deploying next, and what they would worry about. Skipping it means the incoming person meets a known problem as a novel one — and 49.14 covers the special horror of an incident starting exactly at handover.

49.8.2 Paging versus ticketing

Concept

A page wakes a human immediately. A ticket enters a queue and is triaged in working hours.

The rule for a page, and it has exactly two clauses:

Page only if it is urgent (waiting until morning makes it materially worse) and actionable (a human can do something now that improves it).

Both clauses. An urgent alert with no action is a notification that ruins sleep and changes nothing. An actionable alert that is not urgent is a ticket.

Apply it honestly:

Alert Page? Why
Checkout burn rate 14.4x Yes Urgent, and the runbook has mitigations
Checkout burn rate 3x over a day No, ticket A week of runway; nobody needs to be awake
Disk 90 percent full, filling at 1 GB/h Yes ~10 hours to failure; and there is an action
Disk 75 percent full, stable No, ticket Not urgent
CPU above 80 percent No Not a symptom of user pain; it is a dashboard panel
Pod restarted once No That is Kubernetes working
Pod in CrashLoopBackOff for 10 min Yes Capacity is gone and it will not self-heal
Dead-letter queue grew by 50 in 15 min Yes Work is being lost now
Certificate expires in 14 days No, ticket Ticket at 30 days, page at 24 hours
Payment provider error rate above 5 % Yes Revenue, and there is a failover action
A nightly batch job failed Depends Page if it must complete before business hours; otherwise ticket

Note the CPU row. Alerting on causes rather than symptoms is the single largest source of alert fatigue. High CPU that is not hurting users is not a problem; low CPU while users are failing is still an incident. Alert on the symptom — burn rate, backlog age, error ratio — and put the causes on the dashboard the runbook tells you to open.

49.8.3 Rotation health metrics

Measure the rotation the way you measure a service. These four numbers, reviewed monthly, with the on-call engineers in the room:

  1. Pages per shift. Target under 5 per week. Above 10 and people stop reading them carefully; that is when a real page gets acknowledged and ignored.
  2. Out-of-hours pages (22:00 to 08:00, weekends). Target under 2 per week. This is the number that predicts resignations.
  3. Time to acknowledge. p90 under 5 minutes. Rising TTA means either the paging path is broken (test it monthly) or people have stopped trusting the alerts.
  4. Actionability ratio. The fraction of pages where the responder actually did something. Below 70 percent, you have an alerting bug, not an operations problem.

Also track which alert fired most. There is nearly always one alert responsible for a third of all pages, and it is nearly always fixable in a day. Finding it is the highest-leverage reliability work available to most teams.

Alert quality is an engineering deliverable

This is the mindset shift. A noisy alert is a bug in the alerting system, with the same status as a bug in the product. It gets a ticket, an owner and a fix. Acceptable fixes: tune the threshold, add a for: duration, make it a ticket instead of a page, group it with related alerts, automate the response so no human is needed, or delete it.

"Delete it" is a real and underused fix. An alert nobody has acted on in six months is not protecting you; it is training you to ignore your pager.

Every alert must have, before it is allowed to page:

  • An owning team named in the labels.
  • A link to a runbook that exists and has been read.
  • A for: duration so a 30-second blip does not fire it.
  • A description of user impact, not internal state.
  • A severity that matches the paging policy above.

An alert without a runbook is a page that says "good luck". Make the runbook a required field in your alerting config and this problem disappears permanently.

49.9 Runbooks

49.9.1 Structure

Concept

A runbook is a document written for a specific person: a competent engineer, at 03:00, who has never seen this alert, is not an expert in this service, and is slightly panicking. Everything about its structure follows from that reader.

The seven sections, always in this order:

  1. Symptom — what fired and what it means, in one sentence.
  2. Impact — who is affected and how badly. Determines urgency.
  3. Dashboards — direct links. Not "the Grafana folder". Links.
  4. Diagnosis — ordered, concrete steps with the exact commands, each with an "if this, then that".
  5. Mitigation — how to make it stop. Before the root cause is known.
  6. Escalation — who to call, when, and how.
  7. Verification — how to confirm it is actually fixed, from the user's side.

Rules that keep runbooks useful:

  • Commands must be copy-pasteable, with real cluster names and namespaces, no <placeholders> you have to guess.
  • Mitigation comes before deep diagnosis, mirroring the first-ten-minutes rule.
  • Every runbook is dated and owned. A runbook that has not been touched in a year is a liability, because it will confidently tell you to do something that no longer exists.
  • Test them in game days. A runbook that has never been executed is fiction.

49.9.2 A complete worked runbook

Markdown
# RUNBOOK: Checkout latency SLO burning at 14x

Alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn (latency variant)
Owner: Orders team  |  Slack: #orders  |  On-call: orders-primary
Last reviewed: 2026-08-14 by A. Sharma  |  Last executed: 2026-08-27 (game day)

### 1. Symptom

The fraction of POST /api/orders requests completing under 800 ms has dropped
far enough that we are consuming the 30-day error budget 14.4 times faster than
sustainable. At this rate the entire month's latency budget is gone in ~50 hours.

This alert requires both the 1-hour and 5-minute windows to be burning, so it is
not a blip. Something is genuinely slow right now.

### 2. Impact

Customers pressing "Place order" are waiting more than 800 ms. Above ~2 s a
measurable fraction abandon; above the 30 s gateway timeout they get an error
and may retry, creating duplicate order attempts.

Rough revenue impact: at peak (400 orders/min) each 1 % of abandonment is
about 4 orders/min, roughly 12,000 rupees/min.

Severity: SEV2 if p99 is between 800 ms and 5 s. SEV1 if requests are timing out
or the success rate has also dropped below 99 %.

### 3. Dashboards

- Checkout SLO:        https://grafana.internal/d/checkout-slo
- Orders API service:  https://grafana.internal/d/orders-api
- PostgreSQL primary:  https://grafana.internal/d/pg-primary
- Redis:               https://grafana.internal/d/redis-prod
- Deploy timeline:     https://grafana.internal/d/deploys?var-service=orders-api
- Traces (last 15m, >800ms): https://tempo.internal/explore?q=checkout-slow

### 4. Diagnosis (do step 5 first if a deploy happened)

4.1 Where is the time going? Open the Orders API dashboard, row "Latency by span".

    Look at the p99 breakdown: db, redis, payment_gateway, inventory_service, app.

    - db dominant            -> go to 4.2
    - payment_gateway        -> go to 4.3
    - inventory_service      -> go to 4.4
    - app (no dependency)    -> go to 4.5
    - nothing dominant, gaps -> go to 4.6

4.2 PostgreSQL is slow.

    kubectl -n prod exec deploy/psql-jump -- psql -c "
      SELECT pid, now()-query_start AS dur, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
             left(query,120) AS q
      FROM pg_stat_activity
      WHERE state <> 'idle' AND now()-query_start > interval '2 seconds'
      ORDER BY dur DESC LIMIT 20;"

    - Many rows with wait_event_type='Lock'   -> lock contention, go to 5.4
    - One long query repeated                 -> plan regression, go to 5.5
    - Connections near max_connections        -> pool exhaustion, go to 5.2
    - High CPU on the instance, no locks      -> go to 5.2 then 5.6

    Check for a stuck migration or a long transaction:
    kubectl -n prod exec deploy/psql-jump -- psql -c "
      SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS xact_age, left(query,120)
      FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start < now() - interval '5 minutes';"

4.3 The payment gateway is slow.

    Check https://status.<provider>.com and our client metrics:
    - p99 of payment_client_duration_seconds
    - circuit breaker state gauge: payment_circuit_breaker_state
    If their p99 > 3 s: go to 5.3 (fail over to the secondary provider).

4.4 The inventory service is slow.

    Open its own SLO dashboard and page its on-call (#inventory, rota
    inventory-primary). Meanwhile consider 5.7 (serve from the cached snapshot).

4.5 The application itself is slow.

    Check event loop lag: nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds on the orders-api
    dashboard. Above 200 ms means we are CPU-blocked in-process.
    - Correlate with a deploy (step 5.1).
    - Check for a large-payload endpoint being hammered:
      sum by (route) (rate(http_request_size_bytes_sum[5m]))
    - Check GC: nodejs_gc_duration_seconds. Sustained major GC means a leak;
      restart the pods (5.6) to buy time and capture a heap snapshot first.

4.6 Time is unaccounted for (gaps in traces).

    Usually queueing before the handler: not enough replicas, or a saturated
    connection pool, or the ingress is at its worker limit.
    Check: replica count, HPA status, pg pool pending_requests gauge,
    ingress nginx_ingress_controller_nginx_process_connections.

### 5. Mitigation (prefer these over finishing diagnosis)

5.1 A deploy or flag change in the last 2 hours? ROLL BACK NOW.

    kubectl -n prod rollout undo deployment/orders-api
    kubectl -n prod rollout status deployment/orders-api --timeout=180s
    # Feature flags:
    curl -X POST -H "$FLAG_TOKEN" https://flags.internal/api/flags/checkout-v2/off

    Do not wait to confirm the theory. Verify with section 7 afterwards.

5.2 Scale out and relieve the pool.

    kubectl -n prod scale deployment/orders-api --replicas=12
    # If PgBouncer pools are saturated, raise default_pool_size in the
    # pgbouncer configmap and reload. Do NOT raise Postgres max_connections.

5.3 Fail over the payment provider.

    curl -X POST -H "$FLAG_TOKEN" \
      https://flags.internal/api/flags/payment-primary -d '{"value":"provider-b"}'
    Watch payment_client_duration_seconds for provider-b. Expect ~90 s to settle.

5.4 Break lock contention.

    Identify the blocking pid from 4.2, confirm with the team, then:
    SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<pid>);      -- try this first
    SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);   -- only if cancel does not work
    Never terminate a pid you have not identified. Check it is not a migration.

5.5 Disable the expensive code path.

    Kill switches available for checkout:
      checkout.recommendations   -> hides the upsell panel
      checkout.loyalty_preview   -> skips the loyalty tier calculation
      checkout.address_validation-> falls back to basic format validation
    Turning all three off removes ~180 ms of p99 and 3 database queries.

5.6 Restart the unhealthy pods (buys time, destroys evidence).

    # Capture first:
    kubectl -n prod logs deploy/orders-api --previous > /tmp/incident-$(date +%s).log
    kubectl -n prod exec <pod> -- kill -USR2 1   # heap snapshot, if enabled
    kubectl -n prod rollout restart deployment/orders-api

5.7 Shed load.

    Raise rate limits on non-critical routes to protect checkout:
    curl -X POST -H "$FLAG_TOKEN" https://flags.internal/api/flags/shed-search -d '{"value":true}'
    This returns 429 to search and browse traffic above 200 RPS, freeing
    database capacity for checkout.

### 6. Escalation

- No mitigation working after 20 minutes -> page the secondary (orders-secondary)
  and declare SEV1.
- PostgreSQL-specific and unclear         -> page @db-oncall.
- Payment provider unresponsive           -> page @payments-oncall and email
  their support alias (support@<provider>) with our merchant id.
- Suspected security or data issue        -> page @security-oncall immediately
  and stop mitigating until they advise.
- Customer-visible for over 30 minutes    -> Comms Lead updates the status page
  and notifies the Head of Support.

### 7. Verification

Do NOT declare resolved by looking at the thing you changed. Check the SLI.

1. sli:checkout_latency:ratio_rate5m is back above 0.99 and stable for 10 min.
2. The fast-burn alert has resolved (both windows below threshold).
3. Place a real test order end to end and confirm it completes in under 800 ms:
   ./scripts/synthetic-checkout.sh prod
4. Order confirmation queue: job_queue_oldest_waiting_seconds{queue="notifications"}
   is under 60 s, confirming the downstream pipeline drained.
5. Post the resolution in the incident channel with start time, end time,
   mitigation applied, and the estimated number of affected requests.
6. Schedule the postmortem before you close the channel.

That is what a finished runbook looks like. It is long, and that is fine — nobody reads it top to bottom; they jump to section 4 or 5. The length is what makes it usable at 03:00 by someone who does not know this service.

Common mistakes

  • Runbooks that explain the architecture instead of giving commands. Architecture belongs in the design doc.
  • Placeholders like <your-namespace> that require knowledge the reader does not have.
  • No mitigation section, so the reader diagnoses for forty minutes.
  • Links to dashboards that were reorganized six months ago.
  • A runbook stored somewhere the alert does not link to.

Interview questions

  1. What are the three incident roles and why must they be different people?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: IC decides, Ops executes, Comms informs; diagnosis and coordination compete for the same attention, and comms is a full-time job during an incident.
  2. What is the first thing you do when paged for a checkout outage?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: acknowledge, confirm impact in a minute, declare, check for recent changes, and roll back before diagnosing.
  3. Why roll back before confirming the deploy is the cause?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: asymmetric costs — a wasted rollback costs minutes, a delayed one costs the incident.
  4. What earns a page?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: urgent and actionable, both clauses; symptoms not causes; everything else is a ticket.
  5. How do you know your on-call rotation is unhealthy?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: pages per shift, out-of-hours pages, time to acknowledge, actionability ratio; plus the single alert responsible for most pages.
  6. What sections must a runbook have and who is it written for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: symptom, impact, dashboards, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, verification; written for a competent engineer at 3 a.m. who does not know this service.

Practical exercise

Write a complete runbook for the alert that has paged your team most often in the last quarter, using the seven-section structure.

Acceptance criteria: every command is copy-pasteable with real names; the mitigation section comes before deep diagnosis and contains at least three options including a rollback; verification checks a user-facing SLI and includes a synthetic transaction; the alert definition links to it; and a teammate who does not own that service executes it in a game day without asking you a question.

49.10 Postmortems

49.10.1 Blameless in practice, not just in name

Concept

A postmortem is a written analysis of an incident: what happened, why, what we are changing. "Blameless" means the document and the meeting focus on why the action made sense at the time rather than on who took it.

That phrasing matters. Blameless does not mean "nobody is responsible" or "we do not name people". It means we assume everyone acted reasonably given what they knew, and we ask what made the wrong action look right.

Why does it exist?

Because a blameful culture gets you fewer postmortems, not fewer incidents. If naming a mistake gets an engineer criticized in front of their manager, the next engineer will describe the incident vaguely, omit the part where they were confused, and not mention the two things they tried that made it worse. You lose exactly the information that would have prevented a recurrence.

There is also a deeper reason. If one person's mistake could take down production, that is a system design defect, not a personnel problem. Firing them leaves the defect in place for the next person.

Blameless in practice: the concrete tests

Most teams say they are blameless and are not. Four tests:

  1. Language. "Priya deployed without running the migration check" is blameful. "The deploy pipeline allowed a deploy without running the migration check, and the engineer had no signal that it had been skipped" is blameless and, importantly, more accurate.
  2. Action items. If every action item is "be more careful" or "add a review step", you are still blaming humans, just politely. Real action items change systems: add a guard, add a test, add an alert, remove the sharp edge.
  3. Attendance. If the person closest to the trigger avoids the meeting, or is unusually quiet in it, you are not blameless regardless of your wiki page.
  4. Counterfactuals. "If only she had checked the dashboard" is a counterfactual and it is useless — it describes a world that did not happen. Ask instead: why did the dashboard not make it obvious?

Blameless has one boundary worth stating: it applies to mistakes, not to deliberate policy violations. Someone who disables the alerting to make their week quieter is not a postmortem topic; that is a management conversation. In fifteen years I have seen that maybe twice, and both times the underlying cause was still an alerting system that was unusable.

49.10.2 The template

Text
POSTMORTEM: <short descriptive title>

Status: draft | in review | final
Incident: INC-2026-0142      Severity: SEV2
Date: 2026-09-03             Duration: 1h 47m (impact), 3h 12m (incident)
Authors: <names>             Reviewers: <names>
Postmortem meeting: <date>   Published: <date>

1. Summary
   Three to five sentences. What broke, who was affected, how long, what fixed it.
   A reader who stops here should understand the incident.

2. Impact
   Numbers, not adjectives. Users affected, requests failed, revenue, support
   tickets, error budget consumed, data correctness effects.

3. Timeline
   Timestamped, in one timezone, stated. Include when it started, when we knew,
   when we mitigated, when we resolved. Include the wrong turns.

4. Detection
   How did we find out? Alert, customer, or luck? Time from start to detection.
   Would our alerts have caught it if the customer had not called?

5. Root cause
   The chain of conditions. Distinguish trigger from root cause.

6. Contributing factors
   Everything that made it worse, longer or harder to detect.

7. What went well
   Genuinely. Recognizing effective response reinforces it.

8. What went badly
   Honest. This section is where the value is.

9. Where we got lucky
   The near misses. What would have made this far worse.

10. Action items
    Table: description, type (prevent/detect/mitigate/process), owner (a person,
    not a team), priority, due date, ticket link.

11. Lessons learned
    What we now believe that we did not believe before.

Two mandatory fields people leave out. "Where we got lucky" surfaces the incident you have not had yet — "the replica happened to be healthy" or "this happened at 4 a.m. instead of during the sale". And an owner who is a person: action items assigned to "the platform team" are not done six months later, every time.

49.10.3 A complete worked postmortem

Text
POSTMORTEM: Duplicate order notifications after a Kafka consumer group rebalance

Status: final
Incident: INC-2026-0142      Severity: SEV2
Date: 2026-09-03             Duration: 1h 47m impact, 3h 12m incident
Authors: A. Sharma (IC), R. Menon (Ops Lead)
Reviewers: P. Iyer (Orders lead), S. Kaur (Platform), D. Rao (Head of Engineering)
Postmortem meeting: 2026-09-08   Published: 2026-09-09

1. SUMMARY

Between 13:41 and 15:28 IST on 3 September, customers received duplicate order
confirmation emails and SMS messages, up to 6 copies of the same message. The
cause was a Kafka consumer group that entered a continuous rebalance loop after a
routine node drain, combined with a notification consumer that committed offsets
after sending rather than deduplicating on a stable key. Orders, payments and
inventory were not affected; no customer was charged twice. Mitigated by pinning
the consumer to static group membership and increasing session timeouts;
permanently fixed by adding an idempotency ledger keyed on the notification's
business key.

2. IMPACT

- 41,300 duplicate notifications sent (28,900 email, 12,400 SMS) to 9,740
  distinct customers. Peak 6 copies of one message.
- SMS provider cost: about 74,000 rupees of unbudgeted spend.
- 312 support tickets ("did I order twice?"), 4 of which escalated to refunds
  that were not actually needed.
- 2 merchants publicly complained on social media.
- No orders were duplicated. No payments were duplicated. Verified by
  reconciliation query (see appendix): orders created in the window = 24,117,
  payments = 24,117, matched 1:1.
- Error budget: the notification freshness SLO (99 % within 5 minutes) was not
  breached; delivery was fast, just repeated. The correctness SLI for
  notifications, which we did not have, would have been at ~63 % for the window.
  ACTION: we did not have an SLI that would have caught this. See AI-6.

3. TIMELINE (all times IST, 2026-09-03)

13:38  Platform begins a routine node drain on node ip-10-2-41-88 as part of the
       weekly kernel patch rollout. This is a normal, approved change.
13:39  Two notification-consumer pods are evicted and rescheduled.
13:41  Consumer group "notifications-v2" begins rebalancing. First duplicate
       notifications are sent. IMPACT STARTS.
13:41  Rebalance does not converge: pods are still starting (cold JVM-free Node
       start is ~14 s, but the consumer's first poll waits on a schema fetch that
       took 38 s under load), exceeding max.poll.interval.ms of 30 s. The group
       evicts them and rebalances again. Loop begins.
13:52  First customer support ticket: "I got 3 confirmation emails".
14:04  Second and third tickets. Support asks in #eng-help.
14:11  On-call engineer (R. Menon) acknowledges in #eng-help. Note: NO ALERT HAD
       FIRED. Detection was via support, 30 minutes after impact started.
14:14  Incident declared, SEV3 initially. Channel #inc-2026-0142 created.
14:19  Kafka consumer lag dashboard checked: lag is LOW (the consumers are
       processing, repeatedly). This misleads the responder for ~15 minutes;
       the team's mental model was "duplicates mean lag".
14:22  A. Sharma joins as IC. Comms Lead assigned (V. Nair). Upgraded to SEV2
       after estimating volume from provider dashboards.
14:31  R. Menon finds the rebalance loop in the consumer logs:
       "Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing" repeating every
       ~40 s across all pods.
14:38  MITIGATION 1: scale the notification consumer from 6 to 2 replicas to
       reduce rebalance participants. Partial improvement; loop continues.
14:52  MITIGATION 2: increase max.poll.interval.ms from 30 s to 300 s and
       session.timeout.ms from 10 s to 45 s; redeploy. Rebalance converges at
       15:04 but a final rebalance during the deploy causes another burst.
15:04  Rebalance converges. Duplicate rate drops sharply.
15:22  MITIGATION 3: enable static group membership (group.instance.id from the
       StatefulSet pod ordinal) so pod restarts do not trigger a rebalance.
15:28  Last duplicate notification observed. IMPACT ENDS.
15:31  Comms Lead posts to the status page and sends a note to support with
       approved wording for affected customers.
16:50  Incident closed after 60 minutes of clean metrics and a manual audit of
       provider send counts.

4. DETECTION

Detected by customers, via support, 30 minutes after impact began. This is the
most serious finding in this document.

Why our monitoring missed it:
- We alert on consumer LAG. A rebalance loop that reprocesses the same messages
  produces LOW lag and HIGH throughput. Our dashboards looked healthy.
- We had no alert on rebalance frequency.
- We had no correctness SLI for notifications; we measured whether we sent, not
  whether we sent once.
- The SMS provider spend alert exists but is a daily budget check that would
  have fired at 23:00.

5. ROOT CAUSE

The notification consumer was not idempotent. It performed the side effect
(calling the email and SMS providers) and then committed the Kafka offset. Any
event that causes a partition to be reassigned before the commit results in the
messages since the last commit being reprocessed and re-sent.

Kafka's delivery guarantee for a consumer that commits after processing is
at-least-once. The consumer was written as if it were exactly-once. This is a
design defect that had been latent since the service was written in March 2026;
it required a rebalance storm to become visible at scale.

6. CONTRIBUTING FACTORS

a) max.poll.interval.ms was 30 s, shorter than the consumer's own cold-start
   path (schema registry fetch under load took up to 38 s). Any restart under
   load therefore risked a rebalance loop rather than a single rebalance.
b) Dynamic group membership meant every pod restart triggered a full rebalance.
   Static membership was available and not used.
c) The node drain was performed during business hours. It is an approved,
   routine change, but it removed two consumer pods simultaneously.
d) Monitoring measured lag, not rebalance rate or duplicate sends.
e) The consumer had no ledger, no deduplication key, and the providers were
   called without idempotency keys, so neither we nor the provider could
   deduplicate.
f) The responder's mental model ("duplicates imply lag") cost ~15 minutes. The
   dashboard reinforced it by putting lag at the top and having no rebalance panel.

7. WHAT WENT WELL

- Support escalated quickly and with specifics (customer ids, message counts),
  which made estimating impact fast.
- The IC/Ops/Comms split worked: R. Menon was never interrupted while debugging.
- The reconciliation query proving orders and payments were 1:1 was written
  within 12 minutes and prevented a much larger panic about double charging.
- Static group membership was implemented and shipped during the incident, and
  it was the right permanent mitigation, not a hack.

8. WHAT WENT BADLY

- 30 minutes to detect, and only because customers told us.
- Initial severity was too low; it was set on ticket count rather than on
  estimated blast radius. Fifteen minutes were lost at SEV3 urgency.
- The lag dashboard actively misled the responder.
- The first mitigation (scaling down) was a guess and did not help.
- The config-change mitigation required a deploy, which itself caused another
  rebalance and another burst of duplicates. We made it worse for 90 seconds.
- We had no way to tell customers "ignore the duplicates" other than a status
  page most of them never saw.

9. WHERE WE GOT LUCKY

- The same consumer group also drives the loyalty-points topic. Points are
  awarded idempotently by a unique constraint, so no customer received duplicate
  points. Had that constraint not existed, we would have had a financial incident.
- The node drain touched 2 of 6 pods. A full-cluster patch would have produced a
  much longer loop.
- This was a Wednesday afternoon, not the sale weekend, when volume is 9x.

10. ACTION ITEMS

| # | Action | Type | Owner | Priority | Due | Ticket |
|---|--------|------|-------|----------|-----|--------|
| AI-1 | Add a notification_deliveries ledger with a unique key on (channel, template, business_key) and check it before sending | Prevent | R. Menon | P0 | 2026-09-12 | ORD-4471 |
| AI-2 | Send provider-side idempotency keys on all email and SMS calls | Prevent | R. Menon | P0 | 2026-09-12 | ORD-4472 |
| AI-3 | Enable static group membership on all 7 consumer groups | Prevent | S. Kaur | P0 | 2026-09-15 | PLT-2210 |
| AI-4 | Raise max.poll.interval.ms to 300 s and audit cold-start time for every consumer | Prevent | S. Kaur | P1 | 2026-09-19 | PLT-2211 |
| AI-5 | Alert on consumer group rebalance rate above 3 per 10 minutes | Detect | S. Kaur | P0 | 2026-09-12 | PLT-2212 |
| AI-6 | Define and instrument a notification correctness SLI: unique notifications sent / notifications intended | Detect | A. Sharma | P1 | 2026-09-26 | ORD-4473 |
| AI-7 | Add a "Rebalances" panel above "Lag" on the Kafka dashboard | Detect | S. Kaur | P2 | 2026-09-19 | PLT-2213 |
| AI-8 | Move routine node drains to the 01:00-04:00 window and require them to be one node at a time | Mitigate | S. Kaur | P1 | 2026-09-26 | PLT-2214 |
| AI-9 | Add a "suppress notifications" kill switch that can be flipped in under 60 seconds | Mitigate | P. Iyer | P1 | 2026-10-03 | ORD-4474 |
| AI-10 | Severity guidance: estimate blast radius, not ticket count. Update the incident policy and the on-call training | Process | A. Sharma | P2 | 2026-10-03 | ENG-991 |
| AI-11 | Game day: force a rebalance storm in staging and verify AI-1, AI-3 and AI-5 | Process | R. Menon | P1 | 2026-10-10 | ORD-4475 |

11. LESSONS LEARNED

- Consumer lag is a throughput metric, not a correctness metric. A system can
  process every message promptly and still be badly wrong.
- Any consumer that commits offsets after performing a side effect is
  at-least-once. Either make the effect idempotent or do not pretend otherwise.
- A mitigation that requires a deploy will itself trigger the failure mode you
  are mitigating. Prefer runtime configuration and kill switches.
- Severity should be set from estimated blast radius, not from how many people
  have complained so far.

That document is roughly what a good postmortem looks like: specific, numeric, honest about the wrong turns, and ending in eleven action items each owned by a named person with a date.

49.10.4 Making action items actually ship

The most common postmortem failure is not a bad document; it is a good document whose actions never ship. Four practices that fix it:

  1. Create the tickets during the meeting. Not after. The ticket link goes in the table before anyone leaves.
  2. P0 action items go into the current sprint, displacing something. If nothing is displaced, it was not really a P0.
  3. Review open postmortem actions monthly in the same forum that reviews the SLOs, and report the count and age. An action item older than 90 days is either done, cancelled with a reason, or a standing lie.
  4. Tie it to the error budget policy. When the budget is exhausted, the reliability work that gets prioritized comes from this list. That is the mechanism that turns postmortems into engineering time.

49.11 Root cause analysis

49.11.1 Trigger, root cause, contributing factors

Concept

Three different things, constantly conflated:

  • Trigger — the event that started this particular occurrence. The node drain.
  • Root cause — the condition that made the trigger capable of causing harm. The consumer was not idempotent.
  • Contributing factors — everything that made it worse, longer, or harder to see. Short poll interval, dynamic membership, lag-only monitoring, business-hours drain.

Fixing only the trigger is the classic mistake. "We will not drain nodes during business hours" makes this exact incident less likely and leaves the defect fully armed for the next rebalance, which will come from a broker upgrade, a network blip, or a pod OOM. Fixing the root cause — idempotency — makes rebalances harmless forever.

The useful heuristic: the root cause is the thing that, if fixed, makes the entire class of incident go away, not just this instance.

49.11.2 Five whys, and its limits

Five whys is a ladder: ask "why" repeatedly until you reach something worth fixing.

Text
Customers received 6 duplicate emails.
  Why? The consumer reprocessed the same Kafka messages repeatedly.
    Why? The consumer group rebalanced continuously, so offsets were never committed.
      Why? Pods exceeded max.poll.interval.ms during a slow cold start under load.
        Why? The schema registry fetch on startup took 38 s under load and the
             interval was 30 s.
          Why? The interval was left at a default nobody had reviewed against
               actual startup behaviour.

Useful. But notice what this ladder missed entirely: the consumer was not idempotent. That is the real root cause, and it is not on the "why" chain at all, because the chain follows one thread and idempotency is a parallel condition.

That is the central limitation of five whys: it produces a single linear chain, and real incidents are trees. Every serious incident has several conditions that all had to be true at once. Following one branch gives you a confident, narrow, incomplete answer.

Better tools when the incident matters:

  • Ask "why" in several directions. Why did it happen? Why did it take 30 minutes to detect? Why did the first mitigation not work? Why was the blast radius this large? Each question yields its own chain, and together they cover the tree.
  • The contributing factors list, deliberately kept long. Aim for six to ten. If you have two, you stopped early.
  • Counterfactual pruning: for each factor, ask "if this had been different, would the impact have been materially smaller?" If yes, it is a real factor and deserves an action item. If no, drop it from the list so it does not dilute the document.

49.11.3 "Human error" is never a root cause

Concept

When an analysis lands on "the engineer made a mistake", the analysis has stopped one step too early. Every time.

Humans make errors at a stable, well-studied rate. That rate is a property of being human and it does not go down because you asked people to be careful. So "human error" is not a finding; it is the point where the interesting question starts: what made the error possible, likely, or undetectable?

Translate, always:

Do not write Write instead
"The engineer deployed the wrong image tag" "The deploy command accepts any tag string and does not verify the image exists in the registry or was built from the target branch"
"The engineer forgot to run the migration" "Migrations are a separate manual step that the deploy pipeline neither runs nor checks"
"The engineer ran DELETE without a WHERE clause" "Production database access is direct and unaudited, with no dry-run, no transaction wrapper, and no row-count confirmation for destructive statements"
"The on-call did not follow the runbook" "The runbook was 14 months stale and its first command referenced a deleted namespace"
"The engineer misread the dashboard" "The dashboard's top panel was lag, which is unrelated to this failure mode, and there was no panel for the metric that mattered"
"The reviewer approved a bad PR" "The change had no test covering the failure path, and review is the only control we had"

Every right-hand entry is fixable by engineering. No left-hand entry is.

There is a sharper version of this test. Ask: "Would a competent, well-rested, well-intentioned engineer have plausibly done the same thing?" If the answer is yes — and it almost always is — then the system permitted it, and the system is what you change.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They are suspicious of a postmortem that ends after one clean causal chain, because reality is messier. They push for the second and third contributing factor. They ask "how would we have detected this without a customer telling us?" as a mandatory question, because detection gaps compound every future incident. And they never, ever let "be more careful" survive into the action items table.

49.12 Change management, game days and drills

49.12.1 Most incidents follow a change

The single most useful prior in incident response: roughly 60 to 75 percent of incidents are caused by a change your organization made. A deploy, a config edit, a feature flag, a migration, an infrastructure update, a certificate rotation, a dependency bump.

Two consequences. First, "what changed in the last two hours?" belongs at the top of every diagnosis, which is why it is step 4 of the first-ten-minutes checklist. Second, the highest-leverage reliability investment is usually making changes safer, not making the steady state more redundant.

Safer changes, concretely:

  • Small and frequent beats large and rare. Ten small deploys a week have a smaller blast radius each and a much easier bisection than one weekly release. The instinct to batch changes because deploys are risky makes each deploy riskier.
  • Progressive delivery. Canary a small fraction of traffic, watch the SLI, then ramp. Automate the rollback on burn rate: if the canary's error ratio exceeds the baseline by a threshold, abort without a human.
  • Feature flags decoupled from deploys. Ship the code dark, enable it separately, and you can turn it off in seconds without a rollout. This converts a 6-minute rollback into an 11-second flag flip, which directly moves your MTTR and therefore your availability.
  • Every change has a documented rollback, and the rollback is tested. A migration that cannot be reversed is not a change, it is a commitment (Part 24 — Database Migrations).
  • An audit trail with timestamps for deploys, flags, config and infrastructure, all on the same timeline and annotated on your dashboards. "What changed?" should take ten seconds, not ten minutes.

49.12.2 Freeze windows and when they are theatre

A freeze stops changes during a high-risk period: the sale weekend, the last week of the financial year, the two days before a big customer's audit.

Freezes are legitimate when three things are true: the period is genuinely exceptional, the freeze is short, and there is a documented exception path for security and P0 fixes.

Freezes are theatre when they are long or routine. A four-week December freeze produces a January release containing 400 commits, which is the most dangerous deploy of the year — you have converted many small risks into one enormous one, and you have destroyed your ability to bisect. Worse, teams learn to smuggle changes in through config and flags, which is the same risk with none of the review.

The better instrument is a heightened-care period: deploys continue, but only during business hours, only with two reviewers, only one service at a time, with a named engineer watching the SLI dashboard for thirty minutes after each. You keep the ability to fix things, which during a sale weekend is exactly what you need.

49.12.3 Game days and chaos experiments

Concept

A game day is a scheduled exercise where you deliberately break something in a controlled way and practise responding. A chaos experiment is the narrower automated version: inject a specific fault and assert the system behaves as designed.

The purpose is not to discover that things break. It is to discover that the things you believed would save you do not work: the failover that was never exercised, the runbook whose first command references a deleted namespace, the alert that was silenced eight months ago, the secondary on-call whose phone number is wrong.

Run it properly:

  1. Write the hypothesis first. "If we kill the PostgreSQL primary, the replica is promoted within 60 seconds, checkout sees fewer than 30 seconds of errors, the failover alert fires, and no orders are lost." A prediction you can be wrong about.
  2. Announce it. Game days are not surprise attacks. Surprising your team teaches them to distrust you, and a real incident during the exercise becomes very confusing.
  3. Have an abort condition and a person who owns it, decided before you start.
  4. Run it in production eventually. Staging game days find staging bugs. Start in staging, graduate to production during low traffic with a small blast radius.
  5. Write it up like an incident, with action items. Most of the value is in the write-up.

A useful starter menu for a NestJS-on-Kubernetes stack:

Experiment Hypothesis to test
Kill a random API pod Requests drain gracefully; no 5xx; the readiness probe removes it before the SIGTERM
