Kill the PostgreSQL primary Failover under 60 s; the connection pool reconnects; checkout errors are bounded
Add 300 ms of latency to Redis Requests degrade to the database path; latency SLI dips but no errors
Make the payment provider return 503 The circuit breaker opens; we fail over to provider B; the burn-rate alert fires
Fill a worker's disk The pod is evicted, jobs are requeued, and nothing is lost
Scale workers to zero for 20 minutes Backlog grows, the oldest-waiting-job alert fires, everything drains on recovery
Expire a TLS certificate in staging The renewal alarm fires at least 24 hours before expiry
Page the on-call rotation with a test alert Everyone's device is configured and the escalation path works end to end

That last one is the cheapest and finds a broken paging path roughly once a year in every organization I have worked in.

49.12.4 DR drills and capacity reviews

Disaster recovery drills test the big, rare, terrifying scenarios: the region is gone, the database is corrupted, the account is compromised. The measurements that matter are RTO (how long until service is restored) and RPO (how much data is lost). Both are fiction until you have restored from a backup with a stopwatch running. Part 50 covers backups and disaster recovery in depth; the SRE-side rule is simply that an untested backup is not a backup, and a DR plan that has never been executed is a document, not a capability.

Capacity reviews are the quiet practice that prevents the loudest incidents. Quarterly, ask: what is our peak now, what will it be next quarter, where is the first thing that breaks, and what is the lead time to fix it? Databases have the longest lead times — a bigger instance is a maintenance window, a shard split is a project, a connection-limit ceiling is an architecture change. Find those before the sale, not during it.

49.13 Reliability practice for the NestJS stack

Concretely, here is what "we do SRE" should mean for a NestJS service in front of PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka. Six artefacts, all of which are code or configuration, none of which are slideware.

1. A per-service dashboard with a fixed shape, so any engineer can read any service's dashboard. Five rows: SLI and error budget at the top; RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) by route; dependencies (PostgreSQL pool and query latency, Redis latency and hit rate, Kafka lag and rebalance rate, queue depth and oldest-waiting-job age); runtime (event loop lag, heap, GC, replica count, restarts); and deploy annotations across every panel. Part 43 — Observability builds these.

2. SLO alerts, and almost nothing else that pages. Burn-rate alerts per journey, plus a small set of hard-failure alerts that are urgent and actionable: CrashLoopBackOff, dead-letter queue growth, replication lag above the threshold, certificate expiry within 24 hours, disk filling. Everything else is a ticket or a dashboard panel.

3. A dependency map that is maintained. For each service: what it calls synchronously, what it calls asynchronously, what the timeout is, what happens when each one fails, and whose on-call owns it. Keep it next to the code (a DEPENDENCIES.md reviewed in PRs that add a client) so it cannot rot silently.

4. Documented degradation modes. For every dependency, a written answer to "what does the user see when this is down?" — and code that implements it. This is the table that turns a serial-dependency chain into a resilient one:

Dependency down Designed behaviour Implemented with
Redis Read through to PostgreSQL; latency rises ~40 ms; no errors Cache wrapper with a fail-open path and a short timeout
Recommendation service Panel renders empty 250 ms timeout, empty-array fallback
Inventory service Serve the last known snapshot, flag "stock may be inaccurate" Cached snapshot with a documented 5-minute staleness bound
Payment provider A Automatic failover to provider B Circuit breaker plus a runtime flag
Email provider Queued and retried; the order still completes BullMQ with retries and a DLQ (Part 36)
Kafka Events buffered in the outbox; published on recovery Transactional outbox with a relay
PostgreSQL primary Reads served from the replica; writes fail fast with a clear error Read replica routing plus a fast-fail write path

5. Kill switches, tested. A runtime flag for every non-essential feature in a critical path, flippable in under 60 seconds without a deploy, listed in the runbook, and exercised in a game day. Their value is measured in MTTR, and MTTR is measured in money.

6. DLQ replay tooling behind admin auth: a summary endpoint that groups failures by reason, and a replay endpoint that is capped and spaced. Building this before you need it turns a two-hour manual recovery into a five-minute one, and it is 60 lines of code (Part 36).

49.14 Edge cases and failure modes

SLOs measured server-side only. The pods were down, so they emitted no metrics, so the error ratio was 0/0 and the dashboard was green through a 40-minute outage. Fix: compute availability at the ingress or load balancer, and add a black-box probe as a liveness canary on your monitoring of your monitoring.

Alert fatigue. Forty pages a week, most of them nothing. People acknowledge without reading. Eventually a real one is acknowledged without reading. Fix: treat noisy alerts as bugs with owners and due dates; review the top-firing alert every month; delete anything nobody has acted on in six months.

Unowned services. legacy-sync has no team, no runbook and no dashboard, and it is in the checkout path. Fix: a service catalogue where every service has an owning team, an on-call rota, an SLO and a runbook, and a rule that a service without an owner cannot be deployed to production.

Postmortem actions that never ship. The document is excellent. Six months later, the same incident. Fix: tickets created in the meeting, P0s in the current sprint, monthly review of open actions with an age report, and budget-policy time reserved for them.

Silence during an incident. Engineering is working hard and telling nobody. Support invents answers, the exec escalates, the customer finds out from a competitor's tweet. Fix: a Comms Lead role, a fixed update cadence enforced by the IC, and a status page updated within 15 minutes even when the message is only "we are investigating".

Hero culture. One engineer fixes every incident, at 2 a.m., alone, and is praised for it. This looks like strength and is a single point of failure with a pulse. Fix: rotate the IC role, require runbooks written by the hero and executed by someone else, praise the person who made the incident boring rather than the one who was awake for it.

Single-person knowledge. Only Arun understands the payment reconciliation. Arun is on holiday. Fix: runbooks executed by non-experts in game days, pairing on incident response, and a rule that a system with one knowledgeable person is a P1 risk, tracked like any other.

Stale runbooks. The first command references a namespace deleted last year, so the reader loses trust and improvises. Fix: a review date in every runbook, an automated check that flags any runbook older than 6 months, and execution in game days which finds the rot.

An ignored error budget. The budget has been exhausted for four consecutive months and nothing has changed. The SLO is now decoration and everyone knows it. Fix: the policy's escalation clause — either the target comes down or reliability work gets staffed. Say it out loud to management. An SLO nobody enforces is worse than none, because it creates false confidence.

Retries masking failures. The client retries three times, so the SLI measured at the ingress looks fine, while users wait 9 seconds and a third of them give up. Your dashboard shows 99.97 percent and your conversion rate is falling. Fix: measure at the user journey level — one attempt per user action — and add a latency SLI, not just availability. Also count retries explicitly: a rising retry rate with a flat error rate is the signature of exactly this.

Monitoring down during the incident. Prometheus runs in the cluster that is failing, so during the outage you are blind. Fix: host monitoring outside the blast radius (a different cluster, a different account, or a managed service), and keep an external black-box probe and an out-of-band paging path that does not depend on your own infrastructure.

A status page nobody updates. It exists, it says "all systems operational", and it has said that through the last three outages. It is now actively harmful: it teaches customers your communications are worthless. Fix: make updating it a step in the incident process owned by a named role, and audit it after every incident.

An incident starting at on-call handoff. 09:58, the outgoing engineer is mentally finished and the incoming one has no context. Both assume the other has it. Fix: an explicit handoff protocol — the outgoing on-call stays engaged until the incoming one confirms context in writing; and if an incident is active at handoff, the outgoing engineer remains the IC until the incident is resolved or a formal IC handoff is announced in the channel.

A dependency whose SLA is worse than your SLO. You promise 99.95 percent; the SMS provider offers 99.5 percent and sits in your signup flow. Fix: the arithmetic in 49.6 — remove it from the synchronous path, add a second provider, degrade gracefully, or lower your promise. And check every vendor's SLA against your own SLO before signing, not after the first breach.

The SLI that measures the wrong thing. Availability was 99.99 percent all month because a bug made the API return 200 OK with an empty body. Fix: correctness SLIs and synthetic transactions that assert on content, not status codes. A synthetic checkout that verifies an order row appears is worth more than a hundred /health probes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about all of this

They know reliability is bought, not wished for, and they can say what it costs. They measure from the user's side because that is the only side that matters. They keep a small number of alerts that all mean something. They mitigate before they diagnose, and they can prove they do because their runbooks are ordered that way. They write postmortems that make the system safer rather than making someone feel bad. And they know that the highest-leverage reliability work is almost never more redundancy: it is faster rollback, better alerts, fewer synchronous dependencies, and a team that is not exhausted.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a postmortem blameless, in practice rather than in name?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: system-focused language, action items that change systems, the person closest to the trigger present and comfortable, no counterfactuals; and the recognition that a single mistake taking down production is a design defect.
  2. Distinguish trigger, root cause and contributing factors with an example.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: node drain, non-idempotent consumer, and the poll interval / membership / monitoring gaps; fixing only the trigger leaves the class of incident armed.
  3. What are the limits of five whys?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it yields one linear chain while incidents are trees; ask why in several directions and keep a long contributing-factors list.
  4. Why is "human error" never a root cause?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: human error rate is a constant; the question is what made the error possible or undetectable; translate to a system property that engineering can change.
  5. Your team wants a four-week code freeze before the holidays. What do you say?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it converts many small risks into one enormous January release and destroys bisection; propose a heightened-care period with an exception path instead.
  6. What would you run in your first game day, and what is the hypothesis?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a specific, falsifiable prediction with an abort condition, announced in advance, written up like an incident.
  7. Your availability SLI says 99.99 percent and customers are complaining. Name four reasons.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: measured server-side while pods were down; retries masking failures; wrong SLI (200 with an empty body); journey-level failure spread across services each of which looks fine; a threshold that does not match user experience.

Practical exercise

Run a full incident lifecycle as a drill, end to end, within one week.

  1. Schedule a game day. Write the hypothesis: "if we make the payment provider return 503 for 20 minutes, the circuit breaker opens within 30 seconds, we fail over to provider B, the fast-burn alert fires within 10 minutes, and no order is lost."
  2. Run it in staging with production-like traffic. Assign a real IC, Ops Lead and Comms Lead. Post updates on the real cadence to a real channel.
  3. Have someone who does not own the service execute the runbook.
  4. Write the postmortem using the full template, including "where we got lucky".
  5. Create every action item as a ticket during the meeting.

Acceptance criteria: the hypothesis was written before the exercise and at least one part of it turned out to be wrong; the runbook was executed by a non-expert without asking the owner a question, or the gaps it exposed became action items; the alert fired within the predicted window; the postmortem contains at least six contributing factors and zero instances of "be more careful"; every action item has a named person and a date; and the P0 items are in the current sprint.

Senior Checklist — Part 49

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain reliability as a feature with a cost, and name what we would give up to add a nine
  • I can identify toil in my team's week and name the top item to eliminate this quarter
  • I can define an SLI as a ratio of good to valid events for availability, latency, correctness and freshness
  • My availability SLI is measured at the edge, not inside the service, and I can explain why that matters
  • I have written histogram buckets that bracket my latency SLO thresholds
  • I can write the PromQL and recording rules for every SLI I own
  • I have SLOs per user journey, with targets justified by user need, historical achievability and dependency ceilings
  • I can explain the difference between SLO and SLA and why the SLA must be looser
  • I can compute an error budget in minutes and in failed requests, and state my current remaining budget
  • I can explain and configure multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, and justify the 14.4 / 6 / 3 / 1 rates
  • There is a written, signed error budget policy that says what happens when the budget is exhausted
  • I can multiply a serial dependency chain and tell product why a target is impossible
  • I know my journey's MTTR and I can name the cheapest thing that would halve it
  • We have severity levels with concrete examples, and anyone may declare an incident without permission
  • I can run an incident as IC without touching a terminal
  • I mitigate before I diagnose, and my runbooks are ordered that way
  • Every alert that pages has an owner, a runbook link, a for: duration and a user-impact description
  • I track pages per shift, out-of-hours pages, time to acknowledge and actionability, and review them monthly
  • I can write a runbook a non-expert can execute at 3 a.m. without asking me a question
  • I can write a blameless postmortem with impact numbers, a timeline including wrong turns, contributing factors, luck, and owned action items with dates
  • I never write "human error" as a root cause
  • We run game days, and at least one of our beliefs has been proven wrong by one

Part 49 — Key Takeaways

  • Reliability is a product feature with a price. The right amount is the least that keeps users happy and the business safe; more than that is capital you could have spent shipping.
  • An SLI is always a ratio of good events to valid events. CPU is not an SLI; users do not experience CPU.
  • Measure availability at the edge. A crashed service emits no metrics, and its error ratio looks perfect while customers get 502s.
  • Write SLOs per user journey, not per service, and give different journeys different targets on purpose.
  • The SLA is always looser than the SLO. The gap between them is your warning margin, and it is the difference between a feature freeze and a refund.
  • The error budget turns "it feels risky" into arithmetic both engineering and product can read, and it gives product the right to spend it.
  • Alert on burn rate with paired long and short windows: page for fast burns, ticket for slow bleeds, and let the short window resolve the alert quickly.
  • Serial dependencies multiply. Four services at 99.9 percent give 99.6 percent, and no amount of enthusiasm changes that.
  • You cannot be more available than a dependency you must call synchronously. Remove it, degrade around it, add real redundancy, or lower the promise.
  • MTTR is usually the cheapest lever on availability. A rollback button and a kill switch beat another replica.
  • In the first ten minutes: mitigate. Roll back, scale, shed load, disable the feature. Diagnosis is what the postmortem is for.
  • One person cannot be Incident Commander, Operations Lead and Communications Lead. Decisions and debugging compete for the same brain.
  • A page must be urgent and actionable. Everything else is a ticket, and a noisy alert is a bug with an owner and a due date.
  • A runbook is written for a competent engineer at 3 a.m. who does not know your service: symptom, impact, dashboards, diagnosis, mitigation, escalation, verification.
  • Blameless means asking what made the wrong action look right. "Human error" is never a root cause; it is where the analysis should start.
  • Most incidents follow a change, so making changes safer beats making the steady state more redundant.
  • An untested failover is not redundancy, and an unexecuted runbook is fiction. Game days are how you find out which of your safety nets are real.

Part 50 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery

  • 2 h 8 min read
  • 11 sections
  • 12 diagrams
  • 36 code examples

What you will learn

  1. 50.1Backup
  2. 50.2Restore
  3. 50.3RPO and RTO
  4. 50.4Point-in-time recovery
  5. 50.5Disaster recovery strategies
  6. 50.6Failover and failback
  7. 50.7Database recovery scenarios
  8. 50.8Application-level recovery
  9. 50.9What happens if the PostgreSQL production database disappears
  10. 50.10The DR runbook and drill schedule
  11. 50.11Edge cases and failure modes

Every system in this book has assumed the data is there. This part is about the day it is not.

The running example is a real shape you have probably worked on: an e-commerce platform. NestJS services on Kubernetes (EKS), a primary RDS PostgreSQL instance holding orders, order items, payments, inventory and customers, ElastiCache Redis for sessions and hot product data, Kafka carrying order and inventory events, S3 holding invoices and product images. Roughly 400 requests per second at peak, 25,000 orders a day, a 2 TB database growing 40 GB a month.

The question this part answers is not "do you have backups". Almost everyone has backups. The question is: when the primary database is gone at 02:14 on a Saturday, how long until customers can check out again, and how many orders did you lose? Those two numbers are your RTO and your RPO, and everything else in this part exists to move them.

50.1 Backup

Concept

A backup is a copy of your data that lives somewhere the original failure cannot reach. That last clause is the whole discipline. A copy on the same disk is not a backup. A snapshot in the same AWS account as the database is barely a backup, because one compromised credential deletes both. A copy in another region, in another account, that a human cannot delete without a second approval, is a backup.

PostgreSQL gives you two fundamentally different kinds of copy, and you need to understand both because they solve different problems.

Logical backups export the contents of the database as SQL statements or a portable archive: CREATE TABLE, then the rows. pg_dump dumps one database; pg_dumpall adds cluster-wide objects such as roles and tablespaces. The output is portable across PostgreSQL versions and architectures, and you can restore a single table out of it.

Physical backups copy the files on disk — the data directory, byte for byte — plus the stream of Write-Ahead Log (WAL) records written after the copy started. pg_basebackup takes the base copy; an archive_command or pg_receivewal ships the WAL. The result is not readable as SQL. It restores as an entire cluster, at any point in time covered by the WAL you kept.

Why does it exist?

Without a backup, every failure is permanent. That is obvious. What is less obvious is which failures backups are actually for, because engineers usually design them for the wrong one.

Hardware failure is the failure everybody plans for and the one that almost never causes data loss any more. RDS stores data on replicated EBS with Multi-AZ; a disk dying is a non-event. The failures that actually destroy data in 2026 are:

  1. Human error. DELETE without WHERE. A migration that drops a column with three years of data in it. A cleanup script that reads the wrong environment variable and points at production.
  2. Application bugs. A soft-delete flag inverted in a release, marking 400,000 rows as deleted.
  3. Malicious action. A leaked credential, ransomware that encrypts and then deletes snapshots, a disgruntled insider.
  4. Regional or provider outages. Rare, but when a region has a bad day and you are single-region, you have no lever at all.

Backups exist because none of those are fixed by replication. A replica faithfully replicates your DELETE in under a second. Replication protects against infrastructure failure. Backups protect against time — the ability to go back to a moment before the mistake.

Mental model

Imagine a shop's accounts. A logical backup is a photocopy of the ledger: readable by anyone, you can photocopy just page 42 back into a fresh ledger, but copying 900 pages by hand takes all afternoon and the copy is a snapshot of one moment.

A physical backup is a photograph of the whole safe, plus a tape recorder that has been recording every transaction spoken aloud since the photo was taken. To reconstruct any moment, you develop the photo and then replay the tape up to the second you care about. You cannot read the photo with your eyes, and you cannot pull out page 42 alone — but you can land on 14:31:59 exactly.

You want both. The photograph and tape for "the database is gone" and "go back to before the mistake". The photocopy for "someone truncated one table and everything else is fine".

How it works

Logical backup mechanics. pg_dump opens a transaction with a REPEATABLE READ snapshot, so the dump is internally consistent as of its start time. It reads every table sequentially. Because of MVCC, a long dump holds an old snapshot open, which blocks VACUUM from cleaning up dead tuples for the duration — a 3 hour dump on a busy database causes measurable bloat. It also takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on every table it reads, which conflicts with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — so a migration doing ALTER TABLE will queue behind the dump and then block every query behind itself.

Shell
# Custom format (-Fc): compressed, restorable selectively, parallel-restorable.
pg_dump \
  --host=orders-primary.internal --username=backup_ro --dbname=shop \
  --format=custom --compress=6 --jobs=1 \
  --no-owner --no-privileges \
  --file=/backup/shop-2026-09-09T02-00Z.dump

# Directory format (-Fd) is the only one that supports a PARALLEL dump.
pg_dump --format=directory --jobs=8 --file=/backup/shop-dir --dbname=shop

# Roles, tablespaces and per-database GRANTs live outside any single database.
pg_dumpall --globals-only --file=/backup/globals-2026-09-09.sql

Two things engineers forget. First, pg_dump does not dump roles, so a restore into a fresh cluster fails on every GRANT unless you also ran pg_dumpall --globals-only. Second, --format=plain (the default when you pipe to a file) cannot be restored selectively; use --format=custom so pg_restore --table=order_items works later.

Time cost is the real constraint: pg_dump of a 2 TB database at a realistic 80 to 150 MB/s of compressed throughput takes 4 to 7 hours, and pg_restore of it takes longer because indexes are rebuilt from scratch. That is why logical backups are a surgical tool, not your disaster recovery mechanism, above a few hundred gigabytes.

Physical backup mechanics. This is the mechanism behind every managed snapshot product.

  1. Take a base backup: a consistent copy of the data directory. pg_basebackup calls pg_backup_start(), which forces a checkpoint, then streams every file, then pg_backup_stop(). The copy is "torn" (files change while being copied) but that is fine, because...
  2. ...every change is also written to the WAL. WAL is an append-only record of every page modification, written before the page itself is flushed. Replaying WAL over a torn base copy makes it consistent.
  3. Archive the WAL continuously. PostgreSQL calls archive_command for each completed 16 MB WAL segment. In production that command is wal-g wal-push or pgbackrest archive-push, which uploads to S3.
  4. To restore: unpack the base backup, drop in a recovery.signal file, set restore_command to fetch WAL from the archive, and start PostgreSQL. It replays forward until it reaches the end of the archive or the target you specified.
Text
   base backup taken 02:00              WAL segments archived continuously
   +-----------------------+   +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
   |  data directory copy  |   |02:03|02:07|02:14|02:31|...  |14:32|
   +-----------------------+   +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
              |                                  |
              +---------- replay ----------------+ = database as of any second

The critical property: your recovery point is the last archived WAL segment, not the last base backup. If WAL archiving is healthy, an hourly snapshot plus continuous WAL gives you an RPO measured in seconds, not an hour. If WAL archiving is broken, your RPO silently becomes the age of your last snapshot, and nothing alerts you until you try to restore.

SQL
-- Minimum settings for physical backup + PITR on self-managed PostgreSQL.
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = 'replica';            -- 'logical' if you also use logical replication
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_mode = 'on';
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p';
ALTER SYSTEM SET archive_timeout = '60s';          -- force a segment switch every 60s so a quiet
                                                   -- database still bounds RPO to ~60 seconds
ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_keep_size = '8GB';            -- headroom if the archive is briefly unreachable
-- Verify archiving is actually working; this view is the one you alert on.
SELECT archived_count, last_archived_wal, last_archived_time,
       failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

If failed_count is climbing, or now() - last_archived_time is over a few minutes, your PITR window is broken right now. This is the single most under-monitored metric in PostgreSQL operations.

RDS automated snapshots and manual snapshots. On RDS, AWS runs the physical mechanism for you.

Automated backups Manual snapshots
Created by AWS, daily in the backup window You, via console/API/CLI
Retention 1 to 35 days, then deleted automatically Until you delete them
Enables PITR Yes, with continuous transaction log capture, typically to within 5 minutes No, restores to that one moment
Deleted with the instance Yes, unless you take a final snapshot No, survives instance deletion
Cross-region Copy or use automated backup replication copy-db-snapshot to another region

The snapshot itself is an EBS-level block snapshot: the first is full, later ones are incremental against changed blocks. That is why a daily snapshot of a 2 TB database costs far less than 2 TB per day of storage — you pay roughly for the churn, around 40 to 80 GB a day for our workload, at about $0.095 per GB-month for RDS snapshot storage in us-east-1 (approximate list price, region-dependent).

The trap: automated backups die with the instance. If someone deletes the RDS instance without --final-db-snapshot-identifier, the automated backups go with it. Manual snapshots and cross-region copies do not.

Frequency is driven by RPO, not by habit. If the business accepts losing 5 minutes of orders, a nightly snapshot is irrelevant on its own — you need continuous WAL/transaction-log archiving. If you accept 24 hours for an analytics warehouse, a nightly dump is genuinely enough. Work backwards from the number, never forwards from "daily sounds right". Section 50.3 makes this explicit.

Encryption. Enable RDS storage encryption with a customer-managed KMS key at creation time (you cannot enable it later without a dump-and-reload or snapshot-copy-with-encryption). Snapshots of an encrypted instance are encrypted with the same key. To copy a snapshot to another region or account you must re-encrypt with a key in that region/account and grant the target principal kms:Decrypt and kms:CreateGrant — this is the step that fails during a real incident if you never tested it.

Cross-region and cross-account copies. Two different threats:

  • Cross-region protects against a region-wide event. Either use RDS automated backup replication to a second region, or a scheduled Lambda/EventBridge job that copies the daily snapshot. Expect a 2 TB cross-region snapshot copy to take 1 to 3 hours, and to cost cross-region data transfer of roughly $0.02 per GB.
  • Cross-account protects against your own account being compromised or your own engineers being wrong. Share the snapshot to a locked-down "backup vault" account whose credentials no application and no normal engineer holds. AWS Backup with a vault lock in compliance mode makes those recovery points genuinely immutable: nobody, including the account root, can delete them before their retention expires. This is the control that survives ransomware.

The parts everyone forgets. Ask a team "are you backed up?" and they mean the database. Here is the rest of the system, and what actually happens if you skip each one.

Asset Backup mechanism What breaks without it
Redis (ElastiCache) Daily RDB snapshot to S3; AOF where supported Sessions gone (users logged out), rate-limit counters reset, and any cache-only data such as an unpersisted cart is permanently lost
S3 uploads Versioning + lifecycle for old versions, Cross-Region Replication, optionally Object Lock A bad delete or a wrong lifecycle rule removes invoices you are legally required to keep for 7 years
Secrets (Secrets Manager / Vault) Multi-region replicas, exported and encrypted to the backup account You restore the database and cannot connect to it, because nothing knows the password
Infrastructure state (Terraform) Remote state in S3 with versioning + DynamoDB locking; state stored per environment You can rebuild the database but not the VPC, subnets, security groups or IAM roles around it
Container images ECR with immutable tags and lifecycle rules that keep the last N; a pull-through cache or mirror You cannot redeploy the version that was running, because someone force-pushed :latest
Kafka topic data Tiered storage / MirrorMaker2 to a second cluster, or the source-of-truth-in-DB pattern Events in flight when the cluster died are gone; consumers cannot rebuild state
Kubernetes manifests Git (this is why GitOps matters); plus Velero for stateful cluster resources Rebuilding the cluster is archaeology from someone's shell history
Data warehouse / analytics Reproducible from source systems, if the pipelines are in Git You spend a week reconstructing dashboards nobody can audit

Kafka deserves a note. Kafka is not a database and its retention is not a backup, but it is often the only record of events that were emitted and not yet processed. The senior pattern is not "back up Kafka" — it is make Kafka reproducible: every event that matters is also written to a transactional outbox table in PostgreSQL in the same transaction as the business change. Then the database backup implicitly backs up the event stream, and 50.8 can replay it.

Who owns backups and how you prove they ran. Ownership must be a named team, written down, with the DR runbook (50.10). "AWS does it" is not ownership; AWS runs the mechanism, you own the outcome.

Proof is not "the job exited 0". Proof is three signals, all alerted on:

  1. Existence and freshness. Newest recovery point is younger than the RPO target. Alert if not.
  2. Continuity. WAL/transaction-log archiving has no gap. On RDS, LatestRestorableTime should never be more than about 5 to 10 minutes behind now. On self-managed, pg_stat_archiver.failed_count must be flat and last_archived_time recent.
  3. Restorability. A restore actually succeeded and the data passed checks — within the last 24 hours. That is 50.2, and it is the only one of the three that proves anything.

NestJS example

Backup freshness is an application-observable fact, so expose it like any other health signal. This job polls RDS and Redis recovery points, publishes gauges, and fails a health indicator when the newest recovery point breaches the RPO budget.

TypeScript
// backup-freshness.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { RDSClient, DescribeDBInstancesCommand, DescribeDBSnapshotsCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-rds';
import { InjectMetric } from '@willsoto/nestjs-prometheus';
import { Gauge } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class BackupFreshnessService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(BackupFreshnessService.name);
  private readonly rds: RDSClient;
  private readonly instanceId: string;

  constructor(
    config: ConfigService,
    @InjectMetric('backup_recovery_point_age_seconds') private readonly ageGauge: Gauge<string>,
  ) {
    this.rds = new RDSClient({ region: config.getOrThrow('AWS_REGION') });
    this.instanceId = config.getOrThrow('RDS_INSTANCE_ID');
  }

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_5_MINUTES)
  async checkRecoveryPoints(): Promise<void> {
    // 1. PITR window: how far back can we actually restore to, right now?
    const instances = await this.rds.send(
      new DescribeDBInstancesCommand({ DBInstanceIdentifier: this.instanceId }),
    );
    const latestRestorable = instances.DBInstances?.[0]?.LatestRestorableTime;
    if (!latestRestorable) {
      // No restorable time means automated backups are OFF. This is a page, not a warning.
      this.ageGauge.set({ kind: 'pitr' }, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);
      this.log.error('No LatestRestorableTime: automated backups are disabled');
      return;
    }
    this.ageGauge.set({ kind: 'pitr' }, (Date.now() - latestRestorable.getTime()) / 1000);

    // 2. Newest snapshot, including cross-region copies we own.
    const snaps = await this.rds.send(
      new DescribeDBSnapshotsCommand({ DBInstanceIdentifier: this.instanceId, SnapshotType: 'automated' }),
    );
    const newest = (snaps.DBSnapshots ?? [])
      .filter((s) => s.Status === 'available' && s.SnapshotCreateTime)
      .sort((a, b) => b.SnapshotCreateTime!.getTime() - a.SnapshotCreateTime!.getTime())[0];
    this.ageGauge.set(
      { kind: 'snapshot' },
      newest ? (Date.now() - newest.SnapshotCreateTime!.getTime()) / 1000 : Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER,
    );
  }
}

The alert rule that goes with it is one line, and it is worth more than the code: backup_recovery_point_age_seconds{kind="pitr"} > 900 for 10 minutes, severity page. A broken PITR window is an emergency even when nothing is currently wrong, because it is the moment your RPO silently became 24 hours.

PostgreSQL example

The restore-side checks you will want later are easier if you record facts at backup time. A tiny audit table costs nothing and answers "what was in the database when this backup was taken?" during a restore.

SQL
CREATE TABLE backup_markers (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  taken_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  lsn           pg_lsn      NOT NULL,
  orders_count  bigint      NOT NULL,
  max_order_id  bigint,
  db_size_bytes bigint      NOT NULL
);

-- Run immediately before/with each backup (cheap: counts are approximate from stats where needed).
INSERT INTO backup_markers (lsn, orders_count, max_order_id, db_size_bytes)
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn(),
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders),
       (SELECT max(id) FROM orders),
       pg_database_size(current_database());

After a restore you compare the restored backup_markers row against the restored orders table. If they disagree, the restore is incomplete and you know it in 10 seconds instead of 10 hours.

Production scenario

Our platform's backup posture, written as the numbers a senior would actually defend in a design review:

  • RDS db.r6g.4xlarge, 2 TB gp3 storage, Multi-AZ, storage encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key.
  • Automated backups, 35 day retention, backup window 02:00–02:30 UTC (traffic trough). PITR granularity ~5 minutes.
  • Daily snapshot copy to eu-west-1, retained 14 days. Cost: roughly 60 GB/day of changed blocks, so about $30–60/month of cross-region snapshot storage plus transfer.
  • AWS Backup plan copying the daily recovery point into a separate backup account with a 30 day vault lock in compliance mode. No human in the production account can delete it.
  • ElastiCache: daily snapshot, 7 day retention. Sessions are treated as disposable; carts are persisted to PostgreSQL, not only Redis. This is a design decision made specifically so Redis never needs a real backup.
  • S3 uploads bucket: versioning on, non-current versions expire after 90 days, CRR to eu-west-1, invoices prefix under Object Lock in governance mode for 7 years.
  • Terraform state: S3 with versioning and DynamoDB lock table, in the shared-services account.
  • ECR: immutable tags, lifecycle keeps the last 50 images per repository.

Monthly cost of the entire backup posture: on the order of $300 to $500. Compare that against a single hour of a checkout outage at 25,000 orders a day and an average basket of $60: roughly $60,000 of gross merchandise value per full day, so about $2,500 per hour of complete downtime, before reputational cost. The backup budget is not where you save money.

Failure scenario

A team runs pg_dump nightly from a cron job on a bastion host, uploading to S3. It has "worked" for two years. In March, the DBA adds a new schema analytics and the dump command still says --schema=public. Nobody notices, because the job exits 0 and the file appears in S3 every night at the right size (the public schema is 95 percent of the data).

In September, a bad migration drops analytics.order_facts, 400 GB of derived data with 18 months of history that was never re-derivable because the source events had aged out of Kafka. The restore recovers public perfectly and analytics not at all.

The postmortem finds the cause is not the migration. It is that the backup was never verified against what the database contains — only against whether the command exited successfully. The fix is a check that compares the list of schemas and tables in the dump manifest (pg_restore --list) against information_schema.tables in production, and fails the job on any table present in production and absent from the backup.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • pg_dump running for hours blocks VACUUM from reclaiming dead tuples cluster-wide; on a high-churn table that is measurable bloat by morning. Dump from a replica instead, but see 50.11 for the lag trap.
  • pg_dump takes ACCESS SHARE on every table; a concurrent ALTER TABLE queues behind it and then blocks all reads on that table. Always set lock_timeout on migrations (see Part 24 — Database Migrations).
  • Large objects (pg_largeobject) are not included with --table selective dumps.
  • Sequences are dumped with their current value at dump time; restoring an old dump into a live system reissues ids (50.11).
  • Encrypted snapshots cannot be shared cross-account until copied and re-encrypted with a key the target account can use; and a KMS key scheduled for deletion makes every snapshot encrypted with it permanently unreadable.
  • Snapshot storage bills grow silently: 35 daily snapshots plus every developer's "before I try this" manual snapshot. Tag and expire them (Part 51).
  • A backup that is stored in the same account, same region, with the same credentials that run the application is one compromised token away from deletion.
  • Backups of encrypted-at-rest data are useless if the application-level encryption keys (envelope keys for PII columns) are not also backed up, separately.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start from the loss, not the mechanism. "If we lose everything right now, what do we owe customers?" produces a much better backup plan than "how often should we snapshot?".

They separate replication from backup out loud, every time, because the confusion is universal. Replicas protect against a machine dying. Backups protect against a decision being wrong.

They insist on a second custody boundary. The question they ask an architecture review is: "Which single credential can delete both the data and the backups?" If there is one, the design is not finished.

They treat backup age and archive continuity as SLIs with pages attached, not as dashboards someone looks at quarterly.

And they know the cost of the whole thing is small enough that arguing about it is a waste of a meeting. Explain it to a product manager as insurance: "we spend about $400 a month so that the worst realistic day costs us two hours instead of the company."

Common mistakes

  • Believing a read replica is a backup.
  • Enabling RDS automated backups with 1 day retention because it is the default, so the detection window for a subtle data bug is shorter than the retention.
  • Taking pg_dump from a replica with 40 minutes of lag and recording the wrong recovery point.
  • Never dumping globals, so restores fail on missing roles at the worst possible time.
  • Storing snapshots only in the account that also runs production.
  • Backing up the database but not the secrets, so the restored database is unreachable.
  • Measuring backup success by exit code.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a logical and a physical backup, and when do you use each?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: logical is portable SQL/archive, selective restore, slow at scale, snapshot of one moment; physical is a file-level copy plus WAL, restores whole clusters to any point in time, fast for TB-scale. Use physical for DR, logical for surgical single-table recovery and version migrations. Follow-up: which one lets you restore one table? (Logical, or a physical restore to a side instance then extract.)
  2. Is a read replica a backup? Why not?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no; replication propagates mistakes in under a second. It gives availability, not the ability to go back in time.
  3. What determines your actual RPO on RDS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: transaction log capture frequency, not snapshot frequency; LatestRestorableTime is the honest number, typically ~5 minutes behind. Follow-up: what breaks it? Archive failures, storage full, disabled backups.
  4. How would you protect backups from ransomware or a compromised admin credential?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: separate account, separate credential path, AWS Backup vault lock in compliance mode or S3 Object Lock, MFA delete, no cross-linking of IAM.
  5. What do you back up besides the database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: secrets, IaC state, container images, object storage with versioning, Redis if it holds non-reproducible state, and a plan for in-flight events. Follow-up: why is Kafka usually not backed up? Because the outbox in PostgreSQL is the reproducible source of truth.
  6. Your pg_dump takes 6 hours. What is the operational side effect on production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: an old MVCC snapshot held open blocks VACUUM, causing bloat; ACCESS SHARE locks block DDL; network and CPU load on the source.

Practical exercise

Take a local PostgreSQL in Docker with a shop database containing orders and order_items (seed 500,000 rows). Configure archive_mode=on with an archive_command that copies segments to a local directory. Take a pg_basebackup. Then:

  1. Insert 10,000 more orders and note the time.
  2. Delete the archive directory's newest two segments (simulate an archive gap).
  3. Try to restore to a point after the gap.

Acceptance criteria: you can state exactly which timestamp you can recover to, you can show the error PostgreSQL logs when it cannot find the next WAL segment, and you have a query or script that would have alerted you to the gap before you needed it.

50.2 Restore

Concept

Here is the central argument of this entire part, and it is worth putting in bold:

The restore is the product. The backup is only the input.

Nobody has ever been paid for having a backup. They are paid for having a working database again. A backup you have never restored is a hypothesis, and the incident is a terrible time to test a hypothesis. Teams that take this seriously stop measuring "backup success rate" and start measuring "time to a validated restore", because that number is the one their customers experience.

Why does it exist?

Restore is a separate discipline because it has failure modes that the backup path never exercises:

  • The backup is corrupt, truncated, or missing tables (50.1's failure scenario).
  • The KMS key needed to decrypt is in another region or another account, and the grant does not exist.
  • The restore takes nine hours because you restored to a smaller instance class with lower IOPS.
  • The restored cluster has no roles, so the application's user does not exist.
  • Extensions (pg_trgm, postgis, pgcrypto) are not installed in the target and half your queries fail.
  • The application still points at the old hostname.
  • Nobody on call knows the procedure and the person who wrote it left.

Every one of those is discovered for free in a drill and discovered expensively in an incident.

Mental model

Imagine a fire drill in an office. Having fire extinguishers on the wall is the backup. Knowing that the third-floor stairwell door is locked, that the extinguisher on floor two was discharged last year and never refilled, and that it takes 4 minutes not 90 seconds to get everyone out — that is the restore. You only learn those by walking the route.

How it works

Estimating restore time for a 2 TB database. This is a calculation seniors are expected to do on a whiteboard. Break it into stages; each has a different bottleneck.

Stage What is happening Realistic time, 2 TB
Decide and approve Detect, declare, choose recovery target 5 to 20 min (mostly human)
Provision the instance RDS creates the instance and attaches restored storage 10 to 20 min
Snapshot restore to "available" EBS volume created from the snapshot in S3 20 to 40 min
WAL / transaction log replay Replaying from snapshot time to target time. Recovery is largely single-threaded; expect 100 to 400 MB of WAL per minute replayed 6 hours of WAL at 40 GB total: 20 to 60 min
Lazy block hydration EBS blocks are fetched from S3 on first read. Until then, reads are slow Hours of degraded performance unless you force-read or use fast snapshot restore
Validation Row counts, latest order, checksums, smoke tests 10 to 20 min
Repoint the application Secrets, DNS or config change, rolling restart, pool reconnect 5 to 15 min
Cache warming Redis is empty; the database takes full read load 15 to 60 min of elevated latency

Total for a full PITR restore of 2 TB: realistically 90 minutes to 3 hours to a usable database, and another 30 to 60 minutes before performance is normal. If your published RTO is 1 hour and you rely on restore-from-snapshot, your RTO is fiction. That gap is exactly what 50.3 and 50.5 are for.

Two details that dominate the numbers:

Lazy loading is the hidden cost. A restored EBS volume is not a copy; blocks are pulled from S3 on first access. The instance says "available" long before it is fast. A cold restored 2 TB database can serve queries at a fraction of normal throughput for hours. Mitigations: use Aurora (which has no per-block hydration in the same way), pre-warm by reading the hot tables (SELECT count(*) FROM orders; and friends, or pg_prewarm), or accept the degradation and shed load.

Instance class and IOPS matter more than you think. Restoring a production-sized database onto db.t3.medium "to save money during the drill" produces a 9 hour restore and teaches you nothing useful. Restore to the same class you run in production, or you have not measured your RTO.

Restoring a single table from a logical dump. This is the surgical path, and it is the reason you keep logical dumps despite their cost.

Shell
# What is actually in this dump? Always look before you restore.
pg_restore --list /backup/shop-2026-09-09T02-00Z.dump | grep -i order_items

# Restore ONLY order_items, into a scratch schema in a scratch database.
createdb shop_restore
psql -d shop_restore -c 'CREATE SCHEMA recovered;'

# --data-only avoids recreating the table; --schema/--table select precisely.
pg_restore --dbname=shop_restore --table=order_items --jobs=4 \
  /backup/shop-2026-09-09T02-00Z.dump

Never restore a table directly over the live one. Restore into a scratch database or schema, inspect it, then move exactly the rows you need with an explicit INSERT ... SELECT and an ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. 50.4 walks through the full reconciliation.

Restoring to a separate instance for forensics. When the question is "what did this row look like yesterday?" or "when exactly did this data change?", you do not touch production. You restore to a new, isolated instance:

  • Different security group, reachable only from a bastion or a jump role. No application connects to it.
  • Tagged purpose=forensic, expires=<date>, with an automatic teardown job — forensic instances are a top-5 source of surprise cloud bills (Part 51).
  • Read-only usage. If you must run analysis queries, take a snapshot of the forensic instance first so you can redo the analysis after you inevitably break something.

This is also how you answer legal and compliance questions ("prove what the price was on 3 September") without any production risk at all.

The nightly automated restore verification job. This is the practice that separates teams that have backups from teams that have disaster recovery. Run it every night, in a non-production account, automatically:

The validation suite is where the value is. It must ask business questions, not just "did it start":

SQL
-- 1. Freshness: how far behind the target is the restored data?
SELECT now() - max(created_at) AS newest_order_age FROM orders;

-- 2. Structural completeness: every table production has, the restore has.
SELECT table_schema, table_name
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
ORDER BY 1, 2;

-- 3. Referential sanity: orphans mean a torn or partial restore.
SELECT count(*) AS orphan_items
FROM order_items oi
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- 4. Financial invariant: order totals still equal the sum of their lines.
SELECT count(*) AS mismatched_orders
FROM orders o
JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, sum(unit_price_cents * quantity) AS lines_total
  FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
) t ON t.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.total_cents <> t.lines_total;

-- 5. Extensions and roles exist (the two most common restore surprises).
SELECT extname FROM pg_extension ORDER BY 1;
SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles WHERE rolcanlogin ORDER BY 1;

Publish restore_duration_seconds as a metric with a graph. When it starts creeping from 70 minutes toward 3 hours as the database grows, you find out months before an incident does. That single graph is the most valuable artefact this whole practice produces, because it turns RTO from a promise in a document into a measured number that trends.

NestJS example

The validation suite belongs in your codebase next to your migrations, not in a wiki page. A small Nest standalone application runs it against any connection string, so the same code validates a nightly automated restore, a drill, and a real incident.

TypeScript
// restore-check.command.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export interface CheckResult { name: string; ok: boolean; detail: string }

@Injectable()
export class RestoreCheckService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(RestoreCheckService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async runAll(maxDataAgeSeconds: number): Promise<CheckResult[]> {
    const results: CheckResult[] = [];

    const [{ age }] = await this.ds.query<{ age: string }[]>(
      `SELECT COALESCE(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - max(created_at))), 1e9) AS age FROM orders`,
    );
    results.push({
      name: 'data_freshness',
      ok: Number(age) <= maxDataAgeSeconds,
      detail: `newest order is ${Math.round(Number(age))}s old (budget ${maxDataAgeSeconds}s)`,
    });

    const [{ orphans }] = await this.ds.query<{ orphans: string }[]>(
      `SELECT count(*) AS orphans FROM order_items oi
       LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id WHERE o.id IS NULL`,
    );
    results.push({ name: 'no_orphan_items', ok: orphans === '0', detail: `${orphans} orphans` });

    const [{ mismatched }] = await this.ds.query<{ mismatched: string }[]>(
      `SELECT count(*) AS mismatched FROM orders o
       JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(unit_price_cents * quantity) AS t
             FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) x ON x.order_id = o.id
       WHERE o.total_cents <> x.t`,
    );
    results.push({ name: 'order_totals_match', ok: mismatched === '0', detail: `${mismatched} mismatched` });

    const required = ['pgcrypto', 'pg_trgm', 'uuid-ossp'];
    const rows = await this.ds.query<{ extname: string }[]>(`SELECT extname FROM pg_extension`);
    const present = new Set(rows.map((r) => r.extname));
    const missing = required.filter((e) => !present.has(e));
    results.push({ name: 'extensions_present', ok: missing.length === 0, detail: `missing: ${missing.join(',') || 'none'}` });

    for (const r of results) {
      this.log[r.ok ? 'log' : 'error'](`check ${r.name}: ${r.ok ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL'} - ${r.detail}`);
    }
    return results;
  }
}

Run it with a NestFactory.createApplicationContext entrypoint so it works as a CLI in a Kubernetes Job, exiting non-zero on any failure. Now "verify the restore" is a container image, not a tribal ritual.

Production scenario

The platform's nightly job restores the previous day's recovery point into the DR account on a db.r6g.4xlarge, runs the checks, records restore_duration_seconds, and deletes the instance. Cost: about 100 minutes of a db.r6g.4xlarge per night, roughly $2 to $3 a day, plus storage for the restore duration. Roughly $100 a month to know, every single morning, that the restore works.

That number is the easiest budget conversation you will ever have. "We spend $100 a month to guarantee that our worst day is survivable" needs no further argument.

Failure scenario

A payments company had 90 days of pg_dump files in S3, monitored, alerted, green. In an incident they discovered the dumps were 4 GB when the database was 900 GB. The cron job piped pg_dump into gzip into aws s3 cp, and when pg_dump failed partway through, gzip still produced a valid (truncated) gzip stream and aws s3 cp still exited 0. Pipelines hide failures: the exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of its last command.

The fix was two lines: set -o pipefail in the script, and a post-upload check that the object size is within 20 percent of the previous day's. Both would have caught it on night one. Instead it was caught 90 days later, during a restore, with the CTO on the call.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The restore succeeds but the app cannot connect: roles missing (pg_dumpall --globals-only was never taken), or pg_hba/security group differs in the target.
  • Extensions missing in the target; RDS requires them to be in the allowed list and CREATE EXTENSION to run.
  • Restoring into a smaller instance class silently changes shared_buffers, work_mem and max_connections, so query plans and connection limits differ from production.
  • Parameter groups and option groups are not part of a snapshot in the way people assume; a restored instance gets the default group unless you specify yours.
  • Sequences after a partial logical restore are behind the max id, so the first insert throws a duplicate key error (50.11).
  • Restore time grows superlinearly with unused indexes: pg_restore rebuilds every index. Dropping unused indexes speeds restores and saves money (Part 51).
  • A restore into an existing database with --clean drops objects first; if the restore then fails, you have destroyed the target.
  • Concurrent restores throttle: EBS snapshot restore bandwidth is shared, so restoring six databases at once is not six times faster.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask, in every architecture review that touches data: "When did we last restore this, and how long did it take?" If the answer is a shrug, the backup line item in the design is not done.

They know RTO is a measured number with a trend line, and they refuse to publish an RTO the team has not demonstrated. Saying "our RTO is 1 hour" when the last drill took 3 hours and 40 minutes is not optimism, it is a false promise to the business.

They restore to a separate instance by default. Production is never the place you experiment during an incident; a side instance costs $3 an hour and removes an entire class of "we made it worse" outcomes.

And they automate the verification, because a manual quarterly restore test is a test of whoever happened to be free that afternoon, while a nightly automated restore is a property of the system.

Common mistakes

  • Testing restores "when we have time", which is never.
  • Testing the restore on a 5 GB staging database and claiming the number applies to 2 TB.
  • Restoring over the live database during an incident because it feels faster.
  • Not checking pg_restore --list before restoring, so you do not notice what is missing.
  • Forgetting that the application needs new credentials, a new host, and a rolling restart before the restore counts as finished.
  • Deleting the damaged original instance before the restored one is validated. Keep the evidence.

Interview questions

  1. Estimate the time to restore a 2 TB PostgreSQL database from a snapshot plus 6 hours of WAL.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: staged answer — provisioning 10–20 min, snapshot restore 20–40 min, WAL replay 20–60 min, validation and repoint 15–30 min, plus degraded performance from lazy block loading. Total 1.5 to 3 hours. Follow-up: what makes it faster? Smaller RPO gap, warm standby, Aurora, larger instance class, pre-warming.
  2. How do you restore one table without touching the rest of the database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: logical dump with pg_restore --table into a scratch database, or PITR to a side instance then INSERT ... SELECT the rows across. Never restore over the live table.
  3. What does a nightly restore verification job check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it completes, within the expected time, and passes business invariants (freshness, referential integrity, financial totals, extensions, roles). Follow-up: what metric would you graph? Restore duration over time.
  4. Your backup job exits 0 every night but the file is a tenth of the expected size. How would that happen and how do you catch it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: shell pipeline masking the failure, no pipefail; catch it with size-delta checks, manifest comparison, and restore verification.
  5. Why restore to a separate instance for forensics?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: no production risk, isolation, can be destroyed and repeated, preserves evidence, no contention with recovery.

Practical exercise

Build the nightly restore verification job for a database you control. It must: find the newest recovery point, restore it to an isolated instance, run at least five business-invariant checks, publish a restore_duration_seconds metric, tear the instance down, and page on failure.

Acceptance criteria: it runs unattended for seven consecutive nights; you can show a graph of restore duration; and when you deliberately corrupt or truncate a backup, the job fails loudly and keeps the instance for inspection rather than deleting it.

50.3 RPO and RTO

Concept

Two numbers describe every disaster recovery design. Learn them properly, because every architecture and cost decision in this part falls out of them.

RPO — Recovery Point Objective — is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. "RPO 5 minutes" means: after a disaster, it is acceptable that the last 5 minutes of writes are gone forever. RPO is about the past.

RTO — Recovery Time Objective — is how long you can afford to be down, measured in time. "RTO 1 hour" means: one hour after the disaster starts, customers must be able to use the system again. RTO is about the future.

They are objectives, which means they are business decisions, not engineering ones. Engineering's job is to say honestly what each target costs, and then to build and demonstrate whatever the business chooses.

Why does it exist?

Without these two numbers, DR conversations go in circles. Someone says "we need to be resilient", someone else says "we should go multi-region", a third person says "that's too expensive", and nothing is decided.

With them, the conversation is concrete and takes 20 minutes: "Losing 5 minutes of orders costs us about 90 orders and a support queue we can handle. Losing an hour costs us 1,000 orders and refund disputes. Being down for 4 hours on Black Friday costs us more than the entire year's DR budget." Now you can pick a mechanism.

The other thing they do is stop the most expensive mistake in DR, which is applying one target to the entire system. Not all data is equal.

Mental model

Imagine you are writing a novel.

RPO is how often you hit save. If you save every 5 minutes and the laptop dies, you lose at most 5 minutes of typing. Saving on every keystroke costs you nothing on a laptop, but if each save were a courier riding to another city, you would think harder about the interval.

RTO is how long it takes to get typing again after the laptop dies. If you have a second laptop already open with the file synced, that is minutes. If you have to buy a new laptop, install everything and download the file, that is a day. Both machines can have the same RPO and wildly different RTOs.

The pair is independent. You can have RPO 0 and RTO 8 hours (synchronous replication into a backup you have to restore manually). You can have RPO 24 hours and RTO 2 minutes (a warm standby fed by a nightly copy). Sensible designs move them together, but the mechanisms are separate.

How it works

The RPO window is bounded by how frequently your data leaves the primary in a durable, independent way:

RPO mechanism Achievable RPO Why
Nightly logical dump up to 24 hours Everything since the dump is gone
Snapshots every 6 hours up to 6 hours Same, shorter window
Continuous WAL archiving, 60s archive_timeout 1 to 5 minutes Bounded by segment shipping
RDS PITR (transaction log capture) ~5 minutes typically AWS ships logs continuously
Asynchronous streaming replica seconds (equals replication lag) Lag is normally under 1s but spikes under load
Synchronous replica (synchronous_commit = on, remote_apply) 0 Commit does not return until the standby has it

The RTO window is not one thing; it is a sum, and the human parts are usually the biggest:

Text
RTO = detect + alert + decide + provision + restore + validate + repoint + warm
        3m      2m      10m      15m        45m       10m       10m      20m   = ~115 min

Notice that if you optimise only the restore step you cut 45 minutes out of 115. The other 70 minutes are automation, runbooks and drills. This is why teams that automate detection and repointing beat teams that buy faster storage.

Not all data has the same targets. This is the most useful thing in this section. Classify your data, and let each class have its own numbers.

Data RPO RTO Rationale
Orders, payments, inventory ledger 0 to 1 min 30 min Losing 5 minutes of orders means customers charged with no order record; unacceptable, and a regulatory problem
Customer accounts, addresses 5 min 1 hour Re-enterable but painful; low write rate
Product catalog 1 hour 1 hour Re-importable from the PIM system
Session data in Redis Unlimited 15 min Users log in again; annoying, not damaging
Search index (OpenSearch) Unlimited 2 hours Fully rebuildable from PostgreSQL
Derived analytics / warehouse 24 hours 24 hours Recomputable; nobody checks out through a dashboard
Invoices in S3 0 4 hours Legally required, but not needed for checkout

Two consequences fall straight out of that table. First, your expensive DR mechanism only has to cover the top rows: orders and payments. Second, several rows are cheap because you designed them to be rebuildable — the search index has an unlimited RPO precisely because PostgreSQL is its source of truth. Designing for reproducibility is a DR strategy, and it is usually the cheapest one available.

Mapping targets to mechanisms and cost. These are approximate us-east-1 list prices for our 2 TB, db.r6g.4xlarge-class workload, and they move; use the shape, not the digits.

RPO / RTO target Mechanism Approx. extra cost/month Complexity
RPO 24h / RTO 24h Nightly pg_dump to S3, restore manually $20 to $50 Trivial
RPO 5m / RTO 4h RDS automated backups + PITR, single region, manual restore $80 to $200 (snapshot storage) Low
RPO 5m / RTO 1h Above + cross-region snapshot copies + automated restore runbook + nightly verification $300 to $600 Low to medium
RPO <1m / RTO 5m (AZ failure only) Multi-AZ RDS: synchronous standby in another AZ ~2x instance cost, about +$900 Low, AWS-managed
RPO 1 to 5m / RTO 15 to 30m (region failure) Pilot light: cross-region read replica, minimal infra in region B, scale up on failover +$900 (replica) + ~$150 baseline infra Medium
RPO seconds / RTO 5 to 10m (region failure) Warm standby: cross-region replica plus running-but-small app tier +$900 replica, +$600 to $1,500 app/infra High
RPO ~0 / RTO ~0 Multi-site active-active, both regions serving writes 2x everything plus conflict resolution engineering Very high

The interesting jumps are between rows. Going from RTO 4 hours to 1 hour is mostly automation and drilling, and costs a few hundred dollars. Going from 1 hour to 15 minutes requires a warm replica in another region and roughly doubles your database bill. Going from 15 minutes to near-zero requires active-active and roughly doubles everything else too — plus a permanent engineering tax of conflict resolution, which is the real cost.

Draw that curve for your business and the decision usually makes itself.

Practical example

The e-commerce leadership team is asked for targets. The first answer is "zero and zero, obviously". The engineering answer is a table showing that RPO 0 with region-level RTO near zero means active-active, roughly $8,000 a month more, one extra full-time engineer, and a two-quarter project — plus the honest note that active-active makes some failure modes worse, because now a bad deploy can corrupt data in two regions at once.

The team then asks the right question: what does an outage actually cost? At 25,000 orders a day and $60 average basket, a full checkout outage costs about $2,500 per hour of gross merchandise value, some of which is recovered later when customers return. Reputational damage on Black Friday is worth several times that.

The agreed targets: RPO 5 minutes, RTO 1 hour for normal operations; RPO 15 minutes, RTO 4 hours for a full region loss. That maps to RDS Multi-AZ plus PITR plus cross-region snapshot copies plus a rehearsed, automated runbook — roughly $1,200 a month all in, no new headcount. Everyone can defend that in a board meeting.

Six months later they revisit it before peak season and buy a cross-region read replica for November and December only, temporarily moving region RTO to 30 minutes. That is a good decision precisely because the targets were explicit enough to shop for.

NestJS example

Targets that live only in a document drift. Encode the RPO budget in the application so that a breach is a page.

TypeScript
// rpo-budget.health.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthIndicator, HealthIndicatorResult, HealthCheckError } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

/**
 * Measures the real RPO exposure of the primary: how far behind the durable
 * copy is. On a self-managed primary this is (current LSN - last archived LSN)
 * translated to time; here we approximate with archiver stats, which is the
 * number that actually bounds data loss.
 */
@Injectable()
export class RpoBudgetHealthIndicator extends HealthIndicator {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) { super(); }

  async isHealthy(key: string, budgetSeconds = 300): Promise<HealthIndicatorResult> {
    const [row] = await this.ds.query<{ lag: string; failed: string }[]>(`
      SELECT COALESCE(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - last_archived_time)), 1e9) AS lag,
             failed_count AS failed
      FROM pg_stat_archiver
    `);
    const lagSeconds = Number(row.lag);
    const failed = Number(row.failed);
    const healthy = lagSeconds <= budgetSeconds && failed === 0;

    const result = this.getStatus(key, healthy, {
      archiveLagSeconds: Math.round(lagSeconds),
      budgetSeconds,
      archiveFailures: failed,
    });
    if (healthy) return result;
    // A broken archive means our RPO is silently the age of the last snapshot.
    throw new HealthCheckError('RPO budget breached: WAL archiving is behind or failing', result);
  }
}

Wire it into a /health/dr endpoint that is scraped but not used as the Kubernetes readiness probe. A broken archive must not take your pods out of the load balancer; it must wake a human.

Production scenario

A useful discipline: publish the two numbers on the service dashboard next to latency and error rate, as measured values, not targets.

  • rpo_exposure_seconds — how much data would be lost if the primary died this second. Sourced from archiver lag or LatestRestorableTime.
  • rto_last_demonstrated_seconds — the duration of the most recent successful full restore drill.

When someone asks "what is our RTO?", the answer is a graph, not a claim. When rto_last_demonstrated_seconds is 90 days stale, that is itself an alert: your RTO is now unknown.

Failure scenario

A SaaS company published "RPO 15 minutes, RTO 2 hours" in its enterprise contracts. It had RDS automated backups with PITR, which comfortably meets RPO 15 minutes. Nobody had measured RTO.

A failed migration corrupted a foreign key relationship at 09:12. The team decided to PITR to 09:05. The restore of their 4 TB database took 2 hours 10 minutes to reach "available", then 3 more hours of catastrophic performance while EBS lazily hydrated blocks under full production traffic. Total customer-visible impact: 6 hours 40 minutes against a contractual 2 hours, triggering SLA credits in six-figure territory.

The RPO was met exactly. The RTO was off by a factor of three, because it had never been measured, and because nobody had accounted for the post-restore performance cliff. The fix was not technical at first: it was to change the published number to the demonstrated one, then start a project to bring the demonstrated number down.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RPO and RTO published from a document that has never been demonstrated. This is the norm, and it is a promise you cannot keep.
  • Targets applied uniformly, so you pay for RPO 0 on the analytics warehouse.
  • RPO measured against snapshot age rather than archive lag, understating exposure by hours.
  • Detection time excluded from RTO. If your monitoring takes 20 minutes to notice, your customer-visible RTO includes those 20 minutes.
  • RTO measured to "database available" rather than "customers can check out". Cache warming, queue drain and reconciliation are inside the customer-visible window.
  • Targets that ignore dependencies: your RTO cannot be better than your payment provider's, your identity provider's, or your DNS TTL.
  • Peak-season targets equal to off-peak targets, when the cost of downtime differs by 10x.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They never accept "as fast as possible" as a target. They come to the meeting with the cost table above and force a choice, because an unmade choice defaults to the cheapest mechanism and the most expensive incident.

They separate the numbers per data class, and they look hard for data that can be made rebuildable, because rebuildable data has a free RPO. Moving the search index from "needs backups" to "rebuilt from PostgreSQL in 40 minutes" is a better engineering outcome than backing it up.

They treat the human portion of RTO as the main target. Detection, decision authority and repointing are cheaper to improve than storage.

And they know a target that has not been drilled is not a target. The sentence they use in reviews: "What is the last date we demonstrated this number, and what was it?"

Common mistakes

  • Confusing the two: "our RPO is 4 hours" when they mean RTO.
  • Treating Multi-AZ as a region-level DR answer. It is an AZ-level answer.
  • Assuming an asynchronous replica gives RPO 0. It gives RPO equal to lag, which spikes exactly when you need it most.
  • Forgetting that RTO includes the time to reconcile payments and replay queues, not just to boot a database.
  • Setting a target once and never revisiting it as the database grows from 200 GB to 2 TB; restore time grows with it.

Interview questions

  1. Define RPO and RTO with an example.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: RPO is acceptable data loss in time, RTO is acceptable downtime; e-commerce example where 5 minutes of lost orders is unacceptable but 24 hours of lost analytics is fine.
  2. How do RPO and RTO drive architecture?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: RPO drives replication and archiving frequency; RTO drives standby posture and automation. Walk the ladder from nightly dumps to active-active with cost at each rung.
  3. What is your real RPO if you take hourly snapshots and WAL archiving is broken?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: up to one hour, and you will not know until you restore. Follow-up: how do you detect it? pg_stat_archiver, LatestRestorableTime age, alerting.
  4. Does a synchronous standby give you RPO 0 for all failures?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: for the loss of the primary, yes; not for logical corruption, which replicates instantly. Follow-up: what covers that? PITR.
  5. Your RTO is 1 hour and your last drill took 3 hours. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: change the published number to the truth, then attack the biggest term in the sum, usually human decision time and repointing, before buying faster infrastructure.
  6. How would you set different targets for different data?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: classify by business impact and rebuildability; pay only for the top class.

Practical exercise

Write the RPO/RTO table for a system you work on. Every row must name the data, the target, the mechanism that achieves it, the approximate monthly cost, and the date the target was last demonstrated. Then measure one row for real.

Acceptance criteria: at least one row has a demonstrated RTO with a timestamp; at least one row is downgraded because the data turns out to be rebuildable; and at least one row is discovered to have no mechanism at all.

50.4 Point-in-time recovery

Concept

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) is restoring a database to any chosen moment, not just to the moment a backup was taken. You pick a timestamp — 14:31:00 on 9 September — and the database is reconstructed exactly as it existed at that second.

It is the only tool that fixes logical damage. Replication does not (it replicates the damage). Snapshots alone do not (they land you on a snapshot boundary, potentially hours off). PITR lets you land one minute before the mistake.

Why does it exist?

Because the most common data disaster is a correct database faithfully executing a wrong command. DELETE FROM order_items; is valid SQL. PostgreSQL executes it, WAL records it, replicas apply it, and the snapshot taken 10 minutes later contains the empty table.

The only escape is time travel: reconstruct the state before the command ran. That requires a base copy plus an ordered record of every change, which is precisely what WAL is.

Mental model

Imagine a video recording of a whiteboard. The base backup is a photo of the board at 02:00. The WAL is the video of every hand movement since. To see the board at 14:31, you print the photo and then fast-forward the video to 14:31, redrawing each stroke. Stop the video one second before the person wipes the board, and you have the content back.

The catch, and it matters: you must have the unbroken video. A missing 10 minutes in the middle means you cannot get past that point at all. This is why a WAL archive gap is fatal to PITR from that moment forward (50.11).

How it works

WAL replay to a timestamp, mechanically.

  1. Restore the most recent base backup taken before your target time. If you target 14:31 and your base backup is from 02:00, you restore the 02:00 copy.
  2. Configure recovery. In PostgreSQL 12 and later this is in postgresql.conf plus a recovery.signal file:
INI
# Fetch archived WAL segments as recovery needs them.
restore_command = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p'
# Stop exactly here.
recovery_target_time = '2026-09-09 14:31:00+00'
# 'pause' lets you inspect before promoting; 'promote' opens for writes immediately.
recovery_target_action = 'pause'
# Do not overshoot: stop BEFORE the first transaction that committed after the target.
recovery_target_inclusive = off
  1. Start PostgreSQL. It replays WAL from the base backup's start LSN forward, applying every page change in order, and stops at the first commit record whose timestamp is at or after the target.
  2. With recovery_target_action = 'pause', the instance sits read-only. You connect, run SELECT count(*) FROM order_items;, and confirm you landed where you meant to. If you are one minute off, you throw it away and redo with a different target rather than promoting a wrong state.
  3. SELECT pg_promote(); ends recovery and opens the database for writes. This creates a new timeline (timeline 2).
