Any WAL from the original timeline after your target point still exists in the archive but is now on a divergent branch — which is how you can, if you must, restore again to a different point later and extract more.

Other recovery targets exist and are occasionally exactly what you want: recovery_target_lsn (precise, if you know the LSN), recovery_target_xid (stop before a specific transaction id), and recovery_target_name (a label set earlier with pg_create_restore_point('before-migration-2026-09-09') — worth doing before every risky migration).

RDS PITR. AWS wraps all of this. You call:

Shell
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier shop-prod \
  --target-db-instance-identifier shop-recovery-1431 \
  --restore-time 2026-09-09T14:31:00Z \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.4xlarge \
  --db-subnet-group-name private-db \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-0recovery \
  --no-multi-az \
  --no-publicly-accessible

Points that matter in an incident:

  • RDS always restores to a new instance. You cannot PITR in place. This is a feature: the damaged original is preserved as evidence and as a fallback.
  • The window is EarliestRestorableTime to LatestRestorableTime. LatestRestorableTime is typically about 5 minutes behind now. You cannot restore to 30 seconds ago.
  • Granularity is one second, but the underlying log shipping means the practical floor is the ~5 minute lag above.
  • The restored instance gets the default parameter group unless you pass yours. Pass yours.
  • Restore it into the same VPC with a different security group so the application cannot accidentally connect to it before you are ready.

Practical example

The scenario every engineer eventually meets. At 14:32 on a Tuesday, an engineer running a data cleanup in a psql session against what they believed was staging executes:

SQL
DELETE FROM order_items;

No WHERE. Autocommit on. 8.4 million rows gone in 40 seconds. The orders table is intact; only the line items are gone.

Here is the full walkthrough. The timings are what a drilled team actually achieves.

14:33 — Detection. Two signals fire almost together: the checkout error rate alert (order confirmation pages throw because order_items is empty), and a business metric alert on "items per order" dropping to zero. Support tickets start 4 minutes later. Detection speed here comes from having a business metric alert, not just an infrastructure one.

14:35 — Stop the bleeding. The first action is not recovery, it is containment. The on-call revokes the engineer's session (SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)), and the team decides whether to keep taking orders. Decision: keep the site up, disable order-history and invoice pages behind a feature flag, because new orders write new order_items rows correctly and blocking checkout would multiply the damage. This is a judgement call and it is the most important one of the incident.

14:38 — Establish exactly what happened and when. Not "roughly 14:32". You need a defensible boundary:

SQL
-- What was the last good moment? Ask the audit log / pg_stat_statements / CloudTrail-equivalent.
-- If you have pgaudit or a WAL-based CDC stream, find the transaction.
SELECT xact_start, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE query ILIKE 'delete from order_items%';

-- Cheap, universal fallback: the highest id that still exists tells you nothing here
-- (all rows are gone), so use the orders side to bound it.
SELECT max(created_at) FROM orders;  -- orders kept flowing; items did not

The team settles on a recovery target of 14:31:00, one minute before the transaction started, with recovery_target_inclusive = off. Rounding backwards is always right: you can replay forward from the outbox, you cannot un-restore.

14:40 — Choose the strategy. Two options are on the table:

Option What it means Downside
Fail over: restore to 14:31 and make it the new primary Everything after 14:31 is lost, including ~40 minutes of real orders Loses good data. Almost never right for a single-table incident
Repair in place: restore to a side instance, extract order_items, copy the rows back Production keeps running; only the deleted rows are restored More work, needs careful reconciliation

The team picks repair in place. The rule of thumb: if the damage is scoped to some rows or tables and the rest of the database is healthy, repair in place. Fail over only when the whole database is untrustworthy or unavailable.

14:41 — Provision the recovery instance. restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time to shop-recovery-1431, same instance class, --no-multi-az, isolated security group.

15:35 — Instance available. 54 minutes, in line with the estimate in 50.2. Validation first: does it actually contain the rows?

SQL
SELECT count(*) FROM order_items;                 -- 8,412,904 rows: good
SELECT max(created_at) FROM order_items;          -- 14:30:58: correct target
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2026-09-09 14:00Z';  -- sanity

15:40 — Extract only the affected rows. Do not copy 8.4 million rows blindly. Copy what production is missing. postgres_fdw makes this a single query and avoids a dump-and-load round trip:

SQL
-- On PRODUCTION, reaching into the recovery instance read-only.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgres_fdw;
CREATE SERVER recovery_1431 FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER postgres_fdw
  OPTIONS (host 'shop-recovery-1431.abc.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com', dbname 'shop', port '5432');
CREATE USER MAPPING FOR CURRENT_USER SERVER recovery_1431
  OPTIONS (user 'recovery_ro', password_required 'true', password 'from-secrets-manager');

CREATE SCHEMA recovered;
IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA public LIMIT TO (order_items)
  FROM SERVER recovery_1431 INTO recovered;

-- Now the reconciliation query. Three rules:
--   1. Only rows whose parent order still exists in production.
--   2. Only rows that are actually missing now (some may have been re-created).
--   3. Idempotent, so re-running it is safe.
INSERT INTO order_items (id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents, created_at)
SELECT r.id, r.order_id, r.product_id, r.quantity, r.unit_price_cents, r.created_at
FROM recovered.order_items r
JOIN orders o ON o.id = r.order_id
LEFT JOIN order_items live ON live.id = r.id
WHERE live.id IS NULL
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;

Run it in batches, not as one 8.4 million row transaction, or you will hold locks and bloat WAL:

SQL
-- Batched variant: 20,000 rows at a time, resumable, low lock footprint.
DO $$
DECLARE moved bigint;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    WITH batch AS (
      SELECT r.* FROM recovered.order_items r
      JOIN orders o ON o.id = r.order_id
      LEFT JOIN order_items live ON live.id = r.id
      WHERE live.id IS NULL
      LIMIT 20000
    )
    INSERT INTO order_items (id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents, created_at)
    SELECT id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents, created_at FROM batch
    ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS moved = ROW_COUNT;
    EXIT WHEN moved = 0;
    COMMIT;  -- requires a procedure or a client-side loop; in psql use \gexec batches
  END LOOP;
END $$;

16:20 — Reconcile everything that happened since 14:32. This is the step teams skip and regret. Between the deletion and the repair, the system kept running. Things to check:

  1. Orders placed after 14:32 wrote their own order_items rows normally. The ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and the live.id IS NULL filter protect them. Verify: no order created after 14:32 has duplicated items.
  2. Cancellations and returns processed after 14:32 may have deleted order_items rows legitimately. Restoring them resurrects cancelled lines. Check the audit log or order_status_history for cancellations in the window, and delete the resurrected rows for those orders.
  3. Sequences. If order_items.id uses a sequence, production's sequence advanced during the window while the restored rows use old ids. No conflict here (old ids are lower), but if you had restored the whole table the sequence would need setval to max(id).
  4. Financial invariants. Re-run the totals check from 50.2. Any order whose total_cents no longer matches the sum of its items is a row that needs human review.
  5. Downstream systems. The warehouse, the search index and the accounting export all consumed the "items deleted" state. Each needs a targeted re-sync (50.8).
SQL
-- The invariant that tells you whether the repair actually worked.
SELECT o.id, o.total_cents, COALESCE(sum(oi.unit_price_cents * oi.quantity), 0) AS items_total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-09-01'
GROUP BY o.id, o.total_cents
HAVING o.total_cents <> COALESCE(sum(oi.unit_price_cents * oi.quantity), 0)
ORDER BY o.id;

16:45 — Re-enable the disabled pages, keep the recovery instance for 48 hours, then delete it. Do not delete it the same day. You will find one more discrepancy tomorrow.

Total: 4 hours 13 minutes from deletion to full repair, with no customer-facing checkout downtime and zero lost orders. Compare to a naive "fail over to 14:31" which would have been faster to execute and would have destroyed 40 minutes of real business.

NestJS example

The reconciliation should be code you can review and test, not a psql session someone types under pressure.

TypeScript
// order-items-recovery.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class OrderItemsRecoveryService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderItemsRecoveryService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /**
   * Copies missing order_items from the foreign `recovered` schema in batches.
   * Idempotent: safe to run repeatedly, and safe to stop and resume.
   * Excludes orders cancelled during the incident window so we do not
   * resurrect legitimately removed lines.
   */
  async repair(batchSize = 20_000, incidentStart = '2026-09-09T14:32:00Z'): Promise<number> {
    let total = 0;
    for (;;) {
      const result = await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
        const rows = await em.query(
          `INSERT INTO order_items (id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents, created_at)
           SELECT r.id, r.order_id, r.product_id, r.quantity, r.unit_price_cents, r.created_at
           FROM recovered.order_items r
           JOIN orders o ON o.id = r.order_id
           LEFT JOIN order_items live ON live.id = r.id
           WHERE live.id IS NULL
             AND NOT EXISTS (
               SELECT 1 FROM order_status_history h
               WHERE h.order_id = r.order_id AND h.status = 'CANCELLED' AND h.changed_at >= $2
             )
           ORDER BY r.id
           LIMIT $1
           ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING
           RETURNING 1`,
          [batchSize, incidentStart],
        );
        return rows.length as number;
      });
      if (result === 0) break;
      total += result;
      this.log.log(`recovered ${total} order_items so far`);
    }
    return total;
  }
}

Note what makes this production-safe: a bounded batch, an explicit transaction per batch, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for idempotency, an exclusion for cancellations, and structured logging so the incident timeline is reconstructable afterwards.

Production scenario

PITR is not only for disasters. Uses that earn their keep every month:

  • Before every risky migration, call SELECT pg_create_restore_point('pre-migration-add-status-column'); (self-managed) or take a manual snapshot (RDS). It costs seconds and gives you a named target.
  • Investigating a data bug: restore to before the suspected bad release, diff the affected rows, and prove or disprove the hypothesis without touching production.
  • Legal and compliance: "what was this customer's shipping address on 3 September" is answered by a forensic restore.
  • Testing the restore path: the nightly verification job in 50.2 is itself a PITR.

Failure scenario

A team hit exactly the DELETE scenario, restored to a side instance, extracted the rows and copied them back — and then discovered three days later that their order confirmation emails had been re-sent to 40,000 customers. The reason: the reconciliation INSERT fired an application-level trigger via a CDC stream, which the notification service consumed as "new order item created", which the templating layer turned into "your order has shipped".

The lesson is in 50.8 and worth stating here: restoring data can trigger side effects. Before any bulk repair, pause the CDC connector, the outbox publisher and the notification consumers, then resume them with a filter or a watermark that ignores the repair window.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Target time outside the retention window: PITR simply refuses. Retention must be longer than your detection time (50.11).
  • Target time inside a WAL archive gap: recovery stops at the gap and cannot proceed. You get the state at the gap, not your target.
  • recovery_target_inclusive = on (the default) can include the very transaction you were trying to escape when your timestamp is exactly the commit time. Use off and round backwards.
  • Time zones. recovery_target_time without an offset is interpreted in the server's timezone. Always write UTC with an explicit offset.
  • Promoting the restored instance creates a new timeline; if you later need to restore to a different point on the original timeline, you must set recovery_target_timeline explicitly.
  • On RDS, restoring uses the default parameter group unless specified; work_mem and max_connections differ and your app pool may fail to connect.
  • A PITR restore is a whole cluster. There is no "PITR one table" — you restore everything and extract.
  • Extracting via postgres_fdw pulls rows across the network; 8 million rows is minutes, 800 million is not. For very large extractions use COPY to a file and COPY back, or restore into a staging instance in the same AZ.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Their first instinct in a logical-damage incident is not to restore. It is to stop the damage from spreading and to preserve evidence. The damaged database is the most valuable artefact you have; do not overwrite it.

Their second instinct is to round the recovery target backwards and repair forward, because forward repair is reconcilable and a too-late target is not.

They default to repair-in-place over failover for scoped damage, and they say the reason out loud: failing over to 14:31 throws away every good transaction since 14:31 to fix a subset of bad ones.

They think about side effects before they think about rows. "If I insert these 8 million rows, what fires?" Triggers, CDC, outbox, cache invalidation, notification consumers, search indexers, the accounting export. Every one is a potential second incident.

And they keep the recovery instance around for two days, tagged with an expiry, because the follow-up question always comes.

Common mistakes

  • Restoring over production because it feels like the fastest path.
  • Picking the recovery target from memory instead of from evidence.
  • Copying the whole restored table back instead of only the missing rows, creating duplicates and resurrecting legitimately deleted data.
  • Running the repair as one enormous transaction, blocking writes and bloating WAL.
  • Forgetting the sequences after a full-table restore, so the next insert throws a duplicate key error.
  • Leaving CDC and notification consumers running during the repair, so customers get thousands of duplicate emails.
  • Deleting the recovery instance immediately, then needing it the next day.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through recovering from DELETE FROM order_items with no WHERE, discovered 3 minutes later.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: contain, preserve evidence, decide scope, PITR to a new instance one minute before the transaction, validate the target landed correctly, extract only missing rows joined against surviving parents, batch the insert idempotently, reconcile with events since, handle downstream side effects. Follow-up: why not fail over? Because you would lose all good writes since.
  2. How does WAL replay to a timestamp work?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: restore base backup, replay WAL records in LSN order, stop at the first commit at or after the target, promote to a new timeline.
  3. What is recovery_target_inclusive and why does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: whether the transaction committing exactly at the target is included; set off to stop strictly before.
  4. What is the practical minimum recovery point on RDS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: LatestRestorableTime, usually about 5 minutes behind now; you cannot restore to 30 seconds ago.
  5. You restore rows back into a live table. What could go wrong beyond duplicates?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: triggers, CDC streams, outbox publishers and notification consumers firing side effects such as duplicate emails or re-charges; sequences behind; resurrecting legitimately deleted rows; downstream indexes now inconsistent.
  6. How do you pick the recovery target defensibly?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: from audit logs, pg_stat_activity, CloudTrail, application logs and business metrics; round backwards; validate on the restored instance before promoting.

Practical exercise

On a local PostgreSQL with continuous archiving, seed orders and order_items. Note the time, then run DELETE FROM order_items;. Keep the database running and insert 200 new orders (with items) afterwards to simulate ongoing business.

Now recover: PITR to one minute before the delete on a second instance, connect them with postgres_fdw, and write an idempotent batched repair that restores only the missing rows without touching the 200 new orders.

Acceptance criteria: after the repair, count(*) on order_items equals the pre-delete count plus the new orders' items; the financial invariant query returns zero mismatched orders; running the repair script a second time inserts zero rows.

50.5 Disaster recovery strategies

Concept

There are four canonical DR postures. They form a ladder: each rung costs more, and each rung buys a lower RTO. Almost every real architecture is one of these four, or a deliberate hybrid where the critical data sits one rung higher than everything else.

  1. Backup and restore. Nothing is running in the second region. On disaster, you build it.
  2. Pilot light. The data is continuously replicated to the second region; the compute is defined but switched off.
  3. Warm standby. A scaled-down but running copy of the whole system in the second region.
  4. Multi-site active-active. Both regions serve production traffic all the time.

Why does it exist?

Because "be resilient" is not a design. These four names give a team a shared vocabulary and force the cost conversation into the open. When an architect says "pilot light", everyone in the room knows the database replica is running, the app is not, the RTO is tens of minutes, and someone has to write the promotion runbook.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that wants to survive its kitchen burning down.

  • Backup and restore: you keep the recipes and supplier list in a safe. After a fire, you rent a new space, buy equipment and reopen in three weeks.
  • Pilot light: you already rent a second empty unit with the gas and water connected and the recipes on the wall. After a fire, you move in ovens and staff and open in two days.
  • Warm standby: the second unit is a small working kitchen serving five tables. After a fire, you hire more staff, open the rest of the dining room, and you are at full capacity in an hour.
  • Active-active: two full restaurants in two cities, both serving customers. One burns down and the other absorbs the bookings. But you also now have two of every problem: two inventories to keep in sync, and an argument every time both take the last table.

How it works

1. Backup and restore.

Nothing exists in region B except backups. On disaster you run terraform apply for the whole stack, restore the newest snapshot, repoint DNS. RTO is hours to a day and depends entirely on how good your infrastructure-as-code is; if the VPC was clicked together by hand three years ago, your RTO is "unknown, probably days". RPO is your snapshot/WAL copy frequency, typically 15 minutes to a few hours because cross-region copies are not continuous.

Right for: internal tools, analytics platforms, anything where a day of downtime is survivable. Also right as the baseline under every other strategy, because pilot light and warm standby both fail if the data is corrupt and backups are your only escape from logical damage.

2. Pilot light.

The database replica is running and continuously replicating; the application tier exists as manifests and images but zero replicas; the load balancer and networking are provisioned by Terraform and idle. On disaster: promote the replica, scale the deployment from 0 to N, switch DNS.

RTO 15 to 45 minutes, dominated by three things: replica promotion (1 to 5 minutes on RDS), pod startup and readiness (2 to 10 minutes including image pulls and connection pool warm-up), and DNS propagation (your TTL). RPO is replication lag, normally under 5 seconds, but see 50.11 for what happens to lag at exactly the wrong moment.

Right for: most serious e-commerce and SaaS platforms. It is the best value on the ladder.

3. Warm standby.

Everything is running in region B, just small. Pods are healthy and answering health checks; Kafka consumers may be running against a mirrored cluster; Redis is up but cold. On disaster you promote the database, scale the app up, and shift traffic — but the app tier never had to cold-start.

RTO 5 to 15 minutes. RPO seconds. Cost is significant: you are paying for a real (if small) second environment, plus the operational burden of keeping two environments actually identical — which is the part teams underestimate. A warm standby that has not been deployed to in six weeks is a cold standby with a bigger bill.

Right for: systems where an hour of downtime costs more than the standby costs per month. Do the arithmetic; sometimes it genuinely does.

4. Multi-site active-active.

Both regions take writes. Losing one is a capacity event, not an outage. RTO approaches zero and RPO approaches zero for infrastructure failures.

The cost is not the second region. It is that you now own a distributed database problem. Two customers can buy the last unit of stock in two regions simultaneously. Two writes to the same order row can conflict. You need globally unique ids (UUIDv7 or ULID rather than sequences), conflict resolution rules per table, idempotency everywhere, and a team that understands what "eventual consistency" means for a refund. Aurora Global Database gives you fast cross-region replication with a single writer and a managed failover in typically under a minute, which is warm standby with excellent ergonomics; true multi-writer requires Aurora multi-master style architectures or application-level partitioning by region.

The honest senior take: most companies that say they want active-active want fast failover, which is Aurora Global Database or warm standby, not multi-writer. Ask what they actually need.

Comparison table.

Strategy RTO RPO Complexity Approx. extra $/month (our 2 TB platform) Failure it covers
Backup and restore 4 to 24 h 15 min to 24 h Low $100 to $400 Everything, slowly. The only one that covers logical corruption
Pilot light 15 to 45 min seconds to 5 min Medium $1,000 to $1,500 Region loss, primary loss
Warm standby 5 to 15 min seconds High $2,500 to $4,000 Region loss with capacity preserved
Multi-site active-active near 0 near 0 Very high $8,000+ and one FTE Region loss with no customer impact

Every row also needs backup and restore underneath it, because replication does not protect you from DELETE FROM order_items.

Practical example

Our platform runs pilot light, deliberately:

  • RDS Multi-AZ in us-east-1 (this is availability, not DR).
  • Cross-region read replica in eu-west-1.
  • Terraform modules that build the entire eu-west-1 stack, applied nightly in plan-only mode so drift is visible.
  • ECR images replicated to eu-west-1 automatically.
  • Kubernetes manifests in Git, ArgoCD in region B pointed at the same repo with replicas: 0 on the workloads.
  • Secrets replicated to eu-west-1 via Secrets Manager multi-region secrets.
  • Route 53 health-check-based failover records with a 60 second TTL.

Drilled quarterly, the measured failover is 22 minutes. Cost: about $1,200 a month. RTO target of 4 hours for region loss is met with a wide margin, which is the point — you want headroom, because the drill is calm and the incident is not.

Production scenario

The upgrade path matters as much as the destination. A team can move up the ladder incrementally, and each step is independently valuable:

  1. Get backups verified nightly (50.2). Now "backup and restore" is real rather than theoretical.
  2. Put the whole stack in Terraform, including the parts built by hand. This alone often cuts RTO from days to hours.
  3. Add a cross-region replica. Now you are pilot light.
  4. Automate the promotion and repointing in a script, and drill it. RTO drops by half because human steps disappear.
  5. Only then consider warm standby, and only if the arithmetic says an hour of downtime costs more than the standby.

Teams that jump to step 5 without step 1 have an expensive second environment and no protection from the failure that actually happens.

Failure scenario

A fintech built an active-active deployment across two regions with bidirectional replication. It worked beautifully for eight months. Then a schema migration was applied in region A and, because of a pipeline race, not in region B for 40 minutes. Replication from B to A began failing on rows with the new column; the operator, under pressure, disabled the failing replication direction "temporarily" to stop the alert storm.

Six hours later the two regions had diverged on 190,000 rows, including balances. Reconciliation took nine days and a temporary halt on withdrawals. The postmortem's key line: "active-active doubled our availability and squared our consistency problems". They moved to Aurora Global Database with a single writer, gave up sub-second regional failover for roughly 60 second failover, and never had the class of incident again.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Pilot light where the manifests in region B have drifted; the deploy fails at exactly the wrong moment. Fix: deploy to region B on every release even at zero replicas, or run ArgoCD there against the same repo.
  • Warm standby whose ECR images are not replicated; pods enter ImagePullBackOff during the failover.
  • Cross-region replica whose instance class is smaller "to save money"; after promotion it cannot carry production load and falls over.
  • Quotas: region B's account limits (EIPs, instance vCPU, NAT gateways) are lower because nothing runs there. Failover hits a quota error. Raise quotas in advance and check them in the drill.
  • The second region's Kubernetes cluster is a version behind and your CRDs do not apply.
  • Active-active with sequence-based primary keys: two regions generate id 1,000,001 for different orders.
  • Every strategy above region-local assumes DNS. If your clients cache DNS aggressively or pin IPs, your failover does not reach them (50.11).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick the rung by arithmetic, not by aspiration: cost of an hour of downtime, multiplied by the realistic probability of the event, against the monthly cost and the engineering time. For most businesses the honest answer is pilot light.

They insist that whatever rung you choose, backup and restore sits underneath it, because the failure that actually happens is logical, not physical.

They ask "what is the drift cost?" A second environment that must be kept identical is a permanent tax on every release. If your team cannot commit to that tax, warm standby will silently decay into a broken pilot light.

And they reframe active-active requests: "Do you need both regions serving writes, or do you need to fail over in under a minute? Because those are very different projects."

Common mistakes

  • Calling Multi-AZ "disaster recovery". It covers one AZ failing, not a region, and not a bad DELETE.
  • Building a warm standby and never deploying to it.
  • Assuming a cross-region replica gives RPO 0. It is asynchronous.
  • Choosing active-active for a system whose write conflicts have no defined resolution.
  • Forgetting that S3, Redis, Kafka, secrets and DNS all need a region-B story, not just the database.

Interview questions

  1. Compare the four DR strategies on RTO, RPO, cost and complexity.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the table above, with the point that all four need backups underneath.
  2. Why is Multi-AZ not disaster recovery?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it protects against one AZ; it replicates logical damage instantly; a region event or a bad delete defeats it.
  3. You have a pilot light setup. Walk me through the failover.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: promote replica, update secrets/config with new endpoint, scale deployment, verify health, shift DNS/traffic, warm caches, replay queues, verify writes are landing. Follow-up: what is your longest step? Usually DNS and pod warm-up.
  4. When is active-active the wrong answer?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when write conflicts have no business resolution, when the team is small, when what is really wanted is fast failover; recommend Aurora Global Database or warm standby instead.
  5. What breaks in a DR region that you only discover in a drill?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: quotas, image replication, secrets, manifest drift, undersized instances, IAM roles, security group rules, certificate issuance.

Practical exercise

Take a service you own and write the four-row table for it with your numbers: cost of an hour of downtime, monthly cost of each rung, and current rung. Then identify the single cheapest change that moves you one rung.

Acceptance criteria: the table has real dollar figures for at least three rows, the current rung is named honestly (including "we think it is pilot light but region B has not been deployed to in four months"), and the identified change costs less than $500 a month.

50.6 Failover and failback

Concept

Failover is moving production traffic from a failed primary to a standby. Failback is moving it back afterwards. Failover gets all the attention. Failback is usually harder, and it is where teams get hurt.

Why does it exist?

A standby that is never promoted is just an expensive backup. Failover is the act that converts standby capacity into availability, and it has to work under conditions where nothing else is working.

Mental model

Imagine a relay race where the runner collapses. Failover is the next runner taking the baton. That is not the hard part — the hard part is that the collapsed runner may still be holding the baton (a split brain), the crowd may still be cheering at the old runner's position (DNS and connection pools), and afterwards you must decide whether the first runner ever rejoins the race and how they catch up.

How it works

Automatic Multi-AZ failover on RDS, and what the application experiences.

RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in a second AZ. Writes are not acknowledged until they are durable on both. When AWS detects a primary failure (or you reboot with failover, or during patching), it promotes the standby and moves the DNS CNAME shop-prod.abc.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com to the new instance's address.

The application experience, in order:

  1. All existing connections break. Every pooled connection returns an error. In Node.js with pg you see Connection terminated unexpectedly or ECONNRESET. In-flight queries fail. In-flight transactions are rolled back.
  2. New connections fail for 30 to 90 seconds while the standby is promoted, with ECONNREFUSED or timeouts.
  3. DNS still resolves to the old address for up to the record's TTL. RDS uses a 5 second TTL, but Node.js caches DNS lookups at the OS/libuv level and some environments (and dns.lookup behaviour with certain resolvers) hold on longer. The classic symptom is a pod that keeps failing for minutes after the database is healthy.
  4. The pool reconnects and traffic recovers.

Typical total customer impact for RDS Multi-AZ: 60 to 120 seconds of errors. That is only true if your application handles it. Make it true:

TypeScript
// database.config.ts — TypeORM DataSource options tuned for failover.
export const dataSourceOptions = {
  type: 'postgres' as const,
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  // Pool behaviour during failover.
  extra: {
    max: 20,
    // Do not let a dead connection sit in the pool.
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
    // Fail fast on connect so retries can happen quickly, rather than hanging.
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
    // Kill queries that outlive the failover instead of piling up.
    statement_timeout: 15_000,
    query_timeout: 15_000,
    // TCP keepalive so the OS notices a black-holed connection quickly.
    keepAlive: true,
    keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 10_000,
  },
  // TypeORM will retry the initial connection at startup; important because a pod
  // that restarts mid-failover would otherwise CrashLoopBackOff.
  retryAttempts: 20,
  retryDelay: 3_000,
  // Never in production; a failover is not the time to auto-alter your schema.
  synchronize: false,
};

The three settings that matter most in practice: a short connectionTimeoutMillis so a broken endpoint fails fast instead of hanging for 30 seconds; statement_timeout so queries do not accumulate; and generous startup retries so pods restarting during the event do not enter CrashLoopBackOff and get backed off for five minutes.

Also, force Node.js to re-resolve DNS. Long-lived processes that cached the old address are a real and frequently misdiagnosed cause of "the database is up but the app is still broken":

TypeScript
// main.ts — bound the DNS cache so a failover CNAME change is picked up quickly.
import { setDefaultResultOrder } from 'node:dns';
setDefaultResultOrder('ipv4first');
// If you use a DNS caching layer (cacheable-lookup, dnscache), cap its TTL at ~5s
// so it can never outlive an RDS failover CNAME change.

Manual promotion. For a cross-region read replica there is no automation; you decide. On RDS:

Shell
# Promote the cross-region replica in eu-west-1 to a standalone writable instance.
aws rds promote-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier shop-replica-euw1 \
  --region eu-west-1

Promotion is irreversible. The replica becomes an independent primary on a new timeline; it will never resume replicating from the old primary. That single fact is why failback is hard.

Before promoting, ask two questions and write the answers in the incident channel:

  1. Is the old primary really gone, or is it isolated? Promoting while the old primary is still accepting writes gives you two writable databases: split brain. If the old primary is reachable at all, fence it first — revoke its security group ingress, or stop it.
  2. How far behind is the replica? That is your data loss.

Verifying whether data was lost with asynchronous replication.

SQL
-- On the OLD primary if you can still reach it:
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

-- On the replica, before promotion:
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() AS received,
       pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()  AS replayed,
       EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp())) AS lag_seconds;

-- The gap in bytes between what the primary had and what the replica got:
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff('0/AB12C340'::pg_lsn, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn());

lag_seconds is the honest RPO for this event. On RDS the equivalent is the CloudWatch ReplicaLag metric, and AuroraGlobalDBRPOLag for Aurora Global Database.

Then translate bytes and seconds into business facts, which is what people actually need:

SQL
-- After promotion, on the new primary: what is the newest order we have?
SELECT max(id), max(created_at) FROM orders;
-- Compare against the payment provider's records for the same window (38.8).
-- Every payment they have with no order here is a customer charged with nothing to show.

The failback problem. You failed over to region B at 03:00. By 09:00 region A is healthy. Now what?

This is harder than the failover for four reasons:

  1. The old primary is stale and divergent. It has writes that never reached B (the RPO gap) and it is missing six hours of writes that happened in B. You cannot just start replicating A from B; A's timeline has diverged.
  2. The only clean path is to rebuild A as a replica of B. That means a fresh base backup or replica creation from B, which for 2 TB is 1 to 3 hours plus catch-up, plus cross-region transfer costs.
  3. The failback itself is a second planned outage. Switching writes from B back to A means another promotion, another DNS change, another window of broken connections. You are choosing to have a second incident.
  4. You must extract the orphaned writes from A first. Those writes in the RPO gap are real customer actions. Snapshot A before rebuilding it, restore that snapshot to a forensic instance, and reconcile those rows into B (the technique is 50.4's).

The senior answer is often: do not fail back at all. If region B can carry production indefinitely, make B the new primary, rebuild A as the new standby, and schedule the "failback" as a routine planned maintenance months later, or never. Failing back at 09:00 the same day because "A is our real region" is an emotional decision that causes a second outage.

If you must fail back, do it during a low-traffic window, announce it, drain writes, verify replication lag is zero, and treat it as a planned migration with a rollback plan.

Practical example

At 03:12 the us-east-1 primary becomes unreachable. Multi-AZ failover fires automatically; 74 seconds of elevated errors; the application recovers on its own; nobody is paged beyond the automated notification. This is the 95 percent case and it is why Multi-AZ is worth its doubled instance cost.

At 03:40 the same night, a broader us-east-1 networking event takes out the application subnets too. Multi-AZ cannot help. The on-call declares a region failover, promotes the eu-west-1 replica (replica lag at promotion: 4 seconds, so roughly 30 orders potentially affected), scales the ArgoCD-managed deployment from 0 to 12 pods, updates the Route 53 health-check-driven record, and has checkout working at 04:04 — 24 minutes.

Failback happens 11 days later, on a Tuesday at 02:00, as a planned migration, after us-east-1 has been rebuilt from eu-west-1 and replicating cleanly for three days.

Failure scenario

A team failed over to their DR region during an outage. Twelve minutes later the original region recovered and the original primary came back online, still holding its old DNS entries in some caches and still accepting connections from a subset of pods whose DNS had not refreshed.

For 26 minutes, orders were written to both databases. 340 orders landed only on the old primary and 512 only on the new one. Neither database was complete. Reconciliation required a forensic restore of both, a manual merge, and a customer support campaign.

The missing control was fencing: the runbook did not include "before promoting, make the old primary unreachable". One aws rds stop-db-instance or a security group rule change would have prevented the entire second incident. Fencing is now step one of their failover runbook, before promotion, always.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Split brain: the old primary still takes writes. Fence before promoting, every time.
  • Pods that cached the old DNS answer keep failing after the database is healthy; symptoms look like a database problem and are not.
  • CrashLoopBackOff during failover because the app exits on startup when the database is unreachable, and Kubernetes backs off exponentially to 5 minutes. Use startup retries and a startup probe with a generous failureThreshold.
  • Connection pool sized for steady state stampedes the freshly promoted database with 12 pods times 20 connections at once. Add jitter and pool warm-up.
  • Read replicas of the old primary are now replicating from a dead machine and must be rebuilt.
  • A promoted replica has no read replicas and no Multi-AZ standby of its own; you are running without redundancy until you add them. Add them the same day.
  • Sequences on the promoted replica are correct (they replicate), but any sequence cache on the old primary means small gaps. Gaps are fine; duplicates are not.
  • Aurora Global Database "managed planned failover" is clean and lossless, but "failover" during an actual regional outage is a different, potentially lossy operation. Know which one you are doing.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design the application to survive a database restart as a normal event, not an incident. Failover then becomes 90 seconds of retries rather than a page. That means timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, idempotent writes and a circuit breaker (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure).

They fence before they promote. Always. It is one command and it prevents the worst class of DR incident.

They record the replication lag at the moment of promotion, in the incident channel, before doing anything else. That number is the RPO of this event and everyone will need it later.

They are deeply suspicious of failback urgency. "Region A is back" is not a reason to move production twice in one day.

Common mistakes

  • Promoting without fencing.
  • Not measuring lag at promotion, then being unable to tell customers what was lost.
  • Treating failback as the reverse of failover; it is a fresh migration.
  • Leaving the promoted instance without Multi-AZ or backups configured, so a second failure is unrecoverable.
  • Forgetting that the promoted replica's parameter group, backup retention and monitoring may all differ from the original primary's.

Interview questions

  1. What does an application experience during an RDS Multi-AZ failover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: connections reset, 30–90s of failed connects, DNS CNAME change with TTL delay, pool reconnect; total 60–120s if the app retries correctly.
  2. What is split brain and how do you prevent it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: two writable primaries accepting writes; prevent by fencing the old primary (stop it, revoke network access) before promotion, and by promoting only once.
  3. How do you determine data loss after promoting an async replica?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: replica lag at promotion (pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp, ReplicaLag), LSN diff against the old primary if reachable, then business-level reconciliation against the payment provider and outbox.
  4. Why is failback harder than failover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: divergent timelines, the old primary must be rebuilt as a replica, orphaned writes in the RPO gap must be extracted, and the failback is itself a second planned outage.
  5. Your pods keep failing after the database is confirmed healthy. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: DNS caching in the process, pool holding dead connections, CrashLoopBackOff backoff timer, security groups, secrets pointing at the old endpoint.

Practical exercise

In a test environment, run a NestJS service under sustained load against RDS Multi-AZ and trigger reboot-db-instance --force-failover. Measure: total error duration, number of failed requests, time until the pool is fully re-established, and whether any pod entered CrashLoopBackOff.

Acceptance criteria: total customer-visible error window under 120 seconds, no pod restarts, zero duplicate orders created by client retries, and a documented list of every configuration change you had to make to get there.

50.7 Database recovery scenarios

Concept

Disaster recovery is a set of specific playbooks, not one procedure. This section is the catalogue: seven situations that actually happen, and the first three moves for each.

How it works

Scenario 1: a corrupted table.

Symptoms: queries error with invalid page in block 12345 of relation base/16384/24576, or a checksum failure, or a query returns rows that violate a constraint that should make them impossible.

SQL
-- Confirm and locate. Requires the amcheck extension (available on RDS).
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS amcheck;
SELECT bt_index_check(index => c.oid, heapallindexed => true)
FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind = 'i' AND n.nspname = 'public';

-- Is it just an index? Rebuilding an index is cheap and non-destructive.
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY order_items_order_id_idx;

-- Heap corruption is different. Find the extent of the damage:
SELECT count(*) FROM order_items;   -- may error on the bad block

Moves, in order: (1) if it is an index, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and you are done. (2) If it is the heap, do not set zero_damaged_pages on production as a first response; it silently discards data. (3) PITR to before the corruption on a side instance, extract the affected table, and repair as in 50.4. (4) Investigate the cause: on RDS, hardware corruption is rare and the usual causes are a bug, an unclean shutdown on self-managed hardware without fsync, or storage-level issues. Enable data_checksums if you are self-managed and it is off.

Scenario 2: an accidental DROP TABLE or DROP DATABASE.

A DROP is worse than a DELETE in one way and better in another. Worse: the table's files are gone, so there is nothing to recover in place. Better: it is instantly obvious, so detection time is near zero.

Moves: PITR to one minute before the DROP on a new instance, then pg_dump --table=dropped_table from that instance and pg_restore into production. Because nothing in production references the table (it does not exist), there is no reconciliation problem for the table itself — but foreign keys pointing to it were dropped too, and every write that would have gone into it during the window is lost. Check the outbox and application logs for those.

Prevention beats recovery here: revoke DROP from application roles, require migrations for all DDL, and set ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES so no ad-hoc session has the rights.

Scenario 3: ransomware, or deleted backups.

The attack pattern is specific: the attacker gets a credential, spends time finding backups, deletes or encrypts the backups first, and only then destroys the data. Deleting the primary while snapshots remain achieves nothing, and they know that.

The only defence that works is a second custody boundary:

  • Backups copied into a separate AWS account whose credentials are not in your CI, not in your secrets manager, and not held by anyone with production access.
  • AWS Backup vault lock in compliance mode, or S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. In compliance mode, the retention cannot be shortened by anyone, including the account root user. That is the point.
  • MFA delete on the backup bucket.
  • Alerting on the destructive API calls themselves: DeleteDBSnapshot, DeleteDBInstance, PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration, ScheduleKeyDeletion, DeleteBackupVault. These should page, not appear in a weekly report.

Recovery is then a restore-from-vault into a clean account, with new credentials everywhere, which is slow but possible. Without the second boundary, there is no recovery.

Scenario 4: a replica promoted with missing commits.

You promoted an async replica; it was 12 seconds behind. Those 12 seconds contained real orders. The database is now internally consistent — it just does not contain everything.

Moves: (1) Record the promotion LSN and timestamp. (2) Snapshot the old primary before touching it; that snapshot contains the missing commits. (3) Restore that snapshot to a forensic instance. (4) Diff the window: rows in the forensic instance created after the promotion timestamp minus rows in the new primary. (5) Reconcile the gaps using idempotent inserts, and separately reconcile against the payment provider (50.8) because a charged customer with no order is the case that matters. (6) Fix sequences if you inserted rows with explicit ids: SELECT setval('orders_id_seq', (SELECT max(id) FROM orders));

Scenario 5: a failed migration that needs a data rollback.

A migration ran, the schema change succeeded, and then the data backfill corrupted 200,000 rows. Schema rollback is easy (a down migration). Data rollback is not, because the old values are gone.

Moves: (1) Stop the backfill immediately. (2) Determine the exact affected row set and the window — the migration log has this. (3) PITR to before the migration on a side instance. (4) Extract only the affected columns for only the affected rows and UPDATE ... FROM them back:

SQL
-- Restore only the corrupted column, only for rows the migration touched.
UPDATE products p
SET price_cents = r.price_cents
FROM recovered.products r
WHERE r.id = p.id
  AND p.updated_at BETWEEN '2026-09-09 11:00Z' AND '2026-09-09 11:40Z'
  AND p.price_cents <> r.price_cents;

This is why Part 24's expand-contract pattern matters: a migration that only adds is trivially reversible; a migration that transforms in place needs a recovery plan written before it runs. Create a restore point (pg_create_restore_point) or a manual snapshot immediately before every destructive migration.

Scenario 6: a full disk.

PostgreSQL with no free space cannot write WAL, and a database that cannot write WAL cannot commit anything. On RDS, the instance enters storage-full and stops accepting writes. It is an outage, but usually not data loss.

Common causes, in the order you should check them: unexpected data growth; a replication slot that is not being consumed, so WAL is retained forever; WAL archiving failing, so segments accumulate; pg_stat_statements or logging filling the disk; a runaway temporary file from a bad query.

SQL
-- The single most common cause of a mystery full disk: an abandoned replication slot.
SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots
ORDER BY pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) DESC;

-- If a slot is inactive and retaining hundreds of GB, drop it (after confirming
-- no consumer needs it) and the space is released at the next checkpoint.
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('abandoned_cdc_slot');

-- Where is the space actually going?
SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) DESC LIMIT 20;

Moves: enable RDS storage autoscaling before you need it; alert at 75 percent, not 90; set max_slot_wal_keep_size so a dead slot cannot take the database down; and never let a CDC connector's slot outlive the connector.

Scenario 7: transaction id wraparound.

PostgreSQL transaction ids are 32-bit. Rows are visible based on transaction id comparison in a circular space, so if 2 billion transactions pass without those rows being "frozen" by VACUUM, old rows would appear to be in the future and vanish. To prevent that, PostgreSQL refuses new transactions when the oldest unfrozen transaction id gets within 1 million of the limit. The database goes read-only with a very memorable message: database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss.

This is a slow-motion emergency: it takes weeks or months to develop and gives you many warnings you probably ignored.

SQL
-- Watch this. Alert at 500 million, page at 1 billion.
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age
FROM pg_database ORDER BY xid_age DESC;

-- Which table is holding it back?
SELECT c.relname, age(c.relfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r','m') AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')
ORDER BY age(c.relfrozenxid) DESC LIMIT 10;

Causes are always one of: a long-running transaction or an idle-in-transaction session holding an old snapshot; an abandoned replication slot; a prepared transaction nobody committed; or autovacuum being throttled so hard it cannot keep up on a huge table.

Emergency moves: (1) find and kill the blocker — SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' AND xact_start < now() - interval '1 hour'; (2) check pg_prepared_xacts and ROLLBACK PREPARED any orphans. (3) drop abandoned replication slots. (4) If already read-only, restart in single-user mode (self-managed) or let RDS's protective vacuum run; a manual VACUUM FREEZE on the offending table is the fix and it can take hours on a large table. (5) Afterwards, tune autovacuum_freeze_max_age, increase autovacuum_max_workers and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, and add the xid_age alert you clearly did not have.

See Part 19 — PostgreSQL Internals for the MVCC and vacuum mechanics behind this.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Recovering a table but not its sequences, triggers, or foreign keys.
  • Restoring into a database where the extension version differs, so functions behave differently.
  • A recovery that succeeds but leaves the search index, cache and warehouse stale (50.8).
  • Killing idle in transaction sessions blindly and aborting a legitimate long-running job.
  • Autovacuum tuned so aggressively during a wraparound emergency that it saturates IOPS and causes a performance outage on top of the data emergency.
  • Backup vault lock in compliance mode applied with a 7 year retention "to be safe", creating an unbounded and undeletable storage bill.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They keep this catalogue as runbooks in the repository, one file per scenario, each with the detection query, the first three commands, and the decision points. During an incident nobody invents procedure; they open the file.

They notice that five of these seven scenarios are prevented by ordinary hygiene: alerts on xid_age, on disk usage, on replication slot size, on destructive API calls, and a manual snapshot before every migration. Prevention is cheaper than every recovery in this section.

And they treat the read-only-mode scenarios (full disk, wraparound) as the most dangerous, because the database is up, health checks pass, and the failure is silent until writes start failing everywhere at once.

Common mistakes

  • Setting zero_damaged_pages = on to "fix" corruption, silently deleting rows.
  • Granting DROP to the application's database role.
  • Storing backups only where the application's own credentials can reach them.
  • Ignoring xid_age until the database goes read-only.
  • Leaving a CDC replication slot behind after decommissioning the connector.
  • Running a destructive migration with no restore point taken first.

Interview questions

  1. A query returns invalid page in block. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: determine index vs heap, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY if index, PITR to a side instance and extract if heap, never zero_damaged_pages as a first move, then root-cause the storage or shutdown issue.
  2. Your database disk is full and nothing is writing much data. What is the likely cause?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: an inactive replication slot retaining WAL, or failing WAL archiving. Follow-up: what setting bounds it? max_slot_wal_keep_size.
  3. Explain transaction id wraparound and how you would handle it as an emergency.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: 32-bit xids, freezing, refusal to accept commands within 1 million of the limit; kill long transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions, clear prepared transactions and slots, VACUUM FREEZE, then tune autovacuum and add alerting on age(datfrozenxid).
  4. How do you protect backups from an attacker with production credentials?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: separate account, separate credential path, vault lock or Object Lock in compliance mode, MFA delete, alerts on destructive API calls.
  5. A migration corrupted a column's values. Schema rollback is easy. How do you roll back the data?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: PITR to before the migration on a side instance, extract only that column for only the affected rows in the affected window, UPDATE ... FROM, verify invariants; and take a restore point before every destructive migration.

Practical exercise

Write three runbook files for a database you own: runbook-accidental-delete.md, runbook-disk-full.md, runbook-xid-wraparound.md. Each must contain the detection query, the alert that should have fired, the first three commands to run, the decision point, and the reconciliation step.

Acceptance criteria: someone who has never seen the system can execute each runbook; each runbook names the alert that would have caught the problem earlier; and at least one of the three alerts does not currently exist, so you create it.

50.8 Application-level recovery

Concept

The database being back is not the system being back. An e-commerce platform is a database plus a cache, a search index, a stream of events, a set of queues, and a payment provider that kept working the whole time you were down. Every one of those is now inconsistent with the restored database, and every one needs a deliberate recovery step.

Application-level recovery is the work of making the rest of the system agree with the database again, without causing a second incident by doing it.

Why does it exist?

Because state got out of sync in both directions during the outage:

  • The database went backwards (a restore to 14:31 discarded writes that other systems already saw).
  • Other systems went forwards (Stripe took payments, the warehouse shipped, customers received emails, Kafka accumulated events) while the database was frozen or absent.

If you only restore the database and declare victory, you get: search results for products that no longer exist, carts referencing deleted orders, customers charged with no order record, a warehouse shipping items the database thinks were never sold, and a dead-letter queue full of messages that will fail forever.

Mental model

Imagine a shop whose till was replaced with yesterday's till. The shelves (warehouse), the card machine (payment provider), the customer's inbox (notifications) and the noticeboard (search index) all still reflect today. Recovering the till is step one. Step two is walking the shop and reconciling every one of those against the till, deciding for each discrepancy whether the till is wrong or the world is wrong.

How it works

Work in this order. The order matters, because getting it wrong causes duplicate side effects.

Step 0: pause everything that produces side effects. Before the restored database takes any traffic beyond reads, stop the outbox publisher, the CDC connector (Debezium), the notification consumers and the email worker. If you skip this, restoring 8 million rows re-emits 8 million events and someone receives 40,000 emails (the failure scenario in 50.4).

In Kubernetes this is kubectl scale deployment/outbox-publisher --replicas=0 and friends, and it belongs in the runbook as a single script.

Step 1: reconcile with the payment provider. Do this first, because it is the only source of truth you do not control and the only discrepancy that costs real money and legal exposure.

The question is precise: for the gap window, does every charge at Stripe have a corresponding order in the database, and does every order in the database have a corresponding charge?

TypeScript
// payment-reconciliation.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import Stripe from 'stripe';

export interface Discrepancy {
  kind: 'CHARGED_NO_ORDER' | 'ORDER_NO_CHARGE' | 'AMOUNT_MISMATCH';
  paymentIntentId: string;
  orderId?: string;
  amountCents: number;
}

@Injectable()
export class PaymentReconciliationService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(PaymentReconciliationService.name);
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly stripe: Stripe) {}

  /** Compares the provider's record of truth against ours for an incident window. */
  async reconcile(fromUnix: number, toUnix: number): Promise<Discrepancy[]> {
    const found: Discrepancy[] = [];

    // Stripe is authoritative for money. Page through everything in the window.
    for await (const pi of this.stripe.paymentIntents.list({
      created: { gte: fromUnix, lte: toUnix },
      limit: 100,
    })) {
      if (pi.status !== 'succeeded') continue;

      // Our orders carry the payment intent id; that link is what makes this possible.
      const [order] = await this.ds.query<{ id: string; total_cents: number }[]>(
        `SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE payment_intent_id = $1`,
        [pi.id],
      );

      if (!order) {
        // Customer was charged and we have no order. Highest severity.
        found.push({ kind: 'CHARGED_NO_ORDER', paymentIntentId: pi.id, amountCents: pi.amount });
      } else if (order.total_cents !== pi.amount) {
        found.push({
          kind: 'AMOUNT_MISMATCH', paymentIntentId: pi.id,
          orderId: order.id, amountCents: pi.amount,
        });
      }
    }

    // The other direction: orders we think are paid with no successful charge.
    const orphanOrders = await this.ds.query<{ id: string; payment_intent_id: string; total_cents: number }[]>(
      `SELECT id, payment_intent_id, total_cents FROM orders
       WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at BETWEEN to_timestamp($1) AND to_timestamp($2)`,
      [fromUnix, toUnix],
    );
    for (const o of orphanOrders) {
      const pi = await this.stripe.paymentIntents.retrieve(o.payment_intent_id);
      if (pi.status !== 'succeeded') {
        found.push({
          kind: 'ORDER_NO_CHARGE', paymentIntentId: o.payment_intent_id,
          orderId: o.id, amountCents: o.total_cents,
        });
      }
    }

    this.log.warn(`reconciliation found ${found.length} discrepancies in window`);
    return found;
  }
}

Note what makes reconciliation possible at all: the order row stores the provider's payment_intent_id. If your schema does not carry the external identifier, you cannot reconcile, and you will be matching by amount and timestamp, which is guesswork. This is a design decision made months before the incident.

CHARGED_NO_ORDER never gets auto-fixed. It goes to a human queue: either recreate the order from the payment intent's metadata (if you put the cart in the metadata, which you should) or refund the customer with an apology. Both are acceptable; silence is not.

Step 2: replay the transactional outbox. If you followed Part 28's outbox pattern, every event that should have been published is a row in PostgreSQL, written in the same transaction as the business change. That means the database restore automatically restored the event stream, and republishing is a matter of finding unpublished rows.

SQL
-- The outbox table. published_at NULL means "not yet on the broker".
CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
  id             bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_type text        NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id   text        NOT NULL,
  event_type     text        NOT NULL,
  payload        jsonb       NOT NULL,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at   timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished_idx ON outbox_events (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- After a restore, this is exactly the backlog to replay.
SELECT count(*), min(created_at), max(created_at)
FROM outbox_events WHERE published_at IS NULL;

The subtlety: after a PITR, some rows may be marked published_at = NOT NULL in the restored state but the broker never actually received them (or received them and the consumer had not processed them). The safe posture is at-least-once with idempotent consumers. Republish anything from the incident window, and rely on consumer-side idempotency keys to drop duplicates. If your consumers are not idempotent, the outbox replay is dangerous and you have a design problem to fix before the next incident, not during this one.

Step 3: resume Kafka consumers. Kafka retains events independently of your database, which makes it a recovery asset. Three cases:

  1. The database went backwards past events the consumers already processed. The consumers' offsets are ahead of the restored database's state. Reset the consumer group to the timestamp of the recovery target so it reprocesses:
Shell
# Reset a consumer group to a wall-clock time. Requires the group to be idle.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --group inventory-projector \
  --topic order-events \
  --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-09-09T14:31:00.000 \
  --execute

  1. The database is current but consumers were down. Just restart them; they resume from their committed offsets and catch up. Watch consumer lag drain, and expect a thundering herd of processing that can overload the freshly restored database. Scale consumers up gradually.

  2. Events were produced during the outage that reference rows that no longer exist. These fail and land in the dead-letter queue. That is step 5.

Kafka retention is the constraint: if your topic retains 7 days and you restore to a point 9 days ago, the events are gone. This is another argument for the outbox as the durable source.

Step 4: rebuild caches and search indexes. Both are derived state with PostgreSQL as the source of truth, which is why 50.3 gave them an unlimited RPO.

Redis: the safest action after a database restore is a targeted invalidation, not a FLUSHALL. Flushing everything at 400 RPS causes a cache stampede that hammers the just-restored database.

TypeScript
// cache-recovery.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class CacheRecoveryService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(CacheRecoveryService.name);
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  /**
   * Invalidate only keys affected by the incident, in batches, with a pause
   * between batches so the database is not stampeded. SCAN, never KEYS.
   */
  async invalidatePrefix(prefix: string, batch = 500, pauseMs = 50): Promise<number> {
    let cursor = '0';
    let deleted = 0;
    do {
      const [next, keys] = await this.redis.scan(cursor, 'MATCH', `${prefix}*`, 'COUNT', batch);
      cursor = next;
      if (keys.length > 0) {
        // UNLINK frees memory asynchronously; DEL blocks the Redis event loop on big keys.
        await this.redis.unlink(...keys);
        deleted += keys.length;
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, pauseMs));
      }
    } while (cursor !== '0');
    this.log.log(`invalidated ${deleted} keys under ${prefix}`);
    return deleted;
  }

  /** Warm the keys that carry the most traffic, before reopening to users. */
  async warmTopProducts(ids: string[], loader: (id: string) => Promise<unknown>): Promise<void> {
    const concurrency = 20;
    for (let i = 0; i < ids.length; i += concurrency) {
      await Promise.all(ids.slice(i, i + concurrency).map(async (id) => {
        const value = await loader(id);
        await this.redis.set(`product:${id}`, JSON.stringify(value), 'EX', 3600);
      }));
    }
  }
}

Search index: rebuild from PostgreSQL rather than trying to patch it. For 2 million products a full OpenSearch reindex is typically 20 to 60 minutes with bulk indexing. The pattern is index-into-a-new-index and atomically swap the alias, so search never serves a half-built index:

Text
products_v7 (live, alias "products")  ->  build products_v8  ->  alias swap  ->  delete v7

Sessions in Redis: usually the right decision is to accept the loss and let users log in again. Trying to restore sessions from a snapshot risks resurrecting sessions that were legitimately revoked, which is a security problem.

Step 5: reprocess dead-letter queues. During the outage, thousands of messages failed and went to the DLQ. Some will now succeed; some are genuinely poison; some would cause harm if replayed (a "charge customer" message from an order that has since been refunded).

Never replay a DLQ blindly. The procedure:

  1. Classify. Group by error type and event type. Usually 90 percent are one cause ("connection refused") and are safe.
  2. Filter. Exclude messages whose side effect is no longer valid, using the current database state as the check.
  3. Replay in batches with rate limiting, watching the error rate. If the failure rate on replay exceeds a few percent, stop.
  4. Rely on idempotency. Every consumer must key on a message id or business key so a duplicate replay is a no-op.
TypeScript
// dlq-replay.service.ts (BullMQ example)
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Queue, Job } from 'bullmq';

@Injectable()
export class DlqReplayService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(DlqReplayService.name);
  constructor(private readonly failed: Queue, private readonly main: Queue) {}

  /**
   * Replays failed jobs whose failure reason matches a known-transient pattern,
   * in bounded batches. Everything else stays in the DLQ for human review.
   */
  async replayTransient(pattern: RegExp, batchSize = 200, delayMs = 1000): Promise<number> {
    let replayed = 0;
    for (;;) {
      const jobs: Job[] = await this.failed.getFailed(0, batchSize - 1);
      if (jobs.length === 0) break;

      const eligible = jobs.filter((j) => pattern.test(j.failedReason ?? ''));
      if (eligible.length === 0) break;

      for (const job of eligible) {
        // retry() re-enqueues the SAME job id, so a consumer keyed on job id
        // will treat a duplicate as a no-op.
        await job.retry();
        replayed++;
      }
      this.log.log(`replayed ${replayed} DLQ jobs`);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delayMs)); // rate limit the flood
    }
    return replayed;
  }
}

Production scenario

For our platform, application-level recovery after a 90 minute database outage typically looks like: 8 minutes of payment reconciliation (about 2,100 payment intents in the window, 3 discrepancies), 4 minutes of outbox replay (28,000 events), 12 minutes of Kafka consumer catch-up, 35 minutes of search reindex (running in the background while the site is already up), 6 minutes of cache warming, and 20 minutes of DLQ triage with 9,400 of 9,600 messages replayed automatically and 200 escalated.

Total: roughly 50 minutes of active work after the database is back, most of it parallelisable. If it is scripted, one engineer does it. If it is not scripted, it is four engineers improvising for three hours.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Replaying events that trigger payment capture, re-charging customers. The single worst outcome in this section. Every money-moving consumer must be idempotent on a provider-side idempotency key.
  • Duplicate emails and SMS from replayed notification events. Cheap to prevent (a notifications_sent table with a unique key on event id), expensive in trust.
  • Search index rebuilt from a database that is still missing recovered rows, so it must be rebuilt again.
  • FLUSHALL on Redis at peak, causing a stampede that takes down the recovered database. Always invalidate by prefix, in batches.
  • Consumer offset reset applied to a group that is not idle, silently doing nothing.
  • Kafka retention shorter than the recovery gap, so the events cannot be replayed at all.
  • Webhook endpoints from the payment provider that retried during the outage and gave up; check the provider's failed-webhook list, do not assume they retried forever.
  • Reconciliation run against a payment provider window in the wrong timezone, missing an hour of charges.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design for this recovery long before the incident, by making three choices: an outbox in the same transaction as the write, external identifiers stored on the row (payment_intent_id, shipment_id), and idempotency on every consumer. Those three make application recovery mechanical rather than heroic.

They order the work by irreversibility. Money first, because a wrong refund cannot be un-sent. Derived state last, because it can be rebuilt as many times as you like.

They pause side effects before they touch data. This is the reflex that separates a clean recovery from a second incident.

And they script it. A recovery script that has been run in a drill is worth more than a very good engineer improvising, because the engineer is tired and it is 04:00.

Common mistakes

  • Declaring the incident over when the database is back.
  • Replaying the DLQ with one command and no filter.
  • Not storing the payment provider's identifier on the order, making reconciliation impossible.
  • Flushing the entire cache after a restore.
  • Forgetting that customers received emails about orders that the restore has now erased.

Interview questions

  1. The database is restored to 20 minutes ago. What else is now inconsistent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: payments taken in the gap, events already consumed downstream, caches, search index, warehouse/fulfilment, notifications already sent, DLQ contents. Walk the ordered recovery.
  2. How do you reconcile with a payment provider?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the provider is authoritative; list charges in the window; match on a stored external id; classify charged-no-order, order-no-charge, amount mismatch; escalate money discrepancies to humans.
  3. Why is the outbox pattern a disaster recovery feature?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: events are written transactionally with the data, so restoring the database restores the event log, and replay is a query for unpublished rows.
  4. What makes DLQ replay dangerous and how do you make it safe?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: side effects may no longer be valid and duplicates may re-charge; classify, filter against current state, batch with rate limiting, rely on consumer idempotency.
  5. How do you rebuild a search index without downtime?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: build a new index, bulk load from PostgreSQL, swap the alias atomically, delete the old one.

Practical exercise

Take a service with a queue and a cache. Simulate a restore by rolling the database back 30 minutes while the queue keeps running. Then write and execute the recovery script: pause consumers, reconcile against an external stub API, replay the outbox, reset the consumer offset, invalidate cache by prefix, replay the DLQ with a filter.

Acceptance criteria: no duplicate side effects (assert by counting outbound calls to your stub), all business invariants pass afterwards, and the script is idempotent when run twice.

50.9 What happens if the PostgreSQL production database disappears

This is the walkthrough. One incident, minute by minute, with the decisions named. The setup: pilot light DR (50.5), RPO target 5 minutes, RTO target 1 hour for a primary loss.

02:14 — The event. A storage-level failure in us-east-1 takes out the RDS primary and its Multi-AZ standby (rare, but this is a DR chapter). The instance is not reachable and AWS shows it as failed.

02:14:30 — Detection. Three alerts fire within 40 seconds: the synthetic checkout probe fails, the API error rate crosses 50 percent, and pg_up from the exporter goes to 0. Detection is fast because there is a synthetic transaction, not just infrastructure metrics. Elapsed: 0.5 min.

02:16 — Declare the incident. The on-call pages, opens an incident channel, and takes the incident commander role. First three messages, always the same three: what is broken, what the blast radius is, who is doing what. Someone else is assigned scribe. The customer-communication owner is named now, not later. Elapsed: 2 min.

02:18 — Assess. Is this a database problem or a wider region problem? The pods are healthy, Redis is healthy, S3 is reachable. It is the database. Attempting aws rds describe-db-instances shows failed with no automatic recovery in progress. AWS Health dashboard confirms a storage issue.

The commander makes the call: do not wait for AWS. The RTO clock is running and a "wait and see" of 30 minutes is 30 minutes of the budget. Elapsed: 4 min.

02:20 — Choose the recovery target. Three options are on the table, and the commander states them explicitly:

Option RTO RPO Chosen?
PITR restore in us-east-1 to now-5min ~90 min ~5 min No: too slow, and the region's storage is suspect
Promote the eu-west-1 cross-region replica ~20 min replica lag, currently 6 s Yes
Restore the newest snapshot in eu-west-1 ~70 min ~11 h Fallback if promotion fails

Replica lag at 02:14 was 6 seconds, from the CloudWatch metric captured before the failure. That is the RPO for this event, and it is written in the channel immediately: "expected data loss: approximately 6 seconds of writes, roughly 2 to 4 orders." Elapsed: 6 min.

02:21 — Fence the old primary. Even though it appears dead, the runbook says fence first. The security group ingress rule allowing the application subnets is revoked. This takes 30 seconds and eliminates split brain entirely. Elapsed: 7 min.

02:22 — Promote. aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier shop-replica-euw1 --region eu-west-1. Elapsed: 8 min.

02:27 — Promotion complete. The instance is writable. Immediately, in parallel:

  • Enable Multi-AZ and automated backups on the new primary (it has neither; a promoted replica inherits nothing).
  • Capture SELECT max(id), max(created_at) FROM orders; for the reconciliation record. Elapsed: 13 min.

02:28 — Repoint the application. This is the step that is either 90 seconds or 40 minutes depending on preparation. Ours is 90 seconds because the endpoint is not hardcoded anywhere:

Shell
# One secret holds the connection string. Everything reads it.
aws secretsmanager update-secret \
  --secret-id prod/shop/database-url \
  --secret-string "postgresql://app:***@shop-replica-euw1.xyz.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/shop" \
  --region eu-west-1

# The External Secrets Operator syncs it into the cluster; a rollout picks it up.
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api deployment/worker -n shop

If instead the endpoint had been in a ConfigMap in three namespaces, a Helm value, a Terraform variable and two Lambda environment variables, this step would have been the longest of the incident. Elapsed: 14 min.

02:33 — Pods healthy in eu-west-1. The ArgoCD-managed deployments scale from 0 to 12. Image pull is fast because ECR replication put the images in eu-west-1. Readiness probes pass. Elapsed: 19 min.

02:35 — Shift traffic. Route 53 weighted records move to the eu-west-1 ALB. TTL is 60 seconds. Synthetic checkout succeeds at 02:36:40. Elapsed: 22 min. Customers can check out again.

02:36 — Warm the caches. Redis in eu-west-1 is empty. Without warming, 400 RPS of cache misses hits a database that is also serving the write path. The warming script loads the top 5,000 products and the category tree, then the site is opened to full traffic. p99 is 480 ms for the first 10 minutes, settling to 140 ms by 02:52. Elapsed: 22 to 38 min.
