02:40 — Replay the outbox and queues. 1,240 unpublished outbox rows are republished. Kafka consumers in eu-west-1 connect to the MirrorMaker-replicated cluster and start from their mirrored offsets; lag drains over 9 minutes. Elapsed: 26 to 35 min.

02:50 — Reconcile payments for the gap. The window is 02:13:50 to 02:36:40 (from just before the last replicated write to the moment writes resumed). Stripe shows 47 successful payment intents in that window. 44 have matching orders. 3 do not — customers were charged, the order write never made it to the replica.

Those 3 are handled by hand within the hour: the payment intent metadata contains the cart, so the orders are recreated with their original ids and a note in the audit log. Two customers get an apology email; one had already emailed support. Elapsed: 36 to 55 min.

03:05 — Communicate. The status page was updated at 02:19 ("investigating checkout errors") and 02:37 ("service restored, monitoring"). Now a fuller note goes out. The rule the team follows: update at declaration, at restoration, and every 30 minutes in between, even when there is nothing new. Silence is what customers remember.

03:30 — Stabilise. Multi-AZ is enabling on the new primary. A new read replica is being created in eu-west-1. Backups are confirmed running. Only now does the commander stand down. Running without redundancy is not "recovered".

Total: 22 minutes to customers checking out, 55 minutes to fully reconciled, against a 60 minute RTO and 5 minute RPO. Actual data loss: 6 seconds, 3 orders, all recovered manually.

The honest list: what would have made this four hours faster

This incident went well because of decisions made months earlier. The postmortem's most valuable output is the list of things that would have made a worse version of this incident better. Here it is honestly:

  1. One place for the database endpoint. The single biggest lever. Teams with the endpoint scattered across ConfigMaps, Helm values, Lambda env vars and a hardcoded fallback in an old service spend 30 to 60 minutes hunting. One secret, read by everything, turns that into 90 seconds.
  2. A cross-region replica instead of only snapshots. Promotion took 5 minutes; a snapshot restore would have taken 70. That single line item is worth roughly $900 a month and it saved an hour.
  3. A drilled runbook. The team had run this exact procedure in a drill 7 weeks earlier. Nobody had to think about the order of steps, and nobody forgot to fence.
  4. A synthetic checkout probe. Detection in 30 seconds instead of "when a customer complains", which is typically 8 to 15 minutes at 02:00.
  5. ECR image replication and manifests in Git. No ImagePullBackOff, no hand-editing YAML at 02:30.
  6. payment_intent_id on the order row. Reconciliation was a query. Without it, it would have been a spreadsheet exercise taking days.
  7. A scripted cache warmer. Without it, the site comes back and immediately falls over from a cold-cache stampede, and you have a second outage inside the first.
  8. Raised service quotas in the DR region, checked quarterly. A vCPU quota that only allows 4 pods would have capped capacity at exactly the wrong moment.
  9. The decision to not wait for AWS. Twenty minutes of hoping is twenty minutes of RTO.
  10. A named incident commander and scribe. Five engineers all typing commands is slower than one deciding and two executing.

And the honest gaps this incident revealed, which became action items:

  • The promoted replica had no backups or Multi-AZ. Should be automated in the promotion script, not remembered.
  • Kafka MirrorMaker offsets were mapped approximately; two consumer groups reprocessed about 15 minutes of events. Idempotency saved it, but the offset mapping needs work.
  • The status page update at 02:19 was written from scratch under pressure. Pre-written templates now exist.
  • Nobody checked the DR region's quotas in the last two drills.

50.10 The DR runbook and drill schedule

Concept

A runbook is an executable document: the steps, in order, with the commands, the decision points and the verification for each. A drill is a scheduled rehearsal of that document against real infrastructure. Together they convert DR from a design into a capability.

Why does it exist?

Because at 02:14 nobody reasons well. Cognitive load is the enemy. Every decision you can pre-make, pre-write and pre-test is a decision that does not have to be made badly under pressure.

Also because knowledge decays. The person who built the DR setup leaves. The endpoint changes. A new service is added that hardcodes the database host. Without a drill, you find all of this during the incident.

How it works

The runbook template. One file per scenario, in the application repository, in Git, reviewed like code.

Text
RUNBOOK: Primary database loss
==============================

APPLIES WHEN
  The RDS primary is unreachable and Multi-AZ failover has not restored
  service within 5 minutes.

TARGETS
  RTO 60 minutes. RPO 5 minutes.

ROLES
  Incident Commander - decides, does not type
  Operator           - runs commands
  Scribe             - records the timeline in the incident channel
  Comms              - status page and customer email

PRE-FLIGHT (2 minutes)
  [ ] Confirm scope: kubectl get pods -n shop, Redis PING, S3 HEAD
  [ ] Check the AWS Health dashboard for a regional event
  [ ] Record current replica lag from CloudWatch, post it in the channel

DECISION
  If replica lag < 60s and region B healthy -> promote the cross-region replica
  If the replica is unavailable             -> PITR restore from newest recovery point
  If a region-wide event affects both       -> escalate, use snapshots in the third region

STEPS
   1. FENCE the old primary (revoke SG ingress).       command: ...
   2. Promote the replica.                             command: ...
   3. Enable Multi-AZ and backups on the new primary.  command: ...
   4. Update the database secret.                      command: ...
   5. Restart deployments.                             command: ...
   6. Verify: the synthetic checkout must pass.        command: ...
   7. Shift DNS.                                       command: ...
   8. Warm caches.                                     command: ...
   9. Replay the outbox, reset consumer offsets.       command: ...
  10. Reconcile payments for the gap window.           command: ...

VERIFICATION
  [ ] Synthetic checkout passes
  [ ] Error rate below 1 percent for 5 minutes
  [ ] SELECT count(*) FROM outbox_events WHERE published_at IS NULL is draining
  [ ] Payment reconciliation reports zero unresolved discrepancies

ROLLBACK
  There is no rollback after promotion. If promotion fails, go to
  runbook-pitr-restore.md.

AFTER
  [ ] New read replica created
  [ ] Backups verified running on the new primary
  [ ] Postmortem scheduled within 48 hours
  [ ] Timeline exported from the incident channel

Two rules that make runbooks actually work: every step is a copy-pasteable command, and every step has a verification. A step that says "ensure the application is healthy" is not a step.

The quarterly drill. Four levels, escalating. Do not start at level 4.

Level What you do Frequency Disruption
1. Tabletop Walk the runbook aloud in a meeting; find the stale command Monthly, 30 min None
2. Component Restore a backup to a scratch instance and validate Nightly, automated None
3. Non-production failover Full failover in staging, timed, with the real runbook Quarterly Staging down for an hour
4. Production game day Real failover in production, announced, in a low-traffic window Annually Real, planned

Level 4 frightens people, and it should be earned by passing level 3 twice. But a team that has never failed over production does not know whether it can.

What to measure during a drill. Record these every time, and graph them across drills:

  • Time to detect (from the injected failure to the first alert).
  • Time to declare (first alert to incident channel open).
  • Time to decide (channel open to recovery target chosen).
  • Time to first successful write on the new primary.
  • Time to synthetic transaction passing (this is your real RTO).
  • Time to full performance (caches warm, lag drained).
  • Data loss measured, in seconds and in business records.
  • Number of runbook steps that were wrong, missing or ambiguous. This is the most valuable number. A drill that finds seven broken steps was a great drill.
  • Number of people needed.

Publish the trend. When time-to-synthetic-passing goes from 74 minutes to 38 minutes to 22 minutes across three drills, that is the DR programme visibly working.

Backup verification automation. Covered in 50.2, but it belongs in the drill schedule too: the nightly restore is your level-2 drill, running 365 times a year while the humans drill four times.

Common mistakes

  • A runbook in a wiki nobody can find at 02:00. Put it in the repository and link it from the alert.
  • Runbook steps written as prose intentions rather than commands.
  • Drills run by the person who wrote the runbook. Have someone else execute it; that is the test.
  • Drilling only the happy path. Inject a failure mid-drill ("the replica will not promote") and see what happens.
  • Treating a drill that found problems as a failure. That is a successful drill.
  • Never drilling the communication path, so the status page password is unknown at 02:20.

Interview questions

  1. What is in a DR runbook?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: applicability, targets, roles, decision table, copy-pasteable steps with verification, rollback, post-incident actions.
  2. How often should you drill, and at what levels?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: automated nightly restores, monthly tabletop, quarterly non-production failover, annual production game day.
  3. What do you measure in a drill?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: the time breakdown, data loss, and the count of broken runbook steps; graph them across drills.
  4. A drill found nine problems. Was it a good drill?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: yes, emphatically; those nine would have been found during a real incident otherwise.

Practical exercise

Write the primary-database-loss runbook for your system using the template above. Then hand it to an engineer who did not write it and have them execute it in staging while you time each step and say nothing.

Acceptance criteria: they complete it without asking you a question; you record the six timing measurements; and you file at least three issues for steps that were wrong or ambiguous.

50.11 Edge cases and failure modes

The catalogue. Each of these has taken a real production system down or made a recovery far worse.

  • Backups never tested, and corrupt. The pg_dump piped into gzip without set -o pipefail, producing a valid truncated archive every night for 90 days. Fix: nightly automated restore with business-invariant checks and a size-delta alert.
  • A backup taken from a lagging replica. The dump ran against a replica 40 minutes behind, so the recorded recovery point is 40 minutes older than believed, and your RPO is silently wrong by that amount. Fix: check pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() before dumping and fail the job if lag exceeds a threshold; record the actual replay timestamp as the backup's recovery point.
  • WAL archive gaps that silently break PITR. archive_command fails (S3 permission changed, disk full, network policy) and PostgreSQL retries forever while the PITR window quietly ends at the gap. Nothing alerts, because the database is healthy. Fix: alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count > 0 and on now() - last_archived_time; on RDS, alert on the age of LatestRestorableTime.
  • A nine-hour restore because of instance and IOPS limits. Restored to a smaller class to save money; gp2 at 3 IOPS/GB throttled; EBS lazy loading hydrated blocks at a trickle under production read load. Fix: restore to production-equivalent class and storage, measure it nightly, and pre-warm hot tables.
  • Application secrets still pointing at the old host. The database is healthy; the app is not, because a Helm value, a Lambda environment variable and an old service's hardcoded fallback still resolve the dead endpoint. Fix: one secret, referenced everywhere; grep the whole organisation for the hostname during the drill.
  • Caches inconsistent with the restored database. Redis holds product prices and cart contents from after the recovery point. Customers see prices and carts that the database has never heard of; some of them check out. Fix: invalidate by prefix as part of the runbook, before traffic returns, and treat any cache holding authoritative-looking data as a liability.
  • Sequences reissuing ids and causing duplicate keys. After restoring a table, orders_id_seq is behind max(id), and the next insert throws duplicate key value violates unique constraint. Fix: SELECT setval('orders_id_seq', (SELECT COALESCE(max(id), 1) FROM orders)); for every sequence, as a scripted step. Better: use UUIDv7 or ULID primary keys, which have no sequence to fix and no collision across regions.
  • Replayed events triggering duplicate side effects. The worst one. Republishing order.paid events after a restore causes the payments consumer to capture the same authorisation twice, charging customers a second time. Fix: idempotency keys sent to the payment provider (they deduplicate server-side), a processed_messages table with a unique key on event id, and pausing money-moving consumers before any replay.
  • Retention shorter than the time to detect the problem. A subtle data corruption introduced by a release is discovered 12 days later; backup retention is 7 days. There is no version of the data that is correct. Fix: retention must exceed your realistic detection time for logical problems, which is weeks, not days. 35 days is a reasonable floor; monthly archival snapshots kept for a year are cheap.
  • Cross-region replication lag at failover. Lag is 3 seconds on a normal Tuesday and 4 minutes during the traffic spike that preceded the failure, because that is when replication falls behind. Your RPO is measured at the worst moment, not the average. Fix: alert on replica lag with a threshold tied to your RPO, and record lag at promotion.
  • DNS TTL delaying recovery. A 300 second TTL on the application record means five minutes of traffic still arriving at a dead region after the switch, plus clients and resolvers that ignore TTLs entirely. Fix: 60 second TTLs on failover-relevant records maintained permanently (you cannot lower a TTL during an incident and have it take effect), health-check-based routing, and connection-level retry in clients.
  • One compromised credential deleting both the data and the backups. The CI role has rds:* and s3:* because it was easier. A leaked token deletes the instance, the snapshots and the backup bucket in four API calls. Fix: separate backup account, vault lock in compliance mode, no cross-account trust from CI, alerts on destructive API calls, and least privilege that specifically excludes Delete* on backup resources.

Two more that deserve naming because they are structural rather than technical:

  • The DR plan assumes a person who has left. Every runbook step that begins "ask Priya" is a single point of failure. Fix: drills executed by someone who did not write the runbook.
  • The DR region has never had a deploy. Manifest drift, missing CRDs, an outdated cluster version, expired certificates, un-raised quotas. Fix: deploy to region B on every release, even at zero replicas.

Senior Checklist — Part 50

  • I understand the concept of backup, restore, RPO, RTO and the four DR strategies
  • I can explain simply why a read replica is not a backup
  • I can implement logical and physical backups, and configure PITR
  • I understand the failure modes of each backup and restore mechanism
  • I understand the scaling limitations: restore time grows with data size and instance class
  • I understand the security implications: backups need a separate custody boundary
  • I understand the operational implications: drills, runbooks, and measured RTO
  • I can choose between backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active
  • I can explain the cost tradeoffs of each rung of the DR ladder
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions on recovery
  • I can estimate restore time for a 2 TB database and defend the estimate stage by stage
  • I can execute a point-in-time recovery and extract only the affected rows
  • I can reconcile a restored database with a payment provider for a gap window
  • I know to fence the old primary before promoting a replica
  • I know what pg_stat_archiver tells me and why a WAL gap silently breaks PITR
  • I have a runbook in the repository and I know the date of the last drill

Part 50 — Key Takeaways

  • The restore is the product; the backup is only the input. An untested backup is a hypothesis.
  • Replication protects against machines failing. Backups protect against decisions being wrong. You need both.
  • RPO is acceptable data loss in time; RTO is acceptable downtime. Both are business decisions, and both must be demonstrated, not asserted.
  • Classify data by RPO and RTO. Most of your data is rebuildable, and rebuildable data is free to protect.
  • Your real RPO is bounded by continuous log archiving, not by snapshot frequency, and a broken archive makes it silently worse.
  • For scoped logical damage, repair in place from a side instance. Never fail over to a recovery point just to fix a few tables.
  • Round the recovery target backwards and reconcile forwards. You can replay; you cannot un-restore.
  • Fence the old primary before promoting a replica, or you will have two databases and a much worse day.
  • Failback is a fresh migration, not the reverse of failover. Often the right answer is not to fail back today.
  • The database being back is not the system being back: payments, outbox, queues, caches, search and DLQs all need ordered recovery, and money comes first.
  • Backups need a second custody boundary. Ask which single credential can delete both the data and the backups.
  • Automate the nightly restore verification and graph restore_duration_seconds. It turns RTO from a promise into a measurement.
  • A drill that finds nine broken runbook steps is a successful drill.

Part 51 — Cost-Aware Engineering

  • 1 h 38 min read
  • 9 sections

What you will learn

  1. 51.1Why engineers must understand cost
  2. 51.2Compute cost
  3. 51.3Database cost
  4. 51.4Storage, network egress and observability cost
  5. 51.5Caching, CDN and autoscaling as cost tools
  6. 51.6Architecture cost trade-offs
  7. 51.7The best architecture is not the most sophisticated architecture

Every number in this part is an approximate AWS list price, in us-east-1, at the time of writing. Prices differ by region (often 10 to 30 percent), drop over time, and fall further with Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Enterprise Discount Programs. Never quote these figures to a finance team as fact. Use them the way an engineer uses "a Redis lookup is about 0.5 ms": as an order of magnitude that lets you reason before you measure.

The system we are pricing is the same e-commerce platform as Part 50: NestJS on EKS, RDS PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Redis, Kafka, S3 and CloudFront, roughly 400 to 500 requests per second at peak, 25,000 orders a day.

51.1 Why engineers must understand cost

Concept

Cost is a non-functional requirement, exactly like latency, availability and security. It is a property of the design, decided by engineers, at the moment they choose an instance class, a replication topology, a log level or a service boundary. Finance can renegotiate a contract; only engineering can change the fact that your service makes 40 cross-AZ calls per request.

The uncomfortable truth is that cloud cost is mostly an engineering artefact. The bill is a printout of your architecture.

Why does it exist?

Because the feedback loop is broken by default. When you add an index, you feel the latency change in a benchmark. When you add a read replica, you feel nothing at all — the money leaves 30 days later, aggregated into a bill that no engineer reads, attributed to nothing in particular.

Without deliberate practice, the loop stays broken and three things happen. First, waste compounds silently: every unused environment, oversized instance and debug logger stays forever because nobody owns it. Second, the company reacts late and badly, with a panicked "cut 30 percent" mandate that lands on resilience because resilience is the easiest thing to delete. Third, engineers lose a genuine lever on the business, because a team that can say "we can serve this feature for $0.002 per order" is trusted with decisions that a team quoting only latency is not.

Mental model

Imagine your architecture is a house and the cloud bill is the electricity meter. Nobody plans to waste electricity. But if the meter is in a locked cupboard and the bill goes to a different department, the heating stays on in the empty guest room for three years.

Cost awareness is not frugality. It is putting the meter where the people who flip the switches can see it, and labelling each circuit.

How it works

Unit economics is the number that matters. The total bill is almost useless as an engineering signal, because it moves with traffic. A bill that grew from $18,000 to $24,000 could mean you got 30 percent more efficient (traffic doubled) or 30 percent more wasteful (traffic flat). You cannot tell.

The number to track is cost per unit of business value:

  • Cost per order
  • Cost per API request (or per 1,000 requests)
  • Cost per monthly active user
  • Cost per gigabyte of customer data stored

For our platform: $18,000 a month at 750,000 orders a month is $0.024 per order. That single number changes the conversation completely.

  • It is comparable over time. If traffic doubles and the bill grows 60 percent, cost per order fell and you are winning.
  • It is comparable to revenue. At a $60 average basket with a 4 percent net margin ($2.40 per order), infrastructure is 1 percent of order value. That tells you immediately whether to spend a quarter optimising, or to ship features instead.
  • It makes trade-offs concrete. "This new recommendation service adds $0.004 per order" is a decision a product manager can make. "The recommendation service costs $3,000 a month" is a decision nobody can make, because there is nothing to compare it against.
  • It catches slow regressions that a total bill hides. Cost per order drifting from $0.024 to $0.031 over two quarters is a real signal; the total bill over the same period just looks like growth.

Compute it monthly and put it on the same dashboard as p99 latency. It belongs there.

Tagging and cost allocation. You cannot compute cost per order if you cannot attribute cost. Tagging is the plumbing that makes every other practice in this part possible, and it is boring, which is why it is usually missing.

A workable minimum tag set, enforced rather than requested:

Tag Example Used for
service orders-api Per-service showback
team checkout Ownership, who to ask
env prod, staging, dev Finding non-production waste
cost-center CC-4471 Finance allocation
owner priya@ Who to email about the idle instance
expires 2026-10-01 Temporary resources that must die

Three rules make tags real:

  1. Enforce at creation. An AWS Organizations tag policy plus a Service Control Policy that denies resource creation without required tags. Or, more practically, enforce in Terraform with default_tags at the provider level so every resource inherits them automatically:
HCL
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  default_tags {
    tags = {
      service     = var.service_name
      team        = var.team
      env         = var.environment
      cost-center = var.cost_center
      managed-by  = "terraform"
    }
  }
}
  1. Accept that some cost cannot be tagged. Kubernetes hides this: one EC2 node runs pods from six teams, and the node has one tag. Shared costs (the EKS control plane, NAT gateways, the load balancer, the data transfer between nodes) need an allocation rule. Kubecost, OpenCost or AWS Split Cost Allocation Data can attribute node cost to pods by their CPU and memory requests. Whatever you choose, write the rule down and stop arguing about it.
  2. Publish the untagged percentage. If 40 percent of your bill is untagged, every showback number is fiction. Drive that below 10 percent before you draw conclusions.

The FinOps loop. FinOps is the industry name for the practice, and its three phases are a genuinely useful structure, not just vocabulary.

Inform is visibility. Tags, allocation, a dashboard each team can see, and unit economics. Almost every team that has a cost problem is stuck before this phase, and every optimisation they attempt is guesswork.

Optimise is the engineering. Right-sizing, autoscaling, storage classes, architecture changes. This is 51.2 through 51.7.

Operate is making it stick. Budgets, anomaly detection, cost as a line item in design reviews, and a monthly review with an owner. Without this phase, you optimise once and drift back within two quarters.

The order matters. Optimising before informing is how teams delete a read replica that was actually load-bearing.

Practical example

A team is asked to cut cloud spend by 20 percent. They start with the biggest line item, EC2, and spend three weeks right-sizing nodes for a $2,100 monthly saving.

A second team starts by tagging and building the cost-per-order dashboard. It takes them a week, and it reveals that a single internal analytics service, which serves 40 internal page views a day, costs $4,400 a month because it runs a 6-node OpenSearch cluster refreshed by a Kafka consumer every 30 seconds. Nobody had looked, because it was never anyone's line item. Deleting it and replacing it with a nightly materialised view in PostgreSQL saves $4,300 in two days of work.

The lesson is not "analytics services are wasteful". It is that visibility finds bigger wins than effort does, and it finds them faster.

NestJS example

Unit economics is only real if it is instrumented. Emit the business denominator as a metric so the cost-per-order calculation is a division of two things you already have on a dashboard.

TypeScript
// order-metrics.interceptor.ts
import { Injectable, NestInterceptor, ExecutionContext, CallHandler } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';
import { InjectMetric } from '@willsoto/nestjs-prometheus';
import { Counter } from 'prom-client';

@Injectable()
export class OrderMetricsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(
    @InjectMetric('orders_placed_total') private readonly orders: Counter<string>,
    @InjectMetric('business_requests_total') private readonly requests: Counter<string>,
  ) {}

  intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    // Route label, not the raw URL: raw URLs explode metric cardinality (39.4).
    const route: string = req.route?.path ?? 'unknown';
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => {
        this.requests.inc({ route, method: req.method });
        if (route === '/orders' && req.method === 'POST') {
          // The denominator of cost per order. Label by channel, never by user id.
          this.orders.inc({ channel: req.headers['x-channel'] ?? 'web' });
        }
      }),
    );
  }
}

Then the dashboard panel is one expression: monthly cost from Cost Explorer divided by increase(orders_placed_total[30d]). Put it next to p99 latency and error rate, and it becomes a number the team actually watches.

Production scenario

A useful exercise for any senior engineer joining a team: spend one afternoon producing a single table with five rows.

Metric Value
Monthly cloud spend $18,400
Orders per month 750,000
Cost per order $0.0245
Revenue per order (average basket) $60
Infrastructure as percentage of GMV 0.04 percent

That table reframes every subsequent conversation. At 0.04 percent of gross merchandise value, a 30 percent cost reduction saves $5,500 a month and is worth roughly two engineer-weeks, not two engineer-quarters. But it also shows that a design which triples cost per order is a real problem, because it moves a number leadership can now see.

For a low-margin business the same table produces the opposite conclusion, and that is exactly the point: the table, not the instinct, makes the decision.

Failure scenario

At a Series B startup, cloud spend grew from $22,000 to $61,000 a month over three quarters while traffic grew 40 percent. Nobody noticed until the CFO did, and the response was an emergency mandate: cut 40 percent in one month.

With no tagging and no unit economics, the team cut what was visible: they removed a read replica, dropped RDS backup retention from 35 days to 3, deleted the staging environment, and turned off distributed tracing. Cost fell to $38,000.

Eleven weeks later a data corruption bug introduced by a release was discovered 9 days after the fact. Backup retention was 3 days. There was no correct version of the data, and no tracing to reconstruct what had happened. The recovery cost far more than the entire year of savings, and the company had to rebuild trust with two enterprise customers.

The failure was not the cut. It was cutting without visibility, so the cuts landed on resilience rather than on the $9,000 a month of idle load-test environments that nobody could see.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Untagged shared infrastructure (NAT, EKS control plane, load balancers, data transfer) can be 20 to 40 percent of the bill and is attributed to nobody.
  • Cost per order computed from a bill that includes one-off migration costs, so the trend is noise.
  • Optimising the largest line item rather than the largest waste; the largest line item is usually load-bearing.
  • Savings Plans and Reserved Instances bought against a workload that then changes shape, leaving you paying for capacity you no longer use (51.9).
  • Cost dashboards that only leadership can see, so the people who make the decisions never do.
  • Measuring only the cloud bill and ignoring SaaS: Datadog, Snowflake, PagerDuty and CI minutes are often 30 percent of the total technology spend and grow faster.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat cost as a design constraint they state up front, alongside latency and availability. In a design review they will say, out loud: "this adds roughly $600 a month and about $0.0008 per order; here is what we get for it." That sentence makes them credible with both engineering and finance.

They are deeply anti-panic. They know that the worst cost decisions are made under a deadline mandate, and that the way to avoid one is to keep the number visible so it never becomes a crisis.

They separate waste from cost. A read replica that serves the reporting workload is cost. A read replica that serves nothing is waste. Cutting cost hurts; cutting waste does not, and there is almost always more waste than anyone expects.

And they refuse to trade away resilience for cost without naming the trade explicitly. "We can save $400 a month by dropping to single-AZ, which changes our RTO from 2 minutes to 90 minutes" is a legitimate proposal. Quietly dropping to single-AZ is not.

Common mistakes

  • Tracking the total bill instead of unit economics.
  • Treating cost as finance's problem, then being surprised by a mandate.
  • Starting to optimise before tagging.
  • Ignoring engineer time in the equation: two weeks of engineering to save $200 a month has a payback period of years.
  • Assuming the cloud bill is the whole cost. Observability SaaS and CI often are not.

Interview questions

  1. Why is cost per order more useful than the total bill?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: it normalises for traffic, is comparable over time and to revenue, makes trade-offs decidable, and catches regressions the total hides.
  2. How do you allocate the cost of a shared Kubernetes cluster to teams?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: tag the nodes, then split node cost across pods by CPU and memory requests using Kubecost/OpenCost or AWS split cost allocation; publish the untagged percentage; write the rule down.
  3. Your company mandates a 30 percent cut. How do you approach it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: get visibility first, separate waste from cost, list candidates with their resilience impact, and refuse to cut resilience silently. Follow-up: what is the first thing you look for? Idle non-production environments and orphaned resources.
  4. What is the FinOps loop?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: inform, optimise, operate; and why optimising before informing is dangerous.
  5. When is it not worth optimising cost?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when infrastructure is a tiny fraction of revenue and engineer time is the scarcer resource; quantify with the unit economics table.

Practical exercise

Produce the five-row unit-economics table for a system you work on: monthly spend, monthly business units, cost per unit, revenue per unit, infrastructure as a percentage of revenue. Then compute the percentage of the bill that is untagged.

Acceptance criteria: you can name your cost per order (or per user) to two significant figures; you know your untagged percentage; and you can name the single largest line item that no team currently owns.

51.2 Compute cost

Concept

Compute is CPU and memory you rent by the second: EC2 instances, Fargate tasks, Kubernetes nodes, Lambda invocations. It is usually 30 to 50 percent of a cloud bill, and it is the line item with the most structural waste, because the gap between what you provision and what you use is invisible unless you go looking.

Why does it exist?

You pay for capacity, not for work done. A node that is 12 percent utilised costs exactly the same as one that is 85 percent utilised. Every layer of the stack introduces another opportunity to reserve capacity you do not use: an instance sized for peak, a node pool sized for the instance, a pod request sized for a guess, and a JVM-era habit of over-allocating memory to a Node.js process that will never use it.

Mental model

Imagine renting a van. You pay for the van, not for the boxes. If you rent a 20-cubic-metre van to move 3 cubic metres of boxes, you paid for 17 cubic metres of air. Now imagine you rent that van 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and you only move boxes for 6 hours on weekdays.

Cloud compute waste is exactly that: air, rented continuously.

How it works

Right-sizing. The method is unglamorous and it works: look at actual utilisation over a representative period (at least two weeks including a peak), then size for peak plus headroom, not for the number that felt safe when you created it.

For a Node.js service the profile is distinctive and worth knowing: Node is single-threaded for JavaScript execution, so a pod rarely benefits from more than 1 to 2 CPUs unless you are running the cluster module or heavy libuv thread-pool work (crypto, zlib, fs). Meanwhile the default V8 old-space heap on a 64-bit system is around 1.5 to 2 GB unless you set --max-old-space-size. Giving a Node pod 8 GB of memory and 4 CPUs usually buys nothing at all.

Text
Typical NestJS API pod, measured over 14 days:
  CPU request 1000m, actual p95 220m, actual p99 410m   -> request 500m, limit 1000m
  Memory request 2Gi, actual p95 380Mi, RSS ceiling 620Mi -> request 512Mi, limit 1Gi
Result: 2x more pods fit per node. Node count drops from 8 to 4.

Requests versus limits, and where the waste hides. This is the single most misunderstood cost lever in Kubernetes, so be precise.

  • Request is what the scheduler reserves. It is subtracted from the node's allocatable capacity whether or not the pod uses it. Requests are what you pay for.
  • Limit is the ceiling the kernel enforces. Exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling (CFS quota); exceeding a memory limit causes OOMKilled.

The waste: a pod requesting 2 CPUs and using 0.2 occupies 2 CPUs of schedulable space forever. Ten such pods consume a whole 16-vCPU node while using 2 vCPUs of it. You pay for the node.

The practical policy that most teams land on for Node.js services:

Resource Setting Why
CPU request p95 of measured usage, e.g. 300m Reserves what you actually need
CPU limit 2 to 4x the request, or unset CPU throttling causes latency spikes; unset limits let a pod burst into idle node capacity. Set limits only where noisy-neighbour risk is real
Memory request p99 RSS plus 25 percent, e.g. 640Mi Memory is incompressible
Memory limit equal to the request Prevents one leaking pod from evicting others; makes OOM behaviour predictable

CPU limits deserve a note, because it is a genuine trade-off rather than a rule. Aggressive CPU limits on a latency-sensitive Node.js service cause throttling that shows up as unexplained p99 spikes. Many mature teams set CPU requests carefully and leave CPU limits off, accepting some noisy-neighbour risk in exchange for burst capacity that costs nothing. Memory limits, by contrast, should always be set.

Also set --max-old-space-size to roughly 75 percent of the memory limit, or V8 will happily grow its heap until the kernel kills the container:

Dockerfile
# Dockerfile — keep V8's heap inside the container's memory limit.
ENV NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=768"

Autoscaling and scale-to-zero. Traffic on an e-commerce platform is not flat. Ours runs 500 RPS at 20:00 and 40 RPS at 04:00 — a 12x range. Provisioning for peak 24 hours a day means paying for peak capacity for the 18 hours a day you do not need it.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU is the default and is adequate for API pods:

YAML
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: orders-api
  minReplicas: 3        # never below 3: one per AZ, survives a node loss
  maxReplicas: 24
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 65   # headroom for a scale-up that takes ~90s
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30    # react quickly to a traffic spike
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600   # descend slowly; flapping costs more than it saves

The two settings people get wrong: a scaleDown window that is too short (pods flap, and every scale-up has a cold start), and a minReplicas set to 1 to save money, which removes redundancy for a saving of one pod.

For workers, queue depth is a far better signal than CPU, and workers can genuinely scale to zero. KEDA does this (see 51.5):

YAML
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: invoice-worker
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: invoice-worker
  minReplicaCount: 0        # zero pods when the queue is empty
  maxReplicaCount: 30
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  triggers:
    - type: redis
      metadata:
        address: redis.shop.svc.cluster.local:6379
        listName: bull:invoices:wait
        listLength: "50"    # one pod per 50 queued jobs

An invoice worker that runs for 40 minutes a day costs 3 percent of a worker that runs 24 hours a day. That is a real saving and it requires no cleverness.

Spot instances. Spot is spare AWS capacity at a 60 to 90 percent discount, typically around 70 percent, with a 2 minute interruption notice. The rule is simple: spot for interruptible work, on-demand for the rest.

Workload Spot? Why
Batch jobs, report generation, image processing Yes Retryable and idempotent
Kafka consumers with committed offsets Yes, carefully Rebalancing on interruption is normal behaviour
CI runners Yes A killed build is re-run
Stateless API pods Partially: a mixed node group, e.g. 60 percent spot Needs PodDisruptionBudget, graceful shutdown and multiple instance types
Stateful sets, databases, Kafka brokers No Interruption means data movement or loss
Anything holding a lease or a lock No Interruption mid-lease causes correctness problems, not just latency

A 60/40 spot/on-demand split on an $8,000 monthly EC2 line saves roughly $3,300. The prerequisites are non-negotiable: terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough to drain, a preStop hook, correct SIGTERM handling in NestJS (app.enableShutdownHooks()), PodDisruptionBudgets, and node groups spread over several instance types so one capacity pool draining does not take you out.

ARM and Graviton. AWS Graviton processors (m7g, c7g, r7g, db.r6g) are roughly 20 percent cheaper than the equivalent x86 instance and frequently deliver better performance per vCPU for interpreted, memory-bound workloads. Node.js is a very good fit: it has first-class linux/arm64 builds, and the ecosystem's native modules (sharp, bcrypt, argon2, node-gyp builds) have had arm64 binaries for years.

The migration is usually smaller than teams expect:

Dockerfile
# Multi-arch build; buildx produces a manifest list so the same tag runs on both.
# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t repo/orders-api:1.4.2 --push .
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=768"
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

Expect a 20 percent instance-price saving plus, commonly, 10 to 20 percent better throughput per vCPU on Node.js HTTP workloads — a combined effect that often lands near 30 percent on the compute line. The work is: build multi-arch images, verify every native dependency, and run a canary. For a $8,000 EC2 line that is a ~$2,400 monthly saving for a few days of work, which is one of the best returns available anywhere in this part.

Fargate versus EC2. Fargate charges per vCPU-second and GB-second of the task, with no node to manage. Approximate list prices: $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour.

A 1 vCPU / 2 GB task running continuously: (0.04048 + 2 x 0.004445) x 730 hours = about $36 per month.

An m7g.large (2 vCPU, 8 GB) at about $0.0816 per hour is about $60 per month for 2 vCPU, so roughly $30 per vCPU — slightly cheaper than Fargate per vCPU, before you account for the fact that you never achieve 100 percent bin-packing, you pay for the node's OS and DaemonSet overhead, and you pay for the EKS control plane ($73 per month per cluster).

The honest comparison:

Fargate EC2 / managed node groups
Price per vCPU Slightly higher list price Lower, but only at high utilisation
Effective price You pay exactly what you request You pay for the node, including unused capacity and DaemonSets
Bin-packing waste None 20 to 40 percent typical
Spot Fargate Spot available for ECS Full spot flexibility
Graviton Yes Yes
Operational cost No node patching, no AMI upgrades, no cluster autoscaler tuning Real, ongoing engineer time
Best for Spiky, bursty, small or few workloads; teams without a platform engineer Large, steady fleets where utilisation can be driven above ~70 percent

The rule of thumb: below roughly 20 to 30 continuously-running tasks, Fargate is usually cheaper once you price engineer time. Above that, well-packed EC2 with spot and Graviton wins clearly. Teams that run a small EKS cluster at 25 percent utilisation are paying more than Fargate and paying an engineer to maintain it.

Idle non-production environments. This is consistently the largest pot of pure waste in mid-sized companies, and it is embarrassing how easy it is to fix.

A staging environment that mirrors production costs roughly what production costs. It is used from about 09:00 to 19:00 on weekdays: 50 of 168 hours a week, which is 30 percent. The other 70 percent is pure waste.

Text
Weekly hours          = 168
Used (Mon-Fri, 9-19)  = 50
Waste                 = 118 hours = 70 percent

Staging at $3,000/month, shut down nights and weekends
  -> $900/month. Saving: $2,100/month, for one scheduled job.

Implement it as a scheduled scale-down, not a teardown, so it comes back in minutes:

YAML
# Kubernetes CronJob that scales the staging namespace to zero at 20:00 UTC
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: staging-shutdown
  namespace: staging
spec:
  schedule: "0 20 * * 1-5"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: scaler
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: kubectl
              image: bitnami/kubectl:1.31
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - kubectl scale deployment --all --replicas=0 -n staging

Pair it with aws rds stop-db-instance for the staging database (RDS allows a stopped instance for up to 7 days before it auto-starts, so a weekday schedule works) and a cluster autoscaler that removes the now-empty nodes. Add a self-service "wake staging" button so nobody is blocked at 21:00.

The same applies to: developer sandboxes, load-test environments, preview environments per pull request (add a TTL and delete them on merge), and demo environments created for a sales call two years ago.

The serverless crossover point. Lambda is not "cheaper than containers". It is cheaper for low or spiky average utilisation and dramatically more expensive for sustained load. Here is the arithmetic, which is the thing to remember.

Lambda pricing (approximate): $0.20 per 1 million requests, plus $0.0000166667 per GB-second.

For a 512 MB function averaging 100 ms:

Text
Compute per request = 0.100 s x 0.5 GB x $0.0000166667 = $0.00000083
Request charge      = $0.00000020
Total per request   = $0.00000103   ->  about $1.03 per million requests

A single Fargate task at $36 per month can comfortably serve 150 to 300 RPS of that same light work. At 200 RPS it handles about 518 million requests a month, which is $0.07 per million. Lambda is roughly 15x more expensive per request at that utilisation.

The crossover, for a service that must be highly available (so at least two tasks, about $72 per month, plus a shared ALB at roughly $20 per month):

Text
Container baseline    = $92/month
Lambda at $1.03/M     = $92 / $1.03 = ~89 million requests/month
                      = ~34 requests per second, sustained average

So: below roughly 30 to 50 RPS of sustained average traffic, Lambda is usually cheaper. Above it, containers win, and the gap widens fast. At our platform's 400 RPS average, Lambda for the main API would cost around $1,050 a month against roughly $250 for the equivalent Fargate capacity.

But cost is not the only axis, and the honest senior answer includes the rest:

Factor Favours Lambda Favours containers
Traffic shape Spiky, bursty, mostly idle Steady, high
Cold starts Tolerable (async, batch) Latency-critical p99
Execution time Short (under a few seconds) Long-running, streaming, WebSockets
Database connections Poor fit; needs RDS Proxy Natural connection pooling
Operational overhead Near zero Real
Cost at 5 RPS Pennies ~$92 minimum
Cost at 500 RPS ~$1,300 ~$250

Lambda earns its place on our platform for exactly the right things: the nightly restore verification job (50.2), the snapshot copier, S3 event handlers for image processing, and webhook receivers with bursty traffic. Not for the checkout API.

Production scenario

The platform's compute line before and after a deliberate optimisation quarter:

Item Before After Change
Production EKS nodes (x86, over-requested) $4,800 $2,650 Right-sized requests, Graviton, 40 percent spot
Worker nodes (24/7) $1,200 $310 KEDA scale-to-zero
Staging (24/7) $2,900 $870 Nights and weekends off
Two forgotten load-test environments $1,400 $0 Deleted; expires tag now mandatory
EKS control plane $73 $73 Unchanged
Lambda (image processing, webhooks) $180 $180 Correct workload for it
Total $10,553 $4,083 -61 percent

Roughly three engineer-weeks of work. Nothing in that table reduced resilience: minReplicas stayed at 3, Multi-AZ stayed on, and backup retention was untouched.

Failure scenario

A team enabled cluster autoscaling and aggressive HPA to save money before a sales event. They set minReplicas: 2 and scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30.

Traffic arrived in a burst. The HPA scaled up, the cluster autoscaler requested nodes, and node provisioning took 4 minutes: image pull, kubelet registration, readiness. During those 4 minutes the two existing pods absorbed 100 percent of the burst, saturated their event loops, failed readiness probes, and were removed from the load balancer. The remaining traffic hit the newly starting pods, which were not warm.

Meanwhile the 30 second scale-down window meant that every brief dip in load removed pods that were needed 40 seconds later. The service flapped for 25 minutes.

Three fixes, in order of importance: a longer scaleDown stabilisation window (600 seconds), a higher minReplicas sized for the burst that arrives before autoscaling can react, and over-provisioning with low-priority placeholder pods so the cluster always has warm capacity ready to be preempted. The last one costs about $120 a month and removes the node-provisioning latency from the critical path entirely.

Aggressive autoscaling is a cost optimisation that can buy you an outage. Scale up fast, scale down slowly, and never let minReplicas drop below what a node failure plus a burst requires.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CPU limits causing throttling that presents as mysterious p99 latency, with no error and no OOM.
  • Memory limit set well above the request, so the scheduler packs the node and then evicts pods under memory pressure.
  • --max-old-space-size unset, so V8 grows past the container limit and the pod is OOMKilled at 03:00 under load.
  • Spot interruptions on pods holding a distributed lock or a Kafka partition lease, causing correctness problems rather than latency.
  • Graviton migration broken by one native dependency with no arm64 build; find it in CI, not in production.
  • Scale-to-zero on a worker whose cold start is 40 seconds, so the first job after a quiet period times out.
  • Fargate tasks sized in the allowed CPU/memory combinations only; asking for 0.75 vCPU rounds up and you pay for 1.
  • Cluster autoscaler unable to remove a node because one pod without a PodDisruptionBudget, or a pod with local storage, is pinned to it. One such pod keeps an entire node alive.
  • Reserved Instances or Savings Plans bought for x86 immediately before a Graviton migration.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They measure before they resize. The utilisation graph over two weeks is the input; anything else is a guess dressed as a decision.

They know that requests, not limits, are what you pay for, and that this one sentence explains most Kubernetes cost waste they will ever see.

They are willing to leave headroom on purpose and say why: "we run at 55 percent utilisation because a node loss plus a traffic burst must not page anyone". Cost optimisation that removes headroom is borrowing from the on-call rota.

They pick the cheapest safe compute per workload rather than standardising for tidiness: spot for batch, Graviton everywhere it builds, Lambda for spiky and event-driven, containers for sustained.

And they always price engineer time. A $200 a month saving that takes two weeks and adds a permanent maintenance burden is a bad trade, and saying so out loud is part of the job.

Common mistakes

  • Copying resource requests from another service's manifest.
  • Setting requests equal to limits everywhere "for QoS Guaranteed" without checking utilisation, doubling the reserved footprint.
  • minReplicas: 1 to save money, deleting redundancy for the price of one pod.
  • Running staging 24/7.
  • Choosing Lambda for a sustained high-throughput API because it is "serverless and cheap".
  • Choosing Kubernetes for four services and paying the control plane, the platform engineer and the bin-packing waste.
  • Buying a 3-year Reserved Instance for a workload the team plans to rearchitect next quarter.

Interview questions

  1. In Kubernetes, do you pay for requests or limits?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: requests, because the scheduler reserves them from node capacity regardless of usage; limits only cap runtime. Follow-up: what happens if you set CPU requests too high? Nodes look full, the autoscaler adds nodes, and you pay for idle capacity.
  2. When is Lambda cheaper than a container, and where is the crossover?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: below roughly 30 to 50 RPS sustained average for a small function, using $1 per million requests against a ~$90 per month HA container baseline; above that containers win by roughly an order of magnitude. Follow-up: what non-cost factors matter? Cold starts, execution time, database connections.
  3. How would you cut compute cost by 40 percent without reducing resilience?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: right-size requests from measured utilisation, Graviton, spot for interruptible workloads, scale-to-zero workers, shut down non-production out of hours, delete orphaned environments; explicitly preserve minReplicas, Multi-AZ and backup retention.
  4. What are the risks of aggressive autoscaling?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: scale-up latency during bursts, flapping from short scale-down windows, cold starts, retry storms amplified by scaling; mitigate with longer scale-down stabilisation, sensible minReplicas and over-provisioning placeholder pods.
  5. Which workloads should never run on spot?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: databases, brokers, stateful sets, anything holding a lease or lock, anything where a 2 minute notice is not enough to drain safely.
  6. Why might a Node.js pod not benefit from 4 CPUs?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: single-threaded JavaScript execution; extra CPUs help only via cluster mode or libuv thread-pool work; over-requesting CPU wastes schedulable capacity.

Practical exercise

Pick one production service. Pull 14 days of CPU and memory utilisation. Compute p95 and p99. Set requests to those values plus headroom, remove the CPU limit if one exists, set the memory limit equal to the request, and set --max-old-space-size to 75 percent of it. Deploy behind a canary and watch p99 latency and OOM kills for a week.

Acceptance criteria: node count or Fargate spend for that service falls by at least 25 percent; p99 latency is unchanged or better; zero OOMKilled events; and you can state the monthly dollar saving.

51.3 Database cost

Concept

The database is usually the second largest line item after compute, and it is the one where a single checkbox can double the bill. Unlike compute, database cost is sticky: you cannot scale an RDS instance down at night without a restart, replicas take minutes to create and destroy, and storage that has grown never shrinks on its own.

Why does it exist?

Managed databases price four things independently, and each has its own trap:

  1. Instance — vCPU and memory, billed per hour whether idle or saturated.
  2. Storage — GB provisioned per month, and it only ever goes up.
  3. IOPS and throughput — either included in the storage type or provisioned separately at a price that can exceed the instance.
  4. I/O operations — on Aurora Standard, billed per million reads and writes, which is where write-heavy workloads get an unpleasant surprise.

Getting a design wrong on any of these produces a bill that grows faster than your traffic.

Mental model

Imagine renting a warehouse. The instance is the rent on the building. Storage is the floor space you have leased, and the landlord will not shrink the lease. IOPS is a contract for how many forklift trips per hour you are guaranteed. And on Aurora's standard pricing, there is an additional charge per forklift trip, which is fine until the day you decide to move every pallet twice.

How it works

Instance class. Approximate us-east-1 on-demand list prices for RDS PostgreSQL:

Instance vCPU RAM Approx. $/hour Approx. $/month
db.t4g.medium 2 4 GB 0.065 47
db.r6g.large 2 16 GB 0.24 175
db.r6g.xlarge 4 32 GB 0.48 350
db.r6g.2xlarge 8 64 GB 0.97 705
db.r6g.4xlarge 16 128 GB 1.93 1,410

Two immediate levers. Graviton (r6g, r7g) is roughly 10 to 20 percent cheaper than the equivalent Intel (r6i) class with equal or better PostgreSQL performance, and switching is a modify-with-restart, not a migration. A 1-year no-upfront Reserved Instance is roughly 35 to 40 percent off, and a 3-year all-upfront is around 55 to 60 percent. Databases are the best possible candidate for reservations, because unlike compute they rarely change shape in a hurry.

Our db.r6g.4xlarge at $1,410 on demand is roughly $880 with a 1-year reservation. That is a $530 monthly saving for a purchasing decision, with no engineering work at all. Do this before you do anything else in this section.

Storage and IOPS. RDS gp3 storage is about $0.115 per GB-month, and it includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline regardless of volume size. Our 2 TB database costs about $230 a month in storage.

Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) is priced separately at roughly $0.10 to $0.125 per provisioned IOPS-month. This is where bills explode:

Text
20,000 provisioned IOPS x $0.10  = $2,000/month
That is more than the db.r6g.4xlarge instance it is attached to.

The senior instinct here is to fix the queries before buying the IOPS. A missing index that causes a sequential scan on a 40 million row table can generate tens of thousands of IOPS on its own. Provisioning IOPS to serve a bad plan is paying rent on a mistake, monthly, forever. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on your top queries by total time from pg_stat_statements before you touch the storage configuration.

gp3 also lets you provision extra IOPS and throughput independently and far more cheaply than io2, so for most workloads the ladder is: fix queries, then add gp3 IOPS, and only then consider io2 (which you want for its higher durability guarantees and Multi-AZ cluster support, not usually for price).

Multi-AZ doubles the instance cost. RDS Multi-AZ runs a full standby instance in another AZ with synchronous replication. You pay for two instances and two sets of storage. Our db.r6g.4xlarge goes from $1,410 to $2,820 on demand.

Is it worth it? For the production order database, unambiguously yes: it converts an instance failure from a 90 minute PITR restore into a 60 to 120 second automatic failover (Part 50). For staging, unambiguously no. The mistake teams make is applying the same answer to both.

Multi-AZ cluster deployments (two readable standbys instead of one non-readable standby) cost more still but give you faster failover and two extra read endpoints, which can replace separately-paid read replicas. Compare the two configurations rather than assuming.

Each read replica costs a full instance. This is obvious when stated and constantly forgotten in practice. A db.r6g.2xlarge read replica is $705 a month, every month, whether it serves 4,000 queries per second or zero.

Ask three questions before adding one:

  1. What exactly will use it? "Reporting" is not an answer; name the queries.
  2. Can the primary handle it after the queries are fixed? Most "we need a read replica" requests are really "we have an N+1 query and a missing index". Fixing those is free and permanent.
  3. Does it need to be the same size? A replica serving nightly analytics can often be two classes smaller than the primary. A replica serving user-facing reads generally cannot, because it must survive being promoted.

The pattern that wastes the most money: three read replicas added during an incident two years ago, still running, now serving 3 percent of read traffic between them, because the connection routing was never updated. Check pg_stat_database.xact_commit per replica; a replica with near-zero activity is $705 a month of nothing.

The Aurora I/O pricing trap. Aurora Standard charges about $0.20 per million I/O requests in addition to instance and storage. For read-heavy workloads with a good buffer cache hit ratio this is cheap. For write-heavy workloads it is brutal, because every write generates I/O that no cache can absorb.

Text
Sustained 5,000 write I/O per second:
  5,000 x 86,400 x 30 = 12.96 billion I/O per month
  12,960 million x $0.20 = $2,592/month in I/O charges alone

Plus the instance (~$700) plus storage (~$200). The I/O is the largest line item.

Aurora I/O-Optimized removes per-I/O charges entirely in exchange for roughly 30 percent higher instance pricing and higher storage pricing. The break-even is well known and worth memorising: if I/O charges exceed about 25 percent of your total Aurora spend, I/O-Optimized is cheaper. Check the VolumeReadIOPs and VolumeWriteIOPs CloudWatch metrics and do the arithmetic; teams routinely discover they have been paying a 40 percent premium for months.

Also worth knowing: Aurora's I/O count is driven by cache misses and by write amplification, so the same optimisations that improve latency (larger instance with more buffer cache, fewer indexes, batched writes) directly reduce the bill. On Aurora Standard, a bad query costs you twice.

Connection pooling lets you buy a smaller instance. PostgreSQL allocates a backend process per connection, each with its own work_mem allocations and a base memory footprint of several megabytes. max_connections on RDS defaults to a formula based on instance memory, and pushing it higher trades memory that the buffer cache needs.

A NestJS fleet of 20 pods with a pool of 20 connections each opens 400 connections. That may require an instance class chosen for connection capacity rather than for actual query load — which means you are buying RAM to hold idle backend processes.

PgBouncer (or RDS Proxy) in transaction pooling mode collapses this. 400 client connections multiplex onto 40 server connections. Now the instance is sized for query throughput, and query throughput usually needs a class or two less.

TypeScript
// database.module.ts — a pool sized for the app, behind a pooler sized for the database.
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    type: 'postgres',
    // Point at PgBouncer, not at RDS directly.
    host: config.getOrThrow('PGBOUNCER_HOST'),
    port: 6432,
    extra: {
      // Small per-pod pool: 20 pods x 8 = 160 client connections into PgBouncer,
      // which holds maybe 40 real PostgreSQL backends.
      max: 8,
      min: 2,
      idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000,
      connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
      statement_timeout: 15_000,
    },
    // Transaction pooling does not support session-level features.
    // Prepared statements must be disabled or PgBouncer must be in session mode.
    extra_prepare: false,
  }),
  inject: [ConfigService],
});

The saving is real: moving from db.r6g.4xlarge to db.r6g.2xlarge because connections are no longer the constraint is $705 a month. The cost is one more component to operate, and the constraint that transaction pooling breaks session-level features (LISTEN/NOTIFY, session-scoped advisory locks, some prepared statement behaviour). Know which of those you use before you switch.

Archiving cold data to S3. Storage grows monotonically. An orders table with 5 years of history serves 99 percent of its queries from the last 90 days.

SQL
-- How much of the database is cold? This query usually surprises people.
SELECT
  date_trunc('year', created_at) AS year,
  count(*) AS rows,
  pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_column_size(o.*))) AS approx_size
FROM orders o
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

Moving 4 years of closed orders out of PostgreSQL and into Parquet files on S3 (queryable with Athena when finance asks) turns 1.4 TB of $0.115/GB-month RDS storage into 180 GB of compressed $0.023/GB-month S3 storage:

Text
1,400 GB in RDS gp3    = $161/month
  180 GB in S3 Standard = $4/month     (Parquet compresses 6 to 10x)
  Saving: $157/month, plus faster backups, faster restores (Part 50),
  smaller indexes and better cache hit ratios.

The secondary effects are often larger than the direct saving. A 600 GB database restores in a third of the time of a 2 TB one, its indexes fit in the buffer cache, and VACUUM finishes.

Retention by dropping partitions. If the table is partitioned by month (Part 23 — Database Scaling), retention becomes a metadata operation instead of a DELETE:

SQL
-- Partitioned table: dropping a partition is instant and reclaims space immediately.
CREATE TABLE events (
  id bigserial, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL, payload jsonb
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);

CREATE TABLE events_2026_09 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');

-- Retention job: instant, no bloat, space returned to the filesystem.
DROP TABLE events_2026_03;

-- Compare with the alternative, which is a disaster on a large table:
--   DELETE FROM events WHERE occurred_at < '2026-04-01';
-- It writes as much WAL as the rows it deletes, leaves dead tuples that
-- VACUUM must reclaim, does NOT return space to the OS without VACUUM FULL
-- (which needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and double the disk), and can take hours.

Partitioning for retention is one of the few designs that improves cost, performance and operability simultaneously. If you have a table that grows forever and is queried by time, partition it.

Unused indexes charge you twice. Every index costs storage and write throughput. On a write-heavy orders table, each additional index means another B-tree page to modify per insert, more WAL, more I/O (billed directly on Aurora Standard), and slower VACUUM.

SQL
-- Indexes that have never been used since the last stats reset.
SELECT
  s.schemaname, s.relname AS table_name, s.indexrelname AS index_name,
  s.idx_scan AS times_used,
  pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0
  AND NOT i.indisunique          -- never drop a unique index blindly; it is a constraint
  AND NOT i.indisprimary
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

-- Duplicate / redundant indexes: (a) is redundant if (a, b) exists and is used.
SELECT indrelid::regclass AS table_name, array_agg(indexrelid::regclass) AS indexes
FROM pg_index GROUP BY indrelid, indkey HAVING count(*) > 1;

A typical finding on a mature system: 12 unused indexes totalling 180 GB, on tables taking 3,000 writes per second. Dropping them saves about $21 a month in storage, and — far more valuable — reduces write latency, WAL volume, replication lag, backup size and restore time. Use DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and check idx_scan across all replicas first, because an index used only by a reporting replica shows zero scans on the primary.

Production scenario

The platform's database line, before and after a review:

Item Before After Action
Primary db.r6g.4xlarge on demand $1,410 $880 1-year Reserved Instance
Multi-AZ standby $1,410 $880 Same reservation
Read replica A (analytics) $705 $350 Downsized to xlarge; analytics is not latency-critical
Read replica B (added in an incident, 2 percent of reads) $705 $0 Deleted after routing fixed
Storage 2 TB gp3 $230 $69 Archived 4 years of orders to S3 as Parquet
Provisioned IOPS 12,000 $1,200 $0 Two missing indexes removed the need; gp3 baseline is enough
Snapshot storage $180 $120 Expired 40 orphaned manual snapshots
Total $5,840 $2,299 -61 percent

Backup retention, Multi-AZ and cross-region copies were untouched. Every saving came from waste, purchasing or query work, not from resilience.

Failure scenario

A team migrated a write-heavy event-ingestion workload from RDS to Aurora, expecting better performance. It delivered. The first full month's bill included $4,100 of Aurora I/O charges against a $700 instance.

Investigation found two causes. The obvious one: the workload wrote 8,000 rows per second and every write generated I/O. The less obvious one: the table had 9 indexes, six of which were unused, so each insert generated roughly three times the necessary I/O.

The fix was three actions: drop the unused indexes (I/O fell by about 55 percent), batch inserts into multi-row statements (a further 20 percent), and switch to Aurora I/O-Optimized for the remainder. Final bill: $1,180. The unused indexes alone had been costing $2,200 a month in I/O charges — on RDS they would have cost $8 a month in storage and gone unnoticed for years.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • RDS storage can be increased but never decreased. The only way back down is a dump and reload into a new instance, or pg_repack. Provision conservatively and use storage autoscaling.
  • Storage autoscaling has a cooldown (typically 6 hours) and a maximum; a runaway write can still fill the disk between scaling events (Part 50, scenario 6).
  • A read replica with a long-running query blocks WAL replay (or gets cancelled), so a cheap analytics replica can cause replication lag on your DR path.
  • Aurora Serverless v2 scales ACUs by load and is genuinely cheap for spiky workloads, but its floor ACU setting is billed continuously, and a floor set high "for safety" removes the entire benefit.
  • Deleting an RDS instance without a final snapshot destroys the automated backups with it.
  • DROP INDEX without CONCURRENTLY takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and stops all queries on the table.
  • Reserved Instances are tied to instance family and region; a reservation on db.r6i does not apply after you move to db.r6g.
  • Dropping an index that is only used by a query running once a quarter (a compliance report) turns a 20 second report into a 4 hour one. Check with the owners.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They fix queries before they buy hardware. Provisioned IOPS, a bigger instance and a read replica are all ways of paying money to avoid an EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

They buy reservations for the database first, because it is the most stable workload in the fleet and the discount is the largest single lever available with zero engineering risk.

They treat every read replica as a service with an owner and a documented consumer. A replica with no named consumer gets deleted.

They partition anything that grows forever and is queried by time, because it converts an operational problem (retention) and a cost problem (storage) into a metadata operation.

And on Aurora they check the I/O line every month, because it is the one AWS bill item that scales with your inefficiency rather than with your traffic.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a read replica to fix a query problem.
  • Provisioning IOPS to serve a sequential scan.
  • Leaving Multi-AZ on for staging and off for production (yes, this happens).
  • Running Aurora Standard on a write-heavy workload without checking the I/O charge.
  • Never dropping indexes, because "an index can only help".
  • Deleting old rows with DELETE instead of dropping partitions, then wondering why the disk did not shrink.
  • Buying a 3-year reservation for an instance class the team plans to change.

Interview questions

  1. What are the four things a managed database bills you for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: instance hours, provisioned storage, IOPS/throughput, and (on Aurora Standard) per-I/O charges. Follow-up: which one can exceed the instance cost? Provisioned IOPS, and Aurora I/O on write-heavy workloads.
  2. When is Aurora I/O-Optimized cheaper than Aurora Standard?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: when I/O charges exceed roughly 25 percent of total Aurora spend; typical for write-heavy workloads.
  3. How does connection pooling reduce database cost?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: PostgreSQL is process-per-connection; pooling collapses hundreds of client connections into tens of backends, so the instance can be sized for query throughput rather than connection memory, often one or two classes smaller.
  4. How do unused indexes cost you twice?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: storage, plus write amplification (more pages, more WAL, more I/O, slower VACUUM, more replication lag, longer restores). Follow-up: how do you find them? pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan, checked on every replica, excluding unique and primary key indexes.
  5. You are asked to add a third read replica. What do you ask first?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: which queries will use it, whether the primary could serve them after fixing plans, whether it can be smaller, and who owns it.
  6. Why is dropping a partition better than DELETE for retention?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: instant metadata operation, no WAL for row deletions, no dead tuples, space returned immediately, no VACUUM FULL lock.

Practical exercise

On a production-like database, run the unused-index query and the cold-data query above. Produce a table of: every index with zero scans and its size, and the percentage of rows older than 90 days.

Acceptance criteria: you can state the storage and write-throughput saving from dropping the unused indexes; you can state the monthly saving from archiving cold data to S3; and you have checked idx_scan on every replica before recommending any drop.

51.4 Storage, network egress and observability cost

Concept

These three categories are where cloud bills surprise people, because none of them appear in an architecture diagram. Nobody draws a NAT gateway. Nobody draws the AZ boundary that a service call crosses. Nobody draws the log line inside the for loop. And yet, on a mature system, these three together are routinely 25 to 40 percent of the bill.

Why does it exist?

Storage, network and telemetry are all metered by volume of something an engineer produces incidentally. You do not decide to spend $900 on data transfer; you decide to put a service in three AZs and have it call another service, and $900 is the consequence. The cost is real, but the decision that caused it did not feel like a cost decision.

Mental model

Imagine a factory that charges you per pallet moved between buildings, per truck that leaves the site, and per page of paperwork filed. You would design the floor plan differently. Cloud pricing is that factory, and most architectures are drawn as though moving pallets between buildings is free.

How it works

S3 classes and lifecycle rules. Approximate us-east-1 list prices per GB-month:

Class $/GB-month Retrieval Minimum duration
Standard 0.023 Instant, free None
Intelligent-Tiering 0.023, auto-lowers Instant None (small monitoring fee per object)
Standard-IA 0.0125 Instant, $0.01/GB 30 days
Glacier Instant Retrieval 0.004 Milliseconds, $0.03/GB 90 days
Glacier Flexible Retrieval 0.0036 Minutes to hours 90 days
Glacier Deep Archive 0.00099 ~12 hours 180 days

A lifecycle rule that moves objects through those tiers automatically is a few lines and often halves the S3 bill:

JSON
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "invoices-tiering",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "invoices/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 365, "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR" },
        { "Days": 1095, "StorageClass": "DEEP_ARCHIVE" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "ID": "expire-temp-exports",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "exports/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Expiration": { "Days": 7 }
    },
    {
      "ID": "clean-old-versions",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 90 },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

The last two rules are the ones people forget and they are frequently the largest. Non-current versions on a versioned bucket accumulate forever: a bucket with versioning enabled and no expiry rule, holding files that are overwritten daily, grows without bound while the console shows a small object count. Incomplete multipart uploads are invisible in the console entirely and are billed as storage; buckets with years of failed 5 GB uploads holding hundreds of gigabytes are common.

Watch the minimum-duration charges too: moving an object to Glacier Deep Archive and deleting it a week later bills you for 180 days. Do not lifecycle short-lived data into deep tiers.

Snapshot sprawl. EBS and RDS snapshots are incremental and cheap individually, which is exactly why they accumulate. The pattern is always the same: an engineer takes a manual snapshot before a risky change, the change works, the snapshot stays forever. Multiply by 30 engineers and 4 years.

Shell
# Manual RDS snapshots older than 90 days, with their size and creation time.
aws rds describe-db-snapshots --snapshot-type manual \
  --query 'DBSnapshots[?SnapshotCreateTime<`2026-06-01`].[DBSnapshotIdentifier,AllocatedStorage,SnapshotCreateTime]' \
  --output table

RDS snapshot storage is about $0.095 per GB-month; EBS snapshots about $0.05. Forty orphaned 2 TB-allocated snapshots is not a small number. Fix it with a tag policy (expires), a scheduled job that deletes expired manual snapshots, and AWS Backup lifecycle rules for the ones that must persist.

Surprise one: cross-AZ data transfer. AWS charges roughly $0.01 per GB in each direction for traffic between Availability Zones in the same region — so about $0.02 per GB for a round trip. Traffic within an AZ is free. Traffic to the internet is more expensive still (about $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB).

The arithmetic for a chatty service:

Text
A service moving 2 TB/month across AZs:
  2,000 GB x $0.02 = $40/month

That sounds harmless. Now scale it the way real systems scale:
  - 40 services in a mesh, each doing the same         -> $1,600/month
  - Traffic grows 5x over two years                    -> $8,000/month
  - Add a service mesh: sidecar-to-sidecar hops double -> $16,000/month

The point is not that 2 TB is expensive. It is that cross-AZ transfer is per-gigabyte forever, invisible in any diagram, and it scales with both traffic and service count. It is the classic microservices tax.

Where it comes from, in order of how often it surprises people:

  1. Service-to-service calls landing on a pod in another AZ, because Kubernetes Service load balancing is AZ-agnostic by default.
  2. Application to database when the pod and the RDS writer are in different AZs. Every query result crosses the boundary.
  3. Kafka producers and consumers in different AZs from the partition leader. Kafka replication between brokers in three AZs multiplies this: every message crosses AZ boundaries twice for a replication factor of 3.
  4. Multi-AZ RDS synchronous replication. Included in the Multi-AZ price, but a reason your write path is doing cross-AZ I/O.

The mitigations, in order of value:

YAML
# Topology-aware routing: prefer endpoints in the caller's own zone.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: inventory-api
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto
spec:
  selector:
    app: inventory-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000

Topology-aware routing keeps traffic in-zone when there is enough capacity in the zone, and falls back across zones when there is not — so you get the saving without losing the availability property. Combine it with pod topology spread constraints so each zone actually has capacity:

YAML
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway   # never fail scheduling to save network cost
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels:
