        app: inventory-api

Note whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway. Cost optimisation must never be allowed to prevent a pod from being scheduled during an incident.

For Kafka, the equivalent lever is rack awareness plus client.rack on consumers, which lets a consumer fetch from an in-AZ replica instead of the cross-AZ leader.

Surprise two: NAT gateway charges. A NAT gateway costs about $0.045 per hour (roughly $33 a month) plus $0.045 per GB processed. Most production VPCs run one per AZ for availability, so the baseline is about $100 a month before a single byte moves.

The per-gigabyte charge is the part that hurts, because everything your private pods fetch from the internet goes through it: container images, npm packages, S3 objects, external API calls, telemetry sent to a SaaS vendor.

Text
A cluster pulling 200 GB/day of container images and S3 objects through NAT:
  200 GB x 30 = 6,000 GB/month
  6,000 x $0.045 = $270/month
  Plus 3 gateways x $33 = $100/month baseline
  Total: $370/month

The fix is VPC endpoints, and for S3 it is free. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB cost nothing at all and route traffic over the AWS network instead of through NAT. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs, KMS, STS and the rest cost about $0.01 per hour per AZ (roughly $7.30 per month per endpoint per AZ) plus about $0.01 per GB.

For our platform, adding an S3 gateway endpoint and ECR, Logs and Secrets Manager interface endpoints:

Text
Before: 6,000 GB/month through NAT           = $270 + $100 baseline = $370
After:  S3 traffic (4,000 GB) via gateway EP = $0
        ECR/Logs/Secrets (1,800 GB) via 4 interface endpoints in 3 AZs
          = 12 x $7.30 = $88 + 1,800 x $0.01 = $18  -> $106
        Remaining 200 GB through NAT = $9 + $100 baseline = $109
  Total after: $215/month. Saving: $155/month, and lower latency.

The S3 gateway endpoint in particular is free money: it takes ten minutes, costs nothing, and removes NAT charges for every S3 byte. If you take one action from this section, take that one.

Surprise three: log volume. Logs are the most reliably underestimated line item in the industry, because the cost is per gigabyte ingested and a single misplaced log statement can produce gigabytes.

Approximate prices: CloudWatch Logs ingestion is about $0.50 per GB, storage about $0.03 per GB-month. Third-party platforms charge for both ingestion and indexing: Datadog is roughly $0.10 per GB to ingest and around $1.70 per million log events to index and retain for 15 days.

The arithmetic for a debug-level logger:

Text
A service logging at debug level, writing 500 GB/month:

CloudWatch Logs
  Ingestion: 500 GB x $0.50            = $250/month
  Storage:   500 GB x $0.03, growing   = $15 and rising each month

Datadog (same volume, ~1 KB per line, so ~500 million events)
  Ingestion: 500 GB x $0.10            = $50/month
  Indexing:  500 x $1.70 per million   = $850/month
  Total                                = $900/month

One service. At debug level. Producing almost no diagnostic value,
because 500 GB of debug output is not something a human ever reads.

Now multiply by 12 services, or by an incident in which someone enables debug logging "temporarily" and forgets (51.9).

The levers, from most to least valuable:

  1. Log level is a runtime decision, not a build-time one. info in production, with the ability to raise a single service to debug for 30 minutes via config, with an automatic revert.
  2. Sample high-volume, low-value events. A log line per cache hit is telemetry, not a log; count it as a metric instead.
  3. Structured logs with bounded fields. Never log full request or response bodies by default. A single endpoint returning a 200 KB JSON payload, logged at 100 RPS, is 1.7 TB a month.
  4. Short retention in the expensive tier, long retention in the cheap one. 7 to 15 days indexed and searchable; archive to S3 for the rest and query with Athena when you need to.
  5. Drop what you never query. Health check logs, readiness probe logs and successful 200 OK access logs for static assets are almost always pure volume.
TypeScript
// logger.config.ts — Pino, with production defaults that keep volume sane.
import { LoggerModule } from 'nestjs-pino';

LoggerModule.forRoot({
  pinoHttp: {
    // Runtime-controlled level. Default info; raise deliberately, never by default.
    level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info',
    // Do not log health and readiness probes: pure volume, zero value.
    autoLogging: {
      ignore: (req) => ['/health', '/health/live', '/health/ready', '/metrics']
        .includes((req as { url?: string }).url ?? ''),
    },
    // Redact secrets, and never serialise whole bodies.
    redact: {
      paths: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie', 'req.body.password', 'req.body.card'],
      remove: true,
    },
    serializers: {
      req: (req) => ({ id: req.id, method: req.method, url: req.url }),   // not headers, not body
      res: (res) => ({ statusCode: res.statusCode }),
    },
  },
});

Metric cardinality. A time series is created for every unique combination of metric name and label values. Cardinality multiplies:

Text
http_request_duration_seconds with labels:
  route (40) x method (5) x status (12)              = 2,400 series. Fine.

Add one bad label:
  ... x user_id (250,000)                            = 600 million series.

That kills a Prometheus server outright (each series costs roughly 1 to 3 KB of RAM, so 600 million series is not survivable), and on a per-custom-metric SaaS pricing model at roughly $0.05 per custom metric per month it is an invoice nobody will believe.

The rule: labels must be bounded and low-cardinality by construction. Never label with a user id, order id, request id, email, full URL path with parameters, or an error message. Those belong in traces and logs, which are designed for high cardinality. Use the route pattern (/orders/:id), not the URL (/orders/8f3c...).

Trace sampling. Distributed tracing at 100 percent on a 500 RPS service produces 1.3 billion spans a month, and vendors charge per span or per ingested GB. Head-based sampling at 1 to 10 percent keeps the statistical picture at a tenth of the cost. Tail-based sampling is better still: sample 100 percent of errors and slow requests, and 1 percent of successful fast ones, so you keep the traces you actually open while discarding the ones you never will.

TypeScript
// tracing.ts — OpenTelemetry with parent-based ratio sampling.
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { ParentBasedSampler, TraceIdRatioBasedSampler } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  // Respect an upstream sampling decision; otherwise sample 5 percent of new traces.
  sampler: new ParentBasedSampler({
    root: new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(Number(process.env.OTEL_SAMPLE_RATIO ?? 0.05)),
  }),
});
sdk.start();

Production scenario

The platform's storage, network and observability line after a review:

Item Before After Action
S3 (2.6 TB, no lifecycle) $60 $28 Lifecycle to IA and Glacier IR; expired non-current versions and incomplete multiparts (410 GB recovered)
RDS + EBS snapshot sprawl $310 $140 Deleted 40 orphaned manual snapshots; expires tag enforced
Cross-AZ transfer $640 $290 Topology-aware routing, Kafka rack awareness, pods co-located with the RDS writer AZ where safe
NAT gateway $370 $215 S3 gateway endpoint (free) plus ECR, Logs, Secrets interface endpoints
CloudWatch + Datadog logs $1,900 $560 Log level to info, probe logs dropped, bodies redacted, 15 day indexed retention with S3 archive
Custom metrics $700 $210 Removed three high-cardinality labels
Traces $480 $95 100 percent to 5 percent head sampling with 100 percent on errors
Total $4,460 $1,538 -66 percent

Note that nothing here reduced the team's ability to debug. Dropping health-check logs and 95 percent of successful traces removes noise; keeping 100 percent of error traces keeps the signal.

Failure scenario

A retailer's monthly bill jumped by $31,000 with no traffic change. Cost Explorer showed the growth in "EC2-Other: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes" — cross-AZ transfer.

The cause was a service mesh rollout. Every service-to-service call now traversed two sidecar proxies, and the mesh's default load balancing was round-robin across all endpoints regardless of zone. A request that previously made 6 in-AZ hops now made 6 hops that were each cross-AZ with two-thirds probability, and each hop was counted in both directions.

The fix was locality-aware load balancing in the mesh configuration, which took an afternoon and reduced the charge to $4,200. The lesson the team wrote down: any change to how services find each other is a cost change, and it should be reviewed as one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Versioned S3 buckets with no non-current expiry rule, growing invisibly.
  • Incomplete multipart uploads billed as storage and not visible in the console object list.
  • Lifecycle rules that move short-lived objects to Glacier, triggering 90 or 180 day minimum charges plus retrieval fees.
  • Cross-region S3 replication doubling storage cost and charging cross-region transfer per GB.
  • A NAT gateway per AZ multiplied across three environments: nine gateways, $300 a month of baseline before any traffic.
  • Interface VPC endpoints priced per AZ; creating them in three AZs for six services is $130 a month, which can exceed the NAT charge they were meant to replace. Do the arithmetic per endpoint.
  • CloudWatch Logs with Never expire retention, the default on some log groups, accumulating for years.
  • A metric label added in a hotfix (error_message) creating unbounded cardinality overnight.
  • Topology-aware routing configured with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, so a zone outage prevents pods from being scheduled at all.
  • Egress to the internet for telemetry: shipping 500 GB a month to a SaaS observability vendor costs $45 in egress on top of the vendor's bill.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They read the bill by usage type, not by service. "EC2-Other" hides data transfer; "CloudWatch" hides ingestion versus storage. The usage-type breakdown is where the surprises live, and looking at it once a month takes ten minutes.

They treat AZ boundaries as a design element. When they draw a request path, they mark where it crosses a zone, because that mark is both latency and money.

They put an S3 gateway endpoint in every VPC on day one, because it is free and it removes a whole category of charge.

They treat logs as a product with a budget: every service has a GB-per-day expectation, and exceeding it is a bug to be fixed, not a bill to be paid.

And they hold the line on cardinality, because it is the only one of these mistakes that takes down the monitoring system itself, which means you lose visibility exactly when you need it.

Common mistakes

  • Enabling S3 versioning without a non-current version expiry rule.
  • Logging full request and response bodies at info level.
  • Leaving debug logging on after an incident.
  • Labelling metrics with user or request ids.
  • Assuming traffic between services in the same region is free.
  • Sending observability data to a SaaS vendor through a NAT gateway and paying twice.
  • Deleting logs to save money without checking a compliance retention requirement first.

Interview questions

  1. Name three cost categories that do not appear in an architecture diagram but dominate real bills.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: cross-AZ data transfer, NAT gateway per-GB charges, and log/telemetry volume.
  2. How do you eliminate NAT gateway charges for S3 traffic?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: an S3 gateway VPC endpoint, which is free; contrast with interface endpoints, which cost per AZ-hour plus per GB.
  3. A service moves 2 TB a month across AZs. What does that cost and how do you reduce it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: about $40 at $0.02 per GB round trip, but it scales with service count and traffic; reduce with topology-aware routing, pod spread constraints, Kafka rack awareness, and co-locating chatty components. Note that availability must win over cost when they conflict.
  4. Your logging bill is $900 a month for one service. Diagnose it.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: log level, request/response bodies, health check logs, per-event indexing charges; fix with runtime log levels, sampling, redaction, bounded serializers and tiered retention.
  5. What is metric cardinality and why does it matter for cost?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: one series per unique label combination; unbounded labels like user id produce millions of series, exhausting Prometheus memory and generating per-custom-metric charges. Route patterns, not URLs.
  6. How would you keep useful traces while cutting tracing cost by 90 percent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: head-based ratio sampling for successful requests plus 100 percent retention of errors and slow requests, ideally tail-based.

Practical exercise

Open Cost Explorer, group by usage type rather than by service, and list your top ten usage types for last month. For each, name the engineering decision that produced it.

Acceptance criteria: you can identify your cross-AZ transfer charge, your NAT per-GB charge and your log ingestion charge as separate numbers; you have created an S3 gateway endpoint if one is missing; and you have found at least one usage type nobody on the team could explain.

51.5 Caching, CDN and autoscaling as cost tools

Concept

The previous sections cut cost by removing waste. This one is different: it spends money in one place to remove more of it somewhere else. A cache, a CDN and an autoscaler are all performance tools, but each is also an arbitrage — you buy cheap capacity to avoid buying expensive capacity.

Why does it exist?

Not all compute is priced the same. A Redis GET costs a fraction of a cent-hour of a cache node. The equivalent PostgreSQL query costs a slice of an instance that is 5 to 10 times more expensive per unit of work, plus IOPS, plus (on Aurora Standard) a per-I/O charge. Serving a product image from CloudFront costs about $0.085 per GB; serving it from a NestJS pod costs event loop time, a socket, and egress at $0.09 per GB plus the compute.

When the same work can be done on cheaper infrastructure, moving it there is a cost optimisation that also makes the system faster. Those are rare and you should take them.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. The chef (your database) is expensive and there is exactly one. The hot counter (Redis) holds prepared dishes and any waiter can grab from it. The takeaway fridge by the door (the CDN) holds pre-packed items customers take themselves without entering the building at all.

Every dish served from the counter or the fridge is a dish the chef does not cook. You do not hire a second chef; you buy a bigger counter, which costs a fraction as much.

How it works

Trading Redis cost against a smaller database instance. The arithmetic is usually decisive.

Text
Situation: the orders API does 4,200 reads/second, 78 percent of which are
repeated product and category lookups. The database is at 70 percent CPU on a
db.r6g.4xlarge and the team is being asked to move to db.r6g.8xlarge.

Option A: scale the database up
  db.r6g.4xlarge -> db.r6g.8xlarge, Multi-AZ (both instances)
  +$1,410 x 2 = +$2,820/month

Option B: add a cache layer
  cache.r6g.large ElastiCache, 2 nodes for HA  = ~$300/month
  Absorbs 78 percent of reads. Database CPU falls to ~28 percent.
  Saving vs Option A: $2,520/month.
  Bonus: cached reads are ~0.4 ms instead of ~3 ms.

Redis is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per read than a relational database, and it is faster. That is why caching is the highest-leverage cost tool in most backend systems.

The honest caveats, because this is not free:

  • You now own cache invalidation, stampede protection, and a second failure mode (Part 27 — Caching).
  • The database must still be able to survive a cold cache. If Redis restarts at peak and the database cannot take 4,200 reads per second, you have traded cost for an outage. Size the database for survivable degraded mode, not for the cached steady state.
  • Cache what is read often and changes rarely. Caching a value that changes on every write adds cost and gains nothing.
TypeScript
// product-cache.service.ts — cache-aside with stampede protection and a jittered TTL.
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Injectable()
export class ProductCacheService {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async get<T>(key: string, ttlSeconds: number, loader: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const cached = await this.redis.get(key);
    if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached) as T;

    // Single-flight: only one pod loads on a miss; the rest wait briefly and re-read.
    // Without this, a cold key at 4,000 RPS sends 4,000 identical queries to the database.
    const lockKey = `lock:${key}`;
    const gotLock = await this.redis.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', 10, 'NX');
    if (!gotLock) {
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
      const retry = await this.redis.get(key);
      if (retry) return JSON.parse(retry) as T;
    }

    try {
      const value = await loader();
      // Jitter the TTL so a batch of keys written together does not all expire together.
      const jittered = ttlSeconds + Math.floor(Math.random() * ttlSeconds * 0.2);
      await this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(value), 'EX', jittered);
      return value;
    } finally {
      await this.redis.del(lockKey);
    }
  }
}

CDN offload reduces both egress and origin compute. For our platform, product images are 8 million objects served 50 million times a day.

Text
Serving images from S3 directly:
  GET requests: 50M/day x 30 = 1.5B/month
  At $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs  = $600/month in request charges
  Egress at 300 KB average   = 450 TB/month x $0.09 = $40,500/month  (!)

Serving through CloudFront with a 94 percent cache hit ratio:
  CloudFront egress: 450 TB x ~$0.085 (tiered, lower at volume) = ~$32,000
  Origin fetches: 6 percent of 450 TB = 27 TB from S3 to CloudFront = $0 (free)
  S3 GET requests: 6 percent of 1.5B = 90M = $36/month

The dominant saving here is not the per-GB rate (CloudFront and S3 egress are similar); it is that S3-to-CloudFront origin transfer is free, so only cache misses generate S3 charges, and the request charges fall by the cache hit ratio. At volume, CloudFront's tiered pricing and committed-use discounts widen the gap further.

The bigger structural win is what it does to your compute. If those images were served through NestJS pods (33.2's failure scenario), you would need many times the pod count purely to shuffle bytes, plus the sockets, plus the event loop time stolen from actual business logic. Serving static bytes through your application is the most expensive way to serve bytes available to you.

Cache API responses at the edge too, where they are cacheable: product detail JSON with a 60 second TTL and a stale-while-revalidate directive removes a large fraction of origin requests for a catalog that changes hourly.

Scheduled and event-driven scaling. Two different tools for two different traffic shapes.

Scheduled scaling is for predictable patterns. Our platform's traffic is 12x higher at 20:00 than at 04:00, and every weekday looks the same. A scheduled scale-up at 09:00 and scale-down at 23:00 removes the reaction latency of reactive autoscaling and lets you run a lower minReplicas overnight safely:

YAML
# KEDA supports cron triggers alongside metric triggers.
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: orders-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: orders-api
  minReplicaCount: 3
  maxReplicaCount: 24
  triggers:
    - type: cron
      metadata:
        timezone: Europe/London
        start: "0 9 * * 1-5"      # pre-scale before the morning ramp
        end: "0 23 * * 1-5"
        desiredReplicas: "8"
    - type: prometheus            # reactive scaling still applies on top
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="orders-api"}[2m]))
        threshold: "60"           # requests per second per pod

The value of pre-scaling is that autoscaling always reacts after the traffic arrives. Scheduled scaling puts capacity in place before it does, which means you can run reactive thresholds less conservatively the rest of the time.

Event-driven scaling is for work whose demand is a queue depth, not a CPU number. This is where the biggest savings are, because workers are usually the most over-provisioned part of a system: they are sized for the nightly batch and then idle for 23 hours.

KEDA scaling workers to zero. The invoice generator, the export builder, the image processor, the email sender: all of these do bursts of work and then nothing.

YAML
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: export-worker
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: export-worker
  minReplicaCount: 0            # genuinely zero pods when idle
  maxReplicaCount: 40
  pollingInterval: 15
  cooldownPeriod: 180           # wait 3 minutes of an empty queue before scaling to zero
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/exports
        queueLength: "20"       # one pod per 20 visible messages
        awsRegion: us-east-1
Text
Export worker before: 4 pods x 1 vCPU / 2 GB, 24/7 on Fargate = $144/month
Export worker after:  averages 0.7 pods over the day             = $25/month
Saving: $119/month for one worker. Multiply by nine workers      = ~$1,070/month.

The prerequisites are the same discipline you need anyway: idempotent job handlers, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM so an in-flight job is either finished or re-queued, and a cold start short enough that the first job after a quiet period does not time out. If your worker takes 45 seconds to boot because it warms a large in-memory cache at startup, fix that before enabling scale-to-zero.

For a NestJS worker, the shutdown contract is small and important:

TypeScript
// main.ts — worker process that KEDA can safely scale to zero.
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { WorkerModule } from './worker.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.createApplicationContext(WorkerModule);
  // Enables onModuleDestroy / onApplicationShutdown hooks, so BullMQ workers
  // can finish the current job and stop taking new ones before the pod dies.
  app.enableShutdownHooks();
  await app.init();
}
bootstrap();

Production scenario

The combined effect on our platform:

Lever Cost added Cost removed Net
ElastiCache 2 x cache.r6g.large +$300 Avoided database upgrade -$2,820 -$2,520
CloudFront in front of S3 and the API +$32,000 egress S3 egress and requests -$41,100 -$9,100
KEDA scale-to-zero on 9 workers +$0 Worker compute -$1,070 -$1,070
Scheduled pre-scaling +$0 Lower overnight minReplicas, -$180 -$180

Every one of those also improved latency. That is the signature of a good cost optimisation: when the cheaper option is also the faster one, take it without a meeting.

Failure scenario

A team enabled aggressive caching to avoid a database upgrade. It worked: database CPU fell from 72 percent to 24 percent, and they downsized from db.r6g.4xlarge to db.r6g.xlarge, saving $2,100 a month.

Six weeks later ElastiCache had a maintenance-window failover. The cache was empty for about 90 seconds. In those 90 seconds the full read load — which the cache had been absorbing at a 91 percent hit ratio — hit a database that was now four times smaller than the one that had originally struggled with it. The database saturated, connections queued, the connection pool exhausted, and checkout was down for 11 minutes.

The lesson is a rule worth carrying: size the database for the load it must survive with a cold cache, not for the load it sees with a warm one. You may still downsize, but downsize by less, and prove it with a cache-flush game day in staging. In this case the correct answer was db.r6g.2xlarge (a $700 saving, not $2,100) plus request coalescing so a cold cache produces one query per key rather than thousands.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cold cache after a Redis failover or deploy overwhelming a downsized database.
  • Cache stampede on a hot key when its TTL expires under load. Single-flight locks and jittered TTLs, as above.
  • CDN caching a response that contains user-specific data because Cache-Control was wrong; a privacy incident, not a cost incident.
  • CDN cache hit ratio destroyed by a cache-busting query string on every request.
  • Scale-to-zero on a worker whose consumer group rebalance takes longer than the job timeout.
  • KEDA scaling on a queue whose messages are invisible (in-flight) rather than visible, so the metric reads zero while work is happening.
  • Scheduled scaling that does not account for a public holiday, a marketing email or a flash sale.
  • Redis used as a database rather than a cache, so it holds data that cannot be lost, and now it needs backups, replication and an entirely different cost profile (Part 50).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They look for arbitrage: work being done on expensive infrastructure that could be done on cheap infrastructure. Cache, CDN and queue-driven workers are the three standard trades, and all three make the system faster as well as cheaper.

They never let a cost optimisation remove a safety margin silently. Downsizing the database because a cache absorbs the load is legitimate only with a documented cold-cache plan and a tested degraded mode.

They scale workers on the signal that actually represents demand. CPU-based autoscaling on a queue worker is a category error: a worker waiting on I/O has low CPU and a huge backlog.

And they check the CDN hit ratio like a first-class metric. A hit ratio that drifts from 94 percent to 70 percent is a cost regression and usually also a latency regression, and it is invisible unless someone is watching.

Common mistakes

  • Adding a cache without stampede protection, then blaming Redis for the database outage.
  • Downsizing the database to the cached steady state.
  • Serving images and static assets through application pods.
  • Autoscaling workers on CPU.
  • Scale-to-zero with a 40 second cold start and a 30 second job timeout.
  • Caching data that changes on every read, adding a network hop and a cost for zero hit ratio.

Interview questions

  1. How can adding a cache reduce total cost?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: Redis is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per read than a relational database, so absorbing 70 to 90 percent of reads avoids a database upgrade that costs several times more; it also lowers latency. Follow-up: what must you keep? Enough database capacity to survive a cold cache.
  2. Why does a CDN reduce cost beyond egress rates?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: origin transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, request charges fall with the hit ratio, and origin compute is removed entirely.
  3. What is the right autoscaling signal for a queue worker?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: queue depth or age of the oldest message, not CPU; KEDA with a queue trigger; scale to zero when idle.
  4. What breaks when you scale workers to zero?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: cold start latency, consumer group rebalance, in-flight message visibility metrics reading zero, jobs timing out on the first invocation after idle.
  5. Your team wants to downsize the database after adding a cache. What do you require first?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected: a documented and tested cold-cache degraded mode, request coalescing, and a game day that flushes the cache under load in staging.

Practical exercise

Take the highest-QPS read endpoint in your system. Measure its database cost contribution (queries per second, average duration, share of instance CPU). Add a cache with a jittered TTL and single-flight protection. Then run a game day: flush the cache at peak load in staging and observe whether the database survives.

Acceptance criteria: cache hit ratio above 80 percent; database CPU contribution from that endpoint reduced by at least 60 percent; the system survives a full cache flush at peak without exhausting the connection pool; and you can state the instance class you could safely downsize to, with evidence.

51.6 Architecture cost trade-offs

Concept

Every architectural choice has a recurring monthly price attached, and most of that price is baseline — cost you pay before serving a single request. Baseline cost is where architecture shows up on the bill, and it is the part that scales with the number of moving parts rather than with traffic.

Why does it exist?

Because distributed systems are not free at the boundaries. Every service you split out needs, at minimum: a place to run with a redundant minimum replica count, a way to be reached, a way to be observed, a way to be deployed, and a person who understands it. Those costs are per-service and mostly fixed.

Mental model

Imagine splitting one shop into twelve specialist shops. Each needs its own rent, its own till, its own alarm system, its own insurance, its own opening-hours rota. The total number of customers has not changed. Some of the twelve will genuinely serve customers better. All twelve will send you a rent bill.

How it works

Microservices multiply the baseline. Here is what each additional service costs before it does any work. Approximate monthly figures:

Item Per service Notes
Minimum pod count for HA $40 to $120 2 to 3 pods, even at 5 RPS
Load balancer or ingress rule $0 to $25 Shared ALB with host rules is cheap; a dedicated ALB is about $20 plus LCU charges
Observability agent and telemetry $30 to $150 Per-host or per-container APM pricing, plus that service's metrics, logs and traces
CI pipeline minutes $15 to $60 Build, test, image scan, per commit
Container registry storage $2 to $10 Image history
Secrets and config $2 to $8 Per secret per month, plus API calls
Its own database, if it has one $175 to $700 The big one; see below
Baseline per service $90 to $350, or $300 to $1,000 with its own database

Twelve services is therefore roughly $1,100 to $4,200 a month of baseline before traffic, and considerably more if several own databases. That is the number to put in a design review when someone proposes splitting a module out.

The costs that do not appear on the bill are larger:

  • On-call surface. Twelve services means twelve sets of alerts, twelve runbooks, twelve deploy pipelines to keep green, twelve dependency upgrade streams.
  • Cross-service debugging. A latency regression that spans four services takes far longer to diagnose than one inside a single process, and distributed tracing is a mitigation, not a cure.
  • Cross-AZ and cross-service network traffic (51.4), which grows with the square of chattiness.
  • Data consistency work. Transactions that used to be one BEGIN/COMMIT become sagas, outboxes and reconciliation jobs (Part 30 — Distributed Transactions). That is permanent engineering cost.

None of this is an argument against microservices. It is an argument for knowing the price, so the benefit can be weighed against it.

Managed services versus self-hosted, with engineer time priced in. The comparison people run is "RDS costs $700 a month, an EC2 instance running PostgreSQL costs $250, so self-hosting saves $450". That comparison is wrong because it omits the largest term.

Text
Self-hosted PostgreSQL on EC2, honestly costed:
  Instance (r6g.2xlarge)                       $370/month
  EBS storage + snapshots                      $250/month
  Standby instance for HA                      $370/month
  Engineer time: patching, upgrades, backups,
  monitoring, failover testing, incident response
    ~6 hours/month at a fully loaded ~$120/hour $720/month
  Plus the risk premium: a botched major version
  upgrade or a failed failover has a real cost
  --------------------------------------------------------
  Total                                        ~$1,710/month

RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ (db.r6g.2xlarge, reserved)
  Instances + storage + backups                ~$1,050/month
  Engineer time                                ~1 hour/month = $120
  --------------------------------------------------------
  Total                                        ~$1,170/month

Managed is usually cheaper once engineer time is priced honestly, and it is always cheaper in risk. The cases where self-hosting genuinely wins: very large scale where the managed premium becomes millions, a requirement the managed service cannot meet, or a team that already has deep operational expertise and spare capacity in it.

The same arithmetic applies to Kafka (MSK versus self-managed), Redis (ElastiCache versus a StatefulSet), and search (OpenSearch Service versus running Elasticsearch yourself). In each case, self-hosting on Kubernetes looks cheap on the infrastructure line and expensive on the calendar.

Kubernetes cluster baseline versus ECS. EKS charges about $0.10 per hour per cluster ($73 a month) for the control plane. That is not the real cost.

Text
Realistic EKS baseline, before any application pod:
  Control plane                                        $73
  System workloads: CoreDNS, kube-proxy, CNI, CSI      included in node cost
  Cluster autoscaler / Karpenter                       small
  Ingress controller (2 replicas)                      ~$40 of node capacity
  Observability DaemonSets (agent per node)            ~5 to 10 percent of every node
  Cert-manager, external-secrets, ArgoCD               ~$60 of node capacity
  Node overhead: kubelet + OS reserved, ~10 percent    ~$80 on an 8-node cluster
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Effective baseline                                   $250 to $400/month
  Plus: a person who understands it. This is the real cost.

ECS on Fargate baseline:
  No control plane charge, no nodes, no DaemonSets, no CNI to tune
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Effective baseline                                   ~$0 to $40/month

For a team running 6 services with modest traffic, ECS or App Runner is cheaper in dollars and dramatically cheaper in attention. Kubernetes starts paying for itself when you have enough workloads that bin-packing, spot flexibility, and a shared platform genuinely amortise — typically dozens of services and a team big enough to have someone who owns the platform.

The question to ask is not "is Kubernetes good?" but "do we have enough workloads for a shared platform to be cheaper than a managed one, including the person who runs it?"

Multi-region roughly doubles everything. Not exactly double, but close enough to plan with:

Component Multi-region effect
Compute ~2x (both regions must handle failover load, or you accept degraded capacity)
Database ~2x, plus cross-region replication transfer at about $0.02 per GB
Object storage ~2x with Cross-Region Replication, plus per-GB transfer
Kafka ~2x plus MirrorMaker traffic
Observability ~2x volume
Engineering Every deployment, migration and incident now has two of everything

Part 50's DR ladder is the disciplined way to buy a fraction of this: pilot light gives you most of the resilience for roughly 15 to 25 percent of the cost of full active-active, and that is the trade most companies should make.

Failure scenario

A 14-person startup adopted microservices at the design stage, before they had users. Eighteen months later: 19 services, an EKS cluster, a service mesh, MSK, four RDS instances, and a monthly bill of $23,000 serving 90 requests per second — about 230 million requests a month, which is $0.0001 per request against a product generating very little revenue per request.

Two engineers spent most of their time on platform work. Feature velocity was roughly a third of what it had been at service number four. The CTO's summary in the retrospective: "We bought the operational complexity of a company with 200 engineers and we have 14."

They consolidated to four services and one database over two quarters. The bill fell to $4,800, and — the number that actually mattered — the number of pull requests shipped per week roughly doubled, because a change no longer required coordinating three deploys.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They put the recurring monthly cost of an architecture in the design document, next to the latency and availability targets. Not as an objection, as a fact.

They price engineer time in every build-versus-buy comparison, at a fully loaded rate, and they include the on-call and interrupt cost, not just the build cost.

They count baseline separately from marginal cost. Baseline is what an architecture costs to exist; marginal is what it costs to serve traffic. Distributed architectures have terrible baselines and often good marginal costs, which is exactly why they are wrong for small systems and right for large ones.

And they are willing to say the unpopular thing in a design review: "this split does not pay for itself yet; let us keep it as a module and revisit at 10x traffic."

51.7 The best architecture is not the most sophisticated architecture

This section is an argument, so let me make it concretely, with two systems that serve identical traffic.

System A: a modular monolith. One NestJS application, organised into modules with enforced boundaries (orders, inventory, catalog, payments, notifications), each with its own service layer, its own schema in one PostgreSQL database, and no cross-module imports except through published interfaces. Three pods. One RDS instance. One Redis. One queue for background work.

Text
System A monthly cost, 500 RPS peak:
  3 Fargate tasks (1 vCPU / 2 GB)                     $108
  Workers, KEDA scale-to-zero, ~0.6 avg tasks          $22
  RDS db.r6g.large Multi-AZ, reserved                 $220
  ElastiCache cache.t4g.medium x2                      $90
  ALB                                                  $25
  S3 + CloudFront (modest asset volume)                $60
  Logs, metrics, traces (one service)                 $120
  NAT + endpoints                                     $110
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  Total                                              ~$755/month
  Team: 4 engineers, no platform specialist.
  Deploy: one pipeline, ~7 minutes.
  Debugging a slow request: one stack trace.

System B: twelve microservices. The same product, decomposed: orders, order-items, inventory, reservations, catalog, search, pricing, payments, notifications, users, carts, analytics-ingest. EKS, a service mesh, MSK for inter-service events, three separate RDS instances, OpenSearch, Redis.

Text
System B monthly cost, the SAME 500 RPS peak:
  EKS control plane                                     $73
  Nodes: 6 x m7g.xlarge (mesh sidecars add ~30% CPU)   $714
  Platform workloads (ingress, mesh, agents, ArgoCD)   $180
  MSK: 3 x kafka.m5.large + storage                    $560
  RDS x3 (orders, inventory, catalog), Multi-AZ         $840
  OpenSearch 3 nodes                                   $420
  ElastiCache                                          $150
  ALBs and ingress                                      $90
  Cross-AZ transfer (mesh doubles the hops)            $380
  NAT + endpoints                                      $210
  Logs, metrics, traces (12 services, 12x cardinality) $1,150
  CI minutes (12 pipelines)                            $180
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  Total                                             ~$4,947/month

  Plus one platform engineer, fully loaded ~$12,000/month.
  Deploy: 12 pipelines; a cross-cutting change needs coordination.
  Debugging a slow request: a distributed trace across 6 hops,
  if sampling captured it.

Infrastructure: 6.5x. Including the platform engineer: about 22x. Same traffic. Same product.

The complexity is not free even when the money is available, and the money is rarely the binding constraint. The binding constraint is that System B needs a person, and that person is not building the product.

When the sophisticated option genuinely pays for itself. This is not an argument that microservices are wrong. They are right when the thing they buy is worth the baseline. Real reasons, in rough order of how often they are actually true:

  1. Independent scaling of a genuinely different workload. The image processor needs 32 GB of RAM and GPU-adjacent CPU for 20 minutes a day. Running that inside the API's pods means every API pod is sized for it. Splitting it out saves money rather than costing it.
  2. Team autonomy at scale. Above roughly 30 to 50 engineers, the coordination cost of one deployable becomes the dominant cost, and service boundaries that match team boundaries buy back velocity. Below that, they mostly buy overhead. (This is Conway's Law used deliberately rather than suffered accidentally.)
  3. Genuinely different availability or compliance requirements. The payments module needs PCI scope isolation; keeping it in the monolith drags the whole application into scope. That is a legitimate, expensive-to-ignore reason.
  4. Different technology needs. A machine learning inference service in Python, a real-time gateway in Go. A polyglot boundary is a real boundary.
  5. Independent failure domains that matter. The analytics ingest pipeline must not be able to take checkout down. Sometimes a bulkhead inside one process is enough (Part 31); sometimes it genuinely is not.

Notice what is not on that list: "it is more modern", "it scales better" (a monolith on 30 pods scales fine), "it is what the big companies do" (they have the engineers), and "we might need it later" (you can split later, and splitting a well-modularised monolith is far easier than merging twelve services).

Boring technology. There is a discipline, sometimes called the innovation-token model, that is worth adopting explicitly: you get a small number of tokens to spend on unproven technology, and everything else should be boring. Boring means: you know its failure modes, you can hire for it, its documentation exists, and its problems have been solved publicly by thousands of people.

PostgreSQL is boring. It also does full-text search, JSON documents, queues (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), geospatial, time-series with partitioning, and pub/sub. A very large number of systems that run Elasticsearch, MongoDB, Redis Streams and a message broker could run on PostgreSQL alone until they are considerably larger than they are — with one thing to back up, one thing to monitor, one thing to be on call for, and one set of failure modes to learn.

Spend your tokens where the product is differentiated. Nobody has ever won a market because their queue was interesting.

The cost of complexity, measured in people. This is the part that dollar figures hide, and it is the real argument.

Text
System A: 4 engineers, all building product.
System B: 4 engineers building product, 1 building and running the platform,
          and each of the 4 spends roughly 20 percent of their time on
          cross-service coordination, distributed debugging, and deploys.

Effective product capacity:
  System A: 4.0 engineers
  System B: 3.2 engineers, from a team of 5

System B costs 25 percent more headcount and delivers 20 percent less.
That is a 45 percent swing in the only metric that determines whether
the company survives.

The senior position is not "monoliths good, microservices bad". It is this: complexity must be paid for, in money and in attention, and attention is the scarcer currency. Adopt complexity when you can name what it buys, and when what it buys is worth more than what it costs. Otherwise, choose the boring option, keep your modules clean so you can split later, and spend the difference on the product.

The simplest architecture that meets the requirement wins. That has been the position of this entire book, and cost is simply the most measurable evidence for it.

51.8 Cost review practices

Concept

Optimisation without operation decays. A team that spends a quarter cutting 50 percent will be back to the original number within a year unless the practice becomes routine. These are the routines.

How it works

The monthly cost review. Sixty minutes, a named owner, a fixed agenda:

  1. Total and unit economics. Total spend, cost per order, both against last month and against six months ago. The unit number is the one that gets discussed.
  2. Top five movers. Which line items changed by more than 10 percent, and why. Every one gets an explanation or an action item.
  3. Untagged percentage. If it went up, find out what got created without tags.
  4. Top five by absolute size. Not to cut, but to confirm someone still owns each.
  5. Waste register. A standing list of known waste with owners and dates: idle environments, orphaned volumes, unused replicas, snapshots past their expiry.
  6. Upcoming changes. Anything shipping next month with a cost impact, flagged in advance.

The output is action items with owners, not a document. Thirty minutes of preparation and thirty of discussion.

Anomaly alerts. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection (or the equivalent) learns your normal spend per service and alerts on statistically unusual changes. Configure it per service and per account, with a threshold low enough to catch a $200 a day surprise, because a $200 a day surprise is $6,000 a month.

JSON
{
  "AnomalyDetectorName": "per-service-monitor",
  "MonitorType": "DIMENSIONAL",
  "MonitorDimension": "SERVICE",
  "Subscribers": [{ "Type": "SNS", "Address": "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:cost-alerts" }],
  "Threshold": 100,
  "Frequency": "DAILY"
}

Route it to a Slack channel the team actually reads, not to an inbox. The value of an anomaly alert is entirely in how fast someone sees it: a runaway log loop caught in 24 hours costs $200, and caught in 30 days costs $6,000.

Budgets. Set a budget per environment and per team, with alerts at 80, 100 and 120 percent of the forecast. Budgets are a conversation trigger, not a control. Resist the temptation to attach automated actions that stop resources — the failure mode where a budget action shuts down production is worse than any overspend.

The exception where hard controls are correct: developer sandboxes and ephemeral environments, where an automatic shutdown at a threshold is exactly right.

Cost as an explicit line in design reviews. Add one required section to the design document template:

Text
COST IMPACT
  Recurring monthly cost:      $____ (itemised)
  One-off cost:                $____
  Cost per order impact:       $____
  What we are buying with it:  ____
  Cheaper alternative considered and why rejected: ____

This changes behaviour more than any dashboard. It does not require anyone to say no; it requires the number to exist. Most over-engineering dies quietly at the moment someone has to write "$4,900 a month" in a box.

Showback, not chargeback. Showback means each team sees its own cost, attributed by tag, in a dashboard, monthly. Chargeback means the cost is billed to the team's budget.

Showback works. It creates awareness and mild social accountability without turning cost into a weapon. Chargeback tends to produce gaming: teams hide costs in shared accounts, refuse to adopt shared platforms, and argue about allocation methodology instead of reducing spend. Start with showback, and only consider chargeback if the organisation genuinely needs the financial rigour.

The cost checklist. Run this quarterly. Each row is a specific question with a specific fix.

Item Typical waste Fix Expected saving
Over-provisioned pod requests 40 to 60 percent of reserved CPU unused Right-size from p95/p99 over 14 days 20 to 40 percent of compute
x86 instances for Node.js 20 to 30 percent premium Migrate to Graviton with multi-arch images 20 to 30 percent of compute
Non-production running 24/7 70 percent of hours idle Scheduled scale-down nights and weekends 60 to 70 percent of non-prod
Workers running continuously 90 percent idle KEDA scale-to-zero on queue depth 70 to 90 percent of worker compute
On-demand database pricing 35 to 60 percent premium 1-year Reserved Instance or Savings Plan 35 to 40 percent of database
Unused read replicas A full instance each Audit consumers, delete or downsize $175 to $700 each
Unused indexes Storage plus write amplification pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0, drop concurrently Storage plus 10 to 30 percent write latency
Aurora Standard on write-heavy load I/O charges exceeding the instance Switch to I/O-Optimized above ~25 percent I/O share 20 to 40 percent of Aurora spend
S3 without lifecycle rules Everything in Standard forever Tier to IA and Glacier; expire non-current versions and incomplete multiparts 40 to 60 percent of S3
Snapshot sprawl Manual snapshots never deleted expires tag plus a scheduled cleanup job $100 to $500
S3 traffic through NAT $0.045 per GB avoidable S3 gateway VPC endpoint (free) $50 to $500
Cross-AZ chatter $0.02 per GB round trip Topology-aware routing, rack-aware Kafka 30 to 60 percent of transfer
Debug logging in production 10x volume for no value Runtime log levels, drop probe logs, redact bodies 50 to 80 percent of log spend
Unbounded metric labels Millions of series Route patterns not URLs; ban id labels in review 50 to 90 percent of custom metrics
100 percent trace sampling Vast span volume 1 to 10 percent head sampling, 100 percent on errors 80 to 95 percent of trace spend
Orphaned resources Unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers, old AMIs, unused EIPs Monthly sweep by tag and last-used date $100 to $1,000

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make the number visible and then get out of the way. Engineers are competitive and conscientious; a team that can see its own cost per order will optimise it without being told.

They run the review even in months when nothing changed, because the discipline is the point and the anomaly you catch is the one you were not looking for.

They put cost in the design template rather than in a policy document, because templates change behaviour and policies do not.

And they protect the practice from becoming a cost-cutting programme. The goal is efficiency, which means getting more per dollar, not spending fewer dollars. A team that doubles traffic on a flat bill has done outstanding work, and the review should say so.

51.9 Edge cases and failure modes

The specific ways cost goes wrong, each of which has happened to a real team.

  • A cost spike from a log loop. A retry inside a catch block that logs the full error object, including the response body, on every attempt. One deploy, 40 GB an hour, $500 a day on ingestion and indexing. Fix: anomaly alerts with a daily threshold, log volume per service as a monitored metric with a budget, and a rule that error objects are logged once at the boundary, not at every layer.

  • Runaway autoscaling amplifying a retry storm. A downstream dependency slows down; clients retry; request volume triples; the HPA scales from 8 to 24 pods; the extra pods open more connections to the struggling dependency and make it worse; the autoscaler keeps going. You pay 3x for compute and extend the outage. Fix: circuit breakers, bounded retries with jitter, load shedding, and a maxReplicas that reflects what the downstream can actually take (Part 31).

  • A forgotten load-test environment. Someone clones production to run a capacity test before a launch. The launch happens. The environment stays. Eleven months and $18,000 later, an audit finds it. Fix: mandatory expires tags with a job that deletes or alerts on expiry, and ephemeral environments created by pipeline and destroyed on merge.

  • Cross-region replication egress. S3 Cross-Region Replication charges per GB replicated and stores a second copy. A bucket receiving 30 TB a month of new objects, replicated, costs the transfer plus the duplicate storage indefinitely. Fix: replicate only the prefixes that need it, and check whether a cheaper DR posture (Part 50) meets the actual requirement.

  • S3 request charges from a polling loop. A worker checks for a file's existence every second with HeadObject. That is 2.6 million requests a month per worker, which is small; but the same pattern applied per-tenant across 400 tenants is over a billion requests and thousands of dollars. Fix: S3 event notifications to SQS or EventBridge instead of polling. Push, do not poll.

  • A recursive Lambda. A function writes to the S3 bucket that triggers it. Each invocation spawns another. Concurrency climbs to the account limit within minutes, and it can run for hours before anyone notices. Fix: never write into the triggering prefix, use separate buckets or prefixes for input and output, set a reserved concurrency limit on every function, and configure a billing alarm with a short evaluation period. AWS now has recursive-invocation detection, but do not rely on it as the only control.

  • Over-aggressive scale-down causing an outage. Covered in 51.2's failure scenario, and worth repeating because it is the most common way a cost optimisation causes an incident: short scale-down windows and low minReplicas remove the capacity that absorbs the next burst.

  • Reserved capacity that no longer matches the workload. A 3-year all-upfront reservation on db.r6i bought two months before the team migrates to Graviton, or a Savings Plan sized for a workload that then moves to Fargate. You keep paying. Fix: prefer 1-year no-upfront terms and Compute Savings Plans (which are flexible across instance family, size, region and Fargate/Lambda) over EC2 Instance Savings Plans; buy to 70 to 80 percent of your stable baseline, never to 100 percent; review coverage quarterly against the roadmap.

  • Unbounded queue retention. A dead-letter queue with no retention limit and no consumer accumulates for years. Kafka topics with retention.ms = -1 set "temporarily" during a migration. Both are storage bills that grow forever and, worse, mean a replay would process millions of messages nobody expects. Fix: explicit retention on every topic and queue, and a monitor for DLQ depth that alerts on growth rather than on an absolute number.

  • Developer database snapshots piling up. Every engineer takes a manual snapshot before a risky change. Nobody deletes them. At $0.095 per GB-month against a 2 TB allocated database, forty of them is not free. Fix: expires tag enforced at creation, plus a weekly job that deletes expired manual snapshots and reports what it removed.

  • Cutting cost until resilience drops below the SLO. The most important one on this list. Under a cost mandate, the easiest things to delete are the things that do nothing on a normal day: the standby instance, the extra replica, the backup retention, the staging environment, the distributed tracing, the over-provisioning headroom. Every one of them is insurance, and insurance looks like waste right up until the day it does not.

    The discipline that prevents it: for every proposed cut, write down which SLO or recovery target it affects and by how much. "Drop Multi-AZ: saves $880, changes database failover from 90 seconds to a 90 minute restore, which breaches our 30 minute RTO" is a decision the business can make. Silently dropping Multi-AZ is not a decision, it is an accident waiting for a date.

    A senior engineer's job in a cost-cutting exercise is to make the resilience trade-offs visible and to refuse the invisible ones. You will be right eventually, and being right after the incident is worth far less than being right before it.

Senior Checklist — Part 51

  • I understand the concept of cost as a non-functional requirement
  • I can explain unit economics simply and compute cost per order for my system
  • I can implement tagging, showback and a cost dashboard
  • I understand the failure modes of cost optimisation, especially resilience loss
  • I understand the scaling implications: which costs are baseline and which are marginal
  • I understand the security implications of cost decisions, such as reduced backup retention
  • I understand the operational implications: reviews, budgets, anomaly alerts
  • I can choose between Lambda, Fargate, EC2 and Kubernetes on cost grounds
  • I can explain the trade-offs of managed versus self-hosted with engineer time priced in
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions on cloud cost
  • I know the difference between Kubernetes requests and limits and which one I pay for
  • I can find cross-AZ transfer, NAT per-GB and log ingestion as separate line items on my bill
  • I know the Aurora I/O break-even and can check it for my workload
  • I can identify unused indexes and idle read replicas in my database
  • I put a monthly cost figure in every design document I write
  • I can name what each proposed cost cut does to an SLO or a recovery target

Part 51 — Key Takeaways

  • Cost is a non-functional requirement decided by engineers at design time; the bill is a printout of your architecture.
  • Track cost per order, per request or per user, not the total bill. The total moves with traffic and tells you nothing.
  • Tag first, optimise second. Optimising without visibility deletes load-bearing things.
  • In Kubernetes you pay for requests, not limits. Over-requested pods are the largest source of structural compute waste.
  • Graviton, spot for interruptible work, scale-to-zero workers and shutting down non-production out of hours routinely cut compute by half with no resilience loss.
  • Lambda is cheaper below roughly 30 to 50 RPS sustained and roughly an order of magnitude more expensive above it.
  • Reserve your database capacity first: it is the most stable workload and the discount is the biggest zero-risk lever you have.
  • Unused indexes and idle read replicas charge you twice, in storage and in write throughput; on Aurora Standard a bad query is billed per I/O.
  • The three invisible line items are cross-AZ transfer, NAT gateway per-GB charges and log volume. The S3 gateway endpoint is free and removes a whole category of the second one.
  • Caches and CDNs are arbitrage: cheap capacity replacing expensive capacity, and faster as well. Size the database for a cold cache, not a warm one.
  • Microservices multiply the baseline: every service costs $90 to $1,000 a month before serving a request, and needs an on-call owner.
  • The best architecture is the simplest one that meets the requirement. Complexity is paid for in attention, and attention is scarcer than money.
  • Never cut cost without naming which SLO or recovery target it affects. Insurance looks like waste until the day it does not.

Part 52 — Infrastructure as Code

What you will learn

  1. 52.1Why infrastructure as code
  2. 52.2Terraform fundamentals
  3. 52.3State management
  4. 52.4Structuring Terraform and the alternatives
  5. 52.5IaC in CI/CD and policy as code

  8. 52.8Layout, blast radius, environments and testing

The servers, databases, load balancers, networks and permissions your application runs on are infrastructure, and how you create and change that infrastructure matters as much as how you write code. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining infrastructure in text files, version-controlled and applied by tooling, instead of clicking through a cloud console by hand. This Part teaches IaC from the ground up for a backend engineer: why it exists, Terraform fundamentals, state management, structuring it for many environments, the alternatives (Pulumi, CDK, CloudFormation), IaC in CI/CD, policy as code, GitOps for Kubernetes, secrets handling, and the real incident that explains why the guardrails matter.

The running example is the infrastructure for a NestJS service on AWS — a network, a PostgreSQL database, a Redis cache, a container runtime and the permissions tying them together — defined as code. This Part builds on cloud services (see Part 46 — Cloud Architecture, especially 46.13 and 46.16), Kubernetes (see Part 45 — Kubernetes, 45.19) and CI/CD (see Part 47 — CI/CD and Deployment Strategies), turning the "how do you create this infrastructure" question those raise into a disciplined, codified answer. Sections 52.1 to 52.6 introduce each idea. Sections 52.7 to 52.13 go to production depth: the Terraform language features that cause and prevent incidents (for_each, moved, import and removed blocks, lifecycle rules), layout and module versioning, Pulumi and CDK side by side, a real plan-and-apply pipeline, Rego policies, Argo CD and Kustomize, and secrets that never touch state. Section 52.14 is the full worked example in Terraform, and 52.15 retells the terraform apply that deleted a production database, minute by minute, with every guardrail that would have stopped it.

52.1 Why infrastructure as code

52.1.1 Clickops, reproducibility and the case for IaC

Concept

The alternative to IaC is clickops: creating and changing infrastructure by hand in the cloud provider's web console. IaC replaces that with text files that describe the desired infrastructure, which a tool reads and makes real. The infrastructure's definition becomes code: versioned in Git, reviewed in pull requests, repeatable across environments, and auditable — the same engineering discipline you apply to application code, applied to the servers it runs on.

Why does it exist?

Clickops does not scale and is not safe. Infrastructure built by clicking is undocumented (the only record is what exists, and you cannot easily see why or who changed it), unrepeatable (recreating it in another region or after a disaster means remembering every click), inconsistent (staging and production drift apart because they were clicked separately), and unreviewable (a wrong click in production has no pull request and no second pair of eyes). IaC exists to fix all of this: the infrastructure is described once, applied identically everywhere, changed through reviewed pull requests, and recoverable from the code. It brings version control, review, repeatability and auditability to infrastructure.

Mental model

Clickops is assembling furniture from memory with no instructions — it might work once, but you cannot reliably build the same thing again, nobody can check your work, and if it breaks you are guessing at what you did. IaC is having the assembly instructions written down: anyone can build the identical thing, the instructions are reviewed before use, you can see exactly what changed between versions, and if something breaks you consult the written plan. Infrastructure as code turns "I think I set it up like this" into a precise, shared, versioned document that also builds the thing.

How it works

Text
Clickops:                                   Infrastructure as Code:
  open the console                            write a .tf file describing the infra
  click to create a database                  commit it, open a pull request
  click to set its size, network, backups     a teammate reviews the change
  ...no record of why or who                  CI shows a plan of what will change
  recreate elsewhere = remember every click   apply -> the tool makes it real, identically

With IaC you write files declaring the desired state ("a PostgreSQL database of this size, in this network, with these backups"), and the tool figures out what to create, change or leave alone to match that declaration. The files live in Git, so changes go through pull requests and review (see Part 5 — Git Basics, 5.3, and Part 48 — Git from Intermediate to Senior, 48.13), and the history shows every infrastructure change with its reason. The same files applied to staging and production produce consistent environments. If the infrastructure is lost, you reapply the code. (Reapplying rebuilds the infrastructure, not the data in it: a recreated database is empty until you restore a backup, see Part 50 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery.)

Practical example

A team runs a NestJS orders API on AWS that was built by hand two years ago: one VPC, an RDS PostgreSQL instance, an ElastiCache Redis cluster, an ECS service behind an ALB, about 15 security groups and 30 IAM policies. Nobody can say which security group rules are still needed. Staging was cloned by hand and differs in 40-odd settings. A new region launch is planned. The IaC path is incremental: write Terraform for the existing resources, adopt them into state with import blocks (52.7) without recreating anything, run terraform plan until it shows "No changes", then make every future change through a pull request. After that, the new region is the same code with a different variable file.

Production scenario

A company with 25 services and three environments manages about 4,000 AWS resources in roughly 60 Terraform root configurations (52.8). A typical week has 40–60 infrastructure pull requests; each shows its plan in the PR, policy checks run in about 30 seconds, and applies run from CI. The nightly drift job runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode against every root and reports 2–5 drifted resources a week, almost all from emergency console fixes or AWS-side changes, each turned into code or reverted within a day. Rebuilding a full staging environment from scratch takes about 50 minutes of apply time, most of it RDS and ElastiCache creation.

Failure scenario (clickops disaster)

A critical production database's automated backups had been disabled months earlier — someone had clicked the setting off during a one-time maintenance task and never re-enabled it, with no record of the change. When the database later suffered corruption, there was no recent backup to restore from, and data was lost. In an IaC world, the backup setting would be declared in code (backup_retention_period = 30), any change to it would be a reviewed pull request with a visible reason, and drift detection (52.2) would have flagged that the live setting no longer matched the code. The invisible, unreviewed, forgotten click is exactly the failure mode IaC prevents. The lesson: infrastructure changed by hand has no record, no review and no safety net, and the gap stays hidden until it causes an incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • IaC that reverts an emergency fix. Someone raises a connection limit by hand during an incident; the next unrelated apply quietly puts it back, and the incident recurs. Codify emergency changes the same day.
  • Partial IaC. Half the resources in code, half by hand; the code looks authoritative but is not. Track coverage (resources in state versus resources in the account).
  • Resources created by other tools. Auto Scaling creates instances, ECS creates tasks, Kubernetes creates load balancers; do not try to manage those in Terraform, manage the thing that creates them.
  • Console read access is still fine. IaC does not mean nobody may look at the console; it means changes go through code.
  • IaC itself can destroy at scale. One wrong apply can delete more in a minute than clickops could in a day; that is why 52.5 and 52.15 exist.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats all infrastructure as code and clickops as a liability to be eliminated, because unmanaged manual changes are undocumented, unrepeatable, inconsistent and unreviewable — the conditions under which quiet, dangerous drift accumulates until it causes an incident. They want every piece of infrastructure declared in version-controlled files, changed only through reviewed pull requests with a visible plan of the effect, and applied identically across environments so staging genuinely resembles production. They value the audit trail (who changed what and why) and the disaster-recovery property (the infrastructure can be rebuilt from code). They allow manual console changes only in genuine emergencies and then immediately bring the change back into code, because a live environment that no longer matches its code is drift waiting to surprise someone.

Common mistakes

  • Managing production infrastructure by clickops, leaving it undocumented and unrepeatable.
  • Making a quiet manual change (disabling a backup, opening a port) with no record or review.
  • Letting staging and production drift apart because they were built by hand separately.
  • Making an emergency manual change and never codifying it, creating drift.

Interview questions

  1. What is infrastructure as code and why use it over clickops?
    Show answerHide answer
    Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files applied by tooling instead of manual console clicks; it brings version control, review, repeatability, consistency across environments, and auditability to infrastructure.
  2. What are the dangers of clickops?
    Show answerHide answer
    Undocumented changes, unrepeatable setups, environment drift, no review of production changes, and no audit trail — conditions that hide dangerous misconfigurations until an incident.
  3. How does IaC help disaster recovery?
    Show answerHide answer
    The infrastructure is described in code, so it can be reapplied to rebuild the environment identically, rather than recreated from memory.
  4. What should you do after an emergency manual change?
    Show answerHide answer
    Bring it back into the code immediately, because a live environment that diverges from its code is drift that will surprise someone later.

Practical exercise

List the infrastructure for a simple web service (network, database, cache, compute, permissions) and, for each, note the problems of managing it by clickops (documentation, repeatability, review, drift) and how IaC addresses each. Then describe how the disabled-backup incident above would have been prevented by IaC. Acceptance criteria: you can articulate the four clickops problems and map each to an IaC benefit.

52.2 Terraform fundamentals

52.2.1 Providers, resources, plan and apply

Concept

Terraform is the most widely used IaC tool. You write declarations in its language (HCL) describing the resources you want — a network, a database, a server — and Terraform's workflow has two key steps: plan (show what changes it would make to reach the desired state) and apply (make those changes). A provider is a plugin that knows how to manage a particular platform's resources (AWS, GCP, Kubernetes). You declare the desired state; Terraform computes and applies the difference.

Why does it exist?

You need a tool that reads your infrastructure declarations and reconciles reality to match them — creating what is missing, changing what differs, leaving what matches, and removing what you deleted from the code. Doing this by hand (figuring out the API calls to create each resource in order, with dependencies) would be enormous and error-prone. Terraform exists to do that reconciliation declaratively and across many platforms via providers: you say what you want, it figures out how to get there, and it shows you the plan before it acts so there are no surprises.

Mental model

Terraform is like a meticulous contractor working from a blueprint. You hand over the blueprint (your declarations) describing the finished building. The contractor compares it to what is currently built (the current state), produces a punch list of exactly what will be added, changed or demolished (the plan), shows you that list for approval, and then does precisely that work (apply). You describe the end result; the contractor handles the ordering and the mechanics and never acts without showing you the plan first.

How it works

HCL
# A provider: which platform, and its configuration.
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

# A resource: a declaration of something you want to exist.
resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  identifier              = "orders-db"
  engine                  = "postgres"
  engine_version          = "17"
  instance_class          = "db.r6g.large"
  allocated_storage       = 100
  backup_retention_period = 30          # declared, reviewed, cannot be quietly disabled
  multi_az                = true
  db_subnet_group_name    = aws_db_subnet_group.orders.name   # private subnets (64.14)
  vpc_security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.orders_db.id]
  username                = "orders_admin"
  manage_master_user_password = true    # RDS generates the password in Secrets Manager (64.13)
  storage_encrypted       = true
  deletion_protection     = true        # AWS refuses to delete it, whatever Terraform says (64.15)
}

# Variables parameterize the config across environments.
variable "environment" { type = string }

# Outputs expose values (e.g. the database endpoint) for other code to use.
output "db_endpoint" { value = aws_db_instance.orders.endpoint }
Shell
terraform init      # download providers and set up the working directory
terraform plan      # show what Terraform WOULD change (no changes made) -- review this
terraform apply     # make the changes (after you confirm the plan)

The workflow's heart is plan before apply: terraform plan shows exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed, so you review the effect before anything happens. This is the safety mechanism — you never apply blind. Terraform is declarative: you describe the desired end state, not the steps, and it computes the difference from the current state (the state, 52.3) and makes only the needed changes. Modules (52.4) package reusable groups of resources; variables parameterize them; outputs expose values.

The destroy in the plan

A plan can show resources to be destroyed — this is where the danger lives. If you remove a resource from the code, or change a property that forces replacement, the plan shows a destroy. Reading the plan carefully for destroys, especially of stateful resources like databases, is critical: a plan that says it will destroy the production database must never be applied casually. This is the heart of the IaC incident in 52.6 and 52.15, and why the plan step and guardrails exist.

Here is what that looks like in a real plan. Changing identifier (or engine, or the subnet group, among others) cannot be done in place, so the AWS provider replaces the database:

Text
Terraform will perform the following actions:

  # aws_db_instance.orders must be replaced
-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
      ~ address                 = "orders-db.c9xk2l1abcd.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com" -> (known after apply)
      ~ arn                     = "arn:aws:rds:ap-south-1:111122223333:db:orders-db" -> (known after apply)
      ~ identifier              = "orders-db" -> "orders-primary" # forces replacement
        instance_class          = "db.r6g.large"
        # (41 unchanged attributes hidden)
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

Three symbols to know: + create, ~ update in place, -/+ destroy then create (or +/- create then destroy, with create_before_destroy). The comment # forces replacement names the argument responsible. For a database, -/+ means a new, empty database and the old one deleted. Changing instance_class instead shows ~ (an in-place modify, applied by AWS during the next maintenance window unless apply_immediately = true).

Production scenario

For a team applying 10–20 changes a day, plans for a root configuration with 300 resources take 20–60 seconds, most of it refreshing state against AWS APIs. Applies of routine changes (a task count, a security group rule) take under a minute; creating an RDS instance takes 8–15 minutes, a Multi-AZ ElastiCache replication group 10–20 minutes. The plan is posted to the pull request, the reviewer scrolls straight to the summary line (Plan: N to add, N to change, N to destroy) and then to every -/+ and -.

Failure scenario

An engineer bumped engine_version on a staging database from "16.4" to "17" to test an upgrade, and the plan said ~ update in-place, which looked harmless. On apply, RDS rejected it because a major version upgrade needs allow_major_version_upgrade = true. After adding that, the apply succeeded, and the staging database was unavailable for about 20 minutes during the upgrade, in the middle of a QA session. Nothing was wrong with Terraform; the plan was accurate about what would change, but it does not show how long a change takes or whether it causes downtime. The lesson: a plan tells you what changes, not what it costs; for stateful resources you also need to know the provider's behaviour for that argument (in-place but with downtime, deferred to a maintenance window, or forcing replacement).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • (known after apply) hides the real value. A plan cannot show what AWS will generate; changes that depend on those values only surface at apply.
  • Plan is a snapshot. If someone changes the infrastructure between plan and apply, the saved plan fails to apply as "stale"; that is a feature.
  • Provider upgrades change plans. A new provider version can add a default or change how an argument is read, showing diffs nobody wrote. Pin versions (52.7).
  • Long applies get interrupted. A CI job killed mid-apply leaves resources created but not recorded, or a stale lock; rerun plan and reconcile before doing anything else.
  • Destroy of a resource you did not touch. A resource that depends on a replaced one (a parameter group, a security group) can be replaced too; read the whole plan, not only the lines you expected.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats terraform plan as a mandatory review step and reads it carefully every time, with particular attention to anything marked for destruction or replacement, because the plan is the last chance to catch a change that would delete a database or recreate something stateful. They keep the configuration declarative and let Terraform compute the diff, rather than reasoning about imperative steps. They parameterize with variables so one configuration serves multiple environments consistently (52.4), and expose values via outputs rather than hardcoding. They know that a Terraform apply is a powerful, potentially destructive action, so they wrap it in the guardrails of the rest of this Part — plan on pull request, review, approvals, and protection on stateful resources (52.5) — and never run a casual apply against production without reading the plan.

Common mistakes

  • Running apply without reading the plan, missing a destructive change.
  • Not noticing a resource marked for destroy or replace, especially a stateful one (database).
  • Hardcoding environment-specific values instead of using variables.
  • Not using modules, so configuration is copy-pasted and drifts.

Interview questions

  1. What do terraform plan and terraform apply do, and why is plan important?
    Show answerHide answer
    plan shows exactly what would be created, changed or destroyed without acting; apply makes the changes; plan is the mandatory review step that catches destructive changes before they happen.
  2. What is a provider and a resource in Terraform?
    Show answerHide answer
    A provider is a plugin that manages a platform's resources (AWS, GCP, Kubernetes); a resource is a declaration of a piece of infrastructure you want to exist.
  3. Why is Terraform declarative, and what does it compute?
    Show answerHide answer
    You declare the desired end state; Terraform computes the difference from the current state and makes only the needed changes.
