  4. What is the most dangerous thing a plan can show, and how do you handle it?
    Show answerHide answer
    A destroy or forced replacement of a stateful resource (like a database); read plans carefully for these and guard stateful resources against accidental destruction (52.5).

Practical exercise

Write a Terraform configuration declaring a PostgreSQL database with backups enabled and multi-AZ, parameterized by an environment variable, with the endpoint as an output. Run terraform plan (against a sandbox or with a dry setup) and read the plan to identify what it would create. Then change the instance class and observe whether the plan shows a modify or a replace. Acceptance criteria: you can read the plan, identify creates versus replaces, and explain why a replace of a database would be dangerous.

52.3 State management

52.3.1 Remote state, locking and drift

Concept

Terraform keeps a state file recording what it created and how the declarations map to real resources. This state is how Terraform knows the current reality to compute the diff against. State management — where the state lives, how concurrent access is controlled (locking), and detecting when reality has diverged from state (drift) — is one of the most important and error-prone parts of using Terraform.

Why does it exist?

Terraform needs to know what already exists to decide what to change, and it cannot reliably rediscover every resource from the cloud each time, so it records a mapping in the state file. That file becomes critical: it is the source of truth for what Terraform manages. If two people apply at once, they can corrupt it or make conflicting changes, so locking exists. If someone changes a resource by hand (clickops), reality diverges from the state — drift — and Terraform's plan will try to "correct" it, so drift must be detected and understood. State management exists because the state file is both essential and fragile, and sharing it safely across a team requires deliberate handling.

Mental model

The state file is Terraform's memory of what it built — its inventory list mapping "the database I call orders" to the actual cloud resource. If this memory is lost, Terraform forgets it owns those resources and may try to recreate them; if two people edit the memory at once, it gets scrambled; if someone changes a resource without updating the memory, Terraform's view and reality disagree. Remote state is keeping this memory in a shared, safe place rather than on one person's laptop; locking is ensuring only one person edits the memory at a time; drift detection is noticing when the memory and the real world have diverged.

How it works

  • Remote state: the state file is stored in a shared remote backend (an S3 bucket, a Terraform Cloud workspace), not on an individual's laptop, so the whole team works from one state and it is not lost if a laptop dies. Local state on one machine is a recipe for disaster on a team.
  • Locking: the backend locks the state during a plan or apply so two people cannot write simultaneously and corrupt the state or make conflicting changes. With the S3 backend, Terraform 1.10 and later can lock with a lock file in the bucket itself (use_lockfile = true); the older mechanism, a DynamoDB table (dynamodb_table), still works but is deprecated.
  • State drift: when a resource is changed outside Terraform (a manual console change), the real resource no longer matches the state. terraform plan detects this (it shows the resource would be changed back to match the code) — so drift surfaces as unexpected changes in a plan. The response is to either bring the change into code or let Terraform reconcile it, but never ignore it.
  • Importing existing resources: resources created before Terraform (or by hand) can be brought under management with terraform import, which adds them to the state so Terraform manages them going forward — the path from clickops to IaC for existing infrastructure.
Text
Remote state in a shared backend (S3 + a lock table):
  developer A: terraform apply -> acquires lock -> reads state -> plans -> applies -> updates state -> releases lock
  developer B: terraform apply while A holds the lock -> waits (locking prevents a clash)

Drift:
  someone changes the DB instance class by hand in the console
  -> terraform plan now shows it would change it BACK to the code's value
  -> the drift is visible; you codify the change or let Terraform reconcile it

Practical example

The backend for the production network and data layer of the orders service, plus the bucket that holds it (the bucket itself is created once by a small bootstrap configuration with local state, then never touched):

HCL
# envs/production/data/backend.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10.0"
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-tfstate-prod-111122223333"
    key          = "orders/production/data.tfstate"   # one state file per root configuration
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    kms_key_id   = "arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:111122223333:key/0a1b2c3d-4e5f-6789-abcd-ef0123456789"
    use_lockfile = true                               # S3-native locking (Terraform 1.10+)
  }
}
HCL
# bootstrap/state-bucket.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "tfstate" {
  bucket = "acme-tfstate-prod-111122223333"
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "tfstate" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.tfstate.id
  versioning_configuration { status = "Enabled" }      # every state write is a recoverable version
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "tfstate" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.tfstate.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

Useful state commands, all of which take the lock: terraform state list (what is managed), terraform state show aws_db_instance.orders (what Terraform believes), terraform plan -refresh-only (show drift without proposing to change real resources), and terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> (only after confirming the holder is truly dead).

Failure scenario

At 16:20 a CI apply for the production data layer was cancelled by a runner timeout halfway through modifying an ElastiCache parameter group. The lock stayed in place, so the next pipeline failed with Error acquiring the state lock. An engineer, under pressure to ship a fix, ran terraform force-unlock and then an apply from a laptop with an older checkout of the code. That apply saw the state the cancelled job had partially written and planned to revert two changes merged that morning; it was caught only because the plan showed unexpected ~ lines on resources the engineer had not touched. The recovery: restore nothing, stop, rerun plan from the main branch in CI, and let the pipeline finish the interrupted change. The rules added: force-unlock only from CI with a second person, never apply from a stale checkout, and S3 versioning on the state bucket so a bad write can be rolled back. The lesson: a lock error is a question ("is someone else changing this?"), not an obstacle to remove.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lost state. Without versioning, a corrupted or deleted state file means Terraform no longer knows it owns anything; a plan would propose creating everything again. Version the bucket; restore the previous object.
  • Secrets in state. Any attribute a provider returns is stored, including generated passwords; encrypt, restrict, and avoid putting secrets there at all (52.13).
  • One giant state. 3,000 resources in one state means slow plans (minutes), one lock for every team, and a huge blast radius; split by layer and service (52.8).
  • Cross-state references. terraform_remote_state gives a consumer read access to the whole other state, secrets included; prefer publishing specific outputs to SSM Parameter Store and reading them with a data source.
  • Hand-editing state JSON. Never; use state mv, state rm, or better, moved, removed and import blocks (52.7), which are reviewable.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior always uses remote state with locking for any shared infrastructure, never local state on a laptop, because local state is lost when the laptop dies and offers no protection against two people applying at once. They treat the state file as sensitive and critical — it maps to real resources and can contain secrets (52.6) — so it is stored securely with access control. They watch for drift: an unexpected change in a plan means someone changed something by hand, and they investigate rather than blindly applying, because the plan might be about to undo a necessary emergency fix or reveal an unauthorized change. They use terraform import to bring existing clickops resources under management incrementally. State discipline is, in their view, the difference between Terraform being a reliable tool and a source of its own incidents.

Common mistakes

  • Local state on one laptop for shared infrastructure, risking loss and conflicts.
  • No locking, so concurrent applies corrupt the state.
  • Ignoring drift shown in a plan instead of investigating its cause.
  • Treating the state file as non-sensitive when it can contain secrets and maps to real resources.
  • Not importing existing resources, so Terraform tries to recreate things that already exist.

Interview questions

  1. What is the Terraform state file and why does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    A record mapping declarations to real resources, used to compute the diff; it is the source of truth for what Terraform manages, so losing or corrupting it is serious.
  2. Why use remote state with locking?
    Show answerHide answer
    Remote state lets a team share one state safely and survives a lost laptop; locking prevents concurrent applies from corrupting the state or making conflicting changes.
  3. What is state drift and how do you handle it?
    Show answerHide answer
    When a resource is changed outside Terraform so reality diverges from state; it shows up as unexpected changes in a plan, and you investigate and either codify the change or let Terraform reconcile — never ignore it.
  4. How do you bring existing (clickops) resources under Terraform management?
    Show answerHide answer
    terraform import adds them to the state so Terraform manages them going forward.

Practical exercise

Configure a remote state backend with locking (for example S3 plus a lock table) for a Terraform project, then simulate drift by changing a managed resource by hand and running terraform plan to see the drift detected. Finally, describe how you would import an existing manually-created resource into Terraform management. Acceptance criteria: state is remote and locked, the plan detects the manual change as drift, and you can explain the import path from clickops to IaC.

52.4 Structuring Terraform and the alternatives

52.4.1 Modules, environments and versioning

Concept

Real infrastructure spans many environments (dev, staging, production) and many services, and copy-pasting Terraform for each is unmaintainable. Modules package a reusable group of resources (a "service" module creating a database, cache and compute) with inputs and outputs, so you define the pattern once and instantiate it per environment and service. Structuring Terraform well — modules, per-environment configuration, module versioning — is what keeps IaC maintainable at scale.

Why does it exist?

Without modules, the Terraform for staging and production is duplicated, so they drift apart and a change must be made in many places. A module lets you define "a standard service's infrastructure" once and instantiate it with different inputs per environment (smaller database in staging, larger in production) and per service, keeping them consistent by construction. Versioning modules means a change to the standard pattern can be rolled out deliberately rather than instantly affecting everything. Good structure exists because infrastructure, like code, needs reuse, consistency and controlled change as it grows.

Mental model

A module is a recipe card in a restaurant chain. Head office writes "the standard burger" once; every branch cooks from the same card and only changes what the card allows (the size, the sauce). When head office improves the recipe, they print version 2 and branches switch when they are ready, test kitchen first. Copy-pasted Terraform is every branch improvising its own burger from memory.

How it works

HCL
# A reusable module: infra/modules/postgres/main.tf (trimmed to the essentials)
variable "name"              { type = string }
variable "environment"       { type = string }
variable "instance_class"    { type = string }
variable "subnet_ids"        { type = list(string) }
variable "security_group_id" { type = string }

variable "multi_az" {
  type    = bool
  default = true                                    # safe default: callers must opt out
}

resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "this" {
  name       = "${var.name}-${var.environment}"
  subnet_ids = var.subnet_ids
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "this" {
  identifier                  = "${var.name}-${var.environment}"
  engine                      = "postgres"
  engine_version              = "17"
  instance_class              = var.instance_class
  allocated_storage           = 100
  username                    = "${var.name}_admin"
  manage_master_user_password = true
  db_subnet_group_name        = aws_db_subnet_group.this.name
  vpc_security_group_ids      = [var.security_group_id]
  multi_az                    = var.multi_az
  backup_retention_period     = 30
  deletion_protection         = true
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

output "endpoint" { value = aws_db_instance.this.endpoint }
HCL
# Per-environment usage: infra/environments/production/main.tf
module "orders_db" {
  source            = "git::https://github.com/acme/terraform-modules.git//postgres?ref=v2.3.0"  # pinned version
  name              = "orders"
  environment       = "production"
  instance_class    = "db.r6g.large"               # bigger in production
  subnet_ids        = module.network.private_data_subnet_ids
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.orders_db.id
}

# infra/environments/staging/main.tf instantiates the SAME module with smaller inputs
# (instance_class = "db.t4g.medium", multi_az = false), so staging and production
# share one definition and stay consistent.

The structure: a modules/ directory (or a separate modules repository, as in the source above) of reusable building blocks, and an environments/ directory that instantiates them with per-environment inputs. This keeps environments consistent (same module, different sizes) and changes DRY (fix the module once). Module versioning — referencing a module by a version tag rather than always the latest — lets you adopt a change to the standard pattern environment by environment, so a module update does not instantly and simultaneously alter every environment (a safety and rollout control, the same compatibility thinking as Part 25). Section 52.8 covers layout, blast radius and why Terraform workspaces are a poor way to separate staging from production.

Failure scenario

A platform team changed the shared ecs-service module so every service got a new target-group health check path, and because twelve services referenced the module by ?ref=main rather than a tag, the next apply of each service picked up the change. Four services did not serve /health/ready; their targets went unhealthy within a minute of apply and the ALB returned 503s for those services until the change was reverted 25 minutes later. The fix was to pin every module source to a tag, release module changes with a changelog, and roll them out staging-first. The lesson: an unpinned module is a deploy to every environment that nobody reviewed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Renaming inside a module. Renaming a resource inside a module changes the address in every caller's state; ship a moved block in the module (52.7) or every caller plans a destroy.
  • Breaking input changes. Removing or renaming a variable breaks callers; treat module inputs like a public API with semantic versioning.
  • Too many knobs. A module with 80 variables is the provider re-exported; expose the decisions a service team should make and hard-code the standards.
  • Providers inside modules. Declaring provider blocks in a reusable module prevents callers from using for_each on it and makes removal painful; pass providers in from the root.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior structures Terraform into reusable modules instantiated per environment, so environments are consistent by construction (staging is production at a smaller size, from the same code) and changes are made once. They version shared modules so a change to the standard infrastructure pattern can be rolled out deliberately — staging first, then production — rather than hitting every environment at once, which is both a safety control and an echo of the compatibility discipline from Part 25. They keep the structure simple enough to understand (over-abstracted Terraform with deeply nested modules is as bad as copy-paste), and they treat the module library as a paved road (Part 85) — the standard, reviewed way to provision a service's infrastructure. The goal is consistency, reuse and controlled change, matching how they structure application code.

Common mistakes

  • Copy-pasting Terraform per environment, causing drift and multi-place changes.
  • No module versioning, so a module change instantly affects every environment.
  • Over-abstracting into deeply nested modules that are hard to understand.
  • Inconsistent environments because they were defined separately rather than from a shared module.

Interview questions

  1. Why use modules in Terraform?
    Show answerHide answer
    To define a reusable group of resources once with inputs/outputs and instantiate it per environment and service, keeping environments consistent and changes DRY.
  2. How do you keep staging and production consistent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Instantiate the same module with different inputs (sizes) per environment, so they share one definition and differ only by parameter.
  3. Why version shared modules?
    Show answerHide answer
    So a change to the standard pattern can be rolled out environment by environment deliberately, rather than instantly altering every environment at once.

Practical exercise

Refactor duplicated Terraform for staging and production into a shared service module instantiated per environment with different instance sizes, and reference the module by a version. Acceptance criteria: staging and production use the same module (differing only by inputs), a change to the module is made in one place, and the version reference allows a staged rollout.

52.4.2 Pulumi, CDK, CloudFormation and choosing

Concept

Terraform is the most common IaC tool but not the only one. Pulumi lets you write infrastructure in real programming languages (including TypeScript). AWS CDK also uses programming languages and compiles to CloudFormation. CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service using YAML/JSON. They occupy the same role — declaring infrastructure as code — with different languages and tradeoffs.

Why does it exist?

Teams differ. A platform team managing AWS, Cloudflare, Datadog and GitHub from one workflow needs a tool with providers for all of them. A TypeScript product team that wants to unit-test its infrastructure and share types between application and infrastructure code wants a real language. An AWS-only enterprise with strict change control may want the provider's own managed service so there is no state file to run. The alternatives exist because "declare infrastructure" has several reasonable answers, and the right one depends on who writes it, what it targets, and what the organization already runs. One fact shapes the landscape: in August 2023 HashiCorp moved Terraform to the Business Source License, and the Linux Foundation's OpenTofu fork continues under an open-source license with the same HCL and largely compatible state, so "Terraform" in this Part applies to OpenTofu too, except for features added after the fork by either side.

Mental model

All four are ways of writing the same blueprint. Terraform and CloudFormation are blueprints drawn with a fixed set of symbols: limited, but anyone can read any blueprint. Pulumi and CDK are blueprints produced by a program: you can generate a hundred similar floors with a loop and test the program, but a reader must now understand the program to know what the building looks like.

How it works — the decision table

Tool Language Scope Strength Tradeoff
Terraform HCL (declarative) Multi-cloud (providers) Mature, huge ecosystem, cloud-agnostic, widely known Its own language; state management to run
Pulumi Real languages (TypeScript, Python, ...) Multi-cloud Full programming power, familiar language, testable State management; programming power can over-complicate
AWS CDK Real languages (compiles to CloudFormation) AWS-focused Programming power, AWS-native, no separate state AWS-centric; CloudFormation underneath
CloudFormation YAML/JSON (declarative) AWS only AWS-native, no extra tooling, managed state AWS-only; verbose; slower
Text
Choose Terraform when:               Choose Pulumi/CDK when:            Choose CloudFormation when:
- multi-cloud or cloud-agnostic       - the team strongly prefers a       - AWS-only and you want the
- you want the largest ecosystem        real programming language           native, no-extra-tooling option
  and community knowledge              - you need programming constructs   - you accept AWS lock-in and verbosity
- declarative HCL is acceptable         (loops, conditionals, tests)

For a TypeScript backend team, Pulumi or CDK can appeal because the infrastructure is in a familiar language with real abstractions and testability. Terraform remains the common default for its maturity, multi-cloud providers and ubiquity (most engineers know it, most examples use it). The choice is a tradeoff between a dedicated declarative language with the biggest ecosystem (Terraform) and a real programming language with more power but more ways to over-complicate (Pulumi/CDK). Section 52.9 puts the same database in Pulumi and CDK TypeScript next to the Terraform version so you can compare them line by line.

Failure scenario

A team chose CDK for a new service and, a year later, a CloudFormation stack update failed halfway through replacing an ALB listener and went into UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED because a resource it tried to roll back had been changed by hand. CloudFormation refused further updates to the stack until the rollback was continued with that resource skipped (ContinueUpdateRollback with resources to skip), and the team spent an afternoon learning CloudFormation internals they thought CDK had hidden. Nothing about the choice was wrong; the lesson is that every tool's failure modes are those of its engine (CloudFormation for CDK, the state backend for Terraform and Pulumi), and you must learn the engine before production needs you to.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mixing tools on the same resources. Terraform and CDK both managing one security group means each reverts the other; one owner per resource.
  • Programmatic IaC with network calls at synth time. A CDK app that looks things up live produces different templates on different days; CDK caches lookups in cdk.context.json, which must be committed.
  • License and fork drift. Terraform and OpenTofu are diverging slowly; pick one per organization and pin it in CI.
  • Migration cost. Moving between tools means importing every resource into the new tool's state without recreating it; budget weeks, not days.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior chooses the IaC tool by the team's context and needs, not fashion: Terraform as the safe default for its maturity, multi-cloud support and ubiquity; Pulumi or CDK when the team strongly values infrastructure in a real, familiar, testable language and the extra programming power genuinely helps; CloudFormation when fully committed to AWS and wanting the native option. They are wary that programming-language IaC (Pulumi/CDK) makes it easy to over-engineer infrastructure with excessive abstraction, so they keep it as simple as declarative IaC would be. Whatever the tool, the principles are the same — version control, plan/review before apply, remote state, modules, guardrails — so they do not treat the tool choice as the important decision; the discipline around it is.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a tool by fashion rather than team context and needs.
  • Over-engineering infrastructure because a programming language makes abstraction easy (Pulumi/CDK).
  • Assuming the tool choice matters more than the surrounding discipline (plan/review, state, guardrails).

Interview questions

  1. How do Terraform, Pulumi, CDK and CloudFormation differ?
    Show answerHide answer
    Terraform uses declarative HCL and is multi-cloud with the largest ecosystem; Pulumi and CDK use real programming languages (CDK compiles to CloudFormation, AWS-focused); CloudFormation is AWS's native declarative YAML/JSON. They share the IaC role with different languages and tradeoffs.
  2. When would a TypeScript team choose Pulumi or CDK?
    Show answerHide answer
    When they strongly prefer infrastructure in a familiar, testable language with real programming constructs and the power helps; the risk is over-abstraction.
  3. Why is Terraform a common default?
    Show answerHide answer
    Maturity, multi-cloud providers, a huge ecosystem, and ubiquity (most engineers know it), with declarative HCL that resists over-engineering.

Practical exercise

For a TypeScript backend team on AWS, write a short comparison of Terraform versus Pulumi/CDK for their IaC, considering language familiarity, multi-cloud needs, ecosystem, and the risk of over-abstraction, and make a recommendation. Acceptance criteria: the recommendation follows from the team's stated context, and you note that the surrounding discipline (plan/review, state, guardrails) matters more than the tool choice.

52.5 IaC in CI/CD and policy as code

52.5.1 Plan on pull request, apply pipelines and preventing destructive changes

Concept

IaC becomes safe and collaborative when integrated into CI/CD (Part 47): a change to infrastructure code opens a pull request, CI runs terraform plan and posts the result for review, an approval gate guards the apply, and the apply runs in a pipeline rather than from someone's laptop. Guardrails prevent destructive changes (especially to stateful resources) from being applied casually. This turns infrastructure changes into the same reviewed, automated, controlled flow as application changes.

Why does it exist?

Running terraform apply from a laptop against production is dangerous: no review of the plan, no approval, no audit, and the risk of an unnoticed destructive change. Integrating IaC into CI/CD brings the plan into the pull request so reviewers see exactly what will change, gates the apply behind approval, runs it from a controlled pipeline with proper credentials, and records every change. Guardrails that block or require extra approval for destroying stateful resources prevent the catastrophic accident. This exists because infrastructure changes are high-stakes and deserve at least the same rigor as code changes — arguably more, since a bad one can delete a database.

Mental model

Imagine a bank vault with a two-person rule. One employee prepares the transfer and prints the slip (the plan); a second checks the slip against the request (review); the vault's own lock refuses certain transfers no matter who asks (policy and deletion_protection); and the transfer is executed by the machine from the approved slip, not retyped by hand (apply the saved plan). No single tired person at 18:00 can empty the vault.

How it works

Text
Infrastructure change flow in CI/CD:
  1. Engineer changes a .tf file, opens a pull request
  2. CI runs `terraform plan` -> posts the plan as a PR comment (reviewers SEE the effect)
  3. Reviewers check the plan: creates? changes? any DESTROY of a stateful resource?
  4. Policy checks run (64.5.2): block disallowed changes automatically
  5. Approval gate: a human approves the apply
  6. Merge -> the apply pipeline runs `terraform apply` with controlled credentials
  7. The change is recorded (who, what, when, the plan)

The key safety steps: the plan on the pull request makes the effect visible and reviewable before merge; policy as code (52.5.2) auto-blocks disallowed or dangerous changes; an approval gate requires human sign-off; the apply runs in the pipeline, not on a laptop, with scoped credentials and an audit trail. Preventing destructive changes specifically means guarding stateful resources — Terraform's prevent_destroy lifecycle flag on a database, required extra approval for any plan containing a destroy, and policy that blocks destruction of production data stores.

HCL
# Guard a stateful resource against accidental destruction.
resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  # ...
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true   # a plan that would destroy this fails -> no accidental DB deletion
  }
}

Know the limit of prevent_destroy: it is part of the resource block, so it protects against a plan that destroys or replaces the resource while the block is still in the code. If someone deletes the block, or renames the resource address without a moved block (52.7), the protection disappears with it and the plan happily shows a destroy. That is why the guardrail that actually stops deletion is on the AWS side, deletion_protection = true on the RDS instance, enforced by the RDS API itself, plus skip_final_snapshot = false and policy that rejects any plan deleting a database (52.11). Section 52.10 shows the pipeline in full.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior runs all infrastructure changes through CI/CD with plan-on-pull-request, review, policy checks, approval gates and pipeline-based apply, never a laptop apply against production, because the plan-in-the-PR is where a reviewer catches a change about to destroy a database. They layer explicit protection on stateful resources (prevent_destroy, extra approval for any destroy in a plan, policy blocking production data-store destruction), treating the destruction of a stateful resource as the highest-stakes operation in the whole system. They keep the apply credentials in the pipeline, scoped and audited, not on individuals' machines. In their view, infrastructure changes deserve more rigor than code changes, because a bad code deploy can be rolled back while a destroyed production database with no backup cannot.

Failure scenario

A team had plan-on-PR and approvals, but the apply job ran a fresh terraform plan and apply -auto-approve at merge time instead of applying the reviewed plan file. Between review and merge, another PR to the same root had merged and changed a shared security group. The reviewed plan showed one change; the apply executed three, including removing an ingress rule the payments service relied on, and payments could not reach its database for 11 minutes. The fix: save the plan as an artifact (terraform plan -out=tfplan), apply exactly that file, and serialize applies per root with a CI concurrency group so a stale plan fails instead of silently becoming a different plan. The lesson: "we review plans" only means something if the thing applied is the thing reviewed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Plan artifacts contain secrets. A saved plan file includes values from state; store it as a short-lived, access-controlled CI artifact.
  • Two PRs, one root. Plans computed in parallel go stale on the first merge; serialize per root and re-plan on conflict.
  • Apply fails halfway. Terraform records what it created; rerun plan, read it, and continue. Do not delete state or retry blindly.
  • Approvals rubber-stamped. Fifty routine plans a week train reviewers to click approve; highlight destroys automatically so the dangerous ones look different.
  • Break-glass. Real emergencies need a documented, audited path to apply outside the normal flow, used rarely and reviewed afterwards.

Common mistakes

  • Running terraform apply from a laptop against production, with no review or audit.
  • No plan on the pull request, so reviewers cannot see the effect.
  • No guard on stateful resources, allowing an accidental destroy to be applied.
  • No approval gate on apply.
  • Apply credentials on individuals' laptops instead of scoped in the pipeline.

Interview questions

  1. How do you integrate Terraform into CI/CD safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Plan on the pull request (post the plan for review), policy checks, an approval gate, and apply from the pipeline with scoped credentials and an audit trail — never a laptop apply against production.
  2. Why is the plan-on-pull-request step important?
    Show answerHide answer
    It makes the exact effect of the change visible and reviewable before merge, so reviewers catch destructive or wrong changes.
  3. How do you prevent accidental destruction of a database?
    Show answerHide answer
    deletion_protection = true on the instance (enforced by AWS), prevent_destroy on the resource (enforced by Terraform, but only while the block exists), a final snapshot and retained automated backups, required extra approval for any plan containing a destroy, and policy blocking destruction of production data stores.
  4. Why do infrastructure changes deserve more rigor than code changes?
    Show answerHide answer
    A bad code deploy can be rolled back; a destroyed production database with no backup cannot — the stakes are higher.

Practical exercise

Set up (or describe) a CI/CD flow for Terraform: a pull request runs terraform plan and posts it as a comment, an approval is required, and merge triggers an apply pipeline. Add prevent_destroy to a database resource and verify that a change which would destroy it fails the plan. Acceptance criteria: the plan is visible on the PR before merge, apply runs in the pipeline not locally, and the database cannot be accidentally destroyed.

52.5.2 Policy as code

Concept

Policy as code enforces rules about infrastructure automatically, as code, in the pipeline — "no public S3 buckets", "all databases must have backups enabled", "no untagged resources", "no instance types above a cost threshold". Tools like OPA/Conftest and Sentinel evaluate the Terraform plan against these policies and block the apply if a rule is violated. It is automated governance (Part 85) for infrastructure, catching security and cost problems before they are applied.

Why does it exist?

Relying on humans to remember every security and cost rule in every infrastructure review does not scale and misses things — someone forgets to enable backups, opens a bucket to the public, or picks an oversized instance. Policy as code encodes these rules once and enforces them automatically on every change, so a violation is blocked before it reaches production, not caught later (or never). It exists to make governance automatic, consistent and un-forgettable, the same shift from manual to codified that IaC itself represents, applied to the rules about the infrastructure.

Mental model

Policy as code is a building inspector who reads every blueprint before construction starts, using a written checklist, and who never gets tired, never makes an exception for a friend, and stamps "rejected: no fire exit" with the page number. The human architect (reviewer) still judges whether the design is good; the inspector guarantees the non-negotiables.

How it works

Text
Policy as code in the pipeline:
  terraform plan -> policy engine (OPA/Conftest) evaluates the plan against rules:
    - every S3 bucket must block public access          -> violated? FAIL the pipeline
    - every database must have backup_retention >= 7     -> violated? FAIL
    - no resource may lack a cost-center tag             -> violated? FAIL
    - no instance type above the approved list            -> violated? FAIL (cost guardrail)
  -> the apply is blocked until the change complies.

Policies codify security rules (no public data stores, encryption required, no overly-broad permissions), cost rules (no oversized instances, required cost tags), and standards (naming, tagging) — the governance standards of Part 85, enforced automatically. Because they run on the plan in CI, they catch violations before anything is applied, turning "we have a policy that databases need backups" (which someone can forget) into "a change that disables backups cannot be merged" (which is enforced). Section 52.11 has the Rego for these rules, run with Conftest against terraform show -json output, and their unit tests.

Failure scenario

A cost policy capped instance types at *.2xlarge and below. A team needed a db.r6g.4xlarge for a month-end batch, the policy blocked it, and the team "fixed" the pipeline by adding || true after the Conftest step. Six weeks later, a public S3 bucket with customer invoices went through the same pipeline unchallenged and was found by a security scanner, not by a customer, luckily. The lesson: a policy with no exception path gets disabled, and a disabled policy protects nothing. Real policy-as-code needs a documented waiver (an annotation or tag with an owner and expiry, reviewed by the policy owners; see Part 85 — Architecture Governance, 85.6) and a pipeline in which the policy step cannot be edited by the teams it governs.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Policies on configuration, not plan. Checking .tf files misses values computed from variables and modules; evaluate the plan JSON.
  • Unknown values. Some attributes are (known after apply); a policy must decide whether "unknown" passes or fails.
  • Deletes are not in after. A deleted resource has after = null; policies that only inspect after never see the destroy. Check change.actions.
  • Too many advisory rules. Hundreds of warnings nobody reads hide the one that matters; keep a small set of hard-fail rules.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior encodes the important infrastructure rules — security (no public data stores, encryption, least-privilege permissions; see Part 40 — Security, 40.10, and Part 46 — Cloud Architecture, 46.11), cost (instance-size limits, required tags), and standards (Part 85) — as policy-as-code that runs on every plan in CI, so violations are blocked automatically rather than relying on human reviewers to remember them. They see this as the automated-governance paved road (Part 85): the rules are consistent, un-forgettable and catch problems before they are applied, which is the only way governance scales across many services and engineers. They keep policies focused on real risks (a public production bucket, a database with no backups, a wildly oversized instance) rather than nitpicking, because over-strict policy becomes a nuisance people route around. Policy as code is, to them, the enforcement layer that makes IaC genuinely safe at scale.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on human reviewers to remember every security and cost rule, which misses violations.
  • No automated enforcement, so a change disabling backups or opening a bucket can slip through.
  • Over-strict policies that nitpick and get routed around.
  • Not enforcing cost guardrails, allowing oversized resources to inflate the bill.

Interview questions

  1. What is policy as code and why use it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Encoding infrastructure rules (security, cost, standards) as code that automatically evaluates each Terraform plan in CI and blocks violations; it makes governance automatic, consistent and un-forgettable, catching problems before apply.
  2. Give examples of policies worth enforcing.
    Show answerHide answer
    No public data stores, backups/encryption required, least-privilege permissions, instance-size/cost limits, required tags, naming standards.
  3. How does policy as code relate to governance (Part 85)?
    Show answerHide answer
    It is the automated-enforcement form of architecture standards — the paved road enforced in the pipeline rather than relying on human memory.

Practical exercise

Write (or describe) policy-as-code rules with OPA/Conftest that fail a Terraform plan if any S3 bucket allows public access, any database has backups disabled, or any resource lacks a cost tag, and wire them into the plan step of the CI pipeline. Acceptance criteria: a plan violating any rule fails the pipeline before apply, and the rules focus on real security and cost risks.

52.6 GitOps, secrets and the apply-gone-wrong incident

52.6.1 GitOps for Kubernetes and secrets in IaC

Concept

GitOps applies IaC principles to running applications on Kubernetes (Part 45): the desired state of the cluster (deployments, services, config) lives in Git, and a controller (Argo CD or Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster to match Git. Helm and Kustomize are tools for templating and customizing Kubernetes manifests. Secrets (database passwords, API keys) must never be stored in IaC code or state in plaintext — they come from a secret manager, referenced by the code.

Why does it exist?

Deploying to Kubernetes by running kubectl apply by hand has the same problems as clickops: no review, no audit, drift between what is declared and what is running. GitOps makes Git the single source of truth for the cluster's state and a controller enforces it continuously, so the cluster always matches reviewed, version-controlled manifests, and drift is auto-corrected. Helm and Kustomize exist because raw Kubernetes manifests are verbose and need per-environment customization. Secret handling exists because IaC code and state are stored and shared (in Git, in remote backends) where a plaintext password would be exposed — so secrets are externalized to a secret manager and only referenced.

How it works — GitOps

Text
GitOps reconciliation loop:
  Git (desired cluster state: deployments, services, config)
        |  Argo CD / Flux continuously watches Git
        v
  Controller compares Git (desired) to the cluster (actual)
        |  differs?
        v
  Controller applies the difference -> cluster matches Git
        |  someone changes the cluster by hand (drift)?
        v
  Controller detects it and reconciles back to Git -> drift auto-corrected

The cluster's state is declared in Git; a controller (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the actual cluster to the declared state, so deploys happen by merging to Git (reviewed, audited) and manual drift is corrected automatically. Helm packages Kubernetes manifests as reusable, parameterized charts; Kustomize overlays per-environment customizations on base manifests — both solve the manifest-reuse-and-customization problem, analogous to Terraform modules (52.4).

How it works — secrets

Text
NEVER put secrets in IaC code or state in plaintext:
  BAD:  password = "hunter2"   in a .tf file (committed to Git, visible to all)
  BAD:  a plaintext secret ends up in the Terraform state file (stored in the backend)

Instead:
  - store secrets in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)
  - IaC/code REFERENCES the secret (fetches it at deploy/run time), never embeds it
  - for Kubernetes: sealed secrets / external secrets operators pull from the manager
  - restrict and audit access to the secret manager and the Terraform state (Part 40.32, Part 46.11)

The rule: secrets never live in IaC code (which is in Git) or in state (which is in a shared backend) in plaintext; they live in a secret manager and are referenced. A database password committed to a .tf file is in Git history forever (see Part 48 — Git from Intermediate to Senior) and visible to everyone with repo access — a breach. Even values Terraform fetches can land in the state file, so the state itself must be treated as sensitive, encrypted and access-controlled. This is the secrets discipline of Part 40 — Security (40.32) and Part 47 — CI/CD (47.4) applied to infrastructure code; section 52.13 shows the concrete Terraform patterns (RDS-managed master passwords, ECS secrets, External Secrets Operator).

Failure scenario (the terraform apply that deleted a production database)

An engineer, intending to update a staging environment, ran terraform apply from their laptop. They had the wrong workspace/state selected — it pointed at production. The plan included a destroy of the production database (a refactor had renamed the resource's address without a moved block, so Terraform saw "old one removed, new one added"), but, rushing, they did not read the plan carefully and confirmed the apply. The production database was destroyed. Because backups and point-in-time recovery were in place, the data was recoverable, but there was a painful outage. Nearly every guardrail in this Part would have stopped it: plan-on-pull-request with review would have surfaced the destroy; deletion_protection = true would have made the AWS API refuse the delete; policy-as-code blocking production data-store destruction would have blocked it; a moved block would have turned the rename into a no-op. One guardrail would not have helped: prevent_destroy, because it lived in the old resource block that the refactor removed; running apply from a reviewed pipeline, not a laptop, with no human able to casually apply to production, would have prevented it; and the wrong-workspace mistake would have been caught by the pipeline targeting a fixed environment. The lesson: a Terraform apply is one of the most dangerous commands in the whole system, and it must be wrapped in every guardrail — review, prevent_destroy, policy, pipeline-only apply — because the cost of getting it wrong is a destroyed production database.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses GitOps for Kubernetes so the cluster's state is version-controlled, reviewed and continuously reconciled from Git, with Helm/Kustomize for reuse and customization, treating kubectl apply by hand as the clickops of Kubernetes. They never put secrets in IaC code or state, externalizing them to a secret manager and treating the state file as sensitive, encrypted and access-controlled. Above all, they treat terraform apply as a dangerous, high-stakes operation and wrap it in the full set of guardrails from this Part — plan-on-pull-request and review, prevent_destroy on stateful resources, policy-as-code, and pipeline-only apply against fixed environments — because the apply-gone-wrong incident is a database deletion, and the only reliable defense is making it impossible to apply a destructive change casually. They ensure backups and recovery exist regardless (the last line of defense; see Part 50 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery, 50.4), because guardrails reduce but never fully eliminate the chance of a mistake. Section 52.15 retells this incident minute by minute.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Self-heal fights autoscaling. Argo CD with self-heal reverts spec.replicas that the HPA changed; omit replicas from the manifest or use ignoreDifferences (52.12).
  • Prune deletes too much. Automated pruning removes anything no longer in Git, including a resource someone moved to another app; enable prune deliberately and protect critical resources.
  • Secrets synced into the cluster are still Kubernetes Secrets. Base64, not encryption; enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict get secrets RBAC (see Part 45 — Kubernetes, 45.7).
  • Rotation breaks long-lived connections. Rotating a database password in Secrets Manager does not reconnect running pods; plan for reload or dual credentials.
  • The GitOps repo is now production access. Whoever can merge to it can deploy anything; protect branches and require reviews as strictly as for production credentials.

Common mistakes

  • kubectl apply by hand instead of GitOps, losing review, audit and drift correction.
  • Secrets in IaC code or state in plaintext, a breach that lives in Git history forever.
  • Treating the Terraform state file as non-sensitive when it can contain secrets.
  • Running apply from a laptop against production, risking the wrong-workspace disaster.
  • Relying on carefulness instead of guardrails (prevent_destroy, policy, pipeline-only apply).
  • No backups/recovery as the last line of defense.

Interview questions

  1. What is GitOps?
    Show answerHide answer
    Keeping the desired Kubernetes cluster state in Git and having a controller (Argo CD/Flux) continuously reconcile the cluster to match it, so deploys are reviewed Git merges and manual drift is auto-corrected.
  2. How do you handle secrets in IaC?
    Show answerHide answer
    Never store them in code or state in plaintext; keep them in a secret manager and reference them, treat the state file as sensitive (encrypted, access-controlled), and use sealed/external secrets for Kubernetes.
  3. What guardrails would prevent a terraform apply from deleting a production database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Plan-on-pull-request with review, deletion_protection on the instance and prevent_destroy on the resource (knowing the latter vanishes if the block is removed), moved blocks for renames, policy-as-code blocking production data-store destruction, pipeline-only apply against fixed environments (no laptop apply, no wrong-workspace risk), and backups as the last line of defense.
  4. What are Helm and Kustomize for?
    Show answerHide answer
    Templating/packaging and per-environment customization of Kubernetes manifests, solving manifest reuse and customization (analogous to Terraform modules).

Practical exercise

Set up (or describe) a GitOps flow where Kubernetes manifests in Git are reconciled by Argo CD/Flux, using Helm or Kustomize for per-environment config. Ensure no secret appears in the manifests or Terraform state — reference a secret manager instead. Finally, list every guardrail from this Part that would have prevented the production-database-deletion incident and confirm backups exist as the last line of defense. Acceptance criteria: the cluster state is reconciled from reviewed Git, no plaintext secrets appear in code or state, and you can enumerate the layered guardrails that make a casual destructive apply impossible.

52.7 Terraform in depth: addresses, for_each, lifecycle and safe refactoring

Concept

Every resource in Terraform has an address, such as aws_db_instance.orders or module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this or aws_subnet.private["app-a"]. State maps each address to a real resource id. Almost every "Terraform deleted my thing" incident is an address problem: the code changed in a way that made Terraform believe one address disappeared and another appeared. This section covers the language features that create addresses (count, for_each, modules), the blocks that change them safely (moved, import, removed), the lifecycle rules that constrain changes, and version pinning that keeps plans stable.

Why does it exist?

Infrastructure code is refactored like any code: resources get renamed, moved into modules, split out, adopted from clickops, or handed to another team. Before Terraform 1.1 each of those required terraform state mv or state rm commands run by hand against production state, unreviewed and easy to get wrong. The moved (8.1), import (8.5) and removed (8.7) blocks put those operations in code, so they appear in the pull request and in the plan like any other change.

Mental model

State is a phone book: each entry links a name (the address) to a phone number (the AWS resource id). Renaming a resource in code without telling Terraform is like reprinting the phone book with a new name and no number: Terraform calls nobody at the old name ("destroy") and gets a new number for the new name ("create"). A moved block is the forwarding notice: "the person you knew as orders is now module.orders_db.this, same number".

How it works — count versus for_each

HCL
# Fragile: addresses are list positions aws_sqs_queue.jobs[0], [1], [2]
variable "queue_names" { default = ["order-emails", "invoice-pdf", "loyalty-points"] }

resource "aws_sqs_queue" "jobs" {
  count = length(var.queue_names)
  name  = var.queue_names[count.index]
}

# Robust: addresses are keys aws_sqs_queue.jobs["invoice-pdf"], independent of order
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "jobs_by_name" {
  for_each                   = toset(["order-emails", "invoice-pdf", "loyalty-points"])
  name                       = each.key
  message_retention_seconds  = 345600
  visibility_timeout_seconds = 60
}

With count, removing "order-emails" from the front of the list shifts every index: [0] becomes invoice-pdf and [1] becomes loyalty-points. SQS queue names cannot be changed in place, so the plan replaces two queues that were never meant to change and destroys the third. With for_each, removing a key plans exactly one destroy. Use count only for "zero or one" (count = var.enable_bastion ? 1 : 0); use for_each for collections.

How it works — moved, import and removed blocks

HCL
# 1. Rename or move into a module without destroying anything (Terraform 1.1+)
moved {
  from = aws_db_instance.orders
  to   = module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this
}

moved {
  from = aws_sqs_queue.jobs[1]
  to   = aws_sqs_queue.jobs_by_name["invoice-pdf"]
}

# 2. Adopt a resource created by hand (Terraform 1.5+); generate a starting config with
#    terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
import {
  to = aws_elasticache_replication_group.sessions
  id = "orders-sessions"
}

# 3. Stop managing a resource WITHOUT deleting it, for example when handing it to another team (1.7+)
removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy_exports
  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

The plan shows these explicitly: # aws_db_instance.orders has moved to module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this, # aws_elasticache_replication_group.sessions will be imported, # aws_s3_bucket.legacy_exports will no longer be managed by Terraform. A refactor pull request whose plan says 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy plus moves is the goal. Keep moved blocks in shared modules for at least one major version so every caller's state migrates.

How it works — lifecycle rules and checks

HCL
variable "environment" {
  type = string
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "production"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging or production."
  }
}

resource "aws_ecs_service" "api" {
  name            = "orders-api"
  cluster         = aws_ecs_cluster.main.id
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.api.arn
  desired_count   = 3

  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [desired_count]     # Application Auto Scaling owns this after creation
  }
}

resource "aws_db_parameter_group" "orders" {
  name_prefix = "orders-pg17-"           # a prefix lets create_before_destroy work for named resources
  family      = "postgres17"
  parameter {
    name  = "rds.logical_replication"
    value = "1"
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true         # new group exists before the old one is removed
  }
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  # ... arguments as in 64.14 ...
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
    precondition {
      condition     = var.environment != "production" || var.multi_az
      error_message = "Production databases must be Multi-AZ."
    }
  }
}

ignore_changes stops Terraform fighting another controller; create_before_destroy avoids gaps when something must be replaced; replace_triggered_by forces replacement when a dependency changes; precondition and postcondition fail the plan or apply with a clear message when an assumption is broken.

How it works — pin everything

HCL
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.10"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"                 # allow minor and patch updates, never a new major
    }
  }
}

terraform init writes the exact provider versions and checksums to .terraform.lock.hcl. Commit it, and upgrade providers in their own pull request (terraform init -upgrade) so a provider change never hides inside a feature change.

Production scenario

A team migrating 140 hand-built resources into a module-based layout did it in nine pull requests over two weeks: three of import blocks (with -generate-config-out as a starting point, then cleaned up by hand), five of moved blocks into modules, and one of removed blocks for resources handed to the data team. Every plan showed zero creates and zero destroys. The only production change during the migration was tags.

Failure scenario

At 11:05 on a weekday, a pull request removed the retired "order-emails" queue from a count-based list of three SQS queues. The plan said 2 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy; the reviewer, expecting "one queue removed", saw "destroy" and the queue name and approved. On apply, Terraform deleted all three queues and recreated two of them with the same names after AWS's 60-second wait for reusing a deleted queue's name. About 14,000 unprocessed invoice and loyalty jobs were in those queues and were lost; producers got QueueDoesNotExist errors for a minute. The jobs were rebuilt from the orders table over the afternoon. The fix was for_each with moved blocks from each index to its key, and a pipeline rule that any plan destroying an SQS queue, RDS instance or ElastiCache group needs a second approver. The lesson: read the plan's counts against what you expected; "3 to destroy" for a one-line removal is the plan telling you something is wrong.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • moved cannot cross state files. Moving a resource to another root configuration needs removed (with destroy = false) in one and import in the other, applied in that order.
  • Generated config is a draft. -generate-config-out writes every attribute, including computed ones; trim it, or the next plan shows noise.
  • ignore_changes = all. Silences all drift forever; almost never what you want.
  • for_each keys from unknown values. Keys must be known at plan time; keying by a resource id created in the same apply fails.
  • Provider major upgrades. Version 6 of the AWS provider changed defaults and removed deprecated arguments; read the upgrade guide and expect a noisy plan.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior thinks in addresses. Before approving a refactor, they ask "which addresses change?" and expect a moved block for each. They use for_each for anything that is a collection, count only for optional singletons, and they treat the plan summary line as a test assertion: if a rename shows any destroy, the pull request is wrong. They adopt clickops resources with import blocks in reviewed pull requests rather than with CLI commands against production state, and they pin Terraform and provider versions so the only changes in a plan are the ones someone wrote.

Common mistakes

  • count over a list of named things.
  • Renaming a resource or moving it into a module without a moved block.
  • terraform state rm to "fix" a plan, leaving an orphaned real resource nobody manages.
  • Uncommitted .terraform.lock.hcl, so CI and laptops use different provider versions.
  • Using ignore_changes to hide drift instead of finding who changes the resource.

Interview questions

  1. Why is for_each safer than count for collections?
    Show answerHide answer
    Addresses are keys, not positions, so removing one element affects only that element; with count, removing an early element shifts indexes and replaces later resources.
  2. How do you move a resource into a module without recreating it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Add a moved block from the old address to the new one; the plan shows a move and no destroy.
  3. How do you bring a hand-made resource under Terraform?
    Show answerHide answer
    An import block with the resource id, a matching resource block (optionally generated with -generate-config-out), and a plan that shows only the import.
  4. How do you stop managing a resource without deleting it?
    Show answerHide answer
    A removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false } (or terraform state rm in older versions).
  5. What does ignore_changes solve, and how is it abused?
    Show answerHide answer
    It stops Terraform reverting fields another controller owns (autoscaled counts, task definitions deployed by CI); it is abused to hide drift.

Practical exercise

Create three SQS queues with count in a sandbox account, then migrate them to for_each using moved blocks so the plan shows zero changes. Then import a queue created in the console with an import block, and stop managing another with a removed block. Acceptance criteria: every plan in the sequence shows no destroys; terraform state list matches the final code; the unmanaged queue still exists in AWS.

52.8 Layout, blast radius, environments and testing

Concept

How you split Terraform into root configurations (directories you run plan and apply in, each with its own state) decides the blast radius of a mistake: how much infrastructure one bad apply can touch. This section covers splitting by environment, account and layer, why workspaces are a poor boundary between staging and production, how to version modules, and how to test Terraform before it reaches any account.

How it works — the layout

Text
infra/
  modules/                     (or a separate repo with tagged releases)
    network/  postgres/  redis/  ecs-service/
  envs/
    staging/
      network/  data/  app/    each: backend.tf, providers.tf, main.tf, terraform.tfvars
    production/
      network/  data/  app/

Why split by layer: the app layer changes daily (task definitions, scaling), the data layer monthly, the network layer rarely. A routine app change then runs a 20-second plan over 60 resources and holds a lock nobody else needs, and it cannot touch the database because the database is not in that state at all. Why one AWS account per environment: credentials for staging cannot change production, and the provider can refuse to run in the wrong account:

HCL
# envs/production/data/providers.tf
provider "aws" {
  region              = "ap-south-1"
  allowed_account_ids = ["444455556666"]          # fail fast if credentials point anywhere else
  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/terraform-apply-data"
  }
  default_tags {
    tags = { environment = "production", service = "orders", managed_by = "terraform" }
  }
}

How it works — workspaces, directories or a wrapper

Approach How environments differ Risk Use for
Directory per environment Separate backend, providers, tfvars Some duplication of small root files Staging and production (recommended)
Workspaces (terraform workspace select) Same code and backend, one state per workspace Wrong workspace selected = change in the wrong environment; same credentials for all Short-lived copies, such as per-PR preview environments
Terragrunt or a similar wrapper Generated backends and inputs from a hierarchy Another tool to learn Many accounts and regions

The incident in 52.6 and 52.15 began with a laptop pointed at the wrong workspace. With directories and per-account roles, the equivalent mistake requires running in the production directory with production credentials, which only CI has.

How it works — module versions

Publish modules with semantic version tags and reference them by version: source = "git::https://github.com/acme/terraform-modules.git//postgres?ref=v2.3.0" for Git, or source = "app.terraform.io/acme/postgres/aws" with version = "~> 2.3" for a registry. A breaking change to inputs or a change that replaces resources is a major version; ship moved blocks with it. Roll out a new module version to staging, let it soak, then production.

How it works — testing before apply

HCL
# modules/postgres/tests/postgres.tftest.hcl (terraform test, 1.7+ for mock providers)
mock_provider "aws" {}

variables {
  name              = "orders"
  environment       = "production"
  instance_class    = "db.r6g.large"
  subnet_ids        = ["subnet-0a1b2c3d", "subnet-4e5f6a7b"]
  security_group_id = "sg-0123456789abcdef0"
}

run "production_database_is_protected" {
  command = plan

  assert {
    condition     = aws_db_instance.this.deletion_protection == true
    error_message = "Production databases must have deletion_protection enabled."
  }
  assert {
    condition     = aws_db_instance.this.manage_master_user_password == true
    error_message = "The master password must be managed by RDS, never passed in."
  }
  assert {
    condition     = aws_db_instance.this.backup_retention_period >= 7
    error_message = "Backups must be kept for at least 7 days."
  }
}

The pipeline order, cheapest first: terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, a linter (TFLint, with the AWS ruleset catching invalid instance types), a security scanner (Trivy's config scanning or Checkov), terraform test for modules, then plan and policy checks (52.10, 52.11). Integration tests that create real resources in a sandbox account and destroy them are worth it for shared modules, and only there.

Production scenario

A 25-service company runs 3 accounts (dev, staging, production) times about 20 root configurations each. Median plan time is 25 seconds; the slowest root (the shared network) takes 90 seconds. The modules repository has 14 modules with about 120 terraform test runs, all with mock providers, finishing in under a minute in CI. Module releases go to dev and staging the day they ship and to production a week later.

Failure scenario

A single root configuration held an entire environment: network, three databases, Redis, 22 ECS services and their IAM, 1,900 resources. Plans took 6 minutes, so engineers used -target to plan only their resources, which skipped dependencies and made the full state drift from the code. One day a full plan, run for an unrelated change, proposed 40 updates nobody understood, including a change to the main route table. The team spent two days splitting the state into layer roots with removed and import blocks. The lesson: a state too big to plan in full will be planned in part, and partial plans hide drift until it is dangerous.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • -target as a habit. It exists for emergencies; regular use means the root is too big.
  • Circular dependencies between roots. Network needs an app security group, app needs network subnets; move shared pieces down a layer.
  • Shared resources owned by nobody. A Route 53 zone used by every service belongs in its own root with a clear owner.
  • Mock providers return made-up values. Tests of computed attributes against mocks prove nothing; test inputs to outputs and invariants.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior designs the layout around one question: what is the most a single mistake can break? They separate environments by account, layers by state, and make the database unreachable from the root that changes every day. They avoid workspaces for long-lived environments, version modules like libraries, and test the invariants that matter (protection, encryption, backups) in the module itself so no caller can forget them.

Interview questions

  1. How would you lay out Terraform for 3 environments and 20 services?
    Show answerHide answer
    Accounts per environment, root configurations per layer and service with their own state, shared versioned modules, outputs shared through SSM parameters or remote state outputs, CI-only applies per root.
  2. Why are workspaces risky for staging versus production?
    Show answerHide answer
    The same code, backend and usually credentials serve both, so the only thing standing between a staging change and production is which workspace is selected.
  3. What does allowed_account_ids protect against?
    Show answerHide answer
    Running a configuration with credentials for the wrong AWS account; the provider refuses before making any call.
  4. What would you test in a Terraform module, and how?
    Show answerHide answer
    Invariants (protection, encryption, backups, tags) with terraform test and mock providers; formatting, validation, lint and security scans before plan.

Practical exercise

Split a single-root configuration of a VPC, an RDS instance and an ECS service into three roots (network, data, app) without recreating anything, using removed blocks in the old root and import blocks in the new ones; publish the subnet ids from the network root to SSM Parameter Store and read them in the data root with aws_ssm_parameter. Add allowed_account_ids to every provider and a terraform test file for the postgres module. Acceptance criteria: all plans after the split show no changes; a plan run with the wrong account's credentials fails immediately; terraform test passes and fails when deletion_protection is turned off.

52.9 The same database in Pulumi and CDK

Concept

Section 52.4.2 compared the tools in a table. Here is the orders database from 52.4.1 written in Pulumi TypeScript and AWS CDK TypeScript, so you can see what actually differs: how environments are expressed, where state lives, how deletion protection works, and how you test it.

Practical example — Pulumi

TypeScript
// infra/pulumi/orders-data/index.ts  (one Pulumi stack per environment: staging, production)
import * as aws from '@pulumi/aws';
import * as pulumi from '@pulumi/pulumi';

const cfg = new pulumi.Config();
const env = pulumi.getStack();                       // "staging" or "production"
const isProd = env === 'production';

const subnetGroup = new aws.rds.SubnetGroup('orders', {
  subnetIds: cfg.requireObject<string[]>('privateDataSubnetIds'),
});

const ordersDb = new aws.rds.Instance('orders', {
  identifier: `orders-${env}`,
  engine: 'postgres',
  engineVersion: '17',
  instanceClass: isProd ? 'db.r6g.large' : 'db.t4g.medium',
  allocatedStorage: 100,
  username: 'orders_admin',
  manageMasterUserPassword: true,                    // password lives in Secrets Manager, not in state
  dbSubnetGroupName: subnetGroup.name,
  vpcSecurityGroupIds: [cfg.require('dbSecurityGroupId')],
  multiAz: isProd,
  backupRetentionPeriod: 30,
  storageEncrypted: true,
  deletionProtection: true,
}, { protect: true });                               // Pulumi refuses to delete it, even if the code is removed

export const endpoint = ordersDb.endpoint;

Practical example — AWS CDK

TypeScript
// infra/cdk/lib/orders-data-stack.ts
import { Duration, RemovalPolicy, Stack, StackProps } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import * as ec2 from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-ec2';
import * as rds from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-rds';
import { Construct } from 'constructs';

export interface OrdersDataStackProps extends StackProps {
  vpc: ec2.IVpc;
  production: boolean;
}

export class OrdersDataStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props: OrdersDataStackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    new rds.DatabaseInstance(this, 'OrdersDb', {
      engine: rds.DatabaseInstanceEngine.postgres({ version: rds.PostgresEngineVersion.VER_17 }),
      vpc: props.vpc,
      vpcSubnets: { subnetType: ec2.SubnetType.PRIVATE_ISOLATED },
      instanceType: props.production
        ? ec2.InstanceType.of(ec2.InstanceClass.R6G, ec2.InstanceSize.LARGE)
        : ec2.InstanceType.of(ec2.InstanceClass.T4G, ec2.InstanceSize.MEDIUM),
      allocatedStorage: 100,
      credentials: rds.Credentials.fromGeneratedSecret('orders_admin'),  // generated into Secrets Manager
      multiAz: props.production,
      backupRetention: Duration.days(30),
      storageEncrypted: true,
      deletionProtection: true,
      removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.SNAPSHOT,          // CloudFormation snapshots it if the stack ever deletes it
    });
  }
}

And a CDK unit test with the real assertions library, run by Jest:

TypeScript
// infra/cdk/test/orders-data-stack.test.ts
import { App, Stack } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { Template } from 'aws-cdk-lib/assertions';
import * as ec2 from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-ec2';
import { OrdersDataStack } from '../lib/orders-data-stack';

test('production database is protected and Multi-AZ', () => {
  const app = new App();
  const vpc = new ec2.Vpc(new Stack(app, 'Net'), 'Vpc');
  const stack = new OrdersDataStack(app, 'OrdersData', { vpc, production: true });

  Template.fromStack(stack).hasResourceProperties('AWS::RDS::DBInstance', {
    DeletionProtection: true,
    MultiAZ: true,
    StorageEncrypted: true,
  });
});

How they differ where it matters

Concern Terraform Pulumi AWS CDK
Environments Directory and tfvars per environment A stack per environment with its own config A stack instance per environment, props in code
State S3 (or HCP Terraform), you run it Pulumi Cloud or a self-managed backend such as S3 CloudFormation holds it; nothing to run
Delete protection in the tool prevent_destroy, lost if the block is removed protect: true, stored in state, survives removal of the code RemovalPolicy.RETAIN or SNAPSHOT (CloudFormation DeletionPolicy)
Delete protection in AWS deletion_protection = true deletionProtection: true deletionProtection: true
Preview terraform plan pulumi preview cdk diff (CloudFormation change set underneath)
Unit tests terraform test Mocks via pulumi.runtime.setMocks with Jest or Mocha aws-cdk-lib/assertions with Jest
Typical surprise Address changes cause destroys Logical name changes cause replaces (use aliases) Construct id changes cause replaces; stuck rollbacks

The row worth remembering: every tool can protect a database from itself, and every one can lose that protection through a rename or a removed line. Only the AWS-side deletion_protection is enforced by the API whoever calls it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior judges the three by their failure modes and by the people who will read them at 03:00, not by syntax. TypeScript infrastructure is attractive to a TypeScript team, and CDK's high-level constructs remove a lot of boilerplate, but the review artefact (a readable plan or diff) and the engine's failure behaviour matter more. Whatever the tool, the same invariants are tested in code: protection on, encryption on, backups on.

Interview questions

  1. How does Pulumi's protect differ from Terraform's prevent_destroy?
    Show answerHide answer
    protect is recorded in state, so deleting the resource from code still fails until it is explicitly unprotected; prevent_destroy is configuration and disappears with the block.
  2. What does CDK's RemovalPolicy.SNAPSHOT do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Sets the CloudFormation deletion policy so the database is snapshotted before CloudFormation deletes it.
  3. How do you unit-test CDK infrastructure?
    Show answerHide answer
    Synthesize the stack and assert on the template with Template.fromStack(...).hasResourceProperties(...).

Practical exercise

Write the orders database in all three tools in a sandbox account. In each, try to delete it by removing it from the code and record what stops the deletion (or does not). Acceptance criteria: a table of the three results, and in every tool the AWS-side deletion protection blocks the delete even when the tool-level protection is gone.

52.10 The Terraform pipeline in practice

Concept

Section 52.5.1 described the flow. This is a working GitHub Actions implementation for one root configuration: AWS credentials through OIDC (no stored keys), plan on every pull request, policy checks, a production environment approval that reviews the exact plan, and an apply of the saved plan file, serialized so two applies never overlap. It complements the application pipeline in Part 47 — CI/CD (47.11).

How it works

Practical example

YAML
# .github/workflows/tf-production-data.yml
name: terraform production data
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["infra/envs/production/data/**", "infra/modules/**", "policy/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["infra/envs/production/data/**", "infra/modules/**"]

permissions:
  id-token: write          # OIDC token for AWS, no long-lived keys
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: tf-production-data
  cancel-in-progress: false  # never kill a running apply

env:
  TF_DIR: infra/envs/production/data
  TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "true"

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: "1.10.5", terraform_wrapper: false }
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/gha-terraform-plan
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR init -input=false
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR fmt -check -recursive && terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR validate
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR plan -input=false -lock-timeout=5m -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR show -json tfplan > plan.json
      - name: Install conftest
        run: |
          curl -sSL https://github.com/open-policy-agent/conftest/releases/download/v0.56.0/conftest_0.56.0_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz \
            | tar xz conftest && sudo mv conftest /usr/local/bin/
      - name: Policy
        run: conftest test plan.json --policy policy --data policy/waivers.json --namespace terraform.guardrails
      - name: Summarize destroys
        run: |
          jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | index("delete")) | "DESTROY: \(.address)"' plan.json \
            | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR show -no-color tfplan >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        with: { name: tfplan, path: "${{ env.TF_DIR }}/tfplan", retention-days: 3 }

  apply:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: plan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # required reviewers configured on this environment
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: "1.10.5", terraform_wrapper: false }
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/gha-terraform-apply-data
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: tfplan, path: "${{ env.TF_DIR }}" }
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR init -input=false
      - run: terraform -chdir=$TF_DIR apply -input=false tfplan   # exactly the plan the approver saw

The details that carry the safety:

  • Two roles. The plan role is read-only for AWS (plus read on the state bucket and write on the lock file, because use_lockfile writes a .tflock object even during plan). The apply role can write, and its trust policy allows only this repository's production environment, so a workflow on a feature branch cannot assume it.
  • The approver reviews the merge-time plan. The PR plan is for discussion; the plan saved in the push run is what the environment approval shows and what apply tfplan executes. If state changed in between, Terraform rejects the saved plan as stale.
  • Concurrency per root. Two merges queue rather than race.
  • The policy step is owned centrally. policy/ has its own code owners; service teams cannot weaken it in the same pull request that needs the exception.

The trust policy for the apply role, written in Terraform:

HCL
data "aws_iam_policy_document" "gha_apply_trust" {
  statement {
