    actions = ["sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"]
    principals {
      type        = "Federated"
      identifiers = ["arn:aws:iam::444455556666:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud"
      values   = ["sts.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"
      values   = ["repo:acme/infra:environment:production"]   # only the approved environment job
    }
  }
}

A scheduled workflow runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode nightly for every root and opens an issue when the exit code is 2 (changes present), which is drift detection for free (see Part 46 — Cloud Architecture, 46.16). Atlantis, HCP Terraform, Spacelift and env0 package this same flow as a product; the principles do not change.

Failure scenario

A team's apply role was AdministratorAccess and its trust policy allowed repo:acme/infra:*. A contractor's pull request added a workflow file on a feature branch that ran terraform apply directly; because the trust condition matched any ref, the job assumed the production apply role and applied a half-finished change that recreated an ElastiCache parameter group and restarted the Redis nodes during business hours. The fix: trust only environment:production, require environment reviewers, protect workflow files with code owners, and scope the apply role to the services in that root. The lesson: the pipeline's credentials are production access, so the conditions on who can use them are as important as the code it runs.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Plan artifacts hold sensitive values. Keep retention short and the artifact private.
  • Forks. Pull requests from forks must not get OIDC tokens for any AWS role; GitHub withholds secrets and OIDC from fork PRs by default for pull_request, so do not switch to pull_request_target for Terraform.
  • Wrapper output. The setup action's wrapper changes stdout; disable it when piping show -json.
  • Lock timeouts. -lock-timeout=5m lets a queued plan wait for a running apply instead of failing.

Interview questions

  1. Why apply a saved plan file instead of running apply fresh?
    Show answerHide answer
    So what is executed is exactly what was reviewed; Terraform rejects a saved plan if state changed since it was made.
  2. How does CI get AWS credentials without stored keys?
    Show answerHide answer
    GitHub's OIDC token is exchanged for a role via sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, with trust conditions on audience and subject (repository, branch or environment).
  3. How do you detect drift continuously?
    Show answerHide answer
    A scheduled plan -detailed-exitcode per root; exit code 2 means differences, which open an issue or alert.

Practical exercise

Build the workflow above for a sandbox root with a plan role and an apply role. Acceptance criteria: a feature-branch workflow cannot assume the apply role; two merges in quick succession apply one after the other; changing a resource between plan and apply makes the apply fail as stale; the nightly drift job opens an issue after a manual console change.

52.11 Policy as code in practice: Conftest and Rego against the plan

Concept

Conftest runs Open Policy Agent (OPA) policies written in Rego against structured files. For Terraform, the input is the plan rendered as JSON (terraform show -json tfplan), whose resource_changes array lists every resource with its address, type, change.actions (["create"], ["update"], ["delete"], ["delete", "create"] for a replacement) and change.before / change.after attribute values. A policy is a set of rules that produce deny (fail) or warn (report) messages.

Practical example — the guardrails in Rego

Written in Rego v1 syntax (the default in OPA 1.0), these are the rules from 52.5.2 plus the one that would have stopped the incident in 52.15:

Rego
# policy/guardrails.rego
package terraform.guardrails

import rego.v1

data_store_types := {"aws_db_instance", "aws_rds_cluster", "aws_elasticache_replication_group", "aws_s3_bucket", "aws_dynamodb_table"}

allowed_db_classes := {"db.t4g.medium", "db.r6g.large", "db.r6g.xlarge", "db.r6g.2xlarge"}

# 1. No deleting or replacing a data store, unless a current, owned waiver exists.
deny contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.type in data_store_types
    "delete" in rc.change.actions
    not waived(rc.address)
    msg := sprintf("%s: deleting or replacing a data store is blocked (actions %v)", [rc.address, rc.change.actions])
}

# 2. Databases must keep backups and deletion protection.
deny contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
    after := rc.change.after
    after != null
    after.backup_retention_period < 7
    msg := sprintf("%s: backup_retention_period must be at least 7", [rc.address])
}

deny contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
    rc.change.after != null
    not rc.change.after.deletion_protection
    msg := sprintf("%s: deletion_protection must be true", [rc.address])
}

# 3. Every bucket's public access block must have all four flags on.
deny contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block"
    rc.change.after != null
    some flag in ["block_public_acls", "block_public_policy", "ignore_public_acls", "restrict_public_buckets"]
    not rc.change.after[flag]
    msg := sprintf("%s: %s must be true", [rc.address, flag])
}

# 4. Cost guardrail: database instance classes from an approved list.
deny contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
    rc.change.after != null
    not rc.change.after.instance_class in allowed_db_classes
    msg := sprintf("%s: instance_class %s is not on the approved list", [rc.address, rc.change.after.instance_class])
}

# 5. Tags, as a warning: ownership and cost allocation.
warn contains msg if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    rc.change.after != null
    tags := object.get(rc.change.after, "tags_all", null)
    tags != null
    missing := {"service", "environment", "owner"} - {k | some k, _ in tags}
    count(missing) > 0
    msg := sprintf("%s: missing tags %v", [rc.address, missing])
}

waived(address) if {
    w := data.waivers[address]
    time.now_ns() < time.parse_rfc3339_ns(w.expires)
}

A waiver is data, reviewed by the policy owners, with an owner and an expiry:

JSON
{
  "waivers": {
    "aws_db_instance.reports_legacy": { "owner": "data-platform", "expires": "2026-12-15T00:00:00Z", "reason": "Decommission ticket DP-412, final snapshot verified" }
  }
}

Policies get unit tests like any code, run with conftest verify --policy policy:

Rego
# policy/guardrails_test.rego
package terraform.guardrails

import rego.v1

test_replacing_database_is_denied if {
    msgs := deny with input as {"resource_changes": [{
        "address": "aws_db_instance.orders", "type": "aws_db_instance",
        "change": {"actions": ["delete", "create"], "after": {"backup_retention_period": 30, "deletion_protection": true, "instance_class": "db.r6g.large"}},
    }]}
    some msg in msgs
    contains(msg, "data store is blocked")
}

test_compliant_database_passes if {
    count(deny) == 0 with input as {"resource_changes": [{
        "address": "aws_db_instance.orders", "type": "aws_db_instance",
        "change": {"actions": ["update"], "after": {"backup_retention_period": 30, "deletion_protection": true, "instance_class": "db.r6g.large"}},
    }]}
}

How it works — Sentinel and other policy points

HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise run policies (Sentinel, or OPA) between plan and apply, with enforcement levels: advisory (report only), soft-mandatory (fails, but an authorized person can override with a record) and hard-mandatory (cannot be overridden). Conftest in your own CI gives you the same with deny versus warn plus a waiver file. Policy also belongs at other layers: cost estimates in the pull request (Infracost) with a threshold policy on the monthly delta; Kubernetes admission control (OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno) for what GitOps applies (52.12); and AWS Organizations service control policies as the last layer, such as denying rds:DeleteDBInstance in production accounts to every role except a break-glass role.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Replacements look like updates to naive rules. Check for "delete" in actions, which matches both ["delete"] and ["delete", "create"].
  • Resources inside modules. resource_changes lists resources inside modules with full addresses like module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this, so type-based rules still work.
  • Unknown values. Attributes (known after apply) appear in change.after_unknown, not in after; decide whether a rule fails closed on unknown.
  • Policy drift. Policies copied into each repository diverge; publish them from one repository with versions, like modules.

Interview questions

  1. What does a Terraform policy evaluate, the code or the plan?
    Show answerHide answer
    The plan JSON, because it contains the resolved values after variables and modules, and the actions (create, update, delete) the code would cause.
  2. How do you write a policy that blocks replacing a database?
    Show answerHide answer
    Deny when the resource type is a data store and "delete" is in change.actions, which covers both deletion and replacement.
  3. How do exceptions work without disabling the policy?
    Show answerHide answer
    A reviewed waiver with an owner and an expiry, read as data by the policy, or a soft-mandatory override with an audit record.

Practical exercise

Add the policies and tests above to the pipeline from 52.10. Acceptance criteria: conftest verify passes; a plan replacing the database fails with the rule-1 message; a waiver with an expiry in the past does not help; a bucket with block_public_policy = false fails; an untagged resource produces a warning only.

52.12 GitOps in practice: Argo CD, Kustomize, Helm and Flux

Concept

Section 52.6.1 introduced GitOps. In practice there is a clean split of ownership: Terraform creates the cloud resources and the cluster itself (VPC, EKS, node groups, IAM roles for service accounts, RDS, and Argo CD's own installation), and Argo CD or Flux owns everything inside the cluster that changes with application releases (Deployments, Services, HPAs, ConfigMaps, ExternalSecrets). A release is a commit to a deployment repository that changes an image tag; the controller notices and syncs. The Helm chart layout for the orders API is in Part 45 — Kubernetes (45.19); this section shows the Argo CD and Kustomize objects that deploy it.

How it works

  1. CI builds and pushes an immutable image tag (date plus commit SHA, never latest).
  2. CI opens a pull request on the deployment repository: kustomize edit set image ghcr.io/acme/orders-api=ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:2026.11.05-3f9c2ab in the staging overlay; after staging verification, the same change in the production overlay.
  3. Argo CD polls the repository (or receives a webhook), renders the overlay, compares it with the live cluster, and applies the difference.
  4. With selfHeal, a manual kubectl edit is reverted within minutes; with prune, objects deleted from Git are deleted from the cluster.

Practical example

YAML
# deploy/apps/orders-api/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: orders
resources:
  - ../../base                       # Deployment, Service, HPA, PDB, ExternalSecret
patches:
  - path: resources-production.yaml  # bigger requests and limits in production
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/acme/orders-api
    newTag: "2026.11.05-3f9c2ab"     # the only line a normal release changes
YAML
# deploy/argocd/orders-api-production.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: orders-api-production
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: orders
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/deploy.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/orders-api/overlays/production
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: orders
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - PruneLast=true                 # delete removed objects after everything else is healthy
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true  # do not overwrite fields listed below during sync
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff: { duration: 10s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 3m }
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers: [/spec/replicas]   # the HPA owns replicas, not Git

With Helm instead of Kustomize, the source points at the chart and lists value files (helm: { valueFiles: [values-prod.yaml] }); Argo CD renders the chart itself, so there is no Tiller-style release state to drift. Flux expresses the same idea with two objects, a GitRepository (source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1) and a Kustomization (kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1) with interval, path, prune: true and a sourceRef. Choose one per organization; Argo CD has the richer UI, Flux is lighter and fully CRD-driven.

Failure scenario

A refactor of the deployment repository moved the orders API's ConfigMap from base/ into a new base/config/ folder but forgot to add the folder to resources: in kustomization.yaml. The rendered manifests no longer contained the ConfigMap, and with prune: true Argo CD deleted it from the cluster within three minutes of the merge. Running pods kept working (their environment was already loaded), so nothing alerted. Forty minutes later the HPA scaled out for the lunch peak, and every new pod failed with CreateContainerConfigError because the ConfigMap they referenced did not exist; the service ran on its old pods at 100% CPU until someone noticed. The fixes: a CI check that renders every overlay (kustomize build) and diffs the object list against the live cluster in the pull request, the argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false annotation on objects that must never be pruned automatically, and an alert on CreateContainerConfigError. The lesson: in GitOps the repository is the cluster, so a refactor of YAML is a production change and deserves a rendered diff in review.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deleting the Application. With the resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io finalizer, deleting an Application cascades and deletes every object it managed.
  • Mutable tags. Deploying latest makes Git unable to say what is running; use immutable tags or digests.
  • Secrets in the deploy repo. Never; use External Secrets Operator or Sealed Secrets (52.13).
  • Too many Applications to manage by hand. An ApplicationSet with a Git directory or cluster generator creates one Application per service or environment from a template.
  • Sync waves. Database migration Jobs must run before the new Deployment; use argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotations or a PreSync hook.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior draws the Terraform–GitOps boundary explicitly (cloud and cluster in Terraform, workloads in Git reconciled by a controller) and keeps a single owner for every object, because two controllers on one object means an endless fight. They treat the deployment repository as production access, require rendered diffs in review, and configure self-heal to respect fields that autoscalers own.

Interview questions

  1. Where does Terraform stop and Argo CD start?
    Show answerHide answer
    Terraform creates cloud resources and the cluster, including installing Argo CD; Argo CD reconciles the in-cluster workload manifests from Git.
  2. Why does selfHeal fight the HPA, and how do you fix it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Git declares replicas and the HPA changes it; remove replicas from the manifest or list it in ignoreDifferences with RespectIgnoreDifferences=true.
  3. How is a release promoted from staging to production in GitOps?
    Show answerHide answer
    A pull request changing the image tag in the production overlay after staging is verified; the merge is the deploy and the Git history is the audit log.

Practical exercise

Set up Argo CD in a kind cluster, deploy the orders API with a base and two overlays, and automate promotion with a script that runs kustomize edit set image and opens a pull request. Acceptance criteria: a kubectl scale is reverted by self-heal except where the HPA owns replicas; removing a ConfigMap from Git with Prune=false annotation leaves it in place; deleting a pod-only resource from Git prunes it.

52.13 Secrets in IaC in practice

Concept

Terraform stores in state every attribute a provider returns. If Terraform generates a database password, reads one from Secrets Manager with a data source, or passes one as an argument, that password is in the state file in plaintext. sensitive = true on a variable or output only hides it from CLI output; it does not encrypt or remove it from state. The practical patterns below keep secrets out of state, out of Git and out of plan files.

How it works — four patterns

Pattern How Secret in state? Use for
Let AWS generate and own it manage_master_user_password = true on RDS; the password lives in Secrets Manager and rotates (every 7 days by default) No, only the secret ARN RDS master credentials
Write-only arguments (Terraform 1.11+) Pass a value from an ephemeral resource to a *_wo argument with a version counter No Secrets Terraform must set, such as an app user's password in Secrets Manager
Reference at runtime ECS task definition secrets with valueFrom an ARN; External Secrets Operator in Kubernetes No, only the ARN Every application secret
Data source or random_password resource Read or generate during plan Yes Avoid for real secrets
HCL
# Pattern 2: create an application secret without it ever touching state (Terraform 1.11+)
ephemeral "random_password" "reporting_db" {
  length  = 32
  special = false
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret" "reporting_db" {
  name       = "orders/production/reporting-db"
  kms_key_id = aws_kms_key.secrets.arn
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "reporting_db" {
  secret_id                = aws_secretsmanager_secret.reporting_db.id
  secret_string_wo         = ephemeral.random_password.reporting_db.result
  secret_string_wo_version = 1          # bump to rotate: Terraform sends a new value
}
YAML
# Pattern 3 on Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator copies from Secrets Manager into a Secret
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: orders
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: orders-db
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: DATABASE_PASSWORD
      remoteRef:
        key: orders/production/app-db
        property: password

On ECS, the same reference goes in the task definition (52.14.5), and the NestJS app reads DATABASE_PASSWORD from its environment through ConfigService, never from a file in the image.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Rotation versus pooled connections. RDS rotates the managed master secret; existing connections keep working, new ones need the new value. Applications should use their own database user (created by a migration with a secret of its own), not the master user, and re-read the secret on authentication failure.
  • State still needs protection. Even with these patterns, state holds endpoints, ARNs and some provider-generated values; encrypt it with KMS and restrict who can read it.
  • terraform output in CI logs. A sensitive output printed with -json is shown in full; do not print outputs in pipelines.
  • ElastiCache auth tokens. The auth_token argument lands in state; prefer ElastiCache users with IAM authentication, or a write-only workflow.
  • Plan files. Saved plans contain state values; treat them as secrets (52.10).

Interview questions

  1. Does sensitive = true keep a secret out of Terraform state?
    Show answerHide answer
    No. It only redacts CLI output; the value is stored in state in plaintext.
  2. How do you give an RDS database a master password without it appearing in state?
    Show answerHide answer
    manage_master_user_password = true, so RDS generates and rotates it in Secrets Manager and state holds only the secret's ARN.
  3. How does a container get a database password at runtime on ECS?
    Show answerHide answer
    The task definition's secrets list maps an environment variable to a Secrets Manager ARN (optionally a JSON key); the task execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that ARN.

52.14 Worked example: Terraform for a NestJS service on AWS

This section writes the infrastructure for the orders API from start to finish: VPC, PostgreSQL on RDS, Redis on ElastiCache, ECS Fargate behind an ALB, and the IAM that connects them, split into three root configurations as in 52.8. The architecture is the reference design of Part 46 — Cloud Architecture (46.13); here it becomes code.

52.14.1 Requirements and decisions

  • Traffic: about 400 requests per second average, 1,500 at peak, p99 under 250 ms. NestJS tasks at 1 vCPU and 2 GB handle about 250–300 requests per second each at 60% CPU, so 4 tasks minimum, 12 at peak, ceiling 20.
  • Data: PostgreSQL 17, about 300 GB growing 15 GB a month, Multi-AZ, 30 days of point-in-time recovery; Redis for cache, rate limits and idempotency keys, about 6 GB hot set, Multi-AZ with automatic failover.
  • Region: ap-south-1, three Availability Zones.
  • Security: nothing but the ALB in public subnets; database and Redis reachable only from the API's security group; TLS everywhere; no secrets in state or images.
  • Compute choice: ECS Fargate, not EKS. One team, one service family, no Kubernetes platform team. EKS adds a control-plane fee (about $73 a month per cluster) and, more importantly, the cluster upgrades, add-ons and node management of Part 45. If the company already runs EKS with GitOps, the network and data roots below stay the same, and the app root is replaced by the EKS module plus the Argo CD objects of 52.12.
Text
infra/envs/production/
  network/   VPC, subnets, NAT, security groups        changes: rarely
  data/      RDS, ElastiCache, parameter groups        changes: monthly
  app/       ECS, ALB, IAM, autoscaling, logs          changes: weekly

52.14.2 The network root

HCL
# infra/envs/production/network/main.tf
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 6.0"

  name = "orders-prod"
  cidr = "10.20.0.0/16"
  azs  = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b", "ap-south-1c"]

  public_subnets   = ["10.20.0.0/24", "10.20.1.0/24", "10.20.2.0/24"]      # ALB and NAT only
  private_subnets  = ["10.20.10.0/23", "10.20.12.0/23", "10.20.14.0/23"]   # ECS tasks
  database_subnets = ["10.20.20.0/24", "10.20.21.0/24", "10.20.22.0/24"]   # RDS and ElastiCache

  create_database_subnet_group = true
  enable_nat_gateway           = true
  one_nat_gateway_per_az       = true   # an AZ failure does not take egress down for the others
  enable_dns_hostnames         = true
}

resource "aws_security_group" "alb" {
  name   = "orders-alb"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_security_group" "api" {
  name   = "orders-api"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
  name   = "orders-db"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_security_group" "redis" {
  name   = "orders-redis"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "alb_https" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  cidr_ipv4         = "0.0.0.0/0"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "api_from_alb" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.api.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id      # only the ALB reaches the tasks
  from_port                    = 3000
  to_port                      = 3000
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "db_from_api" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.db.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.api.id
  from_port                    = 5432
  to_port                      = 5432
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "redis_from_api" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.redis.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.api.id
  from_port                    = 6379
  to_port                      = 6379
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "all_out" {
  for_each          = { alb = aws_security_group.alb.id, api = aws_security_group.api.id }
  security_group_id = each.value
  cidr_ipv4         = "0.0.0.0/0"
  ip_protocol       = "-1"
}

# Publish what the other roots need (no terraform_remote_state, no access to this state).
resource "aws_ssm_parameter" "network" {
  for_each = {
    vpc_id               = module.vpc.vpc_id
    public_subnet_ids    = join(",", module.vpc.public_subnets)
    private_subnet_ids   = join(",", module.vpc.private_subnets)
    database_subnet_ids  = join(",", module.vpc.database_subnets)
    db_subnet_group      = module.vpc.database_subnet_group_name
    sg_alb               = aws_security_group.alb.id
    sg_api               = aws_security_group.api.id
    sg_db                = aws_security_group.db.id
    sg_redis             = aws_security_group.redis.id
  }
  name  = "/orders/production/network/${each.key}"
  type  = "String"
  value = each.value
}

Three NAT gateways cost about $100 a month plus data processing; a single shared NAT saves about $65 and makes one AZ a single point of failure for all outbound calls (payment providers, email). For production, pay it.

52.14.3 The data root

HCL
# infra/envs/production/data/main.tf
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "net" {
  for_each = toset(["db_subnet_group", "database_subnet_ids", "sg_db", "sg_redis"])
  name     = "/orders/production/network/${each.key}"
}

resource "aws_db_parameter_group" "orders" {
  name_prefix = "orders-pg17-"
  family      = "postgres17"
  parameter {
    name         = "rds.logical_replication"     # CDC for the analytics pipeline (Parts 13 and 383.7)
    value        = "1"
    apply_method = "pending-reboot"
  }
  parameter {
    name  = "log_min_duration_statement"
    value = "500"
  }
  lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  identifier            = "orders-prod"
  engine                = "postgres"
  engine_version        = "17"
  instance_class        = "db.r6g.large"
  allocated_storage     = 300
  max_allocated_storage = 1000                    # storage autoscaling ceiling
  storage_type          = "gp3"
  storage_encrypted     = true

  db_name                     = "orders"
  username                    = "orders_admin"
  manage_master_user_password = true              # no password in code or state (64.13)

  db_subnet_group_name   = data.aws_ssm_parameter.net["db_subnet_group"].value
  vpc_security_group_ids = [data.aws_ssm_parameter.net["sg_db"].value]
  parameter_group_name   = aws_db_parameter_group.orders.name
  multi_az               = true

  backup_retention_period   = 30
  backup_window             = "20:30-21:00"       # UTC, which is 02:00-02:30 IST
  maintenance_window        = "sun:21:30-sun:22:30"
  copy_tags_to_snapshot     = true
  deletion_protection       = true                # AWS refuses DeleteDBInstance
  skip_final_snapshot       = false
  final_snapshot_identifier = "orders-prod-final"
  delete_automated_backups  = false               # keep PITR backups even if the instance is deleted

  performance_insights_enabled = true
  auto_minor_version_upgrade   = true
  apply_immediately            = false            # changes wait for the maintenance window

  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_elasticache_subnet_group" "cache" {
  name       = "orders-prod-cache"
  subnet_ids = split(",", data.aws_ssm_parameter.net["database_subnet_ids"].value)
}

resource "aws_elasticache_replication_group" "cache" {
  replication_group_id       = "orders-prod"
  description                = "orders API cache, rate limits and idempotency keys"
  engine                     = "redis"
  engine_version             = "7.1"
  node_type                  = "cache.r7g.large"   # about 13 GB memory per node
  num_cache_clusters         = 2                   # primary plus one replica in another AZ
  automatic_failover_enabled = true
  multi_az_enabled           = true
  subnet_group_name          = aws_elasticache_subnet_group.cache.name
  security_group_ids         = [data.aws_ssm_parameter.net["sg_redis"].value]
  at_rest_encryption_enabled = true
  transit_encryption_enabled = true
  snapshot_retention_limit   = 3
  apply_immediately          = false
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_ssm_parameter" "data" {
  for_each = {
    db_endpoint     = aws_db_instance.orders.address
    db_secret_arn   = aws_db_instance.orders.master_user_secret[0].secret_arn
    redis_endpoint  = aws_elasticache_replication_group.cache.primary_endpoint_address
  }
  name  = "/orders/production/data/${each.key}"
  type  = "String"
  value = each.value
}

Look at the four lines grouped under the backup settings: deletion_protection, skip_final_snapshot = false with a final_snapshot_identifier, delete_automated_backups = false, and prevent_destroy. Each covers a different way the database can disappear, and 52.15 shows what happens when they are missing. (The ECS tasks below use the master secret for brevity; in production the first migration creates a least-privilege orders_app role with its own secret, created as in 52.13, and the task definition references that one.)

52.14.4 The app root: ECS, ALB, IAM and autoscaling

HCL
# infra/envs/production/app/main.tf
variable "image_tag"       { type = string }        # set by the deploy pipeline
variable "certificate_arn" { type = string }

data "aws_ssm_parameter" "p" {
  for_each = toset([
    "network/vpc_id", "network/public_subnet_ids", "network/private_subnet_ids", "network/sg_alb", "network/sg_api",
    "data/db_endpoint", "data/db_secret_arn", "data/redis_endpoint",
  ])
  name = "/orders/production/${each.key}"
}

locals {
  p = { for k, v in data.aws_ssm_parameter.p : k => v.insecure_value }   # plain String parameters, not secrets
}

resource "aws_ecs_cluster" "main" {
  name = "orders-prod"
  setting {
    name  = "containerInsights"
    value = "enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "api" {
  name              = "/ecs/orders-api"
  retention_in_days = 30
}

# --- IAM: two roles with different jobs -----------------------------------------------
data "aws_iam_policy_document" "ecs_tasks_trust" {
  statement {
    actions = ["sts:AssumeRole"]
    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com"]
    }
  }
}

# Execution role: used by the ECS agent to pull the image, write logs and fetch secrets.
resource "aws_iam_role" "execution" {
  name               = "orders-api-execution"
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.ecs_tasks_trust.json
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "execution_managed" {
  role       = aws_iam_role.execution.name
  policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy"
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "execution_secrets" {
  name = "read-db-secret"
  role = aws_iam_role.execution.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version   = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{ Effect = "Allow", Action = ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"], Resource = [local.p["data/db_secret_arn"]] }]
  })
}

# Task role: what the NestJS code itself may call. Only what it needs.
resource "aws_iam_role" "task" {
  name               = "orders-api-task"
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.ecs_tasks_trust.json
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "task_metrics" {
  name = "put-orders-metrics"
  role = aws_iam_role.task.id
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect    = "Allow"
      Action    = ["cloudwatch:PutMetricData"]
      Resource  = "*"
      Condition = { StringEquals = { "cloudwatch:namespace" = "Orders" } }
    }]
  })
}

# --- Task definition ---------------------------------------------------------------------
resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "api" {
  family                   = "orders-api"
  requires_compatibilities = ["FARGATE"]
  network_mode             = "awsvpc"
  cpu                      = "1024"
  memory                   = "2048"
  execution_role_arn       = aws_iam_role.execution.arn
  task_role_arn            = aws_iam_role.task.arn
  runtime_platform {
    operating_system_family = "LINUX"
    cpu_architecture        = "ARM64"              # Graviton: about 20% cheaper per vCPU-hour
  }
  container_definitions = jsonencode([{
    name         = "api"
    image        = "111122223333.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:${var.image_tag}"
    essential    = true
    portMappings = [{ containerPort = 3000, protocol = "tcp" }]
    stopTimeout  = 30                              # time for graceful shutdown of the NestJS app
    environment = [
      { name = "NODE_ENV", value = "production" },
      { name = "DB_HOST", value = local.p["data/db_endpoint"] },
      { name = "DB_NAME", value = "orders" },
      { name = "REDIS_HOST", value = local.p["data/redis_endpoint"] },
    ]
    secrets = [                                    # resolved by ECS at task start; never in state or image
      { name = "DB_USER", valueFrom = "${local.p["data/db_secret_arn"]}:username::" },
      { name = "DB_PASSWORD", valueFrom = "${local.p["data/db_secret_arn"]}:password::" },
    ]
    logConfiguration = {
      logDriver = "awslogs"
      options = {
        "awslogs-group"         = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.api.name
        "awslogs-region"        = "ap-south-1"
        "awslogs-stream-prefix" = "api"
      }
    }
  }])
}

# --- Load balancer -----------------------------------------------------------------------
resource "aws_lb" "api" {
  name               = "orders-prod"
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  subnets            = split(",", local.p["network/public_subnet_ids"])
  security_groups    = [local.p["network/sg_alb"]]
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "api" {
  name                 = "orders-api"
  port                 = 3000
  protocol             = "HTTP"
  target_type          = "ip"                      # required for Fargate awsvpc tasks
  vpc_id               = local.p["network/vpc_id"]
  deregistration_delay = 30
  health_check {
    path                = "/health/ready"          # @nestjs/terminus readiness endpoint
    healthy_threshold   = 2
    unhealthy_threshold = 3
    interval            = 10
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_listener" "https" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.api.arn
  port              = 443
  protocol          = "HTTPS"
  ssl_policy        = "ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06"
  certificate_arn   = var.certificate_arn
  default_action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.api.arn
  }
}

# --- Service and autoscaling -------------------------------------------------------------
resource "aws_ecs_service" "api" {
  name                               = "orders-api"
  cluster                            = aws_ecs_cluster.main.id
  task_definition                    = aws_ecs_task_definition.api.arn
  launch_type                        = "FARGATE"
  desired_count                      = 4
  deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 100
  deployment_maximum_percent         = 200
  health_check_grace_period_seconds  = 30
  deployment_circuit_breaker {
    enable   = true
    rollback = true                                # a bad image rolls itself back
  }
  network_configuration {
    subnets          = split(",", local.p["network/private_subnet_ids"])
    security_groups  = [local.p["network/sg_api"]]
    assign_public_ip = false
  }
  load_balancer {
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.api.arn
    container_name   = "api"
    container_port   = 3000
  }
  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [desired_count]               # Application Auto Scaling owns it
  }
  depends_on = [aws_lb_listener.https]
}

resource "aws_appautoscaling_target" "api" {
  service_namespace  = "ecs"
  resource_id        = "service/${aws_ecs_cluster.main.name}/${aws_ecs_service.api.name}"
  scalable_dimension = "ecs:service:DesiredCount"
  min_capacity       = 4
  max_capacity       = 20
}

resource "aws_appautoscaling_policy" "api_cpu" {
  name               = "orders-api-cpu-60"
  policy_type        = "TargetTrackingScaling"
  service_namespace  = aws_appautoscaling_target.api.service_namespace
  resource_id        = aws_appautoscaling_target.api.resource_id
  scalable_dimension = aws_appautoscaling_target.api.scalable_dimension
  target_tracking_scaling_policy_configuration {
    target_value       = 60
    scale_in_cooldown  = 120
    scale_out_cooldown = 60
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization"
    }
  }
}

output "alb_dns_name" { value = aws_lb.api.dns_name }

On the application side, NestJS reads exactly the variables the task definition provides, and nothing else:

TypeScript
// app.module.ts (excerpt): configuration comes from the task definition's environment and secrets
TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
    type: 'postgres',
    host: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_HOST'),
    port: 5432,
    database: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_NAME'),
    username: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_USER'),
    password: config.getOrThrow<string>('DB_PASSWORD'),   // injected by ECS from Secrets Manager
    ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true },                     // RDS CA bundle trusted in the image
    extra: { max: 20, connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000 },     // 20 tasks x 20 = 400 < max_connections
    autoLoadEntities: true,
  }),
}),

52.14.5 Applying it, verifying it, paying for it

Apply order is network, data, app, each through the pipeline of 52.10. The first production plans summarize as:

Text
network:  Plan: 41 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.   apply about 3 min (NAT gateways)
data:     Plan: 9 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.    apply about 25 min (Multi-AZ RDS, ElastiCache)
app:      Plan: 17 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.   apply about 4 min (ALB, service steady state)

Afterwards, a routine deploy (new image_tag) shows 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy (a new task definition revision and the service update), and nothing else; any other line in that plan is drift or a mistake. Verification after the first apply: the ALB DNS name returns 200 on /health/ready; the ECS service reaches steady state with 4 tasks; aws rds describe-db-instances shows DeletionProtection: true; a deliberately failing image triggers the circuit breaker and rolls back.

Approximate monthly cost in ap-south-1 at average load:

Component Configuration About per month
RDS PostgreSQL db.r6g.large Multi-AZ, 300 GB gp3, 30-day backups $430
ElastiCache Redis 2 x cache.r7g.large $330
ECS Fargate average 6 tasks, 1 vCPU / 2 GB, ARM64 $175
ALB 1 load balancer plus LCUs $50
NAT gateways 3, plus about 200 GB processed $110
CloudWatch logs and metrics 30-day retention, Container Insights $60
Total about $1,150

The two largest lines are the data stores, which is normal; the most negotiable is NAT (VPC endpoints for ECR, S3, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch Logs remove much of the NAT data processing; see Part 51 — Cost-Aware Engineering).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior's eye goes to four places in this code: the boundaries between roots (the app root cannot destroy the database because it does not contain it), the security group references (nothing reachable that should not be), the two IAM roles (the code gets one CloudWatch permission, not *), and the data-store protection block. They also notice what is deliberately absent: no passwords, no terraform_remote_state, no count, no laptop in the path to production.

Interview questions

  1. Why split this into network, data and app roots?
    Show answerHide answer
    Different change rates and blast radius: the daily-changing root cannot touch the database, plans are faster, and locks do not block other teams.
  2. What is the difference between the ECS execution role and the task role?
    Show answerHide answer
    The execution role is used by ECS to pull images, write logs and fetch secrets at start; the task role is what the application code assumes for its own AWS calls.
  3. Which settings protect the RDS instance, and from what?
    Show answerHide answer
    deletion_protection (API refuses delete), prevent_destroy (Terraform refuses while the block exists), skip_final_snapshot = false (a snapshot is taken if deleted), delete_automated_backups = false (PITR backups survive deletion), backup_retention_period (how far back you can restore).
  4. Why ignore desired_count in the ECS service?
    Show answerHide answer
    Application Auto Scaling changes it; without ignore_changes, every apply would reset the service to 4 tasks during peak.

Practical exercise

Apply the three roots in a sandbox account with smaller sizes (db.t4g.medium, cache.t4g.small, single NAT) and deploy a NestJS app with a /health/ready endpoint. Acceptance criteria: the app reads its database password only from the task's environment; terraform state pull | grep -i password finds nothing; deleting the RDS instance from the console fails because of deletion protection; a plan that changes the database identifier is rejected by the Conftest policy from 52.11.

52.15 Incident story: the terraform apply that deleted a production database

Concept

Section 52.6.1 summarized this incident. Here it is in full, as a blameless postmortem, because the details are where the lessons are. It is a composite of several real incidents at different companies; every individual failure in it has happened in production somewhere.

What happened

  • The setup. One root configuration per environment, selected with Terraform workspaces (staging, production) over one S3 backend. Engineers had an AWS profile with administrator access to both accounts "for emergencies". The database module had been written for staging first: deletion_protection = false and skip_final_snapshot = true ("so we can tear staging down quickly"), and production overrode neither. delete_automated_backups was not set, so it took the provider default, true. prevent_destroy = true was on aws_db_instance.main.
  • The change. An engineer refactored the database into a reusable module on a branch, moving aws_db_instance.main to module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this, without a moved block. The pull request was still open; the plan in CI ran against staging only.

Timeline (local time):

  • 17:38 To test the refactor before going home, the engineer runs terraform plan from the branch on a laptop. The shell's workspace is still production from a morning investigation.
  • 17:41 The plan prints 300 lines ending in Plan: 14 to add, 3 to change, 12 to destroy. The engineer, expecting a large diff from the refactor, scrolls to the bottom and does not read the destroy list. prevent_destroy does not fire: it lived in the old resource block, which no longer exists in the code.
  • 17:44 terraform apply, types yes. Terraform deletes aws_db_instance.main (the old address) before creating the new one. RDS accepts the delete: deletion protection is off. No final snapshot is taken: skip_final_snapshot = true. Automated backups are deleted with the instance: delete_automated_backups defaulted to true.
  • 17:52 The API's error rate climbs to 100% for writes; Redis-cached reads mask it partially. Pager fires at 17:53.
  • 18:06 On-call finds the RDS instance gone and a new, empty orders-db being created by the still-running apply. The apply is stopped.
  • 18:15 Recovery sources assessed: no final snapshot, no automated backups. The last restorable copy is a daily AWS Backup recovery point at 02:00, in a vault in the same account that the deletion did not touch because AWS Backup recovery points are separate resources.
  • 18:30 Restore from the 02:00 recovery point starts (about 300 GB).
  • 19:50 Restored instance available. Data between 02:00 and 17:44 is missing.
  • 19:55 to 23:20 The analytics team's CDC topics (Parts 13 and 383.7) retained seven days of row changes for orders, order_items, payments and refunds. A replay script applies every change with an LSN after the 02:00 snapshot, idempotently by primary key. Tables not captured by CDC (carts, sessions, saved addresses edited that day) are lost for the day.
  • 23:40 Writes re-enabled. About 6 hours of write outage, and the loss of a day of non-CDC tables.

Why every layer failed, and what each would have done

Guardrail Layer Would it have prevented deletion? Would it have prevented data loss?
Applies only from CI; humans have read-only production credentials Process and IAM Yes Yes
Directory and AWS account per environment, allowed_account_ids (52.8) Layout Yes (wrong workspace impossible) Yes
moved block for the refactor (52.7) Code Yes (no destroy in the plan at all) Yes
prevent_destroy Terraform No (removed with the block) No
Conftest deny on data-store delete (52.11) Policy Yes, in CI; no, from a laptop Yes, in CI
deletion_protection = true AWS API Yes, whoever runs it Yes
SCP denying rds:DeleteDBInstance in production except break-glass AWS Organizations Yes Yes
skip_final_snapshot = false AWS No Yes (to the minute of deletion)
delete_automated_backups = false AWS No Yes (point-in-time recovery)
AWS Backup in a separate account with vault lock AWS No Yes (worst case: last backup)
Plan review that highlights destroys (52.10) Process Likely Likely

The pattern is defence in depth: any one of six independent guardrails would have stopped the deletion, and any one of three would have prevented the data loss. The organization had one guardrail (prevent_destroy), and it was the one with a hole shaped exactly like this mistake.

Postmortem actions

  1. Production credentials for humans are read-only; applies run only from the pipeline's role, trusted only from the protected environment (52.10). Break-glass access exists, is time-limited and alerts the team.
  2. Workspaces replaced by directories and one account per environment, with allowed_account_ids in every provider block.
  3. The database module defaults flipped to safe: deletion_protection = true, skip_final_snapshot = false, delete_automated_backups = false; staging must opt out explicitly, and a terraform test asserts the production values (52.8).
  4. Conftest policy denying deletion or replacement of data stores without a waiver; an SCP denying rds:DeleteDBInstance and rds:DeleteDBCluster in the production account for every role except break-glass.
  5. AWS Backup copies to a separate backup account with vault lock; quarterly restore drills that measure real restore time (see Part 50 — Backup, Restore and Disaster Recovery, 50.10).
  6. The plan comment in pull requests lists destroys first, in bold, and any destroy of a stateful type requires a second approver.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads this story and does not conclude "the engineer should have been more careful". Careful people make this mistake at 17:41 on a Friday; systems must make it impossible or survivable. They layer guardrails so that no single one is load-bearing, they prefer guardrails enforced by AWS itself (deletion protection, SCPs, a separate backup account) over guardrails that live in code which can be refactored away, and they test recovery, not just backups, because "we have backups" is a belief until a restore drill turns it into a measured fact.

Interview questions

  1. Why did prevent_destroy not stop the deletion?
    Show answerHide answer
    It is part of the resource block; the refactor removed the block (renaming the address without a moved block), so Terraform saw a resource with no configuration and planned to destroy it with no lifecycle rule attached.
  2. What is the difference between deletion_protection and prevent_destroy?
    Show answerHide answer
    deletion_protection is an RDS setting enforced by the AWS API for any caller; prevent_destroy is a Terraform plan-time check that exists only while the resource's block exists.
  3. Which settings decide whether you lose data when an RDS instance is deleted?
    Show answerHide answer
    skip_final_snapshot (whether a final snapshot is taken), delete_automated_backups (whether point-in-time backups survive), and whether independent backups exist elsewhere, such as AWS Backup in another account.
  4. Design the guardrails so this cannot happen again.
    Show answerHide answer
    CI-only applies with scoped OIDC roles, per-account environments with allowed_account_ids, moved blocks enforced in review, policy denying data-store deletion, deletion_protection, an SCP, safe module defaults with tests, and cross-account backups with restore drills.

Practical exercise

In a sandbox account, reproduce the incident safely: create a small RDS instance with the original unsafe settings, rename its address without a moved block, and apply. Then rebuild it with every guardrail from the table, repeat the same rename, and record which guardrail stops it first, and which stop it if you disable the first. Acceptance criteria: a written table showing, for each guardrail, whether it blocked the delete or preserved the data, and a restore from a final snapshot completed and timed.

Senior Checklist — Part 52

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain why IaC beats clickops and codify infrastructure in Terraform
  • I always read the plan and can tell ~ from -/+, and I know which arguments force replacement of a database
  • I use remote state with versioning, encryption and locking (use_lockfile), and I treat a lock error as a question
  • I think in resource addresses: for_each for collections, moved for renames, import to adopt, removed to hand off
  • I lay out Terraform by account, environment and layer so the daily-changing root cannot touch the database
  • I version modules like libraries and test their invariants with terraform test
  • I can compare Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, CDK and CloudFormation by state, protection semantics and failure modes
  • I run IaC through CI with OIDC roles, plan on PR, policy, approval and apply of the saved plan, serialized per root
  • I can write Conftest/Rego policies against plan JSON, with tests and expiring waivers
  • I keep Kubernetes workloads in Git reconciled by Argo CD or Flux, with one owner per object
  • I keep secrets out of code, state and plans (managed passwords, write-only arguments, runtime references)
  • I protect databases with layered guardrails: deletion_protection, final snapshots, retained automated backups, SCPs, cross-account backups and tested restores

Part 52 — Key Takeaways

  • IaC replaces clickops with version-controlled, reviewed, repeatable, auditable infrastructure; manual changes are undocumented drift that hides until it causes an incident.
  • plan is the review artefact: read the summary line against what you expected, and treat every -/+ or destroy on a stateful resource as a conversation before an approval.
  • State maps addresses to real resources; most "Terraform deleted it" incidents are address changes, prevented with for_each and moved blocks.
  • Remote state must be versioned, encrypted, locked and access-controlled, because it is critical and may contain sensitive values.
  • Split Terraform by account, environment and layer to limit blast radius; avoid workspaces as the boundary between staging and production.
  • Version modules like libraries, ship moved blocks with refactors, and test invariants such as deletion protection and encryption in the module.
  • All IaC tools can protect a resource from themselves and all can lose that protection through a rename; only provider-side settings like deletion_protection hold for every caller.
  • The pipeline is the only path to production: OIDC roles scoped to a protected environment, plan on PR, policy, human approval, and apply of exactly the saved plan.
  • Policy as code evaluates the plan JSON, blocks real risks (data-store deletion, missing backups, public buckets), and needs reviewed, expiring waivers or it gets disabled.
  • GitOps keeps cluster workloads in Git with a controller reconciling them; give every object one owner and review rendered diffs, because the deploy repository is production.
  • Keep secrets out of code, state and plan files: AWS-managed passwords, write-only arguments, and runtime references from ECS or External Secrets.
  • Defence in depth beats carefulness: any one of several independent guardrails should stop a destructive apply, and backups only count once a restore drill has proven them.

Part 53 — AI-Assisted Engineering

What you will learn

  1. 53.1What AI coding tools are and how they work underneath
  2. 53.2The beginner layer: learning with an assistant

  4. 53.4Reviewing AI-written code like a senior
  5. 53.5Delegate, pair or keep: the decision matrix

  8. 53.8The team layer

Parts 37, 38 taught you to build features with language models: an order-support assistant, a catalog search, an agent that can look up an order. This Part is about something different and more personal. It is about engineering alongside AI tools: the completion that appears as you type, the chat panel you paste a stack trace into, and the agent in your terminal that reads files, runs your tests and edits code in a loop while you watch.

Almost every engineer now uses these tools daily, from the person on their first job to the principal setting policy for four hundred engineers. They are genuinely useful. They are also confidently wrong often enough that an engineer who trusts them blindly ships bugs faster than ever before. The skill is not "using AI". The skill is knowing what the tool actually sees, what it is good and bad at, how to check its work, how much power to give it, and who is accountable when it is wrong. (The short answer to the last one: you are.)

The Part is organised by level, so you can find your layer:

Section Who it is for The question it answers
53.1 Everyone What are these tools, and what is happening underneath?
53.2 Beginners How do I learn with an assistant instead of being replaced by one?
53.3 Working engineers What loop reliably turns AI output into shippable code?
53.4 and 53.5 Seniors How do I review AI-written code, and what should I delegate at all?
53.6 and 53.7 Seniors and tech leads How do I give an agent tools and permissions without giving it the keys?
53.8 Team leads How does a team keep quality, ownership and learning intact?
53.9 Principals and architects Policy, vendors, cost, measurement and rollout across an organisation
53.10 Everyone Interview questions by level

The voice here is that of an engineer who uses these tools every day and has cleaned up after them. No hype, no doom. Model mechanics (tokens, temperature, context windows as an API concept) live in Part 37 — Building Backends with LLMs: Foundations, and evaluation lives in Part 38 — Retrieval, Agents and Evaluation; we link there instead of repeating them.

53.1 What AI coding tools are and how they work underneath

53.1.1 Three shapes: completion, chat and agents

Concept

AI coding tools come in three broad shapes, and most products now offer more than one of them.

  1. Inline completion. As you type in the editor, the tool predicts the next few lines and shows them as grey "ghost text". You press Tab to accept. GitHub Copilot made this shape popular; most AI-enabled editors offer it.
  2. Chat. A panel or window where you ask questions in natural language ("why does this query do a sequential scan?", "write a DTO for this payload") and get answers and code blocks back. You copy, apply or discard them.
  3. Agentic tools (agents). You give a goal ("make the failing refund test pass"), and the tool works in a loop: it reads files, searches the code, runs commands such as your test suite, edits files, looks at the result, and repeats until it thinks it is done or it needs you. Claude Code runs this way in a terminal; editors such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot also offer agent modes inside the IDE, and some services run agents in the cloud against a repository and open a pull request.

The product names and feature lists change every few months. The three shapes do not, and each one carries a different amount of risk.

Why does it exist?

Writing software has always involved a lot of typing that is not thinking: boilerplate, glue code, test scaffolding, looking up an API you used last month and forgot. The tools exist to compress that work. Chat exists because a lot of engineering time goes into understanding (unfamiliar code, an error message, a library) rather than typing. Agents exist because a lot of work is a loop of "edit, run, read the error, edit again", and a tool that can run the loop itself saves the human from being the copy-paste mechanism between the editor and the terminal.

Mental model

Imagine three kinds of help in a workshop.

  • Completion is a helper who hands you the next tool before you ask for it. Usually right, sometimes the wrong size, and you notice immediately because you are holding it.
  • Chat is a well-read colleague at the next bench. You describe the problem, they suggest an approach. They have never seen your workshop, so they only know what you tell them.
  • An agent is an apprentice you send off to do a job on their own. They can pick up tools, cut wood and try things. They work fast and never get tired, but they cannot tell a load-bearing wall from a partition unless someone marked it, and they will cheerfully cut through either.

The further down that list you go, the more work happens before a human looks at it, and the more the safety of the result depends on the guardrails around the tool rather than on your attention.

How it works

All three shapes are the same machine underneath: a large language model that takes text in and produces text out (Part 37, 37.1.1). What differs is who builds the input, how big it is, and what happens to the output.

Step by step, for an agent session:

  1. The tool builds a prompt: a system prompt from the vendor, your project instruction file if there is one (53.3.2), your request, and a list of the tools it can call (read file, search, run shell command, edit file).
  2. The model replies either with text or with a tool call, for example "run npm test -- refund.service.spec.ts".
  3. The tool checks its permission settings. Depending on configuration it runs the command, asks you first, or refuses.
  4. The command's output (test results, a file's contents, an error) is appended to the conversation.
  5. The model reads that output and decides the next step. This is the same tool loop Part 38 describes in 38.3.1 for product agents; here the tools happen to be your file system and your shell.
  6. The loop ends when the model says it is done, hits a step limit, or asks you something.
Shape Who builds the context Size of change per step Where the human checks Main risk
Completion The editor, automatically, from nearby code A few lines Every acceptance, in place Small wrong details accepted on autopilot
Chat You, by what you paste or attach A function or a file When you copy or apply it Answer fits the question, not your codebase
Agent The agent, by reading and running things Many files, many commands At the end, or at permission prompts Large, plausible diffs; actions with side effects

Practical example

You need a new endpoint, GET /orders/:id/tracking, in a NestJS orders service.

  • With completion, you write the controller method signature and the tool suggests the body, guessing that you call this.ordersService.getTracking(id). Useful if that method exists. If it does not, you have just accepted a call to a function that is not real, and the compiler will tell you in a second.
  • With chat, you paste the controller, the service and the Order entity and ask for the endpoint plus a unit test. You get decent code that matches what you pasted, but it may not know that your team wraps every response in a ResponseEnvelope because you did not paste that file.
  • With an agent, you ask "add a tracking endpoint following the existing patterns; run the tests". It searches for existing controllers, finds the envelope, writes the code, runs npm test, sees a failing lint rule, fixes it, and presents a diff touching four files. Faster, and now you have four files to review instead of one function.

Production scenario

On a team of twelve backend engineers working on an e-commerce platform, a typical day looks like this: completion is on for everyone all day; chat is used dozens of times per person for explanations, regexes, SQL and test cases; agents are used a few times per person per day for bounded tasks such as "migrate these six controllers to the new validation pipe" or "find why this test is flaky". The team's pull request volume goes up noticeably after adoption. That last fact matters more than any of the others, and we return to it in 53.8: the bottleneck moves from writing code to reviewing it.

Failure scenario

An engineer uses an agent to "clean up unused code" in a payments module. The agent searches for references to each exported function, finds none for reconcileStalePayments, and deletes it. The function was invoked by name from a cron configuration in a separate infrastructure repository that the agent could not see. All tests passed, because no test called it. Nine days later finance notices that stale payments are no longer being reconciled. The agent did exactly what it was asked, using exactly the information it had. The human approved a deletion without asking "who else calls this?"

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Code outside the context. Callers in another repository, a cron definition, a database trigger, a feature flag config: invisible to the tool unless you provide it.
  • Stale knowledge. The model was trained up to some date; a library's API may have changed since, so it suggests the old method name with full confidence.
  • Generated code that compiles but is wrong. Types line up, tests pass, behaviour is wrong in a case nobody tested.
  • Side effects during the loop. An agent that can run commands can run a migration, call an API or delete a directory as part of "trying something".
  • Non-determinism. Ask the same question twice and get two different answers (Part 37, 37.1.2). A result you cannot reproduce is a result you must verify.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats these tools as a new kind of junior collaborator with unusual properties: extremely fast, widely read, never tired, no memory of yesterday unless written down, and no stake in the outcome. They choose the shape by risk. Completion for the boilerplate they could write in their sleep. Chat for exploration and explanation. Agents for bounded, well-tested, reversible tasks, inside a sandbox, with a diff at the end that they read line by line. They never let the tool's speed set the pace of review.

Common mistakes

  • Treating all three shapes as equally safe. Accepting a two-line completion and accepting a forty-file agent diff are not the same act.
  • Believing the tool "knows the codebase". It knows what it has read in this session.
  • Measuring the tool by how much code it wrote rather than how much correct, maintained code reached production.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a chat assistant and an agentic coding tool?
    Show answerHide answer
    Chat returns text and code for a human to apply; an agent calls tools (read, search, run, edit) in a loop and changes the working tree itself. Why it matters: agents have side effects and produce larger diffs, so they need permissions and sandboxing. Follow-up: what would you never let an agent run without asking?
  2. Why can an agent's change pass every test and still break production?
    Show answerHide answer
    Tests only cover what someone thought of, and the agent only sees what is in its context; callers in other repos, configs or schedules are invisible.
  3. Where does the human checkpoint sit for each shape?
    Show answerHide answer
    On each acceptance for completion, on apply for chat, at permission prompts and final review for agents.

Practical exercise

Pick one small, real task in a NestJS project (for example, adding pagination to a list endpoint). Do it three times: once with completion only, once by asking a chat assistant with the relevant files attached, and once with an agent in a separate Git branch. Acceptance criteria: for each run, record time taken, number of files changed, number of defects you found in review, and one thing the tool did not know about your codebase. Write three sentences on which shape fits this kind of task and why.

53.1.2 Context: the tool only knows what it can see

Concept

A model has no live connection to your repository, your database or your production logs. On each request it sees exactly one thing: the context, meaning the text placed into its input for that request. The size limit on that text is the context window (Part 37, 37.1.1, explains it in tokens). Everything the tool "knows" about your project in a given moment is either in that window or was learned in training from public code, which is not your code.

Why does it exist?

The context limit exists because models process a bounded amount of input per request, and cost and latency grow with input size. Tools work around it by selecting what to include: the open file, nearby files, search results, files the agent chose to read, your instruction file. Understanding that selection explains most of the strange things these tools do.

Mental model

Imagine a consultant who is brilliant but works through a letterbox. You can push pages through; they read them and push back advice. They cannot walk into the building. If you push through the controller but not the guard that protects it, the advice will be about an unprotected controller. If the pages you sent were from last year's version of the file, the advice fits last year.

How it works

What this means in practice:

  1. Selection is lossy. Editors include a small window of nearby code for completion; agents decide what to read. If the relevant file is never read, the model reasons without it.
  2. Long sessions drift. As an agent session grows, early details compete with later ones for attention, and many tools summarise or drop older turns to fit. A rule you stated at the start may have fallen out of view by step forty. Part 37 notes the same effect for prompts: models use facts at the start and end of long input better than facts buried in the middle.
  3. Nothing persists between sessions unless the tool writes it somewhere. Yesterday's agreement about naming is gone today. This is why project instruction files exist (53.3.2).
  4. Training data is not your code. The model has seen a great deal of public NestJS and PostgreSQL code. Its default answer is the average of that code, which may be older, less secure or simply different from your conventions.

Practical example

You ask: "Why is GET /orders slow?" and paste the controller. The assistant suggests adding a cache. Then you paste the TypeORM query and the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output showing a sequential scan on 12 million rows, and it correctly suggests a composite index on (customer_id, created_at DESC). The model did not get smarter between the two questions. The context got better.

Production scenario

A team notices that agent-written code keeps using class-validator decorators directly on entity classes, while the team's rule is that validation lives on DTOs only. Nobody wrote that rule down anywhere the tool reads. After adding two lines to the repository's instruction file and one example DTO path, the pattern drops to near zero in new pull requests. Context is configuration.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Secrets in context. Anything you paste or the agent reads (including .env) is sent to the vendor's model. See 53.2.2.
  • Poisoned context. A file, web page or tool output can contain text that reads like instructions to the model. That is prompt injection, covered for coding agents in 53.6.4.
  • Contradictory context. Two files with different patterns (the old service and the new one); the model may copy the wrong one.
  • Context exhaustion. A huge log pasted in full pushes your actual instructions out of effective attention. Paste the relevant fifty lines, not fifty thousand.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

When an AI answer is bad, the senior's first question is "what did it see?", not "is the model dumb?". They curate context the way they would brief a contractor: the relevant files, the schema, the exact error, the constraint that is not obvious ("this table has 80 million rows and takes writes all day"). They also keep sessions short and focused, starting a fresh one for a new task rather than dragging a long, drifted conversation along.

Common mistakes

  • Asking a question about a bug without pasting the error or the code path.
  • Running one enormous agent session for a whole day and wondering why it forgets the rules.
  • Assuming the tool read a file because the file exists.

Interview questions

  1. An assistant keeps suggesting an API your team deprecated. Why, and what do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    It follows its training data and whatever it sees in context; give it the current pattern in context or the instruction file, and remove or mark the old code so it stops being copied.
  2. What does "context window" mean for a coding tool in practice?
    Show answerHide answer
    It is the boundary of what the tool knows during one request; selection decides quality, and anything outside it does not exist for the model.
  3. Why might an agent ignore a rule you gave it an hour ago?
    Show answerHide answer
    Long-session drift and summarisation; restate key rules, keep sessions focused, put durable rules in the instruction file.

Practical exercise

Take a real bug from your team's history. Ask an assistant to diagnose it three times with increasing context: only the error message; error plus the code path; error, code path, schema and the relevant log lines. Acceptance criteria: a short table showing the diagnosis each time and whether it was right, and one paragraph on the minimum context that produced a correct answer.

53.1.3 Plausible, not verified

Concept

A language model produces text that is likely given its input. For code, "likely" usually means "looks like correct code", and very often it is correct. But nothing in the generation step runs the code, checks it against your schema, or confirms that a package or method exists. Output is plausible by construction and verified by nobody until a compiler, a test, a reviewer or production checks it.

Why does it exist?

This is not a bug that the next model version removes; it is what the generation process is. Models are getting better, and agentic tools narrow the gap by running tests and type checkers inside the loop. But a tool that runs your tests is only as good as your tests, and a passing type check says nothing about authorization or concurrency. Part 38 (38.4.1 and 38.6.1) explains how product teams evaluate model output systematically; as an individual engineer, your evaluation is your test suite and your review.

Mental model

Imagine a student who has read every textbook and writes beautifully, sitting an exam where nobody marks the answers. Most answers will be right because they read the books. Some will be wrong with exactly the same handwriting and confidence. Fluency is not evidence.

How it works

The gap between "plausible" and "correct" shows up in predictable places:

Failure What it looks like What catches it
Hallucinated API repository.findOneOrFailBy(...) with a made-up signature Compiler, type checker
Hallucinated package npm install of a name that does not exist, or worse, exists and is malicious Registry check, dependency review (53.4)
Wrong version Uses an option removed two major versions ago Compiler, tests, changelog
Logic error in an untested branch Refund allowed when order is shipped Tests that cover the branch, review
Security gap Missing ownership check, string-built SQL Security review checklist (Part 40, 40.38)
Concurrency bug Check-then-act without a lock Senior review, concurrency tests (Part 41, 41.9)
Fabricated explanation "PostgreSQL automatically indexes foreign keys" (it does not) Documentation, an experiment

The top rows are cheap to catch automatically. The bottom rows are expensive and are exactly where AI-generated code needs a human who understands the system.

Practical example

You ask why a migration locked the orders table. The assistant explains confidently that CREATE INDEX "only takes a lightweight lock". In fact a plain CREATE INDEX takes a lock that blocks writes for the duration of the build; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids that (Part 24, 24.3). The explanation was fluent, specific and wrong. A two-minute check of the PostgreSQL documentation, or a test on a copy of the table while running an INSERT in another session, settles it.

Failure scenario

A developer asks for "a function to validate Indian GST numbers" and gets a tidy regex with a comment claiming it follows the official format. It accepts most real numbers, so manual testing looks fine. It also accepts some invalid ones, because the checksum digit is not verified, and the comment says nothing about that. Invoices with bad tax IDs reach the accounting export, and the finance team spends a week correcting them. Fix: property-based tests against known valid and invalid examples (Part 41, 41.15), and a habit of asking "what does this not check?"

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Confident citations. The tool may cite a documentation section or RFC that does not say what it claims. Open the link.
  • Tests that test the implementation. Ask a tool to write code and tests together and the tests may encode the same misunderstanding as the code.
  • "Fixed" by weakening the check. An agent told to make tests pass may change the assertion instead of the code. Read test diffs as carefully as code diffs.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior applies the same rule to AI output as to a Stack Overflow answer or a colleague's untested branch: it is a hypothesis until something independent confirms it. They push verification as early and as automatic as possible (types, lint, tests, a quick experiment) and reserve human attention for the things machines cannot check: whether the change is the right change, and whether it is safe under failure, concurrency and attack.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a detailed explanation as more trustworthy than a short one.
  • Accepting a test suite written by the same tool, in the same session, as proof that the code works.
  • Skipping the experiment because the answer "sounds right".

Interview questions

  1. Why is AI-generated code "plausible but unverified"?
    Show answerHide answer
    Generation predicts likely text; nothing in that step executes or checks it. Follow-up: which classes of error does a compiler catch, and which need a human?
  2. An agent says all tests pass. What else do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Whether tests were changed or weakened, whether new branches are covered, security and concurrency paths, and whether the change is the right one.
  3. How would you verify an AI's claim about database locking behaviour?
    Show answerHide answer
    Read the PostgreSQL documentation for the statement's lock level and reproduce it with two sessions, checking pg_locks.

Practical exercise

Ask an assistant five factual questions about PostgreSQL or NestJS behaviour that you can verify (for example, "does PostgreSQL create an index for a foreign key automatically?", "what lock does ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT take?"). Acceptance criteria: for each, the assistant's answer, the documentation or experiment that confirms or refutes it, and a tally of correct, partly correct and wrong.

53.2 The beginner layer: learning with an assistant

53.2.1 A tutor and a pair, not an oracle

Concept

For someone early in their career, an AI assistant can be the most patient tutor they have ever had: it explains a stack trace at 23:00, rephrases a concept five ways and never sighs. It can also quietly stop you learning, because it hands you working code before you have built the mental model that would let you write, debug or review it. The difference is how you use it: as a tutor (explain, quiz, critique) and a pair (you drive, it suggests), not as an oracle (it answers, you paste).

Why does it exist?

Juniors become seniors by building mental models: how a request flows through NestJS, why a transaction needs isolation, what an index does. Those models come from struggling with problems, being wrong, and finding out why. An oracle removes the struggle and the model never forms. The engineer who cannot work without the tool is also the engineer who cannot tell when the tool is wrong, which is exactly when they are needed.

Mental model

Imagine learning to drive with an instructor who has dual controls. A good instructor lets you steer, brakes only when needed, and explains what you did wrong. A bad one drives the whole lesson while you sit in the driver's seat. After twenty lessons with the second, you have a log of hours and no ability to drive.

How it works

Prompts that build understanding versus prompts that replace it:

Instead of Ask
"Write a NestJS guard that checks roles." "I wrote this guard. Explain what ExecutionContext gives me and point out anything wrong, without rewriting it."
"Fix this error." "Explain what this error means and where in the request lifecycle it is thrown. Give me a hint, not the fix."
"Write the SQL for top customers." "Here is my SQL. Will it be slow on 10 million rows? Explain the plan I should expect."
"Write tests for this service." "List the cases I should test for this service and why. I will write them."
"What does this code do?" (then nothing) "Explain this function line by line, then quiz me with three questions about it."

Practical example

A junior is stuck on QueryFailedError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uq_users_email". The oracle route: paste error, get a patch that catches the error and returns 409, paste it in, move on.
