The tutor route: ask what the error means, learn that PostgreSQL enforced a unique index, learn why checking "does the email exist?" before inserting is a race (two requests can both see "no" and both insert, Part 21, 21.3), and then write the handler that maps PostgreSQL error code 23505 to 409 Conflict. Same final code; one of them now understands why the database, not the application, must be the source of truth for uniqueness.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors coaching juniors encourage AI use and expect juniors to explain every line they submit. "The AI wrote it" is not an answer in code review, any more than "I found it on a forum" was. The senior also models the behaviour: asking the tool for explanations, saying out loud when it is wrong, and showing how they checked.

Common mistakes

  • Pasting code you cannot explain into a pull request.
  • Never trying for ten minutes before asking. Struggle is where learning happens.
  • Asking for whole features instead of asking about the parts you do not understand.

Interview questions

  1. How do you use AI tools while you are still learning a stack?
    Show answerHide answer
    As a tutor for explanations and critique, writing the code myself first, and verifying everything by running it.
  2. A reviewer asks you why a line works and you do not know. What happened and what do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    I accepted code without understanding it; I learn it before the change merges, or I rewrite it into something I can explain.

Practical exercise

For one week, use an assistant only in "tutor mode": it may explain, critique and quiz, but not write code you commit. Acceptance criteria: a log of ten questions you asked, what you learned from each, and one concept you could now explain to a teammate without notes.

53.2.2 What never goes into a prompt

Concept

Anything you type, paste or let a tool read is sent to a model provider's servers, unless your organisation runs the model itself. Depending on the product and plan, it may be logged, retained for a period, or reviewed for abuse. Treat a prompt like an email to an external company: never include secrets, private keys, customer personal data or anything your data classification says must not leave approved systems.

Why does it exist?

Because the most common AI-tool security incident is not a clever attack; it is an engineer pasting a production .env file to ask "why can't I connect?". Once sent, you cannot un-send it, and the secret must be treated as compromised. Part 40 — Security, 40.32, covers secrets management; this is the AI-shaped hole in it.

How it works

Never paste or expose Why Do instead
.env files, API keys, database URLs with passwords Credentials leave your control; must be rotated Redact: postgres://USER:REDACTED@HOST/db
Private keys, JWT signing secrets, certificates Total compromise of what they protect Describe the setup, never the material
Customer data: names, emails, addresses, phone numbers, payment details Privacy law and contracts; a data breach by another name Use synthetic rows with obviously fake values
Production database dumps or log extracts with personal data Same as above, at scale Anonymise first, or reproduce with generated data
Proprietary code your policy says must not go to unapproved tools Licence, IP and contractual obligations Use only the organisation's approved tools (53.9)

For agents, the risk is that the tool reads secrets on its own: it opens .env to understand configuration, or prints environment variables while debugging. Two habits close most of this gap:

Shell
# Keep real secrets out of the working tree entirely; load them from a manager at runtime.
# For local work, keep a redacted example file that tools may read:
cat .env.example
# DATABASE_URL=postgres://orders_app:CHANGE_ME@localhost:5432/orders_dev
# PAYMENT_API_KEY=test_key_placeholder

# And check your tool's ignore or deny settings so it will not read real secret files.
# Many tools honour .gitignore; some have their own ignore or permission files. Verify, do not assume.
git check-ignore -v .env

Failure scenario

A developer debugging a connection error asks a chat assistant for help and pastes the full output of printenv from a staging container. It includes the payment provider's live secret key, because staging had been wired to the live account "temporarily" months earlier. The security team, alerted by the developer's own message in the team channel, rotates the key within the hour. Nothing was abused, but the rotation broke three services that had the old key cached, and it took an afternoon to recover. Two lessons: redact before you paste, and staging should never hold production secrets in the first place.

Common mistakes

  • Pasting a whole log file without scanning it for emails, tokens or card fragments.
  • Using a personal AI account for company code because "it is faster than asking for access".
  • Assuming the tool will not read .env because you did not mention it.

Interview questions

  1. You accidentally pasted a production database password into an AI chat. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Treat it as leaked: tell the security owner, rotate the credential, check access logs, and follow the incident process; do not just delete the chat.
  2. How do you get help with a bug that involves customer data?
    Show answerHide answer
    Reproduce it with synthetic data, or redact identifying fields before sharing anything.

Practical exercise

Audit your own last twenty AI prompts (most tools keep a history). Acceptance criteria: count any that contained credentials, personal data or internal hostnames; for each, write what you should have sent instead; set up a redacted .env.example and confirm with git check-ignore that the real file is ignored.

53.2.3 Verify every suggestion: run it, test it, read it

Concept

The beginner's single most important habit with AI: nothing is done until you have run it and written a test that would fail if it were wrong. And because you will spend your career reading code you did not write (colleagues', libraries', and now AI's), learn to read AI code the same way: line by line, asking what each line does and what happens when its inputs are bad.

How it works

A five-step check for any AI suggestion, small or large:

  1. Read it before you run it. Can you say what each line does? Look up anything you cannot.
  2. Run it. Locally, against real inputs. Does it even compile and start?
  3. Break it. Feed it the inputs the tool did not think of: empty string, null, a huge number, a duplicate request, a user who is not the owner.
  4. Pin it with a test. Write a test that fails without the change and passes with it (Part 41 — Testing Backend Systems with Jest and NestJS).
  5. Explain it. Could you defend this in review? If not, you are not done.
TypeScript
// A tiny test that pins behaviour an assistant suggested for order cancellation.
// If someone (or some tool) later changes the rule, this fails loudly.
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';
import { ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';

describe('OrdersService.cancel', () => {
  it('refuses to cancel an order that has already shipped', async () => {
    const repo = { findOneBy: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'ord_1', status: 'shipped' }) };
    const service = new OrdersService(repo as any);

    await expect(service.cancel('ord_1')).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(ConflictException);
  });
});

When to switch the assistant off

There are times to close the chat panel and turn completion off:

  • When learning a new fundamental. Your first week of SQL joins, your first transaction code, your first time with NestJS dependency injection. Write it by hand until it is boring.
  • When practising for interviews. Most coding interviews still expect you to reason without an assistant (Part 70 — The Interview Playbook).
  • When you notice you are accepting suggestions without reading them. That is autopilot; switch off for an hour and reset.
  • When debugging something subtle. A concurrency bug or a performance cliff needs your full attention on evidence, not a stream of guesses.

Common mistakes

  • "It compiled, so it works."
  • Running the happy path once and calling it tested.
  • Keeping completion on during a learning exercise and wondering why nothing sticks.

Interview questions

  1. How do you verify code an assistant gave you?
    Show answerHide answer
    Read, run, try bad inputs, add a failing-then-passing test, and make sure I can explain it.
  2. When would you deliberately not use an AI tool?
    Show answerHide answer
    While learning a fundamental, when debugging something subtle that needs focused reasoning, and when I notice I am accepting without reading.

Practical exercise

Take an AI-generated function from your recent work. Write three tests that try to break it (bad input, boundary, unauthorised caller). Acceptance criteria: at least one test either fails and leads to a fix, or you write a short note explaining why the function handles all three correctly, with the evidence.

53.3 The working layer: a reliable loop

53.3.1 Specify, give context, plan, generate small, run, review, commit

Concept

A working engineer does not need clever prompts. They need a loop that reliably turns AI output into small, tested, reviewed commits. The loop is the same one good engineers used before AI, with the tool slotted into the "write the code" step and verification wrapped tightly around it:

  1. Specify what you want and what "done" means.
  2. Give context: the relevant files, the schema, the exact error, the conventions.
  3. Ask for a plan before any code, and correct the plan.
  4. Generate a small diff, one step of the plan at a time.
  5. Run the tests (and the type checker and linter).
  6. Review the diff as if a stranger wrote it.
  7. Commit that step, then repeat.

Why does it exist?

Without a loop, AI-assisted work drifts into one of two failure modes. Either you ask for the whole feature at once and get a 900-line diff you cannot review properly, or you ping-pong with the tool for an hour, each "fix" breaking something else, with no safe point to return to. Small steps with a commit after each one give you checkpoints, readable diffs and an easy git revert or git reset (Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow, 5.7) when the tool goes down a wrong path.

Mental model

Imagine directing a fast but literal builder. You do not say "build me a house" and leave for a month. You agree a plan, then say "lay the foundation", inspect it, then "frame the ground floor", inspect it. Each inspection is cheap because each piece is small. A mistake found at the foundation costs an hour; found at the roof, it costs the house.

How it works

A few rules make the loop work:

  • "Done" is a test, not a feeling. "Done when POST /orders/:id/refund returns 409 for an already-refunded order, and the new e2e test covers it."
  • The plan is the cheapest place to catch a wrong idea. If the plan says "add a refunded boolean to orders" and your system already has a refunds table, you fix it in one sentence instead of one hour.
  • Small means reviewable in a few minutes. As a rule of thumb, aim for steps under about 200 changed lines. Large diffs are where bugs hide (Part 48 — Git from Intermediate to Senior, 48.13).
  • Going in circles is a signal. If the third attempt at a fix still fails, stop. Discard the changes (git restore . or git stash), think about why, and give better context or a smaller step. Agents in particular can spend many iterations "fixing" a symptom when the real problem is a wrong assumption early on.
  • Commit after every green step. Each commit is a save point. You can squash them before merging if your team prefers.

Practical example

The task: add partial refunds to an orders service. A good opening message to an agent or chat assistant:

Text
Goal: support partial refunds on orders.
Done when:
- POST /orders/:id/refunds accepts { amountCents, reason, idempotencyKey }
- total refunded can never exceed the order total (enforced in the DB too)
- a retry with the same idempotencyKey returns the first result, no second refund
- unit tests for the service, one e2e test for the endpoint

Context (attached): src/orders/order.entity.ts, src/orders/orders.service.ts,
src/payments/payments.client.ts, migrations/1730000000000-orders.ts, docs/conventions.md

Constraints:
- orders table has ~30M rows and takes writes all day: no blocking DDL
- follow the existing DTO + class-validator pattern
- do not add new npm dependencies

First: propose a plan as a numbered list of small steps. Do not write code yet.

The tool proposes six steps: migration for a refunds table, entity, DTO, service method with a transaction, controller, tests. You notice step 4 calls the payment provider inside the database transaction, which would hold a row lock during a slow network call (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering). You correct it ("record the refund as pending in a transaction, call the provider after commit, then mark it succeeded or failed") and only then let it generate step 1.

Production scenario

A team that adopted this loop measured the median size of AI-assisted pull requests before and after: it fell from roughly 600 changed lines to under 250, review turnaround roughly halved, and the number of review rounds per PR went down. The tool did not change; the habit did.

Failure scenario

An engineer asks an agent to "add partial refunds" with no plan step and no constraints. The agent generates a migration adding a column with a check constraint, validated immediately on a 30-million-row table, a service, a controller and forty tests, in one go. All tests pass locally against an empty database. The migration runs in production at 11:00, holds a lock long enough to queue every write to orders behind it, and checkout times out for several minutes. A plan step with the constraint "no blocking DDL" would have caught it before a line was written. Part 24 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes covers the safe form.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The tool "fixes" a failing test by editing the test. Always read test changes; require that test changes are called out separately.
  • Hidden scope creep. You asked for one endpoint; the diff also "tidies up" five unrelated files. Reject unrelated changes; they make review harder and blame history noisier.
  • Environment mismatch. Tests pass in the agent's environment but it used a different Node version or skipped integration tests that need Docker.
  • A plan that sounds right but is not. Plans are also plausible text. Check them against the code.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior's loop is visibly the same as their pre-AI loop: understand, plan, small steps, tests, review, commit. The tool speeds up the typing and some of the thinking, but it never removes a checkpoint. When they are tempted to skip one because "it's just AI boilerplate", they remember that boilerplate is where missing authorization checks live.

Common mistakes

  • Asking for the whole feature in one prompt.
  • Never asking for a plan, so design decisions are made implicitly by the model.
  • Letting uncommitted AI changes pile up so there is no clean point to return to.
  • Continuing a failing loop for an hour instead of resetting.

Interview questions

  1. Describe how you work with an AI assistant on a feature.
    Show answerHide answer
    Specify done criteria, give context, get and correct a plan, generate small steps, run checks, review, commit each step. Follow-up: how small is a step?
  2. The agent has tried three times to fix a failing test. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Stop, discard or stash, figure out the wrong assumption, give better context or a smaller step.
  3. Why ask for a plan before code?
    Show answerHide answer
    It is the cheapest point to catch a wrong design, and it makes the design decisions explicit instead of implicit.

Practical exercise

Implement a small feature (for example, soft-deleting products) using the loop. Acceptance criteria: a written spec with done criteria, the plan you received and the corrections you made, at least three commits each under 200 changed lines, all tests green at each commit, and one paragraph on a mistake the plan step caught.

53.3.2 Prompts and project instruction files

Concept

A project instruction file is a plain Markdown file in the repository that an AI tool reads automatically at the start of a session, so that conventions do not have to be repeated in every prompt. Names differ by tool: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md; GitHub Copilot can read .github/copilot-instructions.md; Cursor reads rules from its own rules location; and AGENTS.md has emerged as a shared convention that several tools read. Check your tool's documentation for the current name; the idea is the same everywhere.

Why does it exist?

Because the tool forgets everything between sessions (53.1.2), and because its default is the average of public code rather than your team's decisions. An instruction file is how you move team knowledge from people's heads into the tool's context: which ORM, how errors are shaped, where validation lives, which commands verify a change, what must never be done.

Mental model

Imagine the one-page briefing you would give a contractor on their first morning: "We use these tools. Tests run with this command. Never touch the payments schema without asking. Here is a good example to copy." You would not give them the whole wiki. You give them what prevents the most expensive mistakes.

How it works

A good instruction file is short, specific and testable. It does not explain what NestJS is; the model knows. It records your decisions.

Text
# CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md (example for an orders service)

## Stack
- NestJS 10, TypeORM with PostgreSQL 16, Jest. Node version from .nvmrc.

## Commands (run before saying a task is done)
- npm run typecheck
- npm run lint
- npm test               (unit)
- npm run test:e2e       (needs Docker; uses Testcontainers)

## Conventions
- Validation lives on DTOs with class-validator; never on entities.
- Errors: throw Nest HttpExceptions from services; the global filter shapes the body.
- Money is integer cents (amountCents), never floats.
- Every query on customer data filters by the caller's customerId or tenantId.
- Copy src/orders/orders.controller.ts as the reference controller.

## Never
- Never edit an existing migration; add a new one.
- Never use blocking DDL on orders, order_items, payments (30M+ rows): see docs/migrations.md.
- Never add an npm dependency without saying so in the summary.
- Never read or print .env; use .env.example.

Writing good prompts follows the same principles at a smaller scale:

Principle Weak prompt Strong prompt
State the goal and done criteria "Improve this endpoint" "Make GET /orders return in under 100 ms p95 for a customer with 5,000 orders"
Give the real context "It's slow" Paste the query and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output
Name constraints (nothing) "No new dependencies; table has 30M rows; no blocking DDL"
Ask for reasoning before code "Write it" "First list three options with tradeoffs"
Say what to leave alone (nothing) "Do not change the public response shape"

Production scenario

A platform team maintains one instruction file per service, reviewed like code through CODEOWNERS. When a recurring review comment appears in three or more pull requests ("use amountCents, not amount"), someone adds a line to the instruction file. Over a quarter, the most common AI-related review comments fall off sharply. The instruction file becomes a living list of "mistakes we have stopped making".

Failure scenario

An instruction file grows to 3,000 lines: the full architecture document, every past decision, onboarding notes. Sessions get slower and more expensive, and the tool's adherence to the important rules gets worse, because they are buried in the middle of a long input. The team cuts it back to about 80 lines of decisions and commands, linking to longer documents that the agent can open when a task needs them.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale instructions. The file says Jest; the project moved to Vitest. The tool now follows wrong rules confidently. Review it when the stack changes.
  • Secrets in the instruction file. It is committed to the repository; treat it as public within the company.
  • Instructions are guidance, not enforcement. A model can still ignore a rule. Anything that must hold goes into a linter rule, a CI check or a permission setting (53.6.1), not only into prose.
  • Conflicting files. A monorepo with instruction files at several levels; know which ones your tool reads and how they combine.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the instruction file as executable team memory and as a smell detector: if they keep writing the same correction, the knowledge belongs in the file, or better, in a lint rule. They keep it short, because they know length dilutes attention, and they never rely on it for a security boundary.

Common mistakes

  • No instruction file at all, then complaining that the tool ignores conventions.
  • A file full of generic advice ("write clean code") instead of specific decisions.
  • Putting "never do X" only in prose when a CI check could enforce it.

Interview questions

  1. What goes in a repository instruction file for AI tools?
    Show answerHide answer
    Stack, verification commands, team-specific conventions, reference examples and hard "never" rules; not generic advice or secrets.
  2. Is an instruction file a security control?
    Show answerHide answer
    No. It is guidance the model usually follows; real boundaries are permissions, sandboxes and CI checks.
  3. Your instruction file says one thing and the code does another. What does the tool do?
    Show answerHide answer
    It may follow either; fix the inconsistency, because both are context.

Practical exercise

Write an instruction file for a service you know, under 100 lines. Acceptance criteria: it lists the exact verification commands (checked against package.json), at least five team-specific conventions, one reference file per layer, and at least three "never" rules, one of which you have also turned into a lint or CI check.

53.3.3 Tests first with AI

Concept

The most reliable way to use AI for implementation is to write or approve the tests first, then let the tool write code to make them pass. The tests become the specification, written in a language that is checked by a machine rather than interpreted by a model.

Why does it exist?

Because "plausible" output (53.1.3) needs an independent check, and the strongest independent check is a test that a human has read and agreed with before the implementation exists. If the same tool writes code and tests together, both may share the same misunderstanding. If a human approves the tests first, the implementation has to satisfy the human's intent.

How it works

  1. Write the test cases yourself, or ask the tool to list cases and you choose and edit them.
  2. Have the tool generate the test code; read every assertion.
  3. Run the tests and watch them fail for the right reason (not a typo).
  4. Ask the tool to implement until the tests pass, without changing the tests.
  5. Review the implementation for things tests rarely cover: authorization, concurrency, failure handling.
TypeScript
// refunds.service.spec.ts -- written and approved BEFORE the implementation exists.
describe('RefundsService.create', () => {
  it('rejects a refund larger than the remaining refundable amount', async () => {
    await seedOrder({ id: 'ord_1', customerId: 'cus_1', totalCents: 10_000, refundedCents: 7_000 });
    await expect(
      service.create({ orderId: 'ord_1', amountCents: 4_000, idempotencyKey: 'k1' }, { customerId: 'cus_1' }),
    ).rejects.toThrow('exceeds refundable amount');
  });

  it('returns the first result for a repeated idempotency key, with one provider call', async () => {
    await seedOrder({ id: 'ord_2', customerId: 'cus_1', totalCents: 10_000, refundedCents: 0 });
    const first = await service.create({ orderId: 'ord_2', amountCents: 1_000, idempotencyKey: 'k2' }, { customerId: 'cus_1' });
    const second = await service.create({ orderId: 'ord_2', amountCents: 1_000, idempotencyKey: 'k2' }, { customerId: 'cus_1' });
    expect(second.id).toBe(first.id);
    expect(paymentsFake.refundCalls).toHaveLength(1);
  });

  it('does not let a customer refund another customer\'s order', async () => {
    await seedOrder({ id: 'ord_3', customerId: 'cus_other', totalCents: 5_000, refundedCents: 0 });
    await expect(
      service.create({ orderId: 'ord_3', amountCents: 1_000, idempotencyKey: 'k3' }, { customerId: 'cus_1' }),
    ).rejects.toThrow('not found');
  });
});

Note the third test. AI-generated implementations frequently forget ownership checks (53.4); writing the test first means the tool cannot "forget" it without a red build.

Common mistakes

  • Letting the tool write tests after the code, from the code, so the tests confirm whatever the code does.
  • Accepting a passing build without checking the agent did not alter the tests.
  • Testing only the happy path because the tool's suggested case list did.

Interview questions

  1. Why write tests before asking an AI to implement?
    Show answerHide answer
    The tests become a machine-checked specification approved by a human, so the implementation cannot share the model's misunderstanding unnoticed.
  2. How do you stop an agent from changing tests to make them pass?
    Show answerHide answer
    Instruct it not to, review test diffs separately, and protect key test files with CODEOWNERS or a CI check on test changes.

Practical exercise

Pick a service method you have not written yet. Write five test cases first (at least one authorization case and one duplicate-request case), then let an assistant implement it. Acceptance criteria: tests committed before implementation, implementation passes without test edits, and a note on anything the tests did not cover that review found.

53.3.4 Where AI earns its keep: refactors, migrations, tests, debugging, docs

Concept

Some jobs fit these tools very well because they are pattern-heavy, easy to verify, or both. Knowing them lets you put the tool where it saves real time.

How it works

Task Why it fits How to keep it safe
Mechanical refactors (rename, extract, move to new API) Repetitive, pattern-based, verified by compiler and tests Small batches; compiler and full test run after each
Test generation for existing code Tedious to type; cases are easy to read You approve the case list; check assertions are meaningful, not toBeDefined()
Debugging from a stack trace Good at reading traces and suggesting hypotheses Treat suggestions as hypotheses; confirm with logs or a repro
Writing a migration draft Knows SQL syntax and ORM migration shape Review lock behaviour and data safety yourself (below)
Documentation and comments Good at prose from code Check every claim against the code
Explaining unfamiliar code Fast orientation in a new codebase Verify by reading the paths it names
Small scripts and one-off queries Low risk, quick to check Run against a copy first, never directly on production

Practical example: debugging from a stack trace

Text
QueryFailedError: deadlock detected
    at PostgresQueryRunner.query (node_modules/typeorm/driver/postgres/PostgresQueryRunner.js:219:19)
    at async InventoryService.reserve (src/inventory/inventory.service.ts:48:5)
    at async OrdersService.place (src/orders/orders.service.ts:91:7)
Detail: Process 18231 waits for ShareLock on transaction 99812; blocked by process 18240.

Pasting this with the reserve method, a good assistant points out that two orders locking the same products in different orders can deadlock, and suggests sorting product IDs before locking (Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control, 21.7). That is a strong hypothesis. You confirm it by checking whether the deadlocks involve multi-item orders with overlapping products, and by a concurrency test that places two such orders at once. The assistant shortened the investigation; it did not replace it.

PostgreSQL example: reviewing an AI-drafted migration

You ask for a migration to add a refunds table and an index for looking up orders by customer. The draft:

TypeScript
// AI draft -- looks fine, has two production problems on a large, busy table
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddRefunds1731300000000 implements MigrationInterface {
  async up(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await q.query(`CREATE TABLE refunds (
      id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
      order_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
      amount_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
      idempotency_key text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
      status text NOT NULL,
      created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`);
    await q.query(`CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)`);
    await q.query(`ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_refunded_le_total CHECK (refunded_cents <= total_cents)`);
  }
  async down(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> { /* drops omitted for brevity in the draft */ }
}

What a reviewer catches:

  1. CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a 30-million-row orders table blocks writes for the whole build, which can take minutes (Part 24, 24.3).
  2. ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK validates every existing row while holding a strong lock; use NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately (Part 24, 24.3).
  3. No lock_timeout, so if the DDL waits behind a long transaction, every query on orders queues behind it (Part 24, 24.4).
  4. An empty down. Also no index on refunds.order_id, which you will query by.

The reviewed version splits the work:

TypeScript
// Reviewed: non-blocking index in its own migration, outside a transaction
import { MigrationInterface, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

export class AddOrdersCustomerIndex1731300000001 implements MigrationInterface {
  transaction = false; // CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction; needs migrationsTransactionMode 'each' (22.7)

  async up(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await q.query(`SET lock_timeout = '5s'`);
    await q.query(
      `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)`,
    );
  }
  async down(q: QueryRunner): Promise<void> {
    await q.query(`DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS idx_orders_customer_created`);
  }
}
SQL
-- Reviewed: constraint added without scanning under a heavy lock, validated separately
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_refunded_le_total
  CHECK (refunded_cents <= total_cents) NOT VALID;      -- brief lock, no full scan
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_refunded_le_total; -- scans, but allows reads and writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_refunds_order_id ON refunds (order_id);

The draft saved typing. The review is where the senior's knowledge lives, and no tool supplied it here unasked. You can ask for it ("review this migration for lock impact on a 30M-row table under write load") and a good assistant will often find these issues. The point is that someone has to know to ask.

Common mistakes

  • Letting the tool write tests whose assertions are trivially true.
  • Running an AI-written one-off UPDATE directly against production.
  • Accepting migration drafts without thinking about table size and write load.

Interview questions

  1. Which engineering tasks are AI tools best at, and why?
    Show answerHide answer
    Pattern-heavy, easily verified tasks: refactors, test scaffolding, trace reading, drafts of migrations and docs.
  2. An AI-drafted migration adds an index and a check constraint to a 30M-row table. What do you look for?
    Show answerHide answer
    CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, NOT VALID plus VALIDATE, lock_timeout, a real down, and indexes for new foreign keys.

Practical exercise

Ask an assistant to draft a migration that adds a foreign key and an index to a large table in a test database seeded with a few million rows. Acceptance criteria: list every lock problem in the draft, rewrite it safely, and prove with a concurrent INSERT loop in a second session that the reviewed version does not block writes.

53.3.5 What AI is bad at

Concept

The tools are weakest exactly where the stakes are highest: decisions that depend on things not in the code, and properties that only show up under concurrency, failure or attack.

How it works

Weak area Why the tool struggles What you do
Novel architecture Defaults to common patterns from training; does not know your constraints, team, budget or history Use it to list options and tradeoffs; decide with an RFC (Part 83 — Writing as an Architect)
Subtle concurrency Bugs appear only with specific interleavings; code looks fine line by line Reason about it yourself; concurrency tests (Part 41, 41.9)
Security boundaries Authorization depends on your domain; the "average" code it learned from often has none Explicit review with a checklist (53.4)
Exact library versions Training cut-off and mixed versions in training data Pin versions; check the changelog and installed types
Hallucinated APIs Invents plausible method names and options Compiler and docs
Hallucinated packages Invents plausible package names Verify existence and reputation before installing (below)
Performance at your scale Does not know your row counts or traffic EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), load tests

Hallucinated packages deserve special attention. A model asked how to do something in Node may suggest npm install some-plausible-name. Sometimes the package does not exist. Research has shown that models repeat many of the same invented names across runs, which makes them predictable, and attackers can register those names on npm or PyPI with malicious code. This is called slopsquatting, a cousin of typosquatting (Part 40, 40.28). The defence is cheap:

Shell
# Before installing anything an AI suggested:
npm view nest-refund-guard name version time.created repository.url maintainers
# 404 -> it does not exist: the suggestion was invented. Do not create or install it.
# Exists but created last week, one maintainer, no repository, few downloads -> treat as hostile.

# Prefer packages your organisation already uses, and install without running scripts:
npm install --ignore-scripts some-known-package
npm audit signatures   # verifies registry signatures and provenance attestations where present

Common mistakes

  • Asking an assistant to "design the architecture" and adopting its first answer.
  • Installing a package because the tool named it confidently.
  • Trusting the tool's claim about which version introduced a feature.

Interview questions

  1. What is slopsquatting?
    Show answerHide answer
    Registering package names that AI models tend to hallucinate, so that developers who follow the suggestion install attacker code. Defence: verify existence, age, maintainers and repository before installing; restrict new dependencies by policy.
  2. Why are AI tools weak at concurrency bugs?
    Show answerHide answer
    Each line looks correct; the bug lives in interleavings that are not visible in the text.

Practical exercise

Ask three different questions of the form "what npm package should I use to do X in NestJS?" for niche tasks. Acceptance criteria: for every package named, record whether it exists, its creation date, maintainer count and weekly downloads; flag any that do not exist or look risky; write a one-paragraph rule your team could adopt for AI-suggested dependencies.

53.4 Reviewing AI-written code like a senior

53.4.1 The review checklist

Concept

Reviewing AI-written code is ordinary code review (Part 58 — The Senior Engineering Mindset, 58.9) with the dials turned in specific directions. AI code tends to be clean-looking, consistently formatted and well-named, which lowers a reviewer's guard. Its defects cluster in places that look fine on the page: missing authorization, unhandled failure paths, concurrency, dependency choices and database operations at scale. The checklist below aims attention there.

Why does it exist?

Because the usual signals of quality no longer mean much. In human-written code, sloppy formatting and odd naming often travel with sloppy logic, so a reviewer's eye is drawn to trouble. AI code removes those signals: the bug sits in a beautifully formatted function with a helpful comment above it. And volume goes up, so reviewers are tempted to skim. A checklist replaces "does this look right?" with "have I checked the things that are usually wrong?"

Mental model

Imagine inspecting a house built by a crew that is very fast and very neat. The paint is perfect, the trim is straight. You do not inspect the paint. You go straight to the wiring, the plumbing under pressure, the load-bearing walls and the locks on the doors, because those are what neatness hides and what fails catastrophically.

How it works

The senior's review checklist for AI-assisted pull requests:

Area Questions
Intent Is this the right change? Does it solve the ticket, and only the ticket? Any unrelated edits?
Correctness Does each branch do what it claims? Are edge cases (empty, null, max size, duplicate) handled? Were tests changed or weakened?
The senior mantra Can it time out (is there a timeout on every network call)? Can it fail (what happens on error, is it caught at the right level)? Can it become slow (at 10x data)? Can it duplicate (retry, double click, redelivered message)? Can it return a wrong response (stale data, wrong user's data)? Can it partially succeed (step 2 of 3 fails)?
Security Injection: any string-built SQL, shell commands, or template rendering (Part 40, 40.20, 40.29)? Authorization: is ownership or tenant checked on every object access, not just login (40.12)? Secrets: hard-coded keys, secrets in logs? Unsafe deserialization or prototype pollution (40.27)? Input validation through a DTO, or a plain TypeScript type that validates nothing at runtime?
Data Migrations: lock level, table size, CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID, lock_timeout, reversible (Part 24)? Transactions: right scope, no network calls inside? Locks: check-then-act races? N+1 queries (Part 22, 22.9)? Missing indexes for new query patterns?
Dependencies Was a package added? Does it exist, is it the one you think (spelling, scope), who maintains it, how old is it, what licence, does it run install scripts? Could an existing dependency or a few lines of code do the job?
Operability Logs with context but without personal data? Metrics for the new path? Errors that a human at 03:00 can act on?
Understanding Can the author explain every line? Would the team be able to debug this in six months?

Two practical tricks:

  1. Read the tests first. They tell you what the author (or tool) thought the code should do. Missing cases are the fastest pointer to missing logic.
  2. Read the diff bottom-up for data and top-down for flow. Start with migrations and queries, which are hardest to undo, then follow a request from controller to database.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior does not review AI code more harshly than human code; they review it differently, spending less time on style and more on the boundaries: trust boundaries (authorization, input), failure boundaries (network, transactions) and time boundaries (concurrency, retries). They also hold the line that the author must understand and own every line, regardless of who or what typed it.

Common mistakes

  • Approving because it "looks clean".
  • Reviewing only the files the PR description mentions and missing a changed lockfile or migration.
  • Accepting a TypeScript interface on @Body() as validation.
  • Skipping review of generated tests.

Interview questions

  1. What do you look for first when reviewing AI-generated backend code?
    Show answerHide answer
    Authorization on object access, injection, failure handling and timeouts, concurrency and idempotency, migrations, and new dependencies. Why it matters: those are the defects AI code most often has and the most expensive to ship.
  2. Why is a TypeScript type on a request body not validation?
    Show answerHide answer
    Types are erased at runtime; only a DTO class with class-validator decorators and a ValidationPipe checks what actually arrives.
  3. A PR adds one new npm dependency. What do you check?
    Show answerHide answer
    Existence and exact name, maintainers and age, licence, install scripts, known vulnerabilities, and whether it is needed at all.

Practical exercise

Take three recent AI-assisted pull requests in your team (or generate three small features). Review each with the checklist above, recording findings per area. Acceptance criteria: a table of findings by area for each PR, at least one finding the original review missed (or a note that none were missed, with evidence), and one checklist item you would add for your codebase.

53.4.2 Worked example: a plausible endpoint with three real bugs

Concept

Here is an endpoint of the kind an assistant produces in seconds when asked to "add a refund endpoint for customers to refund their own orders". It compiles, it passes a happy-path test, it is neatly written, and it would cause a security incident and lose money. Read it and find the problems before reading the analysis.

NestJS example

TypeScript
// refunds.controller.ts -- as generated. Compiles. Happy-path test passes.
import { BadRequestException, Body, Controller, NotFoundException, Param, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource, Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { Order } from '../orders/order.entity';
import { PaymentsClient } from '../payments/payments.client';

@Controller('orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class RefundsController {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>,
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly payments: PaymentsClient,
  ) {}

  @Post(':id/refund')
  async refund(@Param('id') id: string, @Body() body: { amountCents: number; reason: string }) {
    const order = await this.orders.findOne({ where: { id } });
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundException('Order not found');

    if (order.refundedCents + body.amountCents > order.totalCents) {
      throw new BadRequestException('Refund exceeds order total');
    }

    // Refund through the payment provider, then record it.
    const result = await this.payments.refund(order.paymentId, body.amountCents);

    await this.dataSource.query(
      `UPDATE orders SET refunded_cents = refunded_cents + ${body.amountCents},
       refund_reason = '${body.reason}' WHERE id = '${id}'`,
    );

    return { refundId: result.id, status: 'refunded' };
  }
}

How it works: the three bugs

Bug 1: authentication without authorization (IDOR). JwtAuthGuard proves the caller is a logged-in user. Nothing checks that the order belongs to this user. findOne({ where: { id } }) fetches any order by ID. Any customer can refund any other customer's order by guessing or enumerating IDs: textbook insecure direct object reference (Part 40, 40.12). Assistants produce this pattern constantly, because most example code on the internet looks up records by ID alone.

Bug 2: SQL injection. body.reason is interpolated into the SQL string. A reason of x', refunded_cents = 0, total_cents = '999999 rewrites the row. And @Body() body: { amountCents: number; reason: string } is a TypeScript type, erased at runtime, so ValidationPipe has nothing to validate: amountCents can be a string containing SQL, a negative number (a "refund" that increases what the customer can refund later), or missing entirely (Part 40, 40.20).

Bug 3: double refunds and partial success. Run the senior mantra against it:

  • Can it duplicate? Yes, three ways. Two concurrent requests both read refundedCents = 0, both pass the check, and both refund: a classic check-then-act race (Part 21, 21.3). A mobile client that times out and retries refunds again, because there is no idempotency key (Part 30 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency). A double tap does the same.
  • Can it partially succeed? Yes. If the provider call succeeds and the UPDATE then fails (connection reset, deploy restart), the money has moved and the database says it has not. The customer can refund again.
  • Can it time out? The provider call has no timeout. A slow provider holds the request, its socket and its memory indefinitely (Part 31, 31.2).

There are smaller findings too: the refund reason overwrites a single column, so the history of multiple partial refunds is lost; there is no audit record of who refunded what; and the response claims status: 'refunded' without knowing.

The fixed version

The fix moves logic into a service, validates input with a DTO, makes ownership part of the query, serialises concurrent refunds with a row lock, records the refund as pending in a short transaction before calling the provider, passes an idempotency key to the provider, and treats "unknown outcome" as its own state for a reconciler job to resolve.

TypeScript
// create-refund.dto.ts and refunds.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { IsInt, IsString, IsUUID, Length, Max, Min } from 'class-validator';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator'; // project decorator built with createParamDecorator
import { RefundsService } from './refunds.service';

export class CreateRefundDto {
  @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(10_000_000) amountCents!: number;  // integer cents, positive, bounded
  @IsString() @Length(3, 500) reason!: string;
  @IsUUID() idempotencyKey!: string;                        // client generates once per refund attempt
}

@Controller('orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class RefundsController {
  constructor(private readonly refunds: RefundsService) {}

  @Post(':id/refunds')
  create(
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) orderId: string,
    @Body() dto: CreateRefundDto,              // global ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }) validates this class
    @CurrentUser() user: AuthUser,
  ) {
    return this.refunds.create(orderId, dto, user);
  }
}
TypeScript
// refunds.service.ts
import { ConflictException, Injectable, Logger, NotFoundException, UnprocessableEntityException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, QueryFailedError } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from '../orders/order.entity';
import { Refund } from './refund.entity';
import { PaymentsClient, PaymentDeclinedError } from '../payments/payments.client';
import { AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { CreateRefundDto } from './refunds.controller';

@Injectable()
export class RefundsService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(RefundsService.name);
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly payments: PaymentsClient) {}

  async create(orderId: string, dto: CreateRefundDto, user: AuthUser): Promise<Refund> {
    // 1. Short transaction: lock the order row, check, reserve the amount, record a pending refund.
    let refund: Refund;
    try {
      refund = await this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
        const existing = await m.findOne(Refund, { where: { idempotencyKey: dto.idempotencyKey } });
        if (existing) {
          if (existing.orderId !== orderId || existing.amountCents !== dto.amountCents) {
            throw new ConflictException('Idempotency key reused with different parameters');
          }
          return existing; // a retry gets the original refund, never a second one
        }
        const order = await m.findOne(Order, {
          where: { id: orderId, customerId: user.customerId }, // ownership is part of the lookup
          lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' },                  // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serialises refunds
        });
        if (!order) throw new NotFoundException('Order not found'); // same answer for "missing" and "not yours"
        if (order.refundedCents + dto.amountCents > order.totalCents) {
          throw new UnprocessableEntityException('Refund exceeds refundable amount');
        }
        await m.increment(Order, { id: order.id }, 'refundedCents', dto.amountCents); // parameterised
        return m.save(m.create(Refund, {
          orderId: order.id, paymentId: order.paymentId, amountCents: dto.amountCents,
          reason: dto.reason, idempotencyKey: dto.idempotencyKey, status: 'pending', requestedBy: user.id,
        }));
      });
    } catch (err) {
      // Two requests with the same key at the same moment: both passed the findOne check above,
      // the second INSERT hit the UNIQUE constraint (23505) and its transaction rolled back.
      // Return the winner's refund instead of a 500; the winner makes the provider call.
      if (err instanceof QueryFailedError && (err.driverError as { code?: string }).code === '23505') {
        const winner = await this.dataSource.getRepository(Refund).findOneByOrFail({ idempotencyKey: dto.idempotencyKey });
        if (winner.orderId !== orderId || winner.amountCents !== dto.amountCents) {
          throw new ConflictException('Idempotency key reused with different parameters');
        }
        return winner;
      }
      throw err;
    }
    if (refund.status !== 'pending') return refund;

    // 2. Network call AFTER commit: timeout, and our refund id as the provider's idempotency key.
    try {
      const res = await this.payments.refund(
        { paymentId: refund.paymentId, amountCents: refund.amountCents, idempotencyKey: refund.id },
        { timeoutMs: 5_000 },
      );
      await this.dataSource.getRepository(Refund).update(refund.id, { status: 'succeeded', providerRefundId: res.id });
      return { ...refund, status: 'succeeded', providerRefundId: res.id };
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof PaymentDeclinedError) {
        await this.release(refund); // definite failure: give the reserved amount back
        throw new UnprocessableEntityException('Refund declined by the payment provider');
      }
      // Timeout or unknown: money may or may not have moved. Stay pending; a reconciler job asks the provider.
      this.logger.warn(`refund ${refund.id} outcome unknown, left pending: ${String(err)}`);
      return refund;
    }
  }

  private async release(refund: Refund): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
      const res = await m.update(Refund, { id: refund.id, status: 'pending' }, { status: 'failed' });
      if (res.affected === 1) await m.decrement(Order, { id: refund.orderId }, 'refundedCents', refund.amountCents);
    });
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

The database backs up the application's rules, so a future bug (or a future AI edit) cannot break them silently:

SQL
CREATE TABLE refunds (
  id                 uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id           uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  payment_id         text NOT NULL,
  amount_cents       integer NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
  reason             text NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key    uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,          -- concurrent same-key inserts: one wins, one gets 23505
  status             text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'succeeded', 'failed')),
  provider_refund_id text,
  requested_by       uuid NOT NULL,
  created_at         timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_refunds_order_id ON refunds (order_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_refunds_pending ON refunds (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- the reconciler's scan

-- Added with NOT VALID then VALIDATE (53.3.4), here tightened to forbid negatives too.
-- ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT chk_refunded_le_total CHECK (refunded_cents BETWEEN 0 AND total_cents);

Production scenario

With the fixed version on a marketplace processing roughly 4,000 refunds a day, a small number each day end in the "outcome unknown" state, typically provider timeouts during their busy periods. A reconciler runs every five minutes, finds pending refunds older than two minutes using the partial index, asks the provider for the status of each idempotency key, and resolves them. The finance dashboard shows a "pending over 30 minutes" count that should be zero; it alerts if not. That is what "partial success handled" looks like in operation: a named state, a job that resolves it, and a metric that proves it.

Failure scenario

The original version shipped at a company once (a composite story, but every piece of it is common). Within a week, the support team noticed customers with refunds larger than their orders. The cause was mobile retries: the app retried on a 10-second client timeout while the provider took 12 seconds during a peak. Two weeks later, a security researcher reported that refunds could be triggered on other customers' orders. The fix took a day. The reconciliation with the payment provider, and the conversations with affected customers, took a month.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reading the original sees a request that touches money, crosses a network boundary and writes to a database, and immediately asks the mantra questions. None of the three bugs is exotic; all three are standard backend failures that this book covers in other Parts. The AI did not invent new categories of bug. It produced the most common categories in fluent, confident code, at a speed that tempts reviewers to skim. The fix is not "do not use AI"; it is "know the checklist and apply it every time money, identity or data is involved."

Common mistakes

  • Treating @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard) as authorization.
  • Calling a payment provider inside a database transaction (holds a row lock across a slow network call) or before recording intent (loses track of money on a crash).
  • Returning "refunded" when the outcome is unknown.

Interview questions

  1. Find the bugs in this refund endpoint.
    Show answerHide answer
    IDOR (no ownership check), SQL injection (string interpolation plus no runtime validation), and double refund or partial success (check-then-act race, no idempotency key, no timeout, provider call before recording intent). Follow-up: how do you test each one?
  2. Why record the refund as pending before calling the provider?
    Show answerHide answer
    So a crash or timeout after the call leaves a durable record of intent that a reconciler can resolve, instead of money moving with no trace.
  3. Why should "not yours" return 404 rather than 403?
    Show answerHide answer
    A 403 confirms the object exists, which leaks information and helps enumeration.
  4. Why not call the provider inside the transaction?
    Show answerHide answer
    It holds the row lock for the duration of a slow, unreliable network call, and the transaction cannot undo the external side effect anyway.

Practical exercise

Reproduce the original endpoint in a test project. Write three failing tests, one per bug: a customer refunding another customer's order, a reason containing a quote that alters the row, and two concurrent refunds that together exceed the total. Then apply the fixed version. Acceptance criteria: all three tests fail on the original and pass on the fix; the concurrency test uses a real PostgreSQL (Testcontainers, Part 41, 41.7), not a mock.

53.5 Delegate, pair or keep: the decision matrix

Concept

Not every task should go to an AI tool, and not every task should be kept from one. A useful rule is to judge each task on two axes: how easy is it to verify the result, and how expensive is it if the result is wrong. Easy to verify and cheap if wrong: delegate. Hard to verify or expensive if wrong: pair (you drive, the tool assists) or keep human.

Mental model

Imagine deciding what to hand an intern. Formatting a report: hand it over and skim the result. Drafting a customer email: let them draft, you edit. Signing a contract or deciding a layoff: you do it, though they can fetch the documents. The intern is not less capable on the third task; the cost of an unnoticed mistake is just too high.

How it works

Task Verifiable? Cost if wrong Decision Notes
Boilerplate DTOs, module wiring High Low Delegate Compiler and tests catch most errors
Mechanical refactor across many files High (with good tests) Medium Delegate Small batches, full test run each
Unit test scaffolding for existing code Medium Low Delegate You approve the case list
Explaining unfamiliar code or a stack trace Medium Low Delegate Verify by reading the paths named
Documentation drafts Medium Low Delegate Check every claim
New CRUD endpoint in an established pattern Medium Medium Pair Authorization and validation reviewed by hand
Database migration on a large table Low (locks only show at scale) High Pair Tool drafts; you own lock analysis (Part 24)
Performance optimisation Medium (with load tests) Medium Pair Measure before and after
Debugging a production incident Low High Pair Tool proposes hypotheses; evidence decides
Authentication, authorization, crypto Low Very high Keep human (tool may review) Use proven libraries; human design and review
Concurrency and money movement logic Low Very high Keep human (pair at most) Design by hand; concurrency tests
Architecture and service boundaries Low Very high Keep human Tool lists options; RFC decides (Part 83)
Choosing a new dependency or vendor Low High Keep human Tool can research; policy decides (53.9)
Running anything against production Low Very high Keep human No agent writes to production (53.6)

The flowchart is the first cut; the table adds judgement. Medium verifiability counts as "mostly" when the check is cheap (reading the paths an explanation names), so those rows are delegated. A large-table migration or a production incident scores low on verifiability and high on cost, which the flowchart sends to "keep human"; we still pair on them because the tool's draft or hypothesis is useful, as long as you own the lock analysis and the evidence.

The matrix shifts with your safety net. A team with strong integration tests, Testcontainers and contract tests can delegate more, because more becomes machine-verifiable. A team with weak tests should delegate less, however good the tool is.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses the matrix to set expectations with the team rather than to police individuals: "agents are welcome on the refactor; the refund flow gets designed on a whiteboard first." They also notice that the "keep human" rows are exactly the ones where the team's long-term expertise lives, and protect the learning that happens there (53.8.3).

Common mistakes

  • Delegating by how boring a task is rather than how verifiable and costly it is.
  • Keeping everything human out of fear, and losing real productivity on the safe rows.
  • Forgetting that weak tests move every row toward "keep human".

Interview questions

  1. How do you decide what to delegate to an AI tool?
    Show answerHide answer
    By verifiability and cost of error: delegate what machines can check and mistakes are cheap; pair or keep human where verification is hard or errors are expensive.
  2. Would you let an agent write an authorization guard?
    Show answerHide answer
    I might let it draft or review one, but I would design and review it myself, use proven libraries, and test it adversarially.

Practical exercise

List the last twenty tasks your team completed. Place each in the matrix. Acceptance criteria: a table with the decision and reason for each, at least three tasks where your team's current practice differs from the matrix, and a proposal for one test or check that would move a task from "pair" to "delegate".

53.6 Agents and tools

53.6.1 Agentic coding in a terminal, and how much power to give it

Concept

An agentic coding tool runs the loop from 53.1.1 on your machine or in a cloud environment: it reads and searches files, edits them, and runs shell commands such as tests, linters, git and package managers. Each of those abilities is a permission. The central engineering decision is not which model to use; it is what the agent may do without asking, what it may do only after asking, and what it may never do.

Why does it exist?

Agents are useful precisely because they can act: run the test, read the failure, fix the code, run it again. But a tool that can run npm test can also run npm install, curl, psql, git push --force or rm -rf. It does so for plausible reasons ("let me check the database schema", "let me clean the build directory"), with the same credentials, network and file access as the user who started it. Permissions exist so that the agent's power matches the task, not the user's full account.

Mental model

Imagine giving a contractor access to your house. You can give them a key to the garage only, a key to the whole house, or a key plus your bank card. Most jobs need the garage key. Some need the house key while you are home. Almost none need the bank card. The trouble is that a terminal session, by default, is the bank card: your SSH keys, your cloud credentials, your production database URL in an environment variable.

How it works

Think of agent permissions as layers, from least to most dangerous:

Level The agent can Typical use Risk
0. Read-only Read and search files in the project Explain code, plan a change, review a diff Leaks what it reads into context (secrets in files)
1. Edit Change files in the working tree Implement a planned step Bad edits; easily undone with Git
2. Run allowlisted commands Run specific commands: tests, lint, typecheck, git diff The edit-run-fix loop Commands with side effects hidden inside (a test that hits a real API)
3. Run arbitrary commands Any shell command Exploratory work in a sandbox Installs, network calls, deletes, anything the user can do
4. External access Network, cloud CLIs, databases, pushing to remotes Rarely justified for coding tasks Data exfiltration, production changes

Most agentic tools let you configure this with allow and deny rules plus "ask me first" for anything not listed. As one concrete example, Claude Code reads project settings from .claude/settings.json; at the time of writing the format looks like this, and other tools have equivalents:

JSON
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run lint)",
      "Bash(npm run typecheck)",
      "Bash(npm test:*)",
      "Bash(git diff:*)",
      "Bash(git status)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Read(./secrets/**)",
      "Bash(curl:*)",
      "Bash(git push:*)",
      "Bash(npm publish:*)"
    ]
  }
}

Two cautions about rules like these:

  1. Command rules are guardrails, not a sandbox. A deny rule on curl does not stop node -e "fetch(...)", wget, or a test file that makes an HTTP call. Pattern-matching on command strings is easy to route around, by an attacker or by a model trying to be helpful. The real boundary is the environment the agent runs in (53.6.2).
  2. "Auto-approve everything" turns a level-2 agent into a level-3 or level-4 agent. Many tools offer a mode that skips permission prompts. It is reasonable inside a disposable container with no secrets and restricted network. It is not reasonable in your normal terminal with production credentials loaded.

Practical example

A sensible default for a NestJS service:

  • Planning and review sessions: read-only. The agent may read code and propose a plan or review a diff.
  • Implementation sessions: edit plus an allowlist of npm run lint, npm run typecheck, npm test, git diff, git status. Everything else prompts.
  • Exploratory or long autonomous sessions: any command, but only inside a container or cloud sandbox with no production credentials, and network limited to the package registry.
  • Never: pushing to protected branches, publishing packages, touching production databases or cloud accounts. Those go through CI/CD (Part 47 — CI/CD and Deployment Strategies) with human approval.

Production scenario

A forty-engineer organisation standardises on a checked-in settings file per repository with a shared allowlist, plus a team rule that "skip permissions" mode is only used inside the team's devcontainer image. Engineers report that the allowlist removes most of the annoying prompts (tests, lint) while the remaining prompts are rare enough that people actually read them. That last property is the goal: a prompt that appears forty times an hour gets approved without reading, which is the same as no prompt.

Failure scenario

An engineer runs an agent in auto-approve mode in a terminal where they had earlier exported a production DATABASE_URL to investigate a support ticket. They ask the agent to "fix the failing migration test". The agent, trying to understand the schema, runs the project's migration command, which reads DATABASE_URL and applies two pending migrations to production at 15:20, outside the deploy process and without the expand/contract sequencing they were designed for. One of them renames a column that the running application still uses. Orders fail for eleven minutes until the change is reversed by hand. The agent did nothing malicious. It had the bank card.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Approval fatigue. Too many prompts and people approve without reading. Allowlist the safe, frequent commands so the rare prompts get attention.
  • Inherited credentials. Environment variables, cloud CLI profiles, SSH agents and Git credential helpers are all available to commands the agent runs.
  • Commands with hidden side effects. npm test that includes an integration test hitting a shared staging API; npm install that runs install scripts.
  • Long autonomy. The longer an agent runs without a checkpoint, the further a wrong early assumption propagates.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior applies least privilege to agents exactly as they would to a service account (Part 40, 40.10): give the minimum for the task, scope it to an environment with nothing valuable in it, and log what happens. They are relaxed about agents editing files, because Git makes edits cheap to undo, and strict about anything with effects outside the working tree: network, installs, databases, pushes. Their question is never "is the model trustworthy?" but "what is the worst thing this session can do if the model is wrong or manipulated?"

Common mistakes

  • Running agents in the same terminal where production credentials are loaded.
  • Using auto-approve outside a sandbox because prompts are annoying.
  • Relying on deny rules as if they were a security boundary.
  • Letting an agent push or merge.

Interview questions

  1. How do you set permissions for a coding agent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Least privilege by task: read-only for planning and review, edit plus allowlisted verification commands for implementation, broad command access only inside a sandbox without secrets, and never production access. Follow-up: why are command deny rules not enough?
  2. What is the risk of auto-approve mode?
    Show answerHide answer
    Every command the model decides to run executes with your credentials and network; acceptable only in a disposable environment with nothing valuable in it.
  3. An agent needs to look at the database schema. How do you give it that safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Give it the migration files or a schema dump, or a read-only role on a local or anonymised database; never production credentials.

Practical exercise

Write a permission configuration for an agent in one of your repositories. Acceptance criteria: an allowlist of verification commands checked against package.json; deny rules for secret files and network tools; a short note on three ways the deny rules could be bypassed and which environment control (53.6.2) closes each.

53.6.2 Sandboxes, worktrees and containers

Concept

Because permission rules can be bypassed, the strongest control is where the agent runs. Three common isolation tools, from lightest to strongest:

  1. Git worktree: a second working directory for the same repository on its own branch, so the agent's edits never touch your main checkout.
  2. Container (or devcontainer): the agent and its commands run inside a container with only the project mounted, no host credentials, and restricted or no network.
  3. Remote sandbox or VM: an ephemeral cloud environment created for the task and destroyed afterwards; the agent opens a pull request as its only output.

Why does it exist?

Isolation turns "what could this agent do?" from "anything I can do" into "anything inside this box", and makes the box disposable. It also lets several agents work in parallel without colliding.

How it works

Shell
# 1. A worktree per agent task: separate directory, separate branch, same repository.
git worktree add ../orders-refunds-agent -b agent/partial-refunds
cd ../orders-refunds-agent && npm ci --ignore-scripts
# ... run the agent here; review with `git diff main...agent/partial-refunds`
git worktree remove ../orders-refunds-agent   # clean up when merged or abandoned

# 2. A container with no network: tests that need a DB run against a local container network only.
docker network create --internal agent-net
docker run -d --name agent-pg --network agent-net -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=localdev postgres:16
docker run --rm -it --network agent-net \
  -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:localdev@agent-pg:5432/postgres \
  node:22 bash
# Inside: no host SSH keys, no cloud profiles, no route to the internet or production.
Isolation Protects against Does not protect against Cost
Worktree Messing up your main checkout; parallel agents colliding Network, credentials, side-effecting commands Seconds; disk for a second checkout and node_modules
Container, restricted network Credential theft, exfiltration, host damage Bad code reaching the PR; secrets you mount in Image maintenance; slower first start
Remote sandbox All of the above, plus local machine exposure Bad code reaching the PR Vendor or platform cost; setup

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mounting the secrets in anyway. A container that mounts ~/.aws or the real .env is not a sandbox.
  • Allowing all network "for npm". Allow the registry (or your internal mirror) only, not the whole internet.
  • Forgotten worktrees and containers. Each worktree has its own node_modules; ten forgotten ones eat disk. Clean up as part of finishing the task.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The senior matches isolation to autonomy: a short, supervised session with an allowlist can run in a worktree; a long, auto-approved session belongs in a container or a remote sandbox whose only output is a pull request. They make the safe setup the easy one, for example a devcontainer definition in the repository, so engineers do not have to choose between safety and convenience.

Interview questions

  1. Why run an agent in a worktree?
    Show answerHide answer
    Its edits live on a separate branch and directory, so your own checkout is untouched and several agents can work in parallel.
  2. What makes a container a real sandbox for an agent?
    Show answerHide answer
    No host credentials mounted, network restricted to what the task needs, and disposable; otherwise it is just a different directory.

Practical exercise

Build a devcontainer or Docker setup for one repository in which an agent can run the full test suite (including a PostgreSQL container) with no access to the internet except the package registry and no host credentials. Acceptance criteria: the suite passes inside it; curl https://example.com fails inside it; ls ~/.ssh ~/.aws shows nothing inside it.

53.6.3 The Model Context Protocol (MCP)

Concept

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and since adopted by many AI tools, for connecting AI applications to external tools and data. Instead of every assistant building a custom integration for every system (the issue tracker, the database, the docs, the monitoring tool), a system exposes an MCP server once, and any MCP-capable application can connect to it as a client.

Why does it exist?

Before a standard, connecting M assistants to N systems needed M times N integrations, each with its own authentication and quirks. MCP turns that into M plus N: each tool speaks the protocol once. For an engineer, that means you can give your coding agent access to, say, your issue tracker, an internal docs search and a read-only view of a database with a few lines of configuration. That convenience is also the risk: each server is new power and new untrusted input.

Mental model

Imagine USB for AI tools. Before USB, every printer had its own cable and driver. With a standard plug, any device works with any computer. And just as with USB, plugging in a device you found in a car park is a security decision, not a convenience.

How it works

The durable concepts:

  1. Host, client, server. The host is the AI application. It runs one client per connected server. The server is a program that exposes capabilities.
  2. What servers expose. Mainly three kinds of thing: tools (functions the model can call, such as search_issues or get_order_status), resources (data the application can read into context, such as a file or a record), and prompts (reusable templates).
  3. Wire format. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. Local servers usually run as a subprocess talking over standard input and output (stdio); remote servers are reached over HTTP, with OAuth-based authorization defined for that case.
  4. Discovery. On connect, the client asks the server what tools it offers, with names, descriptions and input schemas. Those descriptions go into the model's context so it knows when to call them.

Practical example: a least-privilege MCP server

A support team wants their coding agent to answer "what happened to order X?" while debugging. Rather than give it a database URL, they write a tiny MCP server with one narrow tool, backed by a read-only role on a replica:

TypeScript
// orders-mcp/server.ts -- one narrow, read-only tool; no free-form SQL
import { McpServer } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js';
import { StdioServerTransport } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.ORDERS_RO_URL, max: 2 }); // read-only role, replica

const server = new McpServer({ name: 'orders-readonly', version: '1.0.0' });

server.registerTool(
  'get_order_status',
  {
    title: 'Get order status',
    description: 'Status timeline for one order by id. Returns no customer personal data.',
    inputSchema: { orderId: z.string().uuid() },
  },
  async ({ orderId }) => {
    const { rows } = await pool.query(
      'SELECT status, changed_at, actor_type FROM order_status_history_support WHERE order_id = $1 ORDER BY changed_at',
      [orderId], // parameterised; the model never writes SQL
    );
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(rows) }] };
  },
);

await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());

PostgreSQL example

The server's database role enforces the boundary even if the server code is wrong:

SQL
CREATE ROLE mcp_orders_ro LOGIN;                         -- password set from the secrets manager, not here
ALTER ROLE mcp_orders_ro SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
ALTER ROLE mcp_orders_ro SET statement_timeout = '3s';
ALTER ROLE mcp_orders_ro CONNECTION LIMIT 5;

-- A view that exposes only what support debugging needs: no names, emails, addresses.
CREATE VIEW order_status_history_support AS
  SELECT order_id, status, changed_at, actor_type FROM order_status_history;

REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public FROM mcp_orders_ro;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO mcp_orders_ro;
GRANT SELECT ON order_status_history_support TO mcp_orders_ro;

The grants are the real boundary. default_transaction_read_only is a helpful second layer, but any session can switch it off with SET, so never rely on it alone. On PostgreSQL 14 and older, every role (PUBLIC) may also create tables in the public schema by default; there, add REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC; (PostgreSQL 15 and later already ship this way).

The security model

MCP standardises the connection; it does not make any server safe. The questions to ask about every server:

Question Why
Who wrote it, and is the version pinned? A local server runs as a process with your user's permissions; an update can change its behaviour
What credentials does it hold, and how broad are they? The model can call any tool the server exposes, with the server's credentials
Does it read untrusted content (web pages, issues, emails, tickets)? That content goes into the model's context and can carry injected instructions (53.6.4)
Can its tools write, send or delete? Write tools need confirmation; prefer read-only
Are tool descriptions trustworthy? Descriptions are text in the model's context; a malicious server can hide instructions in them
Is there an audit log of tool calls? You will need it after an incident

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats an MCP server like any integration with a third-party service: vet it, pin it, give it its own narrowly scoped credentials, prefer read-only, and assume its output is untrusted. They favour narrow, purpose-built tools ("get order status") over general ones ("run SQL"), because the narrower the tool, the smaller the blast radius when the model is wrong or manipulated. Part 38 (38.3.1 and 38.7) applies the same principles to agents you ship to customers; the reasoning carries over unchanged.

Common mistakes

  • Connecting a server with a personal admin token "just to try it".
  • Exposing a generic "execute SQL" tool on a primary database.
  • Installing community servers without reading what they do or pinning a version.

Interview questions

  1. What is MCP, in one minute?
    Show answerHide answer
    An open protocol that lets AI applications (hosts, via clients) connect to servers exposing tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC, locally via stdio or remotely via HTTP. Follow-up: what does it not solve? Trust in the server and its content.
  2. How would you let an agent query production data safely?
    Show answerHide answer
    Usually not at all; if needed, a narrow read-only tool over a replica, a role with read-only transactions, a statement timeout, a view without personal data, and audit logging.
  3. Why prefer narrow tools over a general SQL tool?
    Show answerHide answer
    Smaller blast radius when the model errs or is manipulated, and easier authorization and review.

Practical exercise

Build the read-only MCP server above against a local database with seeded fake orders, and connect it to an MCP-capable tool you use. Acceptance criteria: the tool can answer a status question using the server; an attempt to make the model run an UPDATE through it is impossible by design; the database role cannot write even if you connect with psql directly as that role.

53.6.4 Prompt injection through tool output and fetched content

Concept
